parties:
DR. A.K.M. MUZTABA AND OTHERS 
Vs. 
AHSAN HABIB KHAN AND OTHERS
full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J: This appeal is directed at the instance of the petitioner-appellants against the judgment and order dated 26.05.2011 passed by the learned District Judge, Bagerhat, in Miscellaneous Case No.10 of 1998 under section 35(1) of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 in rejecting the case.

2. The facts relevant for disposal of the appeal in a nutshell can be stated thus that the present appellants as petitioners filed a Miscellaneous Case being No. 10 of 1998 under section 35(1) of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 in the Court of learned District Judge, Bagerhat for a declaration that the disputed property is not waqf property contending inter alia that the case land along with other lands originally belonged to one Sayed Ali, Abdul Gafur and Abdul Goni. Hasan Ali the predecessor of the petitioners obtained the case land through settlement for the limited period. Subsequently, Hasan Ali executed a kabuliat in favour of Sayed All and others. The kabuliat was registered on 31.10.1939. The period of settlement although was expired in the year 1950, even then; Hasan Ali was possessing the property-in-dispute by handing over. In this way, a tenancy was created in favour of Hasan Ali by the conduct of Sayed Ali and others. Sayed Ali and others instituted a Rent Suit being No. 1788 of 1958 against Hasan Ali for realization of arrear rents. The further case of the petitioners is such that the case land was not recorded wrongly in the name of Hasan Ali in the S.A. khatian and for that reason Hasan Ali filed a Title Suit being No. 02 of 1972 for declaration of title in the disputed property and that suit was decreed on compromise in terms of "solenama". In this way, the petitioners acquired title in the disputed property and a registered Osiotnama ' was subsequently executed by Hasan Ali in favour of the petitioners. Hasan Ali died in the year 1975. The case land is a homestead property and the petitioners are residing therein after constructing their residential sheds. The petitioners had been owning and possessing the case land by payment of rents, taxes etc. and the case property was not a waqf property in the name and style "Karom Ali Khan Waqf Estate". The further case of the petitioners is such that Karom Ali Khan had no title and interest in the case property and he had no right to declare the property Waqf On 02.04.1978 on behalf of the Deputy Commissioner, Bagerhat the Thana Nirbahi Officer concerned issued a notice for eviction directing the petitioners to handover the vacant possession of the disputed property in favour of the opposite parties which constrained the plaintiffs to file a Title Suit being No.86 of 1997 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Bagerhat for permanent injunction against the defendants to that suit. It is also the case of the petitioners that the order of the Administrator of Waqf, Dhaka, Bangladesh vide his office Memo No. 1281/Khu dated 05.01.1997 as well as the order dated 28.05.1998 relating to the eviction of the petitioners treating the case property waqf property are illegal, null and void and without jurisdiction. Challenging the orders of the Waqf Administrator the petitioners filed the miscellaneous case.

3. The contrary case of the opposite parties in short is thus that one Karom Ali Khan, son of Nayan Khan was the owner of' the case property and the owner of the property in the name of 'Almighty Allah' declared the property as waqf estate in respect of 327 bighas of land including the case property. A deed of waqf was executed on 29.09.1921 and Karom Ali Khan became the Motowalli of the property. The further case of the opposite parties is such that at the demise of Karom Ali Khan, his two sons namely Syed Ali Khan and Abdul Gafur Khan and grandson Abdul Goni Khan were appointed Motowalli of the waqf estate. They were the Joint Molowallies of the estate which was enrolled as waqf property in the office of the Waqf Administrator under E.C. No. 11050. Subsequently, the case land was recorded in the name of Motowalli. It is the case of the opposite parties that Hasan Ali was the son-in-law of Abdul Gofur Khan who was a lawyer. Out of love and affection Hasan Ali was permitted to reside in the homestead of the case land from his father-in-law Abdul Gofur Khan and as such he was a permissive possessor in the case property. Taking advantage of that, Hasan Ali fraudulently crated a kabuliat showing settlement of the case land in favour of Syed Ali and others. Subsequently, realizing the fault; Hasan Ali gave up his claim over the suit property by executing a 'nadabipatry' on 09.03.1952. A Refit Suit was filed by Wahed Ali against Masan Ali with regard to the estate for arrear rents, in which a fraudulent `solenama' was filed and in that Rent Suit the Waqf Administrator was not made party intentionally. A Title Suit being No. 02 of 1972 was also filed in respect of the case property and in that suit another fraudulent 'solenama' was filed. The Administrator of Waqf was not a party to that suit also. That suit was filed with regard to the S.A. record of right. The opposite parties knowing about the fraudulent 'solenama' informed the Administrator of Waqf who issued a show cause notice upon Saleh Ahmed, the father of the petitioners. An Inspector of Waqf inquired into the matter and submitted his report to the Waqf Administrator and the Administrator of Waqf being satisfied requested the Deputy Commissioner, Bagerhat to evict Saleh Ahmed from the case property vide Memo dated 05.01.1997 and the Deputy Commissioner, Bagerhat directed the concerned Thana Nirbahi Officer to do the needful. Thana Nirbahi Officer accordingly served a notice upon the petitioners for eviction, against which the petitioners out of ill-motive to grab the waqf property filed a suit for permanent injunction being No.86 of 1997 which is pending for disposal.

4. The learned District Judge, Bagerhat hearing the Miscellaneous Case No. 10 of 1998 passed the impugned judgment and order dated 26.05.2011.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order the petitioners have preferred this appeal with Civil Rule No. 365(FM)/201 1 and obtained an order of stay therein.

6. During hearing of this appeal along with Civil Rule Mr. Mosharraf Hussain the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the appellants while Mr. Mohammad Mutahar Hussain the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the respondents.

7. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the learned District Judge, Bagerhat during disposal of the miscellaneous case committed illegality and failed to appreciate that the predecessor-in-interest of the present appellants Md. Hasan Ali obtained the case property through a settlement by the original owners of the property namely Syed Ali Khan, Abdul Gofur Khan and Abdul Goni Khan. The learned District Judge also failed to appreciate that a kabuliat was executed and registered by the settlement holder Hasan Ali -in favour of the Owners of the property on 31.10.1939. Since the settlement was for a limited period, it was expired in the year 1950 A.D. But the fact remains that the predecessor of the appellants, Hasan Ali had been owning and possessing the property by handing over, and accordingly tenancy right was accrued in favour of Hasan Ali by the conduct of the original owners who brought a Rent Suit being No.1788 of 1958 against Hasan Ali for realization of arrear rents. The learned trial court during disposal of the miscellaneous case could not realize that, against the S.A. record of right in respect of the case property Hasan Ali filed a Title Suit being No. 02 of 1972 which was decreed on compromise by way of solenama' and in this way the appellants acquired title and interest in the case property. A registered `osiotnama' was executed and registered by Hasan Ali in favour of the appellants on 09.11.1974 prior to his death in the year 1975 and all these facts has been corroborated from the evidence of P.W.1, but the learned trial court i.e. the District Judge, Bagerhat without proper assessment of evidence and appreciation of law arrived at an erroneous decision that the case property is a wall-estate, which has been declared as waqf property by the original owner of the land Md. Karam Ali Khan. The learned Advocate also submits that the learned District Judge committed an error in law resulting in an error in the decision in not holding that the disputed deed of waqf dated 29.09.1921 is not related to the case property which was in respect of the land appertaining to Bagerhat Police Station. The property showing in the waqf deed relating to Morelgonj police station is different and not identical with the case property. The learned Advocate submits that in fact, Karam Ali Khan was not the owner of the disputed property and he had no authority to declare the case property waqf estate which is not properly evaluated and appraised by the learned trial Judge during disposal of the Miscellaneous Case No. 10 of 1998. The learned Advocate lastly in support of his contention referred some decisions reported in 19 DLR 106 and 2 BLC 517.

8. As against the aforesaid submission of the learned counsel for the appellants the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents opposing the grounds of the appeal memo submits that, the learned District Judge, Bagerhat during disposal of the original miscellaneous case committed no illegality or irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the present appellants who were the petitioners of the miscellaneous petition under section 35(1) of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 failed to prove their respective case by adducing tangible evidence. The oral and documentary evidences led from the sides of the respective parties were properly evaluated and discussed by the learned trial Judge during disposal of the case on merit. The learned Advocate also submits that the learned District Judge, Bagerhat after proper assessment of evidence and appreciation of law arrived at a conclusive decision relying upon the authentic evidence that the property-in-dispute is a waqf property and the Waqf Administrator was totally empowered to pass an order under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance of 1962 treating the property as waqf property pursuant to E.C. No. 11050. The learned Advocate submits that the Rent Suit which was marked as Exhibit-11 was in fact not tiled by the motowallies or their legal heirs and neither the C.S. recorded tenants nor the heirs of the recorded tenants filed the aforesaid Rent Suit for realization of arrear rents and apart from this; the kabuliat vide Exhibit-'G' allegedly executed by the predecessor of the petitioner-appellants namely Hasan Ali is a created paper, by which no valid title and interest was accrued in favour of Hasan Ali or his successors. Hasan Ali, who is an admitted lawyer of the local Bar, during his life time realizing the fate of his conduct, admitting the case of the respondents executed a `nadabipatra which shows the malafide of the appellants and the learned trial Judge rightly appraised the actual facts of the case. The alleged kabuliat was also not produced from the side of the petitioner-appellants during pendency of the original miscellaneous case while the Gnadabipatra' dated 09.03.1952 was exhibited and marked as Exhibit-GE'. The learned Advocate submits that the S.A. record of right Exhibit-`D' stands recorded in the names of the predecessor-in-interest of the, respondents which have got its presumptive value of correctness and that matter is properly appreciated by the learned court below and it is apparent from the face of the records that the original owner of the property was the predecessor-in-interest of Syed Ali, Abdul Gofur and Abdul Goni Khan namely Karam All Khan. It is a fact that Karam Ali Khan during his life time declared the property as waqf estate by a waqf deed which has been marked as Exhibit-GA' and the positive contention to that effect that Karam Ali Khan in respect of the case property along with other property comprising an area of 327 bighas of land executed the deed of waqf in the year 1321 A.D. and in the waqf deed vide Exhibit-GA' there exist a clear recital that, during the life time of Karam Ali Khan he will remain as Motowalli of the estate and after his death his two sons namely Syed AIi Khan and Abdul Gofur Khan along with his grandson Abdul Goni Khan would be joint motowalli of the estate which has been proved by sufficient cogent evidence before the learned trial Judge. The learned Advocate after filing a supplementary affidavit submitted B.R.S. khatian No. 525 which stands recorded in the name of the present respondents as n2otowalli of the waqf estate namely 'Karam Ali Khan Waqf Estate' and it has been published during pendency of this case. The learned Advocate lastly submits referring some decisions reported in 34 BLD 463 and 2 SCC 642 that a waqf is a permanent dedication of property and once a waqf always a waqf and the learned trial court rightly after proper sifting of evidence in its true perspective arrived at a conclusive decision that the property being waqf cannot be a property a private individual and it is not proved by any cogent evidence that the appellants acquired any valid right, title, interest and possession in the case property, rather; it is on records that the predecessor of the appellants Md. Masan Ali and after his death the appellants are permissive possessors in the case property who in fact have no legal status or character to declare the property a private property or that the property is not a waqf property.

9. In order to appreciate the submission advanced from the sides of the learned counsels of both the parties, I have perused the judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge, Bagerhat in Miscellaneous Case No. 10 of 1998 along with the evidences led from the sides of the respective parties and all other relevant papers with the documentary evidences produced from the sides of the parties to the case.

10. Having gone through the case records ii transpires that the original ease was instituted by the heirs of Saleh Ahmed against the order dated 28.05.1998 passed by the Waqf Administrator in respect of the case property under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 in E.C. No. 11050, treating the disputed property waqf property. The learned trial court by the impugned judgment and order dated 26.05.2011 disallowed the miscellaneous case and being aggrieved the petitioners to that case have instituted this appeal and it’s connected Civil Rule No. 656(FM) of 2011.

11. During hearing of this appeal, from the office of the Waqf Administrator, the connected case records has been called for wherefrom it appears that the Waqf Administrator, Dhaka, Bangladesh vide his office Memo No. শুশা-১/১৫৫২ তাং ৩১/৫/১৯৯৮ requested the Deputy Commissioner, Bagerhat to take necessary action in respect of the disputed property appertaining to Mouza Soroi under J.L. No.156 corresponding to C.S. khatian No. 1195/1 and S.A. khatian No. 672/673 under plot No.607 comprising an area of 0.33 acres. The order of the Waqf Administrator was passed under section 50/64(1) of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 wherein; the Waqf Administrator held that the property being a waqf property is illegally possess by the present appellants and the possession of their predecessor was also not legal. The Waqif Karam Ali Khan by way of a registered waqf deed in the year 1921 declared the property as waqf estate and as such the possessors of the property, who are residing therein in the standing sheds therein, are illegal possessors.

12. Consulting the relevant case records I also find that the waqif Karam Ali Khan by virtue of a deed of waqf declared the suit property along with the other properties comprising total area of 327 bighas of land as waqf. It is also within the recital of Exhibit-'A' that in the deed of waqf Karam Ali Khan was the motowalli of the estate and at the demise of Karam Ali Khan his two sons namely Syed Ali Khan, Abdul Gofur Khan and grandson Abdul Goni Khan were appointed motowallies jointly in respect of the above mentioned properties and it is the case of the appellants that from the sons and grandson of Karam Ali Khan who are the successors of Karam Ali Khan, their predecessor Hasan Ali obtained the case land by way of a settlement for a limited period ended in the year 1950 and a kabuliat was executed by Hasan Ali in favour of Syed Ali Khan and others. It is further case of the appellants that after the expiry of the ending year 1950, the possession was continued by their predecessor Hasan Ali by holding over. It was also contended from the side of the petitioner-appellants that Syed Ali Khan and others for recovery of arrear rents filed a Rent Suit being No.1788/58 against Hasan Ali and when the S.A. khatian was prepared in the name of original owners, Hasan Ali filed a Title Suit challenging the entry of the khatians being Title Suit No.02 of 1972 for declaration of title which was decreed on compromise in terms of `solenama’.

13. Vis-a-vis; the respondents categorically challenged the alleged kabuliat and the subsequent `solenama' and also asserted to the effect that the owner of the property Karam Ali Khan during his life time made the property waqf on 29.09.1921. In respect of the suit property with other property the deed of waqf was executed and registered which has been marked as Exhibit-`A' from the side of the respondents.

14. During trial of the original case apart from documentary evidences the parties to the case examined two witnesses from each side.

15. P.W.1 A.B.M. Sadique is the co-petitioner to the original case, who is the full brother of the original plaintiffs. This witness in his testimony testified that he is deposing on behalf of all the petitioners. P.W.1 further testified in his testimony that the owners of the property filed the rent suit against his grandfather Hasan Ali and in that Rent Suit No. 1788 of 1958 the owners of the property recognized Hasan Ali as of their tenant. P.W.1 admits in his testimony that they are not in a position to file any paper relating to the Rent Suit No. 1788 of 1958. lie also testified that against the S.A. record of right the Title Suit .No.02 of 1972 was filed by their grandfather Hasan Ali, which was decreed in terms of `solenama' and his grandfather died on 09.11.1978 leaving behind the original petitioners along with he (P.W.1) and during the life time of Hasan Ali he made an `osiotnama transferring the suit land in favour of the petitioners.

16. At the time of cross-examination from the side of the opposite party-respondents, P.W.1 testified at a stage that at the request or the father-in-law of Hasan Ali, Hasan Ali started to reside in the case property and in this context; it is the case of the respondents that the father-in-law of Hasan Ali was one of the Molowallies as nominated by Karam Ali Khan in the waqf deed and due to love and affection, Hasan Ali was allowed to reside in the case property for the time being by his father-in-law and because of that reason, Hasan Ali was the permissive possessor under the Motowalli. It is admitted from the side of the appellants that for a particular period Hasan Ali was allowed to reside in the property and after the expiry of that term, Hasan Ali continued his possession. At a stage of cross-examination in a reply- to a question from the side of the opposite parties P.W.1 testified that he cannot recollect as to whether he has seen the papers relating to the rent suit and he has no knowledge about the S.A. record of right. P.W.1 frankly conceded that the present khatian in respect of the case property has been prepared in the names of opposite party-respondents. He expressed his inability in his testimony to state that, what was the amount of rent of the case properly. P.W.1 in his deposition also testified that Hasan Ali went into possession prior to the date of kabuliat, but he cannot say how many days before the kabuliat Masan Ali entered into the possession of the case property. 17. P.W.2 is A.K.M. Nuruzzaman. This witness in his deposition deposed about the registered `osiotnama' executed by Hasan Ali. P.W.2 in his testimony testifies that Hasan Ali on 09.11.1974 executed the osiomama' in which Hasan Ali put six signature. This witness testified in cross-examination that his father also put his signature in the said deed.

18. On the contrary, 0.P.W.1 is the opposite party No.2 Khan Mohammad Rezaul Karim. This witness in his testimony testified in support of the written objection filed by them and corroborated their pleading. 0.P.W.1 categorically testified in his deposition that the original owner of the property was Karam Ali Khan, who executed the deed of waqf on 29.09.1921 which was registered on 02.10.1921 being No. 6864. In the said deed of waqf the waqif Karam Ali Khan was the Motowalli. 0.P.W.1 in his testimony also testified that his predecessor in interest late Abdul Goni Khan who was his father along with other Motowallies did not recognize Hasan Ali as of their tenant and they never realized any rent from Hasan Ali and also did not accept the alleged kabuliat from Hasan Ali and there was no tenancy right of the predecessor of the petitioners and he was asked to handover vacant possession of the case property when the predecessors of this witness came to know about the alleged kabuliat. O.P.W.1 denied the `osiotnama' executed by Hasan Ali and testified specifically that they asked the petitioners to leave the case property. With regard to the `nadabipatra' of Hasan Ali 0.P.W. 1 testified that they have filed the 4nadabipatra' in which Hasan Ali admitted the case of the opposite parties.

19. During cross-examination 0.P.W.1 testified at a stage that by virtue of C.S. khatian No.1195/1 they claim the case property, which has been filed by them. This witness also testified in a reply to a question from the side of the petitioners that his predecessors submitted the account of the waqf property in the office of the Administrator and he/they have filed series of rent receipts to prove their bonafide case.

20. O.P.W.2 Alhaj Abdur Rashid Khan testified before the trial Court and this witness in his testimony testified that Saleh Ahmed is the son of late Advocate Hasan Ali and the `nadabipatra' was given (executed) by Hasan Ali in presence of this witness, which was written by his Mohorar. O.P.W.2 also testified that Hasan Ali put his signature in his presence and in that deed O.P.W.2 as witness also gave his signature. He has identified that `nadabipatra and signature therein, which has been marked as Exhibits-`E' and 'E-1' respectively.

21. In the instant case an Advocate Commissioner, Sheikh Mokbul Hossain by name was examined as O.P.W.3. This witness in his testimony proved his report dated 22.01.2002 marked as Exhibit-'F'. In his deposition the learned Advocate Commissioner categorically testified that, being appointed by the court as Advocate Commissioner he did the commission work lawfully. In the deposition of the learned Advocate Commissioner he has specifically testified that, to the eastern side of plot No.607 there exist a wall, to the northern side there is a road, but there is no pond in plot No. 614.

22. The learned trial court with regard to the evidence adduced from the sides of the respective parties after assessment of the same arrived at a decision that in the evidence of the petitioners it has conic to the notice of the court that they have admitted the case of the opposite parties as to the permissive possession of the petitioners in the case property. I find on meticulous assessment of the evidence on record that the learned District Judge was justified and rightly held that, despite from the side of the petitioners there exist series of rent receipts since 1372 B.S., but inasmuch as they are in possession over the case land as permissive possessors of the opposite parties, the series of rent receipts have got no presumptive value of their title and possession in the case property.

23. Having gone through the relevant papers it also appears that the case property has been made waqf property by the Waqif Karam Ali Khan by a registered deed of Waqf in the year 1921 A.D. and within the relevant list of Waqf Administrator of the year 1946 A.D. the suit property has been enlisted. Admittedly the S.A. record of right stands recorded in the names of the legal heirs of Waqif Karam Ali Khan and the heirs of the wag if according to the deed of waqf became motuwallies jointly to look after the property. The learned court below in his observation and findings evaluating the connected documents, conclusively held that the kabuliat as alleged from the side of the petitioners and the filing of so called Rent Suit No.1788 of 1958 and the subsequent sole decree obtained in Title Suit No. 02 of 1972, which are under challenge have got no legal footings, inasmuch as; by way of registered waqf deed of the year 1921 the property has became waqf property and in this context; the learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite parties rightly cited the decision reported in 2 SCC 642. In the Case of Sayyed Ali and others —vs.- A.P. wakf Board, Hyderabad and others, their lordships held that, "a waqf is a permanent dedication of property for purposes recognized by Muslim law as pious, religious or charitable and property having been found as waqf would always retain its character as a waqf In other words, once a waqf always a waqf and the grant of patta in favour of Mokhasadar under the Mums Act does not, in any mariner, nullify the earlier dedication made of the property constituting the same as wave; After a waqf has been created, it continues to be so for all time to come and further continues to be governed by the provisions of the waqf Act and a grant of patta in favour of Mokhasadar does not affect the original character of the waqf property. "

24. The above mentioned decision is very much applicable in the instant case. Furthermore; consulting the evidence on records it is evident to note that the petitioner-appellants admitted the existence of waqif Karam Ali Khan, which is corroborated by the conduct of their predecessor. From the face of the papers it is also admitted from their side that, for a particular period their predecessor obtained a permission to reside in the case property from one of the Motuwallies, Abdul Gofur Khan, who was the father-in-law of Hasan Ali and it is the specific contention of the opposite parties that out of love and affection the son-in-law of Abdul Gofur was permitted to reside in the case property as permissive possessor and the term of permission was admittedly expired in the year 1950. Hence; Hasan Ali was a permissive possessor in the case property and the subsequent act of Hasan Ali by execution of an osiomama ' on 09.11.1974 is not sustainable in law. It was claimed by the appellants that, Wahed Ali instituted the Rent Suit being No. 1788 of 1958 in which the tenancy of Hasan Ali was confirmed vide Exhibit-11, but from the plain reading of the connected paper viz. the plaint of the Rent Suit, 1 find that the following recital is visible, which reads as follows:

”১১৯৫/১ খতিয়ানে .৩৬ শতক জমির কাত বার্ষিক ৬ টাকা করের যে প্রথা অনুসারে দখলী স্বত্ত বিশিষ্ট কোর্ফা বর্তমান রায়তী স্বত্তের জমা লেখা হয় তাহার হিং ১/৩ অংশে বাদী কৃত করমালী খাঁ কৃত ওয়াকফ নামায় শর্ত অনুযায়ী মোতোওয়াল্লী সূত্রে স্বত্ববান দখলকার আছেন।”

25. Therefore, this documentary evidence itself shows that the appellants frankly admitted that the case property is a waqf property under Karam Ali Khan waqf estate. Furthermore, the above mentioned Rent Suit was not filed by all the Moluwallies or their successors-in-interest. Besides this; the Rent Suit was instituted admittedly after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. It further appears from the case records that the specific case of the present respondents as to the nature and character of the case land there lies a document. The predecessor-in-interest of the present appellants Md. Hasan Ali executed a 'nadabipatra' on 09.03.1952 vide Exhibit-`E, in which Hasan Ali acknowledged that he has got no right, title, interest in the case property and he was allowed to stay in the case land temporarily. The witness in whose presence, Hasan Ali executed the nadabipatra' has been examined from the side of the respondents as O.P.W.2, who was a witness of that deed (Exhibit-`E'). This witness in his testimony identified his signature as well as the `nadabipatra'.

26. Moreover, from the cross-examination of the witnesses adduced form the sides of the respective parties I find that P.W.1, who is a co-petitioner of the case, A.B.M. Sadique, son of Saleh Ahmed and P.W.2 A.K.M. Nuruzzaman are interested witnesses, inasmuch as; they are not independent, competent and credible because of their relationship with one another. No independent, disinterested, competent witness is examined from the side of the petitioners, who can be relied upon to believe the case of the petitioner-appellants. On the other hand 0.P.W.1, who is the opposite party No. 2 during his testimony, corroborated their case and 0.P.W.2 Alhaj Abdur Rashid Khan corroborated O.P.W. 1 in his deposition. From their cross-examination except sonic minor discrepancy no such material contradiction, omission or ambiguity is noticed, by which they can be disbelieved. The learned District Judge, Bagerhat in his observation and findings rightly in this context held that, there is no tangible evidence from the side of the petitioners, by which it can be held that the petitioners have successfully proved their case.

27. The learned Advocate for the respondents during his argument with regard to Exhibit-`E' argued that the appellants are stopped by the doctrine of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence under the ambit of section 115 of the Evidence Act, 1872 from denying that the case land is a waqf property.

28. On perusal of the deed of waqf vide Exhibit-'A' dated 29.09.1921 it is noticed that within the contents of the deed there is a clear mention from the side of the Waqif Karam Ali Khan that the Motuwallies are not entitled to change any of the terms and conditions of the said deed and according to the terms and conditions of the deed of waqf, the purported kabuliat dated 31.10.1939 (Exhibit-`G') cannot create any right or title in favour of Hasan Ali. From the plain reading of the contents of Exhibit-`A' it is evident that, nobody is empowered to change the nature and character of the property which has made waqf through the waqif by this registered instrument. The learned court below with regard to this rightly observed in the impugned judgment and order that the nature and character of the property remain as before and because of that, the Waqif Administrator consulting the connected documents rightly issued the Notice-in-dispute with regard to the eviction of the petitioner-appellants from the case property.

29. The fact remains in view of the schedule Condition No .3 of the deed of waqf and section 56 & 80 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 that the case land being a waqf property cannot be transferred or alienated by any means and the alleged act of compromise in the Title Suit No.02 of 1972 cannot be treated legal and proper. It is found that the motowallies are also without jurisdiction without prior approval of the waqf Administrator to enter into any compromise in respect of the case property. The connected S.A. Khatian vide Exhibit-'D' which stands recorded in the names of the predecessor-in-interest of the respondents have got a presumptive value of correctness as it is not rebutted by any' tangible evidence and that there is nothing on record to hold that the khatian was prepared wrongly. From the record of Waqf Administrator with regard to the nature and character of the case land it transpires that an enquiry was held and there is a report to that effect dated 17.12.1996 and from the contents of that report it is crystal clear that the enquiry officer during his local enquiry clearly observed that the suit property' is a waqf property and there is no existence of any valid document showing transfer of the case property in favour of 3rd party. Furthermore, under section 56(1) of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 there is no such approval or permission by which the alleged transfer or alienation was done.

<u>30. Having regard to the facts, circumstances and the discussions referred to above I .find that the decisions referred to from the side of the appellants are not identical due to distinguishable nature and features of the case. In the instant case, as I have already spelt out that, there is nothing on record to differ with the findings and decisions given by the learned District Judge, Bagerhat as to the fate of the miscellaneous case. The act of the Administrator in the instant case cannot be treated ultra-vires or not legal because of the documentary evidences, especially the conduct of the waqif Karam Ali Khan with regard to the permanent dedication of the suit property along with his other properties done by him pursuant to a registered deed of waqf declaring the property as waqf property'. As to the possession of the present appellants I have already pointed out that they and prior to them their predecessor-in-interest was a permissive possessor under the motowallies. Hence, there is no wrong or illegality or irregularity in passing the order of the Waqf Administrator under section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance, 1962 pursuant to E.C. No. 11050.</u>

31. In the foregoing narrative, I find no such material or substance in this appeal as well as the Civil Rule by which the appeal can be allowed, or the Rule can be made absolute.

32. In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 26.05.2011 passed by the learned District Judge, Bagerhat, in Miscellaneous Case No.10 of 1998 is hereby affirmed.

33. Consequently, the Civil Rule being No. 656(FM)/2011 is hereby disposed of.

34. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule in Civil Rule No. 656(FM)/2011 stands vacated.

34. Send down the Lower Court's Records and communicate the judgment and order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Saifur Reza, Advocate, For the Defendant-Appellant. 
Mrs. Hosnera Begum, Advocate, For the Respondents.
parties:
MASHRIQUI JUTE MILLS LIMITED 
Vs. 
JIBON BIMA CORPORATION AND OTHERS
full_judgment:
S. H. Md. Nurul Huda Jaigirdar, J: This First Appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 10.07.2002 and 16.07.2002 respectively passed by the Joint District Judge and Commercial Court No.2 Dhaka in Title Suit No. 197 of 2001 decreeing the suit on contest against the defendant appellant and others.

2. The suit was filed on 29.10.1988 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka, for sale of the mortgaged properties of defendant No.1 for realization of loan money. The suit eventually was transferred to the Court of Joint District Judge and Commercial Court No.2, Dhaka, and renumbered as Title Suit No.197 of 2001.

3. The plaint case, precisely, is that plaintiff is an Insurance Corporation and defendant No.1, herein appellant, is a private limited company; defendant Nos. 2 to 5, are the directors of the defendant No.1; defendant No. 1 obtained foreign currency loan facilities from the then `Pakistan Industrial Credit And Investment Corporation Limited (PICIC), presently Defendant-Respondent No.7, by way of creating a mortgage by depositing title deeds to establish a jute mill having 50 Nos. broadlooms; in addition to the foreign currency loan already obtained from PICIC, further Rupees 60,00,000.00 (six million) was required for the project and it was resolved that the money would be collected by issuing shares, having face value of Rs.10.00 each; it was further resolved that out of the requirements the sponsors of the company would manage/collect Rs. 30,00,000.00 (three million) and the rest Rs.30,00,000.00 (three million) would be collected from the different financial institutions and accordingly an agreement / contract was entered into, on 27/03/1070, under the name and style "UNDER WRITING-CUM-ADVANCE. 3. AGREEMENT", hereinafter referred to the 'AGREEMENT', between the defendant No.1-Apellant and eight (8) Nos. financial institutions including Pakistan Industrial Credit And Investment Corporation Limited '131C1C' and two predecessors of the plaintiff corporation; the financial institutions, as it reveals from the 'Agreement', are chronologically Nos. ii. Investment Corporation of Pakistan hereinafter referred to ICP iii. Pakistan Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation Limited (PICIC)', iv. Eastern Banking Corporation Limited hereinafter referred to EBCL, v. Premier Bank Limited hereinafter referred to PBL, vi. Habib Enterprises Limited hereinafter referred to KIEL, as being underwriter FIRST SET; Nos. vii. Eastern Federal Union Insurance Company Limited hereinafter referred to EFU, viii. Muslim Insurance Company Limited hereinafter referred to MICL, ix. Eastern Mercantile Insurance Company Limited hereinafter referred to EMIC, being underwriters SECOND SET. Under the said Agreement dated 27.03.70, predecessors of the plaintiff, namely 'EFU and MICL', hereinabove underwriter Nos. vii and viii `EFU and MICL' granted Rs.5,00,000.00 (five hundred thousand) only and Rs.2,50,000.00(Two hundred fifty thousand) only respectively as bridge loan to the defendant No. 1 Appellant on condition to issue 50,000 and 25,000 shares of Rs.10.00 each by the borrower/debtor-defendant No. 1; defendant Nos.2 and 3 are the signatories of the Agreement, Demand Promissory Note and letter of Indemnity etc; after the independence of Bangladesh the properties and obligations of the underwriters, namely `EFU and MICL' were vested with the government of Bangladesh and that in pursuance of President Order (PO) No. 95 of 1972 and Insurance Corporation Act, 1973 the bridge loan or advances of TRY and `MICL' amounting to Rs. 5,00,000.00 and Rs.2,50,000.00, total being Rs.7,50,000.00 along with interests were vested in the plaintiff; as stipulated in the Agreement dated 27.03,1970, the borrower defendants are bound and obligated to pay interests and penal interests on borrowed sum of Rs. 7,50,000.00; the defendant No. 1 did not repay the loan including interests even after repeated notices. Hence the suit.

4. Defendant Nos.1, 7 and 9 filed written statements; the case of defendant No.7, in short, is that the properties and obligations of underwriter No. iii. PICIC and ii. ICP were vested with the defendant No.7 and that PICIC granted the foreign currency loan to the defendant No. 1 to the tune of US $ 1.153 million equivalent to Rs. 5.534 million and to secure the loan the defendant No.1 deposited all its title deeds regarding all its immovable properties with the PICIC only; besides the foreign currency loan was guaranteed by the sponsors (defendant Nos. 2 and 3) of the company personally; the original title deeds of the immovable properties of the defendant No. 1 company are lying with the head office of PICIC at Karachi, Pakistan; the copy of the Agreement dated 27.03.1970 is not available with the defendant-Shangstha and the plaintiff is therefore put to prove their respective case and that this defendant does not have any comment regarding the transactions between plaintiff and defendant No.1 and that as at 01.01.1990 the defendant No. 1 company owes Tk. 1,1800,000.00 to defendant No.7 and that defendant No. 7 is not a necessary/proper party in the suit. Accordingly the contesting defendant No. 7 prayed for dismissal the suit with cost.

5. Defendant No.9-Uttara Bank Ltd. was formerly known as Eastern Banking Corporation Limited (EI3CL), underwriter No.(iv) from the 'First Set' of financial institutions hereinafter referred to as PI to the agreement dated 27.03.1970, and also granted bridge loan to the tune of Rs. 5,00,000.00 against 50,000 Nos. shares and as the defendant No. 1 did not repay, this defendant handed over the shares to the Ministry of Industries and receipt Tk.1,10,4000.00 as compensation and that very recently this defendant requested the defendant No.7,owning corporation of underwriter Nos. ii and iii ICP and PICK for the money and that as at 31.12.1988 the total outstanding is Tk.16,22,683.94 including interest.

6. Defendant No.1, herein appellant, filed written statement alleging that the suit is not maintainable and that the suit is liable to be dismissed as being barred by law and that the suit is bad for defect of parities and that the suit is barred by limitation and also barred by principles of estoppels and acquiescence and that the suit has no cause of action and that after receipt of the legal notice dated 19.11.1987 issued by the plaintiff this defendant approached the managing director of the plaintiff Corporation on 04.12.1987 and proposed to repay the bridge loan amount of Tk. 7,50,000.00 in five years’ time in installments after waiver of the interests accrued therein and further proposed for settlement of the loan and that the calculations of accounts are inflated and that this defendant paid Tk.1,00,000.00 only during pendency of the suit, on 12.08.1989, as a good gesture and that the plaintiff acknowledged the receipt of Tk. 1,00,000.00 only by their letter dated 15.09.1989 and that the suit may be dismissed with cost.

7. On the basis of the aforesaid pleadings of the parties, the learned Joint District Judge and Commercial Court No.2 framed the following issues for adjudication:

a. Is the suit maintainable in its present form and manner?

b. Is the cause of action arose?

c. Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

d. Is the suit barred by limitation?

e. Is the plaintiff entitled to the decree as prayed for?

8. At the trial, the learned Joint District Judge and 2nd Commercial Court, Dhaka, recorded the testimony of I PW admitted the plaintiff documents in evidence which have been marked as exhibit 1-10. The defendant No. 1. contested the suit and examined 1 witness and exhibited the document which has been marked exhibit "L" before the trial court in support of his written statement. The defendant No.7 examined 1 witness who is cited DW.2, in support of his written statement. Considering the facts of the suit and evidences available on record, the learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit by his judgment dated 10.07.2002.

9. Being aggrieved, the defendant No. 1 as appellant preferred this First Appeal.

10. Mr. Saifur Reza, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant No.1 appellant took us through the pleadings of the suit and written statement, evidences, exhibits, and judgment and decree with relevant laws regarding to limitation of the suit. The appellant has nothing to submits regarding to issue Nos. 'a' to 'c' and `e' of the impugned judgment but admitted the facts and so far issue No. "d", of the said judgment is concerned the learned Advocate has submitted that the Court below committed multifaceted error of law and, as such, misdirected himself to arrive at a correct decision. He has further submitted that the learned Joint District Judge erroneously, both on facts and law, held that the suit is for sale of mortgaged property'; the learned Judge has also erroneously held that the suit is one under Artice-147 of the Limitation Act; the learned Judge has decided the issue in favour of the plaintiff relying on the fact that the defendant No. 1 in paragraph No. 20 of the written statement admitted that it had repaid Tk.1,00,000.00 only to the plaintiff on 12.01.1989, Therefore, the learned Judge opined that the loan was renewed and since, the learned Judge added, the suit is one under Article-147 of the Limitation Act the suit could have been filed within sixty(60) years and, the learned Joint District Judge further added, since sixty years’ time is yet to expire form 27.03.1970 the suit is not barred by limitation. He has next submitted that the finding regarding repayment by the defendant No.1 is, on the face of it, incorrect inasmuch as ext.6, 6(1) and (II) envisages that the defendant made repayment on 13.07.1970, 14.01.71 and 30.12.70 respectively. He has further added that admittedly the defendant made the last repayment on 14.01.1971 to the plaintiff after disbursement of the bridge loan by the predecessors of the plaintiff. He has next added that it is also admitted that the repayment dated 12.01.1989 was made after the suit was filed, on 29.10.1988, and it is also admitted that the said repayment was made after, at least, eighteen years after repayment dated 14.01.1971 (Ext. 6(1) of the disbursement of the loan money. He has next added that so far the finding of the learned Joint District Judge, regarding renewal or computation of fresh period of limitation of the loan money, is concerned, as reasoned by the learned Judge to arrive at as such is a wholesale error of law in view of section-20, read with Article-132 (C) and Artice-147 of the Limitation Act. He has next submitted that a plain reading makes it crystal clear that payment should be made on account of a debt before expiration of the prescribed period, but as the case in hand is concerned, payment was made firstly, after the suit was instituted and secondly, after eighteen years from due and thirdly, in view of Article-132 (c) of the Limitation Act, after the prescribed period of 12 (twelve) years; Article-132 ( C ) is the specified article for a suit for money only relating to mortgage by deposit of title deed. He has next added that the learned Judge erroneously found the Agreement dated 27.03.1970 (Ext.02) to be the 'mortgage by deposit of title deed' of which the plaintiff, as found by the learned Judge, to be the mortgaged; the definition of a mortgage by deposit of title deed has been contemplated in Section-58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, hereinafter referred to as 'T.P. Act'. He has next added that a plain reading of the unregistered Agreement / contract, namely' Underwriter-Cum-Advance' Agreement, reveals that the predecessors of the plaintiff were not mortgagees, rather predecessor of defendant No. 7(PICIC) was the mortgagee for the foreign currency loan from earlier without any memorandum of deposit of title deed; while the plaintiffs predecessors were parties to the said Agreement/Contract as financial institutions who did agree to sanction bridge loan to the defendant of which PICIC, being earlier mortgagee, stood security of the future bridge loan. He has further added that the Agreement is not a memorandum of deposit of title deed rather an unregistered Agreement/Contract and therefore inadmissible in evidence. He has next added that should the Agreement, for arguments sake, is considered to be an admissible 'memorandum of deposit of title deed' the expiration of limitation of such mortgage ought to have been read with Article 132 (c) of Limitation Act which provides 12 (twelve) years from the time when the money, sued for, becomes due, as the suit was filed more than 18(eighteen) years after money, sued for, became due the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. He has further submitted that learned Judge erroneously held that the suit is one under Article-147 of the Limitation Act inasmuch as the said Article is applicable only in case of those mortgagees who are qualified to sell the mortgaged property in view of section 67 of the ' T. P. Act'. He has next submitted that a plain reading of Article-132( c ) with Article-147 of the Limitation Act and Section-67 (a) of the 'TT. Act' would make it crystal clear; that Section -67 of the T.P. Act' deals with the rights of the mortgagee to foreclose or sale subject to conditions as contemplated in clause Nos. (a) to (d).

11. Clause (a) of section 67 of the `T.P. Act' contemplates in the following manner: "S.67 Nothing in this section shall be deemed-"(a) to authorize any mortgagee other than a mortgagee by conditional sale or a mortgagee under an anomalous mortgage by the terms of which he is entitled to foreclose, to institute a suit for foreclosure, or an usufructuary mortgagee as such or a mortgagee by conditional sale as such to institute a suit for sale."

12. It has further submitted that the Agreement does not stipulate any term, whatsoever, empowering the alleged mortgagee to sale the alleged mortgaged property. Besides, Article 132 (c ) of the Limitation Act has been specifically provided for filing suit for money/interest by the mortgagee under section 58 (f) of the T.P. Act widely known as mortgagee by depositing title deed'. Besides, he submits that the learned Court below fell into error in holding that the Underwriting —Cum-Advice Agreement dated 27.03.1970 (Exhibit-02) to be a deed of mortgage and the plaintiff is a mortgagee inasmuch as nowhere in the four corners of the agreement none, except the predecessor of the defendant No. 7 PICIC, as divulged in the Agreement, was identified as mortgagor or mortgagee. Neither the recital relating to the purpose of the Agreement uttered for once the term 'mortgage' in any applied form. The Agreement starts with the narration / recital that 'whereas the foreign currency cost of the project is being financed out of a PICIC (defendant No. 7) fund. The agreement further reveals that there were two sets of financial institutions out of which Nos. ii) to vi) being underwriter FIRST SET and from vii) to ix ) being underwriter SECOND SET with several terms. Article 111 (The Advance) was stipulated relating to disbursement and security of the advances and 'statements regarding deposition of title deeds with PICIC were mentioned.

13. In article No. 3.01 (c) of Article-III (The Advance) of the Agreement dated 27.03.1970 reveals the following term:-

"(C) — the advance (including the interim finance) shall be secured by a mortgage by deposit of title deeds relating to all the present and future immovable properties of the company. The title deeds relating to its properties deposited by the company with PICIC to secure the PICIC's foreign currency loan shall thenceforth be held by PICIC and PICIC hereby agrees to hold the same, in representative capacity on behalf of the underwriters and the interim financiers also to secure the advance and the amount of the interim finance actually disbursed not exceeding Rs. 30,00,000.00 to the company and the interest thereon"

14. He has next added that the aforementioned stipulation makes it crystal clear that the defendant-appellant never ever deposited their title deeds with the predecessors (Underwriter Nos. vii & viii of the second set) of the plaintiff. Rather, the appellant deposited their title deeds with PICIC (from the first set and defendant No. 7) to secure the foreign currency loan sanctioned by PICIC, in view of the 'Agreement' is, at best, a contemporaneous unregistered contract. He has next submitted that the learned Judge fell into error of law in holding the unregistered "Underwriting—Cum-Advance" Agreement as a memorandum / deed of mortgage by deposit of title deed and the plaintiff is the mortgagor. He further added that if the finding, for arguments sake is found to be lawful, yet no decree even under Article-132 (c), not to speak of Article-147, of the Limitations Act is maintainable inasmuch suit must be filed within 12 years. He has next added that it is now an established principle of law in view of Section 59 of the T. P. Act, the registration of the document, if it is found to be a contract relating to deposit of title deeds is mandatory, without the registration under section 17 of the Registration Act the memorandum or contract, whatsoever, is inadmissible in evidence in view of the fact that where the parties professing to create a mortgage by deposit of title deeds contemporaneously enter into a contractual agreement in writing which evidences the deposit and contains all the essentials of the transaction, expressly conferring a power of sale on the mortgagee and in fact purports to be an Instrument not merely evidencing the transaction already completed but by itself effective to create an interest in the property in favor of the mortgagee, such a document requires to be compulsorily registered. In support of his submission Mr. Saifur Reza the learned Advocate for the appellant referred the following cases: i). A.I.R. 1941 Privy Council 90; ii) A.I.R. 1939 Privy Council 167; iii) PLD 1969 Karachi 123; PLD 1961 (W.P) Karachi 537.

15. Mrs. Hosenera Begum, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff Respondent No.1 contended that the loan is admitted. She further contended that it is very true that acknowledgement within the meaning of section 19 of the Limitation Act must be made before the expiration of the period of Limitation acknowledgement (Ext-08) by the director (Defendant No. 4) of defendant No.1 company was made after the expiration of the limitation and as such the reply, to the legal notice dated 18.1.1987, being Ref. No. Mash Ji / Head office 87 ka 1388 dated 8.12.1987 (Ext.-8) is needed to be considered an agreement, under section 25(3) of the Contract Act, promising to pay (part of) the debt, and as such another fresh period of limitation for three years would be extended from that date and, added, that in continuation of earlier for promise dated 8.12.1987 defendant paid Tk. 1.00 lac during the pendency of the suit on 12.1.1989. In substantiating her contention the learned Advocate Mrs. Hosne Ara Begum refers to the following cases: (1) 39 DLR 1987 Page-243 to 256  (2) AIR 1938 Lahore Page-505 to 507 (3) 18 C L J Page-369  (4) P1,D 1969 Kar Page-653  (5) AIR 1953 SC Page-225

16. She further contended that in the instant case it was admitted in the written statement that in continuation and confirmation of the earlier fresh promise dated 08.12.1987, the defendant paid Tk.1.00 Lac on 12.01.1989 in favour of the plaintiff. She has next contended that the fresh promise to pay contained in the reply dated 08.12.1987 to the legal notice and actual payment made on 12.01.1989, confirms the earlier fresh promise to pay. She finally contended that since the fresh period of limitation would start from 08.12.1987 and actual part payment was made on 12.01.1989, the suit is not barred by limitation.

17. In reply to the contention as put forward by the Mrs. Hosneara Begum, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.1, Mr. Saifur Reza the learned Advocate for the appellant replied that the alleged acknowledgement (Ext-08) by the director (Defendant No.4) of defendant No.1 company was made after the expiration of the limitation and as such the reply, to the legal notice dated 18.11.1987, being Ref- No. MashJi / Head Office/ /87 Ka 1388 dated 08.12.1987 (Ext.8) is needed to be considered an Agreement, under section 25(3) of the Contract Act (Act X11 of 1872), promising to pay (part of) the debt, and as such another fresh period of limitation for three years would be extended from that date and, added , that in continuation of earlier promise dated 08.12.1987 defendant paid Tk.1.00 Lac during the pendency of the suit on 12.01.1989; to the effect that a fresh period of limitation would start from 08.12.1987 for 3(three) years needs to read with the statement made in paragraph-14 of the plaint that reads that' Defendant No.4, on behalf of defendant No.1, caused an application on 08.12.1987 proposing /urging to facilitate the defendant to pay the principal sum only in five yearly installments and waiver the interest but the defendant is obligated to pay the interest and that P.W. 1, only witness examined by the plaintiff, while making the reply, dated 08.12.1987, as Ext-08 deposed that 'the defendant caused the application for waiver of interest but we are not bound to waiver interest'. In view of the aforementioned averment and deposition made in the plaint and deposition respectively made by the plaintiff make it crystal clear that there were no acceptance, from the plaintiff's end, of the proposal made on behalf of the defendant. The plea of Section 25(3) of the Contract Act does not attract as neither any agreement, written or oral, was entered into nor any written promise in compliance with the aforementioned law was executed by the defendant and therefore on the face of it, and for the following reasons, misconceived:

18. Firstly because the submission is beyond the pleading and evidences on record, thus, affecting the nature and character of the suit consequently triggering requirement of opportunity to controvert by the defendant in the written statement and framing issue and a decision by the Court below in view of the plaint where no statement in this regard was made, instead it was averred that the suit is for realization of money by selling the mortgaged properties of defendant No.1 under Article 147 of the limitation Act as the cause of action arose on 27.03.1970 and thereafter on 08.12.1987.

19. Secondly because section 25 (3) requires an unconditional Agreement, in the form of a promise made in writing and signed by the person to be charged therewith or by his agent generally or specifically authorized in that behalf to pay wholly or in part of the debt. Plain reading of the Ext-8, as alleged, for the first time, to be the Agreement under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act reveals that it was a mere reply to the legal Notice dated 18.11.1987 with a conditional proposal/ offer urging to accept and thereby facilitate the defendant to make part payment after waiver of interest but the plaintiff never accepted the proposal and that should the plaintiff respondent have agreed to its conditions of waiving the interests the proposal .would have ended up in agreement between the parties. He further added to his reply that had the plaintiff agreed to the proposal made by the defendant a formal promise could have been made, but plaintiff neither agreed to the conditional proposal nor facilitated/allowed the defendant to make, any promise; whatsoever complying with the requirements of Section 25(3) of the Contract Act. He next added that the submission to the effect that in confirmation of the promise, made in the reply, defendant paid Tk. 1,00,000.00 has no substance inasmuch as the same transaction was made after the suit was filed and that Section 25(3) of the Contract Act neither require such alleged confirmation nor the section has any role to play in this regard. He next replied that besides, the money paid during pendency of the suit was aimed at entering into a compromise/ solenama in order to obtain a compromise judgment / decree but the plaintiff after receipt did not accept the proposal, instead adjusted the money against their whole claim.

20. Thirdly because the submission relating to Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, made by the respondent, is misconceived inasmuch as the same goes against the plaint as well as the judgment and decree, appealed against, in view of the judgment that decreed for sale of the alleged mortgaged property for which limitation, as held, under Article 147 of the Limitation Act inasmuch as for the fresh cause of action, as submitted , during hearing, limitation is three years, is not under Section 19 of the Limitation Act rather, a fresh extension under section 25(3) of the Contract Act.

<u>21. We have carefully gone through the judgment passed by the Trial Court along with evidence and exhibits as well as record. On hearing the submission and contention made by the learned Advocate for the appellant and respondent No. 1 and considered the pleadings of the parties. Since the learned Advocate for the appellant Mr. Saifur Reza apprises the court that he admit\ the impugned judgment with regard to issue No. "a" to "c and "e" and he will press the appeal so far issue No. "d" is concerned only on the point of limitation so we are considering the appeal only in the point of limitation: the issue, is the suit barred by limitation? On these point the learned Joint District Judge held that the suit is a suit for sale of mortgaged property. He next held that the suit is one under Article-147 of the Limitation Act. He further held that the issue of limitation in favour of the plaintiff on relying of the fact in paragraph No. 20 of the written statement admitted that it had repaid Tk. 1,00,000.00 only to the plaintiff on 12.01.1989 and so, the leaned Judge held that the loan was renewed and since, the learned Judge added, the suit is one under Article-147 of the Limitation Act. The suit could have been filed within 60 years and, the learned Judge further added, since sixty years’ time is yet to expire from 27.03.1970 the suit is not barred by limitation.</u>

<u>22. On perusal of the exhibits, impugned judgment and evidence on record it appears to us that regarding repayment by the defendant No.1 is, on the face of it, appears on perusal of ext.6,6(I) and (11) shows that the defendant No.1 made a repayment admittedly on 13.07.1970, 14.01.1971 and 30.12.1970 respectively, after disbursement of the bridge loan by the predecessors of the plaintiff. It further appears that admittedly repayment dated 12.01.1989 was made after the suit was filed on 29.10.1988. It next appears that so far the finding of the learned Joint District Judge, regarding renewal or computation of fresh period of limitation of the loan money, is concerned, as reasoned held by the learned Judge to arrived at in view of Section 20 of the Limitation Act,1908 read with Article-132(C) and Article-147 of the Limitation Act, 1908.</u>

23. In the awake of rival contentions advanced from both the sides, it is beneficial to a extract of Section 20 of the Limitation Act,1908 read with Article 132(C) and Article-147 of the Limitation Act, 1908, along with Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

24. Section 20(1) reads thus:

"20. (1) Where payment on account of a debt or of interest on a legacy is made before the expiration of the prescribed period by the person liable to pay the debt or legacy, or by his duly authorized agent, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the payment was made.  3, a plain reading makes it crystal clear that payment should be made on account of a debt before expiration of the prescribed period, but as the instant case is concerned, payment was made during pendency of the suit on 12.01.1989 in view of Article 132(C) of the Limitation Act after the prescribe period of 12 years.

25. Article 132 (C) runs thus: "132 (C) Advances secured by mortgage by deposit of title-deeds shall be deemed to be money charged upon immoveable property."

26. Article 132(C) is the specified article for a suit for money only relating to mortgage by deposit of title deed. Article 147 which is as follows: "Article 147 By a mortgagee for foreclosure or sale."

27. The learned Joint District Judge found the agreement dated 27.03.1970 (Ext.No.2) to be the mortgage by deposit of title deed of which plaintiff, as found by the learned Judge, to be the mortgagee; the definition of a mortgage by deposit of title deed has been contemplated in Section -58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. It will be also useful to "quote" Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act which is as follows:

28. Mortgage by deposit of title-deeds: " (f) Where a person in the town of [Dhaka, Narayangonj and Chittagong] and in any other town which the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, specify in this behalf, delivers to a creditor or his agent documents of title to immoveable property, with intent to create a security thereon, the transaction is called a mortgage by deposit of title-deeds."

29. In the present case it appears that the referred laws are applicable in the facts and circumstance of the present suit, so far, as it relates to issue (d) is concern only on the point of limitation. It appears to us that the trial court rightly opined that the suit was for foreclosure as the defendant obtained the loan by depositing the title deeds. Moreso, admittedly the appellant repaid the loan amounting to Tk. 1,00,000.00/- (one lac) admitting the debt during pendency of the suit. It appears to us that the suit is not for only foreclosure, rather, the defendants have waived to raise the question of limitation depositing the part of loan money at the trial, admitting that the defendants had obtained the loan by deposit the title deeds. Question of limitation once waived by the defendants at their own sweet will; therefore, in appeal they cannot raise the same point of limitation.

30. To consider the finding with regard to limitation by the learned Subordinate Judge & Commercial court No. 2, Dhaka as we referred to above, it cannot be at all said that those are tainted with patent illegality, legal infirmity and flagrant error of law and fact warranting any interference by this court.

31. In view of the discussion made herein above we find the submissions as advanced by the learned Advocate for the Appellant bears no merit and decisions and laws as referred by him in support of his submissions also not applicable in the facts and circumstances because of those decisions are quite distinguishable from the facts and circumstance of the instant appeal.

32. On the other hand the contention as put forward by the learned advocate for the respondent bears merits and decisions and laws as referred by her in support of her contentions also squarely applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant appeal.

33. Thus, the appeal having no merits, it fails.

34. In the result, the appeal is dismissed, however without any order as to costs.

35. The judgment and decree dated 10.07.2002 passed by the Joint District Judge and commercial court No.2 Dhaka in Title Suit No. 197 of 2001 is hereby affirmed.

36. Consequently, the connected Civil Rule No. 310(f) of 2003 is hereby discharged without any order as to costs.

37. Send down the lower court record at once.

38. Communicate the judgment to the concerned court at once.

End.
