parties:
Belayet Hossain -------- Defendants-Petitioner 
vs
Md Mizanur Rahman and others ------- Plaintiffs-Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Md Ashraful Kamal J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the order dated 13-10-2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No. 3, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 164 of 2007 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Brief facts, necessary for the disposal of this Rule, are as follows;

2(a). Opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff had filed a Title Suit being No. 164 of 2007 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Court No. 3, Dhaka for a declaration of title in respect of 'ka' schedule property to the plaint and recovery of khas possession with cancellation of registered sale deed dated 30-10-2005.

2(b). The facts of the case of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 are that the government of the then East Pakistan allotted the property in question to one Md Hanif Bhuiyan vide registered deed No. 4015 dated 27-6-1957. Thereafter, Hanif Bhuiyan sold the property to the plaintiff's mother Mrs. Firoza Begum vide registered sale deed No. 796 dated 11-2-1964. By constructing two building thereon Mrs. Firoza Begum had been living there with her family members.

2(c). On 15-5-1992 mother of the plaintiffs made an oral gift in respect of the property in question in favour of the plaintiff and handed over the possession. In such way the plaintiff has been owing and possessing the suit property.

2(d). The plaintiff's 3 (three) sisters, (the defendant Nos. 2-4 to the plaint) in collusion with other brothers of the plaintiff by forging the signature of their mother sworn an affidavit on 29-12-1992 affirming the oral heba dated 17-9-1992 in favour of the said 3 sisters keeping the plaintiff in dark. Thereafter, the defendant No. 2-4 filed Title Suit No. 215 of 1996 in the Court of 1st Assistant Judge, Dhaka against the plaintiff and his brother, the defendant No.5 for evicting them from the suit property and by practicing fraud they obtained ex-parte judgment and decree on 23-6-1999. Against the said ex-parte judgment and decree dated 23-6-1999, the defendant No. 1 of the said suit and the defendant No. 5 of the present suit filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the said ex-parte decree whereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000 was started.

2(e). In the meantime after obtaining the ex-parte decree the plaintiffs of that suit filed Title Execution Case No. 4 of 2000 for evicting the defendants of the said suit. Thereafter, the defendant No.5 of the present suit filed an application in the Title Execution Case No.4 of 2000 for staying the proceeding of the title execution case till hearing of the Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000, which was rejected on 30-10-2003. Against that order dated 30-10-2003 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Narayangonj, the defendant No. 5 of the present suit filed Civil Revision No. 4754 of 2006 before this Division.

2(f) Although, the defendant No. 24 of the present suit had no legal title and possession in the suit property, but they transferred the same along with 'Kha' scheduled property illegally in favour of the defendant No. 1 vide registered sale deed No. 8864 dated 30-10-2005. The cause of action of the present suit arose when the defendant Nos. 2-4 evicted the plaintiff illegally from the suit property. Hence, the suit.

2(g). The petitioner as defendant No. 1 entered appearance and contested the suit by filing an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of plaint. Upon hearing of the said application for rejection of plaint, the court below rejected the same on 13-10-2009.

2(h). Being aggrieved by the said order dated 13-10-2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No. 3, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 164 of 2007, the petitioner preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

3. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the plaintiff stated in the plaint about the ex-parte decree dated 23-6-1999 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 but with a malafide intention he has suppressed the fact that in Civil Revision No. 3834 of 2001 the High Court Division affirmed the said ex-parte decree dated 23-6-1999 which was further affirmed by the Appellate Division in CPLA No. 1413 of 2002. He also submits that the ex-parte decree dated 23-6-1999 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1999 reached its finality when it was affirmed by the Appellate Division and hence the suit is barred by the doctrine of res-judicata and Mr Mokaddas finally submits that the suit is barred by law in view of the facts that the judgment and decree passed in the earlier suit were affirmed by the Appellate Division as such the present suit cannot be maintainable. He referred some decisions namely Islami Bank Bangladesh vs Abdul Jalil reported in 53 DLR 29 and Abdul Jalil vs Islami Bank reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12.

4. Mr Moin Uddin along with Mr Md Kobad Hossain and Mr Abul Hossain, the learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party No. 1 by filing counter-affidavit submits that the matter relating to the application for rejection of plaint is the matter of evidence which may be proved by examination of witnesses on the dock and that the said matter do not come under the purview of Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the court below rightly rejected the application for rejection of plaint.

5. He further submits that the court below did not commit any illegality or that the order passed by the court below does not suffer from any infirmity of law. He also submits that the summon-notices of the Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 were not served upon the defendants and against the ex-parte decree the defendant No. 1 of the said suit as petitioner filed Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2000.

6. He also submits that there was no decree in the said suit but on the strength of the decree the opposite party Nos. 2-4 went to possession of the suit land and the present opposite party No. 1 was dispossessed. He further submits that the name and character are different from each other and parties are also different, thus the present suit does not hit by res judicata or any other law and, as such, the plaint of Title Suit No. 64 of 2007 does not come under the purview of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and he finally submits that the learned Court below rightly rejected the application for rejection of plaint and, as such, the present rule is liable to be discharged with cost.

7. In support of his submissions he referred some decisions namely Shahjahan Siraj (Md) vs Md Rafique Quoraishi reported in 19 BLC (AD) 143, Abdul Jalil vs Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd. reported in 64 DLR (AD) 107, Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman reported in 13 BLD (AD) 217 and Md Mahbubul Haque vs Md A. Kader Monshi reported in 8 BLT (AD) 177 = 52 DLR (AD) 49.

8. We have gone through the revisional application along with annexures therein and the counter-affidavit filed by the opposite party No. 1. We have also considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1.

9. Order VII, rule 11 describes the procedure for rejection of plaint. It is necessary to quote Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs as follows

"11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:—

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action;

(b) where the relief claimed is under-valued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so;

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law.

[Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty-one days].

[(e) where any of the provisions of rule 9 (1A) is not complied with and the plaintiff on being required by the Court to comply therewith within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so.]

10. On a plain reading of the aforesaid rule it is evident that the plaint shall be rejected on the grounds specified above.

11. For deciding an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the averments in the plaint need to be looked into.

12. The trial Court can exercise the power under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure at any stage of the suit before registering the plaint or after issuing summons to the defendants at any time before the conclusion of the trial.

13. For the purpose of deciding an application under clauses (a) and (b) of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code, the averments in the plaint are germane; the pleas taken by the defendants in the written statement would be wholly irrelevant.

14. The basic question to be decided while dealing with an application filed under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code is whether a real cause of action has been set out in the plaint. If on a meaningful and formal reading of the plaint, it appears to be manifestly fictitious and meritless in the sense of not disclosing a clear right to sue, the Court should exercise the power under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.

15. The real object of the Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is to keep out of Court's irresponsible suits. If it is found that the suit is an abuse of the process of the court in the sense that it is a bogus and irresponsible litigation, the jurisdiction under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code can be exercised.

16. Question is whether a real cause of action has been set out in the plaint. Clever drafting creating illusions are not permitted in law and a clear right to sue should be shown in the plaint.

17. The Court should always be vigilant for scrutinizing the pleadings and materials placed before it to ascertain whether the litigation is frivolous or maintainable at all. The Court must exercise its powers at every stage in order to nip the frivolous cases in the bud.

<u>18. It is well settled now that a plaint may be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure merely on a plain reading of the plaint but in exceptional circumstances the Court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and can through the plaint out in limine.</u>

<u>19. It is also well settled that the plea of implied bar should ordinarily be decided on evidence, unless the facts disclosed in the pleading clearly prove that the suit is not maintainable. In exceptional cases recourse may be taken under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

20. In the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd. vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union reported in 18 DLR 709 Mr Justice Murshed held that apart from the question of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court can also exercise its inherent power in order to stop the harassment of the other party.

Justice Murshed has held as follows;

"The principles involved as twofold: in the first place, it contemplates that a still born suit should be properly buried, at its inception, so that no further time is consumed on a fruitless litigation. Secondly, it gives plaintiff a chance to retrace his steps, at the earliest possible moment, so that, if permissible under law, he may find a properly constituted case.

Order VII, rule 11 of the Code, as quoted above enumerates certain categories under which the Court is called upon to reject a plaint, but, it is obvious that they are not exhaustive. It appears from the language of rule 11 of Order VII that it requires that an incompetent suit should be laid at rest at the earliest moment so that no further time is wasted over what is bound to collapse as not being permitted by law."

21. In the case of Abdul Jalil vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Ltd. reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12, it was held that:

"It is well settled that where a plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

It was further held that in the said case—

"As the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as day light such a suit should be hurried at its inception so that no further time is consumed in a fruitless litigation."

22. Coming to the case at hand, the defendants Nos. 24 after getting oral gift of their mother filed Title Suit No. 215 of 1996 in the Court of 1st Assistant Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of the suit property against the defendant No. 5 of present suit making him defendant No. 1 and making defendant No.2, the plaintiff of the present suit. Subsequently, the suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Nawabganj, Dhaka on transfer which was decreed ex-parte on 23-6-1999 in favour of the plaintiffs of the said suit declaring title of the suit property and also decreed for recovery of khas possession of the suit property. Against the aforesaid ex-parte decree, the plaintiff of the present suit as defendant No. 2 filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte decree dated 23-6-1999 of Title Suit No. 127 of 1997 whereupon the Miscellaneous Case No. 35 of 1999 was started. The petitioner of the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case that is, the plaintiff also filed Title Appeal No. 769 of 1999 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka against the said ex-parte decree which was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Court No. 3, Dhaka and after hearing the said appeal was allowed on 29-3-2001 setting aside the ex-parte decree and the suit was sent on remand to the trial court for hearing. Against the aforesaid judgment and order of the appellate court, the respondents of that appeal filed civil revision No. 3834 of 2001 before this Division and obtained Rule. After hearing the said Civil Revision No. 3834 of 2001 the Rule was made absolute on 28-2-2002 setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court and restored the ex-parte decree dated 23-6-1999 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 1999. Against the judgment and order passed in Civil Revision No. 3834 of 2001 the present plaintiff filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1413 of 2002 before the Appellate Division which was dismissed on 18-1-2003.

23. We carefully scrutinized the plaints of both the suits as well as the judgments passed by the Courts up to the Appellate Division. We are of the view that question which in the present plaint is now raising had already been considered and decided in the earlier suit once and for all and, as such, we hold that there was no cause of action for instituting the present suit.

<u>24. The decree passed by the Appellate Division is the law of the land. Article 111 of our constitution provides that the law declared by the Appellate Division shall be binding on the High Court Division and the law declared by either Division of the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts subordinate to it.</u>

<u>25. Since the judgment and decree passed by the earlier suit was affirmed by the Appellate Division the present suit cannot be maintainable in view of the fact that as the suit is barred by law and law declared by the Appellate Division in the judgment passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1413 of 2002.</u>

26. On the admitted facts appearing from the record itself, learned Advocate for the plaintiff- opposite parties were unable to show that all or any of this averments in the plaint disclose any cause of action giving rise to a triable issue. In our opinion, the trial court failed to perform its duty and overlooked this fatal defect.

27. Since the plaint suffers from this fatal defect, the continuance of such a suit tantamount to licensing a frivolous and vexatious litigation. This cannot be permitted as per law.

28. In such a factual situation, in our considered opinion, the court below has fallen into an error of law resulting in an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice in rejecting the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside. If the present suit is allowed to proceed further it would consume the time, energy and money of all the parties concerned. Therefore, this court cannot allow such frivolous malafide proceedings to continue.

29. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and order dated 13-10-2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No. 3, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 164 of 2007 holding the suit to be maintainable is set aside and the plaint is rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

30. There is no order as to costs.

Communicate this judgment and order at once.

End.

parties:
Abul Khair Condensed Milk and Beverage Ltd ----- Petitioner 
Vs.
Commissioner of Customs and ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: In the above Rule Nisi legality of three CRF certificates issued on 20-10-05 in respect of the imported sugar was challenged and a direction was sought for assessment of said goods on the basis of invoice value as normal/transaction value.

2. The petitioner is stated to be a company incorporated in Bangladesh under the Companies Act. It imported 22,700 metric tons of sugar from Brazil by opening three letters of credit on 24-8-05, 27-8-05 and 28-8-05 at the rate of US$ 260 permetricton, Before shipment the goods were inspected by an approved PSI agency and arrived with three CRF certificates issued by said PSI agency. After arrival of the goods at Chittagong Port four bills of entry were submitted on 2-11-05 for clearance of the goods for home consumption. Upon receipt of the bills of entry the customs authority assessed the goods to duty on the basis of the value certified in the CRF certificates at the rate of US$ 262 per metric ton and printed computerised generated bills of entry, Annexure-'E' series to the writ petition.

3. During the vacation, the petitioner challenged such CRF certificates before a Single Bench of this Division and on 9-11-05 obtained an order of  release of the goods on payment of duty and other charges in cash on the basis of invoice value and upon further receipt of 25 percent of the CRF value in cash and rest 75 percent upon receipt of continuing bank guarantee(s).

4. On behalf of the respondent No. 1, the Commissioner of Customs on 15-11-05 made an application for vacating aforesaid interim order of release. In the application, it is denied that the goods were assessed to duty on receipt of the bills of entry on the basis of CRF certified value. It was stated that no assessment of duty was at all made. It was further stated that said CRF agency in collusion with the petitioner certified a price at much lower than the prevalent price. Because of the dishonest valuation, the customs authority suffered loss of Taka 6,42,62,862.42 in revenue.

5. Against the application the petitioner on 20-11-95 filed an affidavit-in-opposition denying what was claimed therein and reiterated what were stated in the writ petition. On 15-11-07 the application was ordered for hearing on 17-11-05 and the above Rule was issued as aforesaid. Ultimately, the application was ordered to be kept with the file by order dated 27-11-05.

6. Then, said respondent No.1 on 7-5-07 submitted an affidavit-in-opposition to the writ petition. In the affidavit, it was stated that pursuant to the order of release of this Division, the goods were released on the basis of a provisional assessment. It was again reiterated that before the goods could be assessed to duty the petitioner moved this Division and first, obtained the release order and then, the Rule.

7. It also annexed a demand notice dated 16-11-05 for aforesaid Taka 6,42,62,862.42 under section 32 of the Customs Act, 1969 and the goods were valued at the rate of US$ 319.74 per metric ton at the prevalent rate of international price.

8. On 30-4-07 the petitioner filed a supplementary affidavit annexing the correspondences between the petitioner and the supplier. In said affidavit, it was stated that the supplier informed the petitioner that the PSI agency did never ask the supplier for any information/data for the present market price nor did it obtain any information/date from the supplier on the price of the goods on any specific form whatsoever.

Said respondent on 13-5-07 submitted a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition seeking some corrections in their affidavit-in-opposition dated 7-5-07.

9. The petitioner on 17-5-07 submitted an affidavit-in-reply. In the affidavit, it is stated mainly that the respondent No. 1 provided no objective basis for the allegations that the invoice value did not reflect the current market price of sugar as prevailing on the date of issuance of invoice i.e. 3rd and 4th October 2005, nor had he taken any necessary steps to determine the current market price through any of the established procedures for doing so.

10. Respondent No. 1 then on 2-8-07 filed further supplementary affidavit-in-opposition in said affidavit, he denied the case of the petitioner that on receipt of the bills of entry the goods were assessed to duty on the basis of the value certified in the CRF certificates and computerised bills of entry were printed out. It was further stated that annexed bills of entry did not contain any order of assessment.

11. The procedure the customs authority has been following what is called "Journey of Computerised Bill of Entry under ASYCUDA "System" meaning Automated System of Customs Data, Plus Plus indicating modifications done twice for betterment of the software of the said computer system was elaborately described as hereunder:

i.To release the consignment of imported goods the importer himself or his C&F agent fills up the Biil of Entry Form and fixes all necessary documents concerning the import along with the said Form, a specimen of which is Annexure-X. The importer or his agent put signatures on two copies of Lodgment Slip, Annexure-X-1. Then, the importer or Agent submits the Bill of Entry to the Import General Manifest (IGM) Section under section 79 of the Customs Act for noting;

ii. Said IGM section examines the particulars of filled up Bill of Entry Form and Bill of Lading, Import Manifest, etc and if found correct, makes noting of the Bill of Entry and sends the same (which is also known as Data Sheet) to the pre-Entry Check Section;

iii. The Pre-Entry Check section puts all the documents with the Bill of Entry in a Plastic Folder and ascertains that all the documents have been attached and then, gives a Folder Number on the lodgement slip and supplies a copy of the Lodgment. Slip to the importer or his Agent. Then this pre-Entry Check section sends the Folder and other copies of Lodgment Slip to the Head Assistant of the Computer Hall. Then the Head Assistant of the Computer Hall distributes the Folders to the Data Entry Operators. The concerned Data Entry Operator enters the particualrs or information given in the filled up Bill of Entry in the computer (which is also known as Making Entry in the ASYCUDA++ programme). According to the programme in the computer, the computer gives a serial number which is known as Registration Number or BE number (Bill of Entry Number). The operator takes out 3 copies of print of the Bill of Entry with the said number. In this way, at the time of registration of the Bill of Entry the name of the Appraiser or officer of Customs who will assess the duty also gets computerised and kept in the computer.

iv. Thereafter, concerned computer operator writes down the name of the appraiser upon the Lodgment Slip and number of Bill of Entry and sends the folder to the lodgment counter, through the Head Assistant of the Computer Hall, From the lodgment counter, the printed Bill of Entry or Data Sheet reaches to the Appraiser through Transit Section. The Bill of Entry at this stage looks like as Annexure-X-2 From the beginning up to this stage, the process is known as Bill of Entry Noting and registration process under section 79 of the Customs Act;

v. The Appraiser then examines the documents and makes Assessment of customs duty under section 80 of Customs Act and sends the papers to the Principal Appraiser for confirmation of assessment and for issue of Assessment Notice. But when there is any necessity for compliance with some regulation say Import Policy such as radiation test of food items, for example Apple, then without making any assessment the Appraiser sends the goods for Readiation Test;

vi. When the Bill of Entry comes to the Principal Appraiser, he examines the papers and follows the principles for assessment in respect of the imported goods and if he finds them correct, confirms the assessment and from his computer takes out 3 copies of prints of the Assessment Notice. At the time of printing the Assessment Notice, an Assessment Number is automatically put on the Bill of Entry according to the computer programme. After assessment and customs duty the concerned Appraiser and Principal Appraiser put their signatures with respective seals on the Assessment Notice. After the completion of all these, it is called that Assessment has been done. The Assessment Notice, looks as Annexure-X-4;

vii. Thereafter, the signed Bill of Entry along with Assessment Notice and all the documents in the Plastic Folder are presented to the Section Assistant who sees whether all the documents are there. From the documents, he finds out the original Bill of Lading, letter of credit, etc and gives them to the C&F Agent. There after Emboss Seals are given on the Bill of Entry and Assessment Notice. After putting seals, 3rd copy of the Bill of Entry is kept in the concerned section of asessment, the other two copies are given to the C&F Agent. And three copies of Assessment Notice are sent to the Delivery Counter. From the Delivery Counter, the Assessment Notice along with other papers are sent to the concerned Sonali Bank. The Bank Authority gives Emboss Seal on the Assessment Notice and realises payment of customs duty. After realisation of the duty the said Bank keeps 3rd copy of the Asessment Notice and sends 2 other copies to the Treasury Speed Branch (or Delivery Branch.);

viii. That computer operators of the Treasury Speed Branch examine as to whether there are seals and signatures of the Delivery Counter, Appraiser and Principal Appraiser and duty is realised and after such scrutiny he prints the Release Order. When the Release Order is printed according to the computer programme a number is automatically put in the Release Order, which is the Release Order Number (or R N) Annexure-X-5. The operator puts his signature on the printed Release Order and then sends it to the Head Assistant of the Section; and

ix. The Head Assistant puts his signature upon the Release Order and Release order Number is perforated by Punch Machine and given to the other Assistant of the section (Treasury Speed Section or Delivery Section. The Assistant keeps the 2nd copy of the Assessment Notice in the Speed Section and hands over the original copy of Assessment Notice to the C and F agent. He also gives the 1st and 2nd copy of the Release Order to the C&F Agent. Then, the C&F Agent takes steps for taking delivery of imported goods.

12. It is further stated that the remedy against CRF certificate in a particular case was available under Paragraph 9 of the Pre-shipment Inspection Order, 1999 and “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি কমিটি” formed under rule 23 of Pre-shipment Inspection Rules 2002 vide office order dated 12-9-05, Annexure-5 to the affidavit. But the remedy was not available to the petitioner since the letters of credit were opened by the petitioner before September 01, 2005, Said order was applicable only in cases where letter of credit was opened after September 1, 2005.

13. The petitioner on 13-9-07 filed another supplementary affidavit. In said affidavit, it was stated that the “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি” which the respondent referred to in the affidavit dated 29-8-07 was established in September, 2005 did not function for some time and, as such the petitioner could not avail of any remedy before such committee. It further reiterated that the review committee was established on 5-7-06 by an order of the National Board of Revenue long after the impugned order was passed. The petitioner therefore could not even seek remedy before the review committee as was stated to be formed on 20-5-01. Pursuant to rule 36 of aforesaid PSI Rules, 2002 it was stated that such rule related to pending matters or proceedings after coming into force of the PSI Rules, 2002 after repeal of the PSI Order, 1999 and did not cover the present case.

14. By filing further explanation, on white sheets of paper on behalf of respondent No. 1, it is stated that in the case the petitioner opened letter of credit on 24-8-05 mentioning the name of respondent No. 4 as PSI agency, which was appointed under the PSI Order, 1999 and whose service was extended up to 31-8-05 by memorandum dated 30-6-05. Then, new PSI agencies were appointed under the PSI Rules, 2002 with effect from 1st September 2005 vide the notification being SRO No. 153 dated 23-8-05, Annexure-F2 to the writ petition. The petitioner could file complaint, if any, in respect of the PSI certificates before the review committee appointed under said Rules.

15. Dr Kamal Hossain, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, challenged the certificates issued by the respondent No. 4, PSI agency mainly on the grounds that those were issued at inflated value without following the mandatory provisions of the PSI Rules, 2002.

16. He submitted that in view of the disclosures of the supplier, Annexure-K series that the PSI Agent did not ask the supplier for any information data of the present market price nor did it obtain any data or information on the price of the imported goods, the customs authority most illegally and arbitrarily assessed he goods to duty upon such PS certified value.

17. He also tried to impress upon us that in view of print out of computerised bills of entry with all necessary information/data entered therein though without the date, signature and seal of the appropriate customs authority the assertion of the customs authority that the goods was not assessed to duty had got no basis.

18. Lastly, he submitted that in view of release of the imported goods pursuant to the interim order of this Division dated 11-9-05 upon receipt of the duty and other charges both in cash and upon bank guarantee(s), the customs authority would now assess the goods finally to duty in accordance with law by ignoring the CRF certificates.

19. In support, he cited Showkat Ali vs Commissioner of Customs 6 BLC 357 and Alhaj Nazir Ahmed vs National Board of Revenue 2001 BLD 59.

20. Mr Fazlul Haque, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of said respondent No. 1, on the other hand, submitted that the goods were not assessed to duty and before any assessment could be made the petitioner obtained the interim release order and got the goods cleared.

21. He submitted that copies of computerised generated bills of entry were never supplied by the customs authority to the petitioner and those copies were no proof of the fact that the goods were assessed to duty on the basis of CRF certified value, which contained no date, signature and/or seal of the appropriate authority and not even an order of assessment and assessment notice.

22. He submitted that the petitioner obtained the CRF certificates by way of collusion with the PSI agency at much lower price than the international price of the imported goods and also release of the goods pursuant to the interim order of this Division, which caused revenue loss of Taka 6,42,62,862.42 if the goods could be assessed to, duty at the rate of US$ 319.74 per metric ton at the relevant time and the customs authority had to issue a demand notice dated 16-11-05.

23. He submitted that the customs authority had never accepted and assessed the duty at the value certified by the PSI agency and the Rule issued before assessment of the goods to duty must be held to be premature and would be liable to be discharged on this count only.

24. In the aforesaid pleadings and on the submissions of the learned Advocate number of issues was raised. But, in view of the order that we may have to pass ultimately in disposing of the Rule, we are afraid we could deal and dispose of them exhaustively in this writ petition.

25. First, both parties seriously differed on the question of assessment of the goods, namely, sugar of Brazilian origin to duty. It is the case of the petitioner, importer that it challenged the CRF certificates when the customs authority assessed the goods to duty on the inflated value certified therein. In support, computer generated bills of entry were annexed. Its main grievance against the CRF certificates is that they were issued violating the mandatory provisions of rule 13 of the PSI Rules, 2002.

26. On the other hand, it is the definite case of respondent No.1, the Commissioner of Customs, that before the imported goods could be assessed to duty the petitioner moved. this Division on the allegations that the goods was assessed to duty on the basis of CRF certified value and upon such misrepresentation obtained the Rule and release of the goods; that the computerised generated print out is no proof of assessment and the petitioner was not supposed to receive such print out before assessment; that such print out is lacking signature, seal and date of respective customs officers and more particularly, order of assessment cannot be read as assessment and that after assessment in all cases, an assessment order and assessment notice are issued and before issue of such order and notice there is no scope for reading any paper that may be obtained from the office of respondent No.1 as assessment.

27. What is assessment has not been defined in the Customs Act, 1969. Section 79 requires only for the owner of the imported goods to make entry of such goods for home consumption or any other purpose by delivering to an appropriate officer the bill of entry in such form and containing such particulars as the National Board of Revenue may direct. After receipt of such bill of entry, under section 80 the goods shall be assessed to duty, if any and the owner of such goods may then proceed to clear the same for home consumption or warehousing subject to other provisions of the Act. Section 79A was though inserted long back on 1st July 1999 but the customs authority is not yet prepared to take step for acceptance of electronically transmitted bills of entry and/or documents. Section 79B to 790 was inserted by Act No. 15 of 2000. Section 79B provides for access as a user to the computer system by being registered with the Commissioner of Customs, None of the benefits thought to be user friendly could be availed of for the delay in the introduction of the system.

28. The procedure for assessment the customs authority has been following as was stated hereinabove in detail is no doubt lengthy and elaborate and nay seem to be complicated. But after the time for completion of assessment is clamped and prescribed, the customs authority is obliged to complete their job with all the limitations in the prescribed time frame. During such time prescribed for assessment, no importer should or could have any grievance. Rather, he should cooperate with the customs authority to obviate all problems in the clearance of the imported goods.

<u>29. Situation is not different in any way in the neighboring countries, which have got rich experience in working under the same for similar law. Mrs Sara Hossain, learned Advocate, studied on the process of assessment in neighboring  jurisdictions but she also could not find any legal rules for assessment. Assessment is really a matter of national revenue and the National Board of Revenue runs the show by issuing notifications etc time to time on the basis of broader guidelines promulgated in the Finance Act of a year.</u>

<u>30 . There should not be any doubt in the fact that every assessment either of income tax or VAT or excise presupposes existence of an order of assessment. It is equally true in the case of assessment of duty under the Customs Act. When no assessment assessing duty on the imported goods could be shown, only conclusion could be arrived at law is that there was no assessment. Any grievance raised or brought against such inchoate assessment must be held to be based on supposition of an assessment and does not deserve any consideration. Consequently, the rights and obligations arising out of assessment could only be agitated and decided only in accordance with law. This Division is generally not empowered to intervene in the process of assessment. In all the cases cited and relied upon by Dr Kamal this Division intervened only after assessment of duty.</u>

31. In the case at hand, the papers annexed and relied upon by the petitioner do not constitute an assessment of duty on the imported goods. In the circumstances, we have got no hesitation to say that the above Rule was obtained before any assessment of the goods to duty could be made and was issued prematurely.

32. Then, the parties differed seriously on the CRF certificates. It is the case of the petitioner that said certificates were issued at an inflated rate much higher than the international price and in violation of some mandatory provisions of the PSI Rules, 2002. On the other hand, the customs authority found the value certified by PSI agency much lower than the international price at the relevant time of submission of bills of entry.

33. We are amazed and, amused at the lengthy and strenuous arguments of the learned Advocates. Few facts may help understand the basis of the bone of contention of the parties. The petitioner imported 22,500 metric ton of sugar of Brazilian origin at the rate of US$ 260 per metric ton. The PSI agency certified the value of sugar at US$ 262 in its certificates. The customs authority found the value certified in the said certificates much lower than the international price. In his demand notice, issued on behalf of respondent No. 1 sugar was valued at the rate of US$ 319.74 per metric ton as the then market price. After hearing such learned submissions one thing becomes clear that none of the parties was happy at the service of the PSI agency.

34. Sections 25A was inserted in the Customs Act by Act No. 11 of 1994 with effect from July 1, 1994 and section 25B and 25C were inserted by Act No. 15 of 2000 with effect from 15-2-2000. Section 25A was time to time substituted to take the present shape, which is effective since July 1, 1999.

35. Section 25A empowers the Government to appoint pre-shipment agencies and audit agencies for certification and audit mainly on the inspection and certification of imported goods. By notification in official gazette, the government is also empowered to declare that the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by a pre-shipment inspection agency shall be accepted as the basis for assessment. Section 25B requires all imported goods to be inspected by an approved preshipment agency subject to exemption granted by the Government by notification in the official gazette. And 25C provides for imposition and collection of pre-shipment inspection service charge as a customs duty at a rate not exceeding one percent ad-valorem.

36. In order to carry out the purpose of the above provisions of pre-inspection of imported goods and certification by approved pre-shipment agency, the notification being SRO No. 316 dated 19-10-99 was published, naming it as the Pre-Shipment Inspection Order, 1999. In such Order, everything right from appointment and service of pre-shipment agencies and resolution of disputes that may arise out of such service and certification of goods and time limit for completion of assessment and release of imported goods at the earliest were prescribed. Then, by notification being SRO No. 255 dated 19-9-2000 as the Pre-shipment Inspection Rules, 2002 was published and the previous Order was repealed. In the present Rules, procedure for certification of the imported goods, forum for resolution of disputes that may arise from the certification and time limit for completion of assessment, etc in all detail were prescribed.

37. In the Order, 1999 a review committee was conceived for resolution of all 'disputes regarding the certification by the PSI agency. Section 193C of the Customs Act, 1969 was accordingly updated providing for review of any matter related to the Clean Report of Findings (CRF) issued by the pre-shipment inspection agencies. Then, after introduction of the PSI Rules, 2002, a five member “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি কমিটি” for resolution of disputes was first thought of, which was replaced by a notification being SRO No. 154 dated 21-6-06 by previous provision of review committee. There is dispute over which was the forum available to the petitioner at the time. On behalf of the customs authority, it was sometimes asserted that the petitioner ought to go to the “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি কমিটি” but on the next breath, asked the petitioner to go the review committee if it has got grievance against the certification of the imported goods. On behalf of the petitioner, it is claimed that the “বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি কমিটি” claimed to be established in September, 2005 was not working and the review committee was formed on 5-7-06 long after the impugned assessment. We must admit that we have failed to ascertain first, what was the forum available during the time of submission of bills of entry on 2-11-05 and second, if there was any, was it working. This dispute over the forum ultimately appears to be of no significance in view of rule 23(2) of the PSI Rules, 2002 that an importer could be aggrieved only after clearance of the goods and then, he may seek redress against the certification of the goods.

38. At the end of the day, in spite of the above detailed and comprehensive provisions providing the basis for assessment of duty, it appears that the system brought into operation could please neither the importer nor the customs authority. Mechanism for resolution of disputes could not satisfy the importers. May be for this reason, this Division was flooded with writs against the certification of the goods and/or delay in the process of assessment of duty. Search for the actual price, that is, "the price actually paid or payable, or the nearest ascertainable equivalent of such price" remains as the golden deer, সোনার হরিণ as before.

39. Now, the grievance against the CRF certificates on the premise of assessment appears to be of no foundation. When the goods were not at all assessed to duty, all submissions against such certificates appear to be premature. It is for the customs authority first to consider and decide on the certification of the goods as to whether the CT certificate was correct and in order with regard quality, quantity, price, description and custom classification of the imported goods and provides the basis for assessment, and could act and assess the duty thereon. This Division is not empowered to preempt the power of the customs authority in respect of such certification and decide on such CRF certificates before assessment. In all the cases cited on behalf of the petitioner, this Division considered and decided on the legality of such CRF certificates only after assessment.

40. Saying all and everything in disposing of the issues raised, we cannot leave here the goods were cleared pursuant to an interim order of this Division, which now needs to be finally assessed. When none of the parties could accept the CRF certificates, only option is now left to the customs authority that is under sub-rule (2) of rule 22 of the PSI Rules, 2002 to ascertain the value and HS Code of the goods in accordance with the Customs Valuation Rules, 2000. It is needless to say that in the process, the petitioner shall be at liberty to produce any document/paper in support of the invoice value, which the customs authority shall consider in finally assessing the goods.

41. Before we part with the case, we must express our view about the demand notice dated 16-11-05, Annexure-4 to supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 7-5-07, which put the petitioner into natural anxiety. It is a fact now that the goods were released on or about 16-11-05 pursuant to the interim order of this Division. On the same date the customs authority issued a demand notice asking the petitioner to pay Taka 6,42,62,862.42, which they arrived at the rate of US$ 319.74 per metric tons of sugar rejecting the CRF certificates. They claim the demand was issued under section 32 of the Customs Act.

42. Section 32 of the Customs Act comprises of 2 parts. Sub-section (1) makes it offence to make or sign or causes to be made or signed, or delivers or causes to be delivered to an officer of customs any declaration, notice, certificate or other document, or makes any statement in answer to any question, or transmits any statement, document, information or record etc and such document or statement is untrue in any material particular.

43. Sub-section (2), on the other hand, makes one liable to pay any amount by reason of any such document or statement as aforesaid or by reason of some collusion any duty or charge has not been levied or has been short-levied or has been erroneously refunded and requires a notice to be served upon such person within three years of relevant date to show cause why he should not pay the amount specified therein. The proviso to sub-section (5) of section 32 describes the expression, "relevant date."

44. In view of above provisions and in the facts of the case, issue of such demand notice has got no legal basis and must be held to be ex facie bad. Moreover, none of the provisions under the section could be invoked before assessment of duty and clearance of the goods. In such view of legal position, and when the entire matter is pending for decision in this Division, issue of such demand notice must be held to be without application of mind and uncalled for, and must be ignored at the time of final assessment of the goods to duty.

45. In the result, the Rule is disposed of in the light of above observations and directions but without any costs.

46. The concerned customs authority is directed to finally assess the goods to duty in accordance with the Customs Valuation Rules, 2000 and taking into consideration of the documents/ paper(s), if any, that may be produced on behalf of the petitioner and shall return the bank guarantee (s) if the amount, if any, that becomes due after such final assessment is paid in cash within a period of two months of receipt of this order.

Communicate at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-9 (both inclusive) to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 15-3-2006 (decree signed on 22-3-2006) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Manikganj in Title Appeal No. 68 of 2005 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 28-2-2005 (decree signed on 7-3-2005) passed by the learned Assistant Judge, (in-charge), Daulatpur Court, Manikganj in Title Suit No. 135 of 2000 dismissing the suit, should not be set-aside.

2. The relevant fact giving rise to this Rule, in short, is that one Nekjan Nessa, mother of the plaintiffs purchased the suit property from Shahjahan Mollah by a registered deed on 23-4-1887 and during the survey operation of cadastral Survey, the property was wrongly recorded and published in the name of her husband namely, Riazuddin under Khatian Nos. 127, 255 and 323. After the death of Riazuddin Sheikh his son namely, Manik Mollah instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 403 of 1916 in the concerned court. One Nekjan Nesa was the defendant No. 7 in the said suit and the entire property of Nekjan Nessa made over to her by compromise decree in the said suit. One Asiruddin purchased the suit property from Nekjannesa by a registered deed dated 10-3-1917. During the survey operation of State Acquisition, the record had been recorded and published in equal share in the name of Asir Uddin and his full brother Tasir Uddin under Khatian No. 337. Tasiruddin had no right, title and interest in the portion of the suit property. Asiruddin had been possessing the entire property. The plaintiffs became the owner by succession after the death of Asiruddin. During the survey operation of revisional survey, the name of Asiruddin had been correctly recorded and published and the successors of Asiruddin had been possessing the suit property peacefully. The descendent of Taseruddin sold out the property to defendant Nos. 1-3 by a registered deed dated 3-12-1995. Thereafter, they had been threatening the plaintiffs to dispossess from the suit property and, as such, the plaintiffs instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 2 of 1996 for permanent injunction against the defendant. After receiving the show cause notice of temporary injunction, the defendants erected a Shapra (ছাপড়া) just South West portion of the suit plot and fill up the western portion by cutting earth from the east portion and raised a but on it and, as such, dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit property on 22-1-1996. Hence, the suit for declaration of title and Khan possession of the suit property.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter-alia, that Asiruddin and Taseruddin were the members of joint family and the two brothers partitioned their property between themselves. Asiruddin executed and registered a deed of relinquishment in favour of Taseruddin on 27-4-1962 and accordingly the SA record was published in the name of two brothers conjointly. Taseruddin died leaving behind two sons and three daughters. After the death of Taseruddin, his heirs instituted a partition suit being No. 169 of 1973. Asiruddin, sons of Taheruddin contested the suit together. Asiruddin made an averment in that suit that he made an oral gift of the half portion of the suit property to Nuru and Hasem. Hasem died leaving behind defendant Nos. 4-11 and the predecessor of defendant sold out 0.40 acre property to defendant Nos.1-3 on 12-12-1995. The defendant Nos. 1-3 purchased the property erected homestead and has been residing thereon. The defendant Nos. 4-8 sold out 0.80 acre on 9-3-1993. Ukil Uddin sold out that property to defendant No.3 on 8-8-1996. The defendant Nos.1-3 have been possessing the property. The plaintiff filed a Title Suit being No. 2 of 1996 praying for permanent injunction which was dismissed. The plaintiffs have not preferred any appeal and the plaintiffs were not dispossessed on 23-1-1996 and the suit of the plaintiff's would be dismissed.

4. The defendant Nos. 25, 26, 28, 40, 46 and 62 supported the plaintiff’s case and stated that the plaintiffs had been dispossessed them since 7 years by erecting but thereon. The defendants did not dispossess the plaintiffs, more so supported them.

5. The defendant Nos. 32-34 made objection against non-impleading of parties in the suit.

6. At the trial, the plaintiffs examined 5 (five) witnesses and the defendants examined 4(four) witnesses and the plaintiffs exhibited their document which were marked as exhibits 1-11. The defendants exhibited their documents which marked as Ka to Umma to prove their respective cases.

7. The learned Judge of the trial court on conclusion of trial, after hearing the parties, considering the evidence and materials on record dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 28-2-2005. Against the said judgment and decree the plaintiffs preferred appeal before the learned District Judge, Manikganj. On transfer it was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Manikganj who after hearing the parties, considering the evidence and materials on record allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court by his judgment and decree dated 15-3-2006.

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendants as petitioners approached this court and obtained the instant Rule.

9. Mr Md Haroon-ar-Rashid, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioners has placed the revisional application, pleadings, evidence, exhibits, judgment and decree of the courts below and submits that finding of the appellate court as to possession of the plaintiffs before filling title suit No. 2 of 1996 is not in accordance with law which is not sustainable in law. He submits that both the courts below failed to consider that the plaintiff has admitted the oral gift made by Asir Uddin in favour of Nuru and Hasham. He submits that both the courts below failed to discuss as regard to SA Khatian which were recorded in the name of Asir Uddin and Tasiruddin. In support of his contention he has referred the decision reported in: (1) 4 BLC 349.

10. Mr Mohammad Ali Azzam, the learned advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite-parties opposed the rule and submits that the plaintiffs have proved their case by oral and documentary evidence which were entered into evidence as ext. 1-1ka (deeds of ownership), ext. 2, RS and SA Khatian. He submits that the plaintiffs have proved their case as to possession and dispossession. He submits that trial court observed that suit land is esmali property and without partition suit it is not maintainable. In this contention he submits that there is no evidence on record as to esmali property and the appellate court on assessing the evidence correctly reversed the finding of the trial court. He submits that the learned Judge of the trial court observed that the defendant although claimed the suit property by way of oral gift from Asir Uddin but failed to prove by adducing any oral or documentary evidence against which the defendants also failed to any cross-examination as such defendant is not entitle to get any relief. He lastly submits that there is no misreading and non-consideration of evidence passed by the appellate court and the learned Judge of the appellate court considering the evidence and materials on record rightly allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the trial court and he prayed for discharged the rule. In support of his contention he has referred the decisions reported in: (1) 14 BLC (AD) 32, (2) 20 BLT (AD) 173 = 14 BLC (AD) 32.

11. In order to appreciate the submissions made by the learned advocates for the parties, I have gone through the revisional application, pleadings, evidence, exhibits and the judgment and decree of the courts below very carefully.

12. Now the question calls for consideration whether the learned Judge of the court of appeal below has committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and decree.

13. On perusal of the record it appears that the plaintiffs brought a suit for declaration of title and Khas possession. The suit land originally belong to Nekjan Nessa and Nesar Uddin who purchased the suit land by registered deed dated 23-4-1887 which were wrongly recorded in the CS record in the name of her husband Riazuddin. After death of her husband a suit being Title Suit No. 403 of 1916 was filed by her son Manik Molla in the court of 2nd Munsif, Manikgonj where Nekjan Nessa was defendant No.7. The suit was disposed of by amicable Solanama where title of Nekjan Nessa was admitted. Thereafter, Asiruddin purchased the suit land from Nekjan Nessa on 19-3-1917 by registered deed ext. 1ka. It further appears from exts. 3, 3ka SA and RS Khatian 337 that the suit land was recorded in the name of Asir Uddin the present plaintiff opposite-party become the owner and successor of the suit land.

14. On perusal of the judgment of the trial court it appears that the Judge of the trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the suit land was esmali property without specific schedule or suit for partition, the suit is not maintainable.

15. On perusal of the judgment of the trial court and the appellate court, evidence and other materials on record it appears to me that the suit land originally belong to Nekjan Nessa who sold the suit land to Asir Uddin by a single sale deed dated 19-3-1917 which were duly recorded in his name and after his death the plaintiff opposite-parties become the owner and possessor of the suit land and therefore the question does not arise to make any partition suit.

16. Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure clearly stated that where the subject matter of the suit land is immovable property, the plaint shall contain a description of the property sufficient to identify it, and, in case such property can be identified by boundaries or numbers in a record of settlement of survey, the plaint shall specify such boundaries or numbers.

17. In the instant case the suit land is well demarkable by plot numbers RS 705, SA 682 and CS 324 sixteen annas measuring of land 0.52 acres.

<u>18. The claimed of the parties cannot be refused on the mere technical ground when substance is made in the pleadings. Parties’ right to be determined when suit is filed. It is absolutely the domain and discretion of the court to grant the relief sought for or to grant any other general or other relief that may be fit and proper.</u>

<u>19. On perusal of the exhibit lka and evidence on record it appears that the suit land was purchased in the name of Asir Uddin. Therefore it appears to me that the learned Judge of the appellate court considering the evidence and materials on record and assessing the evidence rightly allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court.</u>

<u>20. Record of right is evidence of present possession and registered kabala is an evidence of title. The registered document will prevail over the records of rights and would remain in enforce until and unless, such kabala is cancelled by an appropriate civil court. The registered deed dated 19-3-1917 is an old document more than 30 years produced from proper custody presumed under section 90 of the Evidence Act that it was duly executed and genuine documents. This view find supports in the case of:</u>

<u>(1) ADC (Revenue) vs Md Reaz Uddin Pramanik, reported in 5 BLC (AD) 76, wherein their lordships held:</u>

<u>"Once a document more than 30 years old is produced from proper custody under section 90 of the Evidence Act entitles the court to presume that it is a genuine document."</u>

<u>(2) Abdul Mannan Bhuyan vs Md Nasir Hossain, reported in 18 BLC (AD) 44, wherein their lordships held:</u>

<u>"SA and RS records were not an evidence of title and that a registered document would prevail upon the records of rights and that the registered document would remain in enforce unless the same was cancelled by an appropriate civil Court."</u>

<u>(3) Lal Meah vs Haji Md Ibrahim, reported in 28 DLR (AD) 61, wherein their lordships held:</u>

<u>"The record of right raises presumption of possession in favour of person whose name is recorded therein at the time of final publication."</u>

21. On consideration of records it appears to me that findings arrived at by the court of appeal below having been rested upon considerations and discussions of the evidence and the materials on record and also on a correct and proper analysis of the legal aspect involved in the case. Moreover, impugned judgment and decree of the appellate court below in its entirety are well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case and law. Therefore, grounds urged and contentions advanced by the learned advocate for the petitioners are not correct exposition of law. However, I have gone through the decisions cited by the learned advocate for the petitioners reported in 4 BLC 439 are quite distinguishable to that of the instant case and therefore, to that effect I am also unable to accept his submissions. On the contrary the legal pleas taken by the learned advocate for opposite parties prevail and appear to have a good deal of force.

22. In view of the discussions, decisions and reasons stated above, I am of the view that impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below suffers from no legal infirmity which calls for no interference by this court in revision. Thus, I find no merit in the Rule.

23. In the result, the Rule is discharged. However, there will be no order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 15-3-2006 (decree signed on 22-3-2006) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Manikganj in Title Appeal No. 68 of 2005 allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court are hereby affirmed.

24. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Let the Lower Court Records along with a copy of the judgment be sent to the court concerned at once.

End.
