Conversely, Mr Md Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing for the pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1 (after the demise of the pre-emptor his heirs were substituted as pre-emptor-opposite party Nos. 1(a)-1(e) vehemently opposes the contention so have been advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioners and contends that, the learned Judges of the courts below have very perfectly allowed the pre-emption case finding that, all the legal requirement enumerated in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has duly been complied with leaving no reason to interfere with the concurrent judgement and order passed by the learned Judges of the courts below.

18. The learned counsel goes on to submit that, since the learned Joint District Judge, as well as the learned Senior Assistant Judge, very clearly and exhaustively discussed all the material points involved in the petition for pre-emption finding that, the pre-emption case is not barred by limitation nor it is hit by defect of parties and also it is not found to be barred by principle of waiver and acquiescence so there has been no occasion to dismiss the pre-emption proceedings.

19. The learned Counsel further submits that, since under the provision of clause (C) of section 117(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act there has been gulf of difference between separation of holding and separation of jama so mere mutating the name in the khatian by the predecessor of the present-pre-emptors will not deprive the pre-emptor to exercise his statutory right of pre-emption to pre-empt the case land.

20. The learned Counsel further submits that. though the pre-emptees in its written objection allegedly stated that, before selling 5 decimals of land in favour of the pre-emptor by Korban Ali, he had mutated his name in the khatian vide mutation case but nothing of that sort of document has ever been produced by the said pre-emptees during the process of taking evidence so it clearly shows that, the mutation proceedings so have been alleged by the pre-emptees-petitioners has got no existence in the eye of law.

21. The learned Counsel further submits that, though it is alleged by the pre-emptees that, subsequent record has been prepared in the name of the pre-emptees in respect of case land, but from the record it cannot show that, the said record has finally been published in the name of the pre-emptees so until and unless a record is finally published, in that event, is cannot be said that, the holding has been separated or it recorded in the name of the pre-emptees resulting in it cannot be held that the pre-emptees have been holding possession in separate portion of land by splitting up the holding in which the pre-emptor filed the instant pre-emption case.

22. The learned Counsel lastly submits that, since all the statutory provision of law has duly been complied with by the pre-emptor in having the case land so the courts below have very perfectly allowed the pre-emption case having no occasion to interfere with the said concurrent judgement and order.

23. Anyway, in countenance of his such submission, the learned counsel has also placed a plethora of decisions so reported in 3 ALR (AD) 58, 18 BLT 83, 36 DLR 193, 2 ALR 319, 10 BLT 104, 33 DLR (AD) 205, 35 DLR (AD) 339, 39 DLR (AD) 75, 34 DLR 274 and 44 DLR (AD) 62.

24. With such submission and relying on those decisions, the learned Counsel finally prays for discharging the Rule.

25. I have considered the submission so have been advanced by the learned Counsel for the contending parties, perused the revisions) application in particular, the grounds couched thereof, the evidence adduced by the witnesses of the contending parties, the supplementary-affidavit submitted by the pre-emptees-petitioners and other materials and evidence-on-record. On the point of limitation, there has been no dispute among the parties that from the very date of knowledge, the pre-emptor filed the pre-emption case. Insofar as regards to the point of defect of parties, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, while allowing the pre-emption case has very exhaustively discussed the evidence and came to a decision that, the pre-emptor has filed the instant case within the very statutory period of limitation from the date of knowledge and no confusion can be created by the pre-emptees-petitioners upon cross examining the pre-emptor's witnesses. So far as it relates to the point of waiver and acquiescence, it is the case of the pre-emptees-purchasers that, the vendors that is, opposite party No. 2 at first offered to transfer the case land to the pre-emptor and even the father of the pre-emptee Nos. 1-3 and the father-in-law of the opposite party No. 2, Mr Nazrul Islam also went to the house of the pre-emptors and even talked to his father but they refused to purchase the case land leading to the pre-emptees to purchase the case land.

26. However, that very fact so described in the written objection could not be substantiated by any of their witness though as many as 3 witnesses have been produced by the pre-emptees-petitioners, so the point of waiver and acquiescence as alleged by the pre-emptees cannot stand. Though on that very point, the learned Counsel for the petitioners has placed his reliance on the decision reported in 42 DLR (AD) 189 but the facts so have been described and the ratio so have been settled in that very decision is squarely different from that of the facts as has been stated in the instant case. Invariably, the said decision cannot be made applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

27. Now, only point remains, whether the pre-emptor ceased to have any right as a co-sharer by purchase to have the case land by way of purchase. It is alleged by the pre-emptees that, the vendor that is, Korban Ali before transferring 5 decimals of land infavour of the pre-emptees mutated his name in the khatian vide mutation case No. 2762 (9-1) 86/87 dated 11-11-1987 so before transferring the said case land, the khatian since has been spitted up so the pre-emptor cannot claim to be a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding. It has further been claimed by the pre-emptees that, after purchasing the case land even they also mutated their respective name in the khatian vide Mutation Case Nos. 1250, 1251 and 1252 in the year 2001 and 2002. Though there has been no mutation case number ever stated in the written objection but OPW 1 who is the father of pre-emptee purchaser No. 1 and 3 and the father in-law of the pre-emptee No. 2 has deposed that, in the month of March 2002 they got their names mutated in the khatian.

28. But curiously enough, not a scrap of paper as regards to the said mutation case infavour Korban Ali as well as the present-pre-emptees-petitioners has been produced let alone marked as exhibit by the pre-emptees while giving deposition in the case.

29. Now, for argument sake, had the vendor of the pre-emptee ever mutated his name, in that event whether the pre-emptor would have barred in exercising his right to pre-empt the case land or not. It is the contention of learned Counsel for the opposite party that, mere mutating the name in the khatian will never deprive the pre-emptor to exercise his right of pre-emption. In countenance of his submission, the learned Counsel has placed his reliance in the decision so have been reported in 3 ALR 58, which is propounded here:

Section 117(C) Sub-division of holding.

"Section 96- pre-emption of agricultural land by co-sharer or by contiguing land holder. In these cases the pre-emptees resisted the pre-emption cases on two grounds-(1) the pre-emptees after purchase of the case land have duly separated the jama of the holding and (2) the area in which the case land is situated has already been included by the Government in a municipality, thereby taking it out of the purview of section 96 of the SAT Act, 1950. The trial court accepted the contention of the pre-emptees and refused pre-emption. In revision, the High Court Division set aside the judgements of the Courts below rejecting the pleas of the pre-emptees."

30. To support that very submission, the learned Counsel for the petitioner has also placed a slew of decisions. On going through those decisions. I find that their lordship held that, if the holding is separated for paying the rent in that event, the pre-emptor will cease the right to pre-empt the case land in the said holding which is made under clause (C) of section 117(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. So, in view of those decisions it has been settled that, mere separating a jama, the pre-emptor will not be deprived to exercise his right of pre-emption.

<u>31. To substantiate that very submission, the learned Counsel has also placed his reliance in the decision reported in 18 BLT (HC) 83 where it has clearly been held that, as regards to point of law, the later decisions will always prevail over. Though in the decision reported in 3 ALR 58. the decision so have been given by the Hon'ble Appellate Division on that particular point made under section 117(C) has not been referred even though I find substance in it because in all along the subsequent decision always prevails over. And in the decision reported in 3 ALR it has vividly been discussed how a separation of jama and a separation of holding can be distinguished. Because, under the provision of clause (C) of section 117(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, if any-person wants to separate a holding, in that event several procedure has to be performed but in the process of separating a jama which is generally called mutation in the khatian an application is simply filed before the respective Tohsil Office who then refers the same to the Assistant Commissioner (land) and the Assistant Commissioner land upon performing some procedure just mutates the khatian enabling the applicant to pay the rent in respect of his portion of land by which it cannot be said that separation of holding is held. Moreover, in separating a holding there must have some procedure to be carried out by issuing notice to all the co-sharer of the case holding but nothing of this sort has ever been complied with in the instant case.</u>

<u>32. Moreover, as has been stated herein above that, not a scrap of paper has been produced by the pre-emptees in support of separating the holding by the vendor of the pre-emptor though in the written objection the pre-emptees has stated the mutation number separating the jama by the vendor of the pre-emptees named, Korban Ali but that very paper has not been produced by the pre-emptees while giving evidence before the trial court so mere making any assertion in the written objection will not suffice to prove the case of the pre-emptees in absence of any document thereof.</u>

33. In such a panorama, the learned Counsel for the opposite party has also placed a decision with regard to the dictum per curium which has been reported in 2 ALR 319. By submitting those very decisions the learned Counsel goes on to submit that, earlier decision on the point of sub-division of holding or jama has been made as a part of per in curium for which the decision reported in 3 ALR will prevail over. And in that regard, the learned Counsel has also placed his reliance on the legal dictum (per in curium) so have been reported in 10 BLT (HC) 104.

34. I have very meticulously gone through the said 2 decisions on the point of per in curium and find every substance in it.

35. Now let me asses the contention made in two supplementary-affidavits so submitted by the learned Counsel for the petitioner one, at the time of issuance of the Rule and another, on 22-11-2017. By way of first supplementary-affidavit dated 7-2-2013 the petitioners have produced two deeds dated 26-11-1997, 11-9-2001, the khatian No. 437 when the survey reached at the stage of DP and that of the field porcha (মাঠ পর্চা) with regard to khatian No. 721 appertaining to plot No. 629 stands in the name of the present pre-emptees-petitioners. By filing those documents, the learned Counsel for the petitioners tried to give emphasis on the point that, since the present khatian number is different from that of the purchased deed of the pre-emptor dated 26-11-1997 and 11-9-2001 where the recent plot number has been mentioned as 435 and 437 so the khatian has already been changed so the pre-emptor has ceased to have any right to pre-empt the case land for having enjoyed the land that fails in separate khatian. In order to give emphasis to that, the learned Counsel has also placed his reliance in DP khatian No. 437 which has also been marked as exhibit-D-1 and that of (মাঠ পর্চা) appertaining to khatian No. 721 which has been marked as Annexure-E to the supplementary-affidavit filed on 7-12-2013.

36. Anyway, I have very meticulously gone through all those documents but I don't find any iota of substance in those documents because from those documents it does not show the said khatians have finally been published in the name of the pre-emptor or that of the name of the pre-emptees. And in that regard, the learned Counsel for the opposite party has placed his reliance on the decision reported in 36 DLR 193 where it has been held that;

Section 19 and 144:—

"In absence of final publication of record-of-right as provided in section 19 and 144 there cannot be any presumption as to its correctness."

<u>37. It has already been held that, in absence of final publication of record of right as provided in section 19 and section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act there cannot be any presumption as to the correctness. In such a view, it can safely construe that, until and unless a khatian is finally published, the pre-emptee cannot claim to have separated the holding, so that very decision is squarely applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case.</u>

38. Now let me peruse other supplementary-affidavit submitted by the learned Counsel for the petitioner in which the learned Counsel for the petitioner contends that, one of the son of the pre-emptor named, Lutfe Galif Al Zahid had earlier purchased 20 decimals of land from the vendor-opposite-party, Akbar Ali on 15-7-1999 and subsequently that very purchaser retransferred the said portion of land to the vendor, Akbar Ali on 15-7-2001. By annexing that very kabala in the supplementary-affidavit dated 22-11-2017 the learned Counsel for the petitioner wanted to impress this court that, since one of the son of the pre-emptor had earlier purchased 20 decimals of land from the case plot and re-transferred the said portion of land to the vendor, so the pre-emptor had every knowledge about the disputed transfer so have been made infavour of the pre-emptee-purchaser-petitioners. That very alleged assertion taken by the learned Counsel for the petitioner does not hold any water because the pre-emption case was filed on 11-9-2001 and that very re-transfer was made on 15-7-2001 so that very retransfer does not ifso facto prove that, pre-emptor had knowledge about the subsequent transfer. In that regard, the learned Counsel for the opposite party has relied upon a decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 62 where it has been propounded that:

"Right of pre-emption—Waiver and acquiescence-Statutory right of pre-emption cannot be taken away by mere verbal assurance of person having such right, unless other facts and circumstances clearly make out a case of acquiescence or waiver."

<u>39. So from that very retransfer it cannot be proved that, the pre-emptor had negotiated the deal in transferring the case land in favour of the pre-emptees-purchasers so that very principle of waiver and acquiescence will not operate against the pre-emptor in exercising his right to have the case land through pre-emption.</u>

40. However, it has already been established by the decision of our Apex Court that, concurrent finding of facts cannot be interfered with if a grave error of law is apparent on the face of the record but in the instant case I don't find any such error ever been made by the learned Judges of the courts below while passing the impugned judgement because on the point of limitation, defect of parties, as well as very principle of waiver and acquiescence both the courts below found those legal points in favour of the pre-emptor which is based on assessing the evidence

and materials on record which remains uncontroverted by the pre-emptees-petitioners.

41. So only point is left for the pre-emptee-petitioners that, the pre-emptor has ceased to be any co-sharer in the case holding but no documents haw produced which will suffice to prove the said assertion. Because, though in the written objection the pre-emptees claimed that, before being transferred 5 decimals of land by the vendors of the pre-emptor, he mutated his name in the khatian mentioning a certain mutation case number but nothing of that sort document has been produced to that effect.

42. Moreover, it has already been decided by our Apex Court that, mere mutating the name in the khatian will not deprive or will not cease the right of the pre-emptor in exercising its statutory right of pre-emption.

43. So in view of the said decision so have been reported in 3 ALR, I am of the view that, the same is squarely applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

44. Given the above facts and circumstances and evidence and materials-on-record and the law involved in the instant case so discussed herein above, I don't find any merit in this rule.

45. The inevitable consequence that follows the Rule fails.

46. In the result, the rule is discharged, however without any order as to cost.

47. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule thus stands recalled and vacated.

Let a copy of this judgement along with the lower court records be sent to the court concerned at once.

End.

lawyer:
Dr Rajiqur Rahman with Serajur Rahman with ABM Matiur Rahman, Advocates—For the Petitioner of both the Rules. 

Sheikh Muhammad Serajul Islam, Advocate—For the Opposite-Party of both the Rules.
parties:
Abdul Majid (Md) ---------- Defendant-Petitioner 
Vs. 
Md Emdadul Haque and another --------- Plaintiff-Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Both these Civil Revision Nos. 2175 of 2006 and 2176 of 2006 have been filed by the same petitioner against the same opposite parties (spouse) and on similar contentions. Issues to be decided are also substantially similar and common questions of law are involved in both these matters. Hence, both these matters have been taken up together for disposal by a single judgment.

2. Rules have been issued in both these matter calling upon the opposite party No. 1, to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 26-4-2006 (decree signed on 4-5-2006), passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Mymensingh, in Other Class Appeal No. 182 of 2003 and in Other Class Appeal No. 183 of 2003, allowing both the appeals and reversing the judgment and decree dated 31-5-2003 (decree signed on 31-5-2003), passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Haluaghat, Mymensingh, in Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1999 and Other Class Suit No. 6 of 1999 (heard and disposed of together), should not be set-aside and/or pass such other order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. Facts, relevant for disposal of both the Rules, in brief, are that, since there were 2 (two) deeds of exchange executed by and between the same petitioner, Ext. Ka and Ka( 1), and there are two separate opposite parties (who are husband and wife), therefore, two separate suits were filed by these two opposite parties (as plaintiff), being Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1999 filed (Md Emdadul Haque, plaintiff, versus Md Abdul Majid (defendant) and the Other Class Suit No. 6 of 1999, filed by Most. Sufia Begum, wife of Md Emdadul Haque, plaintiff versus Md Abdul Majid (defendant). I have gone through the pleadings of the parties, filed in these two suits, which are in the LCR. Hence, their cases are not reproduced here. It will suffice to record here that, by a deed of exchange No. 2751 dated 12-2-1995, the defendant Md Abdul Majid and Most. Sufia Begum, wife of Md Emdadul Haque have exchanged some properties (the subject matter of Other Class Suit No. 6 of 1999) and the property described in another exchange deed No. 2752 dated 12-2-1995, were exchanged by and between Md Emdadul Haque and the same defendant Md Abdul Majid (the subject matter of Other Class Suit No. 7 of 1999).

4. The party's case as regards their respective chain of title, in respect of the suit property, has been recorded in their respective pleadings and the parties have given depositions in support of their respective cases as well as proved their documents before the trial court, which were duly marked as exhibits, forming part of the LCR along with the depositions of PWs 1 to 7 and the depositions of DWs 1-6. These are also in the lower court's record.

5. Considering the aforesaid evidence and materials on record, the trial court had decreed both the suits, mainly on the finding that, both the deeds of exchange was executed by and between the parties (two plaintiffs and the same defendant) for proper consideration. The appellate court has heard both Other Class Appeal No. 182 of 2003 and Other Class Appeal No. 183 of 2003, simultaneously, and disposed of the same by allowing both the appeals and reversing the judgments and decrees of the trial court. I have gone through both the judgments and have taken notices of the issues framed and the reasons which these judgments are based on.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgments and decrees of the Appellate Court, the defendant-respondent-petitioner filed these applications under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rules.

7. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, Mr Serajur Rahman and Mr ABM Matiur Rahman, learned Advocates, appeared on behalf of the petitioner. Mr Rafiqur Rahman mainly submits that, the petitioner acquired 70 decimals of land in RS plot Nos. 38 and 39, out of which he has given 25 decimals of land from RS plot No. 38 and 5 decimals of land from RS plot No. 39, i.e. total 30 decimals of land to plaintiff Md Emdadul Haque and also gave another 40 decimals of land from RS plot No. 38 to Most. Sufia Begum, wife of Md Emdadul Haque. Hence, both the plaintiffs, have, in exchange thereof, transferred their lands, as mentioned in the schedules to the aforesaid 2 deeds of exchange, to the defendant-respondent-petitioner. The learned Advocate further submits that, all the deeds of title of the defendant and other relevant documents were handed over by the defendant-petitioner to the plaintiffs-opposite parties for their examination and the plaintiffs were also aware of the defendant's possessions in 70 decimals of land given to them by the aforesaid 2 deeds of exchange, Ext 'Ka' and `Ka(1)'. He further submits that, there was no instance of concealment of title or possession, on the part of the defendant, as alleged by the plaintiff and that the said 2 deeds of exchange were done for good and lawful consideration as has been proved by the defendant, who has adduced oral and documentary evidences before the trial court. He next submits that the trial court has rightly dismissed the aforesaid two suits, but the appellate court has utterly failed to appreciate the evidence on record placed before it as well as it has committed grave error of law resulting in error in passing the impugned decisions, occasioning failure of justice, by holding that, the defendant had no perfect title in the suit property given to the plaintiff by the aforesaid 2 deeds of exchange, since the name of Jotindra Mohan Sarker has not been recorded in the SA khatian, therefore, the seller and all the previous sellers (via) of the defendant had derived no title in the concerned SA plots. The contention of the learned Advocate on this issue is that, mere omission of name of the original owner Jotindra Mohan Sarker in the SA khatian was not legally material to decide the title of the defendant or of the previous owners, who acquired title through Jotindra Mohan, inasmuch as the record of right is not a documents of title. Moreover, both the plaintiffs, being aware of the title and possession of the defendant in the property exchanged for, had exchanged their respective properties by executing 2 deeds of exchange and, by this time, the defendant, after deriving the property acquired by him through the said deeds of exchange, has already constructed his homestead on the property given to him in exchange and is living there with his family members. Therefore, he also submits that, in the given facts and circumstances, the findings of the appellate court amounts to misreading and non-reading of the facts and misinterpretation of law. He next submits that, khatian No. 103 of Mouza Kismot Norail records 60 decimals of lands in the name of Kasem Ali, from whom the defendant derived his title and possession in that 60 decimals of land. However, he has frankly admitted that this is an un-partitioned joint property of Kasem Ali, with other co-sharers. He lastly submits that, the impugned judgments of the appellate court are liable to be set aside and these Rules merit to be made absolute.

8. Learned Advocate Mr Sheikh Muhammad Serajul Islam has appeared on behalf of the opposite parties in both the maters. His main contention is that, the appellate court has properly assessed the evidence on record, facts and circumstances of these cases and has properly decided the issues of law and facts in the circumstances of these cases. He further submits that, the defendant has deliberately concealed the fact that, name of Jotindra Mohan Sarker was not recorded in SA khatian No. 223 and, as such, the defendant and his previous buyers (via), from which he claims to have derived title in the property exchanged, had no title in that property. He seriously argued that, the deeds of the defendant as well as the deed of the preceding buyers (via), who have claimed title with reference to the title of Jotindra Mohan Sarker, is absolutely defective, clouded and none of the previous buyers or the defendant had acquired any saleable title in the property transferred by the defendant. The defendant, he proceeds on, having suppressed the fact and having misled the plaintiff, had succeeded to deceive and obtain their consent in getting the two impugned deeds of exchange executed by the plaintiffs. He also submits that, a mere perusal of the impugned deeds of exchange, respectively marked as Ext. 1 and 1(Ka), will show that there is no specific schedule of the property, nor any boundary, which the defendant claims to have purchased and then transferred to the plaintiff in consideration of the property given to him by the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate points out that, transfer of property necessarily implies transfer of specific immovable property, which is lacking in these two deeds of exchange, so far as the 70 decimals of land claimed and purportedly exchanged by the defendant is concerned. Moreover, it is an admitted position that name of Jotindra Mohan Sarker does not appear in SA khatian No. 223 (Ext. 3) of Mouza Kismot Norail, PS Haluaghat, District Mymensingh, while names of Rajanikanta Saha, Sarat Chandra and Surendra Mohan Saha sons of Bhabani Proshad Saha have been recorded as 16 annas owners of land at SA plot Nos. 38 and 39 (which the defendant claims to have owed and transferred by the said two deeds of exchange). So, he submits, nothing was left in this 16 annas of land for Jotindra Mohan Sarker to transfer to anybody in the SA khatian No. 233 (Ext. 3) or in SA plot No. 38 and 39. Moreover, even the defendant himself did not take any step claiming or for declaration that, he is the title holder of 70 decimals of land at SA plot Nos. 38 and 39, nor he has taken any step to rectify or to open any mutation khatian or separation of jamabhagh in his name, pursuant to his title deed, nor he has paid any rent (Khajna) in respect of these 70 decimals of land. In these circumstances, he further submits, the finding of the appellate court that, the claim of the plaintiff side cannot be ruled out that Jotindra Mohan Sarker had no ownership over the property of plot No. 38 at the time of transferring to Kasem Ali on 27-12-1972, is very much based on admitted facts and document. Therefore, the learned Advocate concludes that, in passing the impugned judgment and decree, the appellate court has committed no error of law and, as such, these Rules have no merit and the same are liable to be discharged.

9. I have heard the learned Advocates for both sides, perused the application for revision, lower Court's record as well as the judgment of both the Courts below and other materials in the record.

10. I find that, the appellate court has properly assessed the evidence on record, facts and circumstances and the issues as well as it has independently assessed and decided the issues of law and facts, in the facts and circumstances of these cases.

11. Whether the defendant had deliberately concealed or not, the fact remains that, name of Jotindra Mohon Sarker was not recorded in SA khatian, No. 223 and that, the 16 (sixteen) annas of land in SA plot Nos. 38 and 39 (from which the defendant petitioner has purported to have transferred 70 decimals of land to the plaintiffs through the said two deeds of exchange) are recorded in the names of Rajanikanta Saha, Sarat Chandra and Surendra Mohan Saha sons of Bhabani Proshad Saha. Therefore, I find that, nothing beyond that 16 annas left for Jotindra Mohan Sarker, in the said property, to transfer to Kasem Ali or any other persons claiming Jotindra Mohan or Kasem Ali, by way of purchase or otherwise. The appellate court has, therefore, rightly found that, "It appears from the certified copy of the SA khatian No. 223 (Ext. 3) that the name of Jotindra Mohan Sarker was not recorded in SA khatian. Although Jotindra Mohan Sarker was one of the 4 purchasers on the strength of deed dated 21-3-1945 AD but his name was not recorded in SA khatian. Had Jotindra Mohan Sarker had any ownership over the property of plot No. 38 at the time of SA operation then his name would be included in the SA khatina No. 223 or any other khatian. As such, the claim of the plaintiff side cannot be ruled out that Jotindra Mohan Sarker had no ownership over the property of plot No. 38 at the time of transferring to Kasem Ali on 27-12-1972." This finding of the Appellate Court is very much based on admitted and proved facts and documents. Besides, the further findings of the appellate court to the effect that, " It appears from the evidence on record that, although Jotindra Mohan Sarker has sold out 50 decimal lands to Kasem Ali, but he had no visible ownership over that land as the SA record of the property was not prepared in his name. So, the title of Jotindra Mohan Sarker over the lands of plot No. 38 was defective and the transfer for 50 decimals land from plot No. 38 did not confer Kasem Ali any title over that property. Since the land of plot No. 38 was not recorded in the name of Jotindra Mohan Sarker then it is very natural that Jotindra Mohan Sarker had no ownership over the land of plot No. 38 at the time SA operation", are also based on the oral and documentary evidences as well as on the admitted facts.

12. 1, therefore, find that, the deed of the defendant as well as the deed of his preceding buyers (via), namely, Rajanikanta Saha, Sarat Chandra and Surendra Mohan Saha, who claimed to have derived title with reference to the title of Jotindra Motion Sarker and Kasem Ali is absolutely defective, clouded and neither of their deeds does confer any perfect title to the defendant or to his preceding buyers (via). The defendant even did not take any step, in such a situation, to get any declaration of title in respect of 70 decimals of land claimed and purportedly exchanged by him, with the plaintiffs, nor he has obtained any mutation khatian in his name, nor he has separated any Jama, nor he has paid any land development tax (khajna), nor he could mention any specific property in schedule to the disputed deeds of exchange, namely Ext. 1 and Ext. 1(Ka). I am also of the opinion that, the facts and circumstances of this case leads me to drawing an inference that the defendant, having suppressed these material facts and having mislead the plaintiffs, had succeeded to obtain their consent by practicing fraud in getting the two impugned deeds of exchange executed by them (the plaintiffs).

13. Besides, a mere perusal of the impugned deeds of exchange, marked as Ext. 1 and 1(Ka), shows that there is no specific boundary of the property which the defendant asserts to have acquired title by purchase and then transferred to the plaintiffs in consideration of the property transferred to him by the plaintiffs in the said two deeds of exchange.

14. The transfer of property necessarily implies transfer of title, interest and possession in an specific immovable property (identifiable with reference to plot number, khatian number, mouza, police station and district and specific boundary, which is lacking in these two deeds of exchange, namely Ext. 1 and 1(Ka), so far as the property of the defendant-respondent is concerned.

<u>15. The essence of the transfer of the immovable property is that, the property should be specific and identifiable with reference to the quantum of land, related khatian and plot number, Mouza, Police Station and District and having a specific boundary. In the absence of any specification of the property in the schedule of the said two deeds of exchange, the same does not confer, to the plaintiff-opposite party, any title and possession in any specific immovable property. Therefore, the disputed deeds of exchange are bound to fail and be scrapped for lack of any lawful consideration, disregard of the fact whether defendant has done anything on the property taken from the plaintiff in exchange of lands on which he has no clear title, which is not identifiable and for which he even did not pay any khajna.</u>

16. The fraudulent conduct of the defendant and his dishonesty are apparent from his previous and the subsequent conducts. Not only he abstained from getting his title declared or created any separate khatian and Jamabhag, he even did not pay any rent of the land purportedly exchanged by him as against the lands of the plaintiffs. So, all these illegalities shall be undone at the cost of the defendant within the time specified by the court of appeal.

17. Such type of deed of exchange without any specification and clear title in the property exchanged will lead to multiplicity of the proceeding, if this court encourages them and will cause serious hardship to the victim party.

18. Therefore, in passing the impugned judgments by the appellate court, it has committed no error of law, and as such, none of these Rules have any merit and the same are liable to be discharged.

19. In the result, both these Rules are hereby discharged.

20. The impugned judgment and decree dated 26-4-2006 (decree signed on 4-5-2006), passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Mymensingh in Other Class Appeal No. 182 of 2003 and Other Class Appeal No. 183 of 2003, are hereby upheld.

21. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

22. No costs.

Let a copy of this judgment along with the Lower Court's Records be sent down to the concerned Courts at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md Abdul Awal with Jagadish Chandra Sarker Advocates—For the Appellants. 

Bhabesh Chandra Sarker, DAG—For the Respondents.
parties:
Nipendra Chandra Sarker and others --------- Appellants
Vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Kashefa Hussain J : This appeal is directed against judgment and decree dated 12-11-2013 (decree signed on 17-11-2013) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 65 of 2009 dismissing the suit.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the appeal inter alia is that the instant appellants as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 65 of 2009 in the court of learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka praying for declaration of title and further praying for that the RS khatian No. 4356 in the schedule property was wrongly recorded in the name of government as “হাল সাং ভারত পক্ষে বাংলাদেশ সরকার” and therefore not binding upon the plaintiffs.

3. The plaintiff's case as stated in the plaint in short is that the schedule suit land originally belonged to one Mohin Chandra Gope who was the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiffs and that he was the CS recorded owner and that his name was recorded in the CS khatian No. 2461, dag No. 425 amounting to a property of 678 decimals of land which was subsequently inherited by his 5 (five) sons. In course of time the property devolved upon the 5 sons of the original CS recorded owner Mohin Chandra Gape. Among the 5 (five) sons 2 (two) were childless. The property, devolved upon the heirs in accordance with the relevant laws. Consequently a nephew being their sister's son named Narayan Chandra Gope inherited the shares of the 2 (two) childless brothers namely Darika Nath Gope and Godadhor Gope in proportion to the amount of his shares accordingly to the applicable law. Another brother Meghu Lal Gope being childless died leaving behind his wife Sreemoti Krishno Dasi Gope as his rightful heir. And the property was proportionally recorded in their names. Ultimately the heirs of the CS recorded owner sold the scheduled suit land through 3 (three) different kabala deeds dated 16-6-1978, 23-5-1978 and 24-5-1978 to Sree Otul Chandra Sarker and the father of the plaintiffs. In pursuance Sree Otul Chandra Sarker and the father of the plaintiffs by dint of the 3 (three) different kabala deeds became owner of 443 decimals of land and accordingly enjoyed possession of the land upon duly mutating “নামজারী ও জমাভাগ), due payment of taxes etc. The VP tohshilder upon examining the documents and the census list issued a statement that the property is not a vested property and is not listed as being such. Meanwhile Sree Otul Chandra Sarker transferred a proportion of his property to his son Omal Chandra Sarker through a registered kabala deed on 16-6-1978. Accordingly Sree Otul Chandra Sarker and Omal Chandra Sarker while holding title and in possession of the property sold 551/4 decimals of land to one Hazi Abdul Samad Sayyal by a registered deed dated 29.06.1983 and on the same date that is 29-6-1983 they sold 551/4 decimals of land to one Abdul Hamid Sayyal by registered deed No. 4510. Subsequently, on 16-8-1983 Abdul Samad Sayyal and Abdul Hamid Sayyal sold their land through 6 (six) several registered deeds to the plaintiffs No. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 respectively. Accordingly the plaintiffs Nos. 1-6 in the present suit became owners of 0.0221 decimals of land by dint of purchase and obtained possession of the same. Accordingly the plaintiffs' father Upendra Chandra Sarker held title and was in possession of 0.0221 decimals of land and his 6 (six) sons were holding title and possession of another 0.0221 decimals of land and while continuing as such the plaintiffs duly completed mutation in their name at the concerned revenue office of the Government by mutation (নামজারী ও জমাভাগ) case No. 2425/84-85 dated 29-1-1985 and accordingly paid taxes being owners of the suit land partly by purchase and partly by inheritance amounting to 0.0442 decimals of land and have been residing in the said land with their families upon constructing house, paying taxes etc. While continuing possession of the suit land the plaintiff No. 1 on 5-1-2009 went to the local office of the AC land for purpose of paying taxes. And thereupon the AC land office informed the plaintiffs that the SA record is duly prepared in their names. But the AC land office however refused to accept taxes since the RS was recorded in the name of the Government. On 5-1-2009 the plaintiffs for the first time discovered that the suit land was wrongly RS recorded in the name of the Government and consequently the addresses of the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs were wrongly inserted as “হাল সাং ভারত পক্ষে বাংলাদেশ সরকার” Upon discovery of this wrong record on 5-1-2009 the cause of action to file the suit arose on that date. The plaint further stated that the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiffs had sold the suit land through registered deeds on different dates and the predecessor-in-interest had not left for India prior to the plaintiffs' purchase of the suit land. The plaint also stated that the suit land is not listed in the census list in the name of the Government. And the government was never in possession of such nor did the government ever grant the suit land in lease to any person. The plaint also stated that pursuant to the mutation and the name of the plaintiffs being correctly recorded in the Dhaka City Jorip, the defendants-government filed an appeal under Rule 31 of the Bengal Tenancy Rules, 1955 before the concerned Assistant Settlement Appeal Officer. Upon hearing of appeal, it was dismissed to the effect that the judgment and order of dismissal of the Appeal consequently went in favour of the plaintiffs and the enlisting of record in the plaintiff's name in the City Jorip was thereby affirmed and which was correctly printed as a gazetted khatian in the Dhaka City Jorip Khatian No. 7203. It was also stated in the plaint that although the wrong recording of the RS record as “হাল সাং ভারত পক্ষে বাংলাদেশ সরকার” which amounts to recording the government of Bangladesh as owner in the suit land, however does not create any impediment in the title and interest of the plaintiffs but yet such wrong R.S record in the name of the government has cast a cloud upon the title of the plaintiffs. And hence the suit.

4. The defendant Nos. 1-3 entered appearance by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made against them. Defendants inter alia stated in the written statement that the SA recorded owner had left for India during 1965 and they have never transferred the property to any person. The written statement further alleged that the predecessor of the plaintiff's upon collusion and fraudulent means created some forged deed and other documents. They further claimed in the written statement that since the SA record during 1966-1975, the RS recorded owner could not be found anywhere in the country and therefore the suit land was correctly enlisted as a vested property of the government and was correctly recorded in the RS record as “হাল সাং ভারত পক্ষে বাংলাদেশ সরকার”.

5. Four issues were framed in the suit for points of determination, 6(six) witnesses deposed from the plaintiff's side while 1 (One) witness deposed from the defendant's side in the title suit.

6. The plaintiffs produced 23 exhibits during trial while the defendants produced none.

7. Mr. Md. Abdul Awal, Advocate along with Mr. Jagadish Chandra Sarker, Advocate appeared on behalf of the appellants while the respondents were represented by learned DAG Mr. Bhabesh Chandra Sarker.

8. Learned Advocate Mr. Md. Abdul Awal appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs-appellants submits that the trial court upon total non application of mind unjudiciously and incorrectly dismissed the suit. He contends that the trial court failed to consider the several deeds and documents produced before it as exhibits. He contends that inspite of most of the original deeds except 2 (two) as exhibits but even those two being later authenticated by two of the PWs being employees of the registered office, yet the trial court did not even take these material factors into any consideration. He argues that the trial court did not even apply its mind to the fact that the suit land does not appear anywhere in the list of vested property. He elaborates his submission upon assertion that following the appeal under Rule 31 of the Bengal Tenancy Rules the appeal which was made by the defendants-government, before the relevant authority, the Assistant Settlement Appeal officer dismissed the appeal against the defendants and in favour of the plaintiffs followed by the plaintiffs name being correctly recorded in the Dhaka city Jorip upon publication as a gazetted khatian, yet the trial court turned a blind eye to such material factors. He further contends that the trial court did not even consider the deposition made by the PWs and failed to appreciate another material factor that the defendants-government could not produce any documents in support of their claim to title. He reiterates his contention that contrary to the defendants-government's claims as the property being a vested property and in support of their reliance upon the RS being recorded as “হাল সাং ভারত পক্ষে বাংলাদেশ সরকার” however the defendants failed to produce any documents which could even indicate that the suit land is a vested property of the government nor could the defendants show their title to the suit land through any other documents. The learned Advocate further asserts that the trial court arrived upon its finding upon conjecture and surmise and upon non reliance of any material evidence nor did it discuss the deposition made by the PWs. He further continues that the trial court arrived upon a wrong filing that the suit is barred by limitation and dismissed the appeal upon an incorrect finding. Controverting the trial court's finding on the point of limitation he contends that the suit was filed within time in as much as that the cause of action arose on 5-1-2009 when the plaintiff No. 1 went to the A.0 land office and the suit was filed on 15-2-2009. Therefore the suit was filed well within the statutory time. In support of his submissions on the point of limitation he cites two decisions before us one in the case of Bangladesh vs AKM Abdul Hye reported in 56 DLR (AD) 53 and another decision in the case of Abdul Hafez vs Lal Meah reported in 1988 BLD 497. Upon reliance on his assertion and the deposition of the witnesses, evidences placed as exhibits and the other materials on record, he concludes his submissions upon reiteration that the judgment and decree of the trial court does not comprise of legal or factual basis and ought to be set aside and the appeal ought to be allowed for ends of justice.

9. Learned DAG Mr. Bhabesh Chandra Sarker opposes the appeal. He however in his submissions failed to show anything from the records or the judgment that could lead to any proof that the property is a vested property of the government or that the government in any manner is the rightful owner of the suit land. He however submits that the trial court correctly dismissed the suit on the point of limitation given that the RS record was prepared as “হাল সাং ভারত পক্ষে বাংলাদেশ সরকার” long before the filing of the suit.

10. We have heard the learned Advocates from both sides, perused all materials on records including the judgment of the court below and the deposition of the witnesses from both sides. The plaintiffs produced 23 exhibits which include the kabala deeds and other relevant documents while the defendants failed to produce any documents at all in support of their claims. From perusal of the judgment it transpires that regrettably the trial court did not consider some vital factors which also included the deposition of the PWs. It also transpires that in absence of any documents or any other credible evidence the trial court arrived upon a presumption based on its own conjecture and surmise that the kabala deeds might have been created as a result of "false personation". But however the trial court did not in its finding make any attempt to explain or otherwise analyse the basis of its presumption.

11. It is an admitted fact that the CS recorded original owner was Mohin Chandra Gope and upon examination in the various exhibits and the other materials before us it appears that the plaintiffs-appellants before us based their claims to title and possession in the suit land partly by dint of purchase and partly by inheritance mainly relying upon various kabala deeds earlier executed by the predecessors-in-interest and subsequently by the plaintiffs themselves. It is also an admitted fact that the SA record was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs. The trial court in its finding made an observation that 2 (two) of the original deeds were not placed before the trial court by the plaintiffs during trial as exhibits. It observed that the original of 2 deeds being deed No. 22341 dated 23-5-1978 and deed No. 11510 dated 16-6-1978 were not produced before the trial court. But the trial court however ignored or overlooked a vital material factor that the rest of the kabala deeds were produced in its original. Furthermore from the deposition of the PW 4 (record keeper) it appears that the PW 4 has during his deposition certified the authenticity of the deed No. 21268 dated 16-6-1978 including the authenticity of others deeds. The trial court also made an observation that the name of the sister of Darika Nath Gope and Godadhor Gope is not mentioned anywhere in the plaint. We may presume that the trial court evidently made this observation indicating or rather questioning the existence of the nephew Narayan Chandra Gope who was the heir of Dharika Nath Gope and Godha Dhor Gope since they were childless.

12. In our opinion the name of the mother of Narayan Chandra Gope being the sister of Dharika Nath Gope and Godha Dhor Gope is not a vital factor for deciding the issues before us since we are here placing our reliance on the various deeds executed by the plaintiffs' predecessor-in-interest which have been produced as exhibits and furthermore we are placing our reliance on the various exhibits produced before the court showing rent receipt, taxes etc. in support of the possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. Furthermore we have noticed that the trial court did not take a relevant fact into consideration which we find necessary to take into consideration to arrive at a correct finding, that being exhibit-7, the certified copy of judgment of the appeal case No. 38110 of 2001 filed under Rule 31 of the Bangal Tenancy Rule, 1955 filed by the defendant before the Assistant Settlement Appeal Officer. It is evident from this decision that the listing of the Dhaka City Jorip was correctly recorded in the name of plaintiff's appellants. Exhibit 7 is the material evidence that the listing of the plaintiff's name in the City Jorip was later affirmed upon appeal.

13. We have perused the deposition of the PW 1 being plaintiff No. 2 in the suit. From the deposition of the PW 1 it transpires that he has in his depositions more or less corroborated the statements made in the plaint. Furthermore, he has also referred to the several exhibits in support of his claim including the deeds, namjari, rent receipt, judgment of the appeal case No. 38110 of 2001. PW1 also deposed that the cause of action arose only on 5-1-2009 for the first time upon going to the office of the relevant authorities for the purpose of of payment of taxes. PW1 deposed that on that date the plaintiffs for the first time discovered that the RS was wrongly recorded as “হাল সাং ভারত পক্ষে বাংলাদেশ সরকার”. From the deposition of the PWs 2 and 3 who are kind of neighbours of the plaintiffs, it appears that the deposition of the PWs 2 and 3 are consistent upon the question of possession of the plaintiffs. The PWs 4, 5 and 6 who are the assistant record keepers respectively being government employees, it appears from their deposition that they have authenticated and affirmed the genuinity of the deeds and further positively stated that the various numbers in the volume "(বালাম বই)" and that of the various deeds are the same. We are inclined to opine that the deposition of PWs No. 5 and 6 indicate that there is no inconsistency between the numbers in the list and the deeds pertaining to the suit land and that the deeds are genuine deeds. Conversely DW 1 being land sub-assistant officer of the concerned office deposes that the suit land is a "vested" property and that the original owner left for India many years ago. However the DW 1 failed to produce any documents in support of his claim that the suit land is vested property of the government. Rather in his cross examination he deposes that: “নালিশা জমি সেনসাস তালিকায় আছে কিনা জানা নাই। নালিশা জমির VP দাগ আছে কিনা জানা নাই। সরকার এই জমি লিজ দিয়েছে কিনা বলতে পারবো না।” Such inconsistency between his deposition and the statement upon cross-examination amounts to controverting the defendant's-government's claim to title in the suit land.

<u>14. It is also quite clear from the records that no documents whatsoever were produced by the defendants at any stage nor was the suit land ever listed as a vested property. On the other hand it is evident from the record that plaintiffs appellants produced several deeds and other supporting evidences being rent receipts, taxes etc. including several other documents in support of their claim to title and possession. The trial court while basing its finding mainly upon surmise and conjecture however dismissed the suit on the ground of being barred by limitation. But it is our considered finding that from the records and the materials before us, it appears that the cause of action arose on 5-1-2009 when the plaintiff had gone to the concerned local office to pay taxes.</u>

15. Learned Advocate for the appellant at one point during his submissions made averments that the cause of action arose only on 5-1-2009 when one of the plaintiffs went to the local tahsil office and for the first time discovered the wrong RS record as “হাল সাং ভারত পক্ষে বাংলাদেশ সরকার” in favour of the defendants-government. Controverting the contention of the defendant-respondent the learned Advocate for the appellant agitates that the suit is not barred by limitation since the cause of action rose on 5-1-2009 and the suit was filed on 15-2-2009 and which is well within time. He further relied upon two decisions, one in the case of Bangladesh vs AKM Abdul Hye reported in 56 DLR (AD) 53. The principle enunciated in that decision of our Apex court is reproduced below:

"Against the wrong record-of-rights the person whose interest is affected is required to file the suit seeking declaration of title within six years from the date the person in whose name record has been wrongly prepared and finally published, raises claim on the basis of wrong record."

16. In the other case relied upon by the appellants being the case of Abdul Hafez vs La1 Meah reported in 1988 BLD 497 where the principle relied upon is also reproduced here-under:

"Suit for declaration of title-Question of starting point for limitation- The plaintiff is not bound to institute a suit for declaration that the entry in the record of rights is wrong —He can wait and sue when invasion on his right is made—Limitation Act (IX of 1908) Article 120".

17. We have perused both the decisions and we are in respectful agreement with those including the decision of our Apex court which needless to state is binding upon us. We are inclined to apply the same principle to the case before us and which is relevant for our purpose. We are also of the considered view that the plaintiffs-appellants filed the suit well within time when they first gained knowledge of the invasion into their right. On 5-1-2009 they also learnt that the record has been wrongly prepared and such wrong record gave rise to their cause of action. We are also inclined to observe that the Trial Court's observation and raising doubt on the genuinity of the deeds based on conjecture and surmise and particularly its observation that the deeds were created upon "false impersonation" are inappropriate and unwarranted in as much as that it did not even make any attempt to analyse nor in any other manner tried to explain the basis of its conclusions. Upon an overall appraisal of all materials it is our considered finding that the defendants failed to hopelessly establish their claim with any supporting documentary evidences and their claim of the suit land being "vested" property could not be proved by any supporting evidence.

18. As mentioned elsewhere in the judgment deposition of the DW1 suffers from considerable inconsistency. While on the other hand the plaintiffs-appellants established and vindicated their claim upon production of several relevant documents as exhibits in the form of the various kabala deeds, rent receipt, taxes etc. Relying upon the principles in the two decisions cited by the learned Counsel for appellant it is also our considered view that the plaintiffs-appellants filed the suit well within the statutory time and are as such not barred by limitation.

19. Therefore under the facts and circumstances, relying upon the discussions made above and taking into consideration all materials on record before us and the submissions of the learned Counsels, the decisions relied upon and the applicable laws, we find merit in the appeal.

20. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and decree dated 12-11-2013 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 65 of 2009 is hereby set aside.

Send down the lower court records at once.

Communicate this judgment and order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mizanul Haque Chowdhury with Hassan Mohammad Reyad Advocates—For the Appellant 
Pratikar Chakma, DAG—For the Respondent.
parties:
Mohammad Hanif --------- Appellant
Vs.
Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka, and others ---------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J : This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 7-8-2016 passed by the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka, respondent No. 1 herein.

2. Brief facts are that the appellant as importer in course of his business opened Letter of Credit No. 086215010070 dated 26-1-2015 for importation of 18 Metric Ton Areca Nut with shell at the rate of US$ 0.23/Kg and Areca Nut without shell at the rate of US$ 0.43/Kg from Indonesia under HS Code No. 0802.80.90. After arrival of the consignment at Chittagong port, the importer through his C & F agent submitted bill of entry No. C-14176 dated 5-7-2015 for releasing the goods on payment of duties and taxes as per declaration. Customs Authority conducted 100% physical examination of the consignment and found the same in order as per declaration. Since the importer procured import permit from the plant protection wing of the agriculture directorate to import Betel Nut, Customs Authority sent sample of the imported goods to the Bangladesh Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (hereinafter called 'the BCSIR') to ascertain whether Betel Nut and Areca Nut are same product or not. After examination, the BCSIR delivered test report with following observation:

"FAO Corporation document Repository হইতে প্রাপ্ত Areca Nut composition এর সহিত তুলনা করিলে দেখা যায় যে, সরবরাহকৃত পণ্য দুইটির খাদ্য গুনাগুন অক্ষুন্ন আছে।

(খ)সরবরাহকৃত পণ্য দুইটির সরাসরি খাওয়ার যোগ্য নয়। Areca Nut (with husk) পণ্যটি হইতে প্রথমে husk ছাড়িয়ে শক্ত Areca Nut বাহির হইতে হইবে। শক্ত Areca Nut কে বিভিন্ন processing (air and water cleaning, drying, slicing etc.) এর মাধ্যমে slice এ রুপান্তরিত করে খাওয়ার (chewing) উপযোগী করিতে হইবে। বাংলাদেশ, ভারত, চায়না, ভিয়েতনাম, ফিলিপিন, ইন্দোনেশিয়া এবং মালয়েশিয়ার লোকজন শত বৎসর যাবৎ  Areca Nut slice পণ্যের সহিত অথবা খালি slice চুষে (chewing) খেয়ে আসতেছে এবং কোন নিষিদ্ধ ক্ষতিকারক দ্রব্য পাওয়া যায় নাই। পণ্যটি বিশ্লেষনে ক্ষতিকারক ধাতব পরিমান গ্রহনযোগ্য মাত্রার মধ্যে থাকায় ক্ষতিকর সম্ভাবনা কম।

(গ)Areca nut and Betel Nut একই।”

3. On the basis of report, Customs Authority changed classification of the imported goods to HS Code No. 0802.90.19 from declared H.S Code 0802.80.90 and imposed supplementary duty at the rate of 30%. The assessing authority deter-mined value of Areca nut without shell at the rate of US$ 1.35/kg and value of Areca nut with shell at the rate of US$ 1.00/Kg on the basis of data base as approved by the assessment committee and the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, ICD Kamlapur, respondent No. 2 herein, ignoring the invoice value. Being aggrieved by the arbitrary change of HS Code and determination of value by the customs authority, the importer as appellant filed appeal before the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal. After admission of the appeal, Tribunal passed an interim order allowing the appellant to release the imported goods on the basis of provisional assessment paying duties and taxes in cash as per declared value and HS Code and furnish a Bank Guarantee for the difference of duties and taxes determined by the customs authority. The appellant released the goods pursuant to order of the Tribunal.

4. After hearing the parties and perusing the papers/documents, Tribunal dismissed the appeal vide its judgment and order dated 7-8-2016.

5. Having aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order, the importer preferred instant customs appeal under section 196D of the Customs Act, 1969.

6. Mr. Mizanul Haque Chowdhury, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that the Tribunal committed illegality in passing the impugned judgment and order without considering that though the customs authority on 100% physical examination found the goods as per declaration but arbitrarily changed HS Code of the goods for the purpose of imposing supplementary duty as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. To elaborate his argument, learned Advocate submits that First Schedule of Bangladesh Customs Tariff provides separate customs classification of Areca Nut and Betel Nut under HS Code No. 0802.80.90 and 0802.80.19 respectively fixing customs duty for both the product @ 25% but through Finance Act, 2015, substituted 3rd schedule of the VAT Act, 1991, imposing supplementary duty for the Product 'Betel Nut' against HS Code No. 0802.90.11 and 0820.90.19 at the rate of 30% wherefrom it is clear that no supplementary duty imposed on the product `Areca Nut'. He also submits that Tribunal came to a wrong finding discarding provisions of the Value Added Tax relating to imposition of supplementary duty inasmuch as 3rd schedule of the VAT Act impose supplementary duty for the product described as fresh or dried nuts, without shell or with shell, against HS Code Nos. 0202.90.19 and 0202.90.19 respectively but declared HS Code of the appellant is 0802.80.90 as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. He again submits that the customs authority arbitrarily determined value of the goods ignoring declared value without recording a finding that the value declared by appellant is not the actual transaction value and the value declared to evade revenue in connivance with the buyer and seller but the Tribunal without considering this factual and legal aspect passed the impugned judgment and order which is liable to be set aside. He next submits that the Tribunal committed illegality in not holding that customs authority determined the value arbitrarily without following provision of the Valuation Rules and as such the judgment and order is liable to be set aside. He further submits that the customs authority without affording an opportunity to the appellant to provide evidence in support of invoice value arbitrarily imposed inflated value approved by so-called assessment committee beyond the scope of law and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. In support of his submissions, learned Advocate referred to the case of Collector of Customs vs TK Oil Refinery Ltd. and 22 others, reported in 62 DLR (AD) 217 and two unreported judgments passed in Writ Petition No.6428 of 2001 (the case of Mohammad Mohazid Jamil vs Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong,) and Writ Petition No.1791 of 2014 (the case of Mrinal Lal Dhar vs Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong and others).

7. On the other hand, Mr. Pratikar Chakma learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the respondent No. 2 submits that customs authority rightly determined value of the goods since the appellant obtained permission from the plant protection wing of Agriculture Department for importing Betel Nut and the BCSIR on chemical examination found that 'Areca Nut' and `Betel Nut' are same product and as such there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and order. He also submits that customs authority assessed the goods on the basis of data base value which is correctly affirmed by the Tribunal as such the appeal is liable to be dismissed.

8. Heard learned Advocate for the appellant and learned Deputy Attorney-General for the respondent No. 2. Perused the paper book, additional paper book and relevant papers/documents contained therein.

9. It appears that the appellant imported Areca Nut with shell and without shell under HS Code No. 0802.80.90 at the rate of US$ 0.23/kg and US$ 0.43/kg respectively from Indonesia. Customs authority assessed the goods changing classification of the goods from HS Code No. 0802.80.90 to HS Code No. 0802.90.19 and thereby imposed supplementary duty at the rate of 30% and also determined inflated value of the goods ignoring invoice value. It may be mentioned here that customs authority conducted 100% physical verification of the goods and found the same in order as per declaration. In changing classification of the goods, customs authority noted that though in all the commercial documents the imported goods are described as Areca Nut but the importer obtained import permit from the plant protection wing of agriculture department for importation of Betel Nut and as such sample of the goods sent to the BCSIR for examination whether both the `Areca Nut' and 'Betel Nut' are same product or not. The BCSIR after examination delivered test report with the following comments:

(গ)Areca nut and Betel Nut একই।

10. On the basis of said report, customs authority imposed supplementary duty at the rate of 30% clanging HS Code of the goods.

11. We have perused relevant provisions of the Value Added Tax Act relating to imposition of supplementary duty for the goods and service described in the 3rd schedule of the Act. It appears that 30% supplementary duty imposed against HS Code No. 0802.90.11 and 0802.90.19 respectively describing the goods “তাজা বা শুকনা সুপারি, খোসা ছাড়ানো হউক বা না হউক।”

12. In the First Schedule, the Product "Betel Nut" described against HS Code No. 0802.90.11 and 0802.90.19 respectively but the Product `Areca Nut' wrapped/canned upto 2.5 kg described against HS Code No. 0802.80.10 and the word 'other' mentioned against HS Code No. 0802.80.90 under the description of the product `Betel Nut'. From the description of First Schedule as stated above, it appears that imposition of supplementary duty by the customs authority on the imported product `Areca Nut' is not justifiable inasmuch as if the legislature had intention to impose supplementary duty on the product `Areca Nut' then the HS Code No. 0802.80.90 classified against the product can be placed in the 3rd schedule of VAT Act. From the First Schedule it is apparent that 'Areca Nut' and `Betel Nut' are classified under different HS Code describing both the product separately. Rule 3(c) of General Rules for the Interpretation of the Harmonized System as contained in the First Schedule runs as follows:

"When goods cannot be classified by reference to 3(a) or 3(b), they shall be classified under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those which equally merit consideration".

13. As such, logic of the Customs Act that since the `Areca Nut' and 'Betel Nut' are same product then as per 3(c) of GIR for classification of the goods subsequent HS code has to be followed is not correct.

14. It appears from note sheet as contained in the paper book that Customs Authority discarded invoice value of the goods and determined value on the basis of data base applying method 6 of the Valuations Rules. But on perusal of the note sheet it appears that there was no data base value since `Areca Nut' was not imported earlier. In discarding invoice value and fixing inflated value, Customs authority did not record any finding that the invoice value is not actual transaction value and the value declared in connivance of the buyer and seller to evade Government revenue. Customs authority is under obligation to follow provision of the 'valuations rules' wherein it clearly provides that the assessing authority is to follow the rules in sequential manner. Apart from that, if the customs authority found that the invoice value is not actual transaction value then the authority is duty bound to afford an opportunity to the importer to place evidence in support of invoice value. Our Appellate Division in the case of Collector of Customs vs TK Oil Refinery Ltd and 22 others, reported in 62 DLR (AD) 217, observed:

"the concerned authority is required by strict compliance of law authorizing it to fix a citizen with the liability of payment of tax and the plea of impossibility of fixation of the normal value of the imported merchandise in the case of each individual importer upon hearing him or that upon affording him an opportunity to place his case, if any, in support of the invoice value, cannot be accepted and the respondents, under the law, cannot be allowed to resort to the practice of pre-fixation of the value of the imported goods for assessment of customs duties in that the Government or any other agency authorised by the delegated legislation cannot act in a manner which is not authorized or provided in the law or by the law."

15. In the premises above, we are of the view that the judgment and order passed by the Tribunal is not in accordance with law and liable to be set aside.

16. It appears from record that the appellant released imported goods pursuant to the order of Tribunal through provisional assessment paying duties and taxes in cash for declared value and classification and furnished bank guarantee on 29-10-2015 for the difference of duties and taxes determined by the customs authority.

<u>17. It also appears that Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal vide judgment and order dated 7-10-2016 which is communicated to the appellant on 11-8-2016. The provision of law is that an aggrieved can file appeal against the judgment and order passed by the Tribunal within 90 days as per law. The period for filing appeal in the case in hand started from the date of communication i.e. on and from 11-8-2016 and ended on 10-11-2016.</u>

18. From the order book it is evident that the appellant preferred instant Customs Appeal on 9-10-2016 but the Customs authority issued a letter to the concerned Bank for encashment of the bank guarantee furnished by the appellant and accordingly the concerned Bank issued pay order No. 0106753 dated 3-10-2016 in favour of the respondent No. 2 Commissioner of Customs, ICD, Kamlapur, Dhaka. The appellant is entitled to get back the amount furnished by the bank guarantee at the time of releasing the goods through provisional assessment pursuant to the order passed by the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal.

19. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.

20. The judgment and order dated 7-8-2016 passed by Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal No. 1, Dhaka, under Nothi No. CEVT/ Case (Cus)-351/2015 is set aside.

21. The respondent No. 2 Commissioner of Customs, ICD Kamlapur, Dhaka, is hereby directed to refund Taka 1,25,88,917.39 (One Crore Twenty Five Lac Eighty Eight Thousand Nine Hundred Seventeen and Paisa Thirty Nine) only to the appellant equivalent the amount furnished by the Bank Guarantee No. SAB/AGB/ BG No. 04/2015 dated 29-10-2015 issued by the South Bangla Agriculture and Commerce Bank Ltd. Agrabad Brach, Chittagong, within 45 (forty five) days from the date of receipt of this order.

22. The Commissioner of Customs, ICD Kamlapur, Dhaka, is also directed to make final assessment of the goods covered by bill of entry No. C-14176 dated 5-7-2015 as per declared HS Code and value within 30 days in line with observation made in the judgment and refund excess amount paid by the importer-appellant in accordance with law.

23. Send down records to the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka, alongwith a copy of this judgment at once.

Communicate a copy of this judgment to the respondent No. 2 Commissioner of Customs, Customs House (ICD), Kamlapur, Dhaka, for compliance of the direction.

End.

lawyer:
Bahesti Marjan, Advocate—For the Petitioners. 

Md Golam Mostafa, Advocate—For the Opposite Party No. 1.
parties:
