23. This letter was issued at the instance of Md K Rahman alias Md Katikbur Rahman, the constituted attorney of both the writ petitioners. Before issuance of the letter dated 26-8-2015, the High Court Division delivered its judgment in other writ petitions on 22-7-2010. But a letter cannot override the Gazette Notification dated 19-4-1999 which included all the areas of Mouza, namely, Jhilanja. In that Notification, no exception has been made on the basis of category of land. The Notification dated 19-4-1999 has simply included all lands within Jhilanja Mouza as ECA. Therefore, we are of the view that the letter dated 26-8-2015 is misconceived and contravenes the official Gazette. The said letter is, therefore, of no legal effect.

24. In addition to above, the said letter dated 26-8-2015 was signed by the Assistant Director, Paribesh Directorate, Cox's Bazar. In the affidavit-in-opposition dated 9-7-2017, it has been stated the officer who had signed the letter dated 26-8-2015 was not authorized to issue such letter and that no report was called for from him by any Court or Ministry of Land. The Assistant Director, Paribesh Directorate, Cox's Bazar, had issued the letter without any direction from proper authority and it was issued with ill motive.

25. This Division in the case of Farid Ahmed Chowdhury and another vs Ministry of Land, represented by its Secretary, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others delivered the judgment and order dated 09-12-2018 in Civil Review Petition Nos. 305-306 of 2015 with Civil" Review Petition Nos. 315-316 of 2015 and Civil Review Petition No. 320 of 2015 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2367 of 2010 and held that the plots in question are not excluded from ECA. The exclusions of the writ-petitioners' plots from the ECA being the main thrust of their submissions, we do not find any merit in these review petitions. Therefore, in those cases, this Division directed as under:

"All leases within Jhilanja Mouza granted after 19-4-1999 be cancelled in the same way as those of the writ-petitioners and any constructions made thereon be demolished. Of course, the lease holder shall be compensated for their loss due to such cancellation/demolition. We further direct that henceforth no lease shall be granted within Jhiianja Mouza or any area which has been classified as Ecologically Critical Area (ECA)."

26. The Ecologically Critical Area (ECA) is an environmentally protected zone where the ecosystem is considered to be endangered to reach a critical condition by the changes brought through various human activities. Section 2(gg) of the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995 as amended till date provides that "Ecologically critical Area" means such area which is rich in unique bio-diversity or due to the importance of environmental perspective necessary to protect or conserve from destructive activities. ECA also falls within the category of natural and cultural heritage.

27. The Government of Bangladesh has declared eight areas as ECAs in 1999, e.g. Cox's Bazar and Teknaf Peninsula, St. Martin's Island, Sonadia Island, Hakaluki Haor, Tanguar Haor and Marjat Baor, Gulshan-Baridhara Lake and Sundarbans. Subsequently in 2009, four rivers (e.g. Buriganga, Sitalakhya, Balu and Turag) around. Dhaka city were declared as ECAs.

28. Bangladesh is a signatory to the Ramsar Convention (1971) and the World Heritage Convention (1972) which are the principal instruments ensuring the conservation of natural heritages worldwide. The principal legislations that safeguard ECAs in Bangladesh are the Environment Conservation Act (1995), Environment Conservation Rules (1997), and the Constitution of Bangladesh.

29. The Act of 1995 in its section 5(1) contains provisions regarding declaration of ECA by the DG of the Department of Environment (DoE), which provides that if the Government is satisfied that, an area is in an environmentally critical situation or is threatened to be in such situation, the Government may declare such area as an ECA. Sub-section (2) also points out that, the Government shall under sub-section (1), specify the activities or processes that cannot be initiated or continued in an ECA. The Act also confers power to DoE to order corrective steps to be taken by any person believed to be responsible directly or indirectly, for causing harm to the ecosystem. Again, Rule 3(1) of the Rules of 1997 states that, the Government shall take the following factors into consideration while declaring any area as ECA under section 5(1) of the Act: (a) human habitat;(b) ancient monument; (c) archeological site; (d) forest sanctuary; (e) national park; (f) game reserve; (g) wild animals habitat; (h) wetland; (i) mangrove; (j) forest area; (k) bio-diversity of the relevant area; and (1) Other relevant factors. Furthermore, Article 18A of the Bangladesh Constitution contains provisions regarding the protection and improvement of environment and bio-diversity and states that, the State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to preserve and safeguard the natural resources, bio-diversity, wetlands, forests and wild life for the present and future citizens.

30. Therefore, the lease deed dated 26-1-2003 in favour of Ahsan Habib, the vendor of the writ-petitioners, for construction of hotel, was illegal from its very inception in view of Gazette Notification dated 19-4-1999 made under section 5 of the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995.

31. In addition to above, the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act has a non obstante in section 2A of the Act, which runs as follows:

"Overriding effect of the Act—Notwithstanding anything contained to the contrary in any other law for the time being in force, the provisions of this Act, rules and directions issued under this Act shall have effect."

32. Therefore, it appears that the provisions of this law shall prevail over any other law for the time being in force and, as such, no derogatory act can be done in violation of the Gazette Notification dated 19-4-1999 made under section 5 of the Environment Conservation Act, 1995 as amended till date.

33. In spite of legal prohibitions, the Metro Makers and Developers Limited (MMDL), a private company, undertook a development project and started earth-filling in the project area which was earmarked as Sub-Flood Flow Zone (SFFZ). In such a situation, the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers' Association (BELA), which is an organization of the environmental activist-lawyers, made a survey visiting the project area and felt the necessity of stopping such illegal works against environmental protection. The said group of lawyers (BELA) ultimately brought the matter before the Supreme Court for adjudication. Giving its decision reported in 65 DLR (AD) 181, the Appellate Division held that the right to-life as guaranteed by the Constitution includes the right to protection and improvement of the environment and ecology and, therefore, the said project of Metro Makers and Developers Limited was declared unlawful. The Court further directed the Metro Makers to restore the wetland of that area to its original state.

34. In the recent past, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, on umpteen occasions, has given directives and guidelines to the government to demarcate the rivers as per their original borderlines and to restore free flow of water restraining the illegal attempts of their enforcements and to save them from being perished. Many housing companies and land developers found engaged in changing the nature and features of wetlands and rivers have already been stopped because of the proactive role of the Judiciary of Bangladesh. But, nevertheless, we have a long way to go and take a firm stand to build up public awareness and legislate more stringent laws to cope with the needs of the changing society, otherwise it will be difficult for us to protect the bountiful treasures of nature and ensure environmental security without which the lives of our posterity will be at stake.

35. Public Interest Litigation under Article 32 and 226 of the Constitution of India resulted in a wave of environmental litigations. The leading environmental cases decided by the Supreme Court includes case of closure of limestone quarries in the Dehradun region (Dehradun Quarrying case. Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra, Dehrandun vs State of UP, AIR 1985 SC 652), the installation of safeguard at a chlorine plant in Delhi (MC Mehta vs Union of India, AIR 1988 SC 1037) etc. in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum vs Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647, the Court observed that "the Precautionary Principle" and "the Polluter Pays Principle" are essential features of "Sustainable Development."

36. At local and village level also, Panchayats have been empowered under the Constitution of India to take measures such as soil conservation, water management, forestry and protection of the environment and promotion of ecological aspect.

37. Environment protection is a part of Indian cultural values and traditions. In Atharvaveda (knowledge), it has been said that "Man's paradise is on earth; this living world is the beloved place of all; It has the blessings of nature's bounties; live in a lovely spirit". Earth is our paradise and it is our duty to protect our paradise. The constitution of India embodies the framework of protection and preservation of nature without which life cannot be enjoyed. The knowledge of constitutional provisions regarding environment protection is need of the day to bring greater public participation, environmental awareness, environmental education and sensitize the people to preserve ecology environment.

38. In order to successfully confront the twenty-first century environmental challenges that include managing the current and mitigating the future impacts of climate change; conserving natural resources and bio-diversity and preventing pollution, and to ensure environmental justice, it is incumbent upon the state to develop, implement and enforce environmental laws and upon the Judiciary to see that all parties concerned follow the laws and no one transgresses the same.

39. 19th century Native American leader Chief Seattle said,

"We do not inherit the Earth from our ancestors. We borrowed it from our Children"

40. We will have to return this Earth to our descendants so that they can return it to their future generations.

41. In the light of the findings made above, we find substance in this civil petition for leave to appeal. Accordingly, this civil petition is disposed of and the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division is set aside.

Respondent No.1 is directed to return the consideration money mentioned in the lease deed to both the writ-petitioners if they approach the Secretary, Ministry of Land.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman J: Both the Civil Appeals, by leave, are directed against the judgment and order dated 4-8-2011 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos.5329 of 2006 and 2516 of 2011 making the Rules Nisi absolute, and declared the judgment and order dated 3-5-2006 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka in Case No.83 of 2003 to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Both the civil appeals are heard together, as both the writs were arose out of the same property. Those were disposed of by the High Court Division by the single judgment. They are dealt with by this single judgment.

3. Facts leading, to filing of both the civil appeals, in short, are that:

The present respondent No.1 in both the civil appeals as the writ petitioners preferred the Writ Petition Nos.5329 of 2006 and 2516 of 2011 before the High Court Division challenging the judgment and order dated 3-5-2006 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka in Case No.83 of 2003 (Anx.5/02) (Ka-43 House No.3, Lane-11, Block-C, section 10, Mirpur, Dhaka) allowing the case with direction to exclude the property in House No.3, Lane-11, Block-C, section 10, Mirpur, Dhaka from the list of abandoned buildings stating that the land measuring 131 square yards (1 and 3/4 kathas) of House No.3, Lane-11, Block-C, section 10, Mirpur, Dhaka was allotted/leased out on 21-10-1963 by Mirpur Housing Estate, Dhaka as lessor in favour of Noor Mohammad, displaced person from India, and accordingly possession of the said land was handed over to him. After taking over possession of the said land, the said Noor Mohammad had been possessing the same by erecting dwelling house, and started living therein; during Liberation War, the said Noor Mohammad along with his family left the said house and after liberation he did not come back to the said house and, as such, Government took over possession the same as abandoned property. Thereafter, Mr Ataharul Hoque, the writ petitioner of the Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 entered into possession of the said house on 1-5-1972 and started to live therein with his family. He by dint of possession filed an application to the concerned authority for allotting the said House No.3, Lane-11, Block-C, section 10, Mirpur Housing Estate, Dhaka in his favour. On the basis of the said application, the writ respondent No.2 of the Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 issued a Demand Note on 18-1-1975 upon the applicant with a direction to deposit arrear rent from 1-5-1972 to 31-12-1975 at the rate of Taka 85 per month amounting to Taka 2,720 within 23-1-1975. As per direction of the writ respondent No.2 the writ petitioner deposited the said amount of Taka 2,720 through Challan No.H/47 dated 23-1-1975 as arrear monthly rent of the said house, and on the same date it was duly informed to the Executive Engineer, Housing Settlement, Mirpur Division, Segun Bagicha, Dhaka, and on 29-1-1975, the same was also duly informed to the office of the Administrative Officer, Mohammadpur and Mirpur Housing Estate Area. Subsequently, the writ petitioner on 3-10-1982 deposited an amount of Taka 510/through Bangladesh Bank Chalan No.Uma/10 and on 29-4-1985 also deposited an amount of Taka 13,134.40 through Bangladesh Bank Chalan No.Jha-3/4 as rents for the said abandoned property. In this way the writ petitioner deposited total amount of Taka 16,364.40 as rents of the said house. Since the original allottee of the property in question had been untraceable and the property in question was uncared in 1972, the property was declared by the Government as abandoned property and it took over the possession in the property as abandoned. The writ petitioner of Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 has been possessing the same as tenant under the Government since 1972. The Government included the said abandoned Building in the `Kr' list of the Abandoned Buildings at Serial No.43 published in Gazette Notification dated 23-9-1986 at page No.9762 (58). In the meantime, the writ respondent No.2 of Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 vide Memorandum No.শাখা-৭/এপি-৮৫/৮৪/৪৮০ dated 25-3-1985 issued a letter offering to sell the property in favour of the writ petitioner. As per condition Nos.1, 2 and 3 of the said offer letter the writ petitioner on 17-11-1985 deposited the 1st installment of an amount of Taka 23,465.20 as 20% of the total consideration amounting to Taka 1,17,326 and also submitted an affidavit on 29-10-1985 and certificate with regard to full payment of rent of the property in question obtained from appropriate authority. After completion of all formalities a “বিক্রয় চুক্তি” was executed on 9-10-1986 between the writ petitioner and the Government with regard to the property in question. (as described in the schedule below.) On 28-1 1 - 1 9 8 5 the Ordinance No.LIV of 1985 was promulgated and the list of abandoned properties was published on 23-9-1986, and thereafter “বিক্রয় চুক্তি”was executed by the Government in favour of the writ petitioner on 9-10-1986. From the Memo No.569 dated 8-10-1988 the writ petitioner learnt that the original allottee did not deposit the total  consideration amount against the property in question. The writ petitioner learnt that the writ respondent No.4, Md Murtuza Shah filed Case No.83 of 2003 in the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka praying for exclusion of the property from the abandoned properties List.

4. The writ petitioner of the instant writ petition in Settlement Case No.83 of 2003 submitted an application which pending before the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka enclosing the above mentioned documents including the Municipality Tax and other utilities bills paid by him in connection with the ownership, occupation and possession of the property in question, as, well as certificate issued by the Local Commissioner for addition of party. But the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka refused to accept the said application filed by the writ petitioner. During the trial of the case before the Settlement Court No.1, Dhaka PWs were examined including the said Mr Md Murtuza Shah as PW 1. There are serious of anomalies and contradictions in the depositions of the witnesses, which will be apparent upon perusal of the depositions. The writ respondent No.4 made some false, malafide and irrelevant statements in the applications while filed the alleged application.

5. The First Court of Settlement, Dhaka after hearing the parties, allowed the Case No.83 of 2003 with direction to exclude the property in question from the "Ka" list of the abandoned buildings by the judgment and order dated 3-5-2006.

6. Against the judgment and order dated 3-5-2006 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka, the writ petitioners of Writ Petition Nos.5329 of 2006 and 2516 of 2011, finding no other alternative efficacious remedy, moved the above mentioned writ petitions and obtained the Rules Nisi.

7. The writ-respondent Nos.4 and 5 in Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 and the writ respondent Nos.2 and 3 in Writ Petition No.2516 of 2011 contested the Rules Nisi by filing separate affidavit-in-opposition.

8. A Division Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties in both writ petitions made the Rules Nisi absolute and thereby setting aside the judgment of the Settlement Court by the impugned judgment and order dated 4-8-2011.

9. The leave petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 feeling aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 4-8-2011 of the High Court Division preferred the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.2024 of 2011 and 2025 of 2011 before this Division which raise the instant appeals.

10. Mr Abdul Matin Khasru, the learned Senior Counsel, appearing on behalf of the appellant in both the civil appeals submits that, the High Court Division erred in law having failed to appreciate that the respondent No.1 (writ petitioner) being a third party had no locus stanch' to file the writ petition challenging the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement and, as such, the instant appeals should be allowed. He further submits that, the High Court Division erred in law having failed to appreciate that the Government could not produce any evidence either documentary or oral to show that the property in question comes within the definition of "abandoned property" under Article 2 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 and, as such, the instant appeals should be allowed. He next submits that the High Court Division erred in law having failed to consider that the original allottee late Noor Mohammad (father of the appellants), filed an application to the appropriate authority with proper documents within time stipulated by law to get his property released and the Court of Settlement after meticulous assessment of materials on record passed its judgment excluding the property in question from the 'Ka' list of the Abandoned Buildings as per provision of law enacted under the Ordinance No.54 of 1985 and, as such, the instant appeals should be allowed. He finally submits that the High Court Division erred in law having failed to appreciate that the explanation of delay in filing the writ petition is not satisfactory and, as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside and the instant appeals should be allowed.

11. Per contra, Mr SK Shaifuzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No.3 in Civil Appeal No.64 of 2016 and the respondent No.1 in Civil Appeal No.65 of 2016 submits that the appellants having miserably failed to discharge the burden to prove that the property in question is not an abandoned property on or before 28-2-1972. Since onus of disproving of abandoned property is squarely lies upon them as provided in section 5 of the Ordinance, No. LIV of 1985 and, as such, the instant appeals are liable to be dismissed. He further submits that Mr Ataharul Hague being the Government Demand Note Holder entered into an agreement for sale on 9-10-1986 with the Government as per Sale Offer vide Memorandum No শাখা-৭/এপি-৮৫/৮৪/৪৮০ dated 25-3-1985 and paid 1st installment of Taka 23,465.20 as 20% of the Total consideration and, as such, he had got locus-stanch to file the writ petition before the High Court Division as per section 13 of the State Agreement as “১৩। তফসিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তি সম্পর্কে ভবিষ্যত কোন মামলা-মোকদ্দমার উদ্ভব হইলে ক্রেতা নিজ দায়িত্বে উহা পরিচালনা করিনে।”and, as such, the instant appeals are liable to be dismissed. He next submits that, the Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant and even if, any singular failure on the part of the claimants regarding whereabouts of the Original Lessee at the relevant point of date i.e. on 28-2-1972 is fully and wholly stunning and, as such, the High Court Division has rightly made the Rule absolute. Hence, the instant appeals are liable to be dismissed. He finally submits that the Government has got right to property as Lessor and the Government-writ petitioner filed the writ petition with proper explanation of delay although there is no statutory limitation to challenge the legality and propriety of the judgment passed by the Court of Settlement and the High Court Division, having assessed the evidence on record, made the Rules Nisi absolute and, as such, the instant appeals are liable to be dismissed.

12. Mr Fida M. Kamal, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent No.1 in Civil Appeal No.64 of 2016 and the respondent No.3 in Civil Appeal No.65 of 2016 made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division.

13. We have heard the learned Senior counsel appearing for the appellant in both the civil appeals, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.3 in Civil Appeal No.64 of 2016, the respondent No.1 in Civil Appeal No.65 of 2016, also Mr Fida M Kamal, the learned Senior counsel appearing for the respondent No.1 in Civil Appeal No.64 of 2016 and the respondent No.3 in Civil Appeal No.65 of 2016. Perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division, judgment of the Court of Settlement, other connected materials available on record.

14. In the instant appeals leave were granted to consider as to whether the High Court Division erred in failing to appreciate that respondent No.1 (Writ Petitioner) being third party had no locus standi to file the writ petition challenging the judgment and order of the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka allowing the case and directing the Government to exclude the case property from the "Ka" list of the Abandoned Buildings.

15. Secondly, as to whether the High Court Division erred in law in failing to appreciate that the Government could not produce any evidence either documentary or orally to show that the property in question comes within the definition of "Abandoned Property" under Article 2 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972.

16. Thirdly, as to whether the High Court Division erred in law in failing to appreciate that the explanation of delay in filing the writ petition is not satisfactory and the Court of Settlement passed the judgment and order after proper and meticulous assessment of evidence on record allowing the case and directing the Government to exclude the case property from the "Ka" list of the Abandoned Buildings.

17. As regards to the ground filing of writ petition by the third party is required to scan as to whether he has any legal right over the property in question pending settlement case between the admitted allottee owner and Government Lessor. The original allottee when questioning the vesting of properly, as per section 7 of the said ordinance as to the abandoned property and listing the same in "Ka" list, before the competent Settlement Court to decide the propriety of vesting, there is no reason and scope to resolve any claim made by the third party through Government vide a contract of purchase. Because, the provision of ordinance provides no room to resolve any claim of right and title of contracting party by the Court of Settlement. The Court of settlement only can see as per application under section 7 of the ordinance, as to whether the case property is abandoned or not.

18. The High Court Division in the judgment has already noticed that the respondent No.1 Ataharul Hague had applied to be added as a party in the settlement case before the Court of Settlement which was refused. The respondent No.1 did not challenge the order of refusal, nevertheless, after passing the judgment by the Settlement Court excluding the property from the "Ka" list of the Abandoned Buildings filed the writ petition challenging the aforementioned excluding before the High Court Division. In the above facts and circumstances, this Division is of the firmed view that writ petition by the third party could not be maintainable, rather, it is quite superfluous. In this regard we can safely held that before issuing the Rule the High Court Division ought to have gone through the merit of the Writ Petition and if it is apparent from the statement of the Writ Petition that the Petitioner neither aggrieved person nor have any locus standi to file the Writ Petition, such type of Vexatious application should be rejected summarily .The Writ Petitioner of the Writ Petition No.5329 of 2006 has got no personal interest in the case property either as tenant or so called purchaser. His claim must be governed according to the result of his landlord vendor's case. It is, therefore, our considered view that the High Court Division appears to have misconstrued and misconceived their jurisdiction under article 102 in holding that the Writ Petition is maintainable.

19. As regards to the second ground whether as per definition of "Abandoned Property" under Article 2 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972, the property in question comes within that purview. The concept of abandoned property, according to article No.2(1) of President Order No.16 of 1972 runs as follows:

Defining part

(1)"abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy supervise or manage in person his property, including—

Inclusion clauses

(i)	any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operation against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;

(ii)	any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972), but does not include—

Exclusion clauses

(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh;

(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force.

Explanation.—"Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

20. According to definition it appears clearly that if any person who left his property or is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, during the period of liberation in 1971 was at war with or engaged in military operation against the Bangladesh, his property under the definition shall be included as an abandoned property.

21. On a careful perusal of the judgment of the Court of Settlement it is clearly revealed that the petitioner before the Court of Settlement produced 10 (ten) prosecution witnesses and exhibited so many documents.

22. On the other hand the respondent Government neither produced any oral or documentary evidence for rebutting the prosecution explanation offered in the oral and documentary evidences regarding Noor Mohammod's living in Bangladesh. Rather, from the trend of the cross it reveals that they would like to establish that claimants are not the legal heirs of the late Noor Mohammod. It is must be mentioned here that Noor Mohammod had filed the application on 17-09-1986 under section 7 of the ordinance LIV of 1985, the final gazette was published on 23-9-1986 including the property as abandoned property at page no. 9762 (58) being serial No.43. In respect of the legal heirs, the petitioners before the settlement Court filed the copy of succession certificate vide Succession case No. 631 of 1996, certificate being issued by a competent Court which did not revoke till today. More so, they had deposited some certificate copies of the complaint case being No. 5 of 97 of the tribunal No. 1 of Bangladesh Bar Council and copy of passport of the Noor Mohammod. Noor Mohammod died on 10-2-1987. The leave petitioners were substituted by the settlement Court as the legal heirs. The government did not challenge those events before any court.

<u>23. The Settlement Court found from the evidence on record that Noor Mohammod never left Bangladesh, rather, on 4-2-1972 he shifted from the property in question for fear of his life to House No.7, Land No.4, Block-C, Avenuce-3, section 11 of Mirpur, Dhaka. So, there is no question arises as to Noor Mohammod's leaving the country. There is no iota of evidence on the side of the Government that, Noor Mohammod had not shifted the house nor they had produced any oral and documentary evidences that Noor Mohammod left Bangladesh. It is further depicted from the record that Noor Mohammod could not manage or supervise the case property, for a short period. The such type of absence from the case property does not take away his right and title in respect of case property as he did not left the country, rather had been trying to release the property. Therefore, the Court of Settlement rightly found that Noor Mohammod never left Bangladesh. It was also found by the Court of Settlement that Noor Mohammod had applied for passport and on 24-9-1979 a passport was issued in the name of Noor Mohammod as a permanent resident of Bangladesh. This passport proved that Noor Mohammod was a permanent resident of Bangladesh until death and lived in Bangladesh. He died on 10-2-1987 which has been clearly mentioned in a Death Certificate issued by the Local Commissioner and certificate issued from the concerned authority of the graveyard. Therefore, the Court of Settlement believed the prosecution story thoroughly examining the oral deposition and documentary evidence. The High Court Division without controverting the aforesaid unimpeachable evidence, reversed the facts of finding of the Court of Settlement, as if, it is a Court of appeal which is not only beyond the jurisdiction under article 102 of the Constitution, rather, such exercise is colourable and fenciful which is deprecated by this Division. So, the High Court Division under article 102 could not act as a Court of appeal.</u>

<u>24. This Division in the long line of catena has already held that the High Court Division only could interfere with the finding of the Court of Settlement, if could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made findings upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence causing prejudice to a party or it had acted malafide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. The High Court Division has failed to appreciate any such lacking in the judgment of Settlement Court, even then, it set aside the judgment of settlement Court.</u>

25. Noor Mohammod had filed the application on 17-9-1986 to the abandoned property cell of Ministry of Works for releasing the property vide a receipt No.3712 which has ultimately given rising to Settlement Case No.83 of 2003. So, it is crystal clear that the Late Noor Mohammad had filed the application within time as per provision of Ordinance No.LIV of 1985 though the case Number was recorded in the year 2003.

26. It is, therefore, clearly depicted that the filling of case in the Court of Settlement by the Noor Mohammod not barred by law as opined by the High Court Division. It is therefore obvious, the findings in the judgment of High Court Division as to non-consideration of evidence by the Settlement Court bears no significance. Ratherest, the Judgment of the High Court Division is so inappreciable which justifying calls for interference by this Division.

27. The next ground is whether the High Court Division erred in failing to appreciate that sole respondent of the settlement case Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works filed the writ petition without any delay acting with due diligence. On a careful scrutiny of the record of the Writ Petition No.2516 of 2011 it is apparent on the face of the cause title of the writ petition that the impugned judgment was passed on 3-5-2006, and an affidavit was sworn on 22nd day of March 2011; therefore, filing of the writ petition was not only delayed, ratherest, shockingly and unprecedented delay has been caused in invoking the special original jurisdiction under article 102 of the Constitution, though settlement case was allowed on contest against the writ petitioner Government denying the material allegations, not only that, moreso, they also cross examined all the PWs.

28. Now this Division will look into the behaviorally attitude regarding seeking the redress under article 102 of the Constitution.

<u>29. Though no period of limitation has been prescribed by law for seeking redress under article 102 of the constitution. However, such relief must be sought as early as possible, and must be shown due diligence. There is no special provision of privilege for the Government to explain the delay invoking constitutional jurisdiction. In the case in our hand, the Government even in the relevant paragraph of the Writ Petition did not explain the knowledge about the judgment, filing of application and obtaining of the certified copy, nor cause any reason in the application for what cause it has not filed the writ application as early as possible after passing the judgment.</u>

<u>30. As we have already noticed the date of judgment and swearing the date of affidavit for filing the writ petition, we cannot but to opine that there is no sufficient explanation for condonation of such inordinate delay. It is therefore, well established that the respondent Government was not vigilant for the filing the writ petition, probably it has acted in persuasion of the third party who filed the writ petition in the year 2006, even then, the Government had filed the writ petition in 2011 just before hearing and judgment of the High Court Division.</u>

<u>31. In the facts, circumstances and instant situation of the case we cannot but to hold that, inordinate delay in seeking relief can't be justified according to explanation offered to condone the delay in accordance with law. Ratherest, it is clearly justifying to interference with the judgment of the High Court Division; because the High Court Division in maintaining the writ application acted beyond the settle maxim of law in regard to condonation of delay.</u>

Accordingly, we find substance in both the appeals. The appeals are hereby allowed. The judgment of the High Curt Division is set aside.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 27-12-1988 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No. 300 of 1989 allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 28-12-1986 passed by Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 117 of 1981 should not he set aside.

2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 112 of 1981 to the Court of the then Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet impleading the petitioner as defendant No. 1 and opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 as defendant Nos.2 and 3 for declaration that order of defendant No.2 Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Sylhet dated 13-2-1981 disallowing tire release of the suit land to plaintiff Pourashava and directing to release of the property to defendant No. 1 Shadharon Bima Corporation is illegal, ultra vires, malicious and further for passing decree of permanent as well as mandatory injunction.

3. The case of the plaintiff-appellant, in brief is that the suit land originally belonged to Sylhet Pourashava which was acquired by it in LA case No.109/1901-1902. The Sylhet Pourshava Board was superseded by Government of Assam by Notification dated 10-2-39 for two years and the properties of Sylhet Municipal board were vested to the Crown and during this period of supersession the Governor of Assam granted lease of the suit land for 30 years to Sylhet Industrial Bank Ltd. by a registered Lease deed dated 18-9-1939. The Sylhet Industrial Bank constructed a two-storied building on the suit Land and carried their business. The said bank faced with financial difficulties and later by the order of Hon'ble High Court of Judicature at Ford William in Bengal dated 25-6-47 it was amalgamated with M/s Mohaiakshmi Bank Ltd. M/s Mohaiakshmi bank Ltd. which held the assets of Sylhet Industrial Bank Ltd. and transferred the suit land along with building and other structures thereon to Arjya Insurance Co. by a registered Kabala deed dated 23-2-48. During Last S/S operation of 1956-57, the suit land was recorded in the name of Arjya Insurance Co. The suit land along with building and other structures were requisitioned in LA Case No. 42/B of 1950-51. Subsequently the suit land along with building and other structures were treated as enemy/vested property in VP Case No. 58/68-69. Plaintiff-appellant by its memo No.514 dated 22-3-1978 prayed to Deputy Commissioner Sylhet for release of the suit property in favour of Pourashava and Deputy Commissioner Sylhet by his memo No. DV/LG/3PS-12/(1)/78/909 dated 20-7-1978 directed the plaintiff-appellant to take steps for correction of record of right in the name of Sylhet Pourashava. Accordingly application was made for correction of record of right whereon, after due notices, orders were passed on 28-8-1978 for correcting the record of rights of the schedule land in the name of the plaintiff-appellant. But the property was not being released, so Pourashava moved the matter to Ministry of LA and LR whereupon the Ministry called for a report from Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet but no report has yet been submitted. Plaintiff-appellant Pourashava also, took up the matter for release of the property with Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) who in his reply to the Pourashava stated that record of rights were corrected in the name of the plaintiff-appellant and that the suit land being enemy/vested property by NP Case No. 58/68-69 and under requisition in the Requisition Case No. 42/B/50-51 and thus, he requested for necessary action in such content. On the other hand, the defendant respondent No. 1 Sadaran Birr a Corporation moved to the Ministry of Commerce and Ministry which advised the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Sylhet to look into the case. The defendant-respondent No.1 claimed title of the suit property and prayed for release of the property to them. Without reference to the earlier correspondence with Pourashava the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Sylhet observed that he had nothing to do with regard to the right and title in the land and advised the parties to take recourse to the competent Court of law but instructed the requisition authority by his order dated 13-2-1981 to pay rent to Arjya insurance Company which according to him stood amalgamated with defendant-respondent No.1, Sadaran Bima Corporation and directed de-requisition in favour of defendant No.1 which is illegal, ultra-vires, malicious and void and hence the suit.

4. The case of the defendant-respondent No. 1 Sadharon Bima Corporation, in brief, is that the suit land was vested to the Crown i.e, the then Government of India free from all encumbrances and when the suit land was in possession of the Government of Assam, it granted lease to Indus-trial Bank Ltd. by a registered bilateral lease deed dated 18-9-1939. The said Industrial Bank constructed permanent two-storied building on the suit land by taking permission from the then Sylhet Municipal Board by improving the condition of land at huge cost and paid rent to the Government and subsequently said Industrial Bank was amalgamated with the Mohalakkshmi Bank by the order of the Hon'ble High Court of Judicature of Fort William of Bengal and on such amalgamation assets for the Industrial Bank vested on the Mohalakkshmi Bank, while Mohalakkshmi Bank is in possession of the suit land, the building and other structures thereon transferred the same to Arjya Insurance Co. Ltd. for consideration of Taka 40,000 by a registered deed dated 23-2-1948, whereupon the Arjya Insurance Co. became exclusive owner and named the said building as Arjya Insurance Building. During Last S/S operation, the suit land and building thereon was recorded in the name of Arjya Insurance Co. as statutory tenant under the Government and records of right had been finally printed and published in the name of Arjya Insurance Company without any objection either by the Sylhet Municipality or anybody else and it is maintained till date. The then Government of East Pakistan for Office accommodation requisitioned the said building from the possession of Arjya Insurance Co. Ltd. In RC Case No. 42/B of 1950-51 and paid monthly rent at the rate of Taka 200 per month to the said company admitting the title and possession of Arjya Insurance Company. In exercising Powers conferred by rule 181 of Defense of Pakistan rule by order dated 11-9-1965 the assets and liabilities of the Arjya Insurance company being unit of Life Insurance Co. of India was vested in Pakistan Insurance Corporation established under Pakistan Insurance Act, 1952 and since then all the assets and Liabilities of all units of the life Insurance Co. Ltd. of India falling within the territory of Pakistan vested in the Insurance Corporation and the said corporation settled many claim of Arjya Insurance Company up to 1971. In 1972 after liberation of Bangladesh the Pakistan Insurance Corporation was renamed as Bangladesh Insurance Corporation under PO No. 18/72 and all assests and liabilities of Pakistan Insurance Corporation falling within Bangladesh Territory vested in Bangladesh insurance Corporation and Subsequently the said corporation was dissolved and vested into Teesta Bima Corporation with all assests and liabilities by PO No. 161 of 1972. Then Sadharan Bima Corporation was constituted and all the assets of Teesta and Kamafully Bima corporation vested in the defendant-respondent No. 1 Sadaron Bima corporation which realizes monthly rents from then allottees of the suit property through the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet with the knowledge of the Pourashava and when the suit property was necessitated for their own use and enjoyment, the Sadaran Bima corporation applied for derequisition of the suit property and the collector is considering the necessity of the Sadaran Bima Corporation passed order on 13-2-1981 favouring derequisition of the suit property in favour of the Sadaran Bima Corporation and, as such, suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

5. The parties led evidence in support of their respective claims. After hearing the trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff is not in possession of the suit land while the defendant No. 1 is in possession, who got rent of the suit premises and record of right has been prepared in defendant No. 1's name and without filing suit for recovery of khas possession instant suit is not maintainable; lease was not granted by the Sylhet Pourashava, rather Government of Assam granted lease to the predecessor of the petitioner the defendant No.1 constructed structures in the suit land and as per the provision of section 7 and 8 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act the plaintiff is not entitled to get possession.

6. The appellate Court reversed the finding of the trial Court and decreed suit contending that the Sylhet Municipality being 'local authority' it's interest cannot be vested upon the Government on the ground of lease. The appellate Court found that period of lease is 30 years being granted by Government of Assam during temporary supersession of Sylhet Municipality and, as such, after elapse of 30 years the suit properties reverted back to the Sylhet Municipality, so laying claim by the defendants in the suit land is illegal, arbitrary and is of no legal effect. The appellate Court further found that the suit property cannot be termed as enemy property as the property is leasehold property having granted by Government of Assam for 30 years during temporary supersession of the municipality. The appellate Court further held that the lessee can remove structures being built in the suit land after de-requisition of the suit property and, as such, there will be no obstruction and hindrance is getting the suit property by the plaintiff without laying claim in the structures standing in the suit land. The appellate Court held that the plaintiff may take recourse for de-requisition of the suit land before any competent authority and after the purpose of requisition being over the government may take step for de-requisition of the suit land in favour of real owner.

7. Mr Rafi Ahmed learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the suit is clearly had for the defect of parties but the appellate Court without adverting the vital aspects found the suit is maintainable which caused failure of justice. He next submits that the suit property has been leased out by the government of Assam to Sylhet Industrial Bank Ltd by lease-deed dated 18-9-1939 where structures have been built by the said bank and subsequently the property is transferred to Arjyo Insurance Company by a deed of sale dated 23-2-1948 and, as such, the suit as framed is not maintainable but the appellate Court erroneously decreed the suit. Learned advocate further averred that as per the provision of defense of Pakistan Ordinance, rules, PO 18/72 and 161/72 right, title and interest of Arjyo Insurance Company has been devolved upon the defendant No. I and, as such, the plaintiffs claim over the suit land is not sustainable.

8. On the other hand, Mr Chaudhury Morshed Kamal, learned advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 submits that in lease deed date 18-9-1939 exhibit-1, it was stipulated that after expiry of the period of lease that is for 30 years, the lease shall not be renewed as of right and the lower appellate Court rightly held that the period of lease has been ceased by expiry of time. He next submits that in the subsequent sale deed dated 23-2-1948, exhibit-3 entered into between Mahaiaxmi Bank with Arjya Insurance Company Ltd duration of the original lease has been mentioned for 30 years and, as such, the defendant No.1 cannot claim title to the suit property. He next submits that admittedly the suit property has been acquired for Sylhet Paurashva and during its supersession for two years Assam Government leased out the said property to Sylhet industrial Bank and, as such, after expiry of the lease period, naturally the property reverted back' to the plaintiff and as the government requisitioned the said land for government purposes and, as such, after de-requisition, the plaintiff is entitled to get back the property. He next submits that the defendant No.1 cannot Claim the property by virtue of wrong record of right and, as such, the appellate Court upon consideration of legal aspect as well as facts and circumstances rightly decreed the suit.

9. Having gone through the pleadings, impugned judgment and exhibits it appears that Sylhet Paurashava was owner of the suit land and being its temporary supersession Government of Assam leased out the said property by lease deed dated 18-9-1939 to Sylhet Industrial Bank Ltd for 30 years, and after expiry of the lease period the tenure cannot be extended unless the lessee renewed it by any covenant. It is clear that there is no renewal of lease and, as such, Sylhet Paurashova remained owner of the suit property. Although lease deed has been executed by Assam Government for temporary supersession of Sylhet paurashova being for two years, but after elapse of that period Sylhet paurashova seized of its normal functions and naturally remained owner of the property in question.

10. In the instant case, the positive case of the plaintiff is that the suit property is acquired land of Sylhet Pourashava which has been acquired vide LA case No. 109/1901-1902 and admittedly due to supersession of Sylhet Municipality the government of Assam leased out the suit land to Sylhet Industrial Bank for 30 years on 18-9-1939 and the said bank in amalgamated with Mohalaxmi Bank and the said Mohalaxmi Bank transferred the suit land in favour of Arjyo Insurance Company by deed dated 23-2-1948 for the reminder period of earlier lease. So it is clear that the government of Assam leased out the suit land for 30 years mentioning the ownership of Sylhet municipality and, as such, after elapse of two years Sylhet Municipality resumed its function as before with full ownership of the suit land along with other properties and, as such, the trial Court's finding as vesting of title to defendant No.1 by, successive transfer is not at all tenable. Besides, after expiry of lease period no fresh lease has been granted to the predecessor of defendant No.1 or earlier lessee and it is also clear that 30 years lease of non-agricultural land is not a lease of perpetually. The said view is clearly established by a decision reported in 17 DLR 329.

Which is quoted below:

"Admittedly the suit-land is a Non-Agricultural land and it is also admitted that the defendant-appellants had obtained the lease of the suit land from plaintiffs predecessor in title. The only question to be examined is, whether the suit-land had vested in the Government. If the aforesaid lease is not a lease in perpetuity, the plaintiff is not a "rent-receiver" and, the suit-land has not vested in Government. It is evident from the terms of the lease as stated above, that it is a lease for a fixed term and not a lease in perpetuity. A lease in perpetuity is unknown to English law. In the country a lease in perpetuity can he created by ah express grant to that effect or by a necessary presumption raised by the terms of a grant and by an unambiguous and long possession. In this particular case there can be no manner' of doubt that the lease was for a fixed period and not a lease in perpetuity within the meaning of the Transfer of Property Act. Plaintiff was not, therefore, a "rent-receiver" in respect of the suit land."

11. The contention of the trial Court that Sylhet industrial bank took lease of the suit property from Assam Government and, as such, Sylhet municipality has no ownership therein which is not all correct because in the deed in question Government of Assam clearly mentioned that due to temporary supersession of Sylhet municipality, the lease deed has been executed by Government of Assam and, as such, finding of the trial Court is not all sustainable.

12. The trial Court also wrongly held that as the predecessor of defendant No.1 constructed pacca structure in the suit land, the plaintiff is not entitled to get possession as per section 2(5), 7 and 8 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949. Such view is also not sustainable as because Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 expressly excludes any land vested in or in the possession of any local authority as per section 85A of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act. In 39 DLR (AD) 16 it is held as under-

"The Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 expressly excludes any land vested "in or in the possession of any local authority". See section 85A clause (3). Therefore, the defendants could not take resort even to the provision of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act. The reason in simple, because the application of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act would saddle the Municipality with certain legal obligations and, as such, the legislature expressly omitted the operation of such act insofar as any land vested in or in the possession of any local authority. So that the advantage which it gives and the dis-advantages which it imposes may not come into operation with regard to such land".

<u>13. The trial Court also committed error in holding that the suit is bad for defect of parties for non- impleading the vested property authority as defendant but the said view is an wrong approach as because the suit land is not vested property but even then Additional Deputy Commissioner has been impleaded as defendant No.2 'who looks after the vested property on behalf of the government and, as such, the findings of the trial Court is quite irrelevant. Besides no suit can fail merely for non-joinder or misjoinder of parties as per order 1 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In 49 DLR (AD) 151 it is held that "no suit can fail by reason merely of non-joinder of parties Order I Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes this legal position clear". Apart from this, the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff being not in possession of the suit land his suit is not maintainable without making prayer of khas possession is also not maintainable, since the property is in the possession of the Government, the plaintiffs suit is maintainable without making prayer for recovery of khas possession. In 43 DLR 109 it is held that—</u>

<u>"Hence the Government is holding the property treating the same to be of the plaintiff. If it is declared by the Court that it is not an abandoned property the Government will have no reason to possess the same and will be under obligation to restore possession to the plaintiff and no prayer for recovery of possession as a consequential relief is necessary. Hence the suit is quite maintain-able and it is not barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act."</u>

<u>14. Since the property is presently being used as requisition property, it can be de-requisitioned in favour of the rightful owner after ceasing its necessity.</u>

<u>15. Apart from this if anybody has no title in any property mere record of right will not confer title to him. The trial Court fails to consider the legal provisions and erroneously dismissed the suit.</u>

<u>16. The appellate Court on appreciation, of evidence both oral and documentary and also by proper interpretation of documents rightly reversed the judgment of the trial Court and decreed the suit with appreciable reasons and it is settled position of law that if the lower appellate Court reverse any judgment of the trial Court on proper assessment of the evidence on record, it calls for no interference under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

17. In the above circumstances I find no merit in the Rule and accordingly the rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

Let a copy of the judgment along with the Lower Court Record be sent to the concern Court.

End.

lawyer:

parties:
Younus Miah (Md) ------ Plaintiff-Respondent-Petitioner
Vs
Jarip Ali and others  ------ Defendants-Appellants-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-4, to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 19-1-2017 (decree signed on 24-1-2017), passed by the Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Chattogram, in Other Appeal No.517 of 2011, allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 24-8-2011 (decree signed on 29-8-2011), passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Rangunia, Chattogram, in Other Suit No. 94 of 2004 decreeing the suit, should not be set-aside and/or pass such other order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts, relevant for disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that, one Md Younus Miah, as plaintiff, had filed Other Suit No. 94 of 2004 before the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Rangunia, Chattogram, against the defendants-appellants-opposite parties seeking permanent injunction in respect of the suit property measuring 0.1102 acres of land as mentioned in the schedule to the plaint.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-4 had appeared and contested in that suit by filing written statements on 25-10-2004. The plaintiff examined one PW and defendants have also examined 2 DWs in support their respective cases.

4. However, the trial court, after hearing the parties and assessing the evidence on record, decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 24-8-2011 (decree signed on 29-8-2011).

5. Against the said judgment and decree of the trial court, the defendants preferred Other Appeal No.517 of 2011 before the District Judge, Chattogram, which was heard by the Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Chattogram, who being the Appellate Court, has passed the impugned judgment and decree, allowing the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court, vide judgment and decree dated 19-1-2017 (decree signed on 24-1-2017).

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 19-1-2017 (decree signed on 24-1-2017) of the Appellate Court the plaintiff-respondent-petitioner has filed this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

7. Learned Advocates Mr Md Mostaque Ahmed and Mrs. Sayeda Rofika Khatun appeared for the petitioner. Mr Ahmed, having placed the petition and other materials on record, first of all submits that, the plaintiff has proved his possession in the suit property being present before the court as PW 1. Besides, the plaintiff has also filed some documents marked as exhibit 3 and 4 which shows that, the plaintiff had a grocery shop on the suit plot and that he had a nationality certificate, issued by the Chairman of the No. 1 Rajanagar Union Parishad on 20-3-2008 (Exhibit 4), showing Bochan Ali, as father of the plaintiff Md Younus Miah. As such, he submits that, the plaintiff has been able to prove his title by an oral gift made by his foster mother Albela Khatun and that he was in possession of the suit property. He further submits that, this being a suit for permanent injunction, the plaintiff has proved his prima-facie title and exclusive possession in the suit property and that in such a case, the court need not have to decide the disputed question of title. In support of his contention, he has referred to the decision reported in 56 DLR (AD) 22: between Jobayer Hossain vs Noor Hafez. Accordingly, he maintains that, the trial court has rightly passed the judgment and decree in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner. But, the appellate court has utterly failed to appreciate the legal aspects of this case and the evidence on record and, out of full misconception of law, it has passed the impugned judgment and decree and, as such, this Rule has merit and the same may kindly be made absolute.

8. Learned Advocates Mr Rezaul Karim and Mr Mohammad Samiul Huq appeared on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1-4. The first contention of the learned Advocate Mr Huq is that, the case of the plaintiff Md Younus Miah, PW 1 has not been corroborated by any other competent witness. The learned Advocates pointed out that, during cross-examination of PW I (the sole-witness) he has admitted that Albela Khatun was alive, but he could not make the said Albela Khatun was present before the court as witness to prove the oral gift allegedly made by her in his favour or to support his possession by making a shop on the suit property. Mr Huq next also submits that, the plaintiff possessed the suit property and the certificate issued by the concerned Chairman, No. 1 Rajanagar Union Parishad on 20-3-2008, which can easily be procured by managing the local Chairman of a Union Parishad and this not a proof of alleged gift or of possession. He next pointed out that, during examination of PW 1 he has admitted that —“না: দাগে বিবাদীদের ঘর-বাড়ি চিনি।” The learned Advocates next submits that, the appellate court has rightly held that, the plaintiff (petitioner) did neither call, nor produce Albela Khatun as witness to prove his case. The appellate court has also recorded that, at the time of alleged oral gift and handing over of possession on 15-1-1974, Bochan Ali, Naderuzzaman, Kabir Ahmed and Bodiul Alam were allegedly present. But having examined the record of Other Suit No. 94 of 2004, it appears that, the plaintiff did not call or examine any one of them as witness to prove the fact of handing over of the possession as asserted by him. On the contrary, the appellate court also recorded that, the defendants' case, that they have acquired the suit property from Albela Khatun on the basis of a registered sale deed No. 573 dated 17-3-2004 (Exhibit-Kha) has not been challenged, nor claimed that deed to be a forged deed/documents created by the plaintiff. Besides, the appellate court has also recorded the deposition of DW 2, who is the attesting witness No. 3 of the aforesaid sale deed No. 573 dated 17-3-2004 (Exhibit-Kha). On these basis, the appellate court has found title and possession of the defendant in the suit property and held that, the findings of the trial court were not based on proper appreciation of evidence on record. Hence, the appellate court has set-aside the findings of the trial court. The appellate court has also held that, no one can, in the absence of any lawful title, claim permanent injunction in the suit property, nor anyone having entered into the suit property on the basis of any oral license can deny or refuse to hand over the possession of the suit property as has been claimed by the plaintiff. The appellate court has finally found that, the defendants' had no legal interest in the suit property. The appellate court has, I find, righty set-aside the judgment of the trial court, the learned Advocate continues. Finally, the learned Advocates for the OP Nos. 1- 4 referred to the decision, reported in the case of Md Kamal vs AKM Mohsin, 10 MLR (AD) 100 in which, the Apex Court held that, in a suit for permanent injunction, if the dispute involves complicated question of title the plaintiff must establish his title by filing a regular suit for declaration of title. A simple suit for permanent injunction should not be allowed to be used as a testing devise for ascertainment of title. Therefore, the learned Advocates sum up that, the impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate court is absolutely based on proper appreciation and assessment of evidence on record and of law, and, therefore, they have prayed for discharging the Rule.

9. 1 have heard the learned Advocates for both the parties, perused the application for revision, lower Court's record as well as the judgment of both the Courts below and other materials on record.

10. 1 find that, during cross-examination of PW 1 (the sole-witness) he has admitted that Albela Khatun was alive, but, he could not produce his alleged foster mother Albela Khatun as witness to prove the oral gift said to have been made by her in his favour or to support his possession by making a shop in the suit property. The certificate issued by the concerned Chairman, No. I Rajanagar Union Parishad on 20-3-2008, is not a relevant document to prove either the case of oral gift or of possession, as claimed by the plaintiff. I also find that, during examination of PW 1, he has admitted possession of the defendant on the suit property by admitting that "না: দাগে বিবাদীদের ঘর-বাড়ি চিনি।"

11. Hence, the appellate court has rightly pointed out that, the plaintiff (petitioner) did not produce Albela Khatun to prove his case and that she was his foster mother. The appellate court has also recorded that, at the time of alleged oral gift and handing over of possession on 15-1-1974, Bochan Ali, Naderuzzaman, Kabir Ahmed and Bodiul Alam were present, as per plaintiff's narration of his case. But, having examined the record of Title Suit No. 94 of 2004, he has rightly found that, the plaintiff did neither call, nor examined any one of them as witness, to prove handing over of the possession of the suit property as alleged.

12. The defendant's case that, they have acquired the suit property from Albela Khatun on the basis of a registered sale deed No. 573 dated 17-3-2004 (Exhibit-Kha) has been duly proved by adducing the attesting witness (DW 2) and the genuineness, existence or execution of the exhibit Kha has not been challenged by the plaintiff.

13. Besides, I also find that, the appellate court has recorded the deposition of DW 2, who is the attesting witness No. 3 of the aforesaid sale deed No. 573 dated 17-3-2004 (Exhibit-Kha). On these points, the appellate court has found title and possession of the defendant in the suit property and held that, the findings of the trial court were not based on proper appreciation or assessment of the evidence on record. Hence, the appellate court has set-aside the finding of the trial court.

<u>14. The appellate court has rightly held that, no one can, in the absence of any lawful title, claim permanent injunction in the suit property, nor the plaintiff, having entered into the suit property on the basis of oral license can deny or refuse to hand over the possession of the suit property. The appellate court has correctly found that, the defendant had no legal interest in the suit property.</u>

<u>15. In 10 MLR (AD) 100: between Md Kamal vs AKM Mohsin in which, the Apex Court held that, in a suit for permanent injunction, if the dispute involves complicated question of title the plaintiff must establish his title by filing a regular suit for declaration of title. A simple suit for permanent injunction should not be allowed to be used as a testing devise for ascertainment of title.</u>

16. In view of the discourse made above, I hold that, the appellate court has committed no error of law in passing the impugned judgment and decree, nor the same has resulted in any error of law, nor it has occasioned any failure of justice.

17. I find no merit in this Rule and the same should be discharged.

Order

In the result, the Rule is discharged. The impugned judgment and decree dated 19-1-2017 (decree signed on 24-1-2017), passed by the Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Chattogram, in Other Appeal No.517 of 2011 is hereby affirmed.

The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

No costs.

Copies of this judgment along with the Lower Court's Record be sent down to the concerned Courts at once and another copy to the concerned Chairman, No. 1 Rajanagar Union Parishad, PO: Thandachari, Upzilla: Rangunia, Chattogram. Another copy of this judgment and order be sent to the Up-Zilla Nirbahi Officer, for recording the misconduct of this Union Parishad Chairman.

End.
