full_judgment:
AKM Abdul Hakim J: In all these appeals the plaintiffs-appellants are different but the respondent nos. 1 and 2 and other respondents are different Banks and Financial Institutions, who sanctioned credit facilities to the respective plaintiff and plaintiffs of the suit filed present appeal before this court are common. The aforesaid appeals arose against the judgment and decree dated 10-7-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 298 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 20-5-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 284 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 103 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 5-5-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 248 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 24-7-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 380 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 24-7-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 381 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 111 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 112 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 5-5-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 250 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 7-7-2019 passed in Title Suit No. 317 of 2019, judgment and decree dated 18-2-2018 passed in Title Suit No. 91 of 2018 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka rejecting the respective plaints of the aforementioned suits under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of maintainability.

2. All these suits were filed for a declaration that the inclusion and publication of the names of the plaintiffs-appellants in the Credit Information Bureau (CIB) of Bangladesh Bank showing them as defaulters/guarantors in connection with the credit facilities is illegal, void, without legal effect and not binding upon the appellants-plaintiffs. But containing the similar facts and circumstances and involving the similar issues to the effect that after filing of the respective suits by the plaintiffs-appellants before the Joint District Judge without issuing any summons or notice fixed the suit for maintainability and hearing of injunction application which were filed by the respective parties before the court below. In view of such position all these appeals were heard together and dispose of by a single judgment.

3. The plaint case of aforesaid suits filed by the respective plaintiff are more or less same. The defendant No. 1, Bangladesh Bank and defendant No. 2, General Manager CIB of Bangladesh Bank is responsible for publishing CIB Report naming the loan defaulters and other defendants are the bank and financial Institutions are different in all the suits. Basically, the case stated in the plaint by different plaintiffs are similar. In the plaint, it is stated that the provisions of publishing the names of the defaulters in the CIB Report of Bangladesh Bank as provided under Article 42-48 of the Bangladesh Bank order, 1972 and Section 27 Ka Ka of the Bank Companies Act, 1991 are absolutely unconstitutional, ultra vires and violative of the fundamental rights as guaranteed under Article 31, 32, 40 and 42 of the constitution of the people's Republic of Bangladesh. It is further stated that in case of defaulting issue, the Bank or financial Institution has several legal recourses including filing suits under Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and filing other Civil and Criminal Cases. In the plaints it is also stated that due to non-payment of loan, the respective Bank and financial institutions sent the name of the plaintiff or plaintiffs to the defendant No. 1 as classified as Bad/loss and defendant No. 2 published the name of the plaintiff as "Defaulter" in CIB list. Due to arbitrariness in sending the name of the plaintiffs in the CIB list, business grow a deal lock position and has been suffering hugs loss. As such the plaintiffs prayed for a declaration that the impugned classification and publication of the name of the respective plaintiff in the CIB report of Bangladesh Bank is arbitrary, illegal, void, without legal effect and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

4. At the time of filing of the suit the plaintiffs also filed an application for temporary injunction. The learned Joint District Judge fixed next date for hearing on maintainability of the suit and injunction hearing.

5. Ultimately, the learned Joint District Judge passed the impugned judgment and order rejected the plaint under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of maintainability mainly relying upon three decisions reported in 18 DLR 709, 48 DLR (AD) 50 and 51 DLR (AD) 221.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka in the respective suit as clearly described in the Memorandum of the respective appeal. The order rejecting the plaint is a decree within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure the plaintiffs of the respective suits preferred the aforesaid appeals against the judgment and decree more fully described in the respective Memorandum of Appeal.

7. At the time of filing of the present appeal, the appellant of all the appeal also filed an application under Order XXXIX, rule 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for an order of temporary injunction restraining the defendants-respondents from reporting, sending and publishing the names of the plaintiffs-appellants in the CIB report of the Bangladesh Bank showing them as defaulters in connection of the credit facilities advanced by the defendants-respondents. Upon hearing, this court issued separate rule upon the opposite-parties to show cause and restrained the respondents-opposite parties by an order of ad-interim injunction as stated above.

8. In view of the averments made in the plaint and the reliefs sought for, now the pertinent question which call for determination in these appeal is to see whether the learned Joint District Judge committed any illegality in rejecting the plaint on the ground of maintainability under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure while the suit was also fixed for hearing temporary injunction.

9. Ms Syeda Nasrin, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-appellants in First Appeal No. 424 of 2019, First Appeal No. 450 of 2019 and First Appeal No. 461 of 2019 submits that the trial court erroneously rejected the plaint and dismissed the suit on the question of maintainability by invoking the jurisdiction under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. She further submits that the question of maintainability of the suit could be decided only after framing issues under Order XIV, rule 2 and Order XV, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the maintainability of the suit can be determined at the time of trial and not under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. She next submits that the learned Joint District Judge totally misappreciated and misconstrued the provisions of Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 erroneously rejected the plaint on this ground of maintainability. She also submits that the trial court committed a gross error of law in rejecting the plaint suo-moto and dismissed the suit without any application filed by the defendants under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. She finally submits that maintainability of a suit being a mixed question of fact, the same cannot be decided before filing of the written statement by the defendants. In support her submissions learned Advocate relied on the decisions reported in 30 DLR (SC) 30, 48 DLR 367 and 11 MLR (AD) 2006 58.

10. In First Appeal No. 424 of 2019, Mr Shahjada Al-Amin Kabir, learned Advocate for the respondent No. 8, Mr SM Kamal Hossain Moni, learned Advocate for the respondent No. 9 and Mr KS Salah Uddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the respondent No. 15 filed power on 29-1-2020 and 6-2-2020 respectively but none of them was present before the court at the time of hearing of the Appeal.

11. Mr AKM Fakrul Islam with learned Advocate Mr Redwan Ahmed appeared for the plaintiffs-appellants in First Appeal No. 422 of 2019 and First Appeal No. 308 of 2019 has submitted that the learned Joint District Judge by the impugned judgment and order rejected the plaint on the ground of maintainability which is not specifically provided under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the ingredience upon which a plaint can be rejected on the said rule is no way applicable in the present case. He further submitted that the civil court has wide jurisdiction to examine whether the Bangladesh Bank rightly declared the plaintiff as loan defaulter and published his name in CIB report and that matter should be decided by the civil court. Learned Advocate in support of his submission has relied on the decision reported in I BLC (AD) 159. He also submitted that the trial court wrongly decided the question of maintain-ability without framing proper issues. He finally submitted that there is no express provision in section 27KaKa of the Banking Companies Act. 1991, that the defaulter cannot invoke jurisdiction in civil court declaring that he is defaulter or not. He further contended that Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972 has no manner application in respect of sending the names of the plaintiff to publish in the CM report under section 27KaKa of the Bank Companies Act, 1991.

12. In First Appeal No. 425 of 2019 Mr Md Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant has submitted that the learned Advocate Ms Syeda Nasrin has touched and raised all the points regarding provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and cited several decisions of our apex court. He contends further that the learned Joint District Judge committed gross error of law in rejecting the plaint without applying its judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the decisions of our Apex Court.

13. In First Appeal No. 422 of 2019, Mr Elen Emon Shah, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent No. 3. He find very difficult to oppose the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant. He tried to submit that the plaint of the suit is clearly barred by law under section 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972. He further submits that declaration from a court is not at all necessary for sending the name of defaulting borrower to Bangladesh Bank under section 27KaKa of the Bank Company Act, 1991. Mr Elen Emon Shah, in support of his arguments has relied the case of Al-Amin Bread and Biscuits Ltd. vs Bangladesh Bank, reported in 17 BLC 653.

14. The learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellant in First Appeal No. 314 of 2019, 131-132 of 2019 and 98 of 2018 adopted the submissions of Ms Syeda Nasrin and the decisions referred to above by Ms Syeda Nasrin in support of her contention as the points in issue are similar.

15. It appears that in First Appeal No. 450 of 2019, 461 of 2019, 132 of 2019, 425 of 2019 no one appears for the respondents although notice was duly served upon them.

16. Learned Advocate Md Abul Kalam Azad appeared for respondent No. 4 in First Appeal No. 314 of 2019, Mr Shahjada Al-Amin, learned Advocate appeared for respondent No. 8, in First Appeal No. 308 of 2019, Mr Tushar Kanti Das, Advocate, Mr Monjur Kader, Advocate, Mr KS Salah-uddin Ahmed, Advocate, Mr lftekhar Ahmed, Advocate appeared for the respondent nos. 3/4/5/6 respectively, Mr Shaikh Mohammad Zakir Hossain, Advocate and Shahjada Al-Amin, Advocate filed power on behalf of respondent No. 3 and respondent No. 4 respectively. But none of the Advocate for respondents were present before the court at the time of hearing of the Appeal.

17. It appears that in all the suits after registration of the suit no summons was issued upon the defendants and in some suits impugned judgment and order was passed by the learned Joint District Judge by referring/relying 3 (three) decisions reported in 18 DLR 709, 48 DLR (AD) 50 and 51 DLR (AD) 221, which are in fact different from the facts, circumstances, related laws and other issues of the present case. The differences are summarized below:

18. In BSRS vs Rahman Textile Mills, 51 DLR (AD) 221 (shortly referred as `BSRS Case')- By the majority decision the plaint was rejected upon an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the defendants. But in the present suits, the plaint was rejected just after registration of the suit and before issuing summon/notice upon the defendants.

19. In BSRS case, the plaint was rejected not for the contents of the plaint or barred by any law but on the ground that the very reliefs claimed in the suit are specifically barred under Article 34(5)(a)(i) or (ii) or (iii) of Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha Order, 1972 (Presidents Order No. 128 of 1972). The reliefs were barred under law, thus plaint was barred by law for seeking barred reliefs under law. But in the present cases, the reliefs claimed by the plaintiffs are not barred under any law.

20. In BSRS case, it was further observed that article 34 of President's Order No.128 of 1972 is an independent, substantive and procedural provision regarding bar of entertainment of a suit on grounds different from those described in Order VII, rule 11 Code of Civil Procedure. Article 34(5) specifically lays down that if the prayers in the suit are of the description contained in Article 34(5)(a)(i) or (ii) or (iii) then the suit will not be entertained. In an ordinary civil suit the plaint is rejected, inter alia, "where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law." Therefore in an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the statement in the plaint has to be looked into to determine if the suit if barred by any law. But under Article 34(5) it is not the statement in the plaint but the reliefs claimed in the suit under Article 34(5)(a)(i) or (ii) or (iii) which will determine whether the suit is entertainable or not. Under Order VII, rule 11 Code of Civil Procedure it is the statement in the plaint which is the determining factor but under Article 34(5) it is the relief claimed which is the determining factor.

21. In the said case, it was also observed that the instant cases are governed by Article 34(5) of Presidents Order No.128 of 1972. To the extent that the determining factors of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Article 34(5) are different and inconsistent, the provisions of Article 34(5) will prevail over those of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The defendant-appellant need not have filed application under Order VII, rule 11 Code of Civil Procedure. It could have maintained application under Article 34(5) of President's Order No. 128 of 1972.

22. The stages of BSRS case and the present suit are completely different. The former one was long after filing of the suit, service of summons, after appearing of the parties and contesting the same but in the present cases it was only on the preliminary stage after registration of the suit, where no summons/notice were served, defendants did not appear, and none contested the suit.

23. In WB Industrial Corp vs Deen Mohammad, 48 DLR (AD) 50 (shortly referred to as 'WB Case)—The plaint was rejected by the trial court because there was an application filed by the defendant under Order VII, rule 11 before the Court below on the ground that the suit is barred under Article 34(5) of the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 129 of 1972). But in the present suits, the plaint was rejected suo moto.

24. In this case, though the plea of malafide was taken, however the Court did not allow the plea of malafide and bonafide saying that the issue of malafide or bonafide involved disputed question of fact which required continuation of the suit, and the plaint was rejected on different ground arising out of the ouster provision of law. That ouster provision barred the parties from claiming certain reliefs. But in the present cases, the plaint was rejected suo moto without having any such ouster clause under law. The reliefs prayed in the present suit are not barred under any law.

25. The stage of WB case and the present suit are completely different. The former one was long after filing this suit, service of summons, appearing by the parties and contesting the same; but in the latter case it was only on the preliminary stage just after registration of the suit without issuance of any summon upon the defendants.

26. In the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union, 18 DLR 709 (shortly referred to as 'Burmah Eastern Case )— In that case the plaint was rejected upon the application filed by the defendant Burmah Eastern Ltd. under Order VII, rule 11. But in the present suits, the plaint was rejected suo moto.

27. In Burmah Eastern case, the plaintiff have no 'legal character' or 'status', in filing the suit very question of 'legal character' was questioned. But in the present suits plaintiff have legal character or status, no such question was raised as to 'legal character' of the parties as well as 'nature of the suit'.

28. In the said case, the Court came to the conclusion that from the mere perusal of the plaint, it appeared prohibited as well as barred under and by law. But in the present suits there is no such specific prohibition under law in filing the present suit.

29. The stages of Burmah Eastern and the present suit are completely different. The former one was long after filing the suit, service of summons, appearing by the parties and contesting the same; but in the present cases it was only on the preliminary stage after registered in a register of Civil Suits under Order IV, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure without issuing any summons upon the defendants.

30. Therefore, it appears that the learned trial court below was out of total misreading, misconception and misconstrued the aforesaid cases erroneously applied the ratio in the present case very arbitrarily and also without applying judicial mind.

31. Although the learned Joint District Judge rejected the plaint on the ground of maintain-ability but the above noted decisions as referred by the learned Joint District Judge have no nexus in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

32. On the other hand, the learned Joint District Judge failed to take notice of the following latest decisions relating to the rejection of plaint by our Apex Court reported in 11 MLR (AD) (2006) 58, 4 MLR (AD) (1999) 426 and 30 DLR (SC) 30.

1) 11 MLR (AD) (2006) 58, Wherein it has been held: "Rejection of plaint on ground of maintainability of the Suit is not permissible before filing of written statement

"Preliminary issue as to the maintain-ability of the suit cannot be decided before filing of written statement."

2) 4 MLR (AD) (1999) 426: "Maintain-ability of the suit can be determined at the time of trial and not under Order VII, rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure. Plaint cannot be rejected in limine under Order VII, rule 11 CPC on the question of maintainability of the suit."

3) 30 DLR (SC) 30: The Supreme Court has observed that if a court finds that a suit may be decided on the decision of an issue of law only, the court may try that issue first and may dispose of the suit. The court also observed that rule 2 of order XIV was an exception to general rule prohibiting disposed of a suit piecemeal.

The court further observed that special provision made in Order 14, rule 2 and Order 15, rule 3 form exceptions to the general rule prohibiting disposal of a suit piecemeal.

The main consideration underlying the general rule which deprecates piecemeal trial is to avoid a protracted litigation and unnecessary expenditure. The reason behind the special provisions of the Code which seek to give priority to the determination of certain issues before taking up the hearing of other issues appears to be also precisely the same namely, economy of time and expenses. These special provisions are contained in Order 14, rule 2 and Order 15, rule 3 of the Code and there is hardly any doubt that the main object behind these provisions is the shortening of time and the lessening of expenditure.

As we have already noticed, the provision of Order 14, rule 2 is clearly obligatory but under Order 15, rule 3 of the Code the Court has kind of discretion.

33. In the impugned judgments the learned Joint District Judge found that the suit is explicitly barred by Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972. To appreciate this findings, it will be profitable to quote the Article 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order 1972 which provides that—

"41.—(1) No suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against the Bank or any of its Officer for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of Article 36 or Article 37 or Article 38 or Article 39 or Article 40 or in pursuance of the provisions of Chapter IV.

(2) No suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against the Bank or any of its Officers for any damage caused or likely to be caused by anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of Article 36 or Article 37 or Article 38 or Article 39 or Article 40, or in pursuance of the provisions of Chapter IV."

34. The very words 'good faith' are the riders of Article 41 which are ultimately providing some sort of indemnity or liberty or exemption to the bank or its officers from any suit or legal proceeding for any kind of work or performance in pursuance of some provisions of law thereof done/carried out in course of duty. In no way, it restricts/prohibits/precludes/bars upon filing any suit or other legal proceedings in case of 'dispute' arising between the borrower and the creditor bank. Article 41 does not create any express or implied bar upon any relief or contents of a pleading. Thus reliefs prayed in the present suit are in no way barred under Article 41.

35. Definition of good faith is not given in the Bangladesh Bank Order. "Good Faith" as denified in section 3(20) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. "Section 3(20) Speaks: a thing shall be deemed to be done in "good faith" where it is in fact done honestly, whether it is done negligently or not." But it transpires that dispute in the suit does not come within the definition of good faith. It is a 'dispute' of civil nature which is to be adjudicated by adducing proper evidence and witnesses before the Court of law. But the learned trial court failed to appreciate this difference, and erroneously rejected the plaint on misconception of law by referring Article 41 of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972.

36. In this connection, we have carefully examined the decision reported in 17 BLC 653 as cited by the learned Advocate Mr Elen Emon Shah but the facts and circumstances of the above decision and instant case are completely distinguishable and, as such, this decision has no manner of application in the present case. Therefore, decision does not have any nexus because of the fact that same was passed in writ petition not in a civil suit. Moreover, this decision does not create any bar upon filing a civil suit by any person whose name is published in the CIB report.

37. At this juncture, it can be said that Article 41 does not create any bar upon any relief, and it has no application under Order VII, rule 11(d). The learned courts below totally failed to appreciate such important aspect of the case.

38. Order VII, rule 11 describes the procedure for rejection of plaint. It is necessary to quote Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads as under:—

"11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:—

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action;

(b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so;

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law.

[Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty-one days]

[(e) where any of the provisions of rule 9(1A) is not complied with and the plaintiff on being required by the Court to comply therewith within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so.]"

39. On a close reading of the aforesaid rule, it is evident that under five circumstances, a plaint shall be rejected:

a. where it does not disclose any cause of action;.

b. where the relief claimed is undervalued and the plaintiff fails to correct the valuation within the time fixed by the court:

c. where the plaint is insufficiently stamped and the plaintiff fails to put in requisite stamp papers within the time fixed by the court;

d. where from the statement in the plaint the suit appears to be barred by any law;

e. where any provisions of rule 9 (1A) is not complied with within the time fixed by the court.

40. It has been held in the case of Bangladesh Jatiya Samabaya Shilpa Samity Ltd. vs Shan Hosiety, Proprietor Md Abu Taleb, reported in 2004 (12) BLT (AD) 253 = 10 BLC (AD) 8, which is quoted below—

"With regard to rejection of plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court Division rightly found that in deciding the question as to whether a plaint is liable to be rejected the court is always required to peruse the plaint only and court is not permitted to travel beyond the plaint to dig out grounds to reject the plaint which is a settled principle of law."

41. While disposing of a case concerning rejection of plaint, Justice Fazle Munim, Chief Justice in paragraph No. 46 observed that—If the court does not even persue the plaint and rejects outright the door of arbitrariness is opened and whatever little right a citizen left with is reduced to shadow substances. Reference: 39 DLR (AD) 1.

42. Further, after scrutinizing the series of decisions of our Apex Court in respect of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, we may refer some of decisions reported in 39 DLR (AD) 1, 42 DLR (AD) 244, 49 DLR 531, 564, 53 DLR (AD) 62, 54 DLR (AD) 125 and 57 DLR (AD) 18 wherein the principles laid down as under:

(i) The well settled principle of laws relating to Order VII, rule 11 are the plaint can be rejected only on reference to plaint itself as whether it is barred in any of the four clauses of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

(ii) Plaint cannot be rejected on defense material as well as on mixed question of law and fact.

(iii) Where evidence is required and where there is material, plaint cannot be rejected.

(iv)Plaint can be rejected if it does not disclose a cause of action and barred by any law.

(v) There is no hard and fast Rule when an application for rejection of plaint is to be filed but ends of justice demands that it must be filed at the earliest opportunity.

(vi) Plaint cannot be rejected before filing of the written statement.

43. Now, let us consider whether the court can reject a plaint under section 151 under inherent power of the court even the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure are found not to be applicable.

44. In the case of Abdul Jalil vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Limited, reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12, it has been held that:—

"Now it is a well settled principle of law that if the continuation of the suit is found to be an abuse of the process of the court, if the suit is foredoomed or if the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as the day light, the suit should be buried at its inception by rejecting the plaint by invoking inherent powers of the Court provided under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

45. Further, on perusal of the facts of the present case, it appears to be distinguishable from the case reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12. In exceptional situation a plaint can be rejected under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure even if it does not come within the mischief of the Rule, but such situation is totally absent in the present case.

46. Before rejecting a plaint under Order VII, rule 11, it is desirable to give an opportunity to the plaintiff to remove the defect in the plaint. In a case reported in 58 DLR (AD) 219, the Appellate Division has observed that instead of straightway rejecting a plaint, the plaintiff should be allowed to remove any formal defect therein and suitably amend the plaint to make it maintainable and to get the relief in a single suit.

<u>47. A suit for declaration is maintainable under section 42 as, to any legal character or to any right as to any property of the plaintiff if the defendant denies or is interested to deny his or her title to such character or right. If the above conditions are satisfied, the plaintiff does not need to ask for any further relief than a mere declaration.</u>

<u>48. The concept of 'legal character' in section 42 is wide enough to include the status of a person. In order to entitle the plaintiff to bring a suit under section 42, 'it is riot necessary that the defendant should actually deny the plaintiff's legal, character. If the claim which might be sent up by the defendant is a hindrance to the plaintiff in the exercise of his or her rights or would expose him or her to liability if he or she disregarded, he or she might come to Court for a declaration that the claim so set up by the defendant was not well founded. Thus, 'legal character' denotes a personal and special right not arising out of contract or tort, but of legal recognition. For example, rejection of plaintiff's application for allotment may create legal recognition enforce-able against a person whose similar application is accepted.</u>

49. We have examined the plaint and considered the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate of respective parties, relevant provision of the Code of Civil Procedure, Bangladesh Bank Orders, 1972, Bank Companies Act, 1991 and decisions of our Apex Court very carefully.

50. It appears from the order sheet of the respective suits that after registration of the respective suits, and next date was fixed for maintainability of the suit and hearing temporary injunction matter. Ultimately, the learned Joint District Judge passed an order rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of maintainability. In the order, the learned Joint District Judge erroneously found that the suit is barred by law under section 41(1) of the Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972.

<u>51. We have already held earlier part of the judgment that the learned Joint District Judge acted most illegally in rejecting the plaint on the ground of maintainability on the assumption of facts which are not borne out by the plaint and also sanctioned by law. That the civil court has wide jurisdiction to examine whether the Bangladesh Bank rightly declared the appellants as loan defaulter and published their names in the CIB report and that matter should be decided by the trial court after framing issue on it.</u>

52. In the back ground of the discussions, relevant provisions of law involved in this suit and the decisions cited above, we are of the view that the learned Joint District Judge wrongly decided the question of maintainability and rejected the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. We therefore, find that the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the Fifth Joint District Judge, Dhaka cannot be sustained and same is liable to be set-aside.

53. In the result, all the appeals are allowed without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 10-7-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 298 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 20-5-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 284 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 103 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 5-5-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 248 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 24-7-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 380 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 24-7-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 381 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 111 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 20-2-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 112 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 05-5-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 250 of 2019, the judgment and decree dated 07-7-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 317 of 2019 and the judgment and decree dated 18-2-2018 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 91 of 2018 all are hereby set-aside and the connected Rules being Nos. Civil Rule 514(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 548(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 338(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 343(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 547(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 546(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 144(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 143(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 342(F) of 2019, Civil Rule 550(F) of 2019, are made absolute without any order as to cost.

54. Considering the facts and circumstance of the case the trial court is directed to proceed with the respective suits filed the plaintiffs-appellants in accordance with law.

55. Before parting with the judgment, to make it clear that this should not be taken as a licence by the trial courts to ignore the provision of Order XIV, rule 2 and similar provisions of Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Joint District Judge should be more careful in future and should not pass any order ignoring the mandatory provisions as contained in Order XIV, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the decisions passed by the apex Court, while passing any order on the question of maintainability of the suit.

56. Mr Sk. Tariq Ezaz, learned Joint District Judge, Fifth Court, Dhaka to comply with the direction made in the judgment to follow the procedure in the Code of Civil Procedure but it is matter of great regret that inspite of this the learned Joint District Judge ignore the mandatory provision of Order XIV, rule 2 and similar provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. It should be clearly understood that such omissions suggest that the learned Judge is inefficient therefore he is liable to be proceeded as per law. Now this is the only way to enforce strict compliance.

57. Let a copy of the judgment be sent immediately to the concerned court and a copy of the judgment also be communicated to the learned District Judge, Dhaka for ensuring strict compliance of the orders of the direction given above.

Send down the lower court record along with a copy of judgment at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 21-1-2014 (decree signed on 23-1-2014), passed by the Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj, in Title Appeal No.233 of 2010, allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 19-10-2010 (decree signed on 26-10-2010), passed by the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj, in Title Suit No.354 of 2006, decreeing the suit, should not be set-aside and/or pass such other order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts, relevant for disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that, one Md Solaiman and 2 (two) others, as plaintiffs, had filed Title Suit No.354 of 2006, before the court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj, against Md Hazrat Ali and 7 (seven) others, seeking declaration of title in respect of 16 annas property described in the schedule to the plaint and for correction of RS khatian No. 53 plot No 10 of Mouza Dighiborab PS Rupgonj, District-Narayangonj so far as it relates to entering the name of Md Fozor Ali and others. The case of the plaintiffs is that, the CS recorded owner of the suit plot was one Atorjan Bibi, who died leaving 2(two) sons 2(two) daughters namely, (1) Warif, (2) Abdul Gafur, (3) Atori Bibi and (4) Sabuja Bibi. The further case of the plaintiffs as stated in paragraph Nos. 3 to 5 of the plaint is that, the plaintiffs have derived title in the suit property measuring 0.1930 acres (19.30 decimals) of land out of 0.2900 acres (29 decimals) of land from the other heirs of CS recorded owners Atorjan Bibi excepting Warif @ Warish in the manner as described in paragraph No. 3 to 5 of the plaint. In paragraph No. 6, the plaintiffs described their cause of action for filing the suit.

3. On the contrary, the defendant Nos. 1-2 have contested in this suit by filing written statements on 28-8-2007 in which, they have denied all material allegations made in the plaint stating their case at paragraph No. 17 of their written statements. The crack of the defendant's case is that, admittedly Atorjan Bibi was the CS recorded owner of the suit property, but she died leaving only one son namely, Warish as the sole heir of the suit property and the said Warish (the sole heir of Atorjan Bibi as the version of the defendant's) had sold 0.29 acres of land (29 decimals) to Md Fozor Ali, vide registered sale deed No. 2068 dated 11-6-1936 (Exbihit E) and that SA and RS record have been prepared in the name of Md Fozor All and he, thus, become owner of the suit property, who had sold 0.1450 acres of land to one Abdul Malek, vide registered deed No. 4653 dated 19-12-1972 (Exbihit Kha). By another deed No. 6679 dated 24-4-1983, 0.0650 acres of land was sold to one Hasna Hena Dewan (Exbihit G) and by another deed No. 3420 dated 8-9-1982, 0.08 acres of land was sold to one Md Ibrahim Miah (Exbihit F). As such, Md Fozor All was sold his purchased 0.29 acre of land to above named 3 persons by the separate 3 deeds. The further case of the defendants is that, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have purchased the suit property from the above named Abdul Malek and f'rom Md Momin Uddin Dewan, vide registered deed No. 3512 dated 16-2-1984 and by another deed No. 3156 dated 14-3-2002 [Exbihit E(1)], while defendant No. 2 acquired title in respect of 0.1450 acre of land by virtue of purchase from above named Hasna Hena Dewan and Md Ibrahim Miah by 2 sale deed No. 6028 dated 13-4-1983 (Exbihit 1) and sale deed No. 3157 dated 14-3-2002 (Exbihit (F). Both the parties have adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases.

4. However, the trial court, after hearing the parties and assessing the evidence on record, by its judgment and decree dated 19-10-2010 (decree signed on 26-10-2010) decreed the suit against the defendant Nos. 1-2 and ex-parte against the rest, by the Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj.

5. Against the said judgment and decree of the trial court, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 preferred Title Appeal No.233 of 2010 before the District Judge, Narayangonj which was heard by the Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj, who being the appellate court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 21-1-2014 (decree signed on 23-1-2014), allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, the plaintiff-respondents-petitioners filed this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

7. The decision in this matter is to be taken mainly rest upon a single issue as to whether the CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi (admitted by both the parties) died leaving 2(two) sons 2(two) daughters namely, (1) Warif, (2) Abdul Gafur, (3) Atori Bibi and (4) Sabuja Bibi or only one son namely, Warish as her sole heir. If the defendant succeeded to prove that, the CR recorded owner died leaving only one son Warish as the sole heir, then the plaintiff has no case and evidence (both oral and documentary) would have no relevance to prove that they derived title from their bia through a chain of title developed from 2(two) sons and 2(two) daughters of the CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi namely, (1) Warif, (2) Abdul Gafur, (3) Atori Bibi and (4) Sabuja Bibi ( except Warish).

8. Learned Advocates Mr AFM Mesbah-uddin Ahmed, Mr Subrata Saha and Mr Kamal Hossain appeared for the petitioner. Having placed the petition along with oral and documen-tary evidences the learned Advocates first of all submit that, the plaintiffs have denied title from the heirs of a son from their bia, who got title from daughters of Abdul Gafur (one sons of CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi and from Saburun Nessa, daughter of Sabuja Bibi, one of the two daughters of the said CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi). Their further contention is that no record of right could be produced in the name of Warish (one of sons of CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi) as the case of the plaintiffs. Their further contention is that, although the name of their bia were rightly recorded in RS khatian No. 53, however, against RS plot No. 10, name of Md Fazor All and others as permitted by Abdul Malek has been wrongly recorded and that has created cloud in respect of title of the plaintiffs in the suit property, therefore, they have prayed for declaration of title in the suit property as well as the correction of wrong recording of name of Md Fazor Ali and others against RS plot No. 10 has been challenged other correction of the RS khatian No. 553, vide prayer Kha to the plaint. The learned Advocates submit that, the trial court has rightly discussed oral and documentary evidence on record and decreed the suit upon proper assessment of the case of the parties, but the appellate court, having failed to appreciate the case of the parties and assessing the evidence on record has passed the impugned judgment and decree and therefore, it has committed grave error of law causing serious prejudiced as regard the burden of proof. The learned Advocates has referred the decisions, reported in 54 DLR (AD) 26 between: Ishaque (Md) vs Ekramul Hague Chowdhury decision, reported in 1987 BLD (AD) 103 between: Chinibash Pramanik vs Nurul Hossain Mollah. They conclude that, this Rule has merit and the same may kindly be made absolute.

9. On the other hand, learned Advocates Mr Abdul Quayum with Mr Tapan Kumar Biswas with Mr Md Moklesur Rahman with Mr M Saifuddin Khokon with Mr Mohammad Golam Kibria, Advocates appeared on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2. Their main contention is that, there is no iota of evidence to prove the case of the plaintiffs that, the CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi died leaving 2(two) sons 2(two) daughters namely, (1) Warish, (2) Abdul Gafur, (3) Atori Bibi and (4) Sabuja Bibi as narrated in the plaint. Indeed, Atorjan Bibi died leaving only one son namely, Warish as the sole owner of the 16 annas property to the suit land. The learned Advocates very strenuously argued that invention of another son and 2(two) daughters namely, (1) Atori Bibi and (2) Sabuja Bibi of the CS recorded owner is totally absurd and false and also concocted story. They maintain that, this Abdul Gafur, Atori Bibi and Sabuja Bibi exists only in the pleadings of the plaintiffs, but not in reality. They pointed out that, the CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi died leaving only one son Warish, who is the owner of 0.29 acre of land (29 decimals) and had sold the same to Md Fozor Ali in the year 1936, vide registered deed No. 2068 dated 11-6-1936 (Exbihit E). The learned Advocates clarified that, since the kabala Exhibit-E was executed and registered in the year 1936, at that time SA operation did not took place and since the property was sold, therefore, the SA khatian No. 455 containing the suit plot No. 33 and others, name of Md Fazor Ali has been duly recorded in the name of Md Fazor Ali [Exbihit Ka(1)] and said Md Fazor Ali sold his 0.29 acre of land by 3(three) separate kabalas and by sale deed No. 4653 dated 19-12-1972 Exhibit Kha, whereby he has sold 0.1450 acre (14.50 decimals) of land to Abdul Malek and to Hasna Hena Dewan, vide registered deed No. 6679 dated 24-4-1983 Exhibit-G, whereby Md Fazor Ali had sold 0.0650 acre of land to one Md Ibrahim Miah, vide deed 3420 dated 8-9-1982 (Exbihit F) and he has also sold 0.08 acre of land to Abdul Malek Miah and Md Ibrahim Miah and by this way the defendant got title in the suit property, vide 3(three) sale deeds, marked as Exhibit E(1), Exhibit-I and Exhibit F(1), respectively. Their further case is that, 0.29 acre of land was acquired by the Government (both the parties admits) and the rest 20 decimals of land has been duly recorded in the RS khatian No. 53 of Mouza Dighibora of PS Rubgonj District: Narayangonj against RS plot No. 10 as recorded in the comment column of the said khatain along with the name of Md Fazor Ali and Abdul Malek. However, the learned Advocates for the OP Nos. 1 and 2 also submit that, since the plaintiff has filed a mutation case based on their fake deeds, false and baseless title, therefore, the defendant could have been filed a mutation case and the said case could not be finalized. But, this delay in getting mutation on the basis of mutation case does not confer title of the defendants as has been held by the High Court Division in a case, reported in 20 DLR 1019 Between: SM Lutfullah vs Bibi Badrunnessa and others, wherein it has been held that, "so far as the legality of the mutation effected, it is sufficient to state that this is merely an executive order which cannot confer title". The learned Advocates, therefore, sums up that, the facts and pleadings considered in the light of the entire evidence on record clearly shows that, the CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi died leaving only one son namely, Warish and the chain of title begun from Warish, which is stand and proved by the defendants, derived title of the suit property, which the appellate court has properly appreciated in its judgment. Similarly, the appellate court has also assessing the evidence on record independently allowed the appeal and reversed the findings of the trial court and in passing the impugned judgment and decree, the appellate court has committed no error of law and facts and there is no misreading of evidence or non-reading of evidence. They conclude that, this Rule has no merit and the same may kindly be discharged.

10. I have heard the learned Advocates for both sides, perused the application for revision, lower Court's record as well as the judgment of both the Courts below and other materials in the record.

11. I find that, there is no iota of evidence to prove the case of the plaintiff that, the CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi died leaving 2(two) sons and 2(two) daughters namely, (1) Warif, (2) Abdul Gafur, (3) Atori Bibi and (4) Sabuja Bibi as narrated in the plaint. Indeed, Atorjan Bibi died leaving only one son namely, Warish as the sole owner of the 16 annas property to the suit land. The invention of another son and 2(two) daughters namely, (1) Atori Bibi and (2) Sabuja Bibi of the CS recorded owner could not be proved by the plaintiffs. It also appears thar, Abdul Gafur, Atori Bibi and Sabuja Bibi exists only in the pleadings of the plaintiffs, but not in reality and the CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi died leaving only one son, named Warish, who is the owner of 0.29 acres of land (29 decimals) and had sold the same to Md Fozor Ali in the year 1936, vide registered deed No. 2068 dated 11-6-1936 (Exbihit E). The kabala (Exhibit-E) was executed and registered in the year 1936. At that time SA operation did not took place and since the property was sold, therefore, the SA khatian No. 455 containing the suit plot No. 33, name of Md Fazor Ali has been duly recorded, alongwith others [Exbihit Ka(1)], during SA operation and said Md Fazor Ali sold his 0.29 acre of land by 3(three) separate kabala and by sale deed No. 4653 dated 19-12-1972 (Exbihit Kha), whereby he has sold 0.1450 acre (14.50 decimals) of land to Abdul Malek and to Hasna Hena Dewan, vide registered deed No. 6679 dated 24-4-1983 (Exbihit G), whereby Md Fazor Ali had sold 0.0650 acre of land to one Md Ibrahim Miah, vide deed 3420 dated 08-9-1982 (Exbihit F) and he has also sold 0.08 acre of land to Abdul Malek Miah and Md Ibrahim Miah and by this way the defendant got title in the suit property, vide 3(three) sale deed marked as Exhibit E(1), Exhibit-I and Exhibit F(1). Their further case that, 0.29 acre of land was acquired by the Government (both the parties admits) and the rest 20 decimals of land has been duly recorded in the RS khatian No. 53 of Mouza Dighibora of PS Rubgonj District: Narayangonj against RS plot No. 10, recorded in the comment column of the said khatain alongwith the name of Md Fazor Ali and Abdul Malek. However, the plaintiff has filed a mutation case based on their fake deeds and baseless title; therefore, the defendant's mutation case could not be finalized. But, this delay in getting mutation does not confer title of the defendants as has been held by the High Court Division in a case, reported in 20 DLR 1019 between: SM Lutfullah vs Bibi Badrunnessa and others, wherein it has been held that, "so far as the legality of the mutation effected, it is sufficient to state that this is merely an executive order which cannot confer title".

12. These facts and pleadings considered in the light of the entire evidence on record clearly show that, the CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi died leaving only one son namely, Warish and the chain of title begun from Warish is consistent and duly proved by the defendant, who claims title of the suit property, which the appellate court has properly appreciated in its judgment. Similarly, the appellate court has also assessed the evidence on record independently and allowed the appeal and reversed the findings of the trial court and in passing the impugned judgment and decree, the appellate court has committed no error of law or of facts and there is no misreading of evidence or non-reading of evidence.

13. I also find that, the plaintiff has also failed to prove their title in the suit property by any credible evidence or any consistent chain of title and even the fact of existence of any heirs of CS recorded owner Atorjan Bibi, except her only son Warish.

14. I also respectfully accept the view of the High Court Division in a case, reported in 20 DLR 1019 Between: SM Lutfullah vs Bibi Badrunnessa.

<u>15. Before parting off, I must record that, the local Union Parishad Chairman has issued a certificate dated 25-8-2008 certifying that, the CS owner Atorjan Bibi had 2(two) sons and 2(two) daughters named therein. Mr Mahbubur Rahman Khan, Chairman, Tarab Pourashava, Rupgonj, Narayangonj was neither born during CS operation, nor he or the plaintiff could have furnished any basis for issuing such a certificate, which was not proved before the trial court, nor marked as exhibit by the court below. This kind of conduct of the concerned Chairman is clear abuse of power and this should be taken into the notice of Anti-Corruption Commission. As such, this is a fit case to refer the matter before the concerned Chief Judicial Magistrate for initiation of the criminal proceeding against him on the allegation of attempting to flout the course of justice. However, considering the prayer for the learned Advocate for the petitioner, this Chairman is let off with warning and he should be cautions in future in issuing such kind of certificate by abusing his public office.</u>

16. So far as the mutation case is concerned, it should be made clear that, the purpose of mutation case is to generate the new record of right, creation of new holding for the purpose of payment of tax to the Government. It is not a title deed.

17. In view of the deliberation, recorded above, I am of the considered opinion that, the impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate court suffers from no illegality because there is no misreading, or non-reading of any evidence on record. The appellate court, in passing the impugned judgment and decree, has committed no error of law, resulting in no error in the decision, nor occasioning any failure of justice.

18. This Rule has no merit and the same should be discharged.

Order

In the result, the Rule is discharged.

The impugned judgment and decree dated 21- ]-2014 (decree signed on 23-1-2014), passed by the Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayangonj, in Title Appeal No.233 of 2010, is hereby affirmed.

The order of status-quo granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

No costs.

Let a copy of this judgment along with the Lower Court's Record be sent down to the concerned Courts at once.

Copies of the judgment and order be sent to the Deputy Commissioner, Narayangonj and UpziIIa Nirbahi Officer, Rupgonj, Narayangonj for information and record, and to take initiative, if they have any scope.

End.

parties:
Tanveer Foods Ltd------Appellant  
Vs 
Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal Dhaka and others--------Respondents
full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J: Since all the appeals involve identical point of law based on similar facts and the parties are also same as such we are disposing of the appeals by this common judgment.

2. Brief facts are that the appellant is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act and engaged, amongst others, in the business of importing whole Milk Powder and marketing the same in local market. In course of its business, the appellant opened letter of credit Nos. 154210020015, 154210020016 and 154210020014 all dated 19-8-2010 for importation of 99.925 MT instant Full Cream Milk Powder from Australia, 99.925 MT instant whole Milk Powder from New Zealand and 200 MT instant Whole Milk Powder from New Zealand respectively under HS Code No. 0402.21.90 at the rate of US$ 2,370, US$ 2,375 and US$ 2,370 per metric ton respectively.

3. After arrival of the goods at Chittagong Port, the importer through its C&F agent submitted bills of entry No. 147790 dated 9-11- 2010, 140406 dated 25-10-2010 and 147799 dated 9-11-2010 respectively to release the goods imported under the aforementioned letters of credit as per invoice value. But Customs Authority assessed the goods at the rate of US$ 3,150.00 per MT vide Nothi No. AP/Sec-1/10-11. Under compelling circumstances, the importer released the goods on protest as per assessment of the Customs Authority and thereafter filed three separate appeals before the respondent No.2, Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal) against arbitrary assessment of the customs authority. Upon hearing the parties and perusing relevant papers/documents, Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal) allowed the appeals and directed customs authority to assess the goods at invoice price by his order dated 15-12-2010.

4. Being aggrieved, the Commissioner of Customs (Import) Customs House, Chittagong, respondent No.4 herein, preferred three separate appeals before the Customs, Excise 'and VAT Appellate Tribunal. After hearing the parties and perusing relevant papers/ documents, the Tribunal consisting of two members differed in opinion. Member (Technical) allowed the appeals by setting aside order passed by the Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal) but Member (Judicial) dismissed the appeals and thereby affirmed findings of the Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal). Since members are equally divided in their opinion, president of the Tribunal referred the appeals to another member for hearing and disposal as per provision of section 196(5) of the Customs Act. After hearing the parties and assessing relevant papers/documents, third member concurred with the decision passed by Member (Technical) and thus allowed the appeals by setting aside orders passed by the Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal).

5. Having aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the Tribunal, the appellant moved before this court under section 196D of the Customs Act.

6. Mr Mizanul Haque Chowdhury learned advocate appearing for the appellant in all the appeals submits that customs authority imposed inflated value ignoring invoice value without following provisions of Valuation Rules, 2000 framed under section 25 read with section 219 of the Customs Act but Tribunal without considering provisions of valuation Rules passed the impugned judgment and order which is liable to be set aside. He also submits that it is apparent from the bills of entry that customs authority assessed the goods on the basis of pre-determined value by the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong, beyond the scope of law but Tribunal without considering this legal aspect erroneously passed the impugned judgment and order which is liable to be set aside. He next submits that Tribunal failed to consider that though Valuation Rules, 2000, mandates that assessing authority shall follow the rules sequentially but in the instant case customs authority in violation of said mandate assessed the goods arbitrarily and whimsically as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. He again submits that Tribunal failed to consider that customs authority assessed the goods applying the method prescribed in rule 9 of the valuation Rules without applying rule 4 to 8 though Valuation Rules, 2000, mandates to determine value of the imported goods applying prescribed methods sequentially as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. He further submits that the customs authority arbitrarily imposed inflated value without affording an opportunity of hearing to the importer-appellant to produce evidence in support of invoice value and thus provisions of Valuation Rules, 2000, as well as principles of natural justice are violated as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. In support of his submissions, learned advocate referred to the case of Collector of Customs vs TK Oil Refinery Ltd and 22 other, reported in 62 DLR (AD) 217; the case of Amirul Islam (Md) vs Commissioner of Customs, reported in 18 BLC 77; the case of Transcom Cables Limited vs The Commissioner of Customs, Customs House (Import), Chittagong, reported in 18 MLR 97 and an unreported judgment passed by this Division in Writ Petition No.1138 of 2000 (M/s Shah Dairy Products Ltd. vs The Commissioner of Customs and others).

7. On the other hand, Mr Pratikar Chakma learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.4 by filing additional evidence swearing affidavit submits that customs authority assessed the goods on the basis of contemporary data base value which was affirmed by the Tribunal in accordance with law as such, there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and order. He also submits that customs authority assessed the goods on the basis of contemporary data base value to stabilize market of the country regarding milk powder with a view to create level playing field for all the traders of same product as such Tribunal legally and justly passed the impugned judgment and order. He further submits that the appellant has not come with clean hands to seek redress before this court because the appellant after releasing the goods on the basis of assessment by the customs authority sold the product to end users/consumers with profit and thereafter filed appeal for furtherance of its profit but the end users/consumers are the ultimate losers as such the appeal should be dismissed.

8. Heard learned advocate for the appellant and learned Deputy Attorney-General for the respondent No. 4. Perused the paper book and papers/documents contained therein along with additional evidence filed by the respondent and citations referred by the learned advocate for appellant.

9. Admittedly, customs authority assessed the goods ignoring invoice value declared by the importer. We have gone through the relevant bills of entry annexed in the paper book. It appears from the bills of entry that there is an endorsement in the bills of entry in the following manner:

মাননীয় কমিশনার মহোদয়ের আদেশ মোতাবেক Loaded Value US$ 3,150 per MT হিসাবে Adj. 1.3293 তে বি/ই শুল্কায়ন করা হলো (Bill of Entry No. C-147790 dated 9-11-2010)

মাননীয় কমিশনার মহোদয়ের নথি নং-৫৬৫/এপি/সেকশন-১/১০-১১/মোতাবেক প্রতি মেঃ টন US$ 3,150 হিসাবে শুল্কায়ন করা বি/ই তে এডজাস্ট করা হলো । (বি/ই নং ১৪০৪৬০ তারিখঃ ২৫-১০-২০১০ ইং)

মাননীয় কমিশনার মহোদয়ের নথি নং-৫৬৫/এপি/সেকশন-১/১০-১১/মোতাবেক প্রতি মেঃ টন US$ 3,150 হিসাবে শুল্কায়ন করা বি/ই তে এডজাস্ট করা হলো । (বি/ই নং ১৪৭৭৯০ তারিখঃ ৯-১১-২০১০ ইং)

<u>10. This court time and again directed the customs authority to determine value of the imported goods after considering contemporary international market price by giving an opportunity to the importer to place evidence in support of declared/invoice value and not assess the goods attributing adjective such as commissioner value, loaded value, recorded value etc. which has no sanction of law. Section 25(2) of the customs Act provides that subject to the provisions of sub-section (1), the price referred to in that sub-section in respect of imported goods shall be determined in accordance with the rules made in this behalf.</u>

11. Section 219 of the Act empowers National Board of Revenue to frame rules and accordingly National Board of Revenue vides SRO No. 57 framed Valuation Rules, 2000 providing methods to apply in deterring value of the imported goods. Valuation Rules, 2000, is a guideline for the assessing authority to follow strictly in determining value of the imported goods. Rule 3 of the valuation Rules mandates that methods prescribed in Valuation Rules shall be followed sequentially. In many of the cases, this court directed customs authority to follow the rules strictly in sequential manner which should be reflected in the relevant nothi of customs authority. The apex court of the land in line with earlier decisions directed customs authority to afford the importer an opportunity of hearing to place his case in support of invoice value. Relevant portion from the judgment passed by our Appellate Division in the case of Collector of Customs vs TK Oil Refinery Ltd. and 22 others, reported in 62 DLR (AD) 217, is reproduced below:

"the learned Attorney-General sub-mitted that the fixation of normal value in every case of imports upon notifying the individual importer would be an impossible task and, as such, for the sake of convenience, the revenue authority has fixed the value of the imported merchandise at a prior date through the Circular dated 3-7-94 for making the same as the basis for assessment of the customs duties in disregard of the invoice value, but the above submission cannot be accepted because in fixing the citizen with the liability of payment of tax, the concerned authority is required by strict compliance of law authorizing it to fix a citizen with the liability of payment of tax and the plea of impossibility of fixation of the normal value of the imported merchandise in the case of each individual importer upon hearing him or that upon affording him an opportunity to place his case, if any, in support of the invoice value, cannot be accepted and the respondents, under the law, cannot be allowed to resort to the practice of pre-fixation of the value of the imported goods for assessment of customs duties in that the Government or any other agency authorized by the delegated legislation cannot act in a manner which is not authorized or provided in the law or by the law".

<u>12. Submission made by the Deputy Attorney General that the ultimate losers are end users/consumers of the product merits consideration. It is true that a section of traders by taking recourse of unethical process such as under invoice, over invoice import goods for personal gain. It is also true that because of such unethical process the market becomes unstahilized and small traders face difficulty to compete in the market. Big traders with their large capital try to establish monopoly in the market by abolishing marginal traders which not only create imbalance in the economy of the country but also affect the end users/ consumers who are compelled to buy the essential product with a high price from a syndicate monopolizing market of a particular product/item. But sitting in this jurisdiction in dispensation 'of justice, we cannot go beyond law framed by the legislators as such this court time and again directed the customs authority to follow the Rules, in this particular case, Valuation Rules, 2000. We are aware of the volume of work in the customs house but inspite of that in a civilized society we have to follow the rules framed under the law as such the assessing authority is required to record notes in assessing the imported goods at least briefly in one or two lines which will reflect that the law and rules has been followed. Otherwise, it is difficult for the court to do justice in the context of socio-economic condition of the country.</u>

13. Under the facts and circumstances of the case, and for the reasons stated above, the appeals being Nos. 155 of 2013, 154 of 2013 and 156 of 2013 are allowed with the observation made above.

14. Judgment and order dated 19-3-2013 passed by the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka, under Nothi No. CEVT/Case (Cus)-245/2011; Nothi No. CEVT/Case (Cus)-240/2011 and Nothi No. CEVT/Case (Cus)-254 /2011 are hereby set-aside.

Send down records to the Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka, along with a copy of this judgment at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Fatema Najib J: These First Appeal No. 212 of 2009, First Appeal No. 230 of 2009, Transfer Appeal No. 1 of 2014 and Transfer Appeal No. 2 of 2014 are directed against the judgment and decree dated 30-11-2008 passed by learned Joint District Judge, Third Court, Sylhet in Title Suit No. 51 of 2001, Title Suit No. 93 of 2014 and Title Suit No. 52 of 2001 which were heard analogously and now are being disposed of by this single judgment.

2. The respondent Nos. 1-3 of First Appeal No. 212 of 2009 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 32 of 1997, in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Golapgonj, Sylhet impleading principal respondents Nos.4 and 5 as principal defendant Nos. 1 and 2, pro-forma respondent Nos. 6 and 7 as pro-forma defendant Nos. 3 and 4, Abdus Sattar, the predecessor of appellants Nos. 1 and 2 as the defendant Nos. 5 and appellants Nos.3-13 as 6-16 Nos. defendants for redemption of mortgage and khas possession in respect of 0.34 acres of land as described in schedule to plaint. Subsequently, it was transferred to the Joint District Judge Third Court, Sylhet and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 51 of 2001. The respondent No. 3 Pulin Ram Malakar died during the pendency of appeal and his legal heirs have been duly substituted. The plaintiff No.1 Gakul Ram Malakar of Title Suit No. 32 of 1997 (re-number as 51 of 2001) died during the pendency of the suit and his legal heir Nikhil Ram Malakar has been duly substituted as plaintiff No. 1(ka).

3. The appellant Nos. 1 and 2 of Title Appeal No. 147 of 2009 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 14 of 1994 in the Court of Joint District Judge, First Court, Sylhet impleading Abdus Sattar, the predecessor of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 as defendant Nos. 2, respondents Nos.3-12 as defendants Nos. 3-12, Seraj the predecessor of respondent Nos. 13-17 as defendant No. 13, the respondent Nos. 18 to 24 as defendant Nos. 14-20 praying for partition in respect of 0.7 acres of land as described in schedule 1, declaration of right, title and interest in respect of second schedule property to the plaint. It may be mentioned that the heirs of Abdur Rahman who are also appellants in this Title Appeal No.147 of 2009 were added as plaintiffs 3-7 in the original suit by order No.144 dated 18-11-2008. During pendency of the suit the defendant Nos. 13 and 16 died whose legal heirs has been duly substituted. Subsequently, it was transferred to Joint District Judge, First court, Sylhet and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 93 of 2014. The said Title Appeal No.147 of 2009 was ultimately transferred to the High Court Division by Order dated 14-5-2012 passed in Civil Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 2010 and re-numbered as Transfer Appeal No.1 of 2014.

4. The heirs of Seraj (defendant No.13) of the said Title Suit No. 14 of 1994/93 of 1994 as appellants filed First Appeal No. 230 of 2009 against the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 as pro-forma respondent Nos. 4, 5 and the defendants Nos. 19-20 as pro-forma respondent Nos. 6 and 7, the defendant Nos. 3-12, and 15 as respondent Nos. 8-16, Gakul Ram Malakar, the predecessor of the defendant No.16, the defendant Nos.17 and 18 as principal respondents 1-3.

5. The appellant No. 2, the predecessor of appellant No. 1, the predecessor of appellant Nos. 3-6 of Title Appeal No.108 of 2009 as plaintiff Nos. 1-3 instituted Title Suit No.15 of 1994 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Golapgonj, Sylhet impleading the respondents as defendants Nos. 1-22 for declaration of title by adverse possession for more than 12 years of the statutory period, correction of record in respect of first schedule to plaint as shail in place of canel and Khas possession in respect of second Schedule to plaint. Subsequently, it was transferred to the Sub-Judge, Third Court, Sylhet and re-numbered as Title Suit No.52 of 2001. The said Title Appeal No.108 of 2009 was transferred to the High Court Division by Order dated 14-5-2012 passed in Civil Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 2010 and re-numbered as Transfer Appeal No. 2 of 2014.

6. The case of the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 32 of 1997/51 of 2001 who are the defendant Nos.16-18 of Title Suit No.14 of 1994/93 of 1994 is that Gagan Ram Malakar, Raman Ram Malakar, and Avoy Ram Malakar who are successive owners by in-heritance of the suit land and subsequently executed and registered a sale deed on 24-4-1952 corresponding to 11-1-1359 BS in favour of Jahir Ali, (the predecessor of the defendant Nos.1 and 2) receiving Taka 100 as consideration money in respect of suit land and on the same date Jahir Ali executed a registered Ekrarnama in favour of the aforesaid Gagan Ram Malakar and others in respect of the same suit land promising to reconvey the suit land to the vendors on repayment of the consideration money within, 30th chaitra, 1361 BS. The transaction was not a sale, it was a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period of 7 years in accordance with the provisions of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and after the expiry of 7 years it was redeemable by operation of law. The plaintiffs on several times requested the defendants to redeem the mortgage by receiving the consideration money. But the defendants refused to comply on the end of Bhadra, 1400 BS. Hence the plaintiff is constrained to file the present suit.

7. The heirs of Jahir Ali that is Md Manik Mia and Mst. Sabiya Begum the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 14 of 1994/93 of 1994 who are the defendant Nos.1 and 2 of Title Suit No.32 of 1997/51 of 2001 in brief their case is that Raman Ram Malakar, Gagan Ram Malakar and Ador Ram Malakar were owners of the first schedule land and while possessing the first schedule land Raman Ram Malakar and his two aforesaid brothers sold the first schedule land to Jahir Ali, (the predecessor of the plaintiffs) on 24-4-1952 corresponding to 11 Baisakh 1359 BS through a saf kabala. After getting the scheduled land they paid rent regularly to Zamidar. The core issue in this appeal is that whether the Deed No. 719 dated 24-4-1952 and reconveyance deed No.720 dated 24-4-1952 (Exhibit-X, X(I) are the basic documents upon which the parties claimed their respective title is complete usufructary mortgage or treated to be mortgage under section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and whether the deed in question is attracted to section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.
