“........... ইয়াদি কির্দ্দ ১) রমন রাম মালাকার, ২) গগন রাম মালাকার, ৩) অভয় রাম মালাকার, সাং-ফুল বাড়ী, পং-বরায়া, জাতি-হিন্দু, পিতা-মৃত-চরন রাম মালাকার, ব্যবসা-গৃহসি, জিলা-সিলেট, থানা-গোলাপগঞ্জ বরাবরেষু লিখিতং জহির আলী, পিতা-মৃত সাং-কাজন, সাং-টাকর বাড়ী পং বরায়া, জাতি-মোসলমান ব্যবসা গৃহস্থি, জিলা-সিলেট, থানা-গোলাপগঞ্জ ৷ অদ্য একরারনামা পত্র মিদং, জিলা-সিলেট, থানা-গোলাপঞ্জ। সিলেট সদর সাব রেজিষ্ট্রার সাহেবের এলাকাধীন আমি অদ্য তারিখে তোমাদের নিকট হইতে নিম্নের তপসীলের লিখিত পরগণা ও মৌজা ও মহাল ও কিত্তা সংক্রান্ত মোঃ/১।৪ এক কেদার এক পোয়া চারি জষ্টি জমি বাৎসরিক মং ৪, চারি টাকা খাজনায় মং ১০০ এক শত টাকায় খরিদ করিয়াছি সেমতে আমি অত্র একরারনামা পত্র লিখিয়া দিয়া একরার করিতেছি। সে অদ্য হইতে আগামী সন ১৩৬১ বাংলার ৩০শা চৈত্র তারিখের মধ্যে মদি উপরের লিখিত অজয় মালের মং ১০০, একশত টাকা তোমরা কি তোমরার অভাবে তোমাদের উত্তরাধি কি আমার অভাবে আমার উত্তরাধিকে ফেরত দেন তবে আমি কি আমার উত্তরাধিকারী উক্ত জমা জমি তোমার কি তোমাদের উত্তরাধিকে অজয় মালীর উক্ত মং ১০০, এক শত টাকা গ্রহণ পূর্বক কবলা সম্পাদন করিয়া জমা জমি আপন দখল হইতে ছাড়িয়া দিব। ও তোমাদের দস্তখত অদ্য তারিখের লিখিত কবলা সাক্ষরও সাক্ষী আবদুর রহিম সাং দাড়িপাতন পং বরায়া (২য় ফর্দ) খানা ও তোমাদিগকে ওয়াপেশ দিব, আর যদি উপরের লিখিত ম্যায়াদ মধ্যে অজয় মালীর টাকা ফেরত দিতে না পারেন তবে উক্ত জমাজমি ফেরত দিবায় । কোন প্রকার দাবী কোন আদালতে কি কোন পঞ্চায়তে চলিবে না, এতদর্থে সদজ্ঞানে সুস্থ শরীরে থাকিয়া অত্র একরারনামা পত্র লিখিয়া দিলাম। ইতি ২৪-৪-১৯৫২ মোঃ ১২-১-১৯৫৯ বাংলা তপসীল চতুঃ সীমানা পং বরায়া মৌজা ফুলবাড়ীস্থিত ৬২৮৮/১০ নং তাং মাং হুসন সংক্রান্ত মং ৪, চারি টাকার খাজনা মুক্ত জুত জমির সীমানা ১। কিন্তে জমির তল কেঃ জঃ। ৪৫৭৮ দাগ পুঃ সড়ক পং জুত এজমালী উং বিক্রি ২ দাগের জমি দং জুত বৈকুন্ট রামমালী এহাতে মোং০।। ২ দুঃ কমলা রকম ভূমি ২। কিত্তে এ কেং জঃ ৪৫৭৯ দাগ পুঃ সড়ক পং জুত করম আলী উং সড়ক দং বিক্রিত ১ দাগের জমি ও জুত ব্রজ মালী এহাতে মোং দ২ দুঃ ফসল রকম ভূমি মোট মোঃ......”

33. It appears from the recital of those documents that:

i) Sale deed, ii) separate registered re-conveyance deed, the period of repayment for 3 years i. e. 30th Chaittra 1361 BS, iii) Possession was delivered.

34. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates, now we can look into the definition of "Treated to be mortgage" under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

95A Treatment of certain transaction as usufructuary mortgage—

Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, any transfer of a holding or of portion or share thereof, 2[either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey,] 3[or] where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of such holding or portion or share thereof for a specified period in lieu of such consideration, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding seven years and the provisions of section 95 shall apply to such transfer whether made before or after the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Second Amendment) Order, 1972] (President's Order No. 88 of 1972).

35. On careful reading the registered saf kabala deed dated 24-4-1952 corresponding to 11-1-1359 BS (Exhibit-X) and the deed of reconveyance on the same date (Exhibit-X-(1), it appears that the predecessors of the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.32 of 1997/51 of 2001 sold the suit property i.e. 1 Kader, 1 powa 4 jaista in local measurement to Jahir Ali, father of defendant Nos.1 and 2 of said suit with a condition of re-purchase of the same within 3 years that is 30th chaittra 1361 corresponding to 24-4-1956.

36. The learned Advocate Mr Khair Ezaz Maswood, argued that an out and out sale accompanied by an agreement for reconveyance is within the purview of the Presidents Order Nos. 88 and 136 of 1972 and No.24 of 1973 whereby provisions of section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act have been amended and a new section being section 95A has been inserted in the said Act. The Presidents Order No.88 of 1972 came into effect on 3-8-1972 (PO No.136 of 1972) and the condition giving right of repurchase having expired the sale became a past and closed transaction and on the same reason the plaintiffs are not entitled for redemption of mortgage of the suit land. In this respect he referred the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD), 233.

37. We have gone through the decision reported in 32 DLR, 233. It appears that in that Writ Petition No. 85 of 1974 along with good number of Writ Petitions were heard analogously. The facts of the said Writ Petition was that the respondent No.1 purchased the land from the respondent No.3 with an agreement to reconvey the said land. The agreement was dated 26-4-1963 which stipulated that the land will be reconveyed if the money is repaid within 10 years. The respondent No.3 i.e. mortgagor made an application before Sub-Divisional Magistrate for restoration of the mortgaged property under section 9(4) and 9(5) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and same was allowed on 30-3-1973. Then the said writ petitions were filed challenging the section 95A of the aforesaid Act which were made absolute and against the said judgment appeals were filed. It has been held by Appellate Division in their judgment that: "Our conclusions, therefore, are that the President's Order Nos.88 and 136 of 1972 and No.24 of 1973 are all valid legislation for affecting necessary amendments in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and those laws cannot be attacked on the ground of ultravires. (2) any transfer of a holding or part thereof by a raiyat either way of out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period of maximum 7 years and the provisions of section 95(4) and (5) shall apply to such transfers; (3) and such transfers are not to be understood in the light of the Transfer of Property Act because those are to be understood in the light of the enactment in question: (4) those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to recovery, made whether before or after the promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972: and (5) as for the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed."

38. Though the facts and circumstances of the cited case and the present case are different,

but the decision made to the effect that the transaction which were not alive, at the promulgation of Presidents Order No. 88 of 1972 on 3-8-1972 is within the mischief of doctrine past and closed, that is similar to present transaction that the deed in question being No.719 dated 24-4-1952 was not alive on 3-8-1972 at the promulgation of President Order No.88 of 1972.

39. On the contrary, the learned Advocate Sadananda Rana having referred the decisions reported in 34 DLR (AD) 258, 12 MLR (AD) 329, 52 DLR (AD) 152, and 36 DLR 90 submits the deed in question being No. 719 dated 24-4-1952 with an registered agreement No. 720 dated 24-4-1952 is an out and out sale with a condition to reconvey is a complete usufructuary mortgage.

<u>40. On scrutinize those decisions, the sale deed of the cited cases reported in 34 DLR (AD) 238, 52 DLR (AD) 133 and 12 MLR (AD) 329 is by one single document wherein the condition embodied to reconvey on certain date. But the pr6sent transaction is not made by a single document but the deed in question is out and out sale with an separate registered agreement deed to reconvey within 3 (three) years which expired long before the promulgation of Presidents Order No. 88 of 1972 on 3-8-972. The sale deed of the cited case reported in 36 DLR 90 was registered on 20-5-1970 as well as a registered agreement was executed with condition to reconvey within 10 years which means the transaction was alive on 3-8-1972 at the promulgation of President Order No. 88 of 1972. So, those citations referred by the learned Advocate for respondents of First Appeal No. 212 of 2009 have no nexus with the facts and circumstances of the present case.</u>

<u>41. Therefore Exhibit-X, X(i) coupled with section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233, 16 BLD (AD) 210 = 1 BLC (AD) 90, 1 BLC (AD) 164 clearly proved that the deed in question being No.719 dated 24-4-1952 with registered agreement deed being No.720 dated 24-4-1952 treated to be mortgage but since the transaction was not alive on 3-8-1972, at the promulgation of President Order 88 of 1972, the said transaction is not hit by section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

42. Therefore, we find the trial court held the deed in question being No.719 dated 24-4-1952 with an agreement to reconvey being 720 dated 24- 4-1952 constituted a complete usufructuary mortgage for a maximum period of 7 years based on totally misconception of law and facts. So, the decree passed by the trial court for re-deemption of mortgage and khas possession in favour of the plaintiffs of Title Suit No.32 of 1997/51 of 2001 is erroneous.

43. Similarly in Title Suit No.15 of 1994/52 of 2001 the plaintiffs claimed title on the basis of the sale Deed No.719 dated 24-4-1952 (Exhibit-X) and reconveyance Deed No. 720 dated 24-4-1952 (Exhibit-X-(1) is not proved mortgage at all under section 58 of Transfer of Property Act and the learned trial court rightly dismissed the said suit. Though the trial court dismissed the suit on different findings that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title and possession over the suit land and also failed to prove the dispossession from the suit land. So, we can easily rely on the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD), 233 which has been subsequently followed in the decision reported in 16 BLD (AD) 210 = 1 BLC (AD) 90, 1 BLC (AD) 164.

44. In Title Suit No.14 of 1994/93 of 1994 the heirs of Jahir Ali, Md Manik Mia and Sabiya Begum sought for partition in respect of 0.7 decimals of land as described in First Schedule of land and declaration for 0.02 decimals as described in second Schedule land to the plaint. Manik Mia as PW 1 in Title Suit No. 93 of 1994 in his chief stated:

“………… এই নালিশী ভূমি আমার পিতার খরিদা ভূমি এক কেদার ১ পোয়া ৪ জষ্টি। ইহার মধ্যে ৩৩ শতক বিক্রিত। অবশিষ্ট ভূমি আমি এবং আমার চাচাত ভাইরা যৌথভাবে ভোগ দখলে আছি……. ২ শতক জায়গা সি এন্ড বি এর নামে রেকর্ড হইয়া গেলেও আমরা ভোগ দখলে আছি।”

44. It is important to note that the second schedule land is from Tikorbari Mouja. But the lands of the deed in question being No.719 dated 24-4-1952 situated in Fulbari Mouja. But the present dispute between the parties in respect of land of Fulbari Mouja. So, the land of second schedule has no nexus with the land of Fulbari Mouja which arises the dispute between the parties. On the other hand, the land of second schedule property is unspecified as there is no boundary. Therefore, declaration for unspecified land is not maintainable and further no averment was made in the plaint to show the date of dispossession.

46. The plaintiff No.1, Manik Mia, (son of Jahir Ali) admitted in his deposition that they had no title over 0.2 decimals out of 0.7 decimals. So, in this respect without praying for declaration of title, the suit for partition over 0.7 decimals is not maintainable. Moreover, Md Manik Mia, son of jahir Ali categorically stated in his chief that they sold 0.33 decimals. Thus it is evident that the second schedule land is from different Mouja which is not disputed in the suit and without declaration of title, the relief sought only for partition in respect of 0.7 decimals is not maintainable and the trial court rightly dismissed the suit.

47. The defendant Nos. 5-16 of Title Suit No.32 of 1997/51 of 2001 claimed they purchased 29.875 decimals by Exhibit-খ২,গ৩,ঘ৪,ঙ৫,চ৬, from Jahir Ali. On perusal of those Exhibits it appears by Exhibit- খ২,গ৩,ঘ৪,ঙ৫,চ৬, an area of land is 0.0425, 0.0625, 0.0625, 0.0550, 0.0550 respectively in total 28.75 decimals of land were purchased. Gokul Ram Malakar the plaintiff  No.1 of Title Suit Nos.32 of 1997/51 of 2001 and 15 of 1994/52 of 2001 admitted in cross stating that Jahir Ali sold his maximum property to Abdur Rahman and others. It may be mentioned that defendant Nos.7-16 of Title Suit No.32 of 1997/51 of 2001 are heirs of Abdur

Rahman, the defendant Nos.5-6 are Abdus Sattar and his wife. Manik Mia as PW 1 of Title Suit No.32 of 1997/5 of 2001 in cross admitted that his father sold those lands. Thus it is proved that defendant Nos.5-16 became owners of total 28.75 decimals of land through purchase by Exhibits, খ২,গ৩,ঘ৪,ঙ৫,চ৬, respectively from Jahir Ali, father of plaintiff.

48. Having regard to facts and circumstances, we are of the view that the deed being No. 719 dated 24-4-1952 upon which parties are claiming their respective title, the trial court on misconception of law and facts most illegally held the said deed is out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey constituted to be usufructuary mortgage for 7 years and on that basis decreed the Title Suit No. 51 of 2001 for redemption of mortgage and khas possession. Since we have found that heirs of Jahir Ali failed to prove the suit for partition over 0.7 decimals, and 0.2 decimals for declaration of title which is situated in different mouja and unspecified that has no nexus with the present claim, so the trial court rightly dismissed the Title Suit No. 93 of 1994 and Title Suit No. 52 of 2001.

49. In the result the First Appeal No. 212 of 2009 is allowed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 30-11-2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Sylhet decreeing the Title Suit No.32 of 1997/51 of 2001 is set aside and the suit is dismissed.

50. First Appeal No. 230 of 2009 is allowed with modification that the deed in question being No. 719 dated 24-4-1952 is treated to be a mortgage but since the said deed is not alive on 3-8-1972 at the time of promulgation of Presidents Order No. 88 of 1972 is not hit under section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.

51. Transfer Appeal No.1 of 2014 and Transfer Appeal No.2 of 2014 are hereby dismissed without order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 30-11-2008 are confirmed.

Send down the lower court records along with a copy of this judgment at once.

End.

full_judgment:
SM Maniruzzaman J : In this Rule Nisi, issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the respondents have been called upon to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 29-10-2013 passed under Nothi No. S/4181 /Aa:/ Mongla/12-13/5090(1) by the respondent No. 3 on behalf of the respondent No. 2 (Annexure-F) demanding Taka 5,62,60,670.73 from the petitioner as customs duties should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and hence, of no legal effect; and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. At the time of issuance of the Rule, further operation of the impugned order dated 29-10-2013 passed under Nothi No. S/4181/ Aa:/Mongla /12-13/5090(1) by the respondent No. 3 on behalf of the respondent No. 2 (Annexure-F) was stayed by this Court for a prescribed period.

3. Facts, necessary for disposal of the Rule, in short, are that the petitioner is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994. In course of business it decided to set up an ultra-modern condensate refinery plant under the name and style "Petromax Refinery Ltd" in order to refining, bottling, drumming, transporting, selling, and marketing of all sorts of edible oil including petroleum. The petitioner company duly registered its name with the VAT authority under the Value Added Tax (VAT) Act, 1991 (in short, the Act of 1991) for the purpose of payment of VAT and since its registration it has been paying VAT regularly. It has also been registered with the Board of Investment (in short, BOI) on 19-8-2009 having registration No. L-170309080361-1. However, the Bol by its letter dated 19-8-2009 permitted the petitioner to import machinery, equipment, components and materials to set up a complete automatic condensate refinery plant.

4. After obtaining permission from the government and completing all necessary formalities as required under the law, the petitioner opened a Letter of Credit being No. 086213020075 dated 18-4-2013 to import condensate (Crude oil) from Malaysia under HS Code No. 7209.00.00. After arrival of the goods at Mongla Port, Khulna, it, however, collected shipping documents from its respective bank and submitted Bill of Entry being No. C-4338 dated 29-5-2013 enclosing those documents through its Clearing and Forwarding (C&F) agent for assessing and releasing the same. After submission of Bill of Entry, the imported goods were inspected by the concerned Customs authority and found that the goods were in accordance with declaration. Pursuant thereto the respondent Customs authority made assessment of the goods on 3-6-2013 and upon payment of all customs duty, taxes and other charges those were released in favour of the petitioner and accordingly, it took delivery of the same.

5. Suddenly, the respondent No. 2, the Commissioner of Customs issued the impugned demand notice on 29-10-2013 upon the petitioner demanding Taka 5,62,60,670.73 with request to deposit the said amount within 10 (ten) days, failing which action would be taken under section 202 of the Customs Act, 1969 (in short, the Act of 1969).

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid demand notice the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule Nisi with interim order of stay.

7. The respondent No.2, the Commissioner of Customs entered appearance by filing affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alia, that after 4 (four) months from the date of release of the goods an audit was conducted by the Customs authority and it was found that the previous assessment was made by the Customs authority on the basis of the declaration of the petitioner in its Bill of Entry without following the provision of law.

8. It has been stated further that the invoice value of the petitioner's imported goods was higher than its tariff value and the petitioner was liable to pay customs duty and taxes on the basis of invoice value as per provision of section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 and that the amount of public money was undisputed and was demanded on the basis of the petitioner's invoice value.

9. Considering the context of the case the Rule is liable to be discharged.

10. Countering, the aforesaid assertion of the respondent No. 2, the petitioner submitted affidavit-in-reply on 6-11-2008 contending, inter alia, that the petitioner has executed an agreement with Bangladesh Petroliam Corporation on 17-9-2012 to supply petroleum product and the tariff value of the goods has been fixed by the Government by Gazette notification. Moreover, the petitioner was not allowed to supply its imported goods to any other authority other than Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation.

11. It has been stated that the Government exercising the power as conferred under section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 promulgated SRO No. 159-Ain/2012/2387/Customs dated 7-6-2012 fixing the tariff value of different types of goods under different HS Codes and therein, the Government also fixed the unit of specified goods. Wherefrom it is apparent that the tariff value of the petitioner's imported goods was fixed at the rate of USD $ 32 per barrel (in short, BBL).

12. It has been stated further that the Second Secretary (Customs, Policy and Budget), National Board of Revenue passed an order on 25-8-2014 under Nothi No. ০৮.০১.০০০০.৫৩.০৩.০০৯.১৪/৫৫৩(১) informing all the concerned stating, inter alia, that the Government of Bangladesh, after special consideration and for the general interest of the people has taken a decision to exempt any customs duty and VAT on the additional value e. declared invoice value and the tariff value for all petroleum and petroleum-related goods as per section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 and that the aforesaid decision shall have retrospective effect covering from 9th June, 2005. Said decision is still pending for publication in the Gazette notification.

13. In this regard it has been stated that in the year 2014, the petitioner imported similar kinds of goods and those were assessed on the basis of tariff value and were accordingly released by furnishing bank guarantees for the differential amount. But, the Customs authority did not make final assessment within the prescribed period in law. The petitioner in the year 2018, however, filed writ petition No. 7329 of 2018 before this Hon'ble Court seeking direction upon the respondent Customs authority to return the bank guarantee which was furnished by the petitioner at the time of releasing the goods treating the provisional assessment as final as per section 81(2) of the Act, 1969. Upon hearing of the said writ petition, this Hon'ble Court vide order dated 28-5-2018 issued a Rule Nisi with direction upon the Customs authority to maintain status-quo in respect of encashment of the bank guarantees. Against the said interim order, the National Board of Revenue filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2616 of 2018 before the Hon'ble Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Said Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal was ultimately dismissed on 12-7-2018. The Rule of the said writ petition is still pending for hearing and disposal.

14. Conversely, the respondent No. 2 submitted supplementary affidavit to the affidavit-in-opposition on 10-12-2018 con-tending, inter alia, that pursuant to letter dated 25-8-2015 issued by the Second Secretary, National Board of Revenue (Annexure-Y to the Affidavit-in-reply), a summary was placed before the Hon'ble Minister, Ministry of Finance for approval and the same was ultimately approved. However, prior to publication of the notification in the official Gazette, it was sent to the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for vetting.

Accordingly, said Ministry after vetting furnished an opinion that there was no scope to exempt the said taxes and duties as per the law and further made opinion to take legal steps for recovery of the government revenue in accordance with law.

15. Ms. Shamima Binte Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner by placing the writ petition and the relevant materials on record at the very outset submits that section 32(3) of the Act, 1969 provides the provision for realization of short levied taxes, duties and other charges by reasons of inadvertence, error or misconstruction through issuing show cause notice but, the impugned demand was made for short levied taxes and duties without issuing any show cause notice in violation of section 32(3) of the said Act. She further goes to submit that without amending the assessment under section 83A of the Act, 1969, the respondents have no authority to re-open the assessment file under which the goods had already been assessed and released; consequently, the impugned demand is absolutely illegal and liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority. She again goes to argue that the petitioner being a citizen of Bangladesh has fundamental right guaranteed under Article 27 of the Constitution to be treated equally and its right to be treated in accordance with law and only in accordance with law, as, has also been guaranteed under Article 31 of the Constitution. But, the Customs authority without following the provision of law issued the impugned notice upon the petitioner demanding the additional duty and taxes. Accordingly, she finally canvasses that issuance of the impugned notice being illegal and without jurisdiction is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and hence, of no legal effect.

16. In order to substantiate her contention the learned Advocate has relied upon the decisions of the case of SK Akijuddin Ltd. Vs National Board of Revenue reported in 16 BLC 692, the case of Md Musa Bhuiyan vs The Commissioner of Customs, Dhaka reported in 23 BLC 663, and an unreported decision of the case of Jalal Uddin vs National Board of Revenue, in Writ Petition No 1144 of 2006 (we are the parties of the said judgment).

17. Per Contra, Mr Shamsuddoha Talukder, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2 referring to section 25(3) of the Act submits that said provision of law provides that when the declared value of any imported goods is higher than its tariff value the customs duties and taxes shall be chargeable on the basis of its declared value and the respondent Customs authority issued the impugned notice demanding the actual customs duty and taxes following the said provision of law. He further goes to submit that the impugned demand has been made on the basis of admitted declared invoice value of the petitioner and giving opportunity of time to pay the demand amount, as such there is no requirement to issue any show cause notice for realization of the admitted government revenue. Hence, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

18. We have heard the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 2, have perused the writ petition, the affidavit-in-opposition and the affidavit-in-reply with relevant materials on record so have been appended thereto and relevant provisions of law.

19. As it appears that the petitioner opened a Letter of Credit bearing No. 086213020075 dated 18-4-2013 for US $ 75,00,000 to import 10,000 Metric Ton condensate (Crude oil) under HS Code No. 2709.00.00 from Malaysia (Annexure-B). Accordingly, the supplier made part shipment of the goods i.e 5,562.185 Metric Ton out of 10,000 Metric Ton equivalent to 46308.00 BBL at the rate of US $ 112.643 per BBL, total invoice value of goods US$ 52,16,272.04 (as evidenced vide Annexure-C). After arrival of the goods at Mongla port, lamina, the petitioner, however, collected its shipping documents from its bank and generated Bill of Entry through its C&F agent and submitted the same to the Customs authority vide Entry No. C-4338 dated 29-5-2013 as per section 79 of the Act 1969 for assessment and releasing the goods (Annexure-D).

20. For the purpose of the assessment, the value of imported crude oil under HS Code No. 2709.00.00 was fixed by the government at the rate of US$ 32.00 per barrel (BBL) by publishing notification in the official Gazette vide SRO No 159-Ain/2012/12387 Customs dated 7-6-2013 (Annexure-X to the affidavit-in-reply) under section 25(3) of the Act. For ready reference sections 25(3) and 79 are quoted below:-"Section 25(3):, Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, fix, for the purpose of levying customs duties, tariff values (or minimum values) for any goods imported or exported as chargeable with customs duty ad valorem: Provided that any imported or exported goods, the declared value of which is higher than its tariff value fixed under this sub-section, shall be chargeable with customs duties on the basis of its declared value.

(4)

(5)

(6)

"Section 79:—Entry for home-consumption or ware housing: (1) The owner of any imported goods shall make entry of such goods for home-consumption or warehousing or for any other approved purpose by delivering to the appropriate officer a bill of entry thereof in such form and manner and containing such particulars as the Board may direct: Provided that, if the owner makes and subscribes a declaration before the appropriate officer to the effect that he is unable, for want of (such information as is essential for submitting a bill of entry), then the said officer shall permit him, previous to the entry thereof, to examine the goods in the presence of an officer of customs or to deposit such goods in a public warehouse appointed under section 12 without warehousing the same, pending the production of such information."

21. Vide section 25(3) of the Act the government for the purpose of levying customs duties and taxes may fix tariff or minimum values for any imported or exported goods as chargeable with customs duty advalorem. But, when the declared value of any imported or exported goods is higher than its tariff value the Customs duty and taxes shall be chargeable on the basis of declared value.

22. Section 79 of the Customs Act provides that the owner of any imported goods within specified period as provided under this section shall make entry of such goods or entry in electronic form by delivery to the appropriate office a Bill of Entry duly signed by him or his authorized agent thereof in such form and manner containing such particulars, as the Board may direct or the such information and documents as the Commissioner of Customs may specified.

23. Following section 79 of the Act, the petitioner had generated its Bill of Entry (Annexure-D) mentioning tarrif value of the goods in Box No. 22 US$ 1332592.00 (as per tariff value per BBL US $ 32) and accordingly, took delivery of the goods upon payment of customs duty and taxes being assessed by the Customs authority on the said tariff value. But, it appears from the petitioner's commercial Invoice (Annexure-C) that the actual transaction invoice value of the goods was US$ 52,16,272.04. (unit price 112.643/BBL) which was the actual value of the imported goods and that the said value was not denied by the petitioner before the respondent Customs authority or before this Court. Moreover, the invoice value of the goods i.e. US$ 52,16,272.04 is higher than its tariff/minimum value US$ 13,32,592.00. Accordingly, in view of section 25(3) of the Act when the declared value of any imported or exported goods is higher than its tariff value, the customs duties shall be chargeable on the basis of its declared value. Under the above legal position Cue petitioner was liable to pay customs duty and taxes chargeable on its declared invoice value at US$ 52,16,272.04, but it made payment upon the tariff value at US$ 13,32,592.00.

24. However, the respondent No. 2, the Commissioner of Customs under the signature of the respondent No. 3 has issued the impugned demand letter dated 29-10-2013 stating, inter alia, that—

“০১। সূত্রঃ বি/ই নং-৪৩৩৮, তারিখঃ ২৯-৫-২০১৩ ইং।

উপযুক্ত বিষয়ে আলোকে জানানো যাচ্ছে যে, বি/ই নং-৪৩৩৮, তারিখঃ ২৯-৫-২০১৩ পর্যালোচনা করে দেখা যায় যে, আমদানিকৃত পণ্য চালান CONDENSATE (crude Oil) এর Value তে শুল্কায়ন করা হলেও পণ্য চালানটির Invoice Value Tariff Value এর চেয়ে বেশি হওয়া। The Customs Act, 1969 এর sec-25(3) মোতাবেক Invoice Value ১১২ মাঃ ডলার/ব্যারেল হিসেবে প্রতি কেজি CONDENSATE এর মূল্য ০.৯৩২৪ মাঃ ডলার ধরে শুল্কায়ন করলে পার্থক্য জনিত আদায়যোগ্য শুল্ক-করাদির পরিমাণ দাঁড়ায় ৫,৬২,৬০,৬৭০.৭৩।

২। এমতাবস্থায়, কম আদায়কৃত শুল্ক-করাদি বাবদ ৫,৬২,৬০,৬৭০.৭৩ (পাঁচ কোটি বাষট্টি লক্ষ ষাট হাজার ছয়শত সত্তর দশমিক সাত তিন) টাকা আগামী ১০ (দশ) কার্যদিবসের মধ্যে মংলা কাষ্টমস হাউসের সরকারী কোষাগারে জমা প্রদানের জন্য অনুরোধ করা হলো। অন্যথায়, The Customs Act, 1969 এর sec-202 মোতাবেক আইনানুগ ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করা হবে।”

25. Said impugned demand notice has been challenged by the petitioner on the assertion that without issuing any show cause notice or giving opportunity of being heard, the concerned respondents Customs authority in violation of section 32(3) of the Act has issued the same demanding less payment of customs duty to the tune of Taka 5,62,60,670.73 (five crore sixty two lac sixty thousand six hundred seventy taka and seventy three paisa) on the difference customs duty and taxes between the invoice value and the tariff value.

26. For better understanding the relevant provisions of section 32 of the Act, 1969 is quoted herein below: "32. Untrue statement, error, etc.—(I) If any person, in connection with any matter of customs,—(a) make or signs or causes to made or signed, or delivers or causes to be delivered to an officer of customs any declaration, notice, certificate or other document whatsoever, or (b) makes any statement in answer to any question put to him by an officer of Customs which he is required by or under this Act to answer, [or] (c) transmits any statement, document, information or record through electronic device or produces soft copy thereof, And such document or statement is untrue in any material particular, he shall be guilty of an offence under this section. (2) Where, by reason of any such document or statement as aforesaid or by reason of some collusion, any duty or charge has not been levied or has been short-levied or has been erroneously refunded, the person liable to pay any amount on that account shall be served with a notice, requiring him to show cause why he should not pay the amount specified in the notice. (3) Where, by reason of any inadvertence, error or misconstruction, any duty or charge [amounting to not less than one thousands taka] has not been levied or has been short-levied or has erroneously refunded the person liable to pay any amount on that account shall be served with a notice, within [three years] of the relevant date, requiring him to show cause why he should not pay the amount specified in the notice. (4) The appropriate officer, after considering the representation, if any, of such person as is referred to in sub-section(2) or sub-section (3) shall determine the amount of duty payable by him which shall in no case exceed the amount specified in the notice, and such person shall pay the amount so determined [Provided that where the amount so determined is less than one thousand take, the person concerned shall not be required to make the payment.] (5) For the purposes of this section, the expression "relevant date" means—(a) in any case where duty is not levied, the duty on which an order for the clearance of goods is made; (b) in a case where duty is provisionally assessed under section 81, the date of adjustment of duty after its final assessment;

(c) in a case where duty has been erroneously refunded, the date of its refund;

(d) in any other case, the date of payment of duty or charge."

27. Section 32 (2) and (3) of the Customs Act, 1969 empowers the Customs authority to demand any customs duty and other charges which has not been levied or shortly levied or erroneously refunded from the person liable to pay the said amount but prior thereto a show cause notice must be served requiring the person concerned to show cause as to why he should not be asked to pay the amount specified in the notice.

28. Sub-section (4) of section 32 provides that the appropriate officer after considering the representation, if any. of such person as is referred to in sub-sections (2) or (3) shall determine the amount of duty payable by him and such person shall pay that amount so determined.

29. It appears from a plain reading of section 32 (2), (3) and (4) of the Act that for determination of actual duty and taxes, which has not been levied or shortly levied or erroneously refunded from the person, the show cause notice must be served. In the present case, the amount of duty has been demanded by the respondent No. 2, the Commissioner of Customs by the impugned demand notice after computing the duty and taxes on the basis of declared invoice value of the petitioner as per provision of section 25(3) of the Act and that said value has not been denied by the petitioner as well as the Customs authority. As such, prior to making demand of the admitted amount does not require issuance of show cause upon the petitioner.

30. Furthermore, Section 202 for the Act empowers the Customs authority to demand any duty to any person, which amount is payable to the government by any person. For ready reference the relevant provision of section 202 is quoted below; 1202.Recovery of Government dues.—(1) When, under this Act, any duty or regulatory duty is payable to the Government by any person or a penalty is adjudged against any person or a notice or demand is served upon any person calling for the payment of any amount unpaid which may be payable by way of duty, regulatory duty, penalty or under any bond, security, guarantee or any other instrument executed under this Act or the rules or orders and such duty, regulatory duty, penalty or other sums due are not paid within the time it was required or ordered to be paid , the appropriate officer may at any time—(a) deduct, or require any other officer of customs to deduct, the amount so payable from any money owing to such person or due which may be in the hands or at the disposal of, or under the control of, the customs authorities or of such officer or of the Government; (b) stop clearance of any goods belonging to such person from customs control in the sea port, airport, any other customs station or from bonded warehouse till such amount is paid or recovered in full;

(c) (d) (e)

(f) (2) (3)

31. It appears from the section 202 of the Act that when any person is liable to pay any duty or regulatory duty to the Government under this Act or a penalty is adjudged against any person or notice or demand is served upon any person calling for the payment of any amount of unpaid duty. regulatory duty,  penalty under this Act or the rules or orders and such duty or other sums due are not paid within the time it was required or ordered to be paid, the Customs officer may at any time take any action as provided under sub-section 1(a) to (f).

32. The impugned demand notice has been issued by the concerned respondent Customs authority with request to deposit Taka 5,62,60,670.73 to the Government treasury within 10 (ten) days, which amount the petitioner is liable to pay under section 25(3) of the Act, failing which action under section 202 of the Act would be taken against it. In view of our above observations and findings, the impugned demand appears to have been issued in due compliance of the provisions of the Customs Act, 1969.

33. Another assertion of the petitioner is that whether the impugned demand notice issued by the concerned respondent Customs authority was in violation of the rules of principle of natural justice i.e. a man shall not be condemned unheard and without having the opportunity of making his defence i.e. audio alteram pertem, since the impugned notice has been issued upon the petitioner without giving opportunity of being heard.

34. What is natural justice, in this question the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Dev Dutt vs Union of India reported in AIR 2008 Supreme Court 2513 paragraph No. 2 observed as under;

"The rules of natural Justice are no codified nor are they unvarying in all situations, rather they are flexible. They may, however, be summarized in one word fairness. In other words, what they require is fairness by the authority concerned. Of course, what is fair would depend on the situation and the context."

35. In Russel vs Duke of Norfolk (1949) All ER 109, 118, the Court held that; "The rules of natural Justice must depend on the circumstances of the case, the natural of the inquiry, the rules under which the authority is acting and the subject matter that is being dealt with."

36. We are in agreement with the above observation that the rules of natural justice depend on the situation, context and circumstances of each case.

37. However, in the instant case, no additional amount of duty or any penalty or fine has been imposed upon the petitioner while issuing the impugned demand. Rather, the actual duty and taxes so assessed earlier was on admitted declared value of the petitioner and that as per proviso to section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 the same has been demanded by the Customs authority giving opportunity to pay the said amount of duty and taxes within 10 (ten) days of receipt of the notice. So, it cannot be said that without giving reasonable time for payment of admitted outstanding duty and taxes, the demand has been made; hence, the impugned demand is very much consonant with Section 202 of the Act, 1969. Moreso, the admitted amount of liability need not be adjudicated by hearing of the party.

38. In the case of SK Akijuddin Ltd. vs National Board of Revenue, reported in 16 BLC 692, the case of Md Musa Bhuiyan vs The Commissioner of Customs, Dhaka reported in 23 BLC 663, and an unreported decision of the case of Jalal Uddin vs National Board of Revenue, in writ petition No 1144 of 2006 (supra), as referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, the Customs authority issued the notices demanding to pay additional customs duties and taxes changing the importer's declared HS Code or enhancing invoice value after conducting post clearance audit. While resolving the said dispute this Court has observed inter-alia, that since the demand was not preceded prior to show cause notice as provided under section 32(2)(3) of the Act, 1969 such demand cannot be said to have been made with lawful authority. Even for making any demand under section 83A of the Act, 1969 the principles of natural justice should be applied.

39. In the present case, the notice of demand has been issued on the basis of assessment so made on the declared invoice value of the petitioner, not changing of H.S Code or enhancing the invoice value. Hence, the facts and circumstances of the present case is distinguishable from the cases so referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and hence, not applicable.

40. On perusal of the supplementary affidavit to the affidavit-in-opposition and the affidavit-in-reply, it appears that the National Board of Revenue on considering the request of Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation as well as the petitioner company had tried to resolve the issue of exemption of additional duty, taxes and VAT on the additional value pertaining to the tariff value following the provision under section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 giving retrospective effect from 9th June 2005. The summary of the said proposal was placed before the Hon'ble Minister, Ministry of Finance for approval and by publishing the notification in the official Gazette. But, before publishing the Gazette, it was sent to the Ministry of Law Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for vetting. However, after vetting the Hon'ble Minister gave opinion, that there was no scope to exempt duty and taxes under the existing law.

<u>41. In view of the said context, the petitioner is liable to pay the admitted unpaid duty and taxes under the Act, 1969 which it cannot avoid to pay on the plea of technicality of law that prior to issuance of the impugned demand, no show cause notice under sections 32 or 83A of the Act, 1969 was served thus, committed violation of the principles of natural justice.</u>

42. Considering the above facts and circumstances of case, observations and findings, we find no substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

43. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order as to costs.

44. The impugned order dated 29-10-2013 passed under Nothi No. S/4181 /Aa:/ Mongla/12-13/5090(1) by the respondent No. 3 on behalf of the respondent No. 2 (Annexure-F) demanding Taka 5,62,60,670.73 from the petitioner as customs duties and taxes is hereby declared to have been passed with lawful authority.

45. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated and recalled.

46. The petitioner is hereby directed to pay the long outstanding Government revenue to the concerned respondents within a period of 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment and order; failing which the respondent concern is at liberty to realise the said amount in accordance with law.

Communicate the copy of the judgment and order to the concerned respondents forthwith.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozibur Rahman Miah, J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic in Bangladesh, a Rule Nisi was issued calling in question the imposition of VAT on the Private English Medium Schools as contained in এস.আর.ও.নং-১০৮-আইন/২০১৪/৭০৩-মুসক dated 5-6-2014 under Service Code No. S069 by the National Board of Revenue.

2. At the time of issuance of the said Rule, the operation of the impugned এস.আর.ও. contained in এস.আর.ও.নং-১০৮-আইন/২০১৪/৭০৩-মুসক, so far as it relates to imposing VAT on the private English Medium schools, was stayed for a period of 6 (six) months.

Background of issuance of the Rule

3. The salient facts so figured in the writ petition are as under:

The petitioners are the parents whose children have now been studying in two English Medium Schools in Dhaka. A daughter of petitioner No. 1 is a student of class VII at Sunbeams School, located at Ashulia, Dhaka and the petitioner No. 1 has to pay the tuition fee plus VAT at the rate of (shortly, (4)) 7.5% on that tuition fees. Similarly, the daughter and a son of the petitioner No. 2 have also been studying in class XII and II, respectively, at Sunnydale School, Dhanmondi, Dhaka, and he has also to pay tuition fees along with VAT @ 7.5% on the tuition fees. The copies with regard to payment of tuition fees along with above mentioned rate of VAT has been annexed in the writ petition as Annexure-A and A-1 respectively.

4. As per the provision of section 3 of the Value Added Tax Act-1991 (briefly "the VAT Act") Schedule No. 1 and 2 have been appended therein where it has prescribed the products and services upon which VAT is to be levied as well as exempted. The said provision (schedule) is also amended from time to time by which goods and services are included and excluded from the scheme of paying VAT and up to the year 2012, all Private Educational Institutions enjoyed exemption from paying VAT, which is evident from Annexure-C and C-1 to the writ petition respectively.

5. By virtue of power conferred upon the National Board of Revenue (shortly, "the Board") under section 5 and section 72 of the VAT Act, it (the Board) promulgated a Statutory Regularity Order (shortly, SRO) being SRO No.108-Ain/2014/703-Mushak dated 5-6-2014 imposing VAT @ 7.5% on the monthly tuition fees payable by the Private English Medium Schools.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said imposition of VAT, the petitioners as a parents of their school going children to their respective English Medium schools as aforementioned, came before this Court and filed this writ petition challenging the validity of such imposition of VAT vide the said SRO and obtained the instant Rule and order of stay, as has been stated herein above.

7. During the course of hearing of this writ petition, the petitioners on 24-11-2016 also filed a supplementary affidavit.

8. In the supplementary affidavit, the petitioners further stated that, the Board had also imposed VAT @ 10% through SRO No. 123- Ain/2015 /729-Mushak dated 4-6-2015 on Private Universities and Private Medical and Engineering Colleges under Service Code No. "S070 S070.10 and S070.20" respectively. But subsequently on 1-7-2015, the Board amended the said SRO reducing the said rate of VAT and fixed it 7.5% by issuing another SRO No. 221- Ain/2015/740-Mushak dated 1-7-2015 and the petitioners also annexed those two SROs as Annexures-G and G-1 respectively.

9. It has further been stated in the said supplementary affidavit that, being infuriated by such imposition of VAT, the students of the Private Universities and Private Medical as well as Engineering Colleges of the country, started launching large scale protests demanding cancellation of such VAT on their tuition fees to be paid by the concerned Private Universities and Medical and Engineering Colleges and the said movement, at a certain point, paralyzed Dhaka city on10-9-2015 and again on 13-9-2015 and 14-9-2015 respectively.

10. Bowing down to such protest, the Board was then compelled to withdraw such VAT on the tuition fees of the Private Universities as well as Private Medical and Engineering Colleges by issuing a Special Order being No. 12 /Mushak/2015 dated 14-9-2015.

11. Thereafter, the Internal Resources Division of the Ministry of Finance, vide SRO No. 176-Ain/2016/752-Mushak dated 2-6-2016 totally exempted such institutions from paying VAT in compliance of section 14(1) of the VAT Act and thereby cancelled the earlier "special order" being No. 12/Mushak/2015 dated 14-9-2015, which is also evident from Annexure-H and H-l respectively to the supplementary affidavit.

Submission advanced by the learned counsel for the petitioners

12. Mr. Shahdeen Malik along with Mr. Md. Monzur Alam, the learned counsels appearing for the petitioners upon taking us to the writ petition, supplementary affidavit as well as other materials on record at the very outset submits that, the fundamental principles of the State Policy, as enshrined in Articles 15 and 17 of our Constitution, ensures basic necessities and free and compulsory education to the citizen of the country and State is mandated by the Constitution to take all effective measures to attain and establish those basic necessities to ensure a literate and educated citizenry by giving effect of those fundamental principles, but the impugned imposition of VAT on a certain types of schools is totally contrary to such principles.

13. The learned counsel then submits that, the above principles so enumerated is Articles 15 and 17 of the Constitution, prohibits the state from taking any measures which is detrimental to the right to acquire education by the people and, as such, the imposition of VAT upon English medium school is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

14. The learned counsel goes on to submit that, under Article 19 of the Constitution, the State stands guarantee of ensuring "equal opportunity" to its citizens and this very principle proscribes the state from taking any action which leads to inequality to a particular group or class of citizen. Thus, levying of VAT only upon the Private English Medium Schools, which are being paid ultimately by the parents of the students of those schools, totally negates the principles of 'equality of opportunity' and, as such the said imposition of VAT on the Private English Medium School is without any lawful authority.

15. So far as it relates to the infringement of fundamental rights guaranteed to the citizen of the country, the learned counsel very stoutly asserts that, our sacred constitution, by Articles 27 and 28, guarantee that, all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law meaning, it forbids discrimination in acquiring education and, as such, imposition of alleged VAT only on the Private English Medium School keeping aside all other public and private educational institutions is violate of that fundamental rights guaranteed by our constitution and therefore, the imposition of VAT only upon a particular section of institutions is totally contrary to that fundamental rights to be enjoyed by a citizen and the same is without any lawful authority.

16. The learned counsel further submits that, the very withdrawal of VAT from Private Universities, Engineering and Medical Colleges in its entirety and keeping it in place only on the Private English Medium Schools is patently discriminatory, arbitrary and violate of the universal principle of equality which signify glaring discrimination among the educational institutions in the country and as such, the imposition of alleged VAT is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

17. The learned counsel next asserts that, merely medium of education epso facto should not be any criterion that can ever embolden the Government to impose VAT only on a particular category of schools.

18. The learned counsel also points out that, by imposing VAT upon a certain class of schools, the Government has clearly made a sharp classification in the education system which clearly contradicts the express provision enunciated in Article 17 of our Constitution which demands that State shall adopt effective measures to produce properly trained and motivated citizen.

19. The learned counsel for the petitioners wrapped up his submission contending that, with a malafide intention, the Government has just singled out a certain class of citizens by bringing them into the network of VAT by keeping aside a vast portion of educational Institutions from the clutches of VAT and, as such, on the face of the very discriminatory action, the imposition of VAT is palpably illegal and without any lawful authority and it is liable to be struck down. On such submission, the learned counsel finally prays for making the Rule absolute and strike down the impugned SRO, so far as its relates to imposition of VAT on the private English Medium Schools.

20. However, in countenance of his submission, the learned counsel has also relied upon a slew of decisions. In the first place, the learned counsel has referred to the case of Manzil Morshed vs Bangladesh, reported in 15 BLC 351. The learned counsel then placed his reliance in the case of Chairman, National Board of Revenue vs Advocate Zulhas Uddin Ahmed, reported in 18 BLC (AD) 52 and lastly, Mr Malik has referred a decision passed in the case of M/s AA Engineering Ltd. vs University of Khulna reported in 3 ALR (AD) 139 = 66 DLR (AD) 19.

The case of the Respondent No.2 and contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General

21. Now let us go through the case so have been made out by the Respondent No.2. In order to contest said Rule, the National Board of Revenue, as Respondent No. 2, entered its appearance by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition denying all the material statements made in the writ petition contending, inter-alia, that, the Government has imposed VAT upon the private English Medium Schools, on the total received money by issuing SRO No. 189- Ain/2008/491-Mushak, dated 29-8-2008 but has not imposed VAT on the student of the institutions because VAT shall be payable @ 15% by the suppliers in case of manufacturing of goods and that of the service providers as per section 3(1) of the VAT Act. Aside from that, the National Board of Revenue, in exercise of power conferred upon it under section 72 read with section 5(4) of the Act, assumes the authority to issue notification from time to time and accordingly, the Board, by issuing SRO No. 108-Ain/2014/703-Mushak, dated 5-6-2014 imposed VAT upon the English Medium Schools under Service Code No. S069.00. And in doing so, this Respondent has not violated any provision of VAT Act by realizing the same @ 7.5% on the tuition fees which the school authority is liable to pay.

22. It has further been stated in the Affidavit-in-Opposition that, the Board imposed VAT upon the authority of English Medium Schools by issuing SRO No. 189-Ain/2008 /491- Mushak, dated 29-8-2008, but not under SRO No. 108-Ain/2014/703-Mushak, dated 5-6-2014, so the impugned SRO is not any new imposition of VAT rather continuation of earlier imposition.

23. It further depicts from the Affidavit-in-Opposition that, upto the year 2000, private Educational Institutions, as service providers, were in the exemption list as referred in the 'Second Schedule' of the VAT Act and it was subsequently amended in the year 2015. However, these private Educational Institutions have not been included in the exemption list as outlined in the Second Schedule for which the English Medium School cannot claim to be exempted in paying VAT to the Government.

24. It has also been stated in the Affidavit-in-Opposition that, under section 72 read with section 5(4) of the VAT Act, the Board exercises the power to issue notification and accordingly, it issued a notification duly notified in the official Gazette vide SRO No. 108-Ain/2014/ 703 Musak dated 5-6-2014 imposing VAT under Service Code No. S069 having no illegality in it.

25. To controvert the assertion so contended by the petitioners as regards to the discriminatory actions so taken by the Government against the English Medium Schools, it has been stated in the Affidavit-in-opposition that, the Non-Government Bengali Medium Schools and Colleges are not the institutions run for commercial purpose, and a Managing Committee/Governing body, duly elected by the guardians of the students of such schools or colleges, use to run their respective Institution under the syllabus and curriculum prescribed by the National Curriculum and Textbook Board of Bangladesh and for that, the respondents has not imposed any VAT or tax upon those Bengali Medium Schools and Colleges.

26. With regard to the Constitutional Provision alleged to have been infracted by imposing VAT so asserted by the learned counsel for the petitioners, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, (shortly-'DAG') on the contrary, avers that, under Articles 15 and 17 of the Constitution, the State guarantees the basic necessities and compulsory education to the citizen of the Republic and on the strength of such mandate, the State has established many Government Primary and Secondary Schools and Colleges and has been providing various grants to those institutions whereas, the English medium schools have not been set-up through any statute and follows foreign syllabus and guidelines and hence, no contravention of Articles 15 and 17 of the constitution has ever been made.

27. It has asserted further that, admittedly the students of English Medium Schools got themselves enrolled with the schools and those schools takes permission form the Government for imparting education, but those schools are solely run commercially and follows Inter-national Curriculum & Syllabus and therefore, the Respondents has not violated the provision of Articles 15, 17 & 19 of the Constitution by imposing VAT.

28. Again, it has been stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that, the English Medium Schools are registered under the VAT Act-1991 and they are not exempted from paying VAT as per schedule-2 of the VAT Act and therefore, those schools are bound to pay VAT under section 3 of the Act.

29. The learned DAG further adds that, English Medium Schools have been providing teaching service in a commercially motivated manner and, as such, they have been paying VAT since 2002. However in 2012, the rate of such VAT was fixed at 4.5% of the total received imposed under SRO No. 182-Ain/2012/640- Mushak dated 7-6-2012, but from June, 2014, the said rate of VAT has been enhanced to 7.5% under the impugned SRO and there has been no inequality in so doing.

30. Lastly, the learned DAG asserts that, the writ petitioners have got no lucus standi to file the writ petition because none of the English Medium Schools who were supposed to become aggrieved for imposing VAT have filed this writ petition because the VAT has been imposed upon the schools and not on the parents or the students of the English Medium Schools.

31. The learned DAG, in support of such submission, has also relied upon several decisions, namely the case of Bangladesh Indenting Agent Association vs Bangladesh, reported in 64 DLR 389, and the case of Shat Dairy Products Ltd vs Commissioner of Customs, reported in 5 BLC (AD) 160.

32. Apart from those submission and citations, the learned DAG also asserts that, the point of discrimination as has been raised by the petitioners is not sustainable as the Universities and Colleges from which the VAT has been withdrawn are in fact, run by their own statute. However, as the English Medium Schools have no such statutory backing in running their respective institutions, so they are not entitled to the same treatment that has been extended to the private Universities and Medical as well as Engineering Colleges and therefore, no discrimination has been made to the English Medium Schools merely on withdrawing VAT from those Universities and Colleges.

33. The learned DAG also submits that the Government assumes the authority to pick and choose in imposing or exempting VAT under the provision of section 3(3), section 5(4) as well as section 8(4) of the VAT Act, so no discrimination has occurred in case of the petitioners as well.

34. The learned DAG finally submits that, the decision cited by the learned counsel for the petitioners reported in 18 BLC (AD) is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the instant case and thus prays for discharging the Rule.

Deliberations

35. We have heard the learned counsel for the petitioners and that of the learned Deputy Attorney-General at length, perused the writ petition, supplementary affidavit, Affidavit-in-Oppositions and considered the submission so advanced by the learned counsels for the contending parties.

36. It is the core submission of Mr. Shahdeen Malik, the learned counsel for the petitioners, that a glaring discriminatory treatment is apparent in the action of the Respondents against the English Medium Schools which reflects from the very exemption given to the private Universities and Medical Colleges and Engineering Colleges by issuing a circular amid protest launched by the students of the those institutions. Furthermore, nowhere in the VAT Act has any school, either Government or non-Government, been included in paying VAT. However, since VAT has been imposed considering only the medium of education rendered by a section of Institutions, it palpably demonstrates that, the Government has singled out a certain class of people in the camouflage of mentioning the schools in the impugned SRO and compels the guardian of the students studying in English Medium School to pay VAT.

37. Substantiating his submission, the learned counsel has referred to Articles-15, 17 and 19 of the Constitution, being the fundamental principles of our State policy, that ensures basic necessity free and compulsory educations, and equality of opportunity in acquiring so by a citizen.

38. Now let us examine how far the action of the Respondents in imposition VAT on a certain class of educational institution is justified. So far as it relates to "education", we never find anywhere in the Constitution that the students studying in English Medium School have ever been differentiated from the students studying in Bengali medium schools. Therefore, on the face of the Constitutional mandate, a gross discrimination has been created by imposing VAT upon certain schools, herein English Medium schools, which is totally contrary to the provision as enunciated in Article 15 and Article 17 of the Constitution.

39. Aside from that, "Equality of opportunity" so enshrined in Article 19 of our Constitution, has also been infracted in imposing the impugned VAT upon the English medium school, because if the State fails to make equality towards its citizens, in that event, the aggrieved person or persons has got no other alternative but to take resort to the authority of this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution and the petitioners have rightly done so.

40. Further, it is not a fact that the petitioners have got no lucus standi to file this writ petition to ventilate their grievance as has been claimed by the learned DAG in as much as, by the impugned SRO though VAT is supposed to be paid by the schools but ground reality is that, none but the parents of the student are paying VAT on the tuition fees in separate head which is evident from Annexure A and B to the Writ Petition respectively, though the Government turned a blind eye over this matter since its very imposition.

41. But the point to be adjudicated by us in this writ is totally otherwise. In this writ petition, we are to address whether the imposition of VAT on a certain class of schools is liable to be persisted or not where the mode of payment and person or persons liable to pay such VAT is totally immaterial here because by the instant Rule, the very SRO imposing VAT on English medium schools has been called in question claiming it to be discriminatory one.

42. Then again, from annexure-G and G-1, as well as annexure H and H-1 of the supplementary affidavit dated 24-11-2016, it appears that, the Government had also imposed VAT on private Medical Colleges, private Engineering Colleges as well as private Universities, but in the wake of protest, by the students of those institutions, the Government had to give in to the said demand and eventually, by special order the Board was compelled to withdraw the said VAT within a span of 1(one) month of its imposition by issuing another SRO acting under the provision of section 14(1) of the VAT Act, exempting all those institutions from paying VAT.

<u>43. This very scenario clearly indicates that, a section of the populace has been singled out and are being victimised and also being compelled to pay the VAT since 2014. However, from the above legal analysis and discussion, it goes without saying that, the very SRO imposing VAT itself is discriminatory one. When a law is found to be discriminatory which provide upper hand to a certain section of populace and deprive a small section of citizenry in enjoying same privilege, then it cannot remain in place any more.</u>

44. In that parlance, we may profitably rely on several decisions, both from the jurisdiction of United States of America and India which are as follows:

In the case of New Orleans vs Dukes (1976), 427 US 297, it has been observed that;

"It is not the functions of the court to sit in Judgment over matters of economic policy and it must necessarily be left to the expert bodies and the court will not interfere unless discrimination clearly emerges from the facts of the cases.

Here in the instant case, glaring discrimination is evident from the very SRO.

It was further held in the case of AP vs P lump Devi (2008) 4 SCC 720 that:

A tax law is no exception to equal protection and it will be struck down as infringing Article 27 if there is no reasonable clarification.

We can also rely on another decision, namely Khedive vs Agricultural ITO, reported in AIR 1963 SC 591 where it has been propounded:

To find out discrimination what is decisive is not the language of the statute but the effect of the law.  A law which on the face of it non-discriminatory may be discriminatory if it, in effect, operates unevenly on the persons or property similarly situated".

45. We can also place our reliance on another decision in the case of Kerala Hotel and Restaurant Association vs State of Kerala, reported in AIR 1990 (SC) 913, where it has been held:

"If the classification is made with the object of taxing only the economically stronger while leaving out the economically weaker section of society that would be good reason to uphold the classification if it does not offend any other accepted norm of valid classification. Every taxing legislation makes a genuine attempt to adjust the burden with a fair and reasonable degree of equality.  It also aims to apportion the burden equitably on different categories of properties and persons with distinct economic characteristics."

46. In this regard, we may also rely on the decision in the case of Ram Krishma Dalmia vs Justice Talukder, reported in AIR 1958 SC 538, where it has been held:

"When a statute confers wide discretion on the executive authority without any policy guide lines it clothes the executive authority with naked arbitrary power to select persons of thinks in the exercise of discretion and the statute even though non-discrimination on its face permits discrimination in the exercise of the discretion.

47. Likewise, in the case of Jyoti Pershad vs Administrator for the Union Territory of Delhi, reported in AIR 1961 SC 1602 their Lordships have also taken a similar view on the point of discrimination.

Also, in a number of other cases, the Supreme Court of India struck down statutes for conferring wide discriminatory power to the Government or to the administrative authority without providing any guide lines or policy for the exercise of discretion.

48. On a careful perusal of the core objectives of those decisions, we conclude that, the principle set at rest in those decisions are equally applicable to the facts and circumstances of the instant case, so far as it relates to the discriminatory action taken by the Respondents towards the English Medium schools.

49. However, when we took up the matter for passing the Judgment we drew the attention of the learned DAG as to whether the impugned SRO has found place in any Finance Act or the said SRO has got any parliamentary sanction, but the learned DAG failed to impress us with a plausible reply. Nevertheless, if we go through Article 83 of our Constitution, we find the following provision:

"No tax shall be levied or collected except by or under the authority of any Act of parliament."

50. However, in that aspect, the learned DAG simply repeats that, under the provision of section 3 as well as section 5(4) and section 72 of the VAT Act, the Board has got ample authority to impose or exempt VAT. On such submission we feel it expedient to peruse section 8(4) of the VAT Act, which reads as follows:

“বোর্ড জনস্বার্থের গুরুত্ব বিবেচনা করিয়া এবং যথোপযুক্ত অনুসন্ধান পূর্বক সরকারী গেজেটে জারিকৃত আদেশ দ্বারা কোন নির্দিষ্ট পণ্য শ্রেণী বা সেবা প্রদানকারীকে বার্ষিক টার্ন ওভারের পরিমাণ নির্বিশেষে ধারা ১৫-এর আওতায় নিবন্ধিত হওয়াসহ মূল্য সংযোজন কর প্রদানের আদেশ করিতে পারিবে।”

51. On a bare reading of those provision of the VAT Act, it is true, the Government can impose VAT on any service provider under the provision of section 3(3) and section 5(4) of the VAT Act, but there must be a reasonable satisfaction of the Government or legate objectives in doing so, which should be free from any discriminatory motive and should also be based on proper investigation which clearly lacks in the present case.

52. Further, in the preamble of the statute, or any sorts of legal instruments, herein the SRO, objectives for enacting the Statute ought to be stated. However, nothing of that sort has been mentioned about the objectives in imposing such kinds of VAT upon the English Medium Schools in the impugned SRO, keeping the aggrieved persons totally in the dark as to the circumstances for such imposition as no Government agencies can be allowed to act at their sweet will, merely on the strength of some provision of law, when the same is found to have created discrimination among the citizens and curtail the fundamental rights of the citizen guaranteed by the Constitution.

53. On the point of discrimination the learned DAG also repeats that since there has been no discrimination amongst the English medium Schools as regards the rate of imposition of VAT, which is 7.5% for all the English Medium schools. He also goes on to submit on this point that, though the VAT has been withdrawn and ultimately exempted from the private Medical Colleges, private Engineering Colleges and Universities, but those institutions are run by their own statute, while the English Medium Schools are not run or regulated by any statute rather, it runs at the whim of the respective authority of the schools. We cannot, but observe that this sort of submission really sounds absurd.

<u>54. In that parlance, question naturally crops up, as to why those English Medium Schools have been given such authority to run and charge tuition fees at their sweet will and as to why the Government is not promulgating any Rules, regulation or guide lines to bring them within the statutory frame work like the Government Institutions, so as to prevent them from realising tuition fees and compelling the parents to pay VAT thereon and other charges at their whim. But the answers seem a far cry. In the given situation, the submission so advanced by the learned DAG has got no basis, rather it amounts to give latitude to those schools to do whatever they like in the interest of levying VAT. But, it is our firm and considered view that, there must be an end to such anarchy that is now prevailing in the private English medium schools with regard to charging excessive tuition fees, yearly re-admission charges and other charges, much to the prejudice and predicament of the VAT paying parents.</u>

55. Be that as it may, we have very meticulously gone through the citations so referred by the learned counsel for the petitioners and that of the learned DAG and so far as it relates to the decision so cited by the learned counsel for the petitioners it is our considered view that, though the facts of the cited decisions are different from those of the present case, but the ratio so settled in those decision is quite applicable to the facts and circumstances of the instant case as well. However, we regret to add that, the decision so cited by the learned DAG has got no manner of application to the facts and circumstances of the present case.

56. Over and above, there is no logical basis, let alone any legal authority, to assume that since the English Medium Schools has got no statutory backing, they can be allowed to do whatever they deem right and by allowing their commercial mileage the Govt. will be emboldened to impose VAT upon them.

The submission of the learned DAG has also got no leg to stand on the score that, since the Government colleges and institutions has got their own statute and regulated thereby, so the Government was compelled to withdraw the VAT so imposed earlier. The above argument defending the Government action on discriminatory treatment upon the English Medium Schools bears no legal basis.

57. Given the above discussions, and considering the submissions so advanced by the learned counsel for the petitioners and that of the learned DAG, we find ample substance in the Rule. So the unavailable consequence that follows, the Rule succeeds.

58. Resultantly, the Rule is made absolute however without any order as to costs.

59. The circular, as contained in SRO No. 108-Ain/2014/703- Mushak dated 5-6-2014, so far as it relates to imposition of VAT on the English medium schools at the rate of 7.5% under Service of Code No. S069, issued by the National Board of Revenue (Respondent No. 2) is hereby declared to have been issued without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. Consequently, the imposition of VAT vide said SRO is hereby struck down. Henceforth, no amount of VAT can be levied from the English medium schools by the Respondents.

60. The Secretary, Internal Resources Division, Ministry, of Finance, Respondent No. 1 is hereby directed to issue a notification in pursuance of section 14(1) of the VAT Act exempting the English Medium Schools from paying VAT within 15 days from the date of receipt of this judgment and order.

Office is directed to transmit the copy of the judgment and order to the Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 at once.

End.

Abdus Salam Mondal, Advocate with Abul Kalam Azad, Advocates—For the Respondents.

full_judgment:
SM Emdadul Hoque J: This First appeal at the instance of the defendant appellants is directed against the judgment and decree dated 26-11-1974 passed by the subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla in Partition Suit No. 89 of 1967 decreeing the suit with costs against the defendant Nos. 1(Ka)-1(Kha) the defendant Nos. 2-5, 6-18 and 55-63 and expertly without costs against the rest.

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the appeal, in short, is that the respondents as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 89 of 1967 before the subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla for partition of the suit land contending inter alia, that the property of schedule-1 belonged to Tofani in 12 arenas, Mohammed Ali in 4 annas and land of schedule-2 belonged to Tofani and Mohammed Ali in equal shares and the property of schedule-3 belonged to Tofani in 10 annas 13 gondas 1 kara and 1 kranti and Mohammed Ali 5 annas 6 gondas 2 karas 2 kranti i.e. /3rd and /3rd respectively. Mohammad Ali having owned and possessed the property in dispute in share died leaving behind the defendant No. 1 Abdul Hakim one son and three daughters defendant No. 1, Rokabjan, the predecessor of the plaintiffs, Rupjan defendant No. 64 and defendant No. 65 Phuljan.
