<u>16. The plaintiffs' case was that the suit land was put in auction in Certificate Case No.660 of 1952-53. Ali Ahmed auction purchased the same on 20th June 1953 which was confirmed on 24.08.1953 and said Ali Ahmed got sale certificate on 19.11.1953 and took over possession of the same on 20.01.1954. It appears from Sale Certificate (Exhibit-2) that certificate holder was R.L. Government Acquired Estate and certificate debtors were Khiroda Sundori and Lalit Mohon Saha. Ext.1 C.S. Khatian shows that Khiroda was the only tenant of the holding but in the Sale Certificate name of Lalit Mohan Saha appeared with her which clearly indicated that arrear was chargeable against Lalit Mohan as well. It is not understandable as to why, for charge of Lalit Mohan, requisition was given for holding auction of the property of Khiroda. From the schedule of property as described in sale certificate it appears that in the column of the name of the certificate holder R.L. Government Acquired Estate was mentioned and at second page of the same it appears the Certificate Officer was of the office of Das Group Govt.—AD Estate who put his signature in the Sale Certificate on 19.1 1.1957. We did not find any explanation neither in the plaint nor in the evidence nor from the learned Counsel of the plaintiff-respondents as to why sale certificate of R.L. Government Acquired Estate was issued by the Certificate Officer of 'Das Group Govt.-Ad Estate' on 19.11.1957. There is nothing in the pleading or in evidence as to how and when the rent receiving interest of landlord Laxminarayan was devolved upon to R.L. Govt. AD Estate since C.S. Khatian shows that Laxminarayan was the landlord. Section 4 of the Public Demand and Recovery Act (PDR Act)prescribes the mode of filing of certificate for Public demand payable to the Collector and directs that when the certificate officer is satisfied that any public demand payable to the Collector is due, he may sign a certificate in the prescribed form stating that the demand is due. Section 5 provides that when any public demand payable to any person other than the Collector is due such person may send written requisition in the prescribed form to the certificate officer. Section 6 of the PDR Act provides that on receipt of such requisition the certificate officer, if lie is satisfied that the demand is recoverable and that recovery is not barred by law, may sign a certificate in the prescribed form stating that the demand is due. Section 7 provides that when a certificate has been filed in the office of the certificate officer under section 4 or 6, he shall cause to be served upon the certificate debtor in the prescribed manner a notice in the prescribed form and a copy of the certificate. It is not the case of the plaintiffs that certificate holder R.L. Govt. Acquired Estate had any demand (Public demand?) chargeable from the certificate debtors Khiroda Sundari Saha and Lalit Mohan Saha(?) for which, it made requisition to the Certificate Officer of 'Das Group Govt.-Ad Estate' who issued notice in Form 2 of schedule II and being satisfied that the demand was chargeable or became due so he signed the certificate.</u>

<u>17. 'Public demand' means any arrear or money mentioned or referred to in schedule-1, i and includes any interest which may, by law, be chargeable thereon up to the date on which a certificate is signed under part II of the PDR Act. It is to be mentioned here that as per provision Section 3(3) of the PDR Act "Certificate Officer" means a collector and any officer, appointed by a Collector to perform the functions of a Certificate Officer under the Act. The Court of Wards can send requisition under section 5 of the PDR Act but requirement is that on receipt of a requisition filed under section 5 the Certificate Officer before signing a certificate must be satisfied, far as the demand made in the requisition is concerned, that it is recoverable. There is no evidence that Deputy Collector appointed any one/officer of Das Group Govt. AD Estate as Certificate Officer.</u>

18. From Ext.1 C.S. Khatian No.241 of Mouza Shahar Dhaka it appears that Landlord of the suit holding was Laxminarayan and tenant was Khairoda Sundari Dashya of No.1 Atosh Khan Lane. Mr. M. I. Faruqui in her written submission stated that R.L (Rup Lal) Estate was owner of 7 annas share of Dhaka Collectorate Touzi No.61/1 and Wards Estate being managed by the Government under the Court of Wards Act. R.L.(Rup Lal) Estate, as a Wards Estate, was ultimately acquired by the Government under sections 3(i)(ii) and 4 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act vide Gazette Notification No.2906 L.R. dated 28.02.1952 as appeared in Gazette Notification No.1815 L.R. dated 6th February 1954. Accordingly, he drew our attention to the Dacca Gazette Extra ordinary dated February 12, 1954. He further stated, in his written submission, that after acquiring the rent receiving interest, in order to realise the arrear rent from the defaulted tenant of C.S. holding No.241 of Plot No.390/3940 Khiroda Sundari Dasya of the said Touzi No.61/1, R.L. Government Acquired Estate filed certificate Case No.660 of 1952-53 under section 62 read with sections 139 and 141 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and put in auction of Khiroda Sundari Dashya's said holding measuring .0568 acre on 20.06.1953 and predecessor of the plaintiffs Ali Ahmed @ Dr. Manjurul Haque purchased the said holding in auction. We are unable to accept the submission of Mr. Faruqui for the reasons that there is nothing in the pleadings or in evidence as to how and when the rent receiving interest of Landlord Laxminarayon was devolved upon R.L. Govt. Acquired Estate. Rent receiving interest of all the rent receivers were acquired with effect from 14th April 1956 under section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by East Bengal Ordinance Ill of 1956 in the district of Dhaka vide Notification Nos.4826 L.R. to 4836 LR, respectively, published in Dacca Gazette Extraordinary dated 2nd April 1956, part. From No.4836 LR of the Dacca Gazette dated April 2nd 1956 it appears that Governor acquired, with effect from the 14th April 1956, all interests of all rent-receivers in their respective estates, teluks, tenants, holdings and tenancies situated in the District of Dhaka, including their interests in all sub-soil except the interests and rights which have already been acquired by, and have already vested in, the Provincial Government under the Provisions of the said Act. Mr. Faruqui, drawing our attention to serial No.103 of the Dacca Gazette dated 12.02.1954, submits that the suit land was acquired vide 2906 LR dated 28.02.1952. But serial No.103 shows that names of the ex-rent receivers are Babu Jogesh Chandra Das son of Radhaballav Das, Babu Tarak Nath Das son Romesh Chandra Das, of Farashgonj, Dacca (Wards, Ruplal Wards Estate, Dacca). We do not find anywhere in the pleadings or in evidence as to how and when the rent receiving interest of the disputed holding was devolved upon to Babu Jogesh Chandra Das and others. In such view of the matter, it is difficult to accept that the suit property fell within the purview of exception mentioned in notification No.4836 LR. There is no reason to accept that Ruplal Wards Estate, Dacca and R.L Govt. Acquired Estate are same estate and landlords are same in absence of any pleadings and evidence with that regard. Serial No.103 shows that Babu Jogesh Chandra Das and Babu Tarak Nath Das are of Farashganj but C.S. Khatian shows that the suit land is situated within Mouza Shahar Dhaka under Kotwali Police Station. From C.S. Khatian No.241 it appears that land of holding No.241 is situated under Kotwali Police Station. But Sale Certificate (ext.2) shows that the same is situated under Lalbag Police Station. In C.S. Khatian; Touzi number was mentioned as No.61 but in Sale Certificate Touzi No. was shown as 61/1. In C.S. Khatian, name of the Mouza appeared as Shahar Dhaka but in Sale Certificate Mouza was shown as Atosh Khana. The plaintiffs did not take any step to connect each other.

<u>19. It appears that the forms used in Sale Certificate and writ of delivery of possession are inconsistent with the forms as described in the forms of rule 74 and 75 schedule II of the Act. The terms used in Sale Certificate are generally used for execution of the decree of the civil Court. It is apparent on the face of the record that Sale Certificate and writ of delivery of possession are manufactured one and that the certificate officer acted beyond his powers and jurisdiction as he was nobody to alter or mutilate the Form prescribed on the Act.</u>

<u>20. Another aspect is that it is well settled that the certificate of sale does not, by itself, create the title but is merely evidence of title. In the case of Ahmedabad Municipality Vs. Hazi Abdul reported in AIR 1971 SC 1201 it was observed by the Supreme Court of India that it is axiomatic that the purchaser at auction sale takes the property subject to all the defects of title and the doctrine caveat emptor (let the purchaser beware) applies to such purchaser. It is the "right, title and interest" of the judgment-debtor with all risk and defect and without any warranty of title either by the decree-holder or by the court that passes to a purchaser at a court sale, with the exception that where it is proved that the judgment-debtor had no saleable interest at all the purchaser may recover back the purchase-money. In this case, the alleged auction was held on 20.06.1953 showing Khiroda Sundari Saha and Lalit Mohon Saha as certificate debtors. But we have already found from C.S. Khatian (ext-1) shows that Khiroda Sundari Dashya was only C.S. recorded tenant and before holding auction she sold her rayoti interest to Salimunnessa on 27.03.1953 who was not impleaded in the certificate procedure. That is, Khiroda had no right and title at the time of holding auction in suit property so the auction purchaser had not acquired any title because, at the time of holding auction the certificate debtor had no title in the property, in question. It is not the case of the plaintiffs that Salimunnessa had notice of the alleged charges brought by R.L. Acquired Government Estate either actual or constructive. It is to be relevant here to reiterating that in Title Suit No.221 of 1964, the learned Munsif observed that Khiroda and Lalit Mohon were the certificate debtors who already sold their interest to Salimunessa with the knowledge of the defendant No.1, that is, predecessor of the present plaintiffs. Lalit Mohan and Khiroda had no subsisting interest on the date of holding auction sale and it cannot be said that the defendant No.1 (predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs) acquired 7 annas interest by his purchase in the certificate sale. That judgment was upheld in Second Appeal No. 1095 of 1966. That finding is binding upon the plaintiffs. The effect of a sale under the PDR Act being to pass to the purchaser merely the right, title and interest of the person named as judgment debtor in the certificate, the purchaser acquires no right if the person appears to have i no interest in the property at the date of sale. That is, auction purchaser Ali Ahmed did not get any title under it. In Title Suit No.221 of 1964, Title Appeal No.50 1966 and Second Appeal No.1 095 of 1966, the respective Courts had taken notice of the same. But the plaintiffs did not meet up the issue raised and explain the consequences of the same.</u>

<u>21. Giving our anxious consideration to the pleadings, evidence and circumstances our view is that the instant suit in respect of .0568 acre of land was not at all and maintainable and the certificate as made was not a proper certificate to charge Khiroda and Lalit Mohan with liability and the sale under it did not pass any title. Their Sale Certificate and writ of delivery of possession are created documents. Accordingly, we find substance in the appeal.</u>

22. Thus, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order passed in Civil Petition is set aside. The judgment and decree of the High Court Division is also set aside. The suit is dismissed.

Plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1 and 2's case

Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 appellants' case

Then the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title to the suit land and also for declaration that the plaintiffs are not bound by the judgment and decree dated 15.11.1979 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 62 of 1979. The plaintiff also filed Money Suit No.73 of 2000 in the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for realization of compensation of taka 28,71,900/-(twenty eight lacs seventy one thousand and nine hundred) along with interest @ of 15% till realization, and the Money Suit was transferred to the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and renumbered as Money Suit No. 2 of 2002. Thereafter, the defendants as appellants filed First Appeal No. 181 of 2004 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division by judgment dated 13 day of May, 2008 dismissed the appeals and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Whereupon, the present appellants filed CPLA. No. 1358-1359 of 2009 before this Division and this Division by order dated 13.05.2008 dismissed CPLA No. 1358 of 2009 arising out of Money Suit No. 02 of 2002 and LA No. 1359 of 2009 arising out of Title Suit No. 59 of 1994. Then the present appellants, who were defendants of the aforesaid suits filed Civil Review Petition No. 90 of 2010 before this Division.

Points for consideration in this appeal

30. Upon hearing of the review petition, this Division granted leave to appeal to consider the following points:-

"I. Whether the Gazette notification dated 2nd April 1956 No 4024 LR(sic No.4824 LR) and No.  4836 LR respectively under section 3 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act XXVIII of 1951) (hereinafter mentioned as the SA&T Act) as amended by E.P. Ordinance III of 1956, the rent receiving interest vested in the Government on 02.04. I 956 and exhibit-1 shows Khiroda Shundari Daishya held a Mirash Ijara  interest wider a private land lord and it conclusively proves that the certificate case No. 660 of 1952-53 issued by L.R. Government Acquired Estate are manufactured papers and exhibits-2 and 2(ka) are all also forged papers and the claim of title of the plaintiffs falls through.

II. Whether the finding that the certificate was filed by the Government for arrears of rent in Certificate Case No. 660 of 1952-53 while the exhibits 2 and 2(ka) show that certificate was filed by R.L. Government Acquired Estate against the provision of section 4 of Public Demand Recovery Act, 1913 (hereinafter referred to as the PDR Act) is a mistake apparent on the face of record and in the circumstances, judgment dated 06.05.2010 calls for review."

Arguments of the contending parties

31. Mr. Abdul Quiyum, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellants with Mr. Ali Reza, Advocate and being instructed by Syed Mahbubar Rahman, Advocate-on-Record takes us through the judgment of various suits/cases and exhibits 2 and 2(ka) filed by the plaintiffs in the suit and submits as under:

Khatian. (2) The root of plaintiffs case is that their predecessor in interest Ali Ahmed Dr. Monjurul Haque had purchased the suit property in auction from the R.L. (8) Those facts and legal questions were not raised by the defendants in the suits, appeals and civil petition for leave to appeal due to inadvertence. But the Courts ought to have considered those questions on examining exhibits 2 and 2(ka).

(9) In the above facts and circumstances the order dated 06.05.2010 passed by the this Division suffers from illegality and, as such, the same is liable to be interfered with.

32. In support of his submissions, Mr. Abdul Quiyum, has relied on the decision in the case of Government of the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh and others Vs. Md. Abdul Jabbar Sheikh, reported in 26 BCR (2006) (AD) 327.

Estate on 28.02.1952 legally sold the suit property to the plaintiffs' predecessor in interest in auction. Deliberation of the Court

34. We have examined the judgment of the trial Court dated 31.03.2004 passed in Title Suit No. 59 of 1994, the judgment and decree dated 12th and 13th day of May, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 181 of 2004, the judgment and order dated 06.05.2010 passed by the Appellate Division in CPLA No. 1359 of 2009, sale Certificate No. 660 of 1952-53 (exhibit-2), certificate of delivery of possession (exhibit-2(ka), Dhaka Gazette Extra-ordinary published by the authority on April 2, 1956, Gazette Extra-ordinary dated 12.02.1954 and the judgment and decree passed by various Courts in various suits, appeals, etc. and the connected materials on record.

35. From the judgment of trial Court in Title Suit No. 59 of 1994 decreeing the suit and the judgment of First Appeal No. 181 of 2004 passed by the High Court Division dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment of the trial Court, it appears that the trial Court and High Court Division by elaborate and threadbare discussions on all the issues involved in the suit filed by respondent Nos. 1 and 2-plaintiffs decided merits on the issues on the basis of evidence on record. Both the courts concurrently found that the plaintiff-appellants could prove their title to and possession in the suit property till they were forcibly dispossessed by the defendants. The courts also disbelieved the defendant-appellants case. The CPLA was also dismissed by this Division with reasoning on merit.

36. In view of the above, in deciding this civil appeal, we have mainly to consider the two grounds as quoted hereinbefore on consideration of the relevant materials on record.

37. From the exhibit-1, copy of C.S. Khatian, it appears that Zamindar Lakshmi Narayan and others were seven annas owners of Tauzi No. 61 which includes Tauzi No. 61/1, Khatian No. 241 of Mouza-Sahar, Dhaka, Police Station-Kotwali and Khiroda Shundari Daishya was in possession of No. 1, Atash Khana Lane as a tenant of Zamindar Lakshmi Narayan and others. Exhibit 1 has not been challenged by the defendants side.

38. The ground taken in this appeal are that admittedly Khiroda Shundari Daishya and Lalit Mohon Das were tenants under private landlord and so, the sale certificate in Certificate Case No. 660 of 1952-53 issued by R.L. Government Acquired Estate and the writ of delivery of possession are manufactured documents as the rent receiving interest vested to the Government in the year, 1956 according to Gazette dated 02.04.1956. Thus, both exhibits 2 and 2(ka) are forged documents.

39. We have examined original sale certificate and the writ of delivery of possession as placed before us by Mr. Farooqui at the time of hearing.

40. Relevant part of Exbt.-2 i.e. the auction sale certificate reads as under:

“তপছিল

জিলা-ঢাকা, কোলেক্টরীর ৬১/১ নং তৌজির হিস্যে। আনা শহর ঢাকা, লালবাগ থানাধীন মৌজা আতশ খানা, ৭নং ওয়ার্ডের ১০ নং সিটের ২৪১ নং খতিয়ানের ৩৯০/৩৯৪০ দাগের ভিটি জমি .৫৬৮ অযুতাংশ ইহার বার্ষিক খাজনা……..আনা।”

41. On careful scrutiny of the sale certificate of Certificate Case No. 660 of 1952-53 (exhibit-2) it is found that both the stamps of sale certificate were purchased immediately before the date of issuance of sale certificate. Moreover, it appears that by the said sale certificate the certificate officer sold .568 ajutangsha of property of C.S. 390 Khatian No. 241 and C.S. plot No. 390/3940 Atash Khana, Ward No. 7, Sheet No. 10 under Lalbagh Police Station, Sahar Dhaka, Touzi No. 61/1 of the Collectorate of Zilla Dhaka.

42. We are of the considered opinion that R.L. (Rup Lal) Court of Wards Estate was the owner of 7 annas share of Tauzi No. 61/1, which is a part of original Tauzi No. 61, of Sahar Dhaka of the Collectorate of Zilla-Dacca. It transpires from the C.S Khatian that it is written therein that Khiroda Shundari Daishya was in possession of No. 1, Atash Khana Lane of Mouza Sahar Dhaka of Khatian No. 241. This clearly shows that the words "Sahar Dhaka" as used in the auction sale certificate was the Mouza of the property sold in auction and the word “মৌজে আতস খানা” does not mean Mouza but it was the lane i.e. Mash Khana Lane. Further, from the deed of sale (Exbt-Ka) submitted by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 (appellants) it appears that the Police Station of the suit property has been stated therein as Kotwali at Present P.S.- Lalbag being premises No. 1, Atash Khana Lane, Dhaka. Thus it is evident that C.S. Khatian No. 241 was originally under P.S. Kotwali but subsequently it fell within P.S. Lalbag. Further, we searched the Gazette of establishment of Lalbag Police Station and finally it was found from the Culcutta Gazette, September 22, 19 45 that:

"No. 11312P.- The 20th September 1915.- The Governor in Council is pleased to sanction the establishment of an investigating centre at Lalbagh, within Kotwali (Dacca) thana, in the district of Dacca. 2. In exercise of the power conferred by section 4(1)(S) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Act V of 1898), the Governor in Council is pleased to declare the said Lalbagh investigating centre to be a police-station and to include the local area Comprised within the following boundaries:-

43. North, South and West- Municipal Boundary. East- Meghnath Saha Road from the Municipal boundary to the north-east corner of Dilkusha. Company Bazar Road from the north-east corner of Dilkusha to the south-east corner of the old Government House. Thence to the west by the road which runs alongside the south wall of the old Government House to Thatari Bazar Road railway level crossing. The railway line to the Jail Road level crossing. Thence by the Jail Road, Be um Bazar Road, Becharam's Dewary and Barada Kinkar Ray's Lane to Raja Ghat."

44. So, it appears that P.S. Lalbag was also correctly mentioned in the sale certificate. Therefore, R.L Estate was the owner of 7 annas share of the aforesaid Tauzi and .568 ajutangsha out of the said 7 annas was sold in auction from khatian No: 241 in favour of Ali Ahmed son of Late Munshi Nawab Jan on 20.06.1953. From the writ of delivery of possession (Exhibit 2(Ka) it appears that possession of the aforesaid land was delivered to Ali Ahmed. Relevant part of this document reads as under:

“যেহেতু সন ১৯২/৫৩ সালের ৬৬০ নম্বর মোকদ্দমার ভিটি জমির নিলাম Ali Ahmed, S/0 Late Munshi Nawab Jan of 74, Mirpur Road, P.S. Lalbagh, Dacca নিম্ন বর্ণিত সম্পত্তির ক্রেতা বলিয়া সার্টিফিকেট প্রাপ্ত হইয়াছেন। অতএব আপনার প্রতি এতদ্বারা হুকুম হইল যে, আপনি উক্ত আলী আহাম্মদ সার্টিফিকেট প্রাপ্ত ক্রেতার উক্ত সম্পত্তিতে দখল নিবেন।

অদ্য সন ১৯৫৪ সালের ১৫/১ তারিখে আমার স্বাক্ষর ও আদালতের মোহরযুক্ত মতে দেওয়া গেল।

স্বা/-

তপছিল

জিলা-ঢাকা, কোলেক্টরীর ৬১/১ নং তৌজির হিং। আনা শহর ঢাকা, লালবাগ থানাধীন মৌজা আতশ খানা ৭নং ওয়ার্ডের ১০ নং সিটের ৩৯০/৩৯৫০ দাগের ভিটি জমির পরিমাণ .৫৬৮ অযুতাংশ বিক্রিত বটে।

45. Thus, it appears that after the auction sale the suit property was also delivered to All Ahmed. Admittedly, All Ahmed had been in possession of the suit property since 1954. Thereafter, his successor-in-interests including the plaintiffs had been in continuous possession thereof till they were forcibly dispossessed by the defendants in the year 1997. Admittedly, R.S Khatian stands in the names of the plaintiffs and not the defendants.

46. Mr. Quiyum strenuously argued that vesting of the rent receiving interest to the Government was on 02.04.1956 by Gazette notification and therefore, the sale certificate and writ of delivery of possessions are forged documents.

47. We have examined gazette notification dated February 12, 1954 submitted by Mr. M.I Farooqui, the relevant part of which is as under: `No. 1815 L.R.- 6th February 1954. — In exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (1) of section 46A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (East Bengal Act No. XXVIII of 1951), the Governor is pleased to order that Compensation Assessment-rolls be prepared in respect of the properties of the rent-receivers mentioned in column 2 of the Schedule below which have been acquired under section 3 of the said Act by the notifications referred to in column 3 of the Schedule, on the basis of the returns, papers and documents furnished or taken possession of under sections 3A and 4 of that Act-

Schedule

Name of the ex-rent receiver	Notification Nos. with dates	Remarks

1. Kuma Satya Sudhir Ghosal Bahadur, son of late Satya Bhusan Ghosal Bahadur, Bhukaliash Rajbati, Post Khidderpore, Calcutta.	10321, L.R., dated 17.11.1951, under section 3(1).  	Published in the Dacca Gazette, Extraordinary, dated 8-1-1952.

103. Babu Jagesh Chandra Das, son of Radhaballav Das, Babu Tarak Nath Das, son of Ramesh Chandra Das, of Farashganj, Dacca, (Wards, Ruplal Wards Estate, Dacca).	2906 L.R. dated 28.2.1952, under section 3(1).

Ditto, dated

19-3-1952

48. Whereas the gazette notification dated 02.04.1956 as referred to by Mr. Quiyum reads as under: "No. 4836 L.R. — 2nd April 1956. — In exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (1) of section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (East Bengal Act No. XXVIII of 1951), as amended by the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (East Bengal Ordinance No. III of 1956), it is hereby notified, for the information of all concerned, that the governor is leased to acquire, with effect from the 14th April 1956, all interests of all rent-receivers in their respective estates taluks, tenures, holdings and tenancies situated in the district of Dacca, including their interests in all sub-soil and rights to minerals in such estates, taluks, tenures, holdings and tenancies, except the interests and rights which have already been acquired by, and have already vested in, the Provincial Government under the provisions of the said Act."

49. Thus, Gazette notification dated 02 April, 1956 excludes the property of Rup Lal Acquired Estate as it was acquired earlier in 2906 LR dated 28.02.1952, published in Dhaka Gazette Extra-ordinary dated 19.03.1952, as apparent from Colum 03 of Gazette Notification dated February 12, 1954.

50. Therefore, it appears from the Dhaka Gazette Extra-ordinary published by the authority on February 12, 1954 that the Governor was pleased to order preparation of compensation of assessment roll of the properties which were acquired under section 3(1) of the SA&T Act by notification referred to in Colum 03. It further appears that Rup Lal Wards Estate, Dacca was acquired in 2906 L.R. dated 28.02.1952, under section 3(1) of the SA&T Act and it was notified in the Gazette on 19.03.1952.

51. In view of the above, it is evident that the entire R.L. (Rup Lal) Wards Estate, whether be it Tauzi No. 61 or 61/1, was under the management of the Government at the relevant time as a Wards Estate prior to 19.03.1952. Therefore, it appears that even prior to acquisition of rent receiving interest by the Government, it had the right to auction sale the suit property for arrear rents of Rup Lal Court of Wards Estate.

52. The defendant appellants claim the property through Salimunnesa as successor in interest. Salimunnesa's deed of purchase from Khiroda Shundari Daishya was on 27.03.1953. But it appears that the property was within the court of wards state and it was acquired prior to the sale by Khiroda Shundari Daishya in favour of Salimunnesa vide exhibit-Ka.

53. However, in the Gazette notification it is mentioned that the properties of Jogesh Chandra Das, son of Radhaballab Das, Babu Tarak Nath Das, son of Ramesh Chandra Das of Farashganj, Dacca were being managed by Wards, Rup Lal Wards Estate, Dacca.

54. None of the parties could explain about the Rup Lal Court of Wards Estate's ownership of the property but this Gazette Notification was never challenged by the defendants. Thus, the Government being in management of RL Wards Estate had lawfully auction sold the suit property of Wards Estate in Certificate Case No. 660 of 1952-53 and so, it cannot be said that the certificate of auction sale Exhibit- 2 is a forged document.

55. The writ of delivery of possession is written in a Form under order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure and not on a form under the Public Demand Recovery Rules.

56. Mr. M. I. Farooqui produced before us some other auction sale certificates, showing use of Form under the Code of Civil Procedure for auction under the P.D.R Act and contends that in many cases forms prescribed under the CPC have been used by the Certificate Officers and the main feature of both forms are identical.

57. We have examined the form prescribed under the CPC and the form prescribed under PDR Rules and it appears that both the forms are more or less identical in nature. However, it be mentioned that forms under CPC has been used in the auction sale certificate and writ of delivery of possession and so the word decree of the said printed form remained in it. Therefore, merely because the form under CPC has been used, it cannot be said to be forged. Exhibit 2 and 2(ka) were issued in the year 1953, i.e. these documents are more than 60 years old and produced from genuine custodian of the same.

58. Thus, we do not find Exhibit 2 and 2(ka) are forged documents rather, on perusal of the documents it appears to us that these documents are original/genuine documents.

59. Moreover, admittedly the plaintiffs' predecessor in interest Doctor Monjurul Hoque @ Ali Ahmed had been in possession of the suit property by virtue of those documents as the defendants failed to prove monthly tenancy of Ali Ahmed or his wife under Khiroda Shundari Daishya or anyone else. Admittedly, the plaintiffs had also been in possession of the suit property, till they were dispossessed during the pendency of the suit. Possession follows title.

60. Further, even if for arguments sake it is presumed that Dr. Manjurul Huq @ Ali Ahmed or his wife Khalimunnessa was a monthly tenant under the Khiroda Shundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Das or anyone else, in such case also, the plaintiffs cannot be evicted forcibly without following the process of eviction of a monthly tenant during pendency of the suit filed by the plaintiffs. It may be mentioned that though the defendants claim that Ali Ahmed/his wife was a tenant under Khiroda Shundari Daishya and Lalit Mohan Das but they failed to prove it by any iota of documentary evidence like monthly rent receipts, tenancy agreement, etc.

61. It may be mentioned that Exhibits 2 and 2 (ka) were marked as exhibits by the trial court without any objection from the defendants side. The defendants did not specifically mention with reasons that those documents arc forged documents in their written statement but their assertion was general in nature like the plaintiffs' assertion in the plaint that the defendants predecessors as well as the defendants deeds of purchases, bainapatra, etc. are all forged documents and paper transactions. The defendants also failed to prove that their predecessor-in-interests were ever in possession of the suit property by their so-called purchase. Thus, the registered deed of purchase from Khiroda Sundari Dasiya seems to be merely paper transaction as claimed by the plaintiffs.

62. Further, from the materials on rerecord it appears that some other lands of Tauzi Nos. 61 and 61/1 of R.L. Ward Estate were also sold in auction by mentioning its 7 annas share of the said Tauzi on the same day, i.e. on 20.06.1953 vide Certificate Case No. 659 of 1952-53 and one Golam Mohammad purchased land of Holding No. 246 in auction and got delivery of possession on 28.04.1954. The said Golam Mohammad transferred the said land to Mohammad Iliyas, vide Deed of Lease in Perpetuity No. 3022 dated 16.06.1954. Land of Holding .No. 236 of R.L. Estate was also sold in Certificate Case No. 657 of 1952-53 of Tauzi No. 61/1 mentioning its 7 annas share and Golam Mohammad also purchased the same in auction. Thereafter, Golam Mohammad transferred the said plots to Mst. Habiban Nesa wife of Piru Sardar alias Piru Mia, vide sale Deed No. 3827 dated 03.09.1954. So, it is evident that some other lands of Tauzi No. 61/1 were also sold in auction by R.L. Ward Estate, in certificate cases of 1952-53 of R.L. Acquired Estate.

63. Therefore, we find no merit on the additional new grounds taken by the appellants that Government had no right to auction sale the property prior to 1956.

64. At this stage, after dismissal of CPLA, the new grounds taken by the appellants ought not be considered by this Division as it would undoubtly prejudice the plaintiffs, who were forcibly dispossessed by the defendants unlawfully taking the laws in their own hands during pendency of the suit.

65. It be mentioned that delivery of possession by the plaintiffs to the defendants amicably on receiving money has been rightly disbelieved by all the courts and no ground was taken on this finding of fact in the appeal and no submission was also made by Mr. Abdul Quiyum on this finding and decision.

66. In the case reported in 26 BCR 2006(AD) 327, as referred Mr. Abdul Quiyum, this Division decided as under:

"There is no allegation from defendants' side as to the non-genuineness of the documents of the plaintiff and that also no evidence was lead from the side of the defendant to show that the document placing reliance upon which the plaintiff is claiming the subject matter of the suit is not genuine, the question is in such a situation whether the Court is precluded from making decision in the background of the result of the scrutiny of document or documents of the plaintiff by the Court and thereupon refusing the relief sought by the plaintiff on the finding that the document relied upon by the plaintiff was not genuine. In our view even if there is no pleading from the side of the defendant alleging the non-genuineness of the document on the basis of which plaintiff is claiming the relief in the suit the Court has a duty in the interest of justice to scrutiny the document(s) relied upon by the plaintiff and if on such scrutiny the Court notices elements in the document that makes the same non-genuine, in the instant case as noticed by the appellate Court and stated hereinbefore, then in that situation the Court in spite of the absence of the pleading of the defendant as to the non-genuineness of the document of the plaintiff is quite competent to make its decision on the basis of the result obtained upon scrutiny of the document i.e. if on scrutiny document of the plaintiff is found not genuine the Court is competent to make its decision as against the plaintiff since his documents on which he based his claim not genuine."

67. The proposition of law enunciated in the said decision can hardly be disputed. But in the instant case both the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court (High Court Division) considering the documents and all the facts and circumstances of the suit/appeal decided it in favour of the plaintiffs. The High Court Division on examination of the documents held as under: "We have examined the sale certificate along with the said form and the rule but we have not found any major deviation or non-compliance with the said form and the rule to make the sale certificate or voidable. We are of the view of that the moment the auction sale was confirmed it took its effect from the date of its sale on 20.06.1953 and it was also acted upon with the delivery of possession of the auction sold property. After all these years the defendants cannot be allowed to challenge the same and that too by way of oral submission through their learned Advocate and thus, to deny plaintiffs title to the suit property."

68. Thus, the decision as referred by Mr. Quiyum has no manner of application in this case.

<u>69. On the other hand, this Division in the case of Joynal Abedin and others vs. Mafizur Rahman and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 162 held as under: "It appears that the kabuliyats Ext.D series were filed before the trial Court and those were not wrongly marked as exhibits. Consequently, at an earlier point of time the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division remanded the case to the lower appellate Court and those were marked exhibits without any objection by the parties. From the order of the lower appellate Court dated 09.06.83, it appears that those documents were filed by the defendants as per Firisti with a petition for accepting those in evidence and those were admitted in evidence without any objection from either side. Thereafter the appeal was heard in 1985 and in disposing of the appeal we find that the lower appellate Court did not say a word with regard to these kabuliyats nor had taken those into consideration. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division also on an erroneous view of the law left these vital documents out of consideration by holding that the certified copies of the kabuliyats were filed without calling for the original copies of the kabuliyats. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division on a worng consideration of section 66 of the Evidence Act left those out of consideration as the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was of the opinion that those documents were not admissible in evidence as the originals were not called for. Mr. SR Pal, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellants rightly argued that the documents having been filed and marked Exhibit without any objection the question of admissibility of those documents cannot be raised at a subsequent point of time and the courts below including the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in not considering these kabuliyats Ext. D series and failed to consider the effect of these kabuliyats in the instant case: The learned Advocate in support of his argument has also cited the case of Abdullah and 3 others Vs. Abdul Karim and others reported in 20 DLR (SC) 205. In that decision it has been held that objection as to formal proof of a document is to be taken at the earliest point of time. In the present case, the document was admitted in evidence without any objection from either side in the year 1983. As a matter of fact the appeal came up for hearing in 1985 after a lapse of 2 years. Nobody raised the question of formal proof of those kabuliyats and those were admitted in evidence without objection. This being the position, the kabuliyats, exhibit D series were admissible in evidence and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in not considering those kabuliyats.</u>

70. In the instant case also Exbit-2 and 2(ka), i.e. auction sale certificate and writ of delivery of possession were marked as Exhibits on 05.01.2002 vide statement of P.W. 1, Murshed Kabir and no question was raised by the defendant-appellants before the trial court, the 1st appellate court and this Division in CPLA No. 1359 of 2009. Therefore, the principle laid down in the above noted case is applicable in the instant case.

71. Be that as it may, we have considered the grounds taken in this appeal on merit hereinbefore in detail.

72. Thus, considering the totality of evidence on record, we are of the considered view that the new grounds taken by the review petitioner (appellants) that exhibits 2 and 2(ka) are forged documents are not tenable in law.

73. We have already seen that in fact the Rup Lal Government Acquired Estate was the owner of 7 annas share of the Tauzi and out of it .568 ajutangsha of land was sold in auction. Moreover, the plaintiffs were admittedly in possession of the suit property. Therefore, if any one claims title to or ownership of the same or part of it, they shall have to file a suit for declaration of title, partition and possession. The defendants, under no circumstance were entitled to evict the plaintiffs from the suit property.

74. We do not like to enter into the other facts in this case as we find that observations and findings of the High Court Division are correct and on the basis of materials on record for which the CPLA was earlier dismissed on merit.

<u>75. Since, the new grounds fall through, we find no merit in the appeal. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed. Md. Nuruzzaman, I have gone through the judgment delivered by my brother, Hasan Foez Siddique, J. and my sister Zinat Ara, J. I agree with the reasoning and findings given by Zinat Ara, J.</u>

Courts Order

78. The appeal is dismissed by majority decision.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 30.05.2011, passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4847 of 2004).
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J. This appeal by leave obtained by the plaintiff -appellant has been preferred against the judgment and order dated 30.05.2011 passed by a single bench of the High Court Division in civil Revision No. 4847 of 2004 affirming the judgment and decree dated 4.9.2004 passed by the Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 75 of 1985 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 2.5.1985 passed by the then Munsif Upazila Court, Laksham, now Assistant Judge, Laksham, Comilla, in Title Suit No. 479 of 1983.

2. Short facts necessary for the disposal of this appeal are that the appellants as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 479 of 1983 in the Court of the then Munsif, Upazila court, Laksham, now Assistant Judge, Laksham, Comilla for declaration of Title in the suit land contending inter alia that the suit land originally belonged to Fateh Ali, Mokaram Ali, Hasan Ali and Safar Ali in equal share which was recorded as such in the C.S. record. Mokaram Ali died leaving behind the other quo-sharers as heirs who had been using the same as their homestead. There being shortage of space Fateh Ali and Safar Ali moved elsewhere constructing new homestead in ejmali leaving Hasan Ali as the only owner in possession in the said homestead. Hasan Ali died leaving behind 2 sons Gafur Ali and Kalu Miah but in the S.A. Khatian No. 563 the name of Gafur Ali and Kalu Miah were recorded along with the names of defendants No. 1-3 and 11, (Sekander Ali predecessor of defendant No. 6, Safor Ali, predecessor of defendant No.7 and Nuruzzaman, predecessor of defendant No. 8-10). This wrong recording in the S.A. Khatian transpired recently on the basis of which the defendants denied the title of the plaintiffs who are in of the suit land for more than 12 years. The defendants have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. Hence the suit

3. The defendants No. 1, 2(Ka) and 3 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material statements made in the plaint, contending inter alia that the suit land originally belonged to C.S recorded owners Fateh Ali, Hasan Ali, Makaram Ali and Safar Ali; that for arrears of rent the suit land was put into auction and the landlord purchased the same upon evicting the tenants. Thereafter Alimuddin and his son Sekander Ali executed a Kabuliyat in favour of the landlord and took settlement of the suit land from the Zaminder and had been paying rents regularly. Hasan Ali being a relative of Alimuddin and Sekander Ali were allowed to leave in 6 decimals of land on compassionate ground and as such he was a mere licensee having no right, and interest in the suit land; that the plaintiffs being heirs of Hasan Ali has no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. The S.A. and R.S. records were correctly prepared on the basis of right, title, interest and possession of the suit land. The defendants donated some Land to the local mosque by a deed of waqf and constructed the mosque in front of their homestead. The plaintiffs had no right, title, interest and possession as such the prayer of the plaintiffs should be dismissed.

4. The trial court upon hearing the parties and considering the materials on record decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 2.5.1985. Against the same the defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 75 of 1985 before the learned District Judge, Comilla. The appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Comilla who by his judgment and decree dated 4.9.2004 allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree o the trial court. The plaintiffs thus move( the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4847 of 2004 and obtained Rule which has been ultimately discharged by judgment and order dated 30.5.2011 by a single Bench of the High Court Division affirming the judgment and decree of till lower appellate court.

5. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order of the High Court Division the plaintiff-appellants filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1669 of 2011 an obtained leave to consider that the High Court Division by misreading and upon non consideration of the evidence or record erroneously discharged the Rule. The High Court Division without considering the materials on record though found that the defendants failed to prove the story of auction sale and eviction by adducing oral and documentary evidence but erroneously discharged the Rule. Hence this appeal.

6. Mr. M.A. Quiyom, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the defendants could not produce any single paper to show that the predecessors of the plaintiffs were evicted from the suit land pursuant to auction sale. The court of appeal below as well as the High Court Division without referring to any document of the defendants came to the findings that the defendants were in possession of the suit land. He also submitted that the court of appeal below as well as the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the plaintiffs never paid any rent in respect of the suit property ignoring exhibit-4 series which clearly show that they paid rents. Thus the High Court Division committed error in law in discharging the Rule and dismissing the suit, which is liable to be set aside.

7. Per contra Mr. Farid Ahmed the learned advocate appearing on behalf of defendant-respondents submits that there is no illegality in allowing the appeal by lower appellate court and affirming the same by the High Court Division as the plaintiffs hopelessly failed to prove their title as well as possession in the suit land. He submits that the suit property was sold in auction pursuant to order dated 15.5.1939 in certificate case No. 2 of 1938-1939 and pursuant to the said order the purchaser took possession of the suit land on 15.5.1941 and thereby the title and possession of the original tenants has been extinguished. He also submits that PW 1 himself in his cross examination admitted that his grandfather and others were evicted from the suit and thereafter the same was leased out to Alimuddin and Sekander; that the S.A. and R.S. records were correctly prepared and the defendants having title and possession in the suit land had been paying rents to the Jamimders as well as to the Government vide exhibit B and C series. He also submits that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land by producing any scrap of paper as against the sale certificate in pursuant to order dated 15.5.1941. Lastly, Mr. Ahmed submits that the lower appellate court being the last court of fact specifically found title and possession of the defendants in the suit land pursuant to admission of the plaintiffs No. 2 and 3 (PWS) that they as to the title of defendant No. 3 and their purchased 6 decimals of land from defendant No. 3 by kabala dated 27.11.1968 much earlier to institution of the suit in 1983. This admission of purchase is nothing but actually admitting the title of the defendants in the suit land. Thus he submits that the High Court Division rightly affirmed the judgment of the blower appellate court:

<u>8. On this back drop we have gone through the materials on record and considered the submissions as noted above. Admittedly it is a suit for declaration simpliciter. So it is the duty of the plaintiffs to prove their title in the suit land. Question of possession though is one of the main factors but that may come in such suit as subsidiary evidence on the principle that possession follows title. On perusal of the judgment of the lower appellate court, which has been affirmed by the High Court Division, it appears that upon analysing the evidence of PWs the last court of fact found that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title in the suit land. PW1 in his evidence said that he could not remember whether they paid any rent to the Bangladesh Government any time before or after the suit has been instituted in 1982.</u>

9. On perusal of the exhibits it appears that after eviction of the predecessor of the plaintiffs, pursuant to certificate case, the suit property was settled with Alimuddip and Sekander by registered kabuliat. It further appears That S.A. Khatian was prepared admittedly upon inserting the names of the defendants, though the plaintiffs claimed it to be wrong but they failed to prove by any evidence that such record was wrong. It also appears from the evidence of PW 1 that he never paid rent either to the Jaminder Seresta or to the government of Pakistan. He also admitted that 'he could not remember whether he paid any rent to the Bangladesh Government'. Similarly P.W. 2 could not say whether 'their predecessors were evicted from the suit land pursuant to auction sale. Interestingly, the trial court decreed the suit upon holding that the defendants could not prove the auction sale i.e. on the defect of the defendants forgetting the principle that the plaintiff is to prove his own case. Weakness of the o defendants cannot be the ground for decreeing a suit in favour of the plaintiff.

<u>10. Apart from the above upon going through the evidence of DWs it appears that DW 1 in his deposition categorically stated that the plaintiff’s No. 1, 2 and 3 purchased 6 decimals of land from the defendants by Kabola which PW1 denied in his cross examination but plaintiff no. 2 and 3 admitted the same. From the judgment of the trial court it appears that the said court also found that 'the defendants sold 6 decimals of land to the plaintiffs and 24 decimals of land to other persons. On this score on perusal of exhibit-2, a document filed by the plaintiffs, it appears that the denial of PW-1 as to purchase of 6 decimals of land from the defendants does not have any leg to stand. Thus when the plaintiffs purchased the suit property or any portion thereof from the defendants it is clear that unless the title of the defendants is admitted the plaintiffs could not purchase the same. On the face of such admission of defendant's title the decree of the trial court was not proper which the court of appeal below, upon discussing the evidence on record correctly reversed. Thus we cannot but hold that the court of appeal below as well as the High Court Division did not commit any error/illegality in passing the judgment in favour of the defendants and thereby dismissing the suit.</u>

11. For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove we do not find any merit in this appeal. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is hereby affirmed.

End.
