১। উপ-সচিব, ভূমি প্রশাসন ও ভূমি সংষ্কার মন্ত্রণালয়, বাংলাদেশ সচিবালয়, ঢাকা ।

২। অতিরিক্ত জেলা প্রশাসক, এল, এ, ঢাকা।

স্বাঃ অস্পষ্ট

২৫/৩/৮৫।

উপ-পরিচালক (প্রশাসন)

জাতীয় নিরাপত্তা গোয়েন্দা বিভাগ, ঢাকা ।”

32. From the record of L.A. Case No.27/69-70, we have found that notices issued under Sections 5(la) and 5(3) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act were duly served. In spite of giving opportunity of filing objection, Munshi Ashraf Ali, predecessor-in-interest of the writ petitioner-respondents did not file any objection. The Executive Engineer paid a sum of taka 2,18,246/- from its contingency item under grant no.45 for compensation of the acquired property. The Government took over the actual physical possession of the disputed property on 22.07.1971 and handed over the same to the Sub-Divisional Engineer, Ramna (Bids), Dhaka. An inventory of goods for handing over and taking over of possession of the same was prepared. Provisional compensation of disputed property was duly assessed for a payment of the same to

Munshi Ashraf Ali, predecessor-in-interest of the writ petitioner respondents requesting him to receive the compensation but he did not receive the said compensation.

33. From the record it further appears that the respondent No.1 Sk. Liakat Ali, admitting the fact of acquisition, prayed for release of the disputed property by filing an application addressing the ADC (L.A) Dhaka on 18.11.1984. In that application he, inter alia, stated, "To our utter surprise and dismay, the above holding was subsequently acquired in L.A case No.27 of 1969-70 for construction of Press Club, but the press club subsequently was constructed on a different site/the present site (where it stands now). Thus, the above holding was not used for the purpose for which it was acquired and no compensation was paid to the owner and as such no steps were taken to complete the acquisition proceedings."

34. The disputed property was allotted to the National Security Intelligence (N.S.I) who has been possessing the same repairing structures therein expending huge amount. The High Court Division though called for the record of L.A. Case No.27/1969-70, but without perusing the same meticulously and without taking into consideration of the facts and consequences of subsequent requisition and acquisition most abruptly drew conclusion that the Government is unauthorized possessor of the disputed property as it possessed the same forcibly which was erroneous and contrary to the provisions of law, this Division while deposing of the civil petition also failed to notice the same.

35. Section 3 of the Act provides the pro-vision that when a property is required permanently for a public purpose or in public interest, the Deputy Commissioner may requisition it with a view to its permanent acquisition for such public purpose or in such public interest. From Order No.3 dated 19.07.1971 it appears that the said provision was duly complied with. From the said order it was directed to Nazir to serve notice which was made in view of the provision provided in section 4 of the Act. Order 6 dated 26.07.1971 it is clear that all the steps under section 5 were complied with except publication of notification under section 5(7) of the Act.

36. It is true that the disputed property was acquired for construction of the building of Press Club but the Press Club was established elsewhere. It is also true that the notice under Section 5(7) (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 was not published in official gazette. Since the notices under Section 5(1a) and 5(3) were duly issued and served upon Munshi Ashraf Ali and provisional compensation for acquisition of disputed property was duly assessed and issuing notices, the Acquiring Authority requested the owner to receive the compensation and actual physical possession was taken over by the government, the right, title and possession of the disputed property has been vested in the Government. The writ petitioner respondents claimed that they are entitled to get back the possession of the disputed property since it has not been used for the purpose, for which, it was acquired but the said submission is not acceptable.

37. In the case of Brahmanbaria Pourasava Vs. Govt. of Bangladesh reported in 51 DIAZ (AD) 81 it has been held: " Again there is no principle of law under which once a property has been validly acquired for a public purpose, as admitted by the Government and has vested in the requiring body then even if the said property be utilised for a different purpose, the acquisition shall not stand void. A simple reading of section 8B of the Act shows that it does not come into operation in this circumstances of the case. So the order of withdrawal from acquisition in question cannot be sustained."

38. In the case of Abul Basher being dead his heirs Hosne Ara Begom and others V. Bangladesh and others reported 50 DLR (AD) 11 this Division observed that mere non-use of the acquired land for the purpose for which it was acquired will not give any right to get return of the same.

39. It appears that Munshi Ashraf Ali, the predecessor-in-interest of the writ petitioner respondents managed to get an exparte decree in Title Suit No.307 of 1975 in which it was declared that the disputed land was not requisitioned property and defendants of the said suit was permanently restrained for entering the disputed land but from the papers of L.A. Case No.27/1969-70 it appears that once disputed property was requisitioned and, then derequisitioned and thereafter, the same was acquired in L.A. Case No.27/1969-70. It further appears in the said suit that acquisition of the said property in afore-said L.A. Case was not challenged. Moreover, section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act provides the provision that no Civil Court shall entertain any suit against any order passed or action taken under the said Act.

That is, said suit was not at all maintain-able. Moreover, the N.S.I. who, taking the delivery of possession after getting allotment of disputed property from Government Accommodation Director has been possessing the same, was not impleaded as party in the said suit. Since the Government took over actual physical possession of the disputed property long before passing the decree of permanent injunction upon acquiring the disputed property, the decree passed in the aforesaid suit was inoperative.

40. Since the Government filed Title Suit No.232 of 1997 in the First Court, of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and got decree upto the High Court, against which, the writ petition & respondents filed Civil Appeal No.191 of 2015 and at this stage, the Government has filed an application for withdrawal of the suit, we are not inclined to discuss the merit of the said suit. Order XXII rule 1 gives power to the Court to allow the plaintiff at any time to withdraw his suit unconditionally. The Government is permitted to withdraw Title Suit No.232 of 1997.

41. On perusal of the notings in the note sheet of L.A. Case No.27 of 1969-70, documents and other materials available in the record, it appears to us that there was no procedural irregularity or illegality in the process of acquisition of the disputed property. Only step was left that was the order of acquisition was not published in official gazette. That was the business of acquiring authority in view of section 5(7) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act. For that reason, the process already completed had not been inadmissible.

42. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the Civil Appeal No.191 of 2015 is disposed of. The application for withdrawal of Title Suit No.232 of 1997 of the First Court, Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is allowed. Consequently judgment and decrees passed in Title Suit No.232 of 1997 and F.A.No.157 of 2001 are set aside. Civil Review Petition No.334 of 2019 is disposed of. The order dated 31.07.1997 passed by this Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.595 of 1997 is reviewed and set aside. The judgment and order dated 17.06.1996 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.333 of 19.93 is also set aside.

<u>43. Since the provisional compensation of the disputed property was assessed and the writ petitioners or their predecessor did not withdraw the compensation as assessed and the same is lying in the office of Acquirm Authority, we are of the view that justice would best be met if a lump sum amount of Tk. 3,00,00,000/-(three crore) is paid to the writ petitioner respondents by the Government against the assessed compensation.</u>

<u>44. Accordingly, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka is directed to pay a sum of taka 3 crore as compensation of the disputed property to the writ petitioner-respondents within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment positively without fail.</u>

End.

Vs.
Shimul Rani Saha and others..........Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 2nd of June, 2014 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1134 of 2005)
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali, J:- This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 02.06.2014 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1134 of 2005 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that Palash Chandra Saha, the petitioner herein as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.31 of 2000 in the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiya, Feni seeking a declaration that he is the adopted son of Khitish Chandra Saha, who was the husband of Gouri Rani Saha (defendant No.4) and the father of Simul Rani Saha (defendant No.1).

3. The plaintiff stated, inter alia, that he was born on 3rd Bhadra 1375 B.S. His natural parents were late Nishi Kanta Das and late Charubala Das. His natural mother died when he was six months old. Since late Khitish Chandra Saha and his wife defendant No.4 had no child they decided to adopt the plaintiff. Their offer/proposal to adopt the plaintiff was accepted by his natural father. Accordingly, late Nishi Kanta Das handed over the plaintiff to Gouri Rani Saha (defendant No.4) and her husband Khitish Chandra Saha. On 15th Falgun, 1375 B.S. the adoption ceremony of the plaintiff was held and since then he had been living in his adoptive father’s house. After his adoption, the plaintiff had no relationship with his natural father. While he was brought up in his adoptive parents’ house, their only daughter Simul Rani Saha, defendant No.1 was born. Khitish Chandra Saha got the plaintiff admitted to school and wrote his own name as the father of the plaintiff in all his school documents. In the S.S.C. and H.S.C. certificates of the plaintiff and also in the voter lists the father’s name of the plaintiff has been recorded as Khitish Chandra Saha. On 07.09.1993 Khitish Chandra Saha filed Title Suit No.69 of 1993 and in that suit also he admitted the plaintiff as his adopted son. After the death of Khitish Chandra Saha the plaintiff performed all rituals as his son. Defendant No.4 has been living with the plaintiff and his wife. After the death of Khitish Chandra Saha the plaintiff allowed defendant No.1 and her family to stay with him for a temporary period. Defendant No.1 in order to deprive the plaintiff from the property he inherited from Khitish Chandra Saha, has been declaring that the plaintiff is not the adopted son of late Khitish Chandra Saha. Hence, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit.

4. Defendant No.1 and her 2 sons-defendant Nos.2 and 3 contested the suit by filing written statement. They contended, inter alia, that the plaintiff is not the adopted son of Khitish Chandra Saha. Khitish Chandra Saha never adopted the plaintiff as his son. Khitish Chandra Saha was a rich man having huge property including a sweetmeat shop. The plaintiff was a cashier in that shop. In order to avoid income tax Khitish Chandra Saha purchased some property in the benami of the plaintiff and others. Khitish Chandra Saha having learnt that the plaintiff was trying to dispose of those property purchased by Khitish Chandra Saha in the benami of the plaintiff, filed Title Suit No.69 of 1993 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiyan against the present plaintiff for declaration that the present plaintiff was a mere ‘benamdar’ of the said property. The said suit was decreed. Since Khitish Chandra Saha had no son, defendant No.l and her husband stayed in the house of Khitish Chandra Saha even after her marriage. According to Hindu Law, defendant Nos.2 and 3, the sons of defendant No.l, have inherited all the moveable and immovable properties of late Khitish Chandra Saha. Defendant No.4 developed some bitter feelings with her daughter-defendant No.l and taking advantage of this situation the plaintiff has filed this present suit. The plaintiff is neither the foster son nor the adopted son of late Khitish Chandra Saha which he himself stated in the plaint of Title Suit No.69 of 1993. The plaintiff also did not claim himself to be the adopted son of late Khitish Chandra Saha in his written statement filed in Title Suit No.69 of 1993. The plaintiff filed the present suit long after the death of Khitish Chandra Saha on false claim and allegations.

5. Upon hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiyan, Feni by his judgment and decree dated 22.05.2002 decreed the suit finding that the plaintiff was the legally adopted son of Khitish. Then defendant Nos.1 to 3 preferred Title Appeal No.59 of 2002 before the learned District Judge, Feni. On transfer the appeal was heard by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Feni, who by his judgment and order dated 02.11.2004 dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and order passed by the trial Court 6.

6. Being aggrieved, the contesting defendants filed Civil Revision No.1134 of 2005 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was made absolute. Hence, the plaintiff filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2407 of 2014 and leave was granted to consider the following grounds:

“I. That in this suit the plaintiff adduced sufficient evidence, both-oral and documentary, to prove that he was adopted as son by Khitish Chandra Saha and that both the Courts of facts have examined and considered all these evidence adduced by the plaintiff and came to a concurrent decision that the plaintiff is adopted son of late Khitish Chandra Saha.

II. That these concurrent findings and decision of the Court of facts is not at all based on the findings and decision arrived at in earlier Title Suit No.69 of 1993 as to adoption of the plaintiff by Khitish Chandra Saha; the High Court Division without adverting to the concurrent findings and decision of the Courts of facts and without considering the evidence adduced by the plaintiff, most erroneously held that the Courts below decreed the suit of the plaintiff relying on the decision of the earlier Title Suit No.69 of 1993 only.

III. That the High Court Division did not at all apply its judicial mind in setting aside the concurrent finding of the Courts of facts and most erroneously set aside the concurrent findings of the Courts below without considering the evidence on record at all.

IV. That this impugned judgment of the High Court Division is erroneous and cannot be sustained in law and in the circumstances leave to appeal needs to be granted.”

7. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He also submitted that the appellate Court as well as the trial Court concurrently found on evidence, adduced in the present suit, aside from the finding of adoption given in Title Suit No.69 of 1993, that Khitish Chandra Saha adopted the plaintiff-petitioner and brought him up as his son as per the relevant rules of the Hindu Law, but the High Court Division without referring to the evidence and without adverting to the concurrent findings of fact of the courts below set aside their judgments and decrees. As such, the impugned judgment and order cannot be sustained. He further submitted that the High Court Division could not point out any sort of misreading or non-consideration of evidence by the Courts below in arriving at the concurrent finding that the plaintiff-petitioner was validly adopted and brought up as the adopted son by Khitish Chandra Saha. He also submitted that neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court considered the finding as to adoption given in the judgment of Title Suit No.69 of 1993 to be a res judicata and the Courts below did not base their decision on such finding, which was considered as a piece of evidence simply. He submitted that in earlier Title Suit No.69 of 1993, although no issue was framed as to adoption, both the parties chose to join issue upon that point without protest, and impliedly the said issue was dealt with in the suit; so, the decision on the point will operate as res judicata between the parties.

8. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Advocate appearing for respondent Nos.1-3, made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He also submitted that the High Court Division rightly set aside the judgment and decree of both Courts of facts holding that the findings and decision arrived at in earlier Title Suit No.69 of 1993 as to adoption of the plaintiff by Khitish Chandra Saha will not operate as res-judicata in the present suit and that both the courts below failed to appreciate this vital legal aspect, and thus the Courts committed wrong in decreeing the suit in relying on the incidental findings made in the judgment of the previous Title Suit No.69 of 1993. He further submitted that the appellate Court failed to consider that the limitation for filing the present suit started from the date of filing Civil Suit No.69 of 1993 by late Khitish Chandra Saha who claimed in his plaint that the plaintiff is not his adopted son and as such the appellate Court committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in not holding that the suit in question was barred by limitation having been filed long after six years of accrual of cause of action under clause 119 of Limitation Act, 1908 and as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. He submitted that the appellate Court committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in dismissing the appeal in mis-appreciating the evidence of late Khitish Chandra Saha in Civil Suit No.69 of 1993 denying the present plaintiff as his adopted son, and in taking into consideration the evidence of witnesses in Civil Suit No.31 of 2000 in that the witnesses and both the courts below confused a foster son with an adopted son, the former having no legal status of a son. He lastly submitted that both the Courts below failed to appreciate the distinction between fostering and adoption and in not considering the evidence of plaintiff’s witnesses in the light of the assertion of late Khitish Chandra Saha that the plaintiff was not his adopted son but foster son and thus committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the suit and dismissing the appeal and as such the appeal is liable to be dismissed.

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. The moot question in this appeal concerns the validity of the adoption of the appellant Polash Chandra Saha by Khitish Chandra Saha, husband of Gouri Rani Saha-respondent No.4, father of respondent No.1 Shimul Rani Saha and grandfather of Chayan Chandra Saha and Dahan Chandra Saha (minor).

10. Polash Chandra Saha as plaintiff claims that he was adopted by Khitish Chandra Saha and his wife Gouri Rani Saha under Hindu Law. In support of his claim he relied upon the findings in an earlier judgement in Title Suit No.69 of 1993 where it was found that he was legally adopted. The earlier Title Suit No.69 of 1993 was filed by Khitish Chandra Saha against Krishna Chandra Das @ Polash Chandra Saha with a claim that certain property purchased in the name of Polash was his benami property.

11. When delivering the judgment in Title Suit No.69 of 1993 the trial Court, while decreeing the suit, observed that Polash had been taken into the family of Khitish Chandra Saha at the age of 6(six) months, his name had been changed in all the records, the business established by Khitish was named “Polash Cabin” and the purchase of the property in that suit in the name of Polash was evidence of his adoption. It was further observed that in Bangladesh apart from ‘Duttohom’ if the formalities are observed the adoption will be lawful according to the principle of factum valet. The trial Court in that suit concluded that defendant No.1 of that suit Polash Chandra Saha was indeed the adopted son of the plaintiff of that suit, Khitish Chandra Saha.

<u>12. According to Hindu Law any act done in contravention of the Hindu texts which are in their nature mandatory cannot be said to be lawful by applying the principle of factum valet. Hence, the principle of factum valet is ineffectual in the case of adoption in contravention of the provision of legal texts. So far as adoption under Hindu Law is concerned, we may refer to Molla’s Principles of Hindu Law (18th Edition) wherein article 480 provides as follows: “480. WHO MAY BE ADOPTED Subject to the following rules, any person who is a Hindu, may be taken or given in adoption:</u>

<u>(1) the person to be adopted must be a male;</u>

<u>(2) he must belong to the same caste as his adopting father; thus, a Brahman cannot adopt a Kshatriya, a Vaisya or Sudra; it is not necessary that he should belong to the same sub-division of the caste;</u>

<u>(3) he must not be a boy, whose mother the adopting father could not have legally married; but this rule had been restricted in many cases to the daughter’s son, sister’s son, and mother’s sister’s son. This prohibition, however, does not apply to Sudras. Even as to the three upper classes, it has been held that an adoption, though prohibited under this rule, may be valid, if sanctioned by custom.”</u>

<u>Thus it is quite clear according to article 480(2) that the adoptive father of the child to be adopted must belong to the same caste and that adoption would be valid if they belong to different sub-division of the same caste.</u>

13. There are 4(four) primary castes in the Hindu religion namely, Brahman, Kshatriya, Vaisya and Sudra.

The claim of the appellant before us is that Saha is a sub-caste of Sudra and for that reason the ritual after his death was done after 30 days which is the customary period in case of a person belonging to the Sudra caste. The learned Advocate for the appellant empathetically argued that Saha is a sub-caste of Sudra and hence the adoption was legal.

14. In support of his argument Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, produced before us information obtain from the internet (Quora) where it has been opined that “although most Saha may be of trading community/Baisya but there are some Saha mostly from West Bengal are bootleggers by profession, they are Shudra/ Scheduled Caste. So a Saha can either be Baishya or Sudra community. So for practical purpose some use the term Sunri (bootleger) Saha to avoid this confusion.”

The learned Advocate for the respondent submitted that Saha is of the Vaisya caste and the appellant whose name at birth was Krishna Chandra Das was of the Sudra caste and, therefore, the adoption was unlawful under provisions of Hindu Law as the adoptive father and the adopted son were of two different castes.

15. Mr. Probir Neogi, learned Advocate who appeared for the respondent placed before us certain information obtained from the internet (Wikipedia) where it has been stated that Baishya Saha is a Bengali Hindu trading caste traditionally known to have the occupation of grocers, shopkeepers, and dealers of various goods. Some are money lenders and farmers. Some use Saha as their surname, but others use Bhowmik, Chowdhury, Das, Majumder, Mallick, Poddar, Roy Chowdhury, Sarker and Sikder, Roy, among others.

16. We find from the case of Pankaj Kumar Saha Vs. Sub-Divisional Officers, Islampur and Ors.(1996) 8SCC 264 that in the State of West Bengal Sunri excluding Saha has been declared to be Scheduled caste. It was observed as follows: “Sunri (excluding Saha) is a Scheduled Caste for the purpose of State of West Bengal. The petitioner admittedly bears the name Saha. The authorities found as a fact that for over a century the petitioner’s family are Saha by caste. The President after consultation with the Governor, has excluded ‘Saha’, a liquor business community as Scheduled Caste. Though some Scheduled Castes by name Sunri adopted tapping as profession, they suffer from untouchability while Sahas, liquor business community like Sethi balija, Edigal or Gowda in Andhra Pradesh are not Scheduled Castes.”

17. In view of the above, we conclude that Saha are of the business community and are not of the scheduled caste, therefore not Sudra. Hence, Khitish Chandra Saha being a Baishya could not adopt a child from the Sudra caste.

18. Both the trial Court and the appellate Court found that the plaintiff was able to prove that he was the lawfully adopted son of Khitish Chandra Saha. We note that the trial Court, in particular relied upon the evidence of defendant No.4 who is the adoptive mother of the plaintiff, who deposed in support of the adoption in spite of the fact that the evidence would deprive her of her life interest in the property as well as the interest of her own biological daughter (defendant No.1). However, this conclusion is only partly correct in law because Gouri Rani (defendant No.4) would benefit from having life interest in her late husband’s property whether or not the plaintiff is the lawfully adopted son of her late husband. It is true that her biological daughter and the sons from that daughter (defendant Nos.2 and 3) would be totally deprived if the plaintiff inherited the property as the adopted son of Khitish. In fact Gouri Rani Saha did not depose to the detriment of her own interest.

19. We also see in the record papers relating to Miscellaneous Case No.62 of 1996 wherein Gouri Rani prayed for a succession certificate claiming herself to be the only heir of late Khtish Chandra Saha. This was admitted by defendant No.4 and the plaintiff in their respective cross examinations.

20. The trial Court also considered the evidence to the effect that the “Shradha” ritual after death takes place after 15 days in case of Baishya and after 30 days in case of Sudra and, therefore, Khitish was Sudra by caste. However, it appears that the trial Court did not consider the evidence of P.W.2 who deposed that he is Purohit for Polash’s biological father who was Sudra and he did not attend any rituals of the Saha gutra, thereby confirming that they are a different caste. In his cross examination P.W.2 categorically stated that he conducts the Puja of the Namasudras and does not attend “Shradha” of Sahas. He also explained that he only attended the adoption ceremony of Polash because he was his follower. It is, therefore, clear from the evidence of P.W.2 that Saha and Sudra are two separate castes. We do not find any evidence from the deposition of the witnesses to the effect that Polash and Khtish are of two sub-castes of Sudra caste.

21. In decreeing the suit the trial Court took into consideration the finding of another Court in the earlier Title Suit No.69 of 1993. In that suit, Khitish as plaintiff had claimed that property purchased in the name of Polash was ‘benami’ property which he (Khitish) had purchased with his own money. That suit was decreed holding that the property was purchased by Khitish and that Polash was his benamder. However, although there was no issue with regard to Polash being adopted by Khitish, that Court found that there was a legal adoption. In the instant suit the trial Court took the finding of adoption in the earlier suit as res-judicata observing that Khitish did not challenge the finding that Polash was legally adopted.

22. However, we cannot ignore the fact that the finding in Title Suit No.69 of 1993 with respect to adoption of Polash by Khitish was a mere obiter. It was not an issue in the suit and since the suit was decreed in favour of Khitish he was not required to appeal against an observation which was not the subject matter of that suit.

23. We note from the judgment in Title Suit No.69 of 1993 that having concluded that the defendant (Polash) was the plaintiff’s (Khitish’s) benamder the Court then went on to consider the relationship of the parties as an afterthought for the sake of completeness. That was not at all necessary. We also note that the consequent appeal filed by Krishna Chandra Saha (Polash’s name at birth) being Civil Appeal No.73 of 1994 was dismissed on 17.08.1998 thereby declaring title in the suit land in favour of Khitish finding Polash as his benamder.

24. Although defendant No.4 Gouri Rani deposed in favour of the plaintiff and also submitted a Solenama in his favour, she categorically stated in her cross examination that she is from the Saha gutra and the plaintiff is from Namasudhra caste and that each caste has different Brahman. However, both the trial Court and the appellate Court appear to have overlooked this admission that they are from two distinct castes. She also admitted that after her husband’s death the tax returns for their business was submitted in her name. This tends to support Khitish’s claim in Title Suit No.69 of 1993 that Polash was not his adopted son but only taken as a foster son due to the fact that his mother had died when he was a baby and his wife was childless at that time.

<u>25. From the above discussion of facts and evidence it transpires that Polash was certainly taken into the family of Khitish and he adopted the title Saha. However, even if he was accepted as a family member, the legality of the adoption must be considered. The provision of Hindu Law is clear that there cannot be adoption across castes. In other words, a child from one caste cannot be legally adopted by a member of another caste.</u>

26. Initially Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali argued that the prohibition of cross-caste adoption had been lifted due to the promulgation of the Caste Disabilities Removal Act, 1850. But he abandoned the argument when Mr. Neogi pointed out that the said law was not applicable in Bangladesh.

27. Mr. Neogi has sought to distinguish between the concept of adoption “দত্তক” and fostering “পালক”. He drew our attention to the written statement filed by Polash in Title Suit No.69 of 1993 wherein he stated “…৫-৬ বৎসর বয়স হইতে বাদীর আপন পুত্রের ন্যায় বাদীর সংসারের হাল শক্ত হাতে ধরিয়া বাদীর সংসারের যাবতীয় কার্য সুষ্ঠুরুপে পরিচালনা করিয়া বাদীর সংসারের যথেষ্ট উন্নতি সাধন করিয়াছে এবং করিতেছে। এই বাদী বাদীর পালক পুত্র হইলেও কখনো বাদীকে পালক পিতা হিসাবে না জানিয়া জন্মদাতা পিতার ন্যায় শ্রদ্ধা ভক্তি করিত এবং করিতেছে।” He submitted that Polash never claimed himself to be “adopted son” (দত্তক পুত্র) of Khitish Chandra Saha. We find substance in such submission particularly in view of the admission by Gouri Rani in her application for a succession certificate that Khitish did not have any other heir.

28. Moreover, we cannot overlook the fact that there was no evidence to support the contention that Saha is a sub-caste of Sudra. On the contrary the evidence of Gouri Rani and P.W.2 clearly suggest that the two families are from two distinct castes. Furthermore, the case of Pankaj Kumar Saha cited above clearly shows that Saha are not of a Schedule Caste. Hence there could not be any adoption by a person of the Saha gutra (not being a schedule caste) of a child from a Sudra gutra (being a schedule caste).

29. We find from the cross examination of the Purohit (P.W.2) that as a Brahmin he conducted the ritual/ceremonies of the Sudra caste. He categorically stated that Khitish was a Saha and he never attended any of their Puja or Shradha ceremony. He only conducted the dattak function for Polash because he was his RRevb-(follower). The question of limitation was not discussed by the High Court Division. However, the learned Advocate for the respondents submitted that the appellate Court erred in not holding that the suit was barred by limitation.

<u>30. The relevant law is found in article 119 of the Schedule to the limitation Act, which provides that in order to obtain a declaration that an adoption is valid the suit must be filed within six years from the date when the rights of the adopted son, as such, are interfered with. Mr. Alam submitted that Khitish in his plaint in Title Suit No.69 of 1993 claimed that Polash was not his adopted son, and therefore, the period of limitation commenced in 1993. Hence the suit filed in the year 2000 was barred. We find substance in the submission of Mr. Alam. We find from the plaint of Title Suit No.69 of 1993 that Khitish categorically stated that the defendant (Polash) had no right in law to lay claim as an adopted son. Such denial by the claimed adoptive father gives rise to the cause of action. Hence, we are of the view that the suit is barred by limitation.</u>

<u>31. In view of the above discussion, we do not find any illegality in the impugned judgment, and accordingly the appeal is dismissed, without, however, any order as to costs.</u>

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 20th day of June, 2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1447 of 1998).
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J. This Civil Appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 20.06.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 144 of 1998 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and order dated 10.03.1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Tangail, in Miscellaneous No.38 of 1996 allowing the appeal upon reversing those dated 28.07.1996 of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Mirzapur, in Pre-emption Case No.44 of 1994 allowing pre-emption.

2. Facts giving rise to this civil appeal in short are:

3. That respondent No.1 herein, as Pre-emptor, filed Pre-emption Case No. 44 of 1994 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Mirzapur, Tangail, for pre-empting .48 acre out of 1.51 acre of land in Plot Nos. 5/9/11 of RS Khatian No. 198 and CS Khatian No. 122 situated in Mouza Chhitmamudpur, PS-Mirzapur, Tangail, stating, inter alia, that 14.37 acres of land in C.S Khatian No. 122 originally belonged to two brothers, namely, Osimuddin and Kasimuddin, both sons of late Boksha Mollah, in equal share. While they were in peaceful enjoyment of the same Osimuddin died leaving behind 3(three) sons, namely, Abdul Kuddus Mollah, Abdul Mollah and Ramjan Mollah as his heirs who were possessing the same peacefully in ejmali and got their names finally recorded in the ROR Khatian. Thereafter, Abdul Mollah died leaving behind four sons namely, Sobdar Mollah, Yakub Mollah, Badar MollEih and Nurul Mollah and one daughter, namely Most. Sharifunnessa (respondent Nos. 16-19 and 32 respectively), as his legal heirs. While, in peaceful enjoyment of the same, all the said heirs of Abdul Mollah transferred 1.80 acres of land in Dag No. 392, Khatian No. 123, including the case land in separate Dag Nos. 5/8/9/10/11, Khatian No. 122, to the pre-emptor-respondent No.1 by exchange deed dated 04.01.1988. Accordingly the pre-emptor took over possession thereof and became a co sharer tenant in the case jote along with Kuddus Mollah and others. In the meantime Kuddus Mollah, brother of Abdul Mollah, sold .48 acre of land to Dr. Forman Ali Miah (preemptee-appellant), by registered deed dated 15.06.1994, without giving any statutory notice to the pre-emptor. The Pre-emptee-appellant is thus a stranger purchaser. Hence, the pre-emptor respondent No.1 filed the aforesaid pre-emption case in respect of the said .48 acre of land.

4. The pre-emptee-appellant contested the said case by filing written objection, contending inter-alia, that 14.37 acres of land originally belonged to Boksha Mollah who died leaving behind two sons Osimuddin and Kasimuddin as his heirs whose names were recorded in equal share. Osimuddin died leaving 3 sons, namely, Abdul Mollah, Kuddus Mollah, and Ramjan Mollah as his heirs. While in peaceful enjoyment of the same, Kuddus Mollah and Ramjan Mollah, the two brothers of late Abdul Mollah sold 2.88 acres of land from case Plots No. 5/9 along with other plots to Ghutu Sikdar, father of pre-emptee appellant, by registered deed dated 31.08.1945 and handed over possession of the same to him. Thereafter, while in possession of the same Ghutu Sikdar transferred .80 acre of land from case plots No. 5/9 along with other plots to his son, the appellant by a registered Heba-bil-Ewaz dated 01.11.1988 and handed over possession in his favour. Accordingly the pre-emptee-appellant became a cc sharer-tenant by purchase of the said case land, even otherwise than by purchase'. On the other hand, the said Kuddus Mollah subsequently by another registered deed dated 15.06.1994 sold the case land measuring .48 acre from Plots No. 5/9/11 to the pre-emptee-appellant and handed over possession of the same in his favour. Since then the pre-emptee appellant is possessing the same in ejmali upon erecting dwelling house thereon. On the other hand the pre-emptor respondent after purchasing 1.80 acres of land from Plots No. 5/8/9/10/11 in 1988 is possessing the same upon mutating his name vide Mutation Miscellaneous Case No. 1063(IX-1) of 1990-91 and accordingly, got a separate Khatian/holding in his nale and therefore the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case jote and as such the pre-emption case is not maintainable.

5. The learned Assistant Judge, after hearing the parties and on perusal of the materials on record, allowed the pre-emption case on contest with direction upon the pre-emptee appellant to handover the case land to the pre-emptor respondent No.1 within 45 days in default to take possession of the same through Court, by judgment and order dated 28.07.1996.

6. The pre-emptee-appellant challenged the said judgment and order in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 38 of 1996 before the learned District Judge, Tangail which was ultimately heard and allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge (Now Joint District Judge) and Artharin Adalat, Tangail, by judgment and order dated 18.03.1998. Against which the pre-emptor respondent No.1 moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1447 of 1998 and obtained Rule.

7. A Single Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the Rule absolute and set aside the judgment and order dated 18.03.1998 passed by the court of appeal below and upheld the judgment and order dated 28.7.1996 passed by the trial Court in Pre-emption Case No. 44 of 1994, by the impugned judgment and order dated 20.06.2006. Hence the pre-emptee-appellant preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1703 of 2007 and obtained leave which gave rise to the instant appeal.

<u>8. Mr. Subrata Saha, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant submits that the pre-emptor respondent No.1, Nizamuddin, purchased the land in the jote from the heirs of Abdul Mollah whereas Ghutu Shikder, father of the pre-emptee-appellant, Dr Forman All Miah, purchased 2.88 acres of land in case jote from Kuddus Mollah and Ramjan Mollah, brothers of late Mollah and thereafter transferred .80 acre to the appellant in 1988 thus the appellant became co-sharer in the case jote otherwise by purchase. Therefore, the status of the preemptee and the pre-emptor of the case jote is the same. The learned Advocate further submits that Ghutu S'kdar also sold .24 acre of land to the pre-emptor Nizamuddin at the same time when he transferred .80 acre of land to his son, Dr. Forman Ali Miah. Therefore, in this respect also the status of the pre-emptee and the pre-emptor is the same. The learned Advocate finally submits that the High Court Division commit-ted error in not holding teat failing to pro-duce the process server of the notice upon the co-sharers for the purpose of mutation case, is not the proof of non-service of notice. In this respect Mr. Saha submits that for determination of this question the trial court could have called for the record of the mutation case and without doing so, it cannot be said that notice was not served upon the co-sharers as it is the settled principle of law that any person, who denies a public document like certified copy, the burden of proof lies upon him to prove the same. Accordingly he prayed that the appeal should be allowed.</u>

9. Mr. Probir Neogi, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the pre-emptor-respondent No.1 submits that the respondent is a co-sharer tenant by Ewaznama (Exchange Deed) dated 04.01.1988 and he is also a co-sharer by purchase from the father of the appellant. As such he submits that the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned judgment which is based on proper appreciation of section 96 as well as section 10 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Hence he submits that this appeal should be dismissed.

10. From the above noted submissions of both the sides and on perusal of the materials on record, including the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, it appears that admittedly the case land is an agricultural land and the preemptor respondent, claiming to be a co-sharer-tenant in the case jote by way of exchange and purchase, filed the pre-emption case. He alleged that the preemptee-appellant is a stranger purchaser in the case jote and as such the pre-emptor has right to pre-empt the case land.

11. It also appears that the pre-emptee-appellant's father, Ghutu Sikdar, purchased 2.88 acres of case land from Kuddus Mollah and Ramjan Mollah the two brothers of late Abdul Mollah, all sons of late Osimuddin Mollah who inherited the same from their father late Boksha Mollah. After purchase Ghutu Sikder transferred .80 acre of land to his son, Dr. Forman Ali Miah, (the pre-emptee appellant), by Heba-bil-Ewaz dated 01.11.1988. On the other hand the said Kuddus Mollah transferred .48 acre of case land to the pre-emptee by kabala dated 16.6.1994 and handed over the possession of the same to him and as such the pre-emptee appellant claimed that thus he also became the co-sharer-tenant of the case jote otherwise than by purchase' since long. The pre-emptee claims that since the case land is uneven land, he, after purchasing the same, developed it by earth filling and by planting trees by spending TK.50,000/=. The pre-emptee claimed that he has land in Plot No. 8 which is adjacent to the case Plot No. 5 on the southern side of which he has homestead whereas the pre-emptor has no land nearer, adjacent or surrounding the case plot. Thus he has no necessity of the case land. It is also claimed that the pre-emptor respondent No. 1 after purchasing 1.80 acre of land got his name mutated by opening a separate holding with the Office of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Mirzapur, Tangail, vide Miscellaneous Case No. 1063(IX-I) 90-91 and accordingly paying rents to the government. Thus the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer nor has any nexus with the case jote. The pre-emptee appellant claims that although by kabala of the same date i.e. 15.6.1994 Kuddus Mollah also transferred .34 acre of land adjacent to case Plot No.9 to one Abdul Kader, but the pre-emptor respondent No.1 did not file any pre-emption case over the said land. Accordingly he claimed that the present pre-emption case is liable to be dismissed.

12. Under such circumstances leave has been granted to consider as to (I)'whether the status of the pre-emptor respondent No.1 and that of the pre-emptee-appellant is same'; (II) whether 'the High Court Division committed wrong in not holding that failing to produce the process server of the service of notice upon the co-sharers, for the purpose of mutation case is not the proof of non-servicing of notice'; and (III) whether 'for determination of the question as to non service of notice upon the co-sharer the trial Court should have called for the record of the mutation case and without doing so whether it can’t be said that the notice was not served upon the co-sharers'.

<u>13. As to the first point 'whether the status of the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee is same', it appears that the pre-emptor respondent No.1 got 1.80 acre of land from case plots No. 5/8/9/10/11 by Deed of Exchange dated 04.01.1988 from the heirs of Abdul Mollah. On the other hand, the pre-emptee appellant got .80 acre of land from case Plots No. 5/9 from his father Ghutu Sikder by way of Heba-Bill Ewaz dated 01.11.1988 out of 2.88 acre of land which he purchased from Kuddus Mollah and his brother Ramjan Mollah the other brothers of Abdul Mollah who inherited the same from their father and possessing in ejmali. So it appears that the pre-emptee is one of the existing co sharers in the case jote since 1988 even then the impugned purchase on 15.6.1994. On the other hand the pre-emptor after getting 1.80 acre of land by exchange .got his purchased land separated by opening a different holding/khatian through mutation and paying rents to the government for which he cannot be treated a co-sharer in the case jote and hence he has no right to file pre-emption case as a co-sharer, in the case land under the law. When a person by opening a separate khatian got his holding separated and paying rents accordingly, he cannot be treated as a co-sharer in the same case jote and as such he cannot pre-empt any land of the earlier jote under section 96 read with section 117(1 C) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

14. In determining other two points as to (II) 'whether failing to produce the process server of the service of notice upon the co-sharers for the purpose of mutation case is not the proof of non-service of notice and (III) for determination of the question as to non service of notice upon the co-sharer whether the trial Court should have called for the record of the mutation case and in not doing so whether it can be said that the notice was not served upon the co-sharers', we need to go through the evidences of the PWs and OPWs. In this respect PW.1, Md. Nizamuddin Miah the pre-emptor, deposed that he did not get his name mutated by opening a separate holding. In Cross he stated that it is not true that he filed the application with the office of the Mirzapur Revenue Office for get-ting his name mutated. On the other hand, OPW-1, the pre-emptee deposed that the pre-emptor got his name mutated by opening a separate holding vide Miscellaneous Case No. 1063/1990-91 and in support of his deposition he produced certified copy of the said mutation case and rather the pre-emptee upon getting .80 acre of land from his father in 1988 and after purchase of the said case land in 1994 is a co sharer in the case jote. However, to prove the claim that the pre-emptor got his land separated and opened a separate khatian vide above noted mutation case the pre-emptee filed certified copy of the said mutation khatian in the name of the pre-emptor(Exhibit-'Kha'). But on the face of denial by the pre-emptor, the trial Court held

"এই জমা ভাগের উপর স্বাক্ষ্য প্রদান করা কালে প্রতিপক্ষ আঃ ফরমান আলী প্রতিপক্ষের ১নং সাক্ষীর জেরায় বলেন উক্ত জমাভাগের কেসের উপর কোন শরীক নোটিশ পাইবার প্রমান তাহার কাছে নাই। আর জমাভাগ হইতে হইলে অবশ্যই সকল শরীকের প্রতি নোটিশ জারী হওয়া বাঞ্জনীয়। তাহা ছাড়া দাখিলী আদেশেও কেহ হাজির হইয়াছেন মর্মে উল্লেখ নাই। এই অবস্থায় ইহাকে বিধি সম্মত জমাভাগ বলা য়ায় না।" Hence the trial Court disbelieved the mutation.

<u>15. When the pre-emptee appellant categorically stated in his evidence that the pre-emptor got his name mutated and in support of such statement he produced and filed the certified copy of the Mutation Khatian, which has been proved and marked as Exhibit-'Kha', without any objection from the pre-emptor, the pre-emptor or anyone now cannot raise any objection as to the admissibility of the same in evidence. The objection as to admissibility of any evidence/document is to be taken at the first instance. No objection having been raised at the time of proving "Exhibit-Kha", none can challenge the same at- later stage. The proceeding of Mutation Khatian and opening of a new/separate khatian pursuant to the said proceeding and the order passed therein is a public document under section 74 of the Evidence Act. Certified copy of such public document can be produced and accepted in the court as a secondary evidence. When the original is a public document under section 74 of the Evidence Act and the original is a document of which a certified copy is permitted by the Act or by any other law in force in Bangladesh to be given in evidence the same may be given/filed in a Court and unless any objection is raised to such document when the same is being filed the same is very much admissible in evidence. This view finds support in the case of Hazi Waziullah alias Waziullah Miah and others Vs. The Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, Noakhali and Assistant Custodian of Vested and Non Resident Property and others, reported in 41 DLR(AD)97.</u>

<u>16. Under such circumstances, when the pre-emptor denied opening of new khatian the burden is upon him to prove that the evidence produced by pre-emptee is not correct. The established principle of law is that the burden of proof lies upon the person who denies the 'public document'. In the present case, the certified copy of the Mutation Khatian is a public document and when the pre-emptor denied the same the burden is upon him to prove that the same is not genuine as provided under section 103 of the Evidence Act. But the pre-emptor did not take any step to do the same nor the trial Court called for the record of the mutation case to justify the claim of the pre-emptor. Rather the trial Court as well as the High Court Division disbelieved the certified copy as well as the Mutation without calling for the original record of the said mutation case. As such the pre-emptee appellant rightly pointed out that for determination as to whether there was separate holding opened vide mutation case the trial Court should have called for the record of the mutation case and in not doing so, we are of the view that the finding of the trial Court as well as those of the High Court Division on this point is not correct.</u>

17. Moreover, when the pre-emptor respondent No.1 has no right to file the pre-emption case over the case land for the reasons as stated above, the judgment of thee trial Court as well as the High Court Division is not proper.

<u>18. On the other hand from the judgment of the lower appellate Court it appears that it held that the preemptor has no right to file the pre-emption case over the case land because of the fact that the pre-emptee appellant, Dr. Forman Ali Miah, when purchased the case land the applicant Nizamuddin was not the co-sharer tenant in the case jote and further held that the pre-emptee has residence contiguous to the case land whereas the applicant Nizamuddin has no such residence contiguous to the case land. The Court of appeal below further held that Kuddus Mollah also transferred some land from the case jote to one Abdul Kader on the same day i.e. on 15.6.1994 but the applicant-Nizamuddin, did not raise any objection to that transfer. Considering all these aspects the Court of appeal rightly allowed the appeal upon setting aside the order of pre-emption which the High Court Division failed to consider in its true perspective.</u>

19. For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove we hold that the High Court Division erred in law in making the Rule absolute and thereby allowing the pre-emption case by the impugned judgment and order upon setting aside the judgment of the lower appellate court which is based on proper appreciation of fact and law and as such the impugned judgment is required to be interfered with.

20. Hence, we find merit in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant.

21. Accordingly, this civil appeal is allowed and the judgment and order complained of herein passed by the High court Division is set aside. However, there will be no order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 12.11.2014, passed by the High. Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2700 of 2012 discharging the Rule arising out of judgment and decree dated 11.044.2012 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Manikgonj, in Title Appeal No. 27 of 2011 reversing the judgment and decree dated 16.1.2011 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Harirampur, Manikgonj in Title Suit No. 196 of 2007 dismissing the suit.

<u>2. Facts leading to filing of this civil petition for leave to appeal in short are that the present respondents No. 1 and 2 as plain-tiffs instituted Title Suit No. 271 of 2006 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Singair, Manikgonj, for declaration of their title, on the basis of purchase of the suit land described in the schedule to the plaint and also for declaration that RS record in respect of the said land is wrong. Subsequently the said suit being transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Harirampur, Manikganj, renumbered as Title Suit No. 1.96 of 2007. It is stated that 0.26 acre of land of C.S. Khatian No. 90 corresponding to C.S. plot No. under mouja Binodpur Borokhando, Singair, Manikgonj originally belonged Lc Ghetu Pramanik in 8(eight) annas shares, Hcrinhok- a Pramanik in 4 annas share and Tenu Praman 1A in share; that while in possession Ghetu Pramanik died leaving behind 3 sons namely, Juran, Hridoy and Kurani who inherited the same; that thereafter Hridoy plod leaving behind one son, Nitai; and Kurani died leaving behind one daughter, Monisha; that subsequently, pursuant to amicable settlement between the parties, Juran became the owner of .15 acre of land and Nitai and Monisha together became the owners of .11 acre of land; that Juran transferred his .15 acre of land to Haldar Mondal who died leaving behind two sons, namely, Kutu Mondal and Dudu Mondal and as such they became the owners of .15 acre of land; that subsequently, said Kutu. Mondal and Dudu Mondal transferred their 0.15 acre of land in favour of one Gafur and handed over possession of the same who in his turn transferred the same in favour of the plaintiffs and defendant No. 1 vide kabala No. 4111. dated 09.10.1986 in equal share; that Nitai and Monisha also transferred 0.10 out of 0.11 acre of land in favour of plaintiff No.1 vide kabala No. 11990 dated 18.11.1972 and subsequently on 01.12.1972 they also transferred the rest 0.01 acre of land in favour of plaintiff No.1 by unregistered document as the value of the same was below Tk.100.00 but the Plaintiffs are owning and possessing the said 0.10 acre from Gafur and 0.11 acre from Nitai and Monisha total 0.21 acre of land by purchase; that in the end of Ashaar, 1413 B.S. when the plaintiffs went to pay rents they came to know that out of 0.15 acre of land purchased from Gafur only 0.08 acre of land has been recorded in their names in RS Khatian No. 351 in place of 0.10 and .10 acre of land has been recorded in the name of defendant No.1, Abdul Ali, in R.S. Khatian No. 516 in place of 0.05 acre of land and out of 0.11 acre of land purchased from Nitai and Monisha only 0.08 acre of land has been recorded in the name of Plaintiff No.1 Jinnot Ali; hence the suit.</u>

3. Defendant No. 2 contested the suit, by filing written statement, contending, inter alia, that, the suit land along with other lands measuring 0.26 acre originally belonged to Ghetu Pramanik in 8 annas share, Horibhokta Pramanik in 4 annas share and Tenu Pramanik in 4 annas share; that on the basis of amicable partition, Ghetu Pramanik became the owner of 0.26 acre of land and as such while possessing the same, Ghetu Pramanik died leaving behind three sons namely Juran, Hridoy and Kurani as his heirs; thereafter Hridoy died leaving behind his son Nitai and Kurani died leaving behind his daughter Monisha; that Juran Mondal by amicable partition had been possessing the entire 0.26 acre of land out of which he transferred 0,13 acre along with 0.38 acre in RS Plot no. 219, 0.6 'A acre in RS Plot No. 185 and 0.38k acre in RS Plot No. 186 of Binodpur Boroldwido mouza in total .96 acre of land to Haider Mondal by registered kabala dated 23.02.1956; that Haider Mondal died leaving behind two sons namely, Kutu Mondal and Dudu Mondal and they transferred .15 acre, of the suit land along with acre out of .37 acre of land in SA Plot No. 185 and 0.45½ acre out of 0.88 acre of land in SA Plot No. 186, totalling .70 acre of land to defendant No.2; that the said defendant No.2 although purchased 0.15 acre of the suit land but he possessed the entire 0.26 acre of the suit land; that thereafter the defendant no.2 on 09.10.1986 transferred 0.15 acre; of land out of the suit land along with .11¼ acre of land from Plots no. 185 and 186 in total .26¼ acre of land to the plaintiffs and the defendant No.1; that the defendant no.1 obtained 0.10 acre of land in the western part of the suit land; that pursuant to amicable settlement RS record has been prepared and accordingly he is possessing the same upon erecting houses thereon; that the defendant No.2 is the owner and possessor of 0.08 acre of land situated in the eastern side adjacent to the 0.10 acre of land of the defendant No.1 on the western side which has been recorded in the RS record in his name; that on the basis of settlement the plaintiffs are possessing 0.08 acre on the eastern side of the suit land along with 0.09 acre of land in SA Plot No. 185 in total .17 acre of land which has been recorded in his name; that the RS record has not been prepared in the name of the defendant no.2; that the plain-tiff no.1 fraudulently got .44 acre of land of defendant no.2 in Plot no. 186 recorded in his name in RS Khatian No. 517, Plots No. 345 and 346 and erected some houses in some portion of the same forcibly and dispossessed the defendants; that the plaintiff no.1 expressed about the purchase of .10 acre of land from Nitai and Monisha on 18.11.1972 but had no possession over the same; that Ni tai Left for India during Pakistan regime; that the plaintiffs on false personation fraudulently created the deed by which no title vested upon him and, as such, the suit is not maintainable; hence the suit should be dismissed.

4. The Trial Court, upon hearing, dis-missed the suit by its judgment and decree dated 16.01.2011, against which, the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal. No.27 of 2011 before the learned District Judge, Manikganj, which was ultimately heard and allowed by the learned joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Manikganj, and thereby decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 11.4.2012.

5. Against the said judgment and decree, the defendant No.2 moved the High Court Division in Civil. Revision No. 2700 of 2012 and obtained Rule. On the other hand, the defendant No.1 also moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2415 of 2012 and obtained Rule.

6. A Division Bench of the High Court Division heard both the Rules together and upon hearing the parties and on perusal of the materials on record discharged both the Rules by its judgment and order dated 12.11.2014.

7. Hence defendant No.2 filed this civil petition for leave, to appeal against the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2700 of 2012.

<u>8. Mr. A.S.M Khalaquzzaman, learned advocate appearing for the defendant No.2-petitioner submits that Court Division committed error of law in dis-charginc7 Rule without giving its independent findings. He that when the plain-tiff no.1, as PW 1, admitted in cross examination that the defendant no.1 had been possess:- the western .10 acre of land of the suit plot by erecting houses thereon and that the plaintiffs had boon possessing the eastern 0.08 acre of the suit plot, it is clear that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their possession in their claimed 0.21 acre of land of the suit plot and, as such, the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division committed error in decreeing the suit without discussing the material points resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He also submits that the plaintiffs upon forging and by false personating somebody as Nitai and Monisha created the deed fraudulently and as such by the said forged and fraudulent deed no title has been passed to the plaintiffs because the said Nitai and Monisha left for. India during Pakistan regime but the lower appellate Court as well as the High Court Division basing on the said forged and fraudulent deed passed the impugned judgment which is liable to be set aside.</u>

9. Mrs. Sufia Khatun, the learned Advocate-On-Record, appearing on behalf of the respondents supporting the impugned judgment submits that the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned judgment and order and decreeing the suit.

10. It appears that admittedly the suit land measuring 0.26 acre of land, belonged to Ghetu Pramanik in 8 annas share, Horibhokta Pramanik in 4 annas share and Tenu Pramanik in 4 annas share. It is also admitted that on the basis of family settlement, Ghetu Pramanik became the 1.6 annas owner of 0.26 acre of land, who died leaving behind three sons namely Juran, Hridoy and Kurani as his heirs. It is also admitted that Hrioy died leaving behind only son Nitai and Kurani died leaving behind only daughter Monisha.

11. The plaintiffs claim that there was an amicable settlement between Nitai, Monisha and Juran, on the basis of which Juran became the owner of 0.15 acre of land and Nitai and Monisha together became the owners of 0.11 acre of land. On the other hand, the defendants claim that pursuant to the amicable partition, Juran got the entire 0.26 acre of land of the suit plot. In support of their respective claims and counter claims the plaintiffs adduced 1. Witness as PW 1 along lath papers which were marked as Exhibits 1 to 3 and the defendants adduced 1 witness as DW 1 along with papers Which were marked as Exhibits Ka to Umma.

12. The trial Court, while dismissing the suit held that the plaintiffs have proved their possession over 0.08 acre of land and failed to prove the same over rest of their claimed 0.21 acre of land. That is the plaintiffs have no possession over their entire claimed land. On perusal of the schedule to the plaint the trial Court observed that although the plaintiffs brought the suit claiming 0.20 acre of land but subsequently by amendment they have claimed 0.21 acres of land without correcting the descriptions by meets and bounds of the schedule and, as such, it observed that the schedule of the plaint being indistinct and indefinite the plain-tiffs have failed to prove their claim over the entire suit land.

13. The appellate Court, can the other hand, on perusal of the evidence adduced by the parties and the other materials on record, found that the plaintiffs have been in possession over 0.21 acre of land, after purch4sing the some from Nitai, Monisha and defendant No.2, for more than 30 to 40 years, Further on the question of possession over the said 0.21 acres land of the plaintiffs, DW 1. remained silent which indicates his admission about such possession of the plaintiffs. Thus it held that the plaintiffs' title and possession over their purchased 0.21 acre of land in the suit plot has been proved by the evidence of DW-1. Accordingly, the appellate Court came to the finding that the RS record in respect of the suit land is wrong and without any basis and the suit, is maintainable in its present form and manner and, as such, the plaintiffs are entitled to get relief as prayed for and thereby decreed the suit upon setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

14. The High Court Division, upon hearing the parties and considering the materials on record, found that Court of appeal below rightly considered deed No. 11990, dated 18.11.1972 by which Nitai and Monisha transferred .10 acre of land to the plaintiffs, though the defendants claimed that the said deed is forged and fraudulent as Nitaj and Monisha left for India during Pakistan regime which they miserably failed to prove further held that subsequently Njtai and Monishaalsc-transferred the rest .01 are of land to plaintiff. No.1 which was not registered as the valuation of the same; was less than TK.100/=, even than it cannot be said that the said .01 acre of land has not been transferred the plaintiffs. It also found that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their possession in the suit land since purchase for more than 30 to 40 years and accordingly, it held that the deed being more than 30 years old, the same has the presumptive value as per section 90 of the Evidence Act. In addition to the aforesaid 0.11 acre of land purchased from Nitai and Monisha the High Court Division upon considering deed No. 4111. dated 9.10.1986(Exhibit-2) also found that 0.15 acre of land have been transferred by Abdul Gafur in favour of plaintiffs no. 1 and 2 and defendant no. 1 . Thus, the High Court Division found that PWs 1, 2 and 3 proved possession of the -plaintiffs in their claimed land and also held that there may be minor discrepancy in their depositions but that itself is not sufficient to hold that it vitiated plaintiffs' case of possession and accordingly discharged the Rules by the impugned judgment and order.

<u>15. From the above discussion and on perusal of record it further appears that, the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division believed the plaintiffs' case and disbelieved the claim of the defendants as to the forgery of the deed of Nitai and Monisha rather, held that since the defendants failed to prove their claims that Nitai and Monisha left Bangladesh for India during Pakistan time by sufficient evidence and since the deed is more than 30 years old it has got the presumptive value under section 90 of the Evidence Act.</u>

16. From the submission of Mr. Khalequgzaman it appears that the main contention of the defendants is that Nitaiwhom the plaintiffs claimed to be one of the owners has left the Country for India during Pakistan regime and the plaintiffs by false personation created deed No. 11990 dated 18.11.1972. But it appears that the questioned deed was in the custody of the plaintiffs who submitted the same in the trial Court and proved and marked as Exhibit-3. On the other hand the defendants failed to prove their claim of forgery and false personation by adducing sufficient evidence. Moreover the said registered deed being more than thirty years old it has sufficient presumptive value under section 90 of the Evidence Act.

<u>17. Regarding possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land on the basis of the said deeds, the DW 1 remained silent in reply to the quaries rather than to dislodge its .presumptive value, when he was asked about the same. This has led the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division to come to the conclusion that the plaintiffs have possession, title and interest in the suit land.</u>

<u>18. In the case of Syed Abdul Haque Vs. Surendra. Nath Majumder, reported in 59 DLR(AD) 111 this Division held "since the documents exhibits 1 and 2 are 30 years old and have a presumption of correctness and that presumption having not been dislodged by the defendants there was no occasion for the Court to discard the claim of title of the plaintiffs made on the basis of the said documents." This Division in the case of Bangladesh Railway Vs. Jashimuddin, reported in 5 LM(AD)58 held. "from- the discussions made herein above since the plaintiffs have been successful in proving their genealogy of title and possession in the suit land and since the defendants failed to challenge the documents relied upon by the plaintiffs and also failed to prove their case of title and possession, it can clearly be held that the defendants have no title and possession in the suit land. On the other hand the plaintiffs could prove the title of Yeasin Hazi, the CS recorded tenant and thereafter devolution of title and possession upon his daughter Duburunnessa who in her turn transferred the same to Khodeza Begum by two registered documents in 1955 and 1956 which are more than 30 years old documents and relying on such registered documents Khodeza Begum's name being recorded in the SA record and thereafter Zumuruddin, the predecessor of the plaintiffs having purchased the same got his name mutated in place of Khodeza Begum in the office of the Government, and after his death his heirs, the plaintiffs having got, their names mutated, the title and possession of the plaintiffs are found to be proved".</u>

<u>19. In the instant case, the plaintiffs claimed the suit land on the strength of Deed No. 11990 dated 18.11.1972 from the Nitai and Monisha which is more than 30 years old document and produced by the plaintiffs during trial without being dislodged by the defendants nor the same has been challenged by the defendants in any Court there is no scope to discard the Claim of the plaintiffs' title on the suit land on the basis of the said deed. The trial Court on perusal of the said deed (Exhibit-3) found that the plaintiffs purchased the suit land from Nitai and Monisha, but it misdirected itself in coming to the conclusion that the plaintiffs are in possession of 0.08 acre of land and the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, and, as such, held that the suit is not maintainable.</u>

20. It further appears upon scanning all the evidence on record that the Court of appeal below rightly reversed the findings of the trial Court and the High Court Division was also correct in affirming the same and, 4s such, it did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned judgment and thereby decreeing the suit.

21. The aforesaid findings and decision arrived at by the High Court Division being based on proper appreciation of law and fact the same does not call for any interference by this Court.

22. Accordingly, this civil petition for leave to appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.
