case_source: From the judgment and order dated 7-1-2008 and 8-1-2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4884 of 2003).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain, CJ: This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 7-1-2008 and 8-1-2008 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4884 of 2003 discharging the Rule. 

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this appeal, in a nutshell, are: 
On 10-5-1984, the respondent herein as the plaintiff brought a suit being Title Suit No.290 of 1984 before the Court of 1st Munsif (now Assistant Judge, Dhaka) against the present defendant No.3-petitioner and the present proforma-respondent Nos.9 and 10 and 11 as defendant Nos.1, 2 and 4 respectively. The case of the petitioner is that the property described in the schedule to the plaint originally belonged to one Radhacharan Mondal, who being a CS recorded tenant transferred the land along with the other land to different persons and one Badsha Miah and one Manik Miah by virtue of deed of purchase have become the rightful owner of the said property and the SA record of rights has been recorded in their names. 

3. On the death of the said Badsha Miah, the suit property along with other land devolved upon the plaintiff-respondent by way of inheritance. In the year 1958-1959 the suit property along with other properties was requisitioned by the Government, defendant-proforma-respondent No.15 for the purpose of rehabilitation of Mohajaria from India as well as for the purpose of constructing a Road, namely "The Ring Road" to protect the Nuclear Houses from flood in LA Case No.30 of 1958-1959. The plaintiff-respondents did not draw any compensation money for the suit land with the hope that the same would be given back to them by the Government as they did not have any piece of land in the Dhaka City. 

4. The Nuclear House for rehabilitation of the Muhajirs and the ring road for which the suit land along with other lands of the plaintiffs was requisitioned have already been completed as per plan of the Government and the Ring road has also been constructed to the north of the Nuclear Houses and beyond the Ring Road the suit lands are lying to the adjacent North of the Ring road and the suit land and, as such, are not utilized for the purpose for which the same was requisitioned. It is stated that the plaintiffs did neither take compensation for the suit land nor they have accepted two plots measuring 13/4 katha each allotted to them in the planned area as those could not meet their requirements. 

5. The plaintiffs came to know that the suit property was leased out to defendant No.3. The present petitioner, who, as per the plaintiff, was threatening the plaintiffs with dispossession, had been impleaded as defendant No.3 in the suit for proper adjudication of the matter in his presence. The plaintiffs made a representation to the officials of the Governments requesting them to derequisition of the suit land in their favour without any loss of time in the months of August, 1983 but unlike other occasions instead of giving any assurance to that effect they refused the request of the plaintiffs and hence they were constrained to bring the suit. 

6. Subsequently, in the year 1994 the plaint was amended by inserting paragraph 8(a) wherein it has been averred that defendant No.2 herein proforma-respondent No.10 did not serve any notice under sections 5(A), 5(3) and 7 of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition and Acquisition of Property Act, 1948 and notices are mandatory and, as such, the acquisition is illegal, ultra-vires and malafide. The plaintiff did not withdraw any compensation money in respect of the suit property and defendant Nos.1 and 2 could not lease out the schedule property to defendant No.3 as the same was not requisitioned for any other purpose other than the rehabilitation of Mohajirs/ Refugees and construction of Ring Road to save and protect Nuclear Houses from flood. 

7. After that, the prayer portion of the plaint was amended by the order No.57 dated 5-9-1999 in the following way: 
"For a declaration that the lease deed executed and registered on 23-12-1981 by defendant Nos.1 and 2 in favour of defendant No.3 is illegal, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs." 

8. The present petitioner as defendant No.3 filed a written statements denying all the material statements made in the plaint of the suit, contending, inter-alia that the suit is prima7facie not maintainable as it is not brought in compliance of section 74 of BADC Ordinance, 1974. 

9. The suit is on the face of the record is barred by the law of limitation, it is suffered from non-joinder of parties and is also barred by law of estopple, weaver, and acquiescence and the suit is also hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

10. The Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh being the 16 annas exclusive owner and possessor of the scheduled property of the plaint through acquisition under LA Case No. 30 of 1958-59 defendant No.2, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka allotted a plot measuring 0.71 acre out of the scheduled property to the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) in the year 1975, as required for Nursery/Horticulture and open sale centre in the greater interest of the citizens of the Dhaka Metropolitan City. Accordingly, the BADC took possession of the said plot of land and started Nursery and sale centre thereon in the year 1975. 

11. Thereafter, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works, leased out the said 0.71 acre of land out of the scheduled property of the plaint, to the allottee/tenant Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) by a registered lease agreement dated 23-12-1981 for a period of 99 (ninety nine) years at a premium of Taka 3,75,915 (Taka three lacs seventy five thousand nine hundred and fifteen only) paid by the tenant BADC vide treasury challan No.28 KA dated 03-7-1981. 

12. Being the exclusive and bonafide owner and possessor of the 0.71 acre of land for 99 years under the lease agreement as aforesaid, the BADC continued its Nursery, Horticulture and sale centre thereon. In addition to the aforesaid lease premium of Taka 3,75,915 BADC also spent an approximate amount of Taka 10(ten) lacs for development of the said land by boundary walls, earth filling construction of sale centre, office and staff accommodation etc. 

13. At one stage a portion of the said leased property was forcibly occupied by some bad elements of the locality and the BADC as a legal owner of the said property ousted those bad elements from the land through police force. Accordingly the BADC has been enjoying the leased property peacefully, without interference from any corner. Afterwards, while the BADC was in possession of the leased property being 0.71 acres out of the scheduled property of the plaint as aforesaid, the plaintiffs filed the present suit being TS No.290 of 1984 in the 1st Court of the Munsif at Dhaka praying for derequisition and khas possession of the scheduled land property including the said 0.71 acres of leased property rightfully owned and possessed by the BADC. The Chairman of the BADC has been impleaded in the suit as defendant No.3 but the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation itself and other concerned officers including the Secretary of the Corporation who has entered into the aforesaid 99 years lease agreement with the government have not been impleaded as defendants in the instant suit. 

14. It is stated that before filing written statement by defendant No.3, Title Suit No.290 of 1984 was decreed ex parte on 17-9-1984. Against the said ex-parte decree, the present petitioner preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No.7 of 1985 before learned District Judge, Dhaka. On transfer, the appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Dhaka, who upon hearing the appeal by the judgment and decree dated 30-9-1986 and 10-11-1986 dismissed the said Title Appeal No. 7 of 1984 affirming those dated 17-9-1984 passed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Dhaka. Against the said judgment and decree dated 30-9-1986 and 10-11-1986 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Dhaka, this petitioner preferred a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.29 of 1987. The High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 05-6-1991 made the Rule absolute and remanded the case to the trial court for hearing the suit in accordance with law. Subsequently, Title Suit No.290 of 1984 was remanded to the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka. 

15. At this stage, defendant No.3-present petitioner filed an application under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of plaint on some material grounds as stated therein; the plaintiffs filed written objection against the said application and the learned Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka by his judgment and order dated 20-3-1994 rejected the said application of the petitioner. Thereafter, against the said judgment and order dated 20-4-1994 passed by the learned Assistant judge, 1st Court, Dhaka, the defendant-petitioner preferred a revisioal application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 2761 of 1994. The High Court Division by its judgment and order dated 20-1-1998 discharged the Rule and Title Suit No.290 of 1984 was subsequently transferred to that Court and has been renumbered being Title Suit No.8 of 1994. On 21-9-1999, the suit was fixed for hearing. An application filed on behalf of defendant No.3, (the present petitioner) was rejected and the case was taken up for ex pane hearing. Shahjahan Miah, plaintiff-respondent No. 1 deposed as PW 1 and the documents filed have been marked as exhibits-1 to 8. The learned Assistant Judge with-out satisfying with the minimum requirements of the proposition of law decreed the suit ex parte by the order No. 59 dated 21-9-1999. 

16. The present petitioner being aggrieved by the said ex parte judgment and decree dated 21-9-1999 as appellant took an appeal being Title Appeal No. 847 of 1999 before the District Judge, Dhaka. On transfer, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka, who upon hearing the appeal by the judgment and decree dated 17-5-2003 dismissed the appeal on the findings among others, that the learned Assistant Judge in view of the fact and circumstances committed no illegality in decreeing the suit ex pane and the learned Judge in keeping reliance upon the decision reported in 1987 BLD 689 dismissed the appeal holding that the plaintiffs are entitled to get back the said unutilized property. 

17. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 17-5-2003 passed by Joint District Judge, Commercial Court, Dhaka, the present petitioner filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.4884 of 2003 before the High Court Division. The High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 7-1-2008 and 08-1-2008 discharged the Rule. 

18. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order of the High Court Division, the leave-petitioner filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.556 of 2008 before this Division and obtained leave on 14-5-2009 resulting in Civil Appeal No.618 of 2009. 

19. Mr A.M. Aminuddin, learned Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, itself bars filing a suit in a civil court questioning legality of the order passed or any action taken under this Act and thus, the decree passed by the Courts below is a nullity and the High Court Division committed an error of law in maintaining the decree for derequisition. He further submits that in view of section 5(7) of the (Emergency) Requisition Property Act, 1948, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is the owner and possessor of the said quantum of land acquired in LA Case No.30 of 1958-1959 out of which 0.71 acre of land was allotted to the appellant by way of lease agreement in the year 1975 as required for nursery and opening a sale center in the greater interest of the citizens of the Dhaka Metropolitan City. He then submits that there is no scope to say that the suit land is unused and unutilized and the appellant is not the requiring body, and it has been done without jurisdiction. Therefore, the High Court Division committed error of law in affirming the concurrent judgments of the Courts below. He continues to submit that the burden of proof lies upon the plaintiffs to prove the case as alleged and the question of non-service of notices under sections 5(A), 5(C) and 7 of the said Act and non-receiving the compensation money incorporated in the plaint by way of amendment long after 12 years of filing the suit are required to be proved by the plaintiffs which they have utterly failed and, as such, the High Court Division committed an error of law in failing to consider that the amendment was made after a long lapse of time incorporating of those facts with a view to simply making out a case and those facts, as it appears has not been proved. 

20. Mr Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-8, on the other hand, submits that the ex pane decree passed by the trial Court has been affirmed by the appellate Court and the High Court Division and that there is no scope for interference as the appellant failed to prove his case as it was not present before the trial Court by filing written statement and also by adducing evidence and, as such, no interference is called for. He further submits that the scheme for the purpose of rehabilitation of the refugees/ Muhajirs from India and for the purpose of construction of Ring-Road to save and protect the Nuclear House from flood had been fully materialized and while the Ring-Road had been constructed the suit property was not used for the purpose for which it was acquisitioned and the suit property remains unutilized and, as such, the suit was rightly decreed by the trial Court which was upheld up to the High Court Division. He further submits that section I4A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 mandates no absolute bar in entertainment of a suit by a civil Court and jurisdiction, even if excluded, civil Court has got jurisdiction to examine whether the Statutory Tribunal has acted in conformity with the Fundamental Principles of Requisition and Acquisition and civil Court rightly and legally entertained the suit and judicial verdicts handed down by Courts below had been very rightly maintained and upheld by the High Court Division and no interference is called for by this Division. He also submits that it is admitted by defendant-appellant that the suit property along with other properties had been requisitioned for the purpose of rehabilitation of Refugees/ Mohajirs from India and also for the purpose of construction of Ring-Road to save and protect Nuclear Houses from flood and scheme of requisition for the purpose of rehabilitation of Refugees/Mohajirs from India and also for the purpose of constitution Ring-Road to save and protect the Nuclear Houses from flood had been fully materialized and satisfied and the suit property was not at all used for the purpose of requisition and the suit property remained unused and unutilized. Admittedly, 0.71 acres of land out of the suit property had been leased out to the defendant-appellant though the defendant-appellant as requiring body did not pray for leasing out 0.71 acre of land and, as such, no interference is called for. He lastly submits that the unutilized land is in exclusive possession of the plaintiff-respondents and the only thing Government is required to do is to release/ derequisition 0.71 acre of land in favour of the plaintiff-respondents. 

21. We have considered the submission of the learned Attorney-General for the appellant and the learned Senior Advocate for plaintiff-respondent Nos.1-8, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record. 

22. In order to address the question raised in this appeal, we should have a look on the submissions of Mr Mahbueby Alam, the then learned Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellant, on which, leave was granted. The submissions are quoted below: 
"That section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, itself bars filing a suit in a civil court questioning legality of the order passed or any action taken under this Act and thus, the decree passed by the Courts below is a nullity and the High Court Division committed an error of law in maintaining the decree for derequisition; that the view of section 5(7) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act,1948 the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was the owner and possessor of the said quantum of land and out of which 0.71 acre of land was allotted to the petitioner by way of lease agreement in the year 1975 as required for nursery and opening sale center in the greater interest of the citizens of the Dhaka Metropolitan City and in such circumstances it cannot be said that the land is unused and unutilized and the petitioner is not the requiring body, and it has been done without jurisdiction; that the settled principle of law that the burden of proof lies upon the plaintiffs to prove the case as being alleged and the question of non-service of notice under sections 5(A), 5(C) and 7 of the said Act, 1948 and non-receiving the compensation money incorporate in the plaint by way of amendment long after 12 years of filing the suit and the High Court Division committed an error of law in failing to consider that the amendment was made after a long passage of time incorporating of those facts with a view to simply make out a case and those facts, as it appears has not been proved." 

23. It had been admitted by both the parties that the suit property along with other properties was requisitioned and acquisitioned in LA Case No.30 of 1958-1959 for the purpose of rehabilitation of Refugees/Mohajirs from India and also for the purpose of construction of Ring-Road to save and protect the Nuclear Houses from flood. It is also admitted that after conclusion of rehabilitation programme of the Refugees/Mohajirs and also after construction of Ring-Road, the suit property remains unused. The plaintiffs contended that keeping unused acquired suit property by the government was illegal and the plaintiffs were entitled to get back the suit property on derequisition. The plaintiffs also contended that the lease deed dated 23-1-1981 executed and registered in favour of defendant No.3 appellant by defendant Nos.1 and 2 was illegal and defendant No.3 appellant on the strength of that lease deed did not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit land. 

24. Admittedly, the trial Court decreed the suit ex parte. On an appeal from the ex parte decree, the appellate Court affirmed the decree passed by the trial Court. The High Court Division by an elaborate judgment came to the definite finding that the suit is not barred under section 14(A) of the Act. 

25. In support of its aforesaid finding, the High Court Division relied upon the case of The Federation of Pakistan through the Secretary, Establishement Division, Government of Pakistan Rawalpindi vs Saeed Ahmad Khan, PLD 1974 (SC) 151. In the decision referred to above Hamdur Rahman, CJ held that a malafide act and coram non judice stand on the same footing and no ouster clause in any enactment howsoever widely coached can save them from judicial scrutiny. 

26. Having gone through the decision cited above, we find that it has no manner of application in the case in hand. Admittedly, the plaintiff obtained ex parte decree from the trial Court on 21-9-1999. We have also gone through the judgment delivered by the trial Court and the trial Court did not at all come to the finding that the acquisition proceedings under LA Case No.30 of 1958-1959 was a malafide one. 

27. In this connection, reliance may be placed on the case of Nur Muhammed vs Moulvi Mainuddin Ahmed, 39 DLR (AD) 1, wherein it has been held that this is a well-known proposition of law which this Court has yet no occasion to depart from or express any disagreement with it. The point, however, is whether any bar of suit imposed by the legislature can be disregarded to make such suit which is so barred, maintainable in order to try an issue on mala fide alleged in the plaint. It may, at least in some cases be seen that hardship, or even injustice, may result if, in spite of evident truth in the allegation of mala fide, the suit is held to be not maintainable because there is a bar against such suit in the statute concerned. But, seeker of justice in a court of law should become aware, if not already so, that justice is done according to law. A Judge may have sympathy for a litigant's suffering due to technicalities of law made by the legislature, still in view of the express legislative, intention, he must follow the "hands-off doctrine." Otherwise chaos and anarchy would prevail leading to all sorts of complexities and confusion. Whatever the legislature says, unless it is contrary to the Constitution, its mandate, either express or implied, has been obeyed by Court. 

28. Their Lordship then held that as to the allegation of mala fide, since we are of the opinion that no Civil Court is competent to entertain any suit so as to try such issue it would be inappropriate for us to make any comment on whether there has been lack of bona fide in passing the impugned order. If such suit was entertainable the allegation regarding mala fide could have been examined. Since the Act itself provides remedy in the Act itself and the appellant took advantage by taking recourse to such remedy, he may not have any cause for grievance. 

29. Therefore, the finding of the High Court Division that the appellant resorted to a malafide way while acquiring the suit property and other properties under LA Case No.30 of 1958-1959 does not hold good. The High Court Division also came to the finding that defendant No.2, Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, did not serve any notice under sections 5(3), 5A and 7 of the Act. But having gone through the judgment, we find that the trial Court did not come to a finding that notices under sections 5(3), 5A and 7 of the Act were not served upon the plaintiffs. Mere assertion made in the plaint without producing the relevant documents cannot prove that notices under the aforesaid sections were not served upon the plaintiff. Admittedly, the gazette notification under section 5(7) of the Act was published in the official Gazette on 25-6-1973. Section 5(7) runs as follows: 
"5(7). The Government shall then publish in the Official Gazette a notice to the effect that the Government has decided to acquire the requisitioned property. On and from the beginning of the day on which the notice is so published the requisitioned property shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and the period of such requisition of such property shall end.

30. According to section 5(7) of the Act as soon as gazette notification is published the requisitioned property vests absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and the period of such acquisition of such property shall end. 

31. Illustration of section 114(e) of the Evidence Act provides that the Court may presume that judicial and official acts have been regularly performed. Section 114 of the Evidence Act provides that the Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business, in their relation to the facts of the particular case. 

32. Relying on illustration (e) of section 114 of the Evidence Act, we hold that notices under sections 5(3), 5A and 7 of the Act had been properly served. The plaintiff-respondent amended the plaint and incorporated the statement adding new paragraph 8(1) wherein it has been averred that defendant No.2 did not serve any notice under sections 5A, 5(3) and 7 of the Act and that the notices are mandatory and, as such, acquisition was illegal and ultra vires and malafide; that the plaintiff did not withdraw compensation money in respect of the suit property; that defendant Nos.1 and 2 could not lease out the schedule property to defendant No.3 for 99 years as the same was not acquisitioned for any other purpose than rehabilitation of Mohajirs/ Refugees and construction of Ring-Road to save and protect the Nuclear Houses from flood. 

33. What is remarkable to note here is that this amendment of plaint was filed after lapse of 10 years of institution of the suit and that the trial Court accepted the amendment after long lapse of time. Admittedly, as soon as gazette notification has been published in the official gazette, the acquired property including the suit property vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and the Government is at liberty to use the property for any other purpose and the original owners lost their right over the acquired land for good. Admittedly, the suit property along with other properties was acquired in LA Case No.30 of 1958-1959 and the gazette notification in respect thereof was published in the official gazette on 25-6-1973. Therefore, the suit itself was not maintainable from its very inception. The plaintiff cannot take the plea that the suit is maintainable because of malafide. 

34. In our opinion, section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act has, in clear and unmistakable terms put an express embargo on entertainment of any suit or application against any order or action under the Act. Not only this, if any suit or appeal was pending from before the enactment of this section (this section was inserted by EP Ordinance No.X1II of 1963) against any order or action under the Act it was to abate. 

35. The High Court Division came to the finding that refusal to derequisition of unused and unutilized property in favour of plaintiff-respondent Nos.1-8 appears to be malafide on the part of defendant Nos. I and 2. Admittedly, gazette notification has been published in respect of the suit property along with other properties on 25-6-1973 prior to filing of the suit. According to the spirit of section 5(7) of the Act, the properties so acquired shall vest in the Government free from all encumbrances. Therefore, the Government is at liberty to lease it out to anybody whomever it likes. 

36. Over and above, the property acquired for one public purpose may be used for another public purpose since the property under acquisition vest in the Government free from all encumbrances. In this connection, reliance may be placed on the case of Brahamanbaria Pourashava vs Secretary, Ministry of Land Reforms, Government of Bangladesh, 51 DLR (AD) 84 wherein it has been held that there is no principle of law under which once a property has been validly acquired for a public purpose, as admitted by the Government and has been vested in the requiring body then even if the said property be utilized for a different purpose, the acquisition shall not stand void. 

37. Therefore, it appears that plaintiff-respondent Nos.l-8 cannot claim the acquired property once it has been validly acquired. Admittedly, the suit property has been leased out to Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation in 1975 for nursery/horticulture and sale centre for the greater interest of the citizens of the Dhaka Metropolitan City. The lease deed has been registered on 23-12-1981 for a period of 99 years. The plaintiffs filed Title Suit No.290 of 1984 in the First Court of the then Munsif Court, Dhaka after registration of the lease deed in favour of the appellants. The unused suit property was also utilized for public purpose and the Government is at liberty to do so since the disputed property and other properties vested in it pursuant to the gazette notification dated 26-6-1973 in LA Case No.30 of 1958-1959. 

38. The findings arrived at by the High Court Division are erroneous and contrary to established principles of law and, as such, we find substance in this civil appeal. Accordingly this civil appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment and order dated 7-1-2008 and delivered by the High Court Division affirming the judgments and decrees passed by the appellate Court and the trial Court is set-aside. 

The suit filed by respondent Nos.1-8 is dismissed without any order as to costs. 

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 22-3-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4419 of 2004)
full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman, J: This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 22-3-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4419 of 2004 making the Rule absolute and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 23-6-2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Narayangonj in Title Appeal No.110 of 2002 affirming the judgment and decree dated 15-5-2002 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rupgonj, Narayangonj in Title Suit No.138 of 1999 decreeing the suit. 

2. Facts, leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the appellant, as plaintiff, instituted the Title Suit No.138 of 1999 for declaration of his title in the suit land and also for declaration that the judgment and decree dated 28-4-1999 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rupgonj, Narayangonj, in Title Suit No.58 of 1998, being obtained fraudulently, is illegal and not binding upon him, on the averments that the proforma respondent No.5, on receiving consideration of Taka 10,000, by registered kabala No.4586 dated 12-5-1998 sold in his favour 0.03 acres of land from Plot No.331, 0.03 acres of land from Plot No.330 and 0.011/2 acres of land from Plot No.535, totaling an area of 0.071/2 acres. the proforma respondent No.6, on receiving consideration money of Taka 10,000, by registered Kabala No.4585 on 12-5-1998 sold to him 0.0114 acres from Plot No.331, 0.01½ acres from Plot No.330, 0.01½ acres from Plot No.567, 0.01½ acres from Plot No.566 and non suited 0.01½ acres from Plot No.553, totaling an area of 0.07½, acres, at the time of the above transfers the profoima respondent Nos.5 and 6 also delivered possession of the suit land in his favour. Thereafter the respondent Nos.1-4, in collusion with the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6, created an anti-dated agreement for sale dated 30-9-1997 showing payment of consideration of Taka 2000 and on the basis of the same claimed that they have purchased the suit land by kabala executed on 20-5-1998 and that after preparation of the above kabala dated 20-5-1998 the deed writer failed to read out the contents of those kabalas to the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6 and that is why they refused to register the same and left the SR Office on that day. The respondent Nos.1-4 instituted Title Suit No.58 of 1998 in the Court and by practicing fraud upon the Court obtained judgment and decree dated 28-4-1999. The plaintiff, on 22-8-1999, obtaining the certified copy of the judgment came to know about the said decree which clouded his title in the suit land. 

3. The defendant Nos.1-4 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6 decided to sell the suit land to them at a consideration of Taka 25,000 and accordingly on receiving Taka 10,000 from them the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6 executed a bainanama on 30-9-1997 in their favour wherein it was stipulated that within 2 years after receiving the balance consideration of Taka 15,000 the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6 would execute and register the kabala. On 20-5-1998, the respondent Nos.1-4 paid the rest consideration of Taka 15,000 to the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6 and thereafter, they executed the kabala but due to the delay of presentation of the kabala the same could not be registered on that day. It was then decided that on the next day the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6 would register the kabala but on the next date the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6 did not turn up in the office of the sub-Registrar. Thereafter, in spite of repeated requests, the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6 did not register the sale deed and hence, the respondent Nos.l-4 instituted the above Title suit No.58 of 1998 for specific Performance of Contract. Although notices were duly served upon the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6, they failed to appear and contest the suit and accordingly the said suit was decreed ex-parte. The appellant, in order to grab the suit and some other lands, by way of false personation created 2 kabala deeds dated 12-5-1998 showing the proforma respondent Nos.5 and 6 as executants and as the bainanama in favour of the respondent Nos.1-4 being earlier on point of time they, on the basis of the same, acquired valid title in the suit land and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

4. On conclusion of the trial, the learned Assistant Judge, Rupganj, Narayanganj considering the evidences and docuinents on record, decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 15-5-2002. 

5. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendants as appellants preferred Title Appeal No.110 of 2002 before the District Judge, Narayanganj. On transfer, the said appeal was heard by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Narayangonj, who by his judgment and decree dated 23-6-2004 disallowed the appeal and thereby affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

6. Feeling aggrieved, by the judgment and decree dated 23-6-2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Narayanganj, the defendant-appellant-petitioners preferred Civil Revision No.4419 of 2004 before the High Court Division and obtained the Rule. 

7. In due course, a Single Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the Rule absolute by the impugned judgment and order dated 22-3-2007 and thereby set-aside the judgment and decree dated 23-6-2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Narayangonj, in Title Appeal No.110 of 2002 and the judgment and decree dated 15-5-2002 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rupganj, in Title Suit No.138 of 1999. 

8. The plaintiff-appellant feeling aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 22-3-2007 of the High Court Division preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.921 of 2007 before this Division and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal. 

9. Mr Taufique Anwar Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the kabala deeds of the plaintiff have been executed and registered on 12-5-1998 and the kabala deed of the defendant-respondent Nos.1-4 has been merely executed on 20-5-1998, moreso was not registered. On the basis of the above kabala deeds dated 12-5-1998 which were earlier in point of time, the plaintiff acquired valid title and after considering the evidence on record the trial Court and appellate Court found that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land but the High Court Division committed serious illegality in making the Rule absolute. He further submits that in the trial Court and appellate Court found that the defendants failed to prove the Bainapatra and considered it as collusive and illegal but the High Court Division upon misreading and misconstruing the findings of the trial Court and appellate Court below committed an error of law in making the. Rule absolute. He next submits that the kabalas executed in favour of the defendants in pursuance of the decree as passed in Title Suit No.58 of 1998 was a suit for specific performance of contract is subsequent to that of the kabalas dated 12-5-1998 and, as such, the defendants did not acquire any valid right, title and interest in the suit land but the High Court Division committed an error of law in making the Rule absolute. He finally submits that since both the Court of facts, on consideration of the evidence on record, found the possession of the appellant in the suit land, so the respondent Nos.1-4 will not get any benefit of the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act but the High Court Division committed serious illegality in making the Rule absolute and, as such, the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. 

10. Per contra, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents submit that the High Court Division considering the evidences and the materials on record rightly held that the trial Court without considering the exhibits, depositions of the PWs and DWs, plaint, written statements wrongly and illegally decreed the suit and the Appellate Court below also without considering the exhibits, depositions of the PWs and DWs, plaint and written statements dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree dated 12-5-2002 passed by the trial Court illegally and, as such, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute and set-aside the judgment and decree passed by the Courts below and, as such, no interference by this Division for ends of justice. He further submits that the High Court Division in exercising his power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure has held and found that the findings of the Appellate Court below are not just and sustainable in law and since there is merit in the revision, it must succeed, the plaintiff failed to prove his case. He finally submits that the High Court Division elaborately discussed the evidence 
of the PWs and DWs independently and considering the facts and circumstances of the case made the Rule absolute without any order as to cost and the impugned judgment and decree dated 23-6-2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Narayanganj in Title Appeal No.110 of 2002 and judgment and decree dated 15-5-2002 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Rupganj, Narayanganj in Title Suit No.138 of 1999 have been set-aside and the suit filed by the plaintiff has been dismissed by the judgment and order dated 22-3-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4419 of 2004 which requires no interference by this Division for ends of justice. 

11. We have heard the learned Advocates for the respective, parties. Perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 

12. Having gone through the judgment of the High Court Division it transpires that in the impugned judgment the learned Single Judge opined that both the trial Court and the Court of appeal below committed error of law in non-considering the evidences on records both oral and documentary resulting in error in the decision occasioning failure of justice but did not rebut the findings, discussions and opinions of the Courts below as both Courts of facts concurrently after discussing the testimonies of DW 1 to 3 found that the bainapatra was not proved by the proper and competent witnesses. 

13. The defendants adduced 3 witnesses to prove the unregistered deed claiming that it was executed by the defendant Nos.5 and 6. So, this Division has to answer whether execution of the unregistered deed was proved in accordance with law and both Courts below misread and misconstrued the evidences on records. 

14. From the judgments of the Courts below it is crystal clear that both Courts below discussed and appreciated the testimonies of PWs and DWs in its true perspective and came to definite findings that the defendants appellants respondents have failed to prove the genuineness of the unregistered deed with its execution. The Courts below founds that the defendant Nos.5 and 6 did not turn up in Court to support the execution, the scribe and husband of the executant name Shainsun Nahar were not adduced as witnesses in the Court, though DW No.1 admitted that they were present at the time of bainapatra and execution. In cross he admitted that he could not bring the arbitrators as witnesses those were present in Arbitration, admitted that there is no witness in the baina and deed of this village. Further admitted that Mokbul Hossain, a witness to the Bainapatra is his maternal uncle, however, he did not turn up to prove the Bainapatra, he comes from village Jatra Mura far from 3½/4 kilometers from the Borpa i.e. from the suit place. DW 2 is the maternal uncle of the DW 1. DW 2 in examination-in-cross admitted that he did not receive the Court witness notice albeit; he was present and disposed in Court. DW 3 could not tell the correct plot numbers and quantum of the land. He admitted that he was not present at the time of execution of bainapatra and deed in question. 

15. However, in the pliant 4 persons are the plaintiffs, except one as DW No.1, none of the plaintiffs were appeared and deposed in the Court in support of their plaint case in the suit for Specific Performance of Contract as DWs, as both suits were tried analogously by the same Court. 

16. The DW 1 while deposed on behalf of other plaintiffs, he did not produce any supporting documents i.e. Power of Attorney or Letter of authority to prove that he is a competent witness on behalf of other plaintiffs as required under Rules 1 and 2 of Order III of the Code of Civil Procedure. Thus, it may conveniently be noted the provisions of the same in this context. 
Rule 1 runs thus:-
Any appearance, application or act in or to any Court, required or authorized by law to be made or done by a party in shall Court, 
may, except where otherwise expressly provided by any law for the time being in force, be made or done by the party in person, or by his recognized agent, or by a pleaded appearing, applying or acting, as the case may be, on his behalf: 
Provided that any such appearance shall, if the Court so directs, be made by the party in person. 
Rule 2 runs thus:—
The recognized agents of parties by whom such Recognized appearance, applications and acts may be made or done are—
(a) Persons holding powers-of-attorney, authorizing them to make and do such appearances, applications and acts on behalf of such parties; 
(b) Persons carrying on trade or business for and in the names of parties not resident within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court within which limits the appearance, application or act is made or done, in matters connected with such trade or business only, where no other agent is expressly authorized to make and do such appearances, applications and acts. 

17. On a breviary of the above provisions of law it is clearly panoramic that a person if not authorise by the plaintiff or defendent, except husband and wife, could not depose on his behalf in the Court, if depose, he would be treated as incompetent witness. The DW No.1 deposed on behalf of other plaintiffs without any authority from them as found from record. Thus, it is obviously proved that he was an un-authorized and incompetent witness to prove the case on behalf of other plaintiffs. 

18. It is the cardinal principle of law as enunciated by this Division that revision Court cannot interfere in concurrent finding of facts, when there is no misreading and non-consideration of the material evidence on records. In the instant case the Single Judge of the High Court Division in the judgment wrongly opined that both the Courts misread and non-considered the materials evidence on record or rebutted the facts of finding of the Courts below as both the Courts below correctly found that the case of the defendant for the Specific Performance of Contract was not proved. 

19. We are, therefore, of the view that the judgment of the High Court Division is not a proper judgment of reversal, thus, it cannot be sustained in law, because, the Court of revision when acts beyond its jurisdiction in setting aside the concurrent findings of fact, this Division obviously interfere in the judgment of the High Court Division to secure the ends of justice. 

20. In the present case, at the time of trial two suits were tried analogously, one suit was for declaration of title and cancellation of ex-parte decree; another was for the Specific Performance of Contract. Both the Courts below concurrently found that suit for declaration and cancellation was proved but suit for Specific Performance of Contract was not proved. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division while reversed the judgments did not even discuss the case on the basis of evidence on record nor opined that the plaintiffs of the suit for Specific Performance of Contract was able to satisfy that the execution of bainapatra and deed were proved, consideration was passed and transaction was found genuine, even if, reversed the concurrent findings of fact which calls for interference by this Division. 

21. The discussions made herein above and the material on records, we are of the view that the judgment of the High Court Division is not a proper judgment of reversal, hence, it is set-aside. The judgment of the Court of appeal below is affirmed. 

Accordingly, this Civil Appeal is allowed, however, without any order as to cost. 

End.

full_judgment:
Ahmed Sohel, J: On an application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the inclusion of the case property measuring an area of 39 decimals of land out of SA Plot No.1058 corresponding to RS Plot No.679 appertaining to SA Khatian No.147 and RS Khatian No.42 of Mouza Dakkingaon, Police Station Shabujbagh, Dhaka at serial No.7 in 'Ka' schedule of vested properties published in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 2-5-2012 (Annexure-'H' to the writ petition) should not be declared to be without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to release the case property from "Ka" schedule of vested property in favour of the petitioners and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The facts relevant for disposal of the Rule as set out in the writ petition, in short, are that CS Khatian No.118 of Mouza-Dakkhingaon under Police Station-Sabek Keraniganj, thereafter Tejgaon and at present-Sabujbag within District-Dhaka was prepared and published in the names of Brindaban Koibartta and Tufani Koibartta, both sons of Guru Proshad. In that khatian, 104 decimals of land were recorded under CS Plot No.1058 wherein they were the owners in equal shares. The said Tufani Koibartta died leaving behind his only son Pagol Nath Das who obtained 52 decimals of land in CS Plot No.1058 appertaining to CS Khatian No.118 of the aforesaid Mouza by way of inheritance from his deceased father. Thereafter, Pagol Nath Das sold out the said 52 decimals of land in favour of Abdus Samad Ahmed, son of Moulavi Tasir Uddin Ahmed vide registered sale deed being No.5763, dated 22-5-1957. Accordingly, SA Khatian No.147 covering 52 decimals of land in SA Plot No.1058 was prepared and published in the name of said Abdus Samad. During RS survey, RS Khatian No.42 covering 48 decimals of land in RS Plot No.679 was prepared and published in the name of said Abdus Samad Ahmed. 

3. Thereafter, Abdus Samad Ahmed sold out the said 52 decimals of land in favour of Rai Raman Mitra vide registered sale deed being No.1897, dated 17-1-1978. Out of the said 52 decimals of land, Rai Raman Mitra sold out 13 decimals of land to the instant petitioner No.1, Md Ilias Hossain vide registered sale deed being No.42072, dated 1-12-1978, (Annexure-B(i) of the writ petition). The said Rai Raman Mitra also sold out 26 decimals of land in favour of Mosammat Jahanara Begum, mother of the petitioner Nos.2-5 vide registered sale deed being No.42148, dated 1-12-1978, (Annexure-B(ii) of the writ petition). Thereafter, the petitioner No.I mutated his name in respect of 13.82 decimals of land vide Mutation Case No.5070 P-1/05, dated 12-5-2005. The said Mosammat Jahanara Begum out of her 26 decimals of land, sold out 5.61 decimals of land in favour of the petitioner Nos.6- 7 vide registered sale deed being No.3741, dated 28-6-1995, then 4.49 decimals of land in favour of the petitioner Nos.8-9 vide registered sale deed being No.3742, dated 28-6-1995 and 4.95 decimals of land in favour of Noorjahan Begum, mother of the petitioner Nos.10-12 vide registered sale deed being No.6113, dated 20-6-1988, (Annexure-C,C(i) and C(ii) of the writ petition). Thereafter, during Mohanagar Jarip, Mohanagar Khatian covering the case land were prepared and published in the names of the petitioner No.1, mother of the petitioner Nos.2-5, petitioner Nos.6-7, petitioner Nos.8-9 and mother of the petitioner Nos.10-12 accordingly without any objection from any quarter. The petitioner No.1 sold out 5.85 decimals of land in favour of the petitioner Nos.13-14 vide registered sale deed being No.5320, dated 14-7-2008, (Annexure-E & E(i) of the writ petition) and accordingly, they have mutated the said land in their respective names. The petitioner Nos.2-5 obtained 7.26 decimals of land by way of inheritance from their deceased mother Jahanara Begum and they have mutated the said land in their names (Annexure-F of the writ petition). The petitioners are possessing their 39 decimals of land for a long time since their respective date of purchase by erecting residential houses on the land. They have paid up to date revenue rent as per the latest Mohanagar khatian. 

4. On the 1st week of January, 2016 the petitioner No.1 went to the office of the respondent No.4, Tohsilder, Shabujbagh Tohshil Office for payment of his revenue rent for the year of 1422 BS, but the respondent No.4 refused to accept the rent on the ground that the land has been included in the list of vested property as "Ka" schedule land. Thereafter, on scrutiny, the petitioners found that SA Plot No.1058 corresponding to RS Plot No.679 covering their land has been included in the list of vested property, published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 2-5-2012 (Annexure-H of the writ petition). The property of the petitioners was vested to the Government in connection with VP Case No.523 of 1979. The petitioners came to know about the VP list on the 1st week of the January, 2016 and in the meantime, statutory period of limitation to apply before the Arpito Sampatti Prottorpan Tribunal, which was 31-12-2013 as per section 10 of the "অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পণ আইন, ২০০১" elapsed. Being aggrieved by the inclusion of the said land of the petitioners at serial No. 7 in the list of 'Ka' schedule vested property Gazette, published on 2-5-2012, the petitioners finding no other alternative efficacious remedy filed the instant writ petition before this Hon'ble Court and obtained the present Rule. 

5. The Rule being served upon all the respondents, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, respondent No.2, entered appearance and filed an affidavit-in-opposition. 

6. Mr Md Hamidur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners at the very outset by referring to all the annexures submits that the petitioners have the title and possession over the case property and they never left the country. Therefore, the inclusion of the case property in 'Ka' list of the " অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পণ আইন, ২০০১” is completely without any legal basis. 

7. He further submits that on a perusal of the annexure-H, it is found that the owner of the property in question was Joy Durga Bewa and others, but on perusal of the documents annexed herewith, it is apparent that never the property was recorded in the name of Joy Durga Bewa or others at any point of time, rather, SA, RS and latest Mohanagar Khatian has been prepared in the name of the present petitioners and their vendor or predecessor Abdus Samad. Hence, inclusion of the property in the 'Ka' schedule is not in accordance with law. 

8. Referring to the supplementary affidavit dated 12-11-2019, Mr Rahman submits that from the materials on record, it appears that Abdus Samad Ahmed sold out the said 52 decimals of land in favour of one Rairaman Mitra vide sale deed being No.1 897, dated 17-1-1978 and subsequently the petitioners obtained 39 decimals of land out of the said 52 decimals by way of purchase. Therefore, it is evident that at the relevant time, the case land belonged to Abdus Samad Ahmed, who never left the then East Pakistan. On the other hand, the said Abdus Samad Ahmed, the SA and RS recorded owner of the case land, was a Muslim. In that view of the matter, there is no scope to include the case land as vested property, but the respondents have acted arbitrarily by including the land of the petitioners in the 'Ka' schedule of the vested property, which is liable to be declared to have been done without lawful authority.

9. He finally submits that after 1974, the inclusion of the petitioners property in the list of vested property is illegal and also violative of Article 42 of the Constitution of Peoples Republic of Bangladesh. The petitioners can come directly to the High Court Division for protection of their right to property guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution of Peoples Republic of Bangladesh. Therefore, the writ petition is maintainable. To fortify his submissions, he relied upon the following decisions, which are as follows:-

10. Manabendra Chakrabarty vs Govern¬ment of Bangladesh, reported in 3 SCOB (2015) HCD 52; Government of Bangladesh represented by Ministry of Works and another vs Syed Chand Sultana, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 24; Saju Hosein vs Bangladesh, reported in 58 DLR (AD)1 7 7; Sharif Ashraf Uzzaman vs Bangladesh, reported in 2017 (2) LNJ (HCD) 166 = 70 DLR 857, and the case of Md Abdul Hye vs Government of Bangladesh, reported in LG (HCD) 6 = 70 DLR 313.

11. Per Contra, Mr Amit Das Gupta, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No.2, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka by filing an affidavit-in-¬opposition submits that the Authority rightly and lawfully included the case property in the vested property list, published by Gazette notification dated 2-5-2012. He submits that the petitioners were fully aware about the Gazette notification and without going to the proper forum, being the Arpito Shampotti Tribunal for releasing their property, they filed the instant writ petition. They have no scope to prefer this writ petition as per the existing law of the land. As such, the instant writ petition is not maintainable, since they have alternative remedy.

12. He submits that the list of returnable property was prepared in order to return the property enlisted as vested property to the original owners, according to the Act of অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পণ আইন, ২০০১. Accordingly, on 2-5-2012, the Gazette was published following all the legal formalities.

13. He next submits that the mutation does not establish any right and title over any property, rather, mutation is normally allowed to realize Government Revenue. At the time of mutation of RS Khatian, the vested property Gazette notification was not published, as a result mutation Khatian was prepared in absence of the related vested property list. The property has been declared as vested property and leased out vide VP Case No.523 of 1979 and therefore, the purchase of the vested property by the petitioners is not proper as per law.

14. He finally submits that inclusion of the property in the 'Ka' schedule list of the vested property has been made following all the legal formalities, and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

15. We have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocate of the petitioners and the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the respondent No.2 and perused the writ petition, supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioners, affidavit-in-opposition and relevant annexures annexed thereto with profound attention.

16. It appears that the main cause to file this writ petition is the Gazette notification dated 2-5- 2012 (Annexure-H) wherein the petitioners property was included at serial No.7 as vested property. It appears from the record that the property in question that is CS Khatian No.118 of Mouza-Dakkhingaon under Police Station-Sabek Keraniganj, thereafter Tejgaon, at present¬Sabujbag within District-Dhaka was prepared and published in the names of Brindaban Koibartta and Tufani Koibartta, both sons of Guru Proshad. In that khatian, 104 decimals of land were recorded under CS Plot No.1058, as evidenced from the annexure-X of the writ petition. Thereafter, Tufani Koibartta died leaving behind his only son Pagol Nath Das who obtained 52 decimals of land in the CS Khatian No.118 of the aforesaid Mouza by way of inheritance from his deceased father and the said Pagol Nath Das sold out the said 52 decimals of land in favour of Abdus Samad Ahmed vide registered sale deed being No.5763, dated. 22-5-1957 (Annexure-Y of the writ petition). It appears that before SA survey, the said Abdus Samad Ahmed purchased 52 decimals of land and accordingly, SA Khatian No.147 was prepared and published in the name of said Abdus Samad Ahmed. Thereafter, during RS survey, RS Khatian No.42 was prepared and published in the name of said Abdus Samad Ahmed and 48 decimals of land was recorded in RS Plot No.679 of the said Khatian. Thereafter, Abdus Samad Ahmed sold out 52 decimals of land in favour of one Rai Raman Mitra vide registered sale deed No.1897, dated 17-1-1978. Subsequently, the present petitioners obtained 39 decimals of land out of said 52 decimals of land by way of purchase. It is clear from the record that at the relevant time of inclusion of the case land as vested property, the case land actually belonged to Abdus Samad Ahmed and hence the question of his whereabouts being unknown did not arise at all. Therefore, there is no basis to treat the case land as vested property.

17. From the above facts and upon perusal of the documents, it is clear that the petitioners name have been recorded in the record of right and they had paid rent. Moreover, there is nothing on record to indicate that they left the country. Rather, they have been possessing and enjoying the property since long by dint of their respective purchases.

18. Now, in respect to the issue of maintain¬ability of the present writ petition, it appears from the record that the Government has accepted rent from the petitioners up to 1421 BS and since their respective date of purchase, the petitioners are possessing the land by erecting residential houses on payment of revenue rent as per the latest Mohanagar Khatian as evidenced from annexures G to G (iv) respectively of the writ petition. Moreover, the possession of the petitioners has not been disturbed from any quarter in any way. Therefore, it is natural that they had no knowledge about their land being enlisted as vested property until the office of the respondent No.4 refused to accept the rent for the year of 1422 BS. Admittedly, by this time, the last date for filing a suit before the "অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পণ আইন, ২০০১” expired. As such, they have no other alternative remedy other than filing this writ petition.

19. Further, as the petitioners have alleged of violation of their fundamental right, namely the right to property under Article 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the present writ petition is very much maintainable. For invoking writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution, the petitioners do not require to show alternative, efficacious remedy. In this connection, reliance may be placed on the view of our Apex Court in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Syed Chand Sultana, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 24, wherein it has been held that:—
"The writ-petitioners can come directly to the High Court Division for protection of their fundamental right even though an alternative remedy is available." 

20. In the present case, it appears that the petitioners are in possession and continuously enjoying the case property since long on the basis of their purchase without any interruption of any quarter and they never left the country nor they have been dispossessed from the property in question. In such a situation, inclusion of their property in the "Ka" list of the vested property and treating it as vested property is violative of fundamental right to hold property as guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

21. It further appears that the Vested Property Case No.523 was started in the year of 1979. It has already been settled by our Apex Court in the case of Saju Hosein vs Bangladesh, reported in 58 DLR (AD) 177, that:—
"Since the law of enemy property itself died with the repeal of Ordinance No.1 of 1969 on 23-3-1974 no further vested property case can be started thereafter on the basis of the law which is already dead. Accordingly, there is no basis at all to treat the case land as vested property upon starting VP Case No.210 of 1980." 

22. Therefore, after 23-3-1974, there is no basis at all to start the Vested Property Case No. 523 of 1979. 

23. In light of the above discussions, we are of the view that the case property is not a vested property, rather it has been included in the list of vested property by violating the provision of the law. Therefore, the inclusion of the property in the schedule 'Ka' of the vested property list, published in the Gazette notification dated 2-5¬2012, (Annexure-H) is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

24. In the above facts and circumstances of the case, we find merit in the Rule. 

25. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. 

26. The respondents are hereby directed to exclude the case property from `Ka' schedule of the vested property list published in Bangla-desh Gazette dated 2-5-2012 through a fresh Gazette notification within 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment and order positively.

Communicate the copy of this judgment and order to the concerned respondents at once.

End.
