vs
Md Mazed Sheikh and others ----- Plaintiffs Appellants-Opposite-parties No. 1-10.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the DC, Rajbari and another ------- Proforma defendant-Respondent-Opposite parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties No. 1-10 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 25-10-2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No. 55 of 2010 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 5-4-2010 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Goalanda, Rajbari in Title Suit No. 54 of 2007 dismissing the suit should not be set aside and/ or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 54 of 2007 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Goalanda, Rajbari against the proforma opposite party No. 12 as defendant for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for further declaration that the sale deed being No. 1136 dated 19-7-1984 registered in the Sub-Registry Office of Goalanda in favour of the defendant is illegal, forged, collusive, null and void, malafide and nothing but a mere paper transaction. 

3. The plaintiffs' Case, in short, is that the suit land appertaining to RS Khatian No. 99 corresponding to SA Khatian No. 94 of Mouza Uttar Ujanchar under Police Station Goalanda District Rajbari originally belonged to Fazil Sarder, Jashim Sarder and others. Md Basiruddin. Sarder and others purchased 11 decimals of land from RS Plot No. 5283 through registered sale deed being No. 2063 dated 5-3-1979 from Jashim Sarder. The said Basiruddin Sarder and others sold out the said 11 decimals of land to one Asgar Ali Sheikh through registered sale deed being No. 925 dated 4-5-1981. The said Asgar Ali Sheikh sold out the said 11 decimals of land to the plaintiff No. 1 through registered sale deed being No. 250 dated 12-2-1984. The plaintiff has been enjoying and possessing the suit land peacefully and without any obstruction. The original defendant (proforma opposite party No. 12) is an influential politician and former member of parliament and by exercising his political influence upon the local administration he managed to have a sale deed executed and registered on 19-7-1984 being No. 1136 in his name/favour and claimed title to the suit land on 20-4-2007 on the basis of the said sale deed and after obtaining the certified copy of the said sale deed on 26-4-2007 the plaintiff for the first time came to know that the defendant managed to have the sale deed executed and registered fraudulently and collusively through impersonation and that the said sale deed is without consideration and nothing but a mere paper transaction and hence the suit. 

4. The petitioners as defendants No. 2 and 3 contested the suit. The petitioners were not made party to the suit although the original defendant (proforma opposite party No. 12) transferred the suit land in their favour by a registered sale deed being No. 226 dated 26-11-1996 and became extinguished therefrom and, as such, he did not contest the suit. Subsequently being added as defendant Nos. 2-3 on 29-6-2008, the petitioners contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material facts of the plaint and contending inter alia that there is no cause of action to file the suit; the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner and the suit is barred by limitation and bad for defect of parties and the suit is bared by the provisions of the Suits Valuation Act and Court Fees Act and hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the suit is barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence etc. One Jasim alias Jochon Sarder was one of the co-sharers of the suit khatian who transferred 44 decimals of land from RS Plot No. 5203 in favour of Basiruddin Sarder and others by a registered sale deed being No. 2063 dated 5-3-1979 and delivered possession in their favour. The said Basir Uddin Sarder and others transferred 11 decimals of land in favour of one Asgar Ali Sheikh by a registered sale deed being No. 925 dated 4-5-1981. Thereafter the said Asgar Ali Sheikh transferred 11 decimals of land in favour of the original defendant (proforma opposite party No. 12) by a registered sale deed being No. 276 dated 15-2-1984 and delivered possession of the same in his favour and while the original defendant (proforma opposite party No. 12) had been enjoying and possessing the suit land by erecting homestead thereon, the plaintiff-opposite party' No. 1 claimed title to the suit land and, as such, to avoid complicity the defendant No.1 managed to have executed and registered another sale deed being No. 1136 dated 19-7-1984 from the plaintiff No. 1. The plaintiffs have no right, title, interest, and possession over the suit land. The sale deed No. 1136 dated 19-7-1984 is genuine and voluntary and while the defendant No. I enjoying and possessing the suit land by paying rent and taking mutation in his name the defendant No. 1 (proforma opposite party No. 12) transferred the same in favour of the defendants petitioners No. 2 and 3 by two registered sale deeds being Nos. 1435 and 1436, both dated 26-11-1996 and became extinguished therefrom by delivering possession in favour of the defendants-petitioners No. 2 and 3 and since purchase the defendants-petitioners No. 2 and 3 have been enjoying and possessing the suit land by paying rents and erecting homestead thereon. The suit is barred by limitation since the plaintiffs have specific knowledge about the impugned sale deed No. 1136 dated 19-7-1984 and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

5. The suit was tried by the learned Assistant Judge, Goalanda, Rajbari. During trial the plaintiffs examined 4 witnesses and the defendants-petitioners examined 3 witnesses in support of their respective cases. 

6. The learned Assistant Judge, Goalanda, Rajbari dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 5-4-2010. 

7. Against this, the plaintiffs as appellants preferred appeal before the District Judge, Rajbari and on transfer, the appeal was allowed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Rajbari on 25-10-2011 and thus the defendants-respondents as petitioner moved this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure before the Court and obtained this Rule. 

8. Mr ZH Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate for the defendants petitioners submits that admittedly the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is out of possession and the defendants-petitioners are in possession of the suit land, which is manifestly evident from the testimony of all the PWs including the plaintiff opposite party No.1 who was examined as PW 1. Plaintiff Md Mazed Sheikh as PW 1 admitted in his cross-examination—
“…….. নালিশী জমিতে দখল চাই । ......বর্তমানে এ ঘরগুলোতে লুৎফর মুন্সি বসবাস করে । ৫/৭ বছর যাবৎ লুৎফর এ ঘরে বসবাস করে ।......৩ নং বিবাদীর আগে ১ নং বিবাদী লতিফ মুন্সি ঘরগুলো দখল করত । লতিফ মু্ন্সি সাত বছর ঘর গুলো দখল করেছিল । লতিফ মুন্সি কত বছর আগে দখলে আসে কাগজপত্র না দেখে বলতে পারব না। লতিফ মুন্সি ১৯৮৪ সাল থেকে জমিতে দখলে আছে।......আমি বর্তমানে এই জমি দখল করি না । লুৎফর দখল করে। আমি কবে থেকে বেদখল হয়েছি বলতে পারব না। …”

9. PW 3 Momen Ali Mondal admitted in his examination-in-chief “……. এখন সেখানে লতিফ মুন্সির ভাই থাকে ।”   

10. PW 4 Abdul Gafur Sheikh admitted in his examination-in-chief “…….এখন লতিফ মুন্সির ভাই লুৎফর দুইটা ঘরে থাকে | ....”

11. Therefore, being out of possession, the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 ought to have prayed for recover)' of possession and that not having been done by way of amendment of plaint, the present suit for declaration of title simplifier without recovery of possession is not maintainable as being barred/hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. In support of his contention he has reported to the case of Delipjan being dead his heirs: Fazal Haque vs Shahed Badsha, reported in 66 DLR (AD) 176. 

12. Mr Md Nurul Amin the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-opposite parties opposes the Rule and submits that the trial Court without considering and discussing the evidence on record dismissed the suit and the appellate Court below upon proper appreciation and discussing the evidence on record allowed the appeal and reversing the decision of the trial Court. The trial Court wrongly held that the suit is barred by law of limitation but the learned appellate Court below with consideration of the materials evidence on record correctly held that the suit was filed within time, since the cause of action arisen on 20-4-2007 when the defendant No. 1 claimed the suit land on the basis of the illegal deed No. 1136 dated 19-7-1984 and the plaintiffs filed the instant suit on 16-5-2007. Even though the cause of action is counted from the dated 26-11-1996 when the defendant No. 1 transferred the suit land to the defendant Nos. 2-3, then it is clear that the suit was filed within 12 years but the learned trial Court illegally held that the suit is barred by law of limitation which was properly reversed by the appellate Court below. The learned trial Court illegally held that the suit is not maintainable for defect of parties since all the co-sharers of SA Khatian were not made party. The learned appellate Court below with proper consideration of fact reversed the issue on the ground that since the cases of both the parties that the suit land was belonged to Azgor Ali and the suit was for declaration of title, so all the co-sharers are not the necessary party of this suit and further held that admitted fact need not be proved under section 58 of the Evidence Act. The trial Court without considering the certified copy of the deed submitted by the plaintiffs, dismissed, the suit which is erred in law. If the certified copy of the deed is filed without calling for the original copy and without any objection the question of inadmissibility of this deed cannot be raised at a subsequent point of time. In the instant case the defendants did not raise any objection about the certified copy of the deed and the trial Court acted wrongly in not considering the deed and on the basis of this ground dismissed the suit. In this regard the learned Advocate has referred to the case of Joynal Abedin vs Mafizur Rahman, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 162. The plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration that the deed No. 1136 dated 19-7-1984 is forged, illegal and void, but the learned trial Court without discussing about the deed dated 19-7-1984, only discussed the deed No. 250 dated 12-2-1984 executed by Azgor Ali in favour of the plaintiff No. 1 held that the plaintiff No. 1 was not owner of the suit land. It is admitted by the defendant No.1 that the plaintiff owned the land from his father and as a result the defendant No.1 took a deed No. 1136 dated 19-7-1984 executed by the plaintiff side in favour of the defendant No. 1. If the defendant No. 1 willingly takes a deed from the plaintiff side, how the learned trial Court denied the ownership of the plaintiff, so it is clear that the trial Court erred in law in dismissing the suit and the appellate Court below with proper appreciation reversed the judgment of the trial Court. The trial Court without discussing the important issue regarding the burden of proof illegally dismissed the suit and the appellate Court below properly discussed the issue and held that when a deed is challenged as forged and fabricated documents, the onus of prove lies upon the defendants to prove whether the same is valid and genuine documents. Normally the initial burden of proving the execution of a document when it is denied must rest upon the person alleging its execution according to section 101 of the Evidence Act. In the present case, it is the case of the plaintiff side that the plaintiff side did not execute any sale deed dated 19-7-1984 in favour of the defendant No.1 and it was forged and fabricated document. On the other hand, it is the case of the defendants that the said sale deed is valid and genuine document. The sale deed itself is in possession of the defendant and in such a situation the defendants are in a dominating position to prove the documents affirmatively. In this situation the appellate Court below rightly held that the burden of prove lies upon the defendants to prove the document is valid and genuine. In this regard the learned Advocate referred the decisions delivered in the case of Aim Miah vs Gauranga Chandra Sharma, reported in 1 ADC 462 and Rishi vs Gurbaksh Singh, Supreme Court of India. The trial Court without discussing the issue, whether the suit is maintainable in its present form, just held that the suit is not maintainable in its present form which is barred in law and violated the mandatory provision of law under Order 20 rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The instant suit was filed for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for further declaration that the sale deed No. 1136 dated 19-7-1984 is illegal, forged, collusive, null and void and nothing but a mere paper transaction and for cancellation of the said deed. The suit was filed under section 39 of the Specific Relief Act and ails the requirement of filing the suit was fulfilled by the plaintiffs and, as such, the suit is maintainable in its present form and the appellate Court below properly discussed the issue and rightly decreed the suit. PW 1 stated in his deposition dated 8-2-2009 that he wants possession. The learned Advocate for the defendants-petitioners claimed that since the plaintiff side is not in possession over the suit land, so the suit is not maintainable without praying for recover of khas possession. On 16-5-2005 the plaintiffs filed the Title Suit and prayed for recovery of khass possession if they were dispossessed during pendency of the suit by the defendants. In the instant suit the plaintiffs were dispossessed by the defendants after filing the Title Suit and, as such, the suit is maintainable, since he already prayed for recovery of khass possession in the plaint. It is a settled principle of law that the findings of fact, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the appellate Court below which is the final Court of fact, is binding on the High Court Division' as revisional Court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case. In the instant case, from the judgment of the appellate Court below it is found that in arriving at its findings the said Court carefully considered all the materials fact and circumstances of the case and evidence on record and consequently these findings of facts are immune from attack in revision. Since the learned Advocate for the defendants-petitioners did not point out any misreading, non-reading and non-consideration of material evidence on records, so in revisional jurisdiction, there is no scope for interfere in the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below and, as such, there is no merit in the Rule and the Rule is liable to be discharged. In this regard the learned Advocate has referred to the case of Hazari Bala Sana vs Niron alias Niranjan Mandal, reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 294. 

13. Heard the learned Advocates for both the sides and perused the record. 

14. The instant suit has been filed by the plaintiffs for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for further declaration that the sale deed No. 1136 dated 19-7-1984 is illegal, forged, collusive, null and void and nothing but a mere paper transaction and for cancellation of the said deed. In the present case, it is the case of the plaintiff side that the plaintiff side did not execute any sale deed on 19-7-1984 in favour of the defendant No.1 and this deed is forged and fabricated document but the plaintiff side failed to prove the same and admittedly the plaintiff side is out of possession and the defendants are in possession of the suit land which is manifestly evident from the testimony of the P.Ws. Being out of possession the plaintiff side ought to have prayed for recovery of possession and that not having been done by way of amendment of plaint, the present suit is for declaration of title simplifier without recovery of possession is not maintainable as being barred/hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case I find substance in this Rule. 

15. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. 

16. The impugned judgment and decree dated 25-10-2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge Court, Rajbari in Title Appeal No. 55 of 2010 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 5-4-2010 passed by the learned Assistant judge, Goalanda, Rajbari in Title Suit No. 54 of 2007 is hereby set-aside. 

Let the record be sent down to the appellate Court below with a copy of the judgment at once. 

End.

lawyer:
Abul Kalam Azad with Munshi Abdul Hamid, Advocates—For the pre-emptee-Petitioner.

Mrinal Kanti Biswas, Advocate—For the Pre-emptors-Opposite parties.
parties:
Shaikh Ali Iman ----- Preemptee-Petitioner
VS
Hazari Lal Mondal being dead his legal heirs Subodh Kumar Mondol and others ----- Preemptors-Opposite parties
full_judgment:
Instant Rule was issued at the instance of the pre-emptee-petitioner ((hereinafter referred to either as pre-emptee or the petitioner) and the same is directed against a Judgment of reversal, being Judgment and Order dated 28-5-2001 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Khulna in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 19 of 1999, reversing the Judgment and Order dated 9-2-1999 passed by the Court of Assistant Judge, Fultala, Khulna in Miscellaneous Case No. 9 of 1995.

2. The background facts of filing this revisional application are that the predecessor of this application's opposite parties, late Hazari Lal Mondal, as the pre-emptor, filed the above-mentioned pre-emption case on 19-4-1995 making the averments that he is a co-sharer of the suit-Jote of 1.65 acres of land and the other two co-sharers Fatik Mondol and Ramala Bala Mondol (opposite party Nos. 2 & 3) have sold the suit land through registered sale deed No. 824 of 1991 dated 12-6-1991 to the pre-emptee without serving notice upon the pre-emptor and other co-sharers; that the suit land is situated in 'Bil Dakatia' which was under water for nearly 12 years and no one could cultivate the land; that in the year 1995, some land were ready for cultivation and when on 17-3-1995, the pre-emptee came to possess the land upon disclosing for the first time that he purchased the property, the pre-emptor came to know from the pre-emptee about the sale of the suit land on the said date of 17-3-1995; that thereafter the pre-emptor went to the sub-Registrar's office and got a certified copy of the sale deed on 18-3-1995 and came to know clearly that opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 had sold the suit land on 12-6-1991 to the pre-emptee through registered sale-deed No. 824 of 1991 at a price of Taka 10,000 (ten thousand) only; that the pre-emptee is not a co-sharer of the Joma and he is a stranger and he never made the transaction known to the pre-emptor or any other person before 17-3-1995 and he did never possess the suit land; that the pre-emptor is a farmer owning 5 bighas land and he deposited the value of the land and compensation money. So, by filing the Miscellaneous Case, he prayed for pre-emption and cost. 

3. The opposite party No. 1 (pre-emptee-petitioner) submitted written objection contending, inter alia, that the case is not maintainable, barred by limitation and bad for defect of parties; that the recorded tenants sold share at the highest price and handed over possession to the pre-emptee; that one relative of the pre-emptor, Nira Mondol, was present at the time of sale and the pre-emptee along with Nira Mondol had met the pre-emptor with a proposal to buy the land from the sellers but he refused and, then, the pre-emptee purchased the land; that the seller also went to the pre-emptor and proposed to sell the land to the pre-emptor and when he refused to purchase the land, the seller sold the same to the pre-emptee; that from the date of purchase, the pre-emptee is possessing and enjoying the suit land without any hindrance; that the pre-emptor knows everything about the sale of case-land, because the pre-emptee mutated his name and paid rent and in the recent survey his name was recorded; that the pre-emptors are not co-sharers and they are not tillers/cultivators and they have over 100 bighas of land. So, the case should be dismissed with cost. 

4. On perusal of the application for pre-emption, written objections and evidence adduced by both the parties, the trial Court arrived at the decision that the application for pre-emption is liable to be rejected on the ground of the pre-emptor's failure to approach the Court within the four months’ time from the date of his knowledge of transfer of the case-land and, accordingly, the pre-emption case was dismissed. The pre-emptor-opposite party preferred an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 19 of 1999 and the learned Additional District Judge allowed the appeal by reversing the Judgment and Order passed by the trial Court. 

5. Mr Abul Kalam Azad, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee takes me through the evidence adduced by the PW 1 and submits that since the PW 1 himself has submitted the certified copy of the mutation of the land in question as Exhibit-2 in the trial Court, no further evidence is required to prove the date of knowledge of sale of this property. In an effort to elaborate his submission on this count, he submits that from the aforesaid Exhibit-2 it is evident that the Mutation Case of the land in question was registered as Mutation Case No.10/92-93 and, therefore, the pre-emptor was competent to file the case only within four months of the date of knowledge in the year 1993. Then, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee, by taking me through the deposition of all the PWs, submits that the deposition of the PW I with regard to the place of knowledge is contradictory with that of the PW 2 and PW 3 inasmuch as the PW 1 states that their father came to know for the first time about the sale upon seeing the pre-emptee in the case-land, whereas the PW 2 and PW 3 stated that they saw the pre-emptee to survey/measure the case-land. Mr Azad continues to submit that there is no mentioning about presence of any person who would corroborate the father of PW l's claim as to disclosure by the pre-emptee about the purchase of the case-land. He argues that since the PW 1 has admitted the fact of the seller's migration to India from this country permanently in the year 1991, the normal presumption is that the pre-emptor had the information about the transfer of this property by the seller. By referring .to the case of Abdul Mazid Howlader vs Lehajuddin Howlader, 1996 BLD (AD) 197 = 48 DLR (AD) 160, he submits that since the case was filed long after 4 (four) years of sale of the case-land, a heavy burden lay on the pre-emptor to discharge the onus of proof that he did not have the knowledge about the transfer of property. Mr Abul Kalam Azad, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee, then, takes me through the Judgment of the trial Court and that of the appellate Court and submits that the appellate Court's Judgment is not a proper Judgment of reversal. He submits that while the learned Judge of the trial Court has judiciously dealt with all the issues of the case, the learned Judge of the appellate Court in a slipshod manner reversed the decision of the trial Court by simply trying to find out the loopholes of the OPWs. 

6. Per contra, Mr Mrinal Kanti Biswas, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor-opposite parties, by taking me through the depositions of the PWs and DWs submits that the date of knowledge as to transfer of the case-land has sufficiently been proved by the PWs inasmuch as it has been admitted by the DWs that the case-land was under water for more than 12 years and the pre-emptor came to know about the transfer lately on 17-3-1995 only when the pre-emptee had been in the case land and disclosed to the pre-emptor about the fact of purchasing the case-land. Mr Biswas next submits that there is no contradiction in the depositions of PWs as to the date of knowledge of transfer of the case-land, rather the deposition of PW 1 is corroborated by that of the other PWs inasmuch as when the pre-emptee had been in the case-land to measure the same, the pre-emptor had asked the pre-emptee about the reason of his presence in the case-land and, that is how, the depositions of each of the PWs have been substantiated. With regard to the arguments placed by the learned Advocate for the petitioner as to the mutation-document, which has been marked as Exhibit-2, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor Mr Biswas argues that though the Exhibit-2 contains the Mutation Case Number as 10/1992-93, but there is no date of passing any Order by any officer on this Mutation Case. In elaborating his above count of submissions, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor submits that the pre-emptor obtained this copy only on 14-1-1998, which is long after the filing of this pre-emption case, and, further, the said copy was submitted by the pre-emptor in the Court to show his standing as a co-sharer in the Khatian. 

7. Mr Biswas, in an endeavour to put forward the practical scenario of Bangladesh, contends that the Sub-Registry Office and the Revenue Office of this country usually do not bother to serve notices under section 89 of the SAT Act. He therefore prays for sending the case back on remand in order to enable the pre-emptor to prove the fact that he never received the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act from the Revenue Office. With regard to the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the purchaser that the pre-emptor was aware of the selling of this property long ago as he had knowledge about the seller's migration to' India from this country, Mr Biswas submits that the PW 1 never made any deposition to the effect that Fotik (the seller) had migrated to India permanently. In an endeavour to explain the pre-emptor's deposition on the aforesaid issue, he submits that pre-emptor is the son of the original pre-emptor who simply stated that the seller had visited India with Nagendranath. In corroboration of his submissions, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor refers to the case of Abdul Sattar vs Osimuddin, 42 DLR 24 and submits that mere obtaining information about transfer of any immoveable property does not trigger counting of limitation period. He submits that the limitation period starts only after having definite information of sale of property to a stranger, by obtaining certified copy of the registered deed of sale of the co-sharer's land. 

8. After hearing the learned Advocates for both the sides, perusing the revisional application and counter affidavits together with their annexures, examining the Lower Court Record (LCR) and reading the relevant statutory laws and case-laws, it appears to this Court that the first issue to be adjudicated upon by this Court is—whether the pre-emptor-opposite parties had filed the case within the statutory period as prescribed in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (shortly, SAT Act); i.e. the first issue is about limitation and the second issue is whether a litigant/party (here in this case, the pre-emptor) may seek any remedy from this Court as to the bonafide mistake of his lawyer at the trial Court or if the mistake is committed by the learned Judge of the trial Court and appellate Court. 

9. Given that the case was filed invoking section 96 of the SAT Act (under the provisions of the old law i.e. before the amendment of the said section on 20-9-2006), quotation of the same would assist the Court in effectively adjudicating upon this revisional application. The old version of section 96 of the SAT Act consisted of as many as 12 (twelve) sub-sections with a few Provisos and the amended version is enacted with as many as 18 (eighteen) sub-sections with 2(two) Provisos. Therefore, for the sake of brevity, quotation of the same is being avoided. Instead, I read the entire provisions of both the old and amended versions of section 96 of the SAT Act. From an inquisitive reading of both the versions concurrently, it appears to me that in a case under section 96 of the SAT Act, there may be many issues, such as; (i) whether the case-land is sold to the pre-emptee or the pre-emptee (transferee) has got the case-land as gift or by exchange or by partition or through usufructuary mortgage or vide waqf or as the dedication for religious/charitable purpose, (ii) whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer/contiguous land-owner (by the new law, the categories of the co-sharer by purchase and the contiguous land-owner have been omitted/dropped/discontinued; only the co-sharers by inheritance are currently entitled to claim pre-emption), (iii) whether the case has been filed within the prescribed time (previously the time was four months and presently the time is two months from the date of serving notice under section 89 of the SAT Act), (iv) if it is proved that no notice was served under section 89 of the SAT Act, then, whether the pre-emptor approached the Court within four months (presently two months) from the date of knowledge of transfer (previously, pre-emptor was allowed to file pre-emption case after lapse of even infinite time if the reason for the delay was plausible; but currently no pre-emption case shall be allowed after three years from the date of registration of the sale deed), (v) whether the pre-emptor shall encounter the impediment i.e. incompetent under section 90 of the SAT Act to purchase the case-land, (vi) whether the pre-emptor has deposited the appropriate amount of money in the Court, (vii) whether all the co-shares have been impleaded as the parties of the case, (viii) whether the pre-emptor has deposited the appropriate amount of money in the Court and (ix) whether the sold-land (case-land) is a homestead (newly inserted in the amended law that no pre-emption case shall be filed for the sold homestead). 

10. Since in this case, the core issue is about the statutory time-limit of filing the case, I find it useful to quote the relevant part of section 96, namely, sub-section (1) of section 96 of the SAT Act. Section 96(1) of the SAT Act (as it was before the amendment of this law by Act No. xxxiv of 2006) runs as follows; 
96. Right of pre-emption—(1) If a portion or share of a holding of a raiyat transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding may, within four months of the service of the notice given under section  82, or, if no notice has been served under section 89, within four months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves; and if a holding or a portion or a share of a holding is transferred, the tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred may, within 4 months of the date of the knowledge of such transfer, apply to the Court for the holding or portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves. 

11. It would not be difficult for any reader to have an understanding that there are two time-schedules for filing pre-emption cases, covering two different situations; the first time-schedule for filing a pre-emption case is 4 (four) months from the date of serving the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act. So, the first situation arises when the notice is served upon the pre-emptor under section 89 of the SAT Act. Given the employment of the words, “….four months of the service of notice given under section 89', there is no scope for anyone to read or interpret or assume that 'four months from the date of receipt of the notice' is the limitation of time for filing a pre-emption case. And the second situation is—when the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act has not been received by the premptor, but the pre-emptor has come to know about the transfer of property by some other means and, in that scenario, the time schedule for filing a pre-emption case is 4 (four) months from the date of knowledge about transfer of the land. So, clearly the clock of limitation of time starts immediately after 'serving notice' under section 89 of the SAT Act. To this end, I find it pertinent to look at the provisions of section 89 of the SAT Act, which is quoted below;

89. Manner of Transfer—(1) Every such transfer shall be made by registered instrument, except in the case of a bequest or a sale in execution of a decree or of a certificate signed under the Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913, and a Registering Officer shall not accept for  registration any such instrument unless the sale price, or where there is no sale price, the value of the holding or portion or share thereof transferred is stated therein and unless it is accompanied by—
(a) a notice giving the particulars of the transfer in the prescribed form together with the process fee prescribed for the transmission thereof to the Revenue-officer; and 
(b) such notices and process fees as may be required by sub-section (4). 
(2) ………………..(not relevant) 
(3) ……………… (not relevant) 
(4) If the transfer of a portion or share of such a holding be one to which the provisions of section 96 apply there shall be filed notices giving particulars of the transfer in the prescribed form together with process fees prescribed for the service thereof on all the co-sharer tenants of the  said holding who are not parties to the  transfer and for affixing a copy thereof in the office of the Registering Officer or the Court house or the Office of the Revenue Authority, as the case may be. 
(5) The Court, Revenue Authority or Registering Officer, as the case may be, shall transmit the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (1) to the Revenue-officer and shall serve the notice on the co-sharer tenants referred to in sub-section (4) by registered post and shall cause a copy of the notice to be affixed in the Court house or in the Office of the Revenue Authority or of the Registering Officer, as the case may be: 

12. From a plain reading of the provisions of section 89 of the SAT Act, it is vividly clear that no sale of a property, in which existence of co-sharers would be apparent from the records, can be completed without serving notice upon the co-sharers inasmuch as the law forbids the Registering Officer to register a sale-deed without obtaining the notice together with the process-fees from the seller and, thereafter, the Registering Officer is duty bound to transmit the notice to the Revenue Officer who shall, then, serve the said notice by registered post. And, in the light of use of the word 'shall' by the Legislature in each of the steps mentioned in section 89 of the SAT Act, the legal presumption is that all the State/Government functionaries have performed their duties assigned under section 89 of the SAT Act. If any pre-emptor claims that s/he was never served with the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act, then, in turn, the pre-emptee shall have to prove its service. However, for an effective adjudication of a pre-emption case, the pre-emptor may either apply to the trial Court for production of the 'dispatch book/register' of the Registering Office and that of the Revenue Office of the relevant dates or may apply to the Court for examining the process-server of the Revenue Office to prove contrary to the legal presumption. If the office/person responsible for serving notice under section 89 of the SAT Act proves before the Court the fact of serving the said notice upon the pre-emptor, then, it would be for the notice receiver, being a pre-emptor in a pre-emption case, to rebut before the trial Court by any other ocular evidence with corroboration that he has never received the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act. 

13. And, when the Court shall be satisfied that actually no notice under section 89 of the SAT Act was ever served upon the co-sharers, that would be the second situation under section 96 of the SAT Act and, only in that scenario, the question of application of the second time-schedule under section 96 of the SAT Act comes into play. Because, given the employment of the expression by the Legislature 'if no notice has been served under section 89', it is mandatory for the pre-emptor to satisfy the Court by adducing ocular evidence that the pre-emptor has never received the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act, against the legal presumption of due accomplishment/performance by the Government officials; without first proving as above, section 96 of the SAT Act does not directly/ automatically entitle a pre-emptor to avail the second limitation of time i.e. 'within four months (currently two months) from the date of knowledge of transfer'. 

14. In this case, since the sale-deed has been registered by the Registering Officer i.e. Sub-Register of the concerned jurisdiction, it shall be presumed by the Court that the Sub-Register has registered the sale-deed only after being furnished with the notice containing the particulars (name and address) of the pre-emptor together with process fees for sending the same to the pre-emptor's address by registered post through the Revenue Officer and, further, it shall be the presumption of the Court that the concerned Revenue Officer has also served the notice upon the pre-emptor duly, for, the PW 1 himself has proved the document of mutation as Exhibit-1. Had it been the pre-emptor's case that he never received any notice from the Revenue Officer, it was incumbent upon the pre-emptor to apply for the production of the 'dispatch register' of the Revenue Officer as well as that of the Sub-Register. Since, evidently the pre-emptor neither applied to the Court for production of the dispatch registers of the sub-Registry Office and Revenue Office, nor did examine any relevant witness/es to nullify the legal presumption; further, since from the evidence (Exhibit 1) produced by the PW 1 himself that after completion of transfer of the case-land, the mutation took place in the year 1993, this Court finds that notice was duly served by the Revenue Office and, accordingly, this Court has no option other than to hold that the pre-emptor did not approach the Court in filing the pre-emption case within 4 (four) months from the date of service of notice under section 89 of the SAT Act. 

15. Now, let me take up the second issue, namely, whether this case is worthy of sending back to the trial Court for giving an opportunity to the pre-emptor to call for the 'dispatch registry' of the Revenue Office and Sub-Registry Office and/or examine the process-server as a witness.

16. It was the submission of the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor that while it was the duty of the learned Advocate of the pre-emptor at trial Court to apply for production of 'dispatch book/register' of the Revenue Office, the learned Presiding Judge of the trial Court can not also shrug off his duty to call for the said document on his own towards ensuring fair disposal of the case, in that it is a fact directly linked with the statutory provision; and it was his argument that enjoyment of a right of a citizen engraved in a statute can not be deprived, simply because of the mistake committed by the lawyer dealing with the case or because of the ignorance of the learned trial Judge as to the status of a law endowing a specific right on a litigant party. 

17. The above ground of the lawyer's mistake apparently sounds logical inasmuch as it is a pertinent issue for consideration of this Court that when a litigant, being not conversant with the legal provisions, engages a lawyer and if because of the latter's incompetency or negligence, the litigant loses a legal right, whether this Court should interfere with the impugned Judgment. Since it was the professional duty of the learned Advocates for the pre-emptor at the trial Court and at the appellate Court to apply for production of the 'dispatch book' of the Sub-Registry Office as well as that of the Revenue Office, and because of not performing their professional duty diligently, the pre-emptor has been deprived of contesting and establishing a legal right, this Court is of the view that the pre-emptor shall be at liberty to claim damage/compensation from the learned Advocates whom he had engaged at the trial Court and the appellate Court. 

18. Also, as per the ratio laid down in the case of Akram Ali vs Khasru Miah 73 DLR 82, the learned Judges of the trial Court and the appellate Court ought to have considered the said issue as one of the vital issues inasmuch as when a statute sets out a legal condition for adjudication of a suit/case, the Court is duty bound to deal with the said law-point, even if the said legal issue is not raised or pointed out by the parties of the suit/case. The learned Judges of the trial Courts should bear in their minds that they are duty bound to frame issues of a suit/case, not only on the basis of the pleadings (i.e. plaint, written statements, application and written objections), but also with reference to the list of the documents submitted before them with the pleadings of the parties and, also, on the basis of the laws involved in the particular suit/case. And, further, they are competent to recast the issues even after taking deposition of the witness with the Exhibits, if submitted, subject to allowing the parties of the suit/case to make out their respective cases on the issues recast by the Court by producing their new or corroborative evidence. After completion of deposition and cross-examinations of all the PWs and DWs, the learned Judges of the trial Courts are empowered to call for any documentary and/or oral evidence, if they consider it to be vital for fair and effective adjudication of a suit/case, as laid down in the afore-cited case of Akram Ali vs Khasru Miah, 73 DLR 82 (relevant para-75). 

19. Given that apparently the learned Judge of the trial Court has not framed the issue on serving notice under section 89 of the SAT Ad, my primary view is in favour of sending this case back to the trial Court for framing an issue as to whether the pre-emptor was served with the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act. However, in the light of the production of the document as to the mutation of the case-land by the plaintiff himself as Exhibit-1, my ultimate final view is that the pre-emptor, in fact, was issued with the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act and, that is why, his lawyers have not hammered on the said issue in the lower Courts. 

20. It follows that since the pre-emptor did not file the pre-emption case within four months of being served with the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act, the pre-emption case is destined to be dismissed. Even, for the sake of argument, if this Court remands the case and the pre-emptor succeeds in establishing the above-discussed legal point at the trial Court that he was never issued with the notice under section 89 of the SAT Act, in that scenario, his case would depend upon proving that he has filed the pre-emption case 'within four months of the date of knowledge of transfer'. Given that the aforesaid factual issue has already been adjudicated upon by the trial Court upon finding that the pre-emptor had the knowledge of the transfer in question, this Court is also in agreement with the trial Court's above-mentioned findings, particularly in view of clear admission by the PW 1 that he was aware of the sellers' migration to India immediately after the sale of the case-land; a very vital material evidence which the appellate Court failed to appreciate and assess.

21. Thus, I find merit in the Rule. However, before parting with this Judgment, it appears to me to be pertinent and useful and, in fact, I find it to be the Constitutional as well as statutory duty of this Court, to lay down some guidelines for the learned Judges of the sub-ordinate judiciary for dealing with the pre-emption cases under section 96 of the SAT Act and, also, the necessary directions for the relevant State-functionaries: 
(1) In all the pre-emption cases under section 96 of the SAT Act, if the pre-emptor denies the fact of receiving notice under section 89 of the SAT Act, the learned Judges of the trial Court must frame an issue as to whether or not notice under section 89 of the SAT Act was served upon the pre-emptor by the concerned Registering Officer and the Revenue Officer. 
(2) The Registrar of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh is directed to circulate this Judgment to all the learned District Judges of the country with a direction upon them to arrange an in-house meeting/workshop for 2(two) hours in order to apprise and enlighten all the learned Judges about the guide-lines set out hereinbefore in this Judgment. 
(3) The Secretary, Ministry of Land is directed to prepare a Form/format of the Notice under sub-sections (4) & (5) of section 89 of the SAT Act to be used by the Revenue Officers of Bangladesh as compliance with the above-mentioned provisions of section 89 of the SAT Act. He is further directed to disseminate the said notice to all the Upazillas of the country with an Office Order that the Revenue Officers must serve notice under section 89 of the SAT Act immediately after being informed about the transfer of a land by the Registering Officers, failure of which negative remarks shall be recorded in their respective service books. 
(4) The Inspector-General of Registration under the Ministry of Law is directed to circulate a gazetted notice to all the Registering Officers of the country directing that they must comply with the provisions of Sub-sections (4) & (5) of section 89 of the SAT Act without fail with a consequential order that in case of failure to serve notice under the provision of section 89, they shall face disciplinary action for gross negligence in performing their duties. 
(5) The Secretary, Ministry of Land, the Registrar of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and the Inspector General of Registration are directed to file affidavits of compliance on or before 5-5-2021. 

22. In the result, the Judgment and Order dated 28-5-2001 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Khulna is set-aside and the Judgment and Order dated 9-2-1999 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Fultala, Khulna is restored and upheld. However, there shall not be any Order as to costs. 

Let the matter be posted in the list on 5-5-2021 to ensure the compliance by the Registrar of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, the Inspector-General of Registration and the Secretary, Ministry of Land. 

End.

lawyer:
Monindra Biswas ----- Plaintiffs-Respondents-Petitioners
vs
Khalilur Rahman Chowdhury ----- Defendant-Appellant-Opposite Party
parties:
Md Zakir Hossain with Abdul Jalil, Advocates — For the Petitioners. 

AKM Badrudduza, Advocate — For the Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
This Rule has been issued calling upon the Opposite Party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 22-6-2008 (decree signed on 29-6-2008), passed by the Additional District Judge, Gazipur, in Title Appeal No.141 of 2006, allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 26-2-2006 (decree signed on 3-5-2006), passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Gazipur in Title Suit No.85 of 2005, should not be set-aside and/or pass such other order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts, relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that Sree Monindra Chandra Biswas and two others had filed Title Suit No.66 of 2003 before the Court of 1st Assistant Judge, Gazipur, against Khalilur Rahman Chowdhury (the principal-defendant) and another i.e. the Sub-Registrar, Gazipur Sadar, Gazipur, being the pro-forma defendant, which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No.85 of 2005. The said suit was filed for rectification of a deed No.2347, dated 15-2-1999 (Exhibit-1), which the plaintiff has executed in favour of the defendant No.1. In that suit, the plaintiff has prayed that, the deed should be rectified/ amended by deleting PS Plot No.1406, as described in schedule "Kha" to the plaint, on the allegation that, the said deed was executed to convey and transfer title in PS Plot No.1410, as described in schedule "Ka" to the plaint, and that, possession of the said PS Plot No.1410 was handed over to the defendant. Subsequently, the defendant claimed that, he had purchased 0.1750 acres of land from PS Plot No.1406. Thereafter, the plaintiff made a search in the office of the Sub-Registrar, Gazipur on 17-12-2002 and obtained the certified copy of the said deed No.2347, dated 15-2-1999 (Exhibit-1) and found that, in the schedule of the said deed, PS Plot Nos.1406 and 1410 have also been written in the schedule to the deed. The further case of the plaintiff is that, PS Plot No.1406 has been inserted fraudulently by the plaintiff in-connivance with the witnesses to the deed and the deed writer. Therefore, the plaintiffs had filed this suit for rectification of the said deed by deleting PS Plot No.1406 from the schedule to the said deed. 

3. The defendant has appeared in the suit by filing written statement, on 15-6-2003, wherein he has claimed that, he has purchased 0.1750 acres of land from PS Plot No. 1406, as was proposed by the plaintiff to be sold to the defendant and he has been given possession of 0.1750 acres of land in that plot. His specific case has been stated in paragraph No. 9 of the written statement. 

4. The plaintiff's side adduced 4 witnesses and proved certain documents, marked as exhibits 1-8 respectively, while the defendant adduced 3 witnesses and proved certain documents, marked as exhibits `Ka' and 'Kha'. 

5. The trial Court, after hearing the parties and having assessed the oral and the documentary evidences, had decreed the suit; vide its judgment and decree dated 26-2-2006 (decree signed on 5-3-2006). 

6. Against the said judgment and decree of the Trial Court, the Defendant preferred Title Appeal No.141 of 2006 before the District Judge, Gazipur, which was heard by the Court of Additional District Judge, Gazipur, who, being the Appellate Court, has passed the impugned judgment and decree, allowing the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court, vide its judgment and decree dated 22-6-2008 (decree signed on 29-6-2008) and remanded the suit to the Trial Court with a direction to dispose of the Title Suit No.85 of 2005 and Title Suit No.419 of 2008(filed by the defendant-appellant) analogously. 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, the Plaintiffs-Respondents-Petitioners have filed this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and obtained the present Rule.

8. Learned Advocates Mr Md Zakir Hossain and Mr Abdul Jalil appeared for the petitioners. Mr Md Zakir Hossain, having placed the petition submits that 0.1750 acres of land was sold to the defendants out of PS Plot No. 1410; vide deed No.2347 dated 15-2-1999 (Exhibit-1). He next submits that the appellate court has allowed the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court without at all reversing any finding arrived at by the trial court. He proceeds on that, the plaintiffs have sold 0.1750 acres of land from PS Plot No.1410 and, accordingly, the plaintiffs have handed over the possession of the said land of PS Plot No.1410. The learned Advocate continues that, thereafter the defendant has opened a khatian in his name (Exhibit-3) in respect of PS Plot No.1410, not in respect of RS Plot No.1406. He proceeds on that, the oral evidence as well as the documentary evidence clearly proved the case of the plaintiffs and the trial court, upon framing proper issues, had arrived at correct findings, after assessing all the evidences, and had decreed the suit, but the appellate court, without reversing any finding of the trial court, has most arbitrarily allowed the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and then remanded the Title Suit No.85 of 2005 for analogous hearing of Title Suit No.419 of 208 filed "by the defendant against the plaintiffs about 2(two) years after the disposal of the Title Suit No.85 of 2005. He also submits that, the order for remand was made on the basis of an application filed by the defendant-appellant for analogous hearing of both the Title Suit Nos. 85 of 2005 and 419 of 2008, i.e. not on merit. The learned Advocate next submits that the appellate court has committed error of law in passing the judgment and decree which has resulted in error in the decision, causing serious prejudice to the petitioners. The learned Advocate has referred to a decision reported in 7 BLT (AD) 145 = 4 BLC (AD) 72, between Indrajit Kundu and others vs S Ali, in support of his contention. He lastly submits that, this Rule has merit and the impugned judgment and decree of the appellate court are liable to be set-aside. 

9. Learned Advocate Mr AKM Badrudduza appeared for the defendant-appellant-opposite party. He, at the very outset, points out that there is only one schedule in the disputed deed No.2347 dated 15-2-1999 (Exhibit Kha = Exhibit-1 of the defendant). But in the plaint, the plaintiffs have given two different schedules. He next submits that, in the schedule to the disputed deed, both the PS Plots No.1406 and No. 1410 have been specifically mentioned, out of which 0.1750 acres of land was sold to the defendant and possession has been given in 0.1750 acres of land of PS Plot No.1406, since that was intended to be purchased by the defendant-buyer and was sold to him and that, the defendant is in peaceful and continuous possession of the purchased land by erecting boundary wall and other demarcation. He next submits that, in the report of the Advocate Commissioner, both the PS Plot Nos.1406 and 1410 have been marked with green colour as the disputed land, while the Advocate Commissioner has also marked PS Plot No. 1413 in green colour as the disputed property, which is not in the schedule to the disputed deed. He next submits that, the Advocate Commissioner's report is not correct, rather it is misleading, and reliance on the said report by the trial court was not proper. He proceeds on that, the defendant is the bonafide purchaser for value and, in fact, the plaintiffs have no title in PS Plot No. 1410, which was acquired by the Government and the plaintiffs has handed over possession of 0.1740 acres of land from PS Plot No. 1406 and the defendant-purchaser is still possessing the same. He further submits that, there is no consistency between the prayer portion of the plaint and the schedule of the plaint and that, there is no evidence on record to prove any case of fraud as alleged. He next submits that, exhibit-3, which is claimed to be mutation khatian of the defendant, is an unsigned document and the same was not admissible in evidence. Hence, the trial court should not have marked the said khatian as exhibit No. 3 and the trial court should not have relied upon exhibit-3 to arrive at the finding in passing the judgment and decree in favour of the plaintiff. As regards the judgment of the appellate court, the learned Advocate submits that, the defendant filed Title Suit No. 419 of 2008 for rectification of the sale deed No.2347 dated 15-2-1999 (Exhibit Kha = Exhibit-1) by deleting PS Plot No. 1410 from the said deed, therefore, in order to avoid a conflicting judgments and having found that the judgment of the trial court was not proper, the appellate court has rightly set-aside the judgment of the trial court and that tantamounts to reversal of the findings of the trial court and, therefore, had sent the suit on remand for fresh trial of Title Suit No. 85 of 2005 along with Title Suit No. 419 of 2008, so that the case and evidences of both the parties can be considered together and a proper judgment can be passed. He also submits that, the appellate court is competent to send the Title Suit 85 of 2005 on remand and in passing the judgment and decree of the trial court; the appellate court has committed no error of law causing any prejudice to the parties. He, therefore, submits that, this Rule has no merit and the same may kindly be discharged. 

10. I have heard the learned Advocates for both sides, perused the petition and judgment of both the courts below and also other materials on record. 

11. It is not disputed by either of the parties that, the plaintiffs have executed the deed No. No.2347 dated 15-2-1999 (Exhibit-Kha of the defendant = Exhibit 1 of the plaintiffs), whereby the plaintiffs have transferred 0.1750 acres of land. Admittedly, the only dispute between the parties is that, the plaintiffs are claiming that 0.1750 acres of land was sold from PS Plot No. 1410, not from PS Plot No. 1406. The plaintiff's further case is that, the defendant had inserted PS Plot No. 1406 in connivance with the deed writer and with the witnesses of the deed and that they have come to know about the above insertion of PS Plot No.1406 after obtaining certified copy of the No.2347 dated 15-2-1999 (Exhibit-Kha = 1) on 17-12-2002 and, thereafter, they have filed Title Suit No. 66 of 2003, subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No.85 of 2005. On the contrary, the defendant's case is that, he intended to buy 0.1750 acres of land which he has been possessing since the date of sale and that is lying under PS Plot No. 1406 and that he has been possessing the purchased property within specific demarcated boundary. 

12. I have examined the deed No.2347 dated 15-2-1999 (Exhibit-Kha = Exhibirt-1). I find that there is only one schedule in the said deed and that 0.1750 acres of land was sold from PS plot No. 1410 and PS Plot No. 1406. I also find that the plaintiffs did not deny that the said deed has been executed out of free will and it is duly attested, as per law. I also find that, it has been written, at the end of the said deed that, 
“এতদ্বার্থে স্বেচ্ছায় স্বজ্ঞানে সুস্থশরীরে অন্যের বিনা প্ররোচনায় অত্র সাফ কবলা দলিল লিখাইয়া টাইপ করাইয়া পড়িয়া ও পড়াইয়া এবং ইহার মর্ম অবগত অত্র সাফ কবলা দলিল আমরা সহি সম্পাদন করিয়া দিলাম ।”Hence, the genuineness of the said deed is apparent and the plaintiff's evidence, if any, to prove that the Plot No. 1406 was subsequently inserted, by fraud or connivance, should be inadmissible and be excluded, as per provisions of section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872. 

13. The court below must note that, the only dispute in this case is in which of these 2(two) PS Plots, namely, PS Plot No. 1406 and PS Plot No. 1410, this 0.1750 acres of land was intended to be sold. 

14. However, the appellate court has duty to decide the case on merit, as required by rule 24 of Order 41, of the Code of Civil Procedure, if it finds that the evidence produced before it are sufficient to enable it to pronounce the judgment, otherwise the appellate court can remand the case either under rule 23 or as per provisions laid down in rule 25 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

15. In the instant case the appellate court has remanded the case on the basis of an application for analogous hearing of a disposed of suit No. 85 of 2005 (which was pending as an appeal) for analogous hearing with Title Suit No. 419 of 2008, pending before the court of Assistant Judge, having stated as reason that, unless these 2(two) matters are heard analogously then there is likelihood of conflict of judgment. 

16. In my considered opinion, the appellate court has ample power to send the case on remand, either under rule 23 or rule 25 or Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But, in the instant case the impugned judgment and decree has not been passed as per rule 23 or rule 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On the other hand the appellate court cannot set-aside the judgment of the trial court without reversing the findings of the trial court, which require the appellate court judgment and order on merit. 

17. Hence, I am constrained to hold that, the appellate court has failed to exercise its power as per provisions of rule 24 or, in the case of remand, as per provisions laid down in rule 23 or 25 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

18. The judgment of the appellate court has not been passed either on merit or on preliminary issue. 

19. As such, and in view of the above, I hold that, the appellate court has committed error of law in passing the impugned judgment, resulted in error in its decision and that has caused prejudice to the plaintiffs-respondents. 

20. I have also perused the judgment reported in 7 BLT (AD) 145 = 4 BLC (AD) 72 between Indrajit Kundu and others vs S Ali. In that case, both the courts below have decided the case on merit on the basis of evidence on record and it was held by the Appellate Division that, the High Court Division was not justified in law in sending back the case on remand to the trial court, in that situation, for holding trial afresh. The judgment of the Appellate Division is binding on the High Court Division and it has laid down a clear law, but this judgment is not applicable in this matter, because in the instant case, the appellate court has not decided the appeal on merit. Rather, it has disposed of the appeal on the basis of an application filed by the defendant-appellant for analogous hearing of Title Suit Nos. 85 of 2005 and 419 of 2008. As such, in this case before me, the appellate court has not arrived at its own findings, as the last court of fact. 

21. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order should be set-aside and the appellate court should be directed to re-hear the appeal afresh and to pronounce a proper judgment or order upon hearing the parties, as per provisions of law as stated above. Hence, I am not inclined to make any comment about the merit of the case, except that, the evidence, if any, adduced by the plaintiffs to rebut the contents of Exhibit 1 = Exhibit Kha as well as the evidence adduced to prove that the PS Plot No. 1406 has been subsequently inserted in Exhibit 1 = Exhibit Kha, should be inadmissible and be excluded as per provisions of section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872. Here, it has to be noted that, the defendant-buyer is entitled to get possession of 0.1750 acres of land, from either or both of these two PS Plots No. 1406 and 1410, as per the admitted sale deed (Exhibit 1 = Exhibit 'Kha') therefore, the main point for determination, in this case, is to ascertain from which, out of these two plots, 0.1750 acres of lands was intended to be sold. 

22. Besides, the court below shall keep in mind that, this is a suit for rectification of a deed, as per provisions of section 31 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, not a suit for declaration of title under section 42 of the said Act. The distinction is clear as the issues involved are distinct too. 

23. The appellate court shall, in deciding this appeal, frame amongst other, the following points (issues) for determination, namely, (I) In which out of these 3(three) Plots namely, PS Plot No. 1406 and PS Plot No. 1410, the defendant has been given possession of 0.1750 acres of land. (II) Whether the defendant-appellant-purchaser is in peaceful and uninterrupted possession of 0.1750 acres of land in PS Plot No. 1406 and (III) Which, out of these two PS Plots, 0.1750 acres of land was intended to be sold to the purchaser and then shall pronounce the judgment accordingly, if it considers that the evidence is adequate for deciding the case, otherwise it may remand the case as per rule 23 or rule 25 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or may, in an appropriate case, take additional evidence as per law.

24. In view of the above, the impugned judgment and decree dated 22-6-2008 (decree signed on 29-6-2018) in Title Appeal No. 141 of 2006, passed by the Court of Additional District Judge, Gazipur, is hereby set-aside and the case is remanded back to the appellate court for hearing afresh, in the light of the observations made above. 

25. The Rule is disposed of accordingly. 

26. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated. 

27. Parties will bear their respective costs. Let a copy of this judgment along with LCR be sent to the concerned Courts at once. 

End.

অমিত তালুকদার, ডেপুটি অ্যাটর্নি জেনারেল সঙ্গে মোঃ সারওয়ার হোসেন বাপ্পী, ডেপুটি অ্যাটর্নি জেনারেল মোহাম্মদ আক্তার হোসেন, সহকারী অ্যাটর্নি জেনারেল মওদুদা বেগম, সহকারী অ্যাটর্নি জেনারেল হাসিনা মমতাজ, সহকারী অ্যাটর্নি জেনারেল -প্রতিপক্ষ নং-২ এর পক্ষে ।

মোশফিক উদ্দিন বখতিয়ার, এডভোকেট - প্রতিপক্ষ নং-৩ এর পক্ষে ।

মনোজ কুমার ভৌমিক, এ্যাডভোকেট ---- সংবাদদাতা
