Leave was granted in the leave petition giving rise to this appeal only to decide the propriety of the finding of the High Court Division on the question of non-service of notice upon the appellant under section 5(1) (b) of the Ordinance, as he claimed to be the lawful owner of the property in question and in possession thereof.

107. Therefore, I do not require going into the detail of the case of the appellant. And I consider it profitable to decide the question together along with the first submission on which leave was granted in the leave petition giving rise to CA No. 10 of 2003.

108. Discussions and findings on the submissions of the legal consequences of enlisting the property in question in the `Kha' list without serving notice upon the appellants under section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance for surrendering or taking possession of the property in question:

The learned Counsel appearing in the two appeals very strenuously argued that the notice as required under section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance was not served upon the occupants of the property in question asking them for surrendering or taking over possession thereof. The enlistment of the property in question in the `Kha' list was illegal and without lawful authority; the Court of Settlement ought to have excluded the property in question from the list of abandoned buildings on the said ground alone. Both the learned Counsel submitted that prior notice on or before 31 October, 1988 was a precondition of enlistment of a building in the list of abandoned buildings to give jurisdiction to the Court of Settlement. Mr. Farooqui specially submitted that a statutory notice is a `jurisdictional fact' or a 'collateral fact'. Where no such notice is issued, the Government shall take over possession of "the left-over abandoned building" in execution of a decree or order passed by a Court in a suit filed by the Government under section 4(b)(ii) of the Ordinance after the aforesaid date. This shows that a statutory notice is mandatory before a building is enlisted to give jurisdiction to the Court of Settlement and if no notice was issued, the civil Courts will have exclusive jurisdiction over the 'left-over property' under section 4(b)(ii) of the Ordinance. According to Mr. Farooqui, the Court of Settlement is a Court of stinted or limited jurisdiction, the statutory notice under article 7 of PO 16 of 1972 read with rule 3(1)(8) of the Rules, 1972 is a mandatory requirement of section 4 of the Ordinance within the statutory period expiring on the 31st day of October, 1988. After issuance of such notices, a list would be published under section 5(b) of the Ordinance. This is a list known as `Kha' or 'EV list. Such list alone gives jurisdiction to the Court of Settlement. In absence of the statutory notice which is a `jurisdictional fact' or a 'collateral fact', the Court of Settlement, an inferior tribunal, could not assume jurisdiction and enter into the merit of the case. As in the instant case, notice under section 5(1) (b) of the Ordinance was not issued; the Court of Settlement acted without jurisdiction in assuming jurisdiction under section 10 of the Ordinance and entering into the merit of the cases filed before it.

109. Both the learned Counsel have argued that PO 16 of 1972 has provided the procedure to take possession of the property 'in such manner as may be prescribed.' A statutory notice is to be served for the purpose in term of article 7 of the said PO read with Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking Over Possession) Rules, 1972 (shortly, the Rules, 1972). The Rules, 1972 provides the manner of taking over possession of an abandoned property under article 7 of PO 16 of 1972. A prescribed notice under rule 3(1) in Form No. 1 is to be served upon the person in possession of the property. As per rule 3(8) of the Rules, 1972, the notice shall be served on the person if possession or on any adult male member of his family or, where none of them is available or the' y refuse to receive the notice, by affixing a copy o f the notice to a conspicuous part of the residence o f such person and also, where the abandoned (property consists of any immovable property on a conspicuous part of such immovable property it the presence of two witnesses, but admitted!) neither the possession of the property in question was taken over by the Government nor any notice under section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance was serves upon the occupant for surrendering or taking over possession thereof. But the Court of Settlement as well as the High Court Division failed to consider the provisions of PO 16 of 1972 and the Ordinance with reference to the materials places 1 before them and thus erred in law in taking a wrong decision as to the prayer for exclusion of the property in question from the list of abandoned buildings in rejecting the cases and as such, the impugned judgment and order cannot be sustained.

110. Mr. Farooqui to strengthen his argument referred pp 286-287 of the celebrated treatise `Administrative Law' (seventh edition) by Wade and Forsyth which have said as follows:

"Certain mistakes of fact can carry an administrative authority or tribunal outside its jurisdiction although 'jurisdictional fact' has long been part of the currency of administrative law, English judges have previously preferred to speak of 'collateral questions'."

111. He has also referred to the classical statement from a case of 1853 in which Coleridge J said:

"Now it is a general rule, that no Court of limited jurisdiction can give itself jurisdiction by a wrong decision on a point collateral to the merits of the case upon which the limit to its jurisdiction depends, and however its decisions may be final on all particulars, making up together that subject-matter, which if true is within its jurisdiction, and, however necessary in many cases it may be (in order) to make a preliminary enquiry, whether some collateral matter be or be not within the limits, yet upon the preliminary question, its decision must always be open to inquiry in the superior Court."

112. Mr. Farooqui has also referred Justice CK Thakker c Administrative Law (1912) pages 1008-1011 to the effect—

"Lack of jurisdiction may also arise from absence of some preliminary facts, which must exist before a tribunal exercises its jurisdiction. They are known as 'jurisdictional' or `collateral' facts. The existence of these facts is a sine qua non or a condition precedent to the assumption of jurisdiction by an interior court or tribunal.  To put it simply, the fact the existence of which is necessary to the initiation of proceedings and without which the act of the court is a nullity can be said to be a "jurisdictional fact."

113. Mr. Farooqui has referred to Black's Law Dictionary where jurisdictional fact has been explained as: "jurisdictional fact" is a fact which must exist before a court can properly assume jurisdiction of a particular case. A jurisdictional fact is one, on existence or non-existence of which depends assumption or refusal to assume jurisdiction by a court, a tribunal or an authority.

114. On the question of jurisdiction, Mr. Farooqui in his written submission has also referred the case of Baldwin & Francis Ltd vs Patents Appeal Tribunal, reported in 1(1959) AC 663 at page 695 where Lord Denning has explained jurisdiction as follows:

"In some of those cases it has been said that the tribunal, in falling into an error of this particular kind, has exceeded its jurisdiction. No tribunal, it is said, has any jurisdiction to be influenced by extraneous considerations or to disregard vital matters. This is good sense and enables the court of Queen's Bench to receive evidence to prove the error. But an excess of jurisdiction in this sense is very different from want of jurisdiction altogether which is, of course, "determinable at the commencement, not at the conclusion of the inquiry" (see Reg. vs Bolton 36) Whereas an excess of jurisdiction is determinable in the course of or at the end of the inquiry. But allowing that a tribunal which falls into an error of this particular kind does exceed its jurisdiction, as I am prepared to do, never the-less I am quite clear that at the same time it falls into an error of law too: for the simple reason that it has "not determined according to law." That is, indeed, how Blackburn J. put it in Reg vs De Retzen. And the decision in the Northumberland case itself shows that, even though no evidence is given, nevertheless if such an error appears from the documents properly before the court, or by legitimate inference there from, then certiorari may be granted to quash the decision: and the certiorari can properly be said to be for error of law on the face of the proceedings. It may be excess of jurisdiction as well, but it is certainly error of law."

115. Mr. M. Amirul Islam has further argued that admittedly the Government for the purpose of putting the property in question under `Kha' list should have had documents, papers and information in order to come to a conclusion that the same was an abandoned property. Hence, there was formation of opinion as to the character of the property being abandoned property within the meaning of article 2(1) of PO 16 of 1972. Suppression and/or non-production and non-disclosure of them is sufficient ground for the Court to come to an obvious conclusion that the Government does not have any such documents, information and materials necessary for the formation of opinion that it is an abandoned property. He has further argued that the publication of the list under section 5 of the Ordinance is deemed as conclusive evidence, but non-disclosure of supporting materials on the basis of which conclusion is arrived is rebuttable and the burden is shifted on the Government to give supporting evidence for upholding the conclusion which is rebutted under the law; prior objective satisfaction on the basis of the facts leading to 'formation of opinion' before treating any property as abandoned property is a sine qua non. Section 4(b) and section 5(b) of the Ordinance re-enforces the principle of estoppel incorporating it in the law itself to be treated as statutory estoppel.

116. Mr. Islam has further argued that in the instant case, since no notice under section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance was served upon the owner of the property in question before the 31st day of March, 1986. The inclusion of the same as an abandoned property, besides being ultr vires to sections 4(b) and 5(b) of the Ordinance, is a malice in law and, in fact, thus becomes a dead letter and is beyond the scope of the Ordinance and thus violative of articles 31 and 42 of the Constitution.

117. On the question of legal consequences of the non-service of notice as contemplated under sections 4 and 5 of the Ordinance, both the learned Counsel have referred a number of cases of this Division in support of their contentions, a few of them are the Ministry of Works vs Helauddin Ahmed, 4 MLR (AD) 140, 141; Bangladesh vs Amela Khatoon, 53 DLR (AD) 55, 56; Government of Bangladesh vs Bibi Marium, 54 DLR (AD) 100, 101; Bangladesh vs Rehana Kamal, 56 DLR (AD) 1, 6; Abdur Rashid Mollah vs Bangladesh, 58 DLR (AD) 20, 22, 23 Bangladesh vs Md. Shahjahan, 2 ADC (2005) 411 413.

118. They have also cited some cases from the High Court Division. The cases are: Helal-uddin Ahmed vs Bangladesh, 2 BLC 427, and Jobon Nahar vs Bangladesh, 49 DLR 108.

119. Mr. Murad Reza, learned Additional Attorney General appearing for the Government-respondent has just supported the reasoning and the finding of the High Court Division on the point at issue.

120. Let me now examine the soundness of the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants as well as the learned Additional Attorney General.

121. From the decision of the Court of Settlement, it appears that it, in a very perfunctory manner, disposed of the objection of the petitioners, particularly, those of Case Nos. 586, 588, 589, 590, 591, 592, 593, 594 all of 1988 as to the non-service of notice upon them under section 5(1) (b) of the Ordinance for surrendering or taking over possession of the property in question before enlisting the same in the `Kha' list. The Court of Settlement argued that the argument as to the non-service of notice upon the petitioners "is not obviously acceptable because on perusal of the case petition", they found that the question of non-service of notice required under section 4(1) (b) of the Ordinance was not challenged in the case petition. In holding so, the Court of Settlement totally misread the statements made in the application inasmuch as in paragraph 2 of the application of the appellant in CA No. 77 of 2003, the fact of non-service of notice as contemplated in section 5(1) (b) of the Ordinance for surrendering or for taking over possession was clearly asserted. The said paragraph reads as follows:

"2.The property having never been subject to any notice by the Government or anybody on behalf of the Government for surrendering possession, as contemplated in section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance, 1985, listing of the said property thereunder is illegal and not sustainable. It is further submitted that in view of the provision contained in the proviso to section 5(1) of the Ordinance and the facts of pendency of suits as stated hereinabove, the building in question cannot be included in the list in question."

122. Besides the said objection taken by the petitioner of Case No.586 of 1988, Md.. Shahidul Haque (appellant No.1 in CA No.10 of 2003), one of the petitioners of Case No.649 of 1988, categorically stated in his examination-in-chief that he did not get any notice to surrender possession (in the deposition sheet, in Bangla, it has been recorded as: "দখল ছেড়ে দিবার কোন নোটিশ পাইনি). Abdus Sobhan also categorically stated that no notice as required under section 4 of the Ordinance was served upon him. The Court of Settlement totally failed to consider that when the statute, namely, the Ordinance puts an obligation upon the Government to undergo a process/ procedure in taking an action before enlisting of a property as an abandoned property, it was obligatory upon it to prove the said fact before the Court of Settlement which is a 'jurisdictional fact' or a 'collateral fact' to give it jurisdiction to enter into the merit of the case, i.e. to see whether the property so listed was an abandoned property and vested in the Government under PO 16 of 1972 and whether the same was liable to be excluded from the list of the abandoned buildings. The claimants who examined themselves before the Court of Settlement as witnesses having asserted that they were in possession of the property in question and that they did not get any notice for surrendering or taking over possession thereof and that the notice is surely referable to section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance and the point of such non-service having specifically been agitated before it, the Court of Settlement was obliged to decide the said fact first, or in other words, in fact, the question of non-service of notice under section 5( I )(b) of the Ordinance was the first question, the Court of Settlement ought to have decided, but it did not. Instead, it answered the question last after making the enquiry as to the ownership of the petitioners and thus acted illegally in rejecting the cases.

123. The other reason assigned by the Court of Settlement in discarding the objection as to the non-service of notice under section 5( I)(b) of the Ordinance is that section 5(2) of the Ordinance attaches a presumption of correctness of the list prepared under section 5(1) of the Ordinance completely ignoring the fact that the Government failed to produce any scrap of paper to show that it took over possession thereof and/or that notice for surrendering or taking over possession was ever served upon the occupants, namely, the appellants. In taking the said view, the Court of Settlement failed to consider that the property in question was outside the scope of mischief of section 5 of the Ordinance, in view of the fact that the Ordinance itself prohibits the taking over possession unless a statutory notice is issued before the 31st October, 1988. In the context, it may be stated that as discussed above, in PO 16 of 1972, procedure to take over possession of an abandoned property has been laid down. And according to article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 if a person in possession of an abandoned property failed to surrender possession thereof as he is required to do under clause (2) thereof, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Officer or the authorized officer shall serve a notice on him in the prescribed manner requiring him to surrender possession of the property within seven days of the service of notice to the person mentioned in the notice or show cause against such surrender within the said period and if he fails to do so, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate or the authorized officer shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed of taking over possession of an abandoned property and, in fact, such procedure has been detailed in rule 3 of the Rules, 1972. And rule 3(8) of the Rules, 1972 has mandated that notice has to be served on the person in possession or on any adult male member of his family or, where none of them is available or they refuse to receive the notice, by affixing a copy of the notice to a conspicuous part of the residence of such person and also, where the abandoned property consists of any immovable property on a conspicuous part of such immovable property in the presence of two witnesses. And admittedly, in the instant case, no notice under article 7 of PO 16 of 1972 read with rule 3 of the Rules, 1972 was served. The provisions for service of notice upon the occupant of an abandoned property as provided in article 7 of PO 16 of 1972 read with rule 3 of the Rules, 1972 has, in fact, been re-introduced and re-asserted in clause (b) of section 5(1) of the Ordinance as a precondition before enlistment of a building of which the Government is not in possession and that notice for surrendering or taking over possession as abandoned property under PO 16 of 1972 had been served.

124. The Court of Settlement also failed to consider that the presumption attached to section 5 of the Ordinance is not sacrosanct and is rebuttable and in considering the presumption attached to section 5 of the Ordinance, it totally failed to consider the materials placed before it, particularly, the decree passed in Title Suit No.31 of 1972, the deposition of Rafi Tehrani in this suit, the order of the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (South), Dhaka dropping the property of Purana Paltan of Rafi Tehrani from the list of abandoned buildings, the decree passed in Title Suit No.425 of 1978 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka, the mutation khatian in the name of Hosne Ara Begum and the rent paid by her which prima facie proved that during the relevant period, i.e. 26-3-1971 to 28.021972, Rafi Tehrani was in possession of the property in question and subsequently he divested his ownership on Hosne Ara Begum, his wife, by oral gift and that she was in possession thereof. Therefore, the property in question did not answer the description of an abandoned property within the meaning of article 2(1) of PO 16 of 1972 and the presumption attached to section 5 of the Ordinance was very well rebutted. In the context, it is necessary to state that section 5 of the Ordinance does not say that to get a notice for surrendering or taking over possession as an abandoned property, one need be in possession of the entire property.

<u>125. As discussed hereinbefore, the petitioners of Case No.649 of 1988, particularly, Hosne Ara Begum conclusively proved that Rafi Tehrani, her husband, was a Bangladeshi citizen holding Bangladesh passport and was in possession of the property in question during the relevant period, i.e. from 26-3-1971 to 28-2-1972 as its rightful owner and after she had become the owner of the same by oral gift from her husband on 3-9-1972. She and her transferees were in possession thereof and therefore, they were entitled to get a notice under section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance before the inclusion of the property in question in the list of abandoned buildings. This Court in the cases of the Ministry of Works vs Helaluddin Ahmed (supra), Bangladesh vs Amela Khatun and others (supra), Government of Bangladesh vs Marium (supra), Bangladesh vs Rehana Kamal (supra), Abdur Rashid Molla vs Bangladesh (supra), Bangladesh vs Md.. Shahjahan (supra), has consistently held that statutory notice as contemplated in sections 4 and 5 of the Ordinance is a sine qua non and in the absence of such notice, the inclusion of a disputed property in the `Kha' list of the abandoned buildings is illegal and without lawful authority.</u>

<u>126. This Division in the case of Secretary, Ministry of Works and Urban Development, Government of Bangladesh vs Rowshan Ara Begum, 57 DLR (AD) 167, rejected the objection as to the non-service of notice under section 5(1) of the Ordinance on the ground that no such objection was taken either before the Court of Settlement or before the High Court Division, so this case could not be relied upon or referred to as an authority on the question of non-service of notice under section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance as sought to be relied upon by the learned Additional Attorney General. A review of this judgment was sought and this Division in the review held that "In the instant case the petitioner having not been able to establish before the Court of Settlement that the claimant of the property or for that matter her vendor Anwari Khatun were present in Bangladesh on 28-2-1972 and consequent thereupon the property having had assumed the character of abandoned property, the listing of the property in question, even if without service of notice as per provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, is not material as the property because of non-service of notice for listing in the list of abandoned properties would not cease to be an abandoned property and consequent thereupon the claim of title made by the petitioner in the property in question is not legally sustainable or, in other words, the petitioner cannot raise any claim of title in the property in question since said property is an abandoned property. The ground contending which review of our judgment is sought merits no consideration." And in taking the said view, the earlier decisions of this Court as mentioned hereinbefore, were not at all taken into consideration. So this judgment can be termed to be a judgment per in curium and does not constitute a precedent. In the context, it is necessary to keep on record that at the time of hearing the review petition, the case of Ministry of Works vs Helaluddin Ahmed (supra) was cited, but that case was distinguished in the following way:</u>

<u>"The learned Counsel in support of his contention that listing of the property without serving notice as per provision of Ordinance No.54 of 1985 makes the list so made unsustainable in law referred to the case of Ministry of Works vs Helaluddin Ahmed reported in 4 MLR (AD) 140. The fact of the aforesaid case is quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case and when we drew attention of the learned Counsel to the facts of the case referred by him the learned Counsel felt difficulty to press his contention that the decision reported in the aforementioned law report has application in the facts of the instant case."</u>

127. Therefore, it is obvious that the earlier decisions of this Court on statutory notice creating jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement have not been reconsidered and reviewed. Those judgments still hold the field and those have reached the status of stare decisis.

128. In Sufia Khatoon vs Mahabuba Rahman, 30 BLD (AD) 41 = 62 DLR (AD) 266, this Division has held that a judgment per in curium or a judgment sub silentio does not constitute a precedent. The same view was expressed by the High Court Division in the case of Monju Mia vs Shiraj Mia, 56 DLR 264 in the following: "... It is basic to the rule of precedent that if a later judgment of an apex Court, particularly when given without considering or noticing its earlier decisions on the same issue or point, and comes in conflict or at variance with its earlier' ones, such judgment however latest in time, loses its binding element for being a judgment made per in curium."

<u>129. In view of the consistent view of this Court in the cases as mentioned hereinbefore, find substance in the submission of the learned Counsel for the appellants that a statutory notice is a 'jurisdictional fact' or a 'collateral fact' for inclusion of any property in the `Kha' list published under section 5 of the Ordinance and inclusion of any property in the `Kha' list without issuing notice under clause 1(b) thereof will not give jurisdiction to the Court of Settlement to assume jurisdiction to inquire into the merit of the case. In view of the above, I hold that the enlistment of the property in question in the `Kha' list of the abandoned buildings was illegal and without lawful authority and the High Court Division on misconception of the provisions of section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance read with article 7 of PO 16 of 1972 erroneously held that the enlistment of the property in question in the ' Kha' list without serving notice upon the petitioners was a mere irregularity and for such irregularity "the whole process of inclusion of the property as abandoned property cannot be called in question."</u>

130. The writ petition filed before the High Court Division was a writ in the nature of certiorari. In the case of the Government of Bangladesh vs Md.. Jalil, 48 DLR (AD) 10, it has been held that "The High Court Division was not a Court of appeal required to make determination of facts on its own. It could interfere with the findings of a tribunal of fact under its extra-ordinary jurisdiction under Article 102, only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence/ facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted mala fide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. In the absence of any of these conditions the interference by the High Court Division will itself be an act of without jurisdiction."

<u>131. In the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Ministry of Works vs Nasima Khatoon, 57 DLR (AD) 97, this Division did not interfere with the judgment of the High Court Division which made the Rule Nisi absolute and set aside the decision of the Court of Settlement on the view that "the Court of Settlement did not consider the documents filed by the respondents and while passing the judgment and order did not apply its judicial mind. In this view of the matter, we do not find that the judgment passed by the Court of Settlement is maintainable."</u>

132. As I have found earlier, the Court of Settlement rejected the case of the appellants of CA No. 10 of 2003 on total non-application of mind to their case, non-consideration of the materials placed before it, misreading and misconstruction of some documents and on misconception of the provisions of oral gift under Mohamedan Law and the provisions of article 7 of PO 16 of 1972 and section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance, the High Court Division was quite competent to interfere with the findings and the decision of the Court of Settlement in rejecting the case and thus rejecting the prayer to exclude the property in question from the `Kha' list of the abandoned buildings, but unfortunately the High Court Division discharged the Rule Nisi maintaining those of the Court of Settlement in a mechanical way just reiterating the decision and dittoing the reasoning of the Court of Settlement in a different language without applying its own independent judicial mind in the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials placed before it and again on the mechanical approach that "In writ of certiorari this Court cannot sit over the judgment of the Court of Settlement for reassessing the evidences on record as this court is not a Court of Appeal" and thus erred in law in passing the impugned judgment and order discharging the Rules and as such, the same cannot be sustained and must be interfered with.

133. I have given my anxious thought on the question whether the case be sent back to the Court of Settlement for its decision afresh in view of the fact that the documents in support of the possession of the appellants, particularly, the transferees from Hosne Ara Begum have been filed before this Court, which as it appears from the decision of the Court of Settlement were not filed before it and as such, the Court of Settlement had no chance to consider those, but considering that the cases before the Court of Settlement were filed in 1988 and by now 27 years have elapsed, I do not deem it proper to send the same to the Court of Settlement for another round of legal battle and thus to consume another 20 years if not 27 years. Particularly, in view of my finding that the property in question did not answer the description of an abandoned property within the meaning of article 2(1) of PO 16 of 1972 and the same did not vest in the Government and that the same was enlisted in the `ICha' list illegally and without lawful authority inasmuch as no notice for surrendering or taking over possession thereof as required under section 5(1)(b) of the Ordinance was served upon the occupants, I propose to decide the matter finally.

134. Now another pertinent question that looms large for decision is in whose favour order for exclusion of the property in question from the list of abandoned buildings should be passed. I find no difficulty in answering the question in favour of the appellants in CA No.10 of 2003, in view of the finding as to their title and possession therein given hereinbefore. At the same time, I must say that since the parties, namely, the appellants (CA Nos. 10 of 2003 and 77 of 2003) are litigating in the civil Courts as to their claim of title in the property in question in the suits now pending therein ultimate claim of the parties to the property in question shall be decided by the civil Court in the suits now pending between them.

<u>135. In the result, the appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division affirming the decision of the Court of Settlement in Case Nos. 649 of 1988 and 586 of 1988 rejecting the cases is set aside. The cases are allowed. Respondent No. 2 is directed to exclude the building being holding No. 5, Maghbazar (Outer Circular Road), presently 70/71, Outer Circular Road, from the list of abandoned buildings published in the official gazette, additional issue, on 28th April, 1986 in favour of the appellants of CA No.10 of 2003. But this order of exclusion of the property in question from the list of abandoned buildings in favour of the appellants of CA No. 10 of 2003 in no way shall affect the merit of the suits now pending between the parties, i.e. the appellants in the civil Court. The civil Court shall be at liberty to decide the title of the parties on the evidence to be produced by them keeping in mind that the property in question is not an abandoned property and the same did not vest in the Government.</u>

<u>Nazmun Ara Sultana J: I have gone through the judgments prepared by my learned brothers Surendra Kumar Sinha, CJ and Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the judgment of my learned brother Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J.</u>

<u>Syed Mahmud Hossain J: I have gone through the judgments prepared by my learned brothers Surendra Kumar Sinha, CJ and Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the judgment of my learned brother Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J.</u>

<u>Muhammad Imman Ali J: I have gone through the judgments prepared by my learned brothers Surendra Kumar Sinha, CJ and Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the judgment of my learned brother Surendra Kumar Sinha, CJ.</u>

<u>Hasan Foez Siddique J: I have gone through the judgments prepared by my learned brothers Surendra Kumar Sinha, CJ and Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the judgment of my learned brother Surendra Kumar Sinha, CJ.</u>

AHM Shamsuddin Choudhury J: I have gone through the judgments prepared by my learned brothers Surendra Kumar Sinha, CJ and Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the judgment of my Lord Surendra Kumar Sinha,

Court's Order

Both the Appeals are dismissed by majority decision.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated July 23. 1996 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1835 of 1994).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This is plaintiffs' appeal by leave against the judgment dated July 23, 1996 of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1835 of 1994 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated February 24, 1994 of tile Court of District Judge, Gopalganj in Title Appeal No. 24 of 1992 reversing the judgment and decree dated March 7, 1992 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Sadar, Gopalganj, in Title Suit No. 218 of 1974 dismissing the same. The suit was filed seeking declaration of title by adverse possession and confirmation of possession in respect of 3.25 acres of land.

2. The suit was filed by Abdur Rashid Sheikh predecessor of the appellants stating, inter alia, that land in suit belonged to Karuna Moyee Dasi and she agreed to sell the land in suit for a consideration of Taka 1,800 and she on receiving Taka 1,200 executed a bainapatra on January 1, 1952 and delivered possession, that there was stipulation in the agreement that the kabala would be executed and registered after six months from date of agreement after payment of balance of the consideration money Taka 600. It was the case of the plaintiff that after executing bainapatra and receiving the part of the consideration money Karuna Moyee Dasi left the then East Pakistan for India with the members of her family and started living there, that Karuna Moyee Dasi executed a Power of Attorney in favour of Bijoy Krishna Majumdar appointing him as her attorney in respect of the land of bainapatra and other land, that in spite of approaching Karuna Moyee Dasi to execute and register the kabala upon receiving balance of consideration money she did not execute and register the kabala, that balance of the consideration money was paid to the attorney of Karuna Moyee Dasi and he assured to execute and register the kabala within the shortest possible time, that prior to the execution and registration of the kabala by Karuna Moyee Dasi the defendant No.1 in collusion with some other persons upon resorting to forgery got a kabala registered by false personation, that a case of forgery was filed against the defendant No.1 and others and they were found guilty and were convicted but on appeal they were acquitted on technical ground that trial was held without obtaining sanction since one of the accused was a public servant. It was also the case of the plaintiff that Karuna Moyee Dasi came in the then East Pakistan in 1963 and she affirmed an affidavit on August 24, 1963 before the Magistrate, 1st Class, Faridpur denying execution of any kabala in favour of defendant No.1 and others and admitting execution of agreement for sale in favour of the plaintiff. The plaintiff upon making the above averments filed the suit seeking the relief as stated hereinbefore. As regard cause of action for filing the suit it was stated that plaintiff was constrained to file the suit since the defendants threatened him to dispossess from the land in suit.

3. The suit was contested by defendant Nos. 1 and 36 by filing separate sets of written statement. It may be mentioned defendant No. 36 ultimately did not contest the suit. The defendant No.1 in his written statement denied the material averments made in the plaint and contended, inter alia, that he along with 10 others purchased the land in suit from Karuna Moyee Dasi by the kabala dated April 19, 1962 and since purchase he and the other purchasers are possessing the land in suit, that the bainapatra of the plaintiff is forged and fabricated and that the plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the land in suit on the basis of the forged bainapatra.

4. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence of the parties dismissed the suit on the finding that plaintiff's claim of offering the balance of the consideration money to Karuna Moyee Dasi and refusal by her to execute and register the kabala is baseless, that payment of balance of the consideration money to Karuna Moyee Dasi's attorney in 1962 and his refusal to execute and register the kabala is something absurd and unbelievable and that the said claim is baseless and also has not been established by producing evidence" that plaintiff's claim that writer of the agreement had died was not established by producing evidence, that there is no satisfactory explanation why the suit for specific performance was not filed in between the years 1952 and 1976, that it is not clear whether the plaintiff possessed the land in suit and after his death his heirs are possessing the land in suit, that the witnesses examined by the plaintiff are not disinterested witnesses and that evidence of the said witnesses, particularly of the evidence of PW 2, is contradictory, that PW 2 though claimed himself to be a witness of the bainapatra but his signature in the bainapatra and the deposition-sheet is discrepant, that from the analysis of the evidence of PW 5 it is seen that his evidence is contradictory and he has no regard for truth, that PW 5 has stated that bainapatra was written on a plain paper but, in fact, the same was written on cartridge paper bearing the water mark State of Calcutta and the national symbol of India (সিংহ মার্কা অশোক চক্র) and as such it can be safely concluded that the bainapatra was brought into existence any time after 1952, that on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, there is no occasion for arriving at a conclusion that plaintiff got the possession of the land in suit on the basis of bainapatra and he is possessing the same, that the defendants though claimed that they have purchased the land of Karuna Moyee Dasi by 4 kabalas but the same were not filed in the Court and that they had also not adduced any evidence in support of their claim of purchasing the land from Karuna Moyee Dasi and of possessing the land on the basis of alleged purchase, that plaintiff failed to prove his title and possession in the land in suit, that the plaintiff as well as defendants have no right, title and interest as well as possession and that the papers relied upon by the plaintiff and defendants in support of their respective claim cannot be considered legal and valid document, that the cause of action as stated in the plaint is not correct, rather cause of action arose in 1962 while there was dispute of extreme nature relating to the title and possession of the land in suit, that the plaintiff has filed the suit on imaginary date of cause of action, that the plaintiff's suit is barred by limitation, that plaintiff failed to prove his case as well as the genuineness of the bainapatra.

5. As against the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff took appeal to the Court of District Judge. The appellate Court in arriving at the decision as to genuineness of the agreement said to have been entered into between Abdur Rashid Sheikh and Karuna Moyee Dasi, the owner of the property in suit, placed reliance primarily on an affidavit produced by the plaintiff, said to have been executed by Karuna Moyee Dasi before the Magistrate, 1st Class, Faridpur on August 24, 1963 wherein Karuna Moyee Dasi stated that she entered into a contract to sell the land in suit to Abdur Rashid and that she did not execute and register any kabala in favour of the defendants on April, 1962 and also placed reliance upon the Power of Attorney said to have been executed by Karuna Moyee Dasi appointing certain Bijoy Krishna Majumdar as her attorney in respect of the property of Karuna Moyee Dasi including the land in suit upon overlooking the fact that the said affidavit and the Power of Attorney were not proved by calling the competent witness and because of that the said documents were left out of consideration by the trial Court. The appellate Court while considering the genuineness of the agreement for sale (Exhibit 1) between Abdur Rashid and Karuna Moyee Dasi considered the matter of nonappearance or, in other words, non contesting of the suit by the defendant Nos. 37 and 38, sons of Karuna Moyee Dasi, who are said to have died. The fact of death of Karuna Moyee Dasi was not established by any evidence. It may be mentioned it was the definite case of the plaintiff that Karuna Moyee Dasi after execution of the alleged deed of agreement for sale of the land in suit allegedly on January 1, 1952 left for India with the members of her family including the sons and were residing there. In that state of the matter the trial Court was of the view that impleading of the defendant Nos. 37 and 38 showing their address in Bangladesh was not genuine since plaintiff himself averred that Karuna Moyee Dasi with her children after execution of agreement for sale left for India and was residing in India. The appellate Court also held that the respondents failed to establish their case of purchasing the land in suit. The appellate Court held that since the date of execution of the bainapatra on January 1, 1952 Abdur Rashid and after him his heirs, the substituted plaintiffs, are possessing the land upon assertion of their title and denying the title of Karuna Moyee Dasi as well as her heirs and that possession of the plaintiff being for more than 20 years in assertion of his title upon denying title of the owner Karuna Moyee Dasi, whatever interest Karuna Moyee Dasi had in the land in suit, the same extinguished and thus the plaintiff acquired title by adverse possession. The appellate Court, while accepting the case of the plaintiff that Karuna Moyee Dasi executed the bainapatra, relied upon the evidence of PW 2 upon overlooking the fact that the said witness was not the attesting witness to the bainapatra and because of that trial Court discarded his evidence relating to execution of bainapatra by Karuna Moyee Dasi and payment of part of the consideration money by Abdur Rashid to Karuna Moyee Dasi. The appellate Court while considering the genuineness of the agreement for sale also placed reliance on the evidence of PW 5 who is an attesting witness to the bainapatra. It may be mentioned PW 5 is the close relation of the recipient of the bainapatra and his evidence being not corroborated by any independent witness trial Court discarded the evidence of PW 5. The appellate Court while arriving at the finding that plaintiff acquired title by adverse possession, observed that the appellants are in possession of the land in suit since January 1, 1952 "as part performance of the contract" and thereupon observed that the plaintiffs were claiming the land in suit in assertion of their title and denying the title of Karuna Moyee Dasi the real owner and the defendants failed to prove their possession in the land in suit. The appellate Court while reversing the finding of the trial Court as to question of limitation has observed that the suit is for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and the plaintiff has title and possession in the land in suit and the suit has been filed well within time from the date on which plaintiff's possession was threatened by the defendants and thereupon held that the trial Court was wrong in holding that the plaintiff's suit was barred by limitation. It may be mentioned that the question of limitation was addressed by the trial Court in the context of not filing in due course any suit seeking relief on the basis of the agreement for sale.

6. The defendants i.e. respondents herein as against the judgment of the appellate Court moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute upon observing that the trial Court noticed the internal incongruity in the cartridge paper on which agreement for sale was drawn up in that the water mark in the cartridge paper was the national symbol of the Government of India and consequently, the cartridge paper was not in use in the then East Pakistan when at best there could be in use cartridge paper of British India and thereupon the High Court Division arrived at the finding that the agreement for sale was not a genuine document. It may be mentioned the appellate Court did not at all consider this aspect of the matter noticing which the trial Court held that agreement for sale was not a genuine document. The appellate Court has also not reversed the finding of the trial Court in that regard. The High Court Division considered the case of the plaintiff that he entered into possession of the land in suit on the basis of the bainapatra and it is the case of the plaintiff that the bainapatra is a genuine one. In the background thereof, the High Court Division held since the plaintiff had at no point of time asserted that his entry into the land was on the basis of void document and that there being no case of the plaintiff that he possessed the land denying the title of the real owner and, as such, the claim of the plaintiff that he acquired title in the land in suit by adverse possession is not well founded and that decisions on which the plaintiff placed reliance in support of his case of adverse possession on the basis of void document has no bearing on the facts and circumstances of the instant case and because of the fact stated hereinabove. The High Court Division from the pleading of the plaintiff noticed that plaintiff paid the balance of the consideration  money to the attorney of Karuna Moyee Dasi but there is no evidence on which date, in fact, the plaintiff paid the balance of the consideration money to Karuna Moyee Dasi's attorney whose appointment is said to have been made by Karuna Moyee Dasi on June 9, 1962. The High Court Division also noticed the fact pleaded by the plaintiff that on receiving the balance of the consideration money the attorney of Karuna Moyee Dasi assured the plaintiff that he would execute the kabala in the light of the agreement for sale. There is no case of the plaintiff that at any point of time the attorney refused to execute the kabala. In the background of the aforesaid state of the matter the High Court Division held that as the plaintiff was awaiting for the execution of the kabala, as such, there was no occasion for the plaintiff to possess the land in suit upon denying the title of the real owner and thereupon held that in the absence of establishing the fact of possessing the land on assertion of title by the plaintiff upon denying the title of the real owner the plaintiff's case of acquiring title by adverse possession is not legally well founded. It may be mentioned there is stipulation in the agreement for sale that in case balance of the consideration money is not paid within 6 months from the date of execution of the bainapatra (the bainapatra was executed on January 1, 1952) the plaintiff would pay share of the crops of the land in suit to Karuna Moyee Dasi. In that background the High Court Division observed that there was no occasion for the plaintiff to possess the land claiming his title in the land in suit upon denying title of Karuna Moyee Dasi and, as such, appellate Court was in serious error in holding that the plaintiff acquired title in the land in suit by adverse possession.

7. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant has submitted that plaintiffs' predecessor was in possession of the land in suit since January 1952 and after that plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit and that the last Court of fact having had found the agreement for sale entered into by Karuna Moyee Dasi, the real owner, with Abdur Rashid, the predecessor of the appellants genuine and thereupon the last Court of fact having had decreed the suit declaring the title of the plaintiffs acquired by adverse possession the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction was in error in disturbing the finding of fact arrived at by the last Court of fact on due consideration of the evidence and thereupon setting aside the judgment of the lower appellate Court. The learned Advocate for the appellant also submitted that the trial Court as well as the High Court Division having had held that the agreement for sale was not genuine and consequent thereupon it being the position that the document on the basis of which plaintiff's predecessor entered into possession being void one and on the basis thereof having had possessed the land in suit for more than 20 years denying the title of the real owner and upon assertion of his title by the plaintiff and thereafter by the plaintiff's heirs and thus they have acquired title in the land in suit by adverse possession. In support of the said contention the learned Advocate has referred to the case of Mir Laik Ali vs Standard Vacuum Oil Company (ESSO) and Abdur Razzak reported in 16 DLR (SC) 287 wherein it has been observed "When there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property transferred as transferee, his possession is in his own right and adverse to the transferor. If he continues in possession of immovable property for more than twelve years he will acquire an indefeasible title. Of course, it is open to a transferee if he finds the transaction in his favour to be invalid not to treat the property as his own, but that will be where he accepts the invalidity of the transfer and henceforth proposes to hold the property on behalf of the transferor. If it be his claim that he holds it by virtue of a transfer which he regards as valid he is obviously holding in his own right and not on behalf of the transferor or in trust for him. A large number of cases could be cited wherein it was held that an unregistered deed though it could not effect a valid transfer could be looked as to ascertain the nature of possession of the transferee. In all these cases it is the transferee who relied on this proposition and who put forward the deed as evidence of the fact that his possession was in assertion of the title which the unregistered deed purported to convey and it has always been held, in the absence of some rebutting circumstance, that a person in possession under an invalid deed which he claimed as valid held in his own right and his possession was adverse to the true owner".

8. The learned Advocate appearing for the respondents supported the judgment of the High Court Division submitting that from plaintiff's side there is no evidence to establish that he ever claimed title to the suit land by adverse possession and also there is no evidence to show that at what point of time plaintiff's possession became hostile to the real owner Karuna Moyee Dasi. The learned Advocate also submitted that it is the case of the plaintiff that he paid balance of the consideration money to the Attorney of Karuna Moyee Dasi who assured him to execute the kabala but there is no pleading that he at any point of time had refused to execute the kabala and, as such, there is no case of claim of title in the land by the plaintiff and thereafter by his heirs, the present appellants, by adverse possession.

9. It is the case of the plaintiff that the real owner Karuna Moyee Dasi agreed to sell the land in suit to him and that upon receiving part of the consideration money executing a bainapatra and put him into possession of the land. It is also the case of the plaintiff that he paid the balance of the consideration money to the Attorney of Karuna Moyee Dasi. There is no pleading that Attorney of Karuna Moyee Dasi at any point of time refused to execute the kabala, rather it is the case of the plaintiff that after payment of the balance of the consideration money, he was assured by the Attorney of Karuna Moyee Dasi that the kabala would be executed very soon. This aspect of the matter clearly shows that plaintiff was in expectance of having the kabala to be executed by the Attorney of Karuna Moyee Dasi and this being the position there was no question of possessing the land upon denying the title of Karuna Moyee Dasi. No positive evidence has been led from the side of the plaintiff to establish from what point of time the plaintiff started to possess the land in suit asserting his title upon denying the title of the real owner Karuna Moyee Dasi. There is another aspect of the matter that it is the consistent case of the plaintiff that the agreement executed by Karuna Moyee Dasi was genuine. The learned Advocate for the appellants also made submission that appellate Court on consideration of the evidence having had found the agreement for sale genuine the High Court Division was in serious error in setting aside the said finding of the appellate Court and thereupon setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court. The above being the case of the plaintiff or, in other words, plaintiff's entry on the land in suit being on the basis of a document which he is consistently claiming as genuine, then claim of acquisition of title by adverse possession on the basis thereof does not fit in with the ratio decidendi of the case reported in 16 DLR (SC) 287, referred hereinbefore and, as such, decision made in the said case has no manner of application in the instant case. The decision reported in 16 DLR (SC) 287 shows that the ratio of the said case is applicable in the background of the fact where there is a real transferor. There is nothing in the said decision that in the case of fictitious transferor, claim of title by the transferee of said kind of document would be adverse in respect of the property. In the instant case, document of plaintiff has been found not genuine and accepting the said finding the appellants are claiming title by adverse possession. The claim so made is not legally well founded.

<u>10. The question that called for determination in the instant case is, whether the plaintiff was able to make out a case of acquisition of title by adverse possession in respect of the land wherein he entered on the basis of the document claimed to be genuine. The plaintiff was required to establish from what particular point of time he started to possess the land in assertion of his title upon denying the title of the real owner i.e. Karuna Moyee Dasi. The evidence from plaintiff's side is totally lacking for establishing the fact that from a particular point of time he started to possess the land asserting his title upon denying the title of the real owner to his knowledge as well as to the knowledge of the others and since that date he was possessing the land for more than 12 years. In our view, there is no evidence that at any particular point of time the plaintiff claimed title in the land in suit on the basis of adverse possession or, in other words, claimed his title in the land upon denying the title of the real owner.</u>

<u>11. In that state of the matter we are of the view that High Court Division was quite correct in arriving at the finding that plaintiff did not acquire any title in the land in suit by adverse possession since there is lack of evidence to show that he possessed the land denying title of Karuna Moyee Dasi or her sons to their knowledge.</u>

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed with costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mir Hashmat Ali J: This Rule nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment vide Annexure 'D' should not be declared to have been made without jurisdiction and is of no legal effect and why the holding No. L/1, Block-E, Mohammadpur, Dhaka should not be released from the 'Ka' list of abandoned buildings published on 23-9-1986. 

2. The petitioner filed Settlement Case No. 130 of 1997 before the Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka. 

3. The petitioner challenged the judgment and order dated 22-2-2001 passed by the Chairman, Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka in Settlement Case No. 130 of 1997 (Annexure 'D' to the writ petition). 

4. The short facts of the petitioner's case is that, the then Government of East Pakistan executed and registered the schedule property in favour of Md Nayeem for a period of 99 years. While the said allotec was in possession and enjoying the property peacefully, the Administrative Office of Mohammadpur issued Memo No. 2374(1) AO dated 8-10-1963 a PRF certificate (Annexure-'R-1'). Thereafter, the original lessee Md Nayeem transferred the property to Mrs Asma Khatoon, wife of Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed vide sale deed No. 13999 registered on 12-10-1963 (Annexure-'R-2'). After purchase Asma Khatoon made lot of improvements of the said property. Thereafter, the said Asma Khatoon obtained permission for construction of a house from the office of the Authorised Officer, Dhaka Improvement Trust on 19-3-1964 vide Memo No. 1118 TP dated 19-3-1964 (Annexure-'R-3'). Thereafter, Section Officer of the Deputy Commissioner's office under Ministry of Works vide his Memo No. 1010/CHB, dated 10-8-1964 issued a letter informing Mrs Asma Khatoon regarding mutation certificate (Annexure-'R-4'). Thereafter, said Mrs Asma Khatoon mortgaged the case property to the House Building Finance Corporation, Dhaka under mortgage deed No. 5843 dated 22-6-1965 against loan case No. D1728 and after obtaining loan, said Mrs Asma Khatoon constructed a three-storied building on the case property (Annexure-'R-5'). While the said Mrs Asma Khatoon was enjoying the property peacefully, she desired to sell out the property and the petitioner offered to purchase the same at a consideration of Taka 50,000 and accordingly, Mrs Asma Khatoon accepted the money and entered into an agreement for sale with the petitioner on 13-12-1970 and on the date of agreement, the petitioner was partly put into possession of the case property as part performance of the contract. Subsequently, the petitioner paid five thousand Taka to the said Asma Khatoon and endorsed the same in the back side of the agreement for sale (Annexure-'J'). Subsequently, the said Asma Khatoon was requested to execute a sale deed but she did not. Consequently, the petitioner filed Suit No. 1084 of 1981 for specific performance of contract before the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. Ultimately, the said suit was decreed on 25-5-1983. The aforesaid decree was put into execution in Title Execution Case No. 31 of 1983 and got kabala deed executed and registered on 10-8-1983 and the petitioner was put into possession officially in execution case on 2-1-1984 and the petitioner till date enjoying the same without any hindrance from any quarter (Annexure-F, Fl, F2, F3 and F4). The petitioner applied before the Deputy Commissioner, Housing and Settlement for mutation of the case property in her name on 8-3-1984 and the Assistant Commissioner issued letter vide Memo No. 7706/1(2)ক, মে dated 4-11-1985 asking the writ petitioner to appear before him with all documents in support of her claim (Annexure-C and C1 ). While the petitioner was enjoying the property peacefully; since the name of the petitioner was not yet mutated; the petitioner used to make payment in the name of his earlier owner Asma Khatun and paid all Electric Bills, Water Bills, Gas Bills, etc. to the concerned authority of the Government accordingly (Annexure-G, G1, G2, G3, G4, G5, G6 and 07). While the petitioner was in peaceful possession and enjoyment of the property, the respondent-government, without serving any notice, most illegally enlisted the property of the petitioner in the "ka" list of the abandoned buildings which was published on 23-9-1986 in serial No. 149 9762(24). Thereafter, the petitioner filed an application under section 7(1) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 challenging the inclusion of the property in the list of abandoned property before the Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka. Subsequently, the said case has been marked and numbered as Case No. 130 of 1997. 

5. After hearing of the parties, the Court of Settlement in slipshod manner disposed of the case without proper consideration of the documentary evidence on record (Annexure-'D'). The petitioner during the trial filed an application for calling for the record of the loan Case No. 1728 dated 22-6-1965 from the House Building Finance Corporation as the property was mortgaged to the House Building Finance Corporation. But the said application was neither accepted nor rejected. In the meantime, the House Building Finance Corporation filed Miscellaneous Case No. 377 of 1999 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka under Article 27(1) of the House Building Finance Corporation Act, 1952 (PO 7 of 1973). In the said miscellaneous case, the petitioner was added as opposite party No. 2. After contested hearing the District Judge, Dhaka was pleased to pass the judgment on 29-6-2000 in favour of respondent No. 3, House Building Finance Corporation and the petitioner was directed to pay the entire loan amount within three months (Annexure-'N'). The petitioner paid the entire decretal amount (loan amount) to the respondent No. 3, House Building Finance Corporation within time (Annexure-'O' series). Subsequently, House Building Finance Corporation issued clearance certificate in respect of full payment of the decretal amount (Annexure-'S').

6. The petitioner finding no other alternative filed instant writ petition and obtained Rule. 

7. Mr MA Quddus Sheikh, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the petitioner purchased the property under an agreement which was prior to 25th March, 1971 and that such agreement was binding upon the Government as well as upon the original owner. In such situation the same allotment may be cancelled, amended or terminated by the Government, if it so chooses to do so and that the possessors of the abandoned property could be asked to surrender the possession under the provision of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 (Clause-1 of Article 10 of the PO 16 of 1972). In the instant case there was no such termination of the agreement so as to entitle the Government to take over possession and, as such, the possession of the petitioner on the basis of the agreement for sale cannot be termed to be an unauthorised one. The Government never choose to terminate the agreement but instead left it to be held a valid document and made itself binding on it and in such circumstances the possession is protected under section 53(A) of the Transfer of Property Act entitling the petitioner to exercise his right to maintain possession. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Bangladesh vs Kazi Ashrafuddin Ahmed reported in 55 DLR (AD) 16. He further submits that the government got the abandoned property from the possession of the petitioner as required under section 7 of the PO 16 of 1972. In support of his contention, he has pointed out the Memo No. A M-19/60/7706/1(2)/ka, say, dated 4-12-1985 (Annexure-C1)" requesting the petitioner to appear before the Assistant Commissioner, Settlement with all the valid documents in regard to the property and that in the said letter the administrative officer was asked to inquire into the matter as to who is in possession and whether he has paid all the dues of the government, which shows that at least till 4-12-1985 the property was not declared as an abandoned property and, as such, the question of abandonment under PO 16 of 1972 is misconceived and Court of Settlement failed to consider such aspect of the case. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Mahmuda Begum vs 1st Court of Settlement reported in 13 BLC 247. He further submits that before enlistment of the property in the list of abandoned property no notice was served upon the petitioner as required under PO 16 of 1972 and under Ordinance 54 of 1985. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Abdur Rashid Mollah vs Bangladesh reported in 58 DLR (AD) 20, the case of Bangladesh vs Amela Khatoon reported in 53 DLR (AD) 55 and the case of Bangladesh vs Helaluddin Ahmed reported in 4 MLR (AD) 140. He further submits that the Court of Settlement on misconception of law failed to consider that the original owner Mohammad Nayeem transferred the property to Asma Khatun and Asma Khatun transferred the same to the petitioner under an agreement dated 13-12-70, which was before Liberation and before the promulgation of President's Order 16 of 1972 and all such transfers cannot be disturbed by the government as per Article 10(1) of PO 16 of 1972 because those transfer were made much earlier than 25th March, 1971. He further submits that the Court of Settlement disposed of the case on the basis of the reported case 47 DLR (AD) 71 but in the facts and circumstances of the present case 47 DLR (AD) 71 is not applicable. In the instant case, the ex parte decree was obtained for enforcement of an agreement entered into before promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 and also before 25th March, 1971 and such agreement was not after the promulgation of PO 16 of 1972. He further submits that any ex parte decree obtained in respect of the agreement after 25th March, 1971 cannot be enforceable according to 47 DLR (AD) 71. But in the instant case admittedly, the agreement was executed long before PO 16 of 1972 and 25th March, 1971. He further submits that admittedly the property was mortgaged to the House Building Finance Corporation in Loan Case No. D-1728 before liberation of Bangladesh and before PO 16 of 1972 came into operation and the House Building Finance Corporation (PO 7 of 1973) filed Miscellaneous Case No. 377 of 1999 before the District Judge, Dhaka and the learned District Judge after hearing both the parties decreed the suit against the opposite parties including the petitioner and according to the said decree, the petitioner paid entire dues of the decretal amount to the House Buildings Finance Corporation. 

8. He further submits that the property was mortgaged to the House Building Finance Corporation which was incorporated under Act 18 of 1952. Subsequently, the said Act has been incorporated in Bangladesh in PO 7 of 1973 and, as such, practically, property mortgaged to the House Building Finance Corporation means to the Government and such property which was mortgaged to Government organisation cannot be declared as abandoned property. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Ariff A Shekha vs Bangladesh reported in 47 DLR 289 the case of Gannysons Ltd vs Sonali Bank reported in 37 DLR (AD) 42 and the case of Md Zaher vs Bangladesh reported in 42 DLR 430. 

9. He further submits that the petitioner filed series of documents before the Court of Settlement including the document of allotment and lease of the property from the Government since from 1963. But the Court of Settlement without considering those documents dismissed the case of the petitioner in a slipshod manner and, as such, the impugned judgment and order dated 22-2-2001 passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 130 of 1997 should be declared to have been made and passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

10. Mr Md Mozzammel Hoque, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondents, submits that the petitioner failed to prove the case before the Court of Settlement and the burden of proof lies upon him and, as such, burden cannot be shifted to others. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Kuinbhan Lakshmanna vs Tangirala Venkateswarla reported in 2 DLR 83. 

11. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties at length and perused the writ petition, supplementary affidavits on behalf of the petitioner, application for addition of party and affidavit-in-opposition and the annexure thereof 

12. It appears that in the writ petition, several supplementary affidavits of various days and application for addition of party, the petitioner annexed various documents of the case property. We have checked up the record of the case, it appears that the husband of the petitioner was examined as PW 1 and he has placed all the documents of the case property including the mortgage of the property to the House Building Finance Corporation. But the Court of Settlement rejected all those documents on the ground that the witness PW 1 could not say the whereabouts of the witnesses of the agreement at present. But the Court of Settlement failed to consider that deed of agreement was executed on 13-12-1970 long before the liberation of Bangladesh and the evidence was taken on 10-10-2000 after about 30 years and that such agreement was also tested and believed by the Civil Court and the Court of Settlement failed to appreciate that none could say the whereabouts of the persons who are witnesses and scribe of the document after long 30 years, that too pre-liberation, but the case of the petitioner was dismissed only on that ground without considering the other documents. It further appears that the Court of Settlement rejected plea of ex parte decree of the petitioner on the ground of a reported case 47 DLR (AD) 71 on the ground that the decree was obtained on the basis of an agreement after the promulgation of President's Order 16 of 1972 but fact remains that the agreement was executed long before PO 16 of 1972 came into operation and before 25th March, 1971, before liberation of Bangladesh and, as such, the case of specific performance of contract before the liberation cannot be construed and considered a bar under PO 16 of 1972. It has already been held in the case of Bangladesh vs Kazi Ashrafuddin Ahmed reported in 55 DLR (AD) 16 and the case of Mahmuda Begum vs First Court of Settlement reported in 13 Inc 247, which runs thus: 

"From the provision of Article 10, it seems to be clear that any allotment or lease of or any agreement relating to an abandoned property is binding upon the government as custodian subject to its right as conferred under the said provisions. It appears that any allotment, lease or agreement granted or entered into before the 25th March, 1971 is binding upon the Government in the same way as upon the original owner having entered into the shoes of the lawful owner but the allotment agreement or lease granted or entered into after 25th March, 1971 may be cancelled, terminated or amended by the Government, if it chooses to do so, and if a person is in possession of an abandoned property by virtue of such allotment, lease or agreement can be asked to surrender possession of such property only if the Government cancels or terminates such an allotment, lease or agreement under clause (2) of the Article and, as is provided in clause (3) the Government may eject such a person only when he fails to surrender possession under clause (2) of the Article. 

In the instant Rule, agreement for sale dated 27-12-1970 i.e. prior to 25th March, 1971, and considering from this standpoint it appears that the said agreement dated 27-12-1970 does not come within the purview of Article 10 of the PO of 1972 unconditionally but subject to terms and conditions of the agreement for sale. The provisions of said Order do not confer any power upon the Government, which appears from Article 10, to ignore an agreement entered into after 25th March, 1971 and eject the occupant lawfully in possession of the abandoned property". 

13. In the instant case, we find from Annexure-'C-1' that Assistant Commissioner, Settlement vide Memo No. A M-19/60/7706/1(2)/ka, se dated 4-12-1985 directed the Administrative Officer of Mohammadpur Housing Estate, Dhaka to enquire as to whether any person is living in the house or whether they have paid the dues of the government and in the said letter the petitioner was asked to submit the original lease deed, original agreement, original purchase deed and original judgment of the Civil Court before the Assistant Commissioner, which shows that at least up to 4-12-1985 the property was not declared as an abandoned property and that at least the petitioner was in possession up to 4-12-1985. 

Admittedly, the case property was mortgaged to the House Building Finance Corporation in House Building Finance Corporation Loan Case No. D-1728 dated 22-6-1965 and that the House Building Finance Corporation filed Miscellaneous Case No. 377 of 1999 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka for realisation of loan against petitioner and others and, as such, we find at least up to decree dated 29-6-2000 the property was under mortgage to House Building Finance Corporation. But such aspect of the case has not been considered by the Court of Settlement though the petitioner agitated the matter before the Court of Settlement. 

14. It has been held in the case of Ariff A Shekha vs Bangladesh reported in 47 DLR 289, that: 

"As the company and its shares have been vested under PO 27 of 1972 on the ground that it was vested in the Government as an abandoned property, under PO 16 of 1972 if it is found that the company and shares thereof does not carry abandoned character then the shares of the petitioners who were found to have been away from the country and have been residing as its national in any country which was not at war with Bangladesh could not be treated as abandoned shares." 

In the instant case, admittedly the property was mortgaged to House Building Finance Corporation, which is an organisation under the Government of Bangladesh according to PO 7 of 1973. 

15. Let us see, what is the meaning of the mortgage. According to Judicial Dictionary of KJ Aiyar, mortgage is defined as under, "a mortgage' is the transfer of an interest in specific immovable property for securing the payment of money, or a present or future debt It may be—
(a) simple, that is, without possession or 
(b) usufructuary, that is, with possession. 

16. In a simple mortgage, both the ownership and possession remain vested in the owner. The form of security only entitles the creditor, in default of repayment of his debt, to realise it by eventual sale of the mortgaged property. But, in a usufructuary mortgage, the owner parts with possession of the mortgaged property. It has been held in the case of Zaher vs Bangladesh reported in 42 DLR 430 that the section 2(i)(ii)(b) clearly provides that any property which was taken over by the Government under any other law before President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force could not be located as an abandoned property. Admittedly, the suit property was requisitioned on 14-2-1972 as per order of requisition and was taken over possession as such on 16-2-1972 by the Government before President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force. That being the position the suit property could not be treated as abandoned property. 

17. In the instant case, the House Building Finance Corporation filed Miscellaneous Case No. 377 of 1999 for sale of the property for recovery of debts and obtained decree for the amount and the petitioner on payment of decretal amount released the property from House Building Finance Corporation and, as such, it appears that the property was under House Building Finance Corporation (government organisation), that being the position the property in question cannot be treated as abandoned property but the Court of Settlement failed to consider such aspect of the case in its proper perspective. 

18. It further appears that admittedly up to 4-12-1985 the property was not declared as an abandoned property and, as such, subsequent enlistment of the property is to be made after proper service of notice as contemplated under Article 7(3) of PO 16 of 1972 and section 5(1)(a) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1995. But in the instant case, the respondents Government failed to show any such notice served upon the petitioner or upon her predecessor. Rather, we find from Memo No. A M-19/60/7706/1(2)/ ka, se dated 4-12-1985 that the petitioner was asked to produce the relevant original documents of the property before Assistant Commissioner, Settlement. It appears that the petitioner obtained ex parte decree from the civil Court and by dint of the said decree execution case was filed and she obtained registered deed and also obtained legal possession through Court. Though we find that the petitioner is in possession since from date of agreement 1970. No doubt the petitioner is to prove her case before the Court of Settlement as series of decisions have been made that the person who claims is to prove the case. The husband of the petitioner, on evidence, produced all the documents in accordance with law before the Court of Settlement but Court of Settlement without considering all the documents held an erroneous view that the witness was not able to say whereabouts of the scribe and the witnesses of the agreement. But we find that the evidence was taken long after 30 years and during the period none could say whereabouts of the persons who were present 30 years ago and that the said agreement has been tested before the Civil Court earlier and, as such, finding made by the tribunal is not a proper finding of facts and a perverse proposition and, as such, we find that the Court of Settlement did not consider the case of the petitioner to its proper perspective and, as such, we feel that justice will be met if we send the case on remand to the Court of Settlement for proper consideration and disposal of the case. 

19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. 

20. The impugned judgment and order dated 22-2-2001 passed by the Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka in Settlement Case No. 130 of 1997 (ka-149, Block-E, Mohammadpur, Dhaka) in respect of House No. L/1, Block-E, Mohammadpur, Dhaka is hereby set aside. 

21. The Settlement Case No. 130 of 1997 (ka-149, Block-E, Mohammadpur, Dhaka) in respect of House No. L/1, Block-E, Mohammadpur, Dhaka is remanded back to the Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka for proper disposal of the case in accordance with law. In the meantime, parties are directed to maintain status quo in respect of possession and position of the case property till disposal of the Settlement Case No. 130 of 1997 of the Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka. 

The petitioner is permitted to take back the original documents by substituting photostat of the same within 1(one) month and file the same before the Court of Settlement. 

End.

lawyer:
Md. Ashadullah Advocate ----- For the Petitioner (in both the revisions).
