parties:
Kazi Harun Mia ----- Plaintiff-Petitioner
Vs.
Kazi Abdul Mannan ----- Defendant-Opposite-Party
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Hafiz J: The aforesaid two revisions have been arisen out of the same judgment and decree and the Rules were issued and subsequently heard analogously, thus both the Rules are to be disposed of by one judgment.

2. Both the Rules were issued calling upon the opposite party Kazi Abdul Mannan to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 19-4-2012 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 109 of 2010 heard analogous with Title Appeal No. 110 of 2010 and thereby affirming those dated 29-4-2010 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Comilla in decreeing the Title Suit No. 44 of 2001 heard analogous with Title Suit No. 22 of 2001 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. The plaintiff's Case (Title Suit No. 44 of 2001) in short is that Arfan Bibi and Ashab Uddin Kazi jointly got settlement of 60 decimals of land in dispute from the ex-landlord. Arfan Bibi died leaving behind only daughter Bodrun Nessa who sold 31 decimals land to Kazi Esmail by a registered deed No.47 dated 22-6-1944. SA Khatian No. 149 was finally published in equal shares in the name of Kazi Esmail and Kazi Mannan. Kazi Esmail gifted 29 decimals land to the petitioner Kazi Harun Mia, who is his grandson, by a registered deed of Gift dated 14-2-1960 including 4 decimals land of Plot No. 783 and he is in possession of the said land and since then the defendant Kazi Abdul Mannan threatened him and thus he (Kazi Harun) filed the instant suit for permanent injunction.

4. The opposite parties Kazi Abdul Mannan and others as plaintiff's filed Title Suit No. 22 of 2001 against Kazi Harun Mia in the Court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Comilla for partition of the suit land and the plaintiffs case, in short, is that Ashraf Uddin Kazi and Arfan Bibi by a registered Patta of 1314 BS got settlement of the land and by amicable partition Ashraf Uddin Kazi got 34 decimals land and Arfan Bibi got rest 25 decimals land. After the death of Ashraf Uddin Kazi his brother Bosiruddin Kazi inherited his properties and Arfan Bibi sold 25 decimals land to Bosiruddin Kazi by an unregistered deed of 1317 BS at a price of Taka 40 and as a result Bosiruddin Kazi became owner of the said land. Bosiruddin Kazi died leaving behind the said Kazi Abdul Mannan and two daughters and by amicable partition Bosiruddin Kazi got aforesaid 46.5 decimals land and he made a Waqf in favour of Mosque of an area of 30 decimals land by a deed dated 2-9-1952 and thereafter he exchanged the said land with the Mosque Committee by a Exchange deed No.4593 dated 20-11-1981 and filed the instant suit praying for decree of partition impleading Kazi Harun Mia as defendant No.1.

5. In both the suits, parties filed written statement denying the materials allegations made in the plaint. The trial Court on consideration of the records framed separate issues in both the two suits. From the record it appears that the issues in Title Suit No. 44 of 2001 and Title Suit No. 22 of 2001 were framed at the time of passing of the judgment and on that issues judgment was passed by the trial Court and no separate evidence was recorded by the trial Court in both the suits; only evidence was recorded in Title Suit No. 22 of 2001 and decreed the same (Title Suit No.22 of 2001) and dismissed the Title Suit No. 44 of 2001 by the same judgment on 29-4-2010.

6. As against the aforesaid judgment and decree the petitioner as appellant filed two separate appeals being Title Appeal No. 109 of 2010 and Title Appeal No. 110 of 2010 in the Court of District Judge, Comilla and on transfer the said two appeals were heard analogously by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla and by a common judgment dated 19-4-2012 dismissed the said two appeals and thus the petitioner moved the aforesaid two applications before this Court and obtained the Rules.

7. The petitioner filed Supplementary Affidavits and the opposite party filed Counter Affidavit in the aforesaid Revisions.

8. Mr Ashadullah, learned Advocate for the petitioner by referring "cause of action" and "reliefs prayed" from the plaint of the two title suits submits that the cause of action and the relief prayed for in both the suits disclose that the suits as a whole being different in nature and character and thus analogous judgment and recording of evidence in one suit is contrary to law. The learned Advocate then submits that the petitioner being plaintiff of Title Suit No.44 of 2001 was not allowed to adduce evidence to prove his case as defendant which is against the mandate of Order 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure and principle of natural justice. In support of his contention he has referred to the case of Abdul Latif Chowdhury vs Md Nur Hossain reported in 17 BLD (AD) 230 and emphasized on the following portion of the judgment:

"6. It is however desirable that evidence should be taken separately in respect of five different suits and cases and judgment should also be pronounced separately taking into consideration the evidence adduced in each particular suit and case. Evidence in one suit or case shall not be taken as evidence in the other suits or cases."

9. And the learned Advocate further submits that the trial Court passed the impugned judgment and decree by framing fresh issues at the time of writing of the impugned judgment and decree which is against the provisions of Order XIV, rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure as the issues are to be framed before taking evidence after considering the plaint and the written statement and the evidence is to be adduced as per issues framed and as such framing of issues at the time of passing judgment without notice to the parties is illegal and violative of principle of natural justice and in support of his contention he has referred to the case of Md Abdul Jalil Mia vs Nirupuma Ritchil reported in 17 BLD (AD) 63 = 49 DLR (AD) 61 and the relevant portion of the judgment as referred quoted as under:

"8. Order XIV rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure casts a definite responsibilities upon the trial Court to frame issue upon the material assertions by one party and denied by the other and this can be done at any stage of the suit if found necessary provided that the parties are afforded a chance to contest the issue."

10. And the learned Advocate for the petitioner by referring judgment reported in AIR 1994 Allahabad 81 and the judgment of the Appellate Division reported in 8 BLC (AD) 167 submits that the petitioner as plaintiff filed suit for permanent injunction and the opposite parties filed partition suit and both the suits are different kind of suits and there cannot be the same issue in the said suits and as such hearing of the two suits analogously are not permissible in law but simultaneous hearing is permitted by law.

11. On the other hand Mr Md Anwar Hossain, learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that on prayer of the petitioner both the suits were heard analogously and as such he cannot raise that the hearing of the suits analogously is not permissible in law. The learned Advocate further submits that the Court has the inherent power to pass an order for analogous hearing and the petitioner did not raise objection against analogous hearing and framing of issues. Thus, at this stage the petitioner cannot raise objection against analogous hearing and framing issues. He further submits that the parties are same and both the suit land is same and thus there is no bar for analogous hearing of the suits. In support of his contentions he has referred to the cases reported in 51 DLR 352, 50 DLR 441, 30 DLR (SC) 74, 40 DLR 56, AIR 1984 (Orissa) 209, 9 BLT (AD) 148 and 66 DLR (AD) 37.

12. On the other hand Mr Asadullah submits that the consent of the parties to commit illegalities by the Court of law confers no jurisdiction upon a Court of law and the Court of law must act according to law and otherwise it will lead to chaos and anarchy and the cases referred by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties are distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of instant case and thus those are not applicable in the instant case.

13. Heard the learned Advocates for both the sides and perused the record.

<u>14. Admittedly, petitioner Kazi Harun Mia as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 58 of 2001 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Comilla for permanent injunction against the defendant-opposite party Kazi Abdul Mannan which was eventually transferred to the Court of learned Joint District Judge, Comilla renumbered as Title Suit No. 44 of 2001 and other suit i.e. Title Suit No. 22 of 2001 was filed for partion by Kazi Abdul Mannan and others as plaintiffs against the said Kazi Harun Mia as defendant. The "cause of action" and "the relief prayed for" in both the suits are different which indicates that the suits as a whole being different in nature and character and thus the petitioner as plaintiff of the Title Suit No. 44 of 2001 was not allowed to adduce evidence to prove his case as defendant of Title Suit No. 22 of 2001 which was used in passing the judgment and decree in both the suits by an analogous judgment and this is contrary to law and thus the judgment referred by the petitioner reported in 17 BLD (AD) 230 is the appropriate judgment in the instant case. The opposite party failed to show any judgment contrary to the aforesaid judgment. The judgments as referred by the opposite party are not relevant as the facts and circumstances of the cases are quite distinguishable. Considering the facts and circumstances of the aforesaid cases, analogous hearing of the aforesaid suits are not permissible in law. Moreso, the trial Court passed the impugned judgment and decree by framing fresh issues at the time of passing the judgment and decree which is also contrary to law as the issues are to be framed before taking evidence after considering the plaint and then evidence is to be adduced as per issues. I find substance in the aforesaid Rules.</u>

15. In the result, both the Rules are made absolute.

16. The impugned judgment and decree dated 19-4-2012 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 109 of 2010 heard analogous with Title Appeal No. 110 of 2010 are hereby set-aside. Therefore, I am sending those back on remand for simultaneous hearing to the appellate Court below and to take evidence separately in respect of the two suits after framing issues separately and judgment should be pronounced separately taking into consideration the evidences adduced in each particular suit at the earliest possible time.

The lower Court record be sent down to the appellate Court below with the observations made above.

End.

Vs.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated July 31. 2000 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 356 of 1990).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This is defendants appeal by leave against the judgment dated July 31, 2000 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 356 of 1990 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated October 9, 1989 of the Court of District Judge, Noakhali, in Title Appeal No. 282 of 1987 allowing the same and thereby dismissing the suit upon reversing the judgment and decree dated November 18, 1987 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Upazilla Companiganj, Noakhali in Title Suit No. 54 of 1985 decreeing the same. The suit was filed seeking declaration that the judgment and decree dated 18-2-1980 passed in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 is null and void and the same is inoperative in respect of the land described in the schedule attached to the plaint.

2. The suit was filed stating, infer alia. that land of plot No. 203 of Mouza Dakhin Musapur was recorded in the name of the Government in khas khatian No.1, that the said plot comprises 100.80 acres of land, that Government took decision to settle the said land by sub-plotting to different persons, that Mohammad Mia, father of the plaintiffs, a retired defence person, took settlement of 2.50 acres of land of sub-plot No. 203/31 of plot No. 203 in 1968-69 on payment of salami amounting to Taka 125 through DCR dated April 24, 1970 and paid rent for the year 1376 BS by the rent receipt dated April 24, 1970 and he went into possession in 1970, that on the death of Mohammad Mia the plaintiffs were substituted in the settlement case on December 20, 1972 and kabuliyat was executed in favour of the plaintiffs by the Government on July 11, 1981, that defendant Nos. 1- 5 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 in the 2nd Court of Monsif (now Assistant Judge), Noakhali impleading Government as defendant and obtained decree in respect of the land of sub-plot No. 203/31 on February 14, 1980, that in the said suit i.e. Title Suit No. 43 of 1978, plaintiffs were not made parties, that the defendants on the basis of the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 got their names mutated in respect of the land of sub-plot No. 203/31, that the plaintiffs came to know from the Revenue Officer, that on obtaining the certified copy of the plaint and the decree it was noticed by the plaintiffs that the plaintiffs of the said suit i.e. Title Suit No. 43 of 1978, who are defendant Nos. 1-5 in the instant suit filed the said suit seeking declaration of their title in respect of the land of plot No. 203 and not sub-plot No. 203/31 but the defendant Nos.1-5 surreptitiously inserted in the decree sub-plot No. 203/31, that as the said decree in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 clouded the title of the plaintiffs in respect of the land of plot No. 203/31 they were constrained to file the suit, that cause of action arose on May 20, 1985 on which date they obtained the certified copy of the plaint and the decree of the Title Suit No. 43 of 1978.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1-5 by filing joint written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that Afazuddin Mia was the owner and possessor of 2.50 acres of land of plot No. 7825 in mouza Musapur and in his name DS Khatian No. 2376 was prepared, that Afazuddin Mia died leaving the defendants as his heirs and after the death of Afazuddin Mia defendants continued possession, that during the diara survey land of DS plot No. 7825 was erroneously recorded in plot No. 203/31 and the khatian No.1 was prepared erroneously in the name of the Government. that the said wrong record having had clouded the title of the defendants they were constrained to file Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 seeking declaration of title in respect of 2.50 acres of land of plot No. 203/31 which is identical to the land of DS Plot No. 7825.

4. The Government contested the suit i.e. Title Suit No. 43 of 1978, by filing written statement and having had raised objection as to the identity of the land local investigation was held by survey knowing Advocate Commissioner for ascertaining the identity of the land in suit and the Advocate Commissioner filed his report stating that the land of plot No. 203/31 and land of DS plot No. 7825 are identical, that the Government in its written statement did not disclose that the land in suit was leased out to the plaintiffs predecessor. The suit, i.e. Title Suit No. 43 of 1978, was decreed on contest on February 18, 1980, that the allegation of forgery in the decree of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 is not true. that plaintiffs have no right, title and interest in the land of plot No. 203/31.

5. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record decreed the suit upon holding that Exhibit 2 i.e. kabuliyat, shows that the land in suit i.e. land of plot No. 203/31, was settled to plaintiffs father, that plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 surreptitiously inserted dag No. 203/31 in the decree of the said suit, that the identity of the land which was the subject matter of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was uncertain, that land of plot No. 203/31 was settled to plaintiffs predecessor in 1968-69 and as such, in 1978 when the defendant Nos.1-5 filed Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 they had no right, title and interest, that plaintiffs were necessary parties in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 but without impleading them the defendant Nos.1-5 obtained decree in the said suit, that in the usual course of transaction it can be said that plaintiffs father on payment of salami obtained possession of the land of plot No. 203/31 settled to him, that had the plaintiffs being not in possession they would not have executed the kabuliyat on July 11, 1981, that on perusal of the plaint of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 it is difficult to say that decree in the said suit was in respect of the land in suit i.e. land of plot No. 203/31 that as the defendant Nos. 1-5 had obtained the decree in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 without impleading the plaintiffs, as such, the decree so obtained is not binding on the plaintiffs.

6. Defendant Nos.1-5 went on appeal. The appellate Court on scrutiny of the original plaint (as well as the draft copy of the plaint which was produced before the Court at the time of hearing of the appeal) of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 arrived at the finding that the plaintiffs of the said suit filed the suit seeking declaration of their title in respect of 2.50 acres of land of Plot No. 203/31 which is identical to the land of DS plot No. 7825, that the plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 in the face of objection taken as to the identity of the land by the Government prayed for local investigation for ascertaining the identity of the land of plot No. 203/31 and DS plot No. 7825 and in the petition for ascertaining identity of the land of the said Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 plot No. 203/31 was mentioned and the Civil Court Commissioner on ascertaining the land of DS plot No. 7825 and diara plot No. 203/31 submitted the report to the effect that 2.50 acres of land of DS plot No. 7825 is identical to 2.50 acres of land of plot No. 203/31, that the decree in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was drawn showing plot No. 203/31, that some unscrupulous person interpolated the decree passed in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 by overwriting figure 31 with a motive to show that the said figure has been inserted therein, that in the OCR dated April 24, 1970 whereby plaintiffs father was said to have paid salami originally dag number was 203/11 but later on figure 11 was changed to 31 and the change so made is quite visible in the DCR that no rent receipt has been filed although plaintiffs averred in the plaint that they paid the rent on April 24, 1970, that on the death of plaintiffs father the kabuliyat dated July 11, 1981 was executed in their names and therein plot No. 203/31 was mentioned, that plaintiffs have not filed any paper showing that their father or they were inducted in the land of plot No. 203/31 in 1376 BS, that as the plaintiffs came in the scene in July, 1981 and, as such, they were not necessary parties in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 which was decreed in February, 1980, that as the Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was decreed in presence of the Government in respect of the land of plot No. 203/31, the Government had no right to lease out the land in suit to the plaintiffs, that the plaintiffs have not called for the record to show that their father was the proponent for plot No. 203/31, that the plaintiffs are not competent to build a case on the basis of erroneous certified copy of the plaint upon interpolation of the figure 31 below dag number 203 by unscrupulous person, that the finding of the trial Court that the defendants obtained decree in respect of the block plot No. 203 is not correct since in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 identity of the land i.e. land of DS plot No. 7825 and diara plot No. 203/31, was ascertained and found identical. The appellate Court on consideration .of the evidence of the plaintiffs held that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the land in suit and finally, the appellate Court held that the plaintiffs have neither title nor possession in the land in suit and thereupon dismissed the suit upon setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court. The plaintiffs then moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule.

7. The. High Court Division upon making the findings that the land in suit stands recorded in the name of the Government, that in the plaint of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 dag number 203 was mentioned but in the decree dag No. 203/31 was mentioned, that the trial Court disbelieved the case of the defendants, that land of plot No. 203/31 was settled in the name of plaintiffs father who paid the salami and went into possession, that insertion of plot No. 203/31 in the decree of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was mysterious, that plaintiffs were necessary parties in the Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 and, as such, decree in the said suit is not binding upon the plaintiffs, that the appellate Court did not consider the material fact and thereupon reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court and that the appellate Court wrongly held that the plaintiffs were not in possession in spite of the fact that land in suit was settled to plaintiffs father who on payment of salami went into possession and that plaintiffs case of being in possession of the land has been supported by PW 2, that the land in suit having been recorded in the name of the Government and the Government having had settled the land to the different lessees including the father of the plaintiffs as back as in 1968-69 and the fact of settlement to the father of the plaintiffs having not been denied by the defendant Nos. 1-5 and that on the date when Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was filed by the defendant Nos. 1-5 as the plaintiffs were owning and possessing the land of plot No. 203/31 and their names were recorded in the record of right, that plot No. 203/31 was wrongly inserted in the decree of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 although the said plot was not mentioned in the plaint, that Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was instituted long after the settlement of plot No. 203/31 to plaintiffs' father and that the plaintiffs of the instant suit were necessary parties in the said Title Suit made the Rule absolute upon observing that the trial Court "rightly decreed the suit in part but the learned District Judge reversed the judgment and decree against the weight of evidence, as such, the same is not sustainable in law"

8. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 there was local investigation for establishing identity of land of DS plot No. 7825 and the land of Diara Plot No. 203/31 and the report of the survey commissioner was that the land of the said plots is identical, that the appellate Court on scrutiny of the materials, particularly DCR by which plaintiffs' father paid the salami, noticed that in the DCR plot number was 203/11 but later on by overwriting figure 11 was converted to 31 and that the plaintiffs by calling for record of the settlement case did not establish that the settlement case was initiated in the name of plaintiffs' father for the settlement of land of plot No. 203/31.

9. The learned' Counsel for the appellants submits that the appellants brought sufficient materials on record to establish that Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was filed in respect of the land of plot No. 203/31 and in the said Title Suit Government took objection as to the identity of the land in suit i.e. whether land of DS plot No. 7825 comprising 2.50 acres of land identical to the land of Diara Plot No. 203/31 comprising 2.50 acres of land and thereupon by local inspection the identity of the land was ascertained and the identity of the land having been ascertained the Court decreed the suit, i.e. Title Suit No. 43 of 1978, on February 25, 1980 against the Government. The decree so passed in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was not challenged by the Government. That being the state of the matter the plaintiff-respondents in whose name kabuliyat was executed by tile Government on July 11, 1991 were not competent to challenge the title of the defendant- appellants since prior to the execution of the kabuliyat by the Government, the Government ceased to be the owner of the land of Diara Plot No. 203/31. The learned Advocate also submits that the appellate Court being the last Court of fact on scrutiny of the materials on record as well as the evidence, both oral and documentary, having had arrived at the finding that the plaintiffs i.e. respondent Nos.1-4 herein, filed the instant suit on the basis of fictitious certified copy of the decree in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 and the said finding being based on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, and the appellate Court having had not misread or left out of consideration the evidence in arriving at the said finding the High Court Division without discussing the evidence on record and without arriving at a finding that the aforesaid finding of the appellate Court was based on non consideration or misreading of the evidence was in serious error in reversing the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court. The learned Advocate further submits that the suit i.e. Suit No. 54 of 1985, was filed on the basis of interpolated DCR dated 24-4-1970 (Exhibit 1) and the finding of the appellate Court that Exhibit 1 has been interpolated for the purpose of filing the suit being based on consideration, of the evidence and upon scrutiny of the document itself the High Court Division without reversing the said finding of the appellate Court was in error in setting aside the judgment of the appellate Court. The learned Advocate continues that the High Court Division having had not reversed the aforesaid finding as regard Exhibit 1, nor having had held that the said finding of the appellate Court was not based on evidence or, rather to the contrary, to the evidence on record, was in error in reversing the judgment of the lower appellate Court. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the appellants that there is no holding in the name of the plaintiffs and also there is no khatian in the name of the plaintiffs in respect of the land in suit and that no material was placed on record from the side of the plaintiffs to show that on the partial payment of the salami plaintiffs father was inducted into the land for the settlement whereof the Settlement Case No. 20973 of 1968-69 was started.

10. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants, the leaned Advocate-on-Record submits that the High Court Division has quite legally set aside the judgment of the appellate Court since prior to the filing of the Title Suit No. 43 of 1978, plaintiffs father got settlement of the land as regard which Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was filed and that as in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 plaintiffs were not made parties, the judgment and decree therein is not binding on the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate-on-Record also submits that the High Court Division on consideration of the evidence of PW 2 has quite correctly held that the plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit. The learned Advocate-on-Record further submits that the High Court Division was quite correct in holding on the date of institution of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 the plaintiffs were owning and possessing the suit land and their names were recorded in the records of right but in the decree Dag No. 203/31 was wrongly inserted although it was not written in the plaint. Since the Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was instituted long after the settlement of the suit land in the name of the plaintiffs father, the plaintiffs were necessary parties in the suit and the learned Assistant Judge rightly decreed the suit in part

11. The plaintiffs filed the DCR No. 40388 dated 24-4-1970 (Exhibit 1, though in the judgment of the appellate Court referred as Exhibit 5) to show that their father paid salami having land of plot No. 203/31 settled to him. Lower appellate Court on scrutiny of the said Exhibit 1 arrived at the finding that in the said DCR originally plot number wan 203/11 and subsequently the same was changed to 203/31. It may be mentioned from the plaintiffs side no paper was filed to show that after payment of part of the salami they were inducted into possession. On the death of plaintiffs father kabuliyat was executed in favour of the plaintiffs on July 11, 1981. There is no khatian in the name of the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs also did not file any rent receipt to establish that settlement case was initiated to settle land of plot No. 203/31 in the name of plaintiffs father, the record of settlement case was not brought before the Court.

<u>12. It was the case of defendant-appellants that land measuring 2.50 acres of DS Plot No. 7825 of Mouza Musapur bearing DS khatian No. 2376 was owned by their father Afazuddin Mia and that during diara survey land of the aforesaid plot of DS khatian No. 2376 was wrongly recorded in Diara plot No. 203/31 in the name of the Government and in the background of the said fact defendant- appellants filed Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 impleading the Government as defendant. In the said suit Government took objection as to the identity of the land in suit contending that the land of DS plot No. 7825 of DS khatian No. 2376 is not the land of diara plot No. 203/31. Thereupon plaintiffs of the said suit i.e. Title Suit No. 43 of 1978, filed an application for ascertaining identity of the land in suit by a survey knowing Advocate Commissioner, that the land of DS plot No. 7825 of DS khatian No. 2376 and the land of Plot No. 203/31 was relayed by a survey knowing Advocate Commissioner and he submitted the report in the affirmative i.e. land of diara plot No. 203/31 is identical to the land of DS plot No. 7825 of DS khatian No. 2376. Thereupon suit was decreed on February 25, 1980. It may be mentioned kabuliyat in the name of the plaintiffs was executed on July 11, 1981. In that state of the matter no title as regard the land said to have been settled to the plaintiffs vested on the execution of the kabuliyat. Since kabuliyat in the name of plaintiffs was executed on July 11, 1981 and, as such, while Title Suit No. 43 ofl978 was filed plaintiff-respondents were not necessary parties because at the time of filing the suit title as regard the land of said Title Suit was with the Government and accordingly Government was impleaded as defendant in the said suit and the Government contested the suit and the suit was decreed on contest in favour of the defendant appellants. In the afore state of the matter, the High Court Division, in our view, was in serious error in holding that in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 plaintiff-respondents were necessary parties as kabuliyat was executed in their names on July 11, 1981. It may be mentioned by the decree dated February 25, 1980 in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 title in respect of the land of plot No. 203/31 vested in the defendant-appellants. As stated hereinbefore although High Court Division observed that the record of right was in the name of the respondent Nos.1-4 herein but the said finding was made quite contrary to the materials on record in that, record of right, if any, could be prepared in the name of the respondent Nos.1-4 only after execution of the kabuliyat i.e. after 11th July, 1981. The High Court Division has observed that the possession of plaintiff-respondents in the land in suit was proved by the evidence of PW 2. With due deference to the learned Judge of the said Division we like to observe the learned Judge without discussing the evidence of the PW 2 made the finding as regard possession of plaintiff-respondents. The appellate Court on discussion of the evidence of PW 2 discarded the evidence of the said witness since the witness was of a different village that could not say the land in suit is of which particular mouza. The appellate Court also noticed that the witness is not a man of locality where the land in suit situates and also the witness has no land in the neighbor hood of the land in suit. Since the Court of fact on due scrutiny and consideration of the evidence of PW 2 found him an unreliable witness on the question of possession of the plaintiff-respondent Nos.1-4 in the land in suit the High Court Division in the absence of arriving at a finding that the consideration of the evidence as made by the last Court of fact perverse was in error in holding that PW 2 proved the possession of the plaintiff-respondent Nos.1-4. It may be mentioned that plaintiff No.4 examined himself as PW 1 and examined PW 2 in support of their case. The High Court Division without setting aside the finding of the last Court of fact arrived at on detailed consideration of the materials on record that the plaintiff-respondents filed the suit on the basis of fictitious certified copy of the decree of the Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 reversed the judgment of the appellate Court. It has not been held by the High Court Division that the finding of the lower appellate Court as to that plaintiffs filed the suit on fictitious certified copy was contrary to the evidence on record or that was based on non consideration and misreading of the evidence. In the absence of said situation the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction was not well founded in law to set aside the finding of the last Court of fact. The lower appellate Court on examination of the papers filed by the defendant-respondents in support of their case held that in the plaint of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 plot No. 203/31 was mentioned, but some unscrupulous persons blurred the figure 31 by over writing and thereafter replaced the said figure by different ink "with a motive to show that the number '31' was subsequently inserted below the number '203' with motive to create suspicion". The lower appellate Court also noticed that in DCR No. 40388 dated 24-4-1970 (Exhibit I) originally plot number was 203/11 but later on the same was changed to 203/31. The aforesaid finding of the appellate Court is based on critical examination of the DCR (Exhibit 1). It may be mentioned that had the plaintiff respondent Nos.I-4 been in enjoyment of the land or in other words, had plaintiffs father been inducted into possession of the land on the date of payment of the part of the salami on 24-4-1970 they would have certainly paid rent for the period starting from April 24, 1970 till the date of execution of the kabuliyat on July 11, 1981 but from the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1-4's side no rent receipt was filed although pleading that they paid rent. The lower appellate Court also noticed that no khatian was opened in the name of the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1-4. The appellate Court on consideration of the aforesaid facts as well as the other materials on record as mentioned hereinbefore arrived at a finding that plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1-4 were not in possession of the land in suit. It may be mentioned in Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 the Government raised question of identity of the land of DS Plot No. 7825 of DS khatian No. 2376 with the land of diara plot No. 203/31 of khatian No. 1. In the background of the said objection raised by the Government plaintiff of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 filed an application for relaying the land by survey knowing Advocate Commissioner. The lower appellate Court on perusal of the application so filed noticed that therein plot No. 203/31 was written. The lower appellate Court examined the original plaint of Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 and noticed that the plaintiffs filed the suit seeking declaration of title in respect of plot No. 203/31. The defendant-appellants filed sufficient materials before the Court wherefrom the appellate Court was satisfied that the Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was filed in respect of diara plot No. 203/31. The High Court Division without considering the materials noticed and considered by the lower appellate Court in arriving at the finding that Title Suit No. 43 of 1978 was filed in respect of the land of plot No. 203/31 and the said suit was contested by the Government and the Court decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs i.e. the appellants herein, set aside the judgment of the lower appellate Court. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division set aside the judgment of the appellate Court without arriving at the finding that the findings arrived at by the last Court of fact i.e. lower appellate Court, was not based on evidence or that contrary to the evidence on record or that the lower appellate Court made the findings while dismissing the suit without considering as well as upon misreading the evidence on record The revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division in interfering with the finding of fact arrived at by the last Court of fact is limited to the one or more situations as stated here in over and in the absence of the said state of the matter it is beyond the jurisdiction of the High Court Division to interfere with finding of fact of the lower appellate Court and thereupon to reverse the judgment of the lower appellate Court.</u>

13. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore we find merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed with cost of Taka 5,000.

End.

Bivhas Chandra Biswas with NM Borhan for Probir Haider Advocates ----- For the Petitioners.

parties:
Kamakshya Ranjan Haider and ors ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Prafullya Kumar Haider & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Plaintiffs obtained this Rule from a judgment of reversal. They instituted title suit No. 76 of 1995 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Nazirpur, Pirojpur seeking declaration of title in respect of 1.84 acres of land as described in schedule Ga to the plaint. In course of hearing of the Rule, they filed an application for amendment of the plaint seeking addition of a relief for partition and allotment of saham of 1.84 acres of land. The application was allowed by a separate order. The suit is now for partition on declaring the plaintiffs' title in respect of 1.84 acres of land.

2. Plaintiffs' case, in short is, that the suit lands along with other lands appertained to RS khatian No. 21 measuring an area of 12.95 acres belonged to Rajmohon, Ketu and Panchu. Rajmohon had 4.27 acres of land in his share and on his death, his 8 sons Kailash, Rasik, Rojoni, Surjokanto, Rakhal, Piyari and Choto inherited their respective shares. Ketu died unmarried while he was jointly residing with his brother Rajmohon leaving wife Feli and nephew Kailash Chandra. During his lifetime Ketu executed a registered will in respect of his share of land giving 12 annas share to Kailash Chandra and 4 annas share to his wife Feli, specifically pointing out that on her demise Kailash would inherit the entire lands. Accordingly, after the death of Feli, Kailash got Ketu's share of 4.27 acres and inherited 0.59 acres as son of Rajmohan. Jogesh Chandra being the only son of Kailash inherited the said lands but in the RS khatian 4 annas share was wrongly recorded in his name though he had 6 annas share. Panchu died leaving two sons, Kanai Lal and Kalicharan @ Khoka but in the RS and SA khatians more shares than they were legally entitled to were recorded in their names. Jogesh Chandra transferred 1.34 acres of land out of his 4.86 acres by registered kabala dated 19th August 1957 in favour of the plaintiff No. 1, his mother Maloti and the plaintiff No. 4. On the same day, Jogesh also transferred 1.34 acres of land by another deed in favour of the plaintiffs-predecessors Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish. Kalicharan @ Khoka exchanged 0.84 acres of land by a registered deed dated 2nd June 1958 with plaintiffs-predecessors Mohananda, Kaishore and Satish out of his inherited property and in pursuance of that exchange, the plaintiffs-predecessors got lands in Shakhari Kati mouja and Kalicharan got lands in the suit Gaokhali mouja. Mohananda died leaving no issue and accordingly Kaishore inherited his share and on the death of Kaishore, the plaintiffs Nos. 1-3 got his share. Satish also died leaving no issue while residing jointly with his sister Maloti and accordingly, the plaintiffs Nos. 1-3 got his share as well. In this way the plaintiffs are claiming title in respect of 1.84 acres of land.

3. Defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. According to them, in the suit khatian Rajmohon, Ketu and Panchu had 13.13 acres of land and accordingly, each brother had 4.38 acres of land. Rajmohon died leaving 8 sons and each son inherited 0.49½ acres of land. Ketu died leaving no issue and therefore, his brother Panchu Ram inherited his share. In the premises, Panchu had 8.75 acres of land from his share and as reversionary heir of Ketu. Out of 13.13 acres of land, 1.16 acres were settled to the tenants and therefore, Rajmohon, Panchu and Ketu had  11.79 acres of land and accordingly, Panchu Ram in fact had 7.86 acres and after his death, Kanai and Kalicharan, his two sons, inherited the lands. Kanai died leaving 4 sons, Judhusthir, Nittyananda, Gouranga and Narayan. They by 5 registered deeds transferred 3.93 acres of land in favour of defendant No. 3. They claimed that although the RS record was incorrect but their title was not clouded and that the deed of exchange was forged, collusive and the plaintiffs did not acquire any title on the basis of those deeds.

4. Plaintiffs examined 3 witnesses and exhibited series of documentary evidence in support of their claim in the suit lands. The defendants also examined 4 witnesses and filed some documentary evidence in support of their claim. The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the evidence on record decreed the suit in part declaring plaintiffs' title in respect of 1.39-1/3 acres of land. The defendants preferred title appeal No. 91 of 2000 from the said judgment and decree. The learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Pirojpur by judgment and order dated 11th October, 2002 allowed the appeal and set aside those of the trial Court.

5. Admittedly, the petitioners are the co-sharers in the suit khatian. According to the plaintiffs, they have title in respect of 1.84 acres of land in the suit khatian as described in schedule 'ga' to the plaint. On the other hand, the defendant admitted that the plaintiffs are entitled to only 0.49½ acres of land as their predecessor Kailash did not get the share of Ketu and that Ketu's brother Panchu, the defendants' predecessor, inherited his share. Therefore, the main controversy in this suit is, who has inherited share of Ketu? The learned Joint District Judge observed that the record of 4(four) annas share in RS khatian No. 21 (Exhibit 1) in Kailash's name proved that besides inheritance, Kailash got lands from other source and as a result, the RS khatian was prepared. He further observed that the RS khatian did not prove that Kanai and Kalicharan, sons of Panchu, inherited 7.86 acres of land from his father and from the share of Ketu, inasmuch as, in the said khatian Panchu's 1/3rd share was recorded in their names that proved that Punchu did not get Ketu's share. The trial Court further held that plaintiffs' predecessors purchased 2.68 acres of land out of 4.86 acres by two deeds dated 19th August, 1957 (Exhibits 4 and 5) from Jogesh, son of Kailash and after they exchanged 0.84 acres of land from the suit Mouja with Kalicharan, the plaintiffs had 1.84 acres of land in the suit khatian after excluding 0.84 acres, which is the disputed 'ga' schedule lands. By the deeds of exchange the plaintiffs predecessors got 0.84 acres of lands from Shakhari Kathi Mouja and Kalicharan got 0.84 acres of land from the suit Mouja (Exhibits 6 and 6(ka). He further held that Exhibit 2 indicated that Mohananda, Lalit, Adityo and Dwijabor, were sons of Jagabandhu Haider that proved that Mohananda had three full brothers, and thus, in presence of full brothers, Kaishore being the cousin of Mohananda did not inherit Mahananda's share. In view of the above, the trial Court came to the conclusion that Mohamanda had 0.4475 acres of land out of 1.34 acres he along with his brothers acquired by purchase jointly by kabala dated 19th August 1957 (Exhibit 5) from Jogesh, that as the plaintiffs failed to prove that they inherited the share of Mohananda, they were entitled to 2.2325 acres after deducting 0.4475 acres of Mohananda's share, and that out of that lands their predecessors Kaishsore, Mohananda and Satish exchanged 0.84 acres of land with Kalicharan on 10th June 1958, (Exhibit 6(ka)) and thus, they have title in respect of 1.3925 (2.2325-0.84) acres of land in schedule 'ga'.

6. The trial Court further held that on the death of Panchu his two sons Kanai and Kalicharan inherited 2.135 acres each and on the death of Kanai, his sons Judisthir, Nittyananda, Gouranga and Narayan acquired title of 2.135 acres and not 3.93 acres, that the defendant No. 3 failed to produce title deeds that his predecessors Judisthir, Nittananda, Gouranga and Narayan had title in respect of 3.93 acres of land, that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 being the heirs of Kalicharan inherited 2.135 acres of land and therefore, they are entitled to 2.135 acres of land and that the RS khatian proved that Panchu's sons, Kanailal and Kalicharan have inherited his 1/3rd share.

7. The lower appellate Court observed that in the remark column of RS khatian only 0.70 acres of land was shown in the possession of Kailash and other co-sharers were in possession of other plots, that on the basis of such possession 7.96 acres of land was recorded in the corresponding SA Khatian No. 39, in the names of Kanailal and Kalicharan, and 0.70 acres of land in the name of Jogesh in khatian No. 213 and that these khatians proved that despite mentioning 4 annas share in the khatian Kailash was in possession of only 0.70 acres of land. These findings of the Court of appeal below are based upon hypothesis, inasmuch as if Kailash did not get the share of Ketu on the basis of will, there was no reason for recording /4/ annas share in his name in Exhibit-1. His share in the lands of RS khatian would have been equal with his other seven brothers. The Court of appeal below without assigning any reason observed that Kailash was not in possession on the basis of the record which finding is in conflict with earlier finding. The Court of appeal below also did not reverse the findings of the trial Court that this recording in the khatian proved that Kailash got other lands apart from his father Rajmohan. Plaintiffs claimed that this record of /4/ annas share was due to mistake but, in fact, he was entitled to /6/ annas share on the basis of the registered deed of will dated 17th February, 1913 (Exhibit-7).

8. In the RS khatian (Exhibit 1) 3 annas and odd i.e. 1/3rd share, was recorded in the names of Kanai and Kalicharan, the predecessors of the defendants. The trial Court on consideration of this khatian, rightly held that the RS record did not support the claim of the defendants that Panchu inherited the share of Ketu and that after the death of Panchu, his sons Kanailal and Kalicharan did not inherit the share of Panchu. The lower appellate Court did not at all consider these findings of the trial Court and on a superficial consideration of the khatians held that the RS khatian supported the defendants' claim. The Court of appeal below failed to consider that the defendants had knowledge about the recording of /4/ share in the name of Kailash but their explanation was that despite such record, their title was not clouded; they however, failed to substantiate their claim. They have not challenged the RS khatian at any point of time which has presumptive value.

9. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Advocate, fails to explain the basis of recording /4/ annas share in the name of Kailash and the basis for recording 7.96 acres of laud in the SA khatian in the name of defendants' predecessors. Learned Advocate, however, contends that though in the RS khatian less share has been recorded in the names of Kanailal and Kalicharan than they were legally entitled to, the SA khatian has been correctly prepared as they have inherited Ketu's share. This submission of the learned Advocate is the reiteration of the defendants' claim but the defendants have adduced no legal evidence in support of their claim, other than the SA khatian, The recitals in the will disprove their claim.

10. The Court of appeal below disbelieved the plaintiffs' claim on the reasonings that though in the will Kektu's name was mentioned but no schedule of the land was mentioned in it, that the plaintiffs did not prove the signatures of Ketu Rain and the attesting witnesses, and the contents of the will in accordance with law, that the plaintiffs did not mention the will in the plaint but later on they incorporated the story of will by way of amendment, that there is no evidence to show that Ketu Ram died before the Succession Act, 1925 came into force and that as the will was not probated, it was not acted upon and therefore, Kailash did not inherit Ketu's share of 4.27 acres of land. These findings of the Court of appeal below are not only self-contra-dictory but also based upon misconception of law.

<u>11. An amendment in the plaint is allowed for determining the real question in controversy between the parties and once an amendment of the plaint is allowed the amendment will relate back to the date of the institution of the suit and will be operative from that date. The defendants did not challenge the amendment in the plaint and the Court of appeal below, in the premises, erred in law in disputing the plaintiffs' claim only because those facts were not pleaded in the original plaint. The Court of appeal below fell in an error in failing to appreciate that no particular form is necessary in executing a will. It is sufficient if it contains the testamentary wishes of the deceased; the reference in this connection is sections 377 and 378 of the Hindu Law. A will is the legal declaration of the intention of a testator with respect to his property which he desires to be carried into effect after his death. Primarily, the words of the will are to be considered. They convey the expression of the stator's wishes. In Exhibit 7 the testator stated that on his demise, his wife Feli and nephew Kailash would enjoy his property in /4/ and /12/ annas share respectively and that on the death of his wife, Kailash would get her share as well. It is a registered instrument and executed on 17th February, 1913, more than 86 years prior to its filing in Court on 23rd November, 1999 by the plaintiffs from their custody claiming that Kailash got Ketu's share in the khatian on the strength of this will. It being a document of more than 30 years old produced from the proper custody, the Court may presume that (a) the signature and every other part of it which purports to be in the handwriting of the scribe is in that person's' handwriting, (b) the will was executed by Ketu, and (c) the will was attested by the persons by whom it purported to have been attested under section 90 of the Evidence Act. There is also presumption that the will was prepared at the time it was purported to have been prepared. The Court of appeal below has totally ignored this legal aspect of the matter while considering the will, Exhibit 7.</u>

12. The finding of the Court of appeal below that this will has not been acted upon in the absence of the probate of the will is also based upon misconception of law. Apart from the legal position, there are sufficient documentary evidence on record suggesting that this will has been acted upon. In the RS khatiar (Exhibit 1) 4 annas share was recorded in the name of Kailash and if the will had not been acted upon, his share would have been shown equal with his other brothers. Exhibit-6 proved that Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish exchanged 0.84 acres of land by registered deed of exchange with Kalicharan alias Khoka, son of Panchu out of 1.34 acres of land which they purchased from Jogesh son of Kailash by registered kabala dated 19th August 1957 (Exhibit 5). By this deed of exchange (Exhibit 6) Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish got lands from Shakhari Kati Mouja and Kali Charan got lands from the suit Mouja Goakhali (Exhibit 6(ka)). Kalicharan, the predecessor of the defendants acknowledged the title of Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish, who had got those lands from Jogesh. Kailash inherited only 0.59 acres from the share of Rajmohan according to the plaintiffs, and according to the defendants. he inherited only 0.49-1/3 acres bu this son Jogesh had transferred 1.34 acres of land by Exhibit 5 out of the suit khatian. Therefore, unless the deeds, Exhibits 5 and 7, were acted upon, Kalicharan would not have exchanged lands. Therefore, there is no doubt that the will was acted upon, and the defendants predecessor had acknowledged the acquiring of Kailash's title on the strength of the will, and that these deeds of will and exchange being old registered instruments have presumptive value in the absence of contrary evidence.

13. The Court of appeal below misread the RS khatian and observed that the RS khatian No. 21 and SA khatian No. 39 (Exhibit Kha and Kha(1)) proved that 7.96 acres of land were recorded in the names of Kanailal and Kalicharan, sons of Panchu Rain. In RS khatian (Exhibit Kha) which corresponds to Exhibit-1, only 3 annas and odd share has been recorded in the names of Kanailal and Kalicharan. In the SA Khatian 7.96 acres of lands were recorded in their names but in view of the above findings I find no basis of this record. There is no presumptive value of SA Khatian and the defendants-opposite panties have failed to show the basis of recording lands as such. The Court of appeal below disbelieved the plaintiffs claim of transfer of 1.34 +1.34 acres of land by Jogesh by registered kabalas dated 19th August, 1957 (Exhibits 4 and 5) in favour of Kamakkha Ranjan, the plaintiff No. 1, Malati Rani, mother of plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and Laxmi Rani, the plaintiff No. 4, and Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish respectively on the reasonings that Exhibit 4 was a certified copy, which the deed was entered in Volume No. 2770, but they did not call for the original volume for reception of secondary evidence and that the dag, khatian numbers and the areas of the lands in these deeds were identical.

14. The Court of appeal below was of the view that the deeds were created by the predecessor of the plaintiffs Kaishore Chandra for which the original deed (Exhibit 4) was not produced. The Court of appeal below failed to notice that Exhibit 4 was admitted into evidence without any objection and out of 1.34 acres lands transferred by Jogesh in favour of Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish (Exhibit 5), Kalicharan got 0.84 acres by way of exchange from Kaishore, Mohananda and Satish (Exhibit 6 ka). The registration number of Exhibit 4 is 2776 and it was registered in registration book No. 1 at pages 13-15. It was executed by Jogesh in favour of Kamakkah, Maloti and Laxmi Rani. Whereas, Exhibit 5, is registered deed No. 2777 and the said deed was executed by Jogesh in favour of Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish. This deed was entered in registration book No. 1 at pages 16-19. These facts prove that these deeds have been executed simultaneously and that the recipients of these deeds are distinct persons, and also in respect of separate lands out of the total area of 12.95 acres in the khatian. Therefore, there is no doubt that by these deeds different lands have been transferred to different sets of persons out of the same plot. The Court of appeal below on a superficial consideration of these two deeds observed that these deeds were collusively created by Kaishore Chandra.

15. As observed above, Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish, jointly on one side, and Kalicharan on the other exchanged suit plots No. 2209, 2210 and 2213 of Mouja Gaokhali with the lands of mouja Shakharkati of plot Nos. 1557, 2040, 2005, 20089, 2234, 2204, 2205 and 2208 by executing two registered deeds. The Court of appeal below found fault in the deeds on the reasonings that the second parties in those deeds did not put their signatures and that Exhibit 6(ka) was a certified copy. The Court of appeal below failed to notice that the parties did not execute one deed of exchange, rather they executed two deeds and in their respective deeds they put their signatures. The deeds were very old instruments executed on 10th June 1958 and there was reference in Exhibit '6' about Exhibit 6(ka), the original of which was lying with the defendants predecessor as he was the recipients of the lands. In Exhibit 6(ka) Kalicharan acknowledged the title of Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish in respect of 0.84 acres of land of suit plots No. 2209, 2210 and 2213, who got the said lands from Jogesh by kabala dated 19th August, 1957 (Exhibit 5). The defendants simply said that this deed of exchange was collusive but they did not lead any evidence in support of their claim of collusion. This is a registered deed and this deed proved that the deed of will was acted upon and by dint of this will, Kailash got Ketu's share, and after his death, Jogeshinherited the same and thereafter, Jogesh transferred the same to Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish and thereafter, Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish exchanged three plots with Kalicharan. The lands of Shakharkati mouja have been recorded in RS khatian No. 17 (Exhibit 2). Since Khoka @ Kali-charan acknowledged the title of Kaishore, Mahananda and Satish, the Court of appeal below erred in law in holding that this deed of exchange was a collusive one.

16. The Court of appeal below on a misreading of the evidence on record disbelieved the plaintiffs' possession. In support of plaintiffs' possession, they examined 3 witnesses, of them, PW 1 Kamakkha Ranjan Haider stated that he along with other plaintiffs have been possessing 1.84 acres of land in RS khatian No. 21 excluding 0.84 acres of land and also other lands in RS khatian No. 17. In cross-examination, he said that they have been possessing 2.68 acres of land in plots No. 2208, 2209, 2210 and 2213. PW 2 Motaleb Bepari stated that he has been borga cultivating 0.74 acres of land in plot No. 2208, and 1.14 acres in plot No. 2209. The Court of appeal below observed that PW 2 did not corroborate the plaintiffs claim in the plaint. This witness deposed about the lands he was borga cultivating on behalf of the plaintiffs. He was not deposing on behalf of the plaintiffs in respect of their entire lands. The Court of appeal below also disbelieved PW 3 Abdul Latif Miah observing that though he deposed in support of plaintiffs' possession but in course of cross-examination he failed to say the boundary of the suit lands. The Court of appeal below misread his evidence. He stated in course of cross-examination that "মামলার জমির চৌহদ্দী বলতে পারব" He did not say that he could not say the boundary of the suit lands.

17. Apart from the oral evidence, the defendants also admitted the plaintiffs' title and possession at least in respect of 0.49-1/2 acres of land. They did not altogether deny the plaintiffs' title in the suit lands. The plaintiffs are admitted co-sharers in the khatian. Admittedly the suit lands remain in ejmali and in view of the observations of the appellate Court about the maintainability of the suit, the plaintiffs filed an application for amendment of the plaint seeking partition and the application was allowed.

18. Mr Quayum, learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite parties, while supporting the views of the Court of appeal below, submits that in view of section 213 of the Succession Act, 1925 which corresponds section 187 of Act of 1865, the executor or the legatee cannot claim a right in the properties of the testator unless Probate of the will or Letters of Administration in respect of the will has been obtained and proved. This contention of the learned Advocate is devoid of substance. After the Hindu Wills Act, 1870, came into force, a Hindu will is required to be in writing and signed by the testator and attested by two witnesses. No Probate or Letter of Administration is required to be granted in respect of will executed by a Hindu in respect of joint family property. Before passing of the Hindu Wills Act, the estate of the deceased Hindu did not vest in his executor even if a probate was granted to him; the executor became the legal representative of the testator. The grant of Probate or the Letter of Administration took effect only for the purpose of recovery of debts and securing debtors paying the same. This Act of 1870 incorporated section 179 of the Indian Succession Act, 1865 which provided:

"The executor or administrator, as the case may be, of a deceased person, is his legal representative for all purposes, and all the property of the deceased person vests in him as such."

19. Section 179 of the Succession Act, 1865 corresponds to section 211 of the Succession Act, 1925 and this section did not apply to an executor under the Hindu Will, before the Hindu Wills Act came into force. His position was analogous to that of the manager of a minor heir under the Hindu Law. The Probate and Administration Act altered the law and made this section inapplicable to Hindus by deleting section 179. Although section 4 of the Probate and Administration Act contained a provision similar to section 179 of Act of 1865, that section contained a proviso saving the rights of the members of a joint Hindu family. Under this provision the executor derives his title from the will, immediately upon the testator's death his property vests in the executor, for the law knows no interval between the testator's death and vesting of the property. The executor or administrator, by virtue of his office or, in other words, in the character of executor or administrator, takes an estate in the property of the deceased, and a legal character is vested in him. The executor derives his title from the will and not from the probate. Therefore, I find no force in the contention of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties.

20. The Indian Succession Act, 1865 is applicable in this case since the will was executed before the Succession Act 1925 came into force. The Hindu Wills Act applied to certain wills only being those in respect of (a) wills made by a Hindu on or after 1st day of September 1870 within the territories which at the said date were subject to the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal, (section 369(a) of the Hindu Law), and (b) to such wills made outside the territory so far as related to immovable property situated within that limit. The Hindu Wills Act did not apply to all Hindu wills. The Probate and Administration Act, 1881 applied to all Hindu wills. This Act repealed section 179 of the Indian Succession Act, 1865 as part of Hindu Wills Act, but reenacted it as part of itself in section 4. The Probate and Administrative Act and the Hindu Wills Act have been repealed and reenacted by the Indian Succession Act.

21. In Raja Rama vs Fakruddin Sahib 122 IC 504, though the will was executed by a Mohammedan, on consideration of the provisions of Succession Act and Williams of Executors, Vol-1, page 220, it was observed:

"the executor derives his title from the Will. Immediately upon the testator's death his property vests in the executor, for the law knows no interval between the testator's death and the vesting of the property. It follows that before and without obtaining Probate the executor may do most things which appertain to his office thus, he may take possession of the testator's property, he may pay, or take releases of debts owing from the estate; and he may receive or release debts which are owing to it. The grant of Probate does not give him his title: it makes his title certain."

22. In Kadiyala Venkata Subamma vs Katreddi Ramayya 136 IC, 111 (PC) corresponding to 59 IA 112, the will in question was executed by one Madduru Venkata Subanna, a Hindu, some time in 1916 appointing his widow as executrix but she did not obtain probate of the will. She alienated some properties to her adopted son and others. Some beneficiaries of the will instituted the suit to enforce their right to particular parcels of land claiming that shortly after the testator's death the same was allotted to their share or, in the alternative, they claimed partition of the estate on the allegation that the executrix had, in the absence of probate, no power to make, and which were further charged as fraudulent. The suit was decreed. A single Bench of the Madras High Court referred the matter to a Full Bench for deciding "whether an executor appointed by will made in mufassil of the presidency has vested in him the estate of the testator as set out in the Probate and Administration Act, even though such executor does not obtain probate of the will" The Full Bench took into consideration of different provisions of the Wills Act, the Probate and Administration Act, 1881, and sections 179 and 188 of the Succession Act 1865, and answered the point as under:

"In case of Hindu wills to which Hindu Wills Act does not apply, the estate vests in the executor from the date of testator's death and that the provisions of Probate and Administrative Act are applicable, even though probate has not been obtained."

The matter went to the Privy Council. Their Lordships took into consideration sections 4 and 90 of the Probate and Administration Act; which read:

Section 4—An executor or Administrator, as the case may be, of a deceased person is his legal representative for all purposes, and all the property of the deceased person vests in him as such."

"Section 90(1)—An executor or administrator has, subject to the provisions of this section, power to dispose, as he thinks fit, of all or any of the property for the time being vested in him under section 4."

"(2)—The power of an executor to dispose of immovable property so vested in him is subject to any restriction which may be imposed in this behalf by the will appointing him, unless probate has been granted to him, and the Court which granted the probate permits him by an order in writing, notwithstanding the restriction, to dispose of any immovable property specified in the Order in a manner permitted by the Order."

Their Lordships were of the view that the Hindu Wills Act had no application in the case and that greater part of the Probate and Administration Act applied to the will and observed as follows:

"Section 4 makes no reference to probate, nor does the definition of 'executor' in section 3 (again reproduction from the Act of 1865) suggest that probate is any part of his title; he is merely the person to whom the testator has confided the carrying out of his disposition.

"So, too, section 90(2) clearly conceives of an executor not clothed with probate being able to dispose of the property "vested in him under section 4". It makes such power subject to any restriction imposed by the Will "unless probate has been granted", in which case the Court may relieve him from the restriction. In view of the terms of this section their Lordships think it would be impossible to hold that before probate nothing vested in the executor, and that he had no power of disposal at all,"

<u>23. Mr Quayum has not cited any authority in support of his contention. The intention of section 213 of the Succession Act 1925 is that an executor or legatee cannot establish his right as executor or legatee in a Court without obtaining probate, but there is nothing to prevent the executor from dealing with the property of the testator without obtaining probate, because as per section 211 the executor is the legal representative of the testator for all purposes, and all property vest in him as such, so that the grant of probate is not a condition precedent to such acts.</u>

24. In the will in question (Exhibit 7), it was clearly recited by the testator that his brother Panch Kari Haider did not reside in his house and thus he was not entitled to get anything from his estate and that if Panch Kari had looked after his wife in his absence and if he had maintained cordial relationship with Kailash, the executor would in his discretion give him something from his estate. The defendants did not adduce any evidence that Panch Mari looked after Ketu's wife or that he maintained cordial relationship with Kailash and thus he had got some lands from the share of Ketu. The will was not a conditional one and no restriction seemed to have been imposed upon the executor. In the absence of any restriction in the management of the estate, the executor had acquired absolute discretion to manage the estate of the deceased and the will was effective after the death of the testator and Kailash got the share of Ketu. The principles of law stated by their Lordships of the Privy Council are very much applicable in this case. I find no cogent ground to depart from their Lordships' views.

25. The trial Court thoroughly considered Exhibits 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, (ka) and 7 and rightly held that the plaintiffs have acquired title in respect of 1.3925 acres of land in schedule 'Ga' property excluding 0.84 acres of land which they exchanged. The trial Court has rightly held that the plaintiffs have title in respect of 1.3925 acres of land in schedule 'gha' lands. The Court of appeal below did not reverse all the findings of the trial Court. It had superficially considered the evidence and dismissed the suit by making conflicting findings. In view of the above, I find that the judgment of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal, which is liable to be interfered with. The Court of appeal below has committed error of law in interfering with the judgment of the trial Court which has occasioned as failure of justice. There is merit in this Rule.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment of the Court of appeal below is set aside and restored those of the trial Court subject to the modification that the plaintiffs are entitled to a saham of 1.3925 acres of land in schedule 'ga' to the plaint subject to payment of requisite court fees within one month of the date of receipt of the record. I direct the parties to amicably partition the lands within 60 days from the date of receipt of the record, failing which, the plaintiffs are entitled to get their saham allotted through Court by appointment of an Advocate Commissioner.

End.
