full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: In the aforesaid Rules Nisi, the only issue that is raised is as to whether or not the enhancement of the customs duty on the Grey Portland Cement by the Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-1998 by reducing exemption under section 19 of the Customs Act, 1969, hereinafter referred to as the Act, was lawful, valid and constitutional.

2. In the writ petitions, the petitioners are not the same but all of them imported said cement. According to the petitioners, they were entitled to pay duty pursuant to the Notification being SRO No. 108 dated 11-6-1998, which exempted duty above 15% and was in force at the time of opening of their letters of credit instead of the duty at the enhanced rate in accordance with the Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-1998 exempting duty above 30% ad valorem under section 19 of the Act.

3. The petitioners imported said cement by opening letters of credit on different dates but

before 20-10-1998 the date when the subsequent Notification being SRO No. 233 came into force. The bills of entry for clearance of said cement were also submitted on different dates before and after said date of subsequent Notification.

4. Pursuant to issue of the Rules and directions issued by this Division, the petitioners got release of their respective goods on payment of the duty and other charges on the basis of exemption of duty above 15% in cash and furnishing bank guarantee(s) for the balance between the two rates of exemption.

5. Dr M Zahir, learned Senior Advocate, took us through the relevant provisions of the Act and submitted that the Government acted beyond its jurisdiction in issuing subsequent Notification being SRO dated 20-10-98 enhancing the rate of duty.

6. He submitted that the exemption given by the Notification being SRO No.1 08 dated 11-6-98 and on the basis of which the petitioners opened their letters of credit for import of the cement vested a right in them to get the cement cleared on the basis of earlier rate of exemption that was in force at the time of opening of the letters of credit and the Government was estopped from asking any further duty on the basis of subsequent Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-98.

7. In support, he cited the authorities in the Collector of Customs vs A Hannan: 42 DLR (AD) 167; Collector of Customs vs Ahmed Hossain: 48 DLR (AD) 199; Mustafizur Rahman vs Bangladesh: 51 DLR (AD) 40; Commissioner of Customs vs Monohor Ali and others: 2003 BLD (AD) 51 = 8 BLC (AD) 87 = 8 MLR (AD) 113; Bangladesh and others vs Mizanur Rahman: 52 DLR (AD) 149.

8. Mr Nahid Mahtab, learned Deputy Attorney- General for the respondents, first read the subsequent Notification being SRO 233 dated 20-10-98 and submitted that the Government was fully competent to change the rate of exemption under section 19 of the Act and such discretion is now limited to exercise once in a year so as to change the rate of exemption by introduction of the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 19 of the Act by the Act No. 15 of 2000.

9. At our request, Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Advocate also appeared as an amicus curiae. He took us through the history of development of the concept of vested rights and the principles of estoppel in the matter of levy and collection of customs duty and other charges.

10. He submitted that in view of sections 19,30 and 30A, subsequent Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-98 which reduced only the rate of exemption that was earlier granted under section 19 of the Act vide the Notification being SRO No. 108 dated 11-6-98 is wholly valid and constitutional and an importer has got no vested right in such exemption.

11. He also read the judgment of A Hannan vs Collector of Customs passed by a Division of this division and reported in 40 DLR 273. He submitted that very basis of the concept of vested rights and/or the principles of estoppel were first initiated in our jurisdiction by a Division Bench presided over Mr Justice Mustafa Kamal, as His Lordship was then, on the view that sections 19 and 30 of the Act were mutually exclusive and independent in their course of operations and in the language of section 19 the Government cannot issue notification with retrospective effect with the canons of construction of delegated legislation. At the time, he submitted, section 30A of the Act was not yet added.

12. We have perused the records of the cases as are available. We have also read the decisions cited. In order to appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocates, we need to read the relevant provisions of the Act, in particular, sections 18, 19, 30 and 30A of the Act, which we would do a little later.

13. Before that, we hope the facts of one case would be sufficient to understand the issue raised and the questions of law involved on the concept of vested rights and/or the principles of estoppel in the matter of levy and collection of the customs duty and other charges pursuant to the provisions of exemption under section 19 of the Act.

14. In Writ Petition No. 3541 of 1998, it is stated that the petitioner on 23-9-98 established a letter of credit for import of 7,000 metric tons of Grey Portland Cement from Indonesia at US$ 41,500 then revised to US$ 2,53,150.00 (15% more or less). At the time, the Notification being SRO No. 108 dated 11-6-98 exempting the duty above 15% of said cement ad valorem was in force, Annexure-D to the writ petition. For our understanding, we can say the duty on said cement was 15% only ad valorem at the time, the duty above thereto was exempted. While said cement was on the voyage on the way to Bangladesh, the Government published a Notification being SRO No 233 dated 20-10-98 reducing the exemption from 15% to 30%, thereby enhancing the duty of said cement to 30% ad valorem, Annexure- E. Expecting arrival of the ship at the Chittagong Port by 11-11-98, five bills of entry at the rate of duty at 15% ad valorem were on 5-11-98 submitted. But the customs authority assessed said cement to duty at the rate of 30% on the basis of subsequent Notification being SRO dated 20-10-98 and supplementary duty at the rate of 4% on the basis of the Ordinance No.1 of 1998 for augmenting the rehabilitation of the flood affected people. The petitioner unsuccessfully appealed to respondent No.3, the Commissioner of Customs at Mongla Customs House at Khulna against such assessment. Then, he moved this Division and obtained a Rule nisi and direction for release of the goods at the aforesaid terms.

15. Now, let us read the decisions cited at the Bar. In A Hannan's case, (decided on 9 June, 1998) during the crisis of sugar when the rate of duty was 100%, the Government exempted duty on sugar above 50% by a notification dated 16-10-84. Petitioner opened letter of credit on 31-10-84 for import of 500 metric tons of sugar of South Korean origin and on 24-11-84 the vessel carrying sugar arrived at Chittagong. Meanwhile, the Government by another notification dated 6-11-84 enhanced the rate of duty by exempting duty above 75% ad valorem. Rejection of the customs authority of the prayer of the importer to pay duty at the earlier rate of duty at 50% instead of the new rate of 75% ad valorem was challenged in a writ petition before this Division.

16. A Division Bench of this Division set aside the order on the following views:

"We are absolutely convinced that section 19 of the Customs Act does not provide any "rate of duty" at all. It only provides for exemption of "any goods" from the whole or any part of the customs-duties chargeable thereon. Section 30 does not refer to section 19 at all. To put it plainly. section 30 will operate only insofar as the "rate of duty" levied under section 18 is altered or amended. It has no reference to section 19 at all. To put it plainly, section 30 will operate only insofar as the "rate of duty" levied under section 18 is altered or amended. It has no reference to section 19 at all. Notifications issued under section 19 will follow their own course, independently of section 30, and these notifications will be construed in accordance with the canons of construction of delegated legislation.

.................... .................... .................... ....................

.................... .................... .................... ........................................ ....................

There is nothing in the language of section 19 of the Customs Act to indicate that the Government can issue Notification with retrospective effect."

17. In the appeal therefrom at the instance of the Collector of Customs, the Appellate Division was of the view that,

"That it is a clear case of estoppel, inasmuch as the respondent had acted on the assurance given by the Government and a right vested in him and that could not be taken away. It was no where mentioned in the Notification that the delivery of the bill of entry will be determining factor, as Mr Bhuiyan intends to suggest.

.................... .................... ....................

The respondent acting upon the solemn promise made by the appellant incurred huge expenditures and if the appellant is not held to its promise, the respondent would be put in a disadvantageous position and therefore, the principle of promissory estoppel can also be invoked in this case."

Upon such view, the Appellate Division dismissed the appeal by its decision dated December 6, 1989 reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167.

18. In the case of Ahmed Hossain. 48 DLR (AD) (decided on 9-7-96) forty leave petitions of the Collector of Customs were dismissed. In similar circumstances, the order of this Division setting aside the assessment of duty by the customs authority at the rate of duty as per the Notification issued under section 19 of the Act in force on the date of bill of entry presented and not the Notification in force on the date of opening of the letter of credit for import of Red Cow Condensed Milk was upheld. The Appellate Division considered and approved the case of A. Hannan on the following view:

"We do not think that the difference in facts would make any difference in the application of the principle which is based on interpretation of sections 19 and 30 of the Customs Act, 1969."

19. Insertion of section 30A of the Act was noticed by the Appellate Division for the first time and disposed of the submissions on the change in law with the following view:

"It will be merely academic now to try and resolve the alleged conflict of decisions with regard to the interpretation of sections 19 and 30 as argued by the learned Additional Attorney- General."

20. In the case of Mizanur Rahman, 52 DLR (AD) 149 (decided on 1-6-2000), the Appellate Division set aside the decision of this Division and allowed the appeal accepting the assessment on the enhanced rate of tariff value on the imported G. Plain Sheets that was in force on the date of bill of entry presented and not on the rate of tariff value on the date of opening of letter of credit on the following views:

"The argument of acquiring vested right may be tenable in case of exemption granted in a special circumstance as in Hannan s case but it is difficult to understand the normal importer would acquire vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value prevailing at the time of opening of letter of credit.

.................... .................... ...................

The customs duty payable on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry and not on the basis of invoice value or tariff in force at the time of opening of the letter of credit.

.................... .................... ....................

No vested right is acquired by the importer to pay sales tax and customs duty on the basis of tariff value declared by notification in force on the date of opening the letter of credit. The importer has to pay tax and duty on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of bill of entry."

It also held that

"So, the decision in 51 DLR (AD) 40 (Mustafizur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh and 6 others) appears to us not correctly decided due to the failure of the then Attorney-General to point out the distinction between 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 on the one hand and the case of Mustafizur Rahman on the other."

21. In Monohar Ali, (2003 23 BLD (AD) 59 = 8 MLR (AD) 113 (decided on 13-7-2002) the withdrawal of CRF scheme before the presentation of the bill of entry for clearance of imported goods came up for consideration. Section 30A was considered of course, vis-a-vis section 25A of the Act. In allowing the appeal, the Appellate Division held-

" ........... section 30A came into effect on 1-7-95 and the present consignments were imported subsequent to that date. However, it also appears that both section 30A and section 25A came into operation on the same date i.e. on 1-7-95 but in section 30A there is nothing to suggest that it excluded the operation of section 25A of the Customs Act.

.................... .................... ....................

at the relevant time the section contained non-obstante clause like, "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act; which means that it included 30A of the Customs Act.

Therefore, section 25A would prevail over all other sections including sections 25(7) and section 30A of the Customs Act."

(underlined by us)

22. The ratio decidendi of the decision as under- lined by us appears to be that because of the non-obstante clause, section 25A providing the CRF value of the imported goods would prevail over all other provisions of the Act including sub-section (7) of section 25 (levy of tariff value) and section 30A (value and effective rate of duty) of the Customs Act. In holding such view, it relied upon a number of decisions including that of A Hannan.

23. In the case of Selim (Haji) vs Collector of Customs: 54 DLR 287, a Division Bench of this division considered for the first time the scope of the exemption under section 19 in the context of section 30 and 30A. It discharged the Rule on the following views:

" ... that once exemption is granted as to imposition of customs duty the same cannot be changed or varied does not have any leg to stand and for that reason the said proviso has been added later on with the provision of section 19(1) and in this case, we have already stated that the bill of entries were submitted before the proviso came in and therefore, it is not applicable.

We have already stated that it is neither increasing or decreasing. It can be called a with drawal of the exemption. So, it is very much within the jurisdiction of the customs authority to withdraw the exemption, as was before the addition of the said proviso, up to the ceiling as affixed by the 1st Schedule of the Finance Act. So, the argument of Dr Zahir, having no substance in this respect, it is repelled."

24. We have closely read the aforesaid decisions particularly those of the Appellate Division. We find in the case of A. Hannan only the scope of section 19 of the Act empowering exemption was considered. It is also noted that after said decision, section 30A was inserted in the Act with effect from July 1, 1995. After such insertion, section 30A was just noticed in the case of Ahmed Hossain disposing 40 leave petitions but no interpretation or construction of section 30A in the context of sections 19 and 30 was thought to be necessary since the case was not on the exemption under section 19 of the Act. In the case of Monohar Ali, section 30A was for the first time considered by the Appellate Division and in the context of section 25(7) and section 30 of the Act. In the case of Mizanur Rahman, the Appellate Division in dispelling the argument on the concept of vested rights and principles of estoppel regarding levy of tariff value under section 25(7) observed: "The argument of acquiring vested right may be tenable in case of exemption granted in a special circumstance as in Hannan s case but it is difficult to understand the normal importer would acquire vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value prevailing at the time of opening of letter of credit". So, the decision of the High Court Division in the case of A. Hannan on exemption under section 19 of the Act before the insertion of section 30A in the Act upheld by the Appellate Division was referred to the cases of Ahmed Hossain, Mizanur Rahman and Monohar Ali on different contexts.

25. Now, we shall examine the relevant provisions of the Act with regard to exemption of the duty, in particular sections 18, 19,30 and 30A of the Act, which were at the relevant time as follows:

18. Goods Dutiable: (1) Except as hereinafter provided, customs duties shall be levied at such rates as are prescribed in the First Schedule or under any other law for the time being in force on-

(a) goods imported into, or exported from, Bangladesh ;

(b) goods brought from any foreign country to any customs station, and without payment of duty there, transshipped or transported for, or thence carried to, and imported at, any other customs station; and

(c) goods brought in bond from one customs-station to another.

(2) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, levy, subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions as it may deem fit to impose, a regulatory duty on all or any of the goods specified in the First Schedule at a rate not exceeding fifty percent of the rate, if any specified therein read with any notification issued under sub-section (1) of section 2 or sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Protective Duties Act. 1950 (LXI of 1950) Or at a rate not exceeding hundred percent of the value of such goods as determined under section 25.

(3) The regulatory duty levied under sub- section (2) shall be in addition to any duty imposed under sub-section (1) or under any other law for the time being in force.

(4) Any notification issued under sub-section (2) shall, if not earlier rescinded, stand rescinded on the expiry of the financial year in which it was issued]

19. General power to exempt from customs-duties. If the Government is satisfied, after consultation with the Board, that it is necessary in the public interest to do so, it may, subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions, if any, as it thinks fit to impose, by notification in the official Gazette, exempt any goods imported into, or exported from Bangladesh or into or from any specified port or station or area therein, from the whole or any part of the customs-duties chargeable thereon.

(2) An exemption granted under sub- section (1) shall be effective from the date mentioned in the notification issued under that sub- section.

30. Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff value of imported goods. The rate of duty and tariff value, if any, applicable to any imported goods, shall be the rate of duty and tariff value in force,

a) in the case of goods cleared for home consumption section 79, on the date a bill of entry is presented under section and a bill of entry number is allocated thereto;

(b) in the case of goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumption under section 104, on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse, and

(c) in the case of any other goods, on the date of payment of duty.

Provided that if a bill of entry is presented in anticipation of arrival of a conveyance by which the goods are imported, the relevant date for .the purpose of this section shall be the date on which the manifest of the conveyance is delivered after its arrival.

31A. Value and effective rate of duty- Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or any decision of any court, for the purposes of section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed under section 18, 18A or 18B and the amount of duty, that may have become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for the sale of such goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof.

26. Close reading of the above provisions on exemption make it clear to us that the customs-duty shall be levied at such rates as are prescribed in the First Schedule or under any other law for the time being in force on goods imported into or exported from Bangladesh. First Schedule is always passed by the Parliament along with the Finance Act under section 18 of the Act. Such levy of duty by the Parliament does not appear to be absolute in view of the qualifying clause at the beginning of the section that "Except as hereinafter provided" that subject to other provisions of the Act. Section 19 of the Act, on the other hand, empowers the Government to exempt any goods imported into or exported from Bangladesh by notification in the official gazette from the whole or any part of the customs-duties chargeable thereon, obviously under section 18. Before declaring such exemption, the Government, of course, shall consult with the National Board of Revenue and be satisfied that such exemption was necessary in the public interest.

27. The following proviso was subsequently inserted in sub-section (1) of section 19 of the Act,

Provided that if, in a financial year, exemption under this sub-section is given in respect of any goods the rate of duty cannot be changed more than once in that year so as to increase that rate.

28. Any exemption under section 19 of the Act shall naturally affect the rate( s) of duty levied by the Parliament in the First Schedule or otherwise to change. Such power of the Government to exempt duty is clearly intended by the Parliament to affect the rate(s) of duty levied by it. After insertion of the proviso to sub-section (1), the Parliament clearly ordained that in a financial year the rate of duty cannot be changed more than once in that year in which year if any exemption is given to increase that rate. Plain meaning of such proviso appears to us that the Government cannot exercise its power to declare exemption more than once in a financial year to increase the rate of duty in that very year. Mr. Mahmudul Islam told us that during the crisis of sugar in the country in 1980s exemption of the customs duty was declared many a times in a year causing some kind of unrest in the market of sugar. So, the Parliament had to intervene and insert the proviso limiting the time of exercise of the Government power.

29. Section 30 of the Act clearly provides that the rate of duty and tariff value shall be the rate of duty and tariff value in force on the date the bill of entry is presented under section 79 in case of goods cleared and under section 104 in case of goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumption. Such rate of duty must be the rate which suffered change after any exemption declared by the Government under section 19 of the Act. Introduction of section 30A in the Act, we believe, removed all controversies or confusion created, particularly by the decisions in the case of A. Hannan relating to the effective rate of duty and date of enforcement of such rate.

<u>30. In view of the opening non obstante clause in section 30A, "Notwithstanding any decision of any Court, for the purpose of section 30," the value and rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed by section 18, 18A or 18B and the amount of duty that may become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty say under section 19 whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for sale of goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof. Under the sweep of such obstante clause, the binding effect of the authority of A Hannan decided on 9-7-89 on the doctrine of vested rights and/or the principles of estoppel in the matter of exemption of customs duty deems to have been washed away. After introduction of section 30A, the rate(s) of duty on any goods levied under section 18 if was affected to change by any Notification issued by the Government exempting the whole or any part of the rate(s) of duty on such goods under section 19 such changed rate(s) of duty would be in force on the date of presentation of a bill of entry for clearance of goods under section 30 of the Act without any reference to the date of opening of a letter of credit.</u>

<u>31. For the reasons aforesaid, there is no substance in the submissions of Dr Zahir. We find subsequent Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-98 valid, competent and constitutional and the importers had no vested rights in the rate of exemption first declared by earlier Notification being SRO No. 108 dated 11-6-98, which was changed by subsequent Notification increasing the rate of duty.</u>

32. In the result, all the above Rules are discharged with cost.

The Customs Authority shall be at liberty to encash the bank guarantees if the petitioners do not pay in cash the amount of money covered by respective bank guarantees within a period of thirty days of receipt of this order.

End.

lawyer:
MA Quddus Sheikh, Advocate -----For the Petitioner. 
Md Mozammel Huq, Deputy Attorney-General with Sk Taimur Reza Hasan, Assistant Attorney-General with Md Moslem Uddin, Assistant Attorney-General -----For the Respondents.
parties:
Hamida Begum ----- Petitioner 
Vs.
Bangladesh and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
SM Emdadul Hoque J: In the instant writ petition, the petitioner challenged the legality and propriety of inclusion of the case property in the list of abandoned buildings. The Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 22-7-1995 (Annexure-'E' to the writ petition) passed by the respondent No. 1 should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Briefly, the facts of the case are, that, the case holding No. U/23, Block-D, Noorjahan Road Mohammadpur, Dhaka under Layout Plan No. 127/1961-62 dated 20-7-1961 had originally belonged to the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan and the same was leased out, to one A. Rafique, by a, registered\case deed being No. 9256 (Page Nos. 221-225 Volume No. 100, Book No.1 of Dhaka Sadar Sub-Registry Office) and the possession there of also delivered in favour of the said original allottee A Rafique by virtue of letter No. 7915/1(1) dated 5-10-1961 and he paid the full costs of the house. Before liberation of Bangladesh he got a clearance certificate from the Administrative Officer, Mohammadpur Housing Estate Dhaka on 2-9-1969 vide Memo No. 166-A/O Since then he was in possession of the case property. The original allottee A. Rafique started to construct a two-storied building on the case property in the year 1969 but he could not complete the same for financial crisis for which he had no option but to sell out the suit property and made an agreement with the petitioner on 25-1-1971 and received Taka 15,000 as advance out of total consideration amount of Taka 30,000 and both the parties agreed that the Kabala will be executed arid registered on payment of Taka 15,000 to be paid within 30 days from the date of intimation by original lessee A Rafique who was supposed to execute the same after obtaining income tax certificate and other necessary papers and also to hand over the physical possession of the case property in favour of the petitioner. Subsequently, said lessee A. Rafique received Taka 10,000 from the petitioner endorsing the same in writing on the back page of the said deed of agreement Havins no response from the said A Rafique for a long period petitioner approached to execute and register the sale deed in respect of the case property which was refused by the said A Rafique; consequently the petitioner was compelled to file Title Suit No. 927 of 1981 before the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court Dhaka for specific performance of contract making the said A Rafique as defendant, wherein Government of Bangladesh was also a party. Summons were duly served upon all the parties in accordance with law and the said original lessee A Rafique duly appeared before the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka and filed written statement on 22-4-1982, ultimately the said Title Suit No. 927 of 1981 was decreed ex parte on 4-12-1983. Thereafter the petitioner by depositing Taka 5,000 to execute and register the sale deed and in compliance of the decree the petitioner got the deed of sale executed and registered vide deed No. 2433; dated 5-9-1991 and accordingly, the same was executed and registered by the said court. The petitioner has been in physical possession of the case property from its original owner since from bainapatra and before the commencement of President's Order 16 of 1972 and the physical possession of the said property has never been taken over by the Government. The petitioner subsequently came to know that the case property has been declared as abandoned property and published in the official Gazette on 23-9-1986 in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property. Finding no other alternative, the petitioner filed an application under section 7(1) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 before the Court of Settlement and appeared regularly in the said Court. But for the time being the court was not continuing due to the quorum of the court. Subsequently, the court was resumed and without giving any notice to the petitioner the Court of Settlement rejected the application by his judgment and order dated 22-7-1995.

3. Being aggrieved the petitioner filed this writ petition and obtained present Rule.

4. Mr MA Quddus Sheikh, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the property in question has never been taken over by the Government and no notice was issued or served to hand over possession of the same to the authority but the said property was most illegally included in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property by violating the mandatory provision of law. He further submits that the petitioner filed application before the Court of Settlement and the notice was duly served upon the parties but subsequently, the court was not in session/operation due to the quorum and constitution of the court and thereafter, when the court was reconstituted and was resumed on 20-7-1995 no intimation was given and on the next day the Court of Settlement, without giving the petitioner an opportunity of being heard, rejected the application which is illegal, without jurisdiction and is of no legal effect. He further submits that though the petitioner earlier received notice and accordingly, appeared before the Court of Settlement regularly, taken all steps in accordance with law but due to the quorum of the constitution of the Court the Court of Settlement was not in session for a long period and when the Court was reconstituted and resumed, in such event provisions of transfer of court is to be observed and, in such situation, fresh notice to the parties are to be served. In support of his submission, he referred section 10 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 and submits that to consider the application, the Court of Settlement shall follow the provisions as laid down in the Civil Procedure Code and accordingly, summons to the parties are to be served and examining the witnesses but Court of Settlement, without giving any opportunity of being heard, disposed of the matter. He further submits that according to section 24A, summons to be served to the parties and fixing a day for appearance of the parties before it and in the instant case, the court after resumption of Its constitution/quorum did not issue any notice upon the petitioner and, as such, the petitioner could not appear and produce the documents before the Court of Settlement which is a violation of the principle of natural justice and thus, the judgment of the Court of Settlement is illegal and without jurisdiction. He further submits that the Court of Settlement opined that the case is barred by 135 days which is miscalculation of the date of filing. He further submits that the petitioner filed the application before the Court of Settlement in time and the court itself mentioned that the case was filed on 8-1-87 where the Gazette was published on 23-9-1986 and thus the statutory period of 108 days ended on 9-1-87 but the Court of Settlement miscalculated that the petitioner filed the application after 135 days which amounts to misapplication of facts and, as such the said finding is not sustainable in law and liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. In support of his argument, he referred several cited cases reported in 53 DLR (AD) 99, 57 DLR (AD) 97, 56 DLR (AD) 101 and 48 DLR (AD) 13.

5. Mr Md Mozammel Huq, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondents, submits that the Court of Settlement after considering the evidence on record opined that the case property has been rightly listed in the "Ka" list of abandoned buildings after observing all the formalities by the authority. He further submits that Court of Settlement decided the matter on merit and opined that the petitioner could not prove his case and that the inclusion of the case property was rightly done and in such a situation the same could not be interfered by this Hon'ble Court in writ jurisdiction. He further submits that summons were duly served upon the parties and thus they appeared before the Court of Settlement and the petitioner had knowledge about the next date but he did not appear before the Court of Settlement nor took any steps. Thus, the Court of Settlement had no alternative but no deliver the judgment on merit which should not be interfered and prayed for discharging the Rule.

6. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and perused the record. Admittedly, the petitioner filed the application before the Court of Settlement on 8-1-1987, thereafter he appeared before the court regularly. On perusal of the order Nos. 8-10 of the Court of Settlement it appears that the Court of Settlement was not continuing from 28-1-1995 to 26-7-1995 due to the quorum of the court, but the court resumed on 20-7-95, as such, the petitioner could not appear before the court and the Court of Settlement fixed the date and delivered the judgment on 22-7-95 Order Nos. 8, 9 and 10 are the relevant orders which run as follows:

আদেশ : ৮

২৮-১-১৯৯৫

অদ্য শুনানীর জন্য ধার্য আছে। পক্ষগণ হাজিরা দাখিল করিয়াছে, বর্তমানে আইনগত ভাবে কোর্ট গঠিত না থাকায় পুনরায় আগামী ২৫/৪/১৯৯৫ ইং তারিখ ধার্য্য করা হইল।

আদেশঃ ৯

২৫-৪-১৯৯৫

অদ্য শুনানীর জন্য ধার্য্য। সরকার পক্ষের হাজিরা দিয়েছেন। বর্তমানে আইনগত ভাবে কোর্ট গঠিত না থাকায় আগামী ২০-৭-১৯৯৫ ইং তারিখ শুনানীর জন্য ধার্য্য করা হইল।

আদেশঃ ১০

অদ্য শুনানীর জন্য ধার্য্য। সরকার পক্ষে হাজিরা দিয়েছে বাদী কোন প্রকার পদক্ষেপ গ্রহন করে নাই মামলা শুনানীর জন্য লওয়া হইল। সরকার পক্ষে নালিশী সম্পত্তি সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রণালয়ের নথি দাখিল করিয়াছে। সরকার পক্ষে বিজ্ঞ আইনজীবী বক্তব্য সুনানী অন্তে আগামী ইং- ২২/৭/১৯৯৫ তারিখে রায় প্রচারের জন্য ধার্য্য করা হইল।

7. From the above order sheets it appears that the Court of Settlement was not continuing from 28-1-1995 to 26-7-1995 due to the quorum of the Court and the Court has been resumed on 20-7-1995 but we do not find any evidence that the parties were duly summoned after reconstituting the Court.

8. Section 10 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 provides that for disposal of the case the Court of Settlement should have followed the Code of Civil Procedure. The Court of Settlement was not in session due to the quorum of the Court for some period and when it was constituted and restarted which amounts to transfer of the court. Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows:

(1) Where any suit is transferred under section 22 or any suit appeal or other proceeding is transferred or withdrawn under sub-section (1) of section 24 on the application of a party the Court ordering the transfer or withdrawal shall fix a date for the appearance of the parties before itself, if the suit appeal or other proceeding is to be tried or disposed of by itself or before the Court to which the case is transferred.

Where any suit appeal or other proceeding is transferred from one Court to another otherwise than on the application of a party the parties thereto shall appear before the Court from which the suit appeal or other proceeding is to be transferred on the day already fixed for their appearance before that Court, and such Court shall then communicate the order of transfer to such parties and direct them to appear before the Court to which the suit, appeal or other proceeding is to be transferred either on the same day, or on such earliest day as may be reasonable having regard to the distance at which the other Court is located.

9. From the above section it appears that when the suit was transferred otherwise an application of the party the court shall then issue notice to the parties but in the instant case the parties were not informed to appear before the court when the court resumed after reconstitution, It further appears that the Court of Settlement opined that the case is barred by limitation but we find that the gazette notification was published on 23-9-1986 and the limitation was for 108 days; the petitioner tiled the case on 8-1-1987 within 107 days which is within due time and, as such, it appears that the finding made by the Court of Settlement fully miscalculated and misread the fact of limitation, inasmuch as the court did not apply its judicial mind. In the case of Bangladesh vs Nasima Khatoon reported in 57 DLR (AD) 97 it has been held that it appears the Court of Settlement did not consider the documents filed by the respondents. While passing the judgment and order it did not apply its Judicial mind. In this view, the judgment passed by the Court of Settlement is not maintainable, and in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Hafizur Rahman reported in 53 DLR (AD) 99 it has been held the "the Court of Settlement did not dispose of the application on merit which it is required to do under the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and instead, dismissed the application as the respondents were not present in the Court. By not deciding the case on merit the Court of Settlement acted illegally and without lawful authority."

10. Admittedly, the Court of Settlement was not in session due to quorum for some period and when it was resumed after due reconstitution the petitioner had reasonable expectation that he should be informed, but it was not done. Consequently, the petitioner could not appear before the court when the matter was taken up for hearing and in such a situation we have no alternative but to interfere with the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement.

<u>11. The Court of Settlement ought to have given an opportunity to the parties to hear the matter by serving notice upon them but it was not done by the Court of Settlement. So, we are inclined to send back and remand the case to the 1st Court of Settlement to hear the matter on merit after due service of notice upon the parties.</u>

12. Considering the facts and circumstance of the case and the discussion made above, it is our considered view that the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

13. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order dated 22-7-1995 (Annexure-"E" to the writ petition) passed by the 1st Court of Settlement Segunbagicha, Dhaka in Settlement Case No. 9 of 1992 is declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The case is hereby sent back on remand to the 1st Court of Settlement, Segunbagicha; Dhaka for disposal of the same in accordance with law after due service of notice upon the parties.

14. Since this is a long pending case, the 1st Court of Settlement Segunbagicha Dhaka is directed to dispose of the matter as early as possible preferably within six months from the date of receipt of the judgment. The petitioner is permitted to take back the original document filed before this court by replacing the attested photostat of the same.

Send down the Lower Court Records at once.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 126 and 127 of 2000.
lawyer:
Fida M Kamal, Additional Attorney-General, instructed by B Hossain, Advocate-on-Record------ For the Petitioner.
 (In both the Petitions)------ Not Represented.
parties:
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh & ors ------ Petitioners
vs.
Khashru Miah ------ Respondent
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 12-7-1998 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 428 of 1989 along with other writ petitions).
full_judgment:
Syed JR Mudassir Husain J: Delay is condoned, These civil petitions by the Government for leave to appeal are directed against the judgment and order dated 12-7-1998 passed in Writ Petition No, 428 of 1989 (heard along with other Writ Petitions) by the High Court Division making the Rules absolute.

2. The Rules in all the writ-petitions were issued calling upon the leave-petitioner writ  respondents to show cause as to why the cancellation of the settlement made by the respondent No, 1, Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of Bangladesh and conveyed by Annexure-K in Writ Petition No, 428 of 1989 and Annexure-1 in all the other writ-petitions should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect

3. The case of the writ-petitioner-respondent Khasru Mia and 38 others was that they formed a Krishi Farming Samabay Samity under the name and style "Gulduba Krishi Farming Co-operative Society Ltd." hereinafter referred to as the Samity within PS-Nabigonj, District-Sylhet now Habigonj in 1974 for mechanized cultivation, The said Samity was registered under the Co-operative Societies Act, on 21-3-1974 vide Regd. No. 2109; that all the aforesaid 39 members of the Samity as landless peasants filed applications to the Sub-Divisional Officer, Habigonj in their individual capacity in separate printed and prescribed form for settlement of a total quantum of land measuring an area of 82.53 acres, each claming 2.50 acres of land appertaining to plot Nos. 651, 652 of Mouza Gulduba. The Sub-Divisional Officer got the matter enquired into by a Magistrate, 1st Class on several occasions and on being satisfied granted permanent settlement of 82.53 acres of land individually in the name of all the 39 members of the Samity each having more or less 2.50 acres of land vide Settlement Case No. 1 of 1975 on 18-10-1975. The said settlement was approved by the ADC (Rev), Sylhet on 10-10-1975. The Sub-Divisional Officer executed 39 permanent deeds of settlement which were registered on 15-11-1975. In the manner, aforesaid petitioner and the other applicants each got 2.13 acres of Government khas land through registered deed of settlement for a period of 15 years with effect from the last of Baishak, 1382 BS (till the 30th Chaitra, 1397 BS) under specific terms and conditions enumerated in the said deed of settlement The aforesaid settlement was made in accordance with the provision of section 81 (1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act The settlement was made heritable after 15 years subject to satisfactory observance of the stipulated terms and conditions. There was a prohibitory condition against alienation before 15 years.

4. The further case of the Khasru Mia was that the petitioner paid salami vide DCR dated 17-11-1975 and got delivery of possession on 18-11-1975. The land was mutated in his name in RoR khatian No. 454. The petitioner procured agricultural equipment including tractor for mechanised cultivation of the land. The petitioner brought the land under mechanised cultivation and has been regularly growing crops therein. He paid land revenue vide DCR No. 500731 dated 17-12- 1976.

5. Photocopy of the writ of delivery of possession and the DCR are annexed as Annexures-C and D respectively. The petitioner contends that some greedy persons inimical to the allotees hatched up a conspiracy under the leadership of Abdur Rashid and Ishaque in order to grab the land settled with the petitioner and others and with that end in view filed an appeal being Settlement Appeal No. 42 of 1979 and a Review Petition being No. 378 of 1977 before the then ADC (Rev), Sylhet who having heard both the parties dismissed the appeal and the review petition. Being aggrieved by those orders the appellant filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 223 of 1979 before the Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong who after due consideration rejected the same by order dated 9-3-1981 but the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Nabigonj (respondent No.2) most arbitrarily and illegally cancelled the petitioners settlement by order dated 10-12-1984 and settled the land on yearly basis (Eksona lease) for 1391 BS to 81 persons. This was done behind the back of the petitioner as no notice to show cause was given to the petitioners as to why their settlement should not be cancelled, they had no opportunity to defend the settlement made to them. Having felt aggrieved by the order dated 10-12-1984, the petitioners filed an application to the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of, Bangladesh on 12-6-1985. The Joint Secretary called for a report from the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Habigonj vide Memo dated 15-6-1985 and in the meantime stayed all further proceedings in respect of the case land. Copy of the said Memo which was forwarded to the petitioner is annexed as Annexure-'F'. In obedience to the aforesaid Memo as contained in Annexure-F the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) submitted a, report to the respondent No.1 stating, inter alia, that the Additional Commissioner, Chittagong Division cancelled the purported settlement made by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Nabigonj, a photo copy of which is annexed as Annexure-G. Even though respondent No.1 was apprised about Annexure-G he did not pay any heed. Subsequently, it came to light that the relevant file could not be traced out and in the meanwhile respondent No.2 (the UNO) started a resumption proceeding being No.I/87-88 as another device to deprive the petitioner of the demised land. Having come to know about this the petitioner moved a petition on 9-12-1988 before respondent No.1 who called for a report to be prepared on the basis of spot inspection. All further proceedings in the meantime were stayed. Photo copy of the said memo is annexed and marked as Annexure-H. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) submitted a report to the Deputy Commissioner, Habigonj on 23-2-1989 vide Annexure-1. On the same date the Deputy Commissioner, Habigonj submitted a report to the respondent No.1 recommending resumption of the land for the purpose of rehabilitating landless destitute by using the land for establishment of cluster villages which arrangements are already in progress. He also recommended for vacating the order of stay granted earlier. Copy of the said report was annexed and marked as Annexure-J. On receipt of Annexure-J, the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of Bangladesh under the signature of respondent No. 4 issued memo No.ভূম/শা-৮/খাজব/হবি/৮২/৮৯/১৬৯ dated 27-3- 1989 to the Deputy Commissioner, Habigonj intimating him that the settlement made in favour of the take samity has been cancelled. The said memo also contained a direction to go ahead with the implementation of "Guchha Gram Project". Attested copy of the said order of cancellation was annexed and marked as Annexure-K (impugned before the High Court Division).

6. On similar assertions and averments, the writ-petitioner-respondents, Rathullah filed Writ Petition No. 443 of 1989 and other writ-petitions also were filed by other individual. The writ respondent-petitioners Ratullah in his writ-petition No. 443 of 1989 impugned the order of cancellation passed by writ-respondent No.1 (petitioner herein). In all the writ-petitions, the leave-petitioner No.1 (writ-respondent No.1) represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of Bangladesh filed affidavits-in-opposition denying all the assertions and allegations contained in the writ-petition, stating, inter alia, that the Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Society by order dated 20-7-1988 cancelled the registration of the petitioners samity as the said samity ceased to have any activities of a co-operative societies; that the petitioners failed to bring the demised land under cultivation and that they violated the terms and conditions of the deed of settlement; that many of the members of the so-called samity were not even aware of any settlement made in their favour; that some of the alleged members are residents of foreign countries and Khasru Mia unauthorisedly used their names; that the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Nabigongj has already started Resumption Case No.1 of 1987-88; that after careful consideration of the inquiry report pursuant to application filed by the petitioners against the said Resumption Case, the Government vacated the order of stay, granted earlier and cancelled settlements made in favour of the petitioners as the samity had no existence; that the Government directed the District Administration to implement the Government policy towards the establishment of cluster village. The writ-petitioner- respondent in reply to the affidavit-in-opposition filed affidavit-in-reply, reiterating the assertions made in the writ-petitions. They further stated that the settlement was not dependent on the formation of any co-operative society and that the society was not cancelled in accordance with the Rules. The writ-petitioner-respondents by filing supplementary affidavit also stated that although the lease in their favour was granted initially for a period of 15 years with effect from 1st Baishak, 1382 BS i.e. till the 30th of Chaitra, 1397 BS but before the expiry of the said lease period respondent No.4 on 27-3-1989 arbitrarily and illegally cancelled the said settlement without serving any show cause notice upon them. The petitioners further contended that on 20-8-1990 (before the expiry of the settlement) they approached the concerned authority for extension of the period of settlement by filing application to that effect and respondent No. 3 received the same on the day but refrained from doing anything on the plea that in the meantime the High Court Division has granted an order of stay. Copy of the application seeking extension of the period of settlement was annexed and marked as Annexure-X. It was further contended that during the recent survey operation the petitioners were found to be in physical possession of the demised land and accordingly, the record of right has been prepared in their names in the face of objection raised by respondent No. 3 (Deputy Commissioner, Habigonj).

7. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the Rule absolute.

8. Since both law and facts are similar these two civil petitions are taken up for hearing together and now are disposed of by this single judgment and order.

9. Mr Fida M Kamal, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the petitioners, contended that the writ-petitioner-respondents, Khasru Mia and Ratullah having failed to prove that the demise land under cultivation belonged to them and having violated the terms and conditions of the deed of settlement, the High Court Division committed an error of law in making the Rule absolute. He further contended that the writ- petitioner-respondents having unauthorisedly using the name of many members of the society although some of the members are the residents of foreign countries and some of the writ-petitioners did not even know about the alleged settlement and the High Court Division having failed to notice this aspect, committed an error of law in making the Rule absolute.

10. The learned Additional Attorney-General also submitted that the Assistant Registrar of the co-operative societies by an order dated 20-7-1988 cancelled the registration of the writ-petitioner-respondents samity the same ceased to have any activities of the co-operative society and the High Court Division having failed to consider this aspect, made the Rule absolute without proper application of judicial mind.

<u>11. We have heard and considered the submissions. On perusal of the impugned judgment, we find that learned Judges of the High Court Division having meticulously considered the case of the parities, the provisions of Co-operative Societies Ordinance, 1984 and also considered the decisions of the superior Court and thus came to the finding that the settlements granted in favour of the writ- petitioner respondent Khasru Mia and Ratullah along with others were cancelled without giving them any notice to show cause for alleged infringement of the terms and conditions of such a lease. Admittedly, the writ-petitioner-respondents were granted settlement by the writ petition respondent No.1 by registered instrument and as such the writ petitioners were legally entitled to be heard before any cancellation of the settlement for the alleged violation of terms and conditions of the lease deed. In the instant case, we find that the learned Judges of the High Court Division upon meticulous consideration as well as on the basis of materials on record held that no prior notice was given to the writ-petitioners and along with others before cancellation of the registered deed of settlement. We are fully in agreement with the findings and decisions arrived at by the High Court Division. For all the above reasons, we find no substance in these two petitions. Accordingly, these are dismissed.</u>

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 2nd July. 1996 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 10141 and 10189 of 1991).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: These two appeals, by leave, are against the judgment of 2nd July, 1996 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division making the Rules absolute obtained in Civil Revision Nos. 10141 and 10189 of 1991 against the judgment and order dated 29th June, 1988 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet in Miscellaneous appeal No. 95 of 1985 and Miscellaneous Appeal No. 94 of 1985 reversing the judgment and order dated 30th April, 1985 of the Additional Court of Munsif Sadar Sylhet in Miscellaneous Case No. 12 of 1985 and Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1985 allowing prayer for pre-emption sought under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 by the respondents (pre-emptors) in the appeals against the respective appellant (pre-emptees) in the respective appeals in respect of the transfer that took place on 27th July, 1978.

2. Pre-emptor's case, in short is that the land sought to be pre-empted and the land they purchased on 25 March, 1974 along with other land belonged to one Ilias Miah son of Meherullah and said Ilias Miah died leaving wife Ful Banu, two sisters Rahima Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi and one full brother Younus who died leaving wife Gulesta Banu, two sons and three daughters. The pre-emptors and one Nanu Miah purchased the property from the full sisters of Ilias Miah on 25 March. 1974, that Nanu Miah transferred his share to the pre-emptors on 25 August, 1980, that on 27 July. 1978 Ful Banu wife of Ilias Miah, transferred her share to the pre-emptee in the respective miscellaneous case, that the pre-emptee of the respective Miscellaneous cases are stranger purchasers and that the transfers under pre-emption were made without notice to the pre-emptors.

3. Pre-emptee-appellant in the respective appeals opposed the prayer for pre-emption contending, inter alia that the land sought to be pre-empted originally belonged to Mohiuddin and Ilias Miah came into possession of the land and thereupon land was recorded in his name during the last settlement operation. The pre-emptees denied the claim of the pre-emptors that Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah and that Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi being not the sisters of Ilias Miah they did not acquire any right, title and interest in the land that belonged to Ilias Miah, that transfer by Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi to the pre-emptors and Nanu Miah was unauthorized since the alleged sisters of Ilias Miah had no right, title and interest in the land of Ilias Miah in any manner. It was the specific case of the pre-emptee of the respective Miscellaneous case that Ilias Miah died issueless leaving his wife Ful Banu and two brothers Rais Miah and Yunus, that there was an amicable partition of the land left by Ilias Miah among his successors and that the land transferred to the pre-emptee of the respective Miscellaneous Cases was allotted to Ful Banu, wife of Ilias Miah and that Ful Banu who was in possession of the land got by amicable partition amongst the successors of Ilias Miah ultimately sold the said land to the pre-emptee of the respective Miscellaneous Cases on 27 July, 1978.

4. The Court of first instance on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, allowed the prayer for preemption in both the Miscellaneous Cases. Thereupon the pre-emptee of the respective Miscellaneous Cases preferred appeals before the Court of District Judge, Sylhet and the said appeals were heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, who by the judgment and order dated 29th July, 1998 set aside the judgment and order of the court of first instance and thereupon dismissed the Miscellaneous Cases.

5. As against the judgment of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge in the Miscellaneous Appeals, the pre-emptors moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rules being Civil Revision No. 10141 of 1991 (against the judgment of Miscellaneous Appeal No. 95 of 1985 which was preferred against the judgment passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 12 of 1985) and Civil Revision No. 10189 of 1991 (against the Judgment of Miscellaneous Appeal No. 94 of 1985 which was preferred against the judgment passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1965 which was preferred against the judgment passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1985). The High Court Division made the Rule absolute upon observing:

"Though the successors-in-interest of deceased Ilias Miah or not would be sorted out in the aforesaid Title Suit No. 245 of 1979 and Title Suit No. 344 of 1990 but for the purpose of these Miscellaneous Cases. I am of the view that the pre-emptors have, prima facie made out a case that Rahima and Kulsuma are the sisters of Ilias Miah or at least that they are the heirs of Ilias Miah in respect of the case land and thereby making them co-sharer tenants in the case land. Accordingly, on the basis of purchase from Kulsuma and Rahima by the pre-emptors, they also became the co-sharer tenants in the case land and as such the applications for pre-emption are maintainable at the instance of the pre-emptors as they had an interest in the case holding as co-sharer tenants."

6. It may be mentioned Title Suit No. 245 of 1979 is for the partition of the properties of lIias Miah and therein Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi are the proforma defendants. The other title suit, being No. 344 of 1980, is for declaration of title and for a decree of permanent injunction as well as for declaring the decree in SCC Suit Nos. 2 and 3 of 1976 illegal and void.

7. Pre-emptor's claim of pre-emption solely depends on the establishment of the fact that Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah. The trial Curt in arriving at the finding that Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah placed reliance on the evidence of PW 1, one of the pre-ernptors and PW 2 claimed to be husband of Kulsuma Bibi and the pleadings of the Title Suit No. 245 of 1979 and 344 of 1980. The court of appeal below reversed the finding of the trial Court as regard PW2's claim of being husband of Kulsuma Bibi upon observing that in respect thereof no document, particularly Kabinnama which he admitted was registered and stated that he has the same was not produced, and as such it is not safe to rely on PW2's lone evidence to arrive at a finding that he is the husband of Kulsuma. The court of appeal below further observed that trial court did not discuss the question pertaining to Kulsuma Bibi's and Rahima Bibi's being the sisters of Ilias Mian in detail and that did not arrive at a definite finding in that regard. The court of appeal below further observed that merely because Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi have been made parties in the title suit but from that decision cannot be arrived at that they are sisters of Ilias Miah as because, in the respective plaint of the said suits it has been specifically denied that Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi are not the sisters of Ilias Miah.

8. The High Court Division has reversed the judgment and order of the court of appeal below upon observing that "the pre-emptors have, prima facie made out a case that Rahima and Kulsuma are the sisters of Ilias Miah or at least that they are the heirs of Ilias Miah in respect of the case land and thereby making them co-sharer tenants in the case land."

<u>9. PW 1 in his evidence has stated that Ilias Miah died leaving wife Ful Banu, two sisters Rahima Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi and brother Yunus. But at the same time PW 1 has stated that he has not filed paper to show that Rahima Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah and that he came to know from the papers which he had seen at the time of making purchase that Rahima Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi are the full sisters of Ilias Miah and they are the daughters of Meherullah. It may be mentioned Ilias Miah is the son of Meherullah. Although PW 1 stated that he came to know from the papers which he saw at the time of making purchase but no such paper was placed before the court in support of his statement of knowing about Rahima Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi being the daughters of Meherullah. This witness has further stated that he heard from the relations of Rahim a Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi they are the full sisters of llias Miah but in support of having that information or deriving of the knowledge that Rahima Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi are the full sisters of I1ias Miah, no evidence has been led. There is nothing in the evidence of PW 1 that he had any information from PW 2 who claims him to be the husband of Kulsuma Bibi, that Rahima Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah. So PW 1's evidence as to that Rahima Bibi Kulsuma Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah remains uncorroborated or in other words has not been corroborated by the evidence of any of the witnesses examined by the pre-emptors. Now there remains the evidence of PW 2 who claims himself to be husband of Kulsuma Bibi. This witness has stated that Rahima Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi are the sisters of I1ias Miah and he is the husband of Kulsuma Bibi. The fact of Rahirna Bibi's and Kulsuma Bibi's being the sisters of Ilias Miah has been denied by the pre-emptees and thereupon it was the duty of the pre-emptors to establish the fact of Kulsuma's and Rahima's being the sisters of Ilias Miah because in the absence of establishing the said fact pre-emptors would not be entitled to have the relief prayed in Miscellaneous Cases. The pre-emptors to prove the fact that Rahima Bibi and Kulsuma Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah have examined PW 2. There is no tangible material except the uncorroborated statement of PW 2 that he is the husband of Kulsuma Bibi or in other words PW 2's claim as of being the husband of Kulsuma Bibi has not been corroborated by any other evidence, both oral and documentary. Because of the quality of the evidence of PW 2 it cannot be said that said witness has proved the pre-emptor's claim that Kulsuma and Rahima are the sisters of Ilias Miah. PW 2 claimed that his marriage was registered and that he has the Kabinama. But same has not been produced at any stage of the Miscellaneous Cases. In the background of challenge as to PW 2's being the husband of Kulsuma, said to be the daughter of Meherullah and thereupon full sister of Ilias Miah, the fact of PW 2's being husband of Kulsuma remains legally unestablished. The Kabinnama or any other competent person if would have deposed about the fact of Kulsuma's being wife of PW 2 that could have been the best evidence to resolve the contentious matter' that Kulsuma Bibi is the full sister of Ilias Miah and that PW 2 is the husband of Kulsuma Bibi but that vital material piece of evidence and the evidence of such person has not been brought on record. In the background of the evidence from the side of the pre-emptors as discussed herein above it is seen that the material question i.e. question of Rahima Bibi's and Kulsuma Bibi's being the full' sisters of I1ias Miah has not been resolved by legal evidence and that the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 having not been corroborated by the evidence of independent and reliable witness the same cannot be made the basis for coming to the decision that Rahima and Kulsuma are the sisters of Ilias Miah. Evidence of PWs 1 and 2 in no standard can be considered corroborative evidence of each other's evidence as to the material fact Kulsuma and Rahima are sisters of Ilias Miah or that PW 2 is husband of Kulsuma. The High Court Division in our view was in error in reversing the judgment of the court of appeal below upon observing; "pre-emptors have prima facie made a case that Rahima and Kulsuma are the sisters of Ilias Miah or at least that they are the heirs of Ilias Miah in respect of the case land and thereby making them co-sharer tenants in the case land" as pre-emptees in case of allowing pre-emption would be deprived of their valuable right to hold property in the absence of firm establishment of the fact that Kulsuma and Rahima are the sisters of Ilias Miah and as such the pre-emptors under the law are required to establish a definite and firm case and not a 'prima facie' case of their being co-sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted. Making out of prima case however strong be, in law cannot be the basis for depriving one of holding property and that to deprive one of one's property there must have case of definite and unassailable kind or quality. In pre- emption proceeding one is deprived of one's property through the coercive' process of the Court and as such unless pre-emptor has a positive case of his being co-sharer the court upon a finding of pre-emptor's having a 'prima facie case' of being co- sharer is not permitted by law to grant pre-emption. Right to acquire and to hold property, subject to restriction imposed by law, is a guaranteed right of a citizen and when a citizen by the coercive process of law is compelled to part with his acquired property, then the condition(s) or the provision of law upon resorting to which a citizen is compelled to part with his property, the same is to be fulfilled in entirety and the provision of law as to coercive parting with properly is to be applied only when there is proof of the fact up to the hilt in the background of which parting with property can be compelled or in other words a citizen would only be compelled to part with his acquired property while the other, who is seeking aid of the court to compel a citizen to part with his property, has established the fact that would have entitled him to have the other's property completely. One cannot compel another upon restoring to a particular provision of law to part with his property in making out a prima facie case for such parting with, as in the instant case of pre-emption. One has to establish one's basis of claim for compelling another to part with his property in one's favour to the full or finally but not upon making out a prima facie case for compelling one to part with one's property by the coercive process of law. In the instant case pre-emptors where required to establish that they are co- sharers of the land transferred to the pre-emptee of the respective Miscellaneous cases and for that pre-emptors were required to establish that Kulsuma and Rahima are the full sisters of Ilias Miah as because in the absence of establishing that Kulsuma and Rahima are sisters of Ilias Miah, since the pre-emptors claim they are co-sharers of the land transferred to pre-emptee of the two miscellaneous cases by purchase from sisters of Ilias Miah, the pre-emptors could not claim pre-emption in .respect of the transfers sought to be pre-empted. The appellate court dismissed the miscellaneous case on the finding that pre-emptors failed- to establish that Kulsuma and Rahima are full sisters of Ilias Mia. The High Court Division allowed the prayer for pre-emption on the finding that pre-emptors made out a prima facie case that Kulsuma and Rahima are sisters of Ilias Miah. The law is now settled that concept of "prima facie case" would only receive consideration of the court while disposing of any interlocutory matter at the primary stage of a case or in other words the case has yet not reached the stage of finality. In the final hearing of the case respective parties thereto would certainly be required to establish or prove their respective case completely or in other words conclusively. There would be total absence of alloy as regards establishment of the case either to have a relief sought from the court or for the rejection of the relief sought by the first party (Plaintiff) in the suit. The High Court Division was in serious error in allowing pre-emption only because prima facie it was established that Kulsuma and Rahima are sisters of Ilias Mia upon overlooking the material fact that establishing something prima facie is never the establishing of the said fact conclusively or finally or that said establishment i.e. prima facie establishment, was free from alloy. Making out of a prima facie case is nothing more than making out a case of first impression or something that appears to be true at the first sight or consideration. A prima facie case is not free from alloy or in other words it cannot be said that prima facie case has stood the acid test. As such establishing or making out of a prima facie case in law cannot be considered to have established the case finally or conclusively or said to have proved the case for having the relief sought by the first party in the proceeding conclusively or in other words free from alloy.</u>

10. The High Court Division also was in error in placing reliance on the plaints of Title Suit No. 245 of 1979 and 344 of 1980 in arriving at the finding as to Kulsuma Bibi's and Rahima Bibi's being the sisters of Ilias Miah in that the plaintiffs of the said suits in the respective plaints have made clear averment denying the fact of Kulsuma Bibi's and Rahima Bibi's being the sisters of Ilias Miah. Merely because Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi have been made proforma-defendants in the aforementioned Title Suits it cannot be said the plaintiffs of the title suits accepted the said two defendants as the sisters of Ilias Miah as because there are statements in the plaints denying their being the sisters of Bias Miah and that there is also explanation in the plaints why these two defendants have been made parties in the suit. The said two title Suits are still pending and in the absence of decision in the said two suits or final disposal of the said two suits it can be said that Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah, nor can it be said because of impleading Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi (as defendants) describing them as sisters of Ilias Miah in Tittle Suits a 'prima facie' has been made out by the preemptors as to Kulsuma Bibi's and Rahima Bibi's being the sisters of Ilias Miah. Since the pre-emptors did not establish by legal evidence that Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah and that being so it cannot be said in the absence of legally establishing that Kulsuma Bibi and Rahima Bibi are the sisters of Ilias Miah, the pre-emptors by purchase from the said two persons have become co-sharers in the land left by Ilias Miah and that inherited by Ful Banu wife of Ilias Miah and that have acquired right of pre-emption.

In view of the discussion made herein above we find merit in the appeals. Accordingly, the same are allowed. There is no order as to cost.

End.
