case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated July 21, 1991 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 523 of 1985).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J : This is an appeal, by leave, by the pre-emptee (pre-emption was sought under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949) against the judgment and order dated July 21, 1991 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 523 of 1985 discharging the Rule and consequent thereupon affirming the judgment and order dated July 22, 1985 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 40 of 1985 allowing pre-emption upon setting aside the judgment and order dated January 23, 1985 of the 1st Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 1984 dismissing the same.

2. Facts, in short, are that land sought to be preempted along with some other land belonged to Abdur Rahman who died leaving sons Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Gafur. Abdul Gafur filed Title Suit No. 18 of 1954 seeking partition of the land inherited from Abdur Rahman. After the final decree Abdul Gafur got in his share 335 aurjuthansa and Abdur Razzaque got in his share 1005 aurjuthansa. Decree in the partition suit was made final (subject matter of the partition suit was land measuring 1340 aurjuthansa listed in CS Khatian No. 8282, the corresponding SA Khatian No. 3232). Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land recorded in a separate khatian being Khatian No. 3232/1. Abdul Gafur's heirs, pre-emptors, purchased 335 aurjuthansa of land on 16-6-1981 from Hannan's heirs. ie heirs of Abdur Razzaque's son. Abdur Razzaque's daughter Rowshan Akhter sold 167 aurjuthansa of land to Alfazuddin Ahmed pre-emptee on August 24, 1981. This sale has been sought to be pre-empted by Abdul Gafur's sons claiming to be co-sharers of the land.

3. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed contending, inter alia, that in the light of the decreein the partition suit filed by the pre-emptor's predecessor Abdul Gafur, his brother Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land separated upon opening separate SA Khatian No. 3232/1 by filing Mutation Case in the year 1977 and that after purchase by the pre-emptors they got the purchased land recorded in separate Khatian No. 3232/1/1 by filing Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1/81-82 of the office of Circle Officer (Revenue) Kotwali, Dhaka and thus ceased to be the co-sharer. It was also the contention of the pre-emptee that pre-emptors were aware of the transfer from the time of sale and that the land sought to be pre-empted being recorded as nishkar, section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act has no manner of application.

4. The Court of 1st instance rejected the prayer for pre-emption with the findings that pre-emptors were not co-sharers and that the prayer for pre-emption was barred by limitation. The said Court based its finding as to pre-emptors of not being co-sharers on Exhibit B(3) which later on was re-numbered as Exhibit A ie Khatian No. 3232/1 /1 opened in respect of the purchased land measuring 335 aurjutansha of Abdul Gafur's heirs from Abdur Razzaque's heirs. The said Khatian was started by the order dated 13-8-1981 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1/81-82 of the office of Circle Officer (Revenue), Kotwali, Dhaka.

5. On appeal, the appellate Court allowed the prayer for pre-emption on the finding that the claim of pre-emption is not barred by limitation since no notice under section 24(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was served on the pre-emptors and that the pre-emptors are co-sharers and that pre-emptee opened in his name separate Khatian in respect of the land sought to be pre-empted without serving notice on the co-sharers and, as such, by the said separation of Jama the pre-emptors did not cease to be the co-sharers of the land measuring 1005 aurjutansha ie land that Abdur Razzaque got in his share pursuant to the decree in the partition suit filed by Abdul Gafur. The appellate Court also held that Khatian No. 3232/1/1 in the name of the pre-emptors is in respect of the land allotted in the share of Abdul Gafur in the partition suit.

6. The pre-emptee moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction as against the judgment and order of the appellate Court allowing pre-emption. The High Court Division on the finding that pre-emptee separated the Jama in respect of his purchased land without compliance of the provision of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and, as such, appellate Court did not commit any error in holding that the pre-emptors are the co-sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted. The High Court Division further held that in spite of the opening SA Khatian No. 3232/1/1 the pre-emptors remained co-sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted since the said khatian was opened in respect of the land pre-emptors' predecessor Abdul Gafur got pursuant to the decree in the partition suit and that the said khatian is not in respect of the land purchased from Abdur Razzaque's heirs by the pre-emptors.

7. The pre-emptee as against the judgment and order of the High Court Division obtained leave contending, infer alia, that the High Court Division overlooked that the Court of appeal below without noticing and considering Exhibit B(2) Khatian No. 3232/1 relied upon by the trial Court came to an erroneous finding that the pre-emptors were the co- sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted, that the High Court Division erred in law in not considering that the Court of appeal below was wholly wrong in holding that Khatian No. 3232/1/1, standing in the name of the pre-emptors, was in respect of the land got pursuant to the final decree in the partition suit though there was no such evidence. Leave was also obtained for consideration whether the decisions reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323; 1987 BLD (AD) 122 and 33 DLR (AD) 309 have been properly interpreted in the instant case.

8. The admitted fact is that, property of holding No. 45(1) belonged to Abdur Rahman who died leaving sons Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Gafur. Abdul Gafur filed partition suit No. 18 of 1954 and in view of the decree therein got in his saham land measuring 335 aurjuthansa. The decree in the partition suit was made final is an admitted fact. Abdur Razzaque who was defendant in the partition suit got 1005 aurjuthansa in his share. Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land measuring 1005 aurjuthansa recorded in a separate khatian, being No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3). It may be mentioned land measuring 1340 aurjuthansa which was subject matter of partition was recorded in CS Khatian No. 8282 and later on the said land was recorded in SA No. 3232 (Exhibit B 1). Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land pursuant to decree in partition suit recorded in the separate khatian No. 3232/l as back as in June 1977. Heirs of Abdul Hannan (son of Abdur Razzaque) sold 335 aurjuthansa of land to the sons (pre-emptors') of Abdul Gafur in June 1981. The pre-emptors got the land purchased recorded in Khatian No. 3232/1/1 by order dated 13- 8-1981 in Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1/81-82. On August 24, 1981 Abdur Razzaque's daughter Rowshan Akhter sold 167 aurjuthansa of land to the pre-emptee. This transfer sought to be pre-empted by Gafur's heirs under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, hereinafter in short, the Act, claiming to be the co-sharers of the land so transferred.

9. The question of ceasing of co-sharership in the non-agricultural land amongst the once co-sharers inter se upon partition by metes and bounds or, in other words, upon allotment of separate saham to the co-sharers pursuant to the decree in the partition suit has been set at rest by the decision in the case of SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and another reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 and in the case of Shafiuddin Chowdhury vs Md Abdul Karim and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) 41. In the light of the decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 the question of ceasing of co-sharership in non-agricultural land on partition by metes and bounds has also been considered in the case reported in 40 DLR 466.

10. The land sought to be pre-empted along with the other land belonged to Abdur Rahman and on his death his 2 sons Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Gafur inherited the same. Abdul Gafur had the 4 annas share. He filed Partition Suit No. 18 of 1954 and got his saham to the extent of 335 aurjuthansa. The partition decree was made final. Thus Gafur got his share being partitioned by metes and bounds by the decree in the partition suit. The land which was the subject matter of the partition suit was undoubtedly non-agricultural land. So, after partition by metes and bounds Abdul Gafur ceased to be the co-sharer of the land allotted to the other co-sharer or, in other words, as regards the other quality of land. This is one aspect of the matter as to the situation of co-sharership between Abdur Razzaque, the heirs of Abdur Razzaque and Abdul Gafur or the heirs of Abdul Gafur. Pursuant to the decree in the partition suit Abdur Razzaque's heirs got their land measuring 1005 aurjuthansa recorded in khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3). The pre-emptors are not challenging legality of the fact of opening of this khatian or, in other words, opening of new khatian upon splitting of the original khatian No. 3232 (Exhibit B (1)) in the names of the heirs of Abdur Razzaque. After the purchase by the pre-emptors from the heirs of Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque, they opened in their names separate khatian, khatian No. 3232/1/1 by the order dated 13- 8-1981 in Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1 of 81-82. The appellate Court considered this khatian as of in respect of land measuring 335 aurjuthansa got in the partition suit by Abdul Gafur and after his death inherited by the pre-emptors. The revisional Court concurred with the said finding of the Court of appeal without taking into consideration the materials on record. It may be mentioned trial Court held that khatian No. 3232/1/1 was in respect of the land purchased by the pre-ernptors from the heirs of Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque. The High Court Division as well as the appellate Court on the view that khatian No. 3232/1/1 is in respect of the land allotted to Abdul Gofur in the partition suit held the pre-emptors being the co-sharers were competent to pre-empt the land sought to be pre-empted, while the trial Court held that because of opening of khatian No. 3232/1/1 in respect of land purchased by the pre-emptors from the heirs of Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque they ceased to be the co-sharers and, as such, were not entitled to pre-empt the land sought to be pre-empted. The fact that khatian No. 3232/1/1 was not as regard the land got by Abdul Gafur pursuant to decree in the partition suit but relates to the land purchased by the pre-emptors from Abdul Hannan's heirs is evidenced by the certified copy of the petition whereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1 of 81-82 was started for separation of jama upon splitting up the khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heir. It is seen that after the transfer by Hannan's heirs and by Rowshan Akhter (who sold to the pre-emptee land measuring 167 aurjuthansa) the quantity of land stands at sail? aurjuthansa in Khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit B (2). The endorsements made therein clearly show pre- emptors in respect of their land purchased from Abdul Hannan's heirs got the said purchased land recorded in khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A). Had the Khatian No. 3232/1/1 been in respect of the land got by Abdul Gafur pursuant to the partition decree there was no occasion for deduction of the said land from the khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) prepared in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs. If Gafur's heirs would have got the land which Gafur got by the decree in the partition suit ie land measuring 3535 aurjuthansa listed in a khatian other than 3232 (Exhibit B (1), then the said land would have been deducted from the khatian No. 3232, and not from the split khatian 3232/1 opened as back in 1977 in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs. So, it is seen that the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court upon total misconception that khatian No. 3232/1/1 was opened in respect of the land Abdul Gafur got by the decree in partition suit were in error in holding that pre-emptors are the co- sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted and entitled to pre-empt the land transferred by Rowshan Akhter to the pre-emptee.

11. Leave was also granted to consider whether the principle of law enunciated in the cases reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309; 1987 BLD (AD) 122 and 33 DLR 320 was properly interpreted by the High Court Division in view of the case of the (pre-emptee that prayer for pre-emption was not maintainable since after purchase pre-emptors separated the jama of their purchased land and he also separated jama of his purchased land by opening a separate khatian. It was urged before the High Court Division that since the pre-emptee has got a separate holding in respect of his purchased land by opening a separate khatian and that no appeal having been filed as against the order of the Revenue Officer allowing splitting of the jama the validity thereof cannot be opened in a collateral proceeding ie in a pre-emption proceeding, before the Civil Court and that Civil Court is not competent to ignore the order. In support of the aforesaid contention cases reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309 and in 1987 BLD (AD) 122 were referred to. In refusal of the aforesaid contention and in support of the contention that an order passed under section 117 (1)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 by the Revenue Officer without notifying the co-sharer and consequently, the same totally being violative of the provision of law, legality of such order can very much be seen by the Civil Court in collateral proceeding ie in pre-emption proceeding, from pre-emptor's side case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323 was referred to.

12. The decision in the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323 as to seeing legality of the order of the Revenue Officer splitting jama was made in the background of the facts first, therein it was established that the order splitting the jama was obtained without serving notice on the co-sharers ie pre-emptors, and second, the said order of the Revenue Officer splitting the jama was obtained during the pendency of the pre-emption proceeding. In that background of the facts the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323 is distinguished from the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309 and in 1987 BLD (AD) 122.

13. The question of legality of order of the Revenue Officer splitting up the jama and opening in the name of pre-emptee separate khatian on the oasis whereof there was the contention that by the opening of the said khatian pre-emptors ceased to be the co-sharers of the land sought to be pre-empted has lost its importance and relevancy because of the fact that pre-emptors got their purchased land from Hannan's heirs listed in a separate khatian being No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) upon splitting up the jama of khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) and consequently, the question of competency of Civil Court to examine legality of the order of Revenue Officer passed under section 117 (c) of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the collateral proceeding as well as question of proper interpretation of the principle of law enunciated in the above mentioned 3 cases in the background of the fact of the instant cases are not necessary. The pre-emptors obtained order of the Revenue Officer on August 13, 1981 in Miscellaneous Case No. 198 'G1' P-1/81-82 for opening a separate khatian in respect of their purchased land from Hannan's heirs and this splitting up of the jama and opening of separate khatian, being No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A), in the name of the pre-emptors in respect of the land purchased from Hannan's heirs was before the transfer to the pre-emptee. The transfer by Rowshawn Akhter, daughter of Abdur Razzaque, to the pre-emptee was made on August 24, 1981. In this background of the facts it is seen that the pre-emptors ceased to be the co-sharers of the land recorded in Exhibit 3 ie khatian No. 3232/1, listing name of heirs of Abdur Razzaque.

14. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that in respect of non-agricultural land on the opening of separate khatian upon splitting up of the jama of the land sought to be pre-empted in the name of the per-emptor disentitles him from exercising right of pre-emption in respect of the land whereof he ceased to be a co-sharer because of splitting up of jama and starting of a separate khatian in his name. In support of the aforesaid submission he has referred to the observation in the case of Begum Khodeza Akhter vs Hajera Khatun and others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 212. In the said case the question of separation of jamaby pre- emptors was raised contending that pre-emptors after purchase filed an application before the Revenue Officer for separation of their jama and thereupon, a Separation Case was started and the same ended in an order separating the jama and thereupon the parties paid rent separately. In that background it was observed "If this is a fact then, certainly the pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharers and are debarred from claiming pre-emption". Since the pre-emptee in support of his contention that pre-emptors separated their jama relied upon the statement made in the petition for pre-emption and as there was no other evidence as to separation of jama and the lands were recorded under separate khatian and that as there was also no material as towhether the proposal for opening separate khatian was finally accepted resulting in separation of jama and payment of rent separately by the 2 co-sharers and that as it was contended by the pre-emptors that they filed application for mutation of their names in place of original owner and that proposal for mutation was erroneously referred to as separation of jama and that the said case did not reach its finality and consequent thereupon they continue to be co-sharers, the case was sent back to the lower appellate Court to determine the question as to separation of jama. Since in the instant case there are materials on record to show that pre-emptors after their purchase from Hannan's heirs land measuring 335 filed an application for separation of the jama and the same was allowed by the Revenue Officer and thereupon separate khatian, being No. 3232/1/1, in respect of the aforementioned quantity of land has been opened evidenced by Exhibit A and, as such, we feel there is no necessity of sending back the case to the court below for determination of the fact of separation of jama by the pre-emptors in respect of the land purchased from Hannan's heirs. The pre-emptors by opening separate khatian in their names in respect of the land purchased from Hannan's heirs ceased to be the co-sharers of the land recorded in khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) that stands in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs.

15. The learned Counsel for the respondents has submitted that because of the decree in partition suit same ipso facto would not constitute separation of jama or mutation in the background of the provision of section 117(1)( c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and that for the said one of the purposes ie for separation of jama or mutation, there shall have to file an application seeking separation of jama or for mutation. The question of ceasing of co-sharership in non-agricultural land upon partition by metes and bounds pursuant to a decree in partition suit and question of ceasing of co-sharership in the land on separation of jama and opening of Khatian are two different aspects of ceasing of co-sharership. The two modes of ceasing of co-sharership are two distinct and different modes. The question of ceasing of co-sharership by metes and bounds partition pursuant to a decree in partition suit is now a settled question. In the instant case there was ceasing of co-sharership twice first, because of decree in the partition suit filed by pre-emptors' father and second, by separation of jama or splitting up of jama and opening of separate khatian by the pre-emptors. The contention of the learned Counsel for the respondent that in the absence of application under section 117(1)( c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act there cannot be separation of holding or mutation can hardly be disputed, rather it is the requirements of provision of law that an application for separation of holding or mutation has to be filed and thereupon the Revenue Officer is authorised for separation of the jama or mutation prayed for upon due service of notice to the other co-sharers,

<u>16. As seen from the materials on record the pre-emptors after their purchase from Hannan's heirs land measuring 335 aurjuthansa filed application seeking separation of jama and thereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 198 (u) P-1/81-82 was started and that the Revenue Officer allowed separation of jama by the order dated August 13, 1981 and thereupon separate khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) has been opened in the name of the pre-emptors. So, it is evidenced that khatian (Exhibit A) has been opened in the name of the pre-emptors on their application filed under section 117(1)( c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It is seen from the, judgment of this Division reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 and the case reported in 52 DLR (AD) 41 that upon partition of the non-agricultural land by metes and bounds by a decree in a partition suit there occurs ceasing of co-sharership among the separate specific saham holders. From the respondent's side we have not been referred to any case to take a view different from the ratio of the cases reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 and 52 DLR (AD) 41 that in case of partition of non-agricultural land in pursuant to a decree in a partition suit co- sharership among the specific saham holders ceases.</u>

17. Learned Counsel for the respondents has submitted since Abdul Gafur who" got land measuring 3535 arjutansha pursuant to the decree in the partition suit did not file any application for separation of the land he got by the partition decree by opening separate khatian and, as such, he remained a co-sharer and that 'after his death his heirs remained co-sharers of the land recorded in SA khatian No. 3232 and in support of the said contention has referred to the case reported in 36 DLR 193. This contention is of merit since en the basis of the final decree in the partition suit Abdur Razzaque's heirs splitted up the jama of Khatian SA No. 3232 and get opened in their names separate Khatian, being No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3), Abdul Gafur remained a tenant in khatian No. 3232 in respect of the land he get in the light of the decree in the partition suit filed by him. There is no reason to take a view different from the view expressed in the case reported in 36 DLR 213 that for sub-division of holding as per provision of section 117(c) of SAT Act there shall have to make an application to the Revenue Officer by one or more co-sharer tenants and order for sub-division of holding shall be made after notice to. the parties concerned to appear and upon hearing the party concerned, if appears. No. exception has been taken by Abdul Gafur's heirs as regard splitting of jama of khatian No. 3232 at the instance of Abdur Razzaque's heirs and opening of separate khatian, being No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) in respect of land measuring 1005 arjutansha they get pursuant to the decree in the partition suit.

18. The contention of the learned Counsel for the respondents that as Gafur did not seek for separation of jama in respect of the land he got by the partition decree; as such, he remained to be a co-sharer and that only if Gafur, or for that matter, his heirs would have filed application seeking separation of the jama in respect of the land got in pursuant to the decree in the partition suit and the land purchased from Hannan's heirs or if would have prayed for listing of the land got by the partition decree and by purchase from Hannan's heirs in one khatian only, in that case it could have been said that there has been ceasing of ce-sharership as regard the land recorded in SA Khatian No. 3232. This contention of the learned Counsel for the respondents appears to be of no merit in the background of the materials on record. The undenied position is that Abdur Razzaque's heirs in the light of the partition decree sought separation of jama upon splitting of the jama of SA khatian No. 3232 and on the application of Abdur Razzaque's heirs seeking separation of jama separation proceeding was started and that Revenue Officer made the order on June 1, 1977 for separation of jama and thereupon khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) was opened in respect of the land measuring 1005. This quantity of land Abdur Razaaque got in his share pursuant to partition decree in Partition Suit No. 18 of 1954 wherein final decree was made on May 20, 1967. After the opening of separate khatian in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs pre-emptors purchased 335 aurjuthansa of land from the heirs of Abdul Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque and thereupon pre-emptors approached the Revenue Officer for separation of jama of their purchased land upon splitting up of the jama of khatian No. 3232/1 by filing separation case No. 198 (u) and that the same was allowed by the Revenue Officer by the order dated August 13, 1981 and on the basis thereof khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) has been opened in the name of the pre- emptors fer 3535 arjutansha of land. The pre-emptors contention is that Khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) is in respect of the land Abdul Gafur got pursuant to the decree in the partition suit. This contention is of no merit since after opening of khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) in the name of Abdur Razzaque's heirs, Abdul Gafur remained the recorded tenant in respect of his share in khatian No. 3232 and, as such, there was no occasion or necessity to go for having a khatian in respect of the land he got pursuant to the partition decree. The fact that khatian No. 3232/1 opened in respect of the land purchased by the pre-emptors from Abdur Razzaque's heirs is seen from the material on record ie petition filed by the pre-ernptors seeking separation of jama and whereupon Separation Case No. 198 ‘ল’ P-1-81-82 was started and pursuant to an order allowing the said separation case separate khatian No. 3232/1/1 has been opened. In the aforesaid background of the facts the pre-emptors' claim of remaining co-sharers since their predecessor Abdul Gafur did not apply for separation of the jama in respect of the land he got on the basis of partition decree and that if Abdul Gafur or for that matter his heirs would have gonefor separation of jama there would have been one khatian for the purchased land as well as for the land got by the decree in the partition suit is of no merit. The notings in the khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit B2) (after listing of the land purchased by pre-emptors and the pre-emptee in new khatians) clearly show that khatian No. 3232/1/1 text A) was open upon separation or splitting upon jama of khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3).

19. In the background of the discussions made hereinabove we are of the view that because of the decree in the partition suit as there has been ceasing of co-sharership between the plaintiff and the defendant of the partition suit that ended in final decree upon allotment of separate saham to respective parties and that as the pre-emptors got the jama of khatian No. 3232/1 (Exhibit 3) split up in respect of their land purchased from the heirs of Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque and go to separate khatian opened in their names before the transfer to the pre-emptee and consequent thereupon as they ceased to be the co-sharers ofkhatian No. 3232/1 or, in other words, land of the said khatian pre-emption sought for on the basis of purchase of land made from the heirs of Abdul Hannan, son of Abdur Razzaque against the pre-emptee who purchased the land sought to be pre-empted from heirs of Abdur Razzaque was not available. The High Court Division as well as the appellate Court in disregard of the materials on record as discussed above wrongly assumed that khatian No. 3232/1/1 (Exhibit A) was started in the name of pre-emptors in respect of the land Abdul Gafur got pursuant to the decree in partition suit and thereupon erroneously allowed pre-emption.

In view of the discussion made hereinover the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order of the High Court Division affirming those of the court of appeal below is set aside and the judgment and order of the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge) is restored. The pre-emption case is dismissed.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2520 of 2010
lawyer:
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mohd. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioners, 
Dr M Zahir; Senior Advocate with Mahbubey Alam, Senior Advocate and Abdur Razzaque Khan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Taufique Hossain, Advocate- on-Record ----- For the Respondent No. 2. 
None Represented ----- For the Respondent Nos. 1 & 3-10.
parties:
Hussain Fabrics Ltd,represented by its Managing Director and another ------ Petitioners
VS
Haji Momena Khatun and others ------Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 31-5-2010 passed by the High Court Division in FA No.216 of 2007)
full_judgment:
Md Muzammel Hossain, J: This petition for leave to appeal under Article 103 of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh is directed against the judgment and decree dated 31-5-2010 passed by the High Court Division in FA No. 216 of 2007 allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 19-6-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge and Arbitration Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 102 of 2004 dismissing the suit.

2. The present respondent Nos. 1-6 as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 119 of 2002 in the 4th Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka for Specific Performance of Contract in respect of the suit property which was subsequently transferred to the Court of Joint District Judge, Arbitration: Court, Dhaka and renumbered as Title Suit No. 102 of 2004. In the plaint the plaintiffs stated, interalia, that the defendant No. I-petitioner No. I being a private limited company got allotment of the scheduled property on 30-7-1985 and as per Board Resolution of the Company one Kazi Golam Hussain being the Chairman of the company on 19-3-1990 entered into an agreement for sale of the said property with Alhaj Mansur Rahman for 'Taka 35,40,000. Thereafter Alhaj Mansur Rahman paid Taka 18.50 lakh through cheques as earnest money and possession of the property was delivered to him with a condition that outstanding dues of Taka 11,00 lakh out of the total consideration money be paid to RAJUK by him for which Taka 11,00 lakh would be excluded from total consideration money and the defendant No. I would execute the deed receiving the balance consideration money of Taka 5 lakh. The price was re-fixed at Taka 33.00 lacs out of which Taka 19,00 lakh was already paid by the plaintiff Mansur Rahman to the defendant and the outstanding amount of Taka 14,29,373 was paid by Mansur Rahman to the RAJUK.The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and Kazi Golam Hussain executed a security bond on 18-3-1992 admitting the agreement. Kazi Golam Hussain died leaving behind defendant Nos. 2-4 as his heirs who are all Directors of the defendant No. l-company. The plaintiffs- respondents requested the defendants to execute and register the deed but they refused to execute and register the deed of sale on 30-3-2002 and hence the suit for Specific Performance of Contract.

3.The defendant Nos.1-2-petitioners contested the suit denying the statements made in the plaint stating, inter alia, that as per Memorandum and Articles of Association of the company there is no post of Chairman of the defendant No. l-petitioner-company rather there is a post of Managing Director; that the defendant No.2 is the Managing Director of the company having overall supervision and control over the company. Kazi Golam Hussain was the father of the defendant No.2 who at the relevant time used to serve in the Investment Board of Bangladesh as a Director and, as such, he was neither Chairman nor Director nor anybody in the said company and there is no such expression in the company law, namely, "Authority". In order to grab the property the predecessor of the plaintiffs-respondents, Mansur Rapman, managed to obtain an unregistered deed of agreement executed by Kazi Golam Hussain alleging that he was the Chairman of the M/s Hussain Fabrics Ltd although Kazi Golam Hussain had no authority to deal with the matter as well as to transfer or enter into any contract with anybody for any share or portion of M/s Hussain Fabrics Ltd and, the alleged contract is not a contract in the eye of law and, as such, the same is not legally enforceable. On 18-3-1992 the plaintiff No. 3 with a group of miscreants came to the residence of the defendants and took their signature in a security bond under threat of gun point. Thereafter the plaintiff, not being the owner and possessor and having no right, title, interest and possession over the assets of Hussain Fabrics Ltd: got 10 Ansars posted therein. Some unscrupulous persons had tried to dispossess the defendants from the land allotted to the defendant No. l-the company and finding no other way the defendant No.2 filed a petition case bearing No. 5877 of 2001 before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka alleging, inter alia, that there is a possibility to break the peace and tranquility and prayed for necessary order and the learned Magistrate passed an order of status quo. Shyampur Police Station Case No. 32(12)2001 was started by the plaintiffs wherein the defendant Nos. 2-4 were falsely implicated. The plaintiff No. 2 with the help of police raided the said land and also arrested the employees of the defendant No.2. Finding no other alternative the defendant No. 2 filed Writ Petition No. 242 of 2002 and got an order of injunction against the plaintiff. The plaintiff No. 2-Mahbubur Rahman with the help of bad elements, police force and Ansars entered into the industry of M/S Hussain Fabrics Ltd and looted away valuable goods and machineries violating the order of injunction of the High Court Division and the order of maintaining status quo granted by the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and thereafter, the defendant No. 2 filed Contempt Petition being No.9 of 2002 in the High Court Division wherein a Rule Nisi has been issued. One Mahamuda Begum also filed Petition Case No. 255 of2002 in the Court of the Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka against Mahbubur Rahman and others. The defendant stated that there was no contract for sale of the suit property and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. However, the defendants did not adduce any evidence, oral or documentary, before the trial Court. The learned Joint District Judge dismissed the suit on contest against the defendant Nos.1 and 2 and ex-parte against the rest by the judgment and decree dated 19-6-2007.

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 19-6-2007 the plaintiff preferred an appeal being First Appeal No.216 of 2007 before the High Court Division. 	.

6.While the appeal was pending the defendant-respondents-petitioners filed an application under Order XL, rule 27 of the Code of  Civil Procedure for adducing additional evidence on the ground that the plaintiffs filed various false cases against the Managing Director of Hussain Fabrics Limited and against Darwan, Guard and other employees of the company and out of fear of the plaintiffs, the defendant could not attend the Court and could not examine their witnesses, produce documents in the Court, mark the same as exhibits and also could not cross-examined two witnesses out of four produced by the plaintiffs. A Division Bench of the High Court Division kept the application under Order XL, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 pending for consideration at the time of hearing of the appeal.

7. Subsequently, a Division Bench of the High Court Division by the judgment and decree dated 31-5-2010 allowed the appeal being No. FA No. 216 of 2007 upon setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs-respondents without considering the relevant papers and documents as well as the application submitted by the defendants-petitioners under Order XL, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure for additional evidence on the grounds stated therein.

8. Thereafter the defendants-petitioners being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division preferred the instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before this Division.

9. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendants-petitioners submits that the High Court Division failed to consider that in the Memorandum and Articles of Association, the name of Kazi Golam Hussain does not appear as Chairman of Hussain Fabrics Limited and, as such, said Kazi Golam Hussain has. no authority to enter into any agreement for sale on behalf of Hussain Fabrics Limited. He submits that admittedly series of litigations have been going on between the parties and because of threat by the plaintiffs-respondents,the defendants-petitioners failed to adduce both oral and documentary evidence before the Trial Court and get them marked as exhibits and that considering the above facts and circumstances an opportunity ought to have been given to the defendants-petitioners to adduce additional evidence but the High Court Division having failed to do so committed an illegality and, as such,the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. He submits that Kazi Golam Hussain was the Director of the Investment Board and that he could not be the Director / Chairman of Hussain Fabrics Limited and,assuch, he has no authority to enter into an agreement for sale in respect of the property of Hussain Fabrics Limited but the High Court Division decreed the suit by ignoring the same and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside, He then submits that the alleged deed of agreement dated 19-3-1990 alleging delivery of possession is totally false. He contends that had agreement dated 19-3-1990 been genuine, then there would have been no need of any Security Bond on 18-3-1992 .from the plaintiffs-respondents for Holding No. 14, Satish Barker Road, Gandaria, Dhaka but the High Court Division totally failed to consider the same and illegally allowed the appeal. He contends that the observation made by the Division Bench ofthe High Court Division that the defendants-petitioners are required to prove the facts that Kazi Golam Hossain was not the Chairman is totally misleading inasmuch as the plaintiffs-respondents must prove their own case and the weakness of the defendants-petitioners will not in any way improve the case of the plaintiffs-respondents and that the defendants-petitioners filed an application under Order XL, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure along with important documents, namely, Memorandum and Articles of Association to show that Kazi Golam Hossain was not the Chairman and some other papers to prove that the defendants were prevented by sufficient cause from attending the Court but the High Court Division did not accept those documents and delivered the judgment without considering the same and wrongly shifted the burden of proof on the defendants-petitioners and, as such, the judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. He then submits that the High Court Division illegally rejected the application under Order XL, rule 27 of the Code. of Civil Procedure; inasmuch; the High Court Division-found difficulties for the defendants-petitioners to attend the Court along with witnesses and, as. such, the High Court Division ought to have considered the same and allowed the application for additional evidence and should have sent back the case on remand giving an opportunity to the defendants-petitioners for proving their case as the High Court Division came to the finding that the defendants-petitioners failed to prove that Kazi Golam Hossain was not the Chairman, and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside.

10. Dr M Zahir, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent No.2 submits that there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division and, as such, the leave petition is liable to be dismissed. He submits that the plaintiffs-respondents by adducing evidence and examining natural witnesses proved the original documents and the case. Dr Zahir then submits that since the defendants-petitioners failed to produce the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Company to prove .the fact that the defendants predecessor was actually not the Chairman of the defendant No. l-company, the bainapatra can be treated as proper document to be enforceable in law. Dr Zahir contends that in order to prove that Kazi Golam Hossain was not Chairman of the defendant No.1 company the evidence should have been laid on behalf of the defendants-petitioners to that effect. Dr Zahir submits that the High Court Division rightly found that the learned Subordinate Judge misread the evidence adduced on behalf of the plaintiffs-respondents and thereby wrongly held that the plaintiff is to prove that Kazi Golam Hossain, the predecessor of the defendant- petitioner Nos. 2 and 3 was the Chairman of the defendant No. l-company as the plaintiffs did not produce the Memorandum and the Articles of Association of the defendant No.1 company, Dr zahir on behalf of the plaintiffs-respondents submits that the High Court Division having considered the provisions of section 102 of the Evidence Act to the effect that a person who alleges certain illegality or challenges the correctness of certain fact must prove the allegation of the same or correctness of the said fact and that to prove that Kazi Golam Hossain was not Chairman of the defendant No.1 company the onus squarely lies on the defendant No. l-company to discharge such onus to that effect as they raised the question and, as such, the High Court Division rightly held that the defendant No. 1-company ought to have led evidence to the effect that Kazi Golam Hossain was not Chairman of the defendant No. 1- company who was required to submit the company's documents including Memorandum and Articles of Association 'of the defendant No.1-company. Dr Zahir further submits that the High Court Division rightly found that the plaintiffs-respondents proved their possession on the suit land by examining wit- nesses and they proved the execution of bainapatra by both oral and documentary evidence and that they were inducted into possession pursuant to the bainapatra executed by the defendants. He also submits that the High Court Division having considered material evidence on record found that the learned Judge of the trial court correctly found the possession of the plaintiffs-respondents in the suit land but the trial Court wrongly held that the plaintiffs- respondents got possession through muscleman without the basis of any material evidence on record as the defendants did not examine any witness. Dr Zahir also asserts that the High Court Division on the question of additional evidence rightly referred to the provision of Order XL, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure which contemplates two preconditions in accepting the additional evidence, namely, where the trial court refused to admit evidence which ought to have been admitted or the appellate court requires the additional evidence to pronounce judgment or for any other substantial cause. He finally asserts that it is to be seen whether the required documents were in possession of the parties when the trial was held and that the defendants-petitioners at the appellate stage admitted that the said documents were very much in their custody but they did not produce before the trial Court and, as such, they should not be allowed to adduce additional evidence to fill up the lacuna by sending back the case on remand to the trial Court and, as such, the High Court Division rightly allowed the appeal in decreeing the suit.

11. We have perused the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal, impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the judgment and decree passed' by the learned Joint District Judge and other materials on record. It appears that in order to prove their case the plaintiffs-respondents examined four witnesses and submitted to the trial Court a number of documents which were formally exhibited. These documents include General Power of Attorney (Exhibit 1), photocopy of allotment letter dated 30-7-1985 (Exhibit 2), original bainapatra dated 19-3-1990 (Exhibit 3), original receipt of money issued by City Bank dated 26-8-1993 (Exhibit 4), original paper of handing over machineries and others (Exhibit 5), letter issued by chairman of defendant No. 1 to the Managing Director, Uttara Bank dated 16-9-1990 (Exhibit 6), pay orders, cheques and chalans for payment of Taka 14,29,303 (Exhibit 8 series), original security bond (Exhibit 9) original lease deed (Exhibit 10), letters issued by defendant No. 2 to Alhaj Monsurur Rahman (Exhibit 11 series), complaint petition case No. 5877 of2001 (Exhibit 14), order of appointment of 10 Ansars with payment receipt (Exhibit 15 series), plaint of Title Suit No. lof 1994 in the Court of 4th Artho Rin Adalat (Exhibit 17), Vokalatnama by the chairman (Exhibit 18) and statement filed by the Chairman of defendant No. I in Title Suit No. lof 1994 (Exhibit 19) and other relevant documents. The plaintiffs-respondents before the trial Court by adducing both oral and documentary evidence on record proved that there was an agreement for sale of the suit land on 19-3-1990 by the defendants-petitioners to the plaintiffs-respondents at. a consideration of Taka 34,54,300 and the plaintiffs paid earnest money of Taka 18,50,000 and the bainapatra was executed on the same date and the possession was delivered to the plaintiffs-respondents by' the defendant No. l-petitioner in presence of witnesses. The plaintiffs-respondents also proved their case by adducing evidence to the effect that the Managing Director of Uttara Bank in his letter dated 16-9-1990 (Exhibit 6) admitted the agreement for sale dated 19- 3-1990 and also admitted their possession. The defendants-petitioners in their written statement admitted possession of the plaintiffs-respondents in the suit land but did not adduce any evidence in support of the written statement to that effect. It appears that in this particular case the defendants-petitioners did neither examine any witness nor submit any document before the trial Court in support of their case. The learned Advocate for the defendants-petitioners only made submissions relying on, the written statement which has no legal basis in the eye of law because pleading of the defendants is not a legal piece of evidence and, as such, on the basis of the pleading of the defendants-petitioners their ,case could not be proved before the. Trial Court.

12. What is the true import of "pleadings" has been discussed by the Supreme Court of India in Kalyan Singh Chouhanvs CP Joshi, AIR 2011 SC 1127 in the following terms:

"Pleadings and particulars are required to enable the court to decide the rights of the parties in the trial. Thus, the pleadings are more to help the court in narrowing the controversy involved and to inform the parties concerned to the question in issue, so that' the parties may adduce appropriate evidence on the said issue, It is settled legal proposition that “ as a rule relief not founded on the pleadings should not be granted." Therefore, a decision of a case cannot be based on grounds outside the pleadings of the parties. The pleadings and issues are to ascertain the real dispute between the parties to narrow the area of conflict and to see just where the two sides differ," "

13. In Ram Sarup Gupta (dead) by LRs vs Bishun Narain Inter 'College, AIR 1987 SC 1242 it was held as under:

"It is well settled that in the absence of pleading, evidence, if any, produced by the parties cannot be considered. It is also equally settled that no party should be permitted to travel beyond its pleading and that all necessary and material facts should be pleaded by the party in sUPP0It of the case set up by it. The object and purpose of pleading is to enable the adversary party to know the case it has to meet."

14. In Bachhaj Nahar vs Nilima Mandai, AIR 2009 SC 1103 it was held as under:

"The object and purpose of pleadings and issues is to ensure that the litigants come to trial with all issues clearly defined and to prevent cases being expanded or grounds being shifted during trial. Its object is also to ensure that each side is fully alive to the questions that are likely to be raised or considered so that they may have an opportunity of placing the relevant evidence appropriate to the issues before the court for its consideration. This Court has repeatedly held that the pleadings are meant to give to each side intimation of the case, of the other so that it may be met, to enable courts to determine what is really at issue between the parties, and to prevent any deviation from the course which litigation on particular causes must take. The object of issues is to identify from the pleadings the question or points required to be decided by the courts so as to enable parties to let in evidence thereon it is said that no amount of evidence, on a plea that is not put forward in the pleadings, can be looked into to grant' any relief."

15. The cumulative effect of the above mentioned decisions is that pleadings and evidence are completely two different things. Pleadings prepare the suit for contest and evidence adduced in the case in line with the claims and denials stated in pleadings, actually contest the suit. In pleadings facts are to be described and relieves are to be sought which will narrow the controversy between and among the parties concerned, and will inform each of them of the extent to which they need to adduce evidence in support of their respective claim to prove their case. Where there is no pleading, evidence to that effect cannot be considered and where there is no evidence, pleadings cannot prove the fact and claim.

16. Defendant-petitioner Nos.2 and 3 did not adduce any evidence whether oral or documentary, before the trial court but their learned Counsel cross-examined two of the witnesses for the plaintiffs- respondents and argued before the Court. True effect of this cross-examination is that if it is able to shake the credibility of the witnesses examined on behalf of the plaintiffs-respondents, it can, create a doubt about the case of the plaintiffs-respondents; but it cannot prove .the case of the defendants-petitioners.

17. However, at a belated stage when appeal was filed against the decision of the trial Court the defendants-petitioners filed an application for adducing additional evidence by submitting Articles of Association and Memorandum of the defendant No. 1-company and other documents to show that Kazi Golam Hussain was not the chairman of the company at the relevant time and therefore he did not have any authority to transfer the suit property. Additional evidence can be adduced under Order XL, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. But there are certain preconditions that are to be fulfilled to enable a party to adduce additional evidence. This Division in the case of Sunil Krishna Banikvs Kailash Chandra Saha, 36 DLR (AD) 220 held as under:

"Clause (b) of rule 27 (1) appears to have conferred discretion on the Appellate Court to allow additional evidence in order "to enable it to pronounce Judgment" or for any other substantial cause". This discretion is not subject to any other limitation, or restriction excepting what is indicated by the words used therein.To do justice is the special preserve or domain of a court of law and this has been stressed by the words used in clause (b) as aforesaid. Since the point raised by the appellants required the determination of the Court before, pre-emption could be allowed,' the expression of hesitation and refusal to admit the additional evidence does not seem to be justified. This may have occasioned failure of justice instead of doing it. Before judgment is pronounced by the Court there may be no harm if it considers a vital piece of evidence produced before it, though late, so that it may prevent an injustice being done. It is true that such admission should not be encouraged. Power to admit additional evidence should, therefore, be sparingly used."

18. In the above quoted paragraph it has been clearly identified that for the ends of justice an Appellate Court can allow additional evidence to be adduced subject to the limitation's or restrictions provided in the rule 27 of Order XL of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and such admission should not be encouraged and power to admit additional evidence should be sparingly used. What the limitations are- have also been pointed out in the same judgment referring to a decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Muhammad Siddiq Muhammad Umar vs Australasia Bank Ltd, PLD 1966 SC 684, wherein it was observed:

"The rule merely prescribes that the requirement must be a genuine one and that the need for the additional evidence must be felt by the Court itself after it has examined the evidence already on the record and come to the conclusion that there is apparent some inherent lacuna or defect which hinders the due administration of justice. If it comes to this conclusion, then it has the power to call for additional evidence subject to the condition that it must record its reasons for doing so, in order that a higher Court may be able to ascertain that the -need was not merely imaginary but based upon factual grounds."

19. The Supreme Court of India in Arjan Singh vs Kartar Singh, 1951 AIR SC 193 held as under:

"The discretion to receive and admit additional evidence is not an arbitrary one, but is a judicial one, circumscribed by the limitations specified in Order XL, rule 27, Civil PC If the additional evidence was allowed to be adduced contrary to the principles governing the reception of such evidence, it would be a case of improper exercise of discretion, and the additional evidence so brought on the record will have to be ignored and the case decided as if it was non-existent. Under Order XL, rule 27, it is the appellate Court that must require the evidence to enable it to pronounce judgment. As laid down by the PC in the well-known case of Kessowji vs GIP Railway, 34 IA 115: (31 Born. 381 (PC), "the legitimate occasion for the apply of the present rule is when, on examining the evidence as it stands, some inherent lacuna or defect becomes apparent, not where a discovery is made, outside the Court, of fresh evidence and the application is made to import it.", and they reiterated this view in stronger terms even in the later case of Parsotim vs Lai Mohan 581A 254: (AIR (18) 1931 PC 143). The true test, therefore, is whether the appellate Court is able to pronounce judgment on the materials before it without taking into consideration the additional evidence sought to be adduced.

20. The Supreme Court of India in Syed Abdul Khadervs Rami Reddy, AIR 1979 SC 553 explaining the scope of allowing additional evidence observed:

"Order XL, rule 27, CPC enables the appellate Court to admit additional evidence in the circumstances or situation therein mentioned one such being where the appellate court requires .any document to be produced or any witness to be examined to enable it to pronounce judgment or for any other substantial cause. By a catena of decisions of this Court, it is well established that Order XL, rule 27, CPC does not confer a right on the party to produce additional evidence. But if the Court hearing the action requires any document so as to enable it to pronounce judgment, it has the jurisdiction to permit additional evidence to be produced."

21. From the above discussions it is abundantly clear that Order XL, rule 27 of the CPC does not confer any right to the party to adduce additional evidence. The need for additional evidence must be felt by the Court itself. When evidence was not adduced by the defendant at the trial stages, at the appellate stage he cannot claim as of his right, an opportunity to adduce evidence. Now the question is whether the High Court Division committed an error of  law resulting an error in the decision by rejecting the application for adducing additional evidence occasioning failure of justice. In other words whether the plaintiffs failed to prove their case or by cross-examining the witnesses of the plaintiffs and by arguing at the argument stage of the case learned Counsel of the defendants was able to create any shadow of doubt against the claim of the plaintiffs so as to require the court evidence at appellate stage as applied by the defendants. This is a suit for specific performance of contract and this Division in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Mrs Noor jahan Khan 8 BLT (AD) 1 held that in a suit for specific performance of contract the genuineness of the agreement for sale is the prime consideration. The genuineness of the agreement for sale could not be questioned by the defendants, what they did question was the authority and capacity of Kazi Golam Hussain to execute such a contract. The defendant Nos.2 and 3 did not adduce evidence to prove that Kazi Golam Hussainwas not the Chairman of the company at the relevant time. It is to be seen whether the plaintiffs were able to prove that Kazi Golam Hussain was the chairman of the company and he did hold the capacity and authority to enter into the contract on behalf of the company. Exhibit 6 is a letter issued by the Chairman of the defendant No. I-Company to the Managing Director, Uttara Bank dated 16-9-1990. This letter shows that Kazi Golam Hussain was chairman of the Company. For this reason, there is nothing left for the appellate Court that could require them further evidence to adjudge whether Kazi Golam Hussain was chairman of the company and that's why the High Court Division did not feel the necessity of any additional evidence and therefore there was no illegality in rejecting the prayer for adducing evidence by the defendants at the appellate stage.

22. As to the argument pressed by the learned Advocate for the defendants-petitioners to the effect that they were prevented by sufficient cause from attending court at the trial stage, as they were threatened by the plaintiffs-respondents and; as such, the High Court Division ought to have allowed evidence at the appellate stage, we are of the view that threat by the plaintiffs-respondents cannot be a sufficient ground for not examining witnesses or for not adducing documentary evidence before the trial Court. Because, if threat had been so predominant, the defendants-petitioners would have filed a case or GD entry and would not have been able to file written statement and subsequently contest the suit.

23. We have seen that before the trial Court the plaintiffs-respondents by adducing both oral and documentary evidence proved the agreement for sale, payment of earnest money, delivery of possession and their continuous possession in the suit land and family defendants' refusal to execute and register the deed of sale. But the defendants without adducing any evidence or examining any witness in the trial court in support of their case could not dislodge the plaintiffs' contention. The submissions made by the learned Advocate for the defendants- petitioners or the defendants case as narrated in the written statement not being a legal piece of evidence cannot be considered by the trial Court unless it is supported by both oral and documentary evidence adduced on behalf of the defendants-petitioners. We find that in the instant case, plaintiffs-respondents having proved their case by adducing both oral and documentary evidence which unchallenged because of non-examination of any witness on behalf of the defendants, inasmuch as, in the eye of law there is no legal evidence before the trial Court on behalf of the defendants-petitioners. In other words, the plaintiffs-respondents case was proved unchallenged. As regards the question of additional evidence, we find that the High Court Division rightly dismissed the defendants-petitioners prayer for allowing additional evidence. For the aforesaid reasons, we do not find any illegality in the impugned judgment and decree dated 31-5-2010 passed by the High Court Division in FA No. 216 of 2007. In consideration thereof, we do not find any substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.

Accordingly, the leave petition is dismissed.

End.

Md Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocate -----For the Respondent No.1.
