full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Defendant No. 14 presented the appeal against the decree dated 22-11-01 passed by the Fifth Court of Joint District Judge at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 135 of 1997, which decreed the suit.

2. One ANM Obaidul Islam, predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos. 1 to 8 as plaintiff instituted title Suit No. 120 of 1992 for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the suit land measuring about 51 decimals, which was fully described in the schedule to the plaint. The suit was then renumbered as aforesaid title Suit No. 137 of 1997.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that the suit land along with other land of CS Plot No. 158 originally belonged to one Abdul Kader and the record of rights were finally prepared and published in his name in CS khatian No. 4. Then, by a, registered deed of sale Abdul Kader transferred the entire land of said CS plot to Sharat Chandra Ghosh, Advocate. Sharat Chandra Ghosh possessed the land through 'Bargaders' Sheik Asanullah alias Munshi and Sheikh Mohammad for some time.Sharat Chandra Ghosh left a will giving the entire land of said plot to Premtosh Chandra Gosh and Bimal Chandra Chosh by a registered will dated 24 Ashar 1335 BS. The will was then duly probated on 13-7-35 in Probate Case No. 7 of 1934.

4. By a registered deed of sale dated 24-9-46 Premtosh Chandra Gosh and Bimal Chandra Ghosh transferred 70 decimals of said CS plot No. 158 to Sheikh Hasenuddin and delivered possession to him Sheik Hasenuddin thus possessed said 70 decimals of land and died leaving Samiruddin and others. Samiruddin and seven others sold said 70 decimals of land by two registered sale deeds dated 12-9-55 to aforesaid ANM Obaidul Islam and his wife Mostammat Rowshanara Begum alias Gulshan Begum transferring to each of them 35 decimals and delivered possession.

5. During survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, 66 decimals instead of 70 decimals was equally recorded in their names in SA khatian Nos. 197 and 196 respectively. At the time of RS survey, 33 decimals was similarly recorded in the name of each of them in RS khatian Nos. 202 and 225 respectively.

6. Obaidul Islam instituted Title Suit No. 303 of 1990 for a declaration that he purchased 35 decimals of land in the 'Benami' of his wife Gulshan Begum and on 6-8-92 got a compromise decree to that effect that Gulshan Begum was his 'Benamder'. Out of the suit land, 15 decimals were acquired in LA Case Nos. 40A and 40B of 1989-90 and they got the compensation as per award. Obaidul Islam made a waqf of 35 decimals of land and on 4-6-88 and 27-8-89 made applications for supplementary list with the Engineer Obaidul Islam Waqf Estate being EC No. 16392. While Obaidul Islam was thus in exclusive possession of the suit land, on 9-1-92 defendant Nos. 1 to 8 dispossessed him therefrom. Hence, the suit.

7. During the proceeding of the suit, on 10-4-96 Obaidul Islam died leaving the present plaintiffs as his only legal representatives.

8. Defendant No. 14 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the plaint case. Its case, in short, is that the suit land along with other land belonged to Abdul Kader and CS record of rights was finally prepared and published in his name. Abdul Kader bequeathed the entire land of CS plot No. 158 by a registered deed of gift being 4133 dated 31-5-1917 to his three sons Sheikh Elahi Bux, Sheikh Abdul Karim and Sheikh Abdul Nabi and put them into possession. On 16-4-43 by way of family settlement Sheikh Elahi Bux and Sheikh Karim got the suit plot in their shares. Successive heirs of Sheik Elahi Bux and Sheik Abdul Karim, namely, Aziza Begum, Serajul Islam, Tehera Begum, Sonaban Bibi, Abdul Motaleb, Abdus Shahid and Abdul Hamid, jointly possessed the suit land along with other land by cultivation and growing fruits openly, publicly and adversely to the entire world.

9. Then, by a registered deed of sale dated 4-7-95 all those successors of Elahi Bux and Abdul Karim transferred 49.5 decimals out of said CS plot No. 158 to said defendant No. 14 and delivered possession. Defendant No. 14 had since then been possessing said 49.50 decimals of land. It got its name mutated in respect of said land and had been paying rent. It filled the land with earth and erected boundary walls surrounding said land and also made semi-pucca structures thereon. It got water, gas and electricity connection to the land.

10. Defendant No. 11 RAJUK also filed a written statement denying the case of the plaintiff. It although cross-examined the witness of the plaintiff but did not adduce any evidence. It contended that the suit was not maintainable without prior notice under section 169 of Town Improvement Act, 1953.

11. On the party pleadings the following issues were finally settled:

(a) Was the suit maintainable in the manner and form as framed?

(b) Was the suit barred by limitation?

(c) Had the plaintiff got title and possession in the suit land?

(d) Was the plaintiff entitled to get a decree as prayed for? and

(e) What relief the plaintiff was entitled to.

12. In support of their case, the plaintiffs examined three witnesses and adduced number of documents, which were marked as Exhibits 1 to 20. Defendant No. 14 also examined three witnesses and its documents were marked as Exhibits 'Ka' to 'cha'.

13. PW 1 Md Ruhul Amin testified that he was plaintiff No. 3 and deposing on behalf of all plaintiffs. He deposed in support of the plaint case and tendered the documents into evidence.

14. He stated that the suit land was a part of CS plot No. 158 appertaining to CS khatian No.4. The plot comprised of 5.68 acres. The suit land was finally recorded and published in the name of Abdul Kader. By a deed being No. 351 dated 12-1-1921, Exhibit 1, Abdul Kader transferred the entire land of said CS plot No. 158 to one Sharat Chandra Ghosh, Advocate, Sharat Chandra Ghosh possessed the suit land through 'Bargaders' Sheik Ahsanullah Munshi and Sheikh Mohammad who gave a joint registered 'Barga kabuliyat' being deed No. 2810 dated 19-5-1924, Exhibit 2(ka) for a period of six years. Then, Sharat Chandra Ghosh left a will executed by him on 24 Ashar 1335 BS giving the entire land of said CS plot No. 158 to Premtosh Chandra Ghosh and Bimal Chandra Ghosh. After death of Sharat Chandra Ghosh, they on 19-7-1935 obtained a probate of the will in Probate Case NO.7 of 1934, Exhibits 3 and 6.

15. By a registered deed of sale being No. 4030 dated 24-9-1946 said Premtosh Chandra Ghosh and Bimal Chandra Ghosh transferred 70 decimals of land to Sheikh Hasenuddin. The original deed of Sheik Hasenuddin was adduced and marked Exhibit 4. After the death of Sheikh Hasenuddin, his heirs Samiruddin and others by two deeds being No. 6266 and 6268 dated 12-9-1955 transferred 70 decimals of land to Obaidul Islam and his wife Gulshan Begum and delivered possession. Original deeds were adduced and marked Exhibits 5 and 5(ka). During survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the suit land was recorded equally in SA khatian Nos. 196 and 197 in the name of his father and mother, Exhibit 7 and 7(ka). Similarly, RS khatian Nos. 202 and 225, 7(kha) and 7(ga) were also prepared in the names of his parents. In the RS khatian a road was shown wrongly. Consequently, his father filed two written objections, which were accepted and mistake was corrected vide Exhibits 9 series.

16. He stated that in the suit land, paddy was cultivated by his father and a pond was made by cutting earth. His father let out some huts on the land to different tenants and received rents, Exhibit 10 series. He stated that when the Public Health Engineering Department tried to take a sewerage line over the land his father raised objections: He made applications before different authorities including the Chief Martial Law Administrator. Consequently, construction of sewerage line stopped, Exhibit 11 to 11 (chha). In 1988, his father made waqf of 35 decimals of land and addressed two applications to the Waqf Administrator for supplementary list of the Engineer Obaidul Islam Waqf Estate, being EC No. 16392. After death of his father, the Waqf Administrator however, rejected the applications by his order dated 7-7-97, Exhibit 12.

17. He also stated that his father purchased half of the suit land in the name 'Benami' of his mother. He then instituted Title Suit No. 303 of 1990 in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge for declaration that his mother was 'Benamder' of his father. The suit ended in a compromise decree declaring his mother was 'Benamder' of his father. The plaint, decree and 'Solenama' were adduced and marked Exhibits 13, 13(ka) and 13(kha). Some portion of the suit land measuring 15 decimals was acquired in LA Case No. 40A of 1989-90 and 40B of 1989-90. Award was given in the names of plaintiffs. They withdrew the money. Notices for acquisition and information slips about payment of compensation were marked Exhibits 14, 14(ka), l4(kha) and 14(ga).

18. He stated that defendant Nos. 1 to 8 instituted Title Suit No. 17 of 1993 for perpetual injunction restraining the defendants from receiving the compensation for acquisition. The suit was dismissed on 8-9-93. Appeal therefrom being Title Appeal No. 318 of 1993 was also dismissed on 29-4-95; judgments and decrees were adduced and marked Exhibit 15 series.

19. He stated that said defendants instituted Title Suit No. 296 of 1989, which was renumbered as Title Suit No. 47 of 1990 and got an ex parte decree. Against the ex parte decree, miscellaneous case being No. 12 of 1994, No. 13 of 1994 and No. 14 of 1994 were filed under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree. Ultimately, all the miscellaneous cases were allowed and ex parte decree was set aside by judgment and order dated 28-4-97, Exhibit 17. The plaintiffs also instituted Title Suit No. 221 of 1995, which was renumbered as Title Suit No. 134 of 1997 but ultimately, withdrew the suit after the ex parte decree dated 19-11-90 was set aside, Exhibit 17(chha).

20. Meanwhile, on the basis of said ex parte decree, said defendant Nos. 1 to 8 on 9-1-92 dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land by forcibly entering into the suit land therein and breaking the huts. The defendants then erected furniture shop in the suit land in order to change the nature and character of the suit land.

21. In cross-examination, he stated that total suit land was 66 decimals. Entire land of the suit plot was 5.68 acres. He could not say what was the adjacent east plot of CS plot No. 158 and who possessed. Similarly, he said that he had no knowledge who was on the adjacent west of CS plot No. 158 and what was plot number. He denied that he did not know CS plot No. 158. He stated that he did not know plot No. 158 right on the spot. He was aged 49 years old. He did not see the 'Bargaders'. He did not bring any witness to prove 'Borga'. He did not file the rent receipts of Sheikh Hasenuddin. He did not see him personally possessing the suit land. The Waqf Administrator informed that the suit land was not included in the existing waqf. He was not aware whether there was any partition amongst the owners of plot No. 158. He did not make parties all the owners of the plot.

22. To cross-examination by defendant No. II, he stated that he did not give notice before the suit to the RAJUK but subsequently issued summons.

23. On recall, he stated that to the east of the suit land was Rafiqul Kader Chowdhury and others, to the west 29 Uttar Dhanmondi, Kalabagan (land of Masuda), to the north, road of Panthapath and south 41 and 30 north Dhanmondi, Kalabagan.

24. PW 2 Md Ali Akbar, aged about 90 years. He testified that he knew Obaidul Islam and worked with him. They were lecturers in the Engineering College. He knew the suit land, which was near his house. In 1955, they purchased land of so it plot together. Plaintiff purchased the suit land and got possession. He knew children of Obaidul Islam. They were dispossessed 8/9 years ago. Before dispossession, the plaintiff possessed the suit land. At the time defendant No. 14 possessed but he did not know him. He had no title.

25. In cross-examination, he reiterated that in 1955 they got possession. At the time, there was paddy field. He denied that he did not see the suit land. Defendant No. 14 possessed for 8/9 years. At the time, there were small huts on the suit land. There were tenants of Obaidul Islam on his land. Now they were not there. He did not know the defendants. He again stated that the defendant possessed the suit land for last 8/9 years.

26. PW 3 Monirul Alam Chowdhury, aged about 57 years, testified that he was working as Professor in Kalyanpur Mohila College. He knew Obaidul Islam and also the suit land. He also knew the children of Obaidul Islam. Obaidul Islam became owner by purchase and since then possessed. He also erected huts. In 1992, Obaidul Islam was dispossessed from the suit land. He did not know them who dispossessed him.

27. In cross-examination, he stated that Obaidul Islam was his brother-in-law. He denied that he was deposing for the interest of his nephews and nieces. He could not say who dispossessed the plaintiff in 1992.

28. SyedMd Delawar Hossain was examined as Advocate Commissioner. He deposed that he was the member of Dhaka Bar and appointed an Advocate Commissioner. After holding investigation he submitted his report dated 12-5-98.

29. Abdul Awal Minto on behalf of defendant No. 14 was examined as DW 1 on commission. He deposed in support of its written statement. He admitted that the entire land of plot No. 158 belonged to Abdul Kader and CS record of rights was prepared in his name. He claimed that by a registered deed of gift dated 31-5-17, Exhibit "kha" Abdul Kader transferred the entire land of CS plot No. 158 to his three sons, namely, Elahi Bux, Abdul Karim and Abdul Nabi and delivered possession. In 1943, by way of family settlement Sheikh Abdul Karim and Sheikh Elahi Bux got the suit land in their share. Elahi Bux then died leaving behind two sons Sayeed Hossain and Siddique Hossain, Sheikh Abdul Karim also died leaving one son Miah Hossain, Sayeed Hossain died leaving one son Arju Mia, Siddique Hossain died leaving one wife Aziza, one daughter Tahera Begum and one son Sirajul Islam, Arzu died leaving one wife Tahera Khatun. Miah Hossain died leaving one wife Sonaban Bibi, three sons Abdul Motaleb, Abdul Shahid and Abdul Hamid. The successive heirs of Elahi Bux and Abdul Karim used to possess the suit land by cultivation. SA record of rights was prepared in the names of various persons but not recorded in the names of Sonaban and others as they were illiterate. Accordingly, they instituted Title Suit No. 47 of 1990, which was decreed on 28-11-90. By a deed being No. 2725 dated 4-7-75 Exhibit "ga" he purchased 49.5 decimals of land from Sonaban Bibi and others and got possession. He got his name mutated, Exhibit  gha He filled the suit land with earth and got a boundary wall erected around the suit land. Nobody obstructed them. His people was living there. He got the connection of gas, electricity and water, etc. to the suit land Exhibit "uma" . He got a municipality holding number which is 4412/a, North Dhanmondi Exhibit "cha" series. The plaintiffs and their predecessor had no title and possession in the suit land. He denied that on 12-1-21 Abdul Kader transferred the suit land to Sharat Chandra Ghosh or he possessed ever.

30. In cross-examination, he testified that he was doing business. On 6-4-99 he submitted written statement. He could not say as to whether the papers were submitted along with his written statement. Whether or not on 21-3-01 he submitted the papers, he could not say, his Advocate could say. He could not say whether the deed No. 4133, Exhibit "kha'' was submitted in Title Suit No. 47 of 1990. The seal on the deed reads Mymensingh. He denied that the date 31-5-1917 on the deed was written recently. One page stamp was valued one Taka two Annas and subsequent two papers were cartridges. He denied that those cartridges were Bangladeshi. He denied that there was no entry in the ledger book of the Sub-registry and that cartridge papers were not of the British time, having no mark of lion. He also denied that the deed was of recent writing and created recently. He did not know any of the witnesses to the deed and he was not born then. To the question of the commission as to whether he claimed the land of RS plot Nos. 1207, 1208 and 1209, he answered he could say only by looking through the papers and record. He did not know whether said plots were recorded in the name of the plaintiff. He denied that the suit land was recorded in plot Nos. 1207, 1208 and 1209.

31. DW 2 Md Abdur Rashed, aged about 48 years. He deposed that he knew the defendant but did not know the suit land. The defendant No. 14 possessed the suit land since 1995. Before him Sonaban Bibi and others were in possession. Since 1979-80 he saw them. At the time it was pond, bamboo clumps and paddy field. He never saw the plaintiff possessed any part of the suit land.

32. In cross-examination, he stated that he was doing business. He witnessed the deed of the defendant who purchased from Sonaban Bibi and others. Entire land of CS plot No. 158 was 13.5 acres. He did not receive any summons.

33. DW 3 Md Riazuddin Akand, aged about 50 years, deposed that he knew the defendant and also the suit land. Defendant No. 14 possessed the suit land since 1995. Before him Sonaban and others possessed. They possessed since 1980. There was ditch earlier now that was filled with earth. He did not see the plaintiff before the defendant.

34. In cross-examination, he stated that he was a teacher of Tejgaon Polytechnic Government College. Defendant No. 14 possessed western part of the suit plot. He could not say the quantity of the land in suit. 	.

35. These are all the evidence adduced by the parties.

36. Upon the aforesaid evidence, oral and documentary, learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit on contest against contesting defendants and ex parte against the rest declaring title of the plaintiffs in the suit land and directed the concerned defendant to hand over vacant possession to the plaintiff within sixty days from date.

37. Only issue facing us is, whether the learned Joint District Judge was justified in decreeing the suit.

38. As stated above, admittedly CS plot No. 158 appertaining to CS khatian No.4 including the suit land originally belonged to Abdul Kader and CS record of rights was finally prepared and published in his name.

39. It is the case of the plaintiff that Abdul Kader transferred the entire land of CS plot No. 158 to Sharat Chandra Ghosh, Advocate by a registered deed of sale being No. 351 dated 12-1-1921 and delivered possession. A certified copy of said document was adduced by the plaintiffs and marked Exhibit 2. Sharat Chandra Ghosh possessed the suit land for some time through 'Bargaders'. namely, Sheik Asanullah Munshi and Sheik Mohammad by executing registered 'Barga Kabuliyat' dated 19-5-1924. The plaintiffs adduced a certified copy of the Kabuliyat which was marked Exhibit 2(kha). Sharat Chandra Ghosh gave the suit land to Premtosh Ghosh and Bimal Chandra Ghosh by a registered deed of will executed on 24 Ashar 1335 BS. The will was duly proved on 13-11-1934 and probate granted thereon on 19-7-35 in Probate Case No.7 of 1934. To prove the will and probate, the plaintiffs adduced a certified copy of the will, Exhibit 6 and suit register of said Probate Case No. 7 of 1934, Exhibit 3. In the column, "order made and date" of the suit register, it was recorded that the will was proved on 13-11-1934 and probated on 13-7-1935. Premtosh Chandra Ghosh and Bimal Chandra then transferred 70 decimals of CS plot No. 158 to Hasenuddin by a registered deed of sale dated 24-9- 46. The plaintiff adduced the original deed, which was marked Exhibit 1. After death of Hasenuddin, his heirs Samiruddin and seven others by two registered deeds of sale dated 12-9-1955 transferred equally said 70' decimals of land to Obaidul Islam, original plaintiff and his wife Gulshan Begum. Those deeds were adduced and marked as Exhibit 5 and 5(ka). During survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 66 decimals instead of 70 decimals was equally recorded in the names of Obaidul. Islam and his wife Gulshan Begum in SA khatian Nos. 196 and 197 Exhibit 7 and 7(ka). During RS survey said land was again recorded as RS plot Nos. 1207, 1208 and 1209 in RS khatian Nos. 202 and 225 in their names Exhibit 7(kha) and 7(ga). The plaintiffs adduced rent receipts showing payment of rents, Exhibit 8 series and counterfoils evidencing possession through tenants, Exhibit 10 series.

40. Obaidul Islam made a waqf of 35 decimals of land. But his prayer for supplementary list with the Engineer Obaidul Islam Waqf Estate was rejected by the Waqf Administration by his order dated 7-7-97 Exhibit 12.

41. Out of 66 decimals, 15 decimals were acquired in LA Case Nos. 40A and 40B of 1989-90. The plaintiffs adduced the notices for acquisition and also the information slips showing payment of the compensation to the plaintiffs, Exhibits 14, 14(ka), 14(kha) and 14(ga).

42. Meanwhile Obaidul Islam instituted Title Suit No. 303 of 1990 for a declaration that he purchased 35 decimals of land in the 'Benami' of his wife Gulshan Begum from Samiruddin and others. The suit ended in compromise and Gulshan Begum was declared to be 'Benami' of Obaidul Islam. Plaintiff adduced the plaint, compromise petition and decree of the suit vide Exhibit 13 series. Public Health Engineering Department once wanted to take sewerage line through the land of the plaintiffs. Obaidul Islam raised objections thereto. He even wrote to Chief Martial Law Administrator. The project was ultimately abandoned. In support, the plaintiffs produced the letters written by Obaidul Islam to different authorities, Exhibit 11 series.

43. PW 2 Md Ali Akbar aged about 90 years corroborated PW 1 that he along with Obaidul Islam purchased land out of said CS plot No. 158 together and became owners and in 1955 they got possession. He and Obaidul possessed their land. Then Obaidul Islam was dispossessed from the land 8/9 years ago. PW 3 also corroborated PW 1 on possession. They appear to be respected people. We could not find any reason for them for not telling the truth on oath.

44. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Senior Advocate, submitted that the evidence of the plaintiffs on title and possession were insufficient. The magnitude of above voluminous documentary evidence along with oral evidence adduced by the plaintiffs in support of their title and possession is so great that we cannot appreciate such submission.

45. He particularly stressed that Exhibits 2, 2(ka), 3 and 6 were certified copies and the plaintiffs did not prove them by calling for the orizinal volume from the office of Sub-Registrar. As such, the documents do not prove title of the plaintiffs.

46. In reply, Mr Hasan Foez Siddique, learned Advocate for the respondents, drew our attention to the judgment dated 8-9-93 passed in Title Suit No. 17 of 1993 brought by defendant Nos. 1 to 8, Exhibit 15(kha). In the suit, very same certified copy was adduced by the plaintiffs and marked as Exhibit B. DW 7 Khandker Mosharraf Hossain, record keeper, brought the volume and proved the certified copy as correct tallying with the entries made in the volume. In the judgment dated 29-4-95 passed in Title Appeal No. 318 of 1993, said deed dated 11-1-1921, Exhibit B was considered and the appellate Court found that the plaintiffs. i.e. defendant Nos. 1 to 8 there, failed to prove that the deed was created. Besides, Exhibit 3 certified copy of suit register, which clearly recorded that on 19-7-1935 the will of Sharat Chandra Ghosh was probated in Probate Case No.7 of 1934. In view of the above, we do not think the plaintiffs were required to prove the certified copy again by calling for the volume from the office of the Sub-registrar.

47. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submitted that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession before dispossession. He also referred to the deposition of the plaintiffs' witnesses. Defendant Nos. 1 to 8 who dispossessed the plaintiffs did not contest the suit. So, practically the evidence of the plaintiffs on possession followed by dispossession got a walkover. As defendant No. 14 purchased the suit land in 1995 from said defendant Nos. 1 to 8 and possessed since then, had got no locus standi to contest the case of possession and dispossession of the plaintiffs.

48. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed also submitted that the present suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession without a prayer for partition of CS plot No. 158 was not maintainable as number of people now owned and possessed the land of said plot comprising of about 5.68 acres and no effective decree for title and possession could be passed without the presence of those owners.

49. We find that the suit land was already recorded in the names of original plaintiff Obaidul Islam and his wife Gulshan Begum during survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in plot Nos. 298/302 and 298/303 appertaining to SA khatian Nos. 196 and 197. Such record of rights was published some time in 1964. On the basis of such record of rights the plaintiff possessed the suit land exclusively on payment of rents on proper receipt Exhibit 8 series. Similarly, under the RS survey the suit land was again recorded in the names of Obaidul Islam and his wife Gulshan Begum in RS plot Nos. 1207, 1208 and 1209 appertaining to RS khatian Nos. 202 and 225 and RS record of rights was published in 1980s.

<u>50. In view of such exclusive possession of their specific land under distinct and separate holdings for more than 12 years, the plaintiffs no more need partition of their land. Submission of Mr Khandker has therefore got no substance.</u>

51. Lastly, he submitted the suit land out of 5.68 acres was not clearly and properly identified and in the absence of identification, the plaintiffs were not entitled to a decree prayed for.

52. In view of above discussions, we find no substance in the submission of Mr. Khandker. Moreover, defendant Nos. 1 to 8 never contested the identity of the suit property. Nor defendant No. 14 raised any question about the identity of the suit land.

53. In support of its case, defendant No. 14 adduced a deed 4133 dated 31-5-1917 claimed to have been executed and registered by Abdul Kader giving the entire land of CS plot No. 158 measuring 8.44 acres of land to his three sons, Sheikh Elahi Bux, Sheikh Abdul Karim and Sheikh Abdul Nabi. Said defendant tendered the deed into evidence on 24-7-2001 and got it marked Exhibit kha. It is the case of defendant No.14 that after a family settlement Sheikh Elahi Bux and Sheikh Abdul Karim got said land in their share. But no evidence whatsoever was led in support thereof. After their death, their successive heirs Sonaban Bibi and others transferred 49.5 decimals of land to defendant No. 14.

54. Learned Joint District Judge found that the deed was forged and created. He found two cartridges used for the deed of Bangladeshi origin. There was no sign of British time. On being asked, the officer-in-charge of Mymensingh Sadar Sub-Registry could not say that the deed was registered in their office, Exhibit 18. The officer-in-charge further informed that on 14-4-1918 the office of the Sadar Sub-Registry, Mymensingh was burned down by accidental fire. Besides, there was no reason for registration of the deed by Abdul Kader in Mymensingh. We have closely examined the deed. We find the writings on the deed very fresh and of recent origin. So, we do not have any hesitation to affirm the finding of the learned Joint District Judge that said deed Exhibit 'kha' was created by forgery and fabrication for the suit. Mr Khandker however, did not rely upon the deed, in any way.

55. Having full knowledge that the deed was forged, fraudulent and created, DW 1 Abdul Awal Minto on behalf of defendant No. 14 gave the deed into evidence. DW 1 Abdul Awal Minto thereby committed a serious offence making him liable for prosecution under section 195(i)(c) read with section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

56. In the circumstances, ultimate conclusion of the learned Joint District Judge that the plaintiffs successfully proved their title and possession in the suit land and thereupon, he committed no error in decreeing the suit. Such decree does not suffer from any illegality or infirmity. Appeal, therefore, fails.

57. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with cost. Impugned judgment and decree are hereby affirmed and the defendants, particularly defendant No. 14, are directed to vacate the suit land by removing all their structures within a period of thirty days from date.

58. Connected Rule is also discharged with cost. Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule on 19-6-02 staying further proceeding of the execution case is hereby recalled and vacated.

59. In view of above decision, the application of third party for addition does not deserve any consideration and is accordingly, rejected.

60. Let the deed of gift being No. 4133 dated 31-5-1917 Exhibit 'kha' be impounded. The Registrar is directed to immediately take the document in his custody and send the same in safe cover to the Fifth Court of Joint District Judge for prosecution of DW 1 Abdul Awal Minto in accordance with law.

The learned Joint District Judge, 5th Court at Dhaka is hereby directed to make a complaint against DW 1 Abdul Awal Minto under section 195(1)(c) read with section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for using said deed in the suit knowing it to be forged and fraudulent for criminal prosecution.

Send down the records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
AKM Shahidul Huq J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh at the instance of the petitioner a Rule Nisi has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the discriminatory treatment to the petitioner and inaction of the respondents in giving allotment of a plot in the extended Uttara Third Residential Area (third phase) Project as affected person in compliance with the provision of Article 8 (kba) প্লট বরাদ্দ নীতিমালা Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakba as well as of the decision taken in the Board meeting of Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakba dated 23-9-2010 and 26-9-2010 (Annexure-E) should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why a direction should not be given upon the respondents to give allotment of a plot to the petitioner in the extended Uttara Residential Area (third phase) Project as affected person vide Award Serial Nos. 368/1, 369/3 and 370/2 and security deposit slip No. 10023 and or pass such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. Relevant facts necessary for disposal of the instant rule is that the petitioner acquired 17 decimals of land at District Dhaka, formerly Police Station Mirpur, Mouza Bounia, SA Plot No. 245/246/248 and RS Plot Nos. 366/370/371 from its lawful owner Serajul Haque Prodhan and MrsRokeya Begum, by virtue of a deed of Hebabil-ewaj vide No. 2145 dated 5-6-2000.

3. The petitioner got possession of the said land and got his name mutated under mutation case No. 12421 of 2002, 12412 of 2002 and 12423 of 2002 and paid rents to the Government in respect of his total land measuring 17 decimals.

4. While the petitioner was owning and possessing the said land, the Government decided to acquire the same along with some other lands for the requiring body namely Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakha and ultimately the land was acquired under LA Case No.6 of 2001-2002 and duly served notice upon the petitioner.

5. The petitioner applied for compensation award against his acquired land by submitting all relevant title deeds and papers and the office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) having been satisfied as to the ownership of the petitioner gave compensation money with award.

6. The requiring body namely Rajdhahi Unnayan Kartripakba published and advertisement inviting applications from the interested person for allotment of plots under the project namely, "Extended Uttara Third Residential Area (third phase) project hereinafter referred to. as the "Project" and the petitioner being affected person in response to the said advertisement, filed application for getting a plot measuring 3 katha by depositing required amount of Taka 75,000.

7. The persons whose land is acquired is entitled to get priority of allotment Of the plot if the acquisition is for the residential purpose and in this regard a gazette was published on 15th January 1970 as Dhaka gazette wherein it was provided that "Subject to the provision of clause B of sub-section of section 101 of the Act valid application of the person who had either land or residential house in the area acquired for the development of Township, has have the first preference for allotment provided be applied and fulfill other condition RAJUK set up a nitimala for allotment of plot of the affected person as 8 (ka) and 8(kha) and the petitioner is within the Nitimala of 8(kba). The petitioner's land is acquired and he has fulfilled all the required conditions and made application in proper form.

8. The Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakha already started giving allotment and also allotted many plots to their chosen persons and though already more than 8 years elapsed from the date of filing application with requisite amount of Taka 75,000, the petitioner did not receive any response or information from the authority as to his allotment of the plot as he is entitled to get preference .in allotment of plot under the project.

9. The petitioner acquired the land measuring 17 decimals for residential purpose and except the said acquired land he has no other piece of land within Dhaka City Corporation and due to such acquisition, he become landless in the city.

10. It is evident from the minutes of the Board Meeting of Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakha dated 23-9-2010 and 26-9-2010 that there is clear admission by RAJUK that the people whose 0.1650 acre of land or more than that have been acquired are entitled to have a plot and accordingly, the said Board meeting recommended allotment of plots in favour of 568 affected persons.

11. RAJUK gave allotment of plot to the 568 affected persons as per Nitimala enunciated in 8 (ka) and 8 (kha) and the matter was published in Daily News Paper namely Daily "Samakal" on 24-10-2010.

12. The provision regarding allotment of the plots is that the affected persons shall have first preference for getting allotment, but the respondents without considering the legitimate right of the petitioner already allotted many plots to their chosen person and not taking any steps for giving allotment in favour of the petitioner and, as such, the discriminatory treatment and inaction of the respondents in giving allotment of a plot in the project is liable to be declared to have been done without lawful authority and be of no legal effect.

13. Mr Md Humayun Bashar, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner and no one appears on behalf of the respondent No. 2 to oppose the rule.

14. Mr Md Humayun Bashar, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the provisions regarding allotment of the plots is that the affected persons shall have first preference for getting allotment, but the respondents without considering the legitimate right of the petitioner already allotted many plots to their chosen persons and not taking any steps for giving allotment in favour of the petitioner and, as such, the discriminatory treatment and -inaction .of the respondents in giving allotment of a plot .in the project is liable to be declared to have been done without lawful authority and be of no legal effect.

15. He next submits that since 568 affected persons have been selected for allotment, on the criterion that they are awardees of 0.1650 acre of land, the petitioner being equally' affected standing on the same footing is entitled to have a plot but the respondents with malafide motive discriminating the petitioner with them depriving his legitimate right and, as such, the discriminatory treatment inaction of the respondents in giving allotment of a plot to the petitioner in the project is liable to be declared to have been done without lawful authority and be of no legal effect and the respondents are liable to be directed to give allotment of a plot to the petitioner from the project.

16. Learned Advocate further submits that since the petitioner is an awardee of 0.17 acres of land, he is entitled to have a plot under Article 8 of the প্লট বরাদ্দ নীতিমালা RAJUK as well as the  decision and recommendation taken in the Board Meeting of RAJUK dated 23-9-2010 and 26-9- 2010 and more so, 568 affected persons, having selected for allotment on criterion as above and, as such, the discriminatory treatment and in action of the respondents in giving allotment of a plot in the project is liable to be declared to have been done without lawful authority and be of no legal effect and the respondents are liable to be directed to give allotment of a plot to the petitioner from, the project.

17. He lastly submits that the inaction of the respondents to comply with the Article 8 (kha) of the প্লট বরাদ্দ নীতিমালা of RAJUK as well as its decision equally in respect of the petitioner like as the 568 others who have been selected for allotment of plot is discriminatory, arbitrary, malafide and a clear violation of the fundamental rights of the petitioner guaranteed under Article 27 and 31 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

18. Learned Advocate in support of his contention refers an unreported decision of this Hon'ble Division passed in writ petition No. 1781 of 2011.

19. No one appears to oppose the rule on behalf of the respondent.

20. Heard the learned Advocate perused the writ petition filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the annexure filed thereto and considered the material on record.

21. It appears from annexure H, minutes of the 9th Board meeting of RAJUK dated 23-9- 2010 and 26-9-2010, that the concerned Ministry had recommended for allotment of plots in favour of the awardees of 0.1650 acres of land as affected persons. The Board of RAJUK also decided to allot plots to 560 persons on the criterion that 0.1650 acres of land had been acquired from each of them and, as such, they were entitled to a plot under Article 8 (kha) of the প্লট বরাদ্দ নীতিমালা of RAJUK. However, it appears from the same minutes that, the fate of 54 persons including the petitioners, whose awards had been subsequently added on their applications to make them eligible for allotment on the same criterion, remained pending.

<u>22. Since 560 persons have been selected for allotment of plots on consideration that they are awardees of 0.1650 acres of land, we do not see any valid reason for excluding the petitioner from such benefit. Since they are equally affected, although by subsequent addition of their awards, We do not find any legal reason for denial of their such entitlements when people standing on the same footing were selected for such allotment. Since main criterion as set by RAJUK is awardee of 0.1650 acres of land and names of 560 selected persons have been published in the daily newspaper on such consideration, we are of the view that the petitioner are also jointly entitled to have a 5 (five) katha plot allotted in their favour if lands are available with RAJUK for such allotment.</u>

23. We find support of this view in a decision of our Apex Court held in RAJUK vs Jahanara Begum, reported in 12 BLT (AD) (2004) page 222 = 57 DLR (AD) 80 wherein modifying the order passed by the High Court Division, the Appellate Division directed the RAJUK to scrutiny the petition filed by the writ petitioners for allotment of plot and to allot plots in their favour if they satisfied the condition and criteria set down by the RAJUK entitling a person to have allotment of plot as affected person provided RAJUK has available lands for such allotment.

24. In view of the said decision of our Apex Court, we hold that since the petitioners has prima-facie fulfilled the criterion in the instant case, namely he is awardee of 0.1650 acres of land like other 560 selected allottees, he is also entitled to have a 5 (five) katha plot allotted jointly in his favour as applied for provided RAJUK has available land for such allotment.

Accordingly, RAJUK is directed to scrutinize petitioners' application receiving code No. 15227 for allotment of plot in the extended Uttara 3rd residential project and allot a 5 (five) katha plot in his favour provided RAJUK has available lands for such allotment. The above process should be completed within 2 (two) months from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment and order, with the above directions and observations, the rule is disposed of, without any order as to cost. Transmit a copy of this judgment to the concern authority forthwith for information and necessary action.

End.

lawyer:
AB Roy Chowdhury------For the Petitioners. 
Carib Newaz with Maksuda Aktar------For Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Abdus Sukur (Md) and others  ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Bhasani Mandal and another  ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule was obtained by the plaintiffs upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and decree dated 9-5-2000 passed by Additional District Judge, 3rd Court at Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 748 of 1999 reversing those dated  30-9-1999 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, 6th Court at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 249 of 1998.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs on 28-7-1998 instituted the suit for setting aside the judgment and decree dated 24-5-1998 and 31-5-1998 respectively, exhibit 12 and 12 (ka) obtained by defendant No.1 from 3rd Court of Additional Assistant Judge at *Civil Revision No. 3535 of 2000 Dhaka in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 and also for declaration that those are not operative against and binding upon the plaintiffs.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that after successive transactions, the suit land measuring about 96 decimals of CS and SA Plot No. 1244 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 212 and SA Khatian No. 507 were owned and possessed by defendant No. 1 and his brother Sudhir Mandai. Then, both of them transferred the suit land to Parul Bal by a registered deed of sale dated 14-5-1969 being deed No. 4400, exhibit 4 and delivered possession. Then, on 4-2-1970 Parul Balal transferred the suit land to one Sufia Khatun by a registered deed of sale being deed No. 1126, exhibit 5 and delivered possession. Sufia Khatun got her name mutated and possessed the suit land for quite some time on payment of rents and then, on 9-12-1977 she transferred by a registered kabala being deed No. 35842, exhibit 7 to Sahabuddin and delivered possession. Then, by about 30 sale deeds exhibit 9 series, Sahabuddin transferred the suit land to the plaintiffs from 1979 to 1984 and delivered possession. The plaintiffs after purchase got their names mutated in respect of their respective land and now, possess the same in their specific share by raising dwelling huts, etc. and on payment of rents.

4. On 8-7-1998 the plaintiffs got a notice issued by the local Demra Police Station on the basis of a complaint dated 7-7-1998 lodged by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, and therefrom, they came to learn for the first time that the defendants claimed to have obtained the aforesaid judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997. Obtaining a certified copy of the same, they found that the defendants got the deed of sale to Parul Bala dated 14-5-1969 exhibit 4 cancelled in the said judgment and decree.

5. Defendant No. 1 alone contested the suit by filing a written statement. His case, in brief, is that he and his brother acquired the entire suit land of 96 decimals. The suit land is nal land i.e. agricultural land. He possesses half 48 decimals of land through borgadar, till today. His brother Sudhir died issueless and his wife got the other half in limited interest. And now Parul Bala lives in her said half. On 8-8-1995 he heard from Zinnah and others that he and his brother sold their land to Parol Bala in 1969. Then, he obtained certified copies of the deeds of the land and became sure about the transfer. Then, he instituted Title Suit No.180 of 1995 which was on transfer renumbered as Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 and got the judgment and decree dated 24-5-1998 and 31- 5-1998 on contest against Parol Bala.

6. On the pleadings, 3 issues were raised. Of them, issue No. 1 is whether the suit as framed is maintainable or not and issue No.2 is whether the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 are liable to be set aside as void and not binding upon the plaintiffs or not. Plaintiffs examined 6 witnesses while defendant No. 1 examined 2 witnesses including himself. Plaintiffs' documents were marked as exhibits 1 to 12 series while those of the defendant No. 1 exhibit No. 'Ka' to 'Ja'. But Parul Bala did neither contest the suit nor appeared as a witness.

7. The trial Court decreed the suit as prayed for. On appeal by said defendant No. 1, the Court of appeal below allowed the appeal and set side the judgment, and decree of the trial Court by the impugned judgment and decree.

<u>8. Mr AB Roy Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that all the documents of the plaintiffs were duly admitted without any objection and proved, but the Court of appeal below without seeing the documents on record held that the execution of those documents were not proved and thus, it erred in law in dismissing the suit upon such erroneous view which has resulted in failure of justice. He then submits that the Court of appeal below without reversing the findings of the trial Court and adverting to the reasons given, erred in law in setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court. He also submits that the Court of appeal below also erred in law in considering certain things which are not at all necessary for disposal of the appeal. He cites the decision in the case of Haider Ali vs the State, 47 DLR (AD) 46 and that of Moulavi Abdul Mannan vs Md Rafiqul Islam, 46 DLR 493.</u>

<u>9. Mr Garib Newaz, learned Advocate for opposite party No.1 (defendant No.1) submits that the suit as framed is not maintainable under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for want of further declaration of title in the suit land. He then submits that by judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997, the sale deed dated 14- 5-1969, exhibit 4 was cancelled to the extent of half share of the defendant No. 1 only and the appellate. Court having upheld such cancellation committed no error calling for any interference. He also submits that the finding of the appellate Court that the plaintiffs have no possession in the suit land on consideration of the evidence on record and such finding being a finding on fact must be held to have been concluded by the decision of the final Court of facts. He also supports the view of the Court of appeal below that the plaint was not signed by many of the plaintiffs. He cites, on admission and execution of documents, the decision in the case of Jhanda Singh and another vs Harman Singh and others, AIR 1926 Lahore 415, Sheikh Karimullah vs Gudar Koeri and others, AIR 1925 Allahabad 56 and Gopal Das and another vs Sri Thakurji and others, AIR 1936 Allahabad 422.</u>

10. In reply, Mr Roy Chowdhury submits that the finding of the Court of appeal below on possession is based on misreading and non-reading of the evidence oral and documentary on record. So such finding is not binding in revision. He further submits that all the title deeds of the plaintiffs exhibits 13 series were admitted by the executant thereof, PW 4 Sahabuddin. He also took me through the judgment of the trial Court again and showed the findings on which the trial Court held the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 collusive and fraudulent which were not at all considered by the Court of appeal below.

11. It appears from the record that by judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997, exhibit No. 12 and 12 (ka) the sale deed being No. 4400 dated 14-5-1969, exhibit No.4 executed by defendant No. 1 and his brother Sudhir Mandai in favour of Parul Bala was declared to be forged, false, fraudulent and collusive, and thereby, the title of defendant No. 1 in 48 decimals of land as described in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint of the previous suit was not affected. In the trial of the suit, issue No.2, as stated earlier, is whether the above judgment and decree, exhibit No. 12 and 12 (ka) as obtained by defendant No. 1 in his Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 are liable to be set aside as void, and also not binding upon the plaintiffs or not? On finding of various facts and circumstances, the trial Court held that by impleading only Parul Bala and without making the plaintiffs parties in the suit, defendant No. 1 obtained said judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 through collusion and by practicing fraud. Court of appeal below also formulated issue No. 1 as' whether the decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 was obtained illegally and fraudulently and, as such, liable to be set aside. This is the moot issue in the suit.

12. On the issue, the case of the plaintiffs' in short, is that divested of all their right, title, interest or possession in the suit land about 30 years ago, defendant No.1, Bhasani Mandai and No.2, Parul Bala went to India and settled there permanently. Now, they got the suit instituted and obtained impugned judgment and decree through false personification, and also by collusion with each other and practicing fraud upon the Court. The case of the defendant No.1 is that he has long been living in Bangladesh, possesses the suit land by cultivation through borgadar and Parul Bala lives in her other half of the suit land in three huts. He is now living at 66/A Dinanath Sen Road. But exhibit No. 11, a notice dated 8-7-1998 issued by Demra PS on the complaint dated 7-7-1998 as lodged by defendant No.1, and No.2, Parul Bala shows that they are both living at the time in the same address of Dinanath Sen Road.

13. Let me first see the findings of the appellate Court. It appears that the appeal was allowed on the findings to the effect that from the evidence of the PWs, it appeared to it that they do not have any idea of the suit land and the plaintiffs have no possession; that by the sale deed dated 14-5-1969 exhibit No.4 no title of Parul Bala was established; that by sale deeds, exhibit Nos. 5, 7 and 8 no title was transferred to the subsequent purchasers and they did not acquire any title; and that the plaintiffs failed to prove their title in the suit land and their deeds (exhibit 9 series, numbering 30) are nothing but papers.

14. In the next breath, the appellate Court however held that by the impugned sale deed (exhibit 4) the title of the defendant No. 1 would not be affected. Said sale deed would only be applicable to the share of Parul Bala, successor to Sudhir MandaI. Therefore, the judgment delivered in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 dated 24-5-1998 is valid and in accordance with law.

15. As stated earlier, by said judgment and decree passed in the previous suit the sale deed dated 14-5-1969 exhibit No.4 was cancelled as collusive and forged. The Court of appeal below wants us to accept the said judgment as half invalid in respect of the share of defendant No. 1 only but valid in respect of other half, i.e. in respect of Parul Bala. According to the appellate Court, the trial Court therefore committed mistake in decreeing the suit. But the appellate Court dismissed the suit in its entirety. This view of the appellate Court is preposterous on the face of it.

16. I will now see why the decree dated 12 (ka) as impugned in the instant suit was set aside by the trial Court. On elaborate consideration of the evidence on record, the trial. Court found that defendant No.2 Parul Bala contested the earlier suit by filing a written statement denying the case of the defendant No. 1 but during cross-examination she admitted entire case of defendant No. 1 saying that defendant No. 1 and her husband Sudhir did not execute the sale deed exhibit No.4 dated 14-5-1969. Parul Bala was though living with defendant No. 1 in the same address of Dinanath Sen Road but she did neither contest the instant suit nor appear before the Court to support the defendant No. 1 as before. The predecessors of the plaintiffs possessed the suit land and now, the plaintiffs possess on raising dwellings. Defendant No.1 failed to prove that he had been in Bangladesh from 1970 to 1995. Title documents of the plaintiffs were admitted by the executant Sahabuddin to have been executed by him as PW 4 and that defendant No. 1 obtained the judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 without impleading the plaintiffs. In coming to such findings various reasons were also given by the trial Court.

17. But the above facts and circumstances as weighed with the trial Court did not find any favour of the Court of appeal below. It appears from the plaint of earlier Title Suit No. 51 of 1997. Parol Bala was made defendant No. 1 and the Sub-Registrar, Mohammadpur, Registration Complex, Tejgaon, Dhaka was made defendant No.2. Address of both the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were given same of Dogar, Demra, Parul Bala appeared in the suit and filed a written statement contending that defendant No. 1 and his brother executed sale deed dated 14-5-1969 in her favour. Having learnt that the original deed was not in her custody, defendant No. 1 now denied the execution. But during the cross-examination she as DW-1 made a u-turn and stated that her husband and defendant No. 1 never gave her any deed. She enjoyed the share of her husband. She did not' claim the share of Bhasani Mandai, defendant No. 1. She could not say how a deed of sale came into existence. It is on record that after purchase from Parul Bala by sale deed, exhibit No. 5 Sufia Khatun got her name mutated and she possessed the suit land for some time on payment of rents and RS record of rights was also prepared in her name. Then, Sahabuddin possessed the suit land till he sold to the plaintiffs from 1979 to 1984. The notice dated 8-7-1998 exhibit No. 11 issued by Demra Police upon a complaint dated 7-7-1998 lodged by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 informing that the plaintiffs were felling earth and raising dwellings on the suit land shows that defendant No. 1 and 2 are living in the same address of Dinanath Sen Road. Case of defendant No.1 on knowledge is that on 8-8-1995 he came to know from Zinnah and others for the first time about the existence of the deed exhibit No. 4 and then, he obtained the deeds of the suit land. So, he came to know about all subsequent transfers and the appearance of the plaintiffs on the suit land. But he did neither make the plaintiffs parties in his suit nor did he challenge the subsequent transactions. In the present suit, why Parol Bala who is living with him did not contest the suit nor was she examined has not been explained. Moreover, defendant No. 1 failed to adduce an iota of documents to show his presence and enjoyment of the suit land over the period from May, 1969 to 1995. To prove his claim that he was still a citizen of Bangladesh, defendant No.1 produced a passport issued at Dhaka on 11-2-1998 giving permanent address as Bangladesh. Trial Court was of the view that such a passport could be easily obtained in Bangladesh. The defendant No. 1 could adduce no other evidence oral or documentary. Above facts and circumstances as found by the trial Court are sufficient to justify its conclusion but did not find any consideration-in the judgment of the Court of appeal below.

18. For decision in the appeal, the appellate Court just relied upon the opinion of the handwriting expert in the earlier suit and the findings in the judgment on title and possession to justify its conclusion forgetting the fact that the very judgment has been impugned in this suit. When, a judgment and decree are impeached in a subsequent suit as collusive and fraudulent, the Court is required to consider the facts and circumstances upon which subsequent suit is based, and transpired at the trial. Findings of such impugned judgment cannot given any answer to the issues of collusion or fraud in the subsequent suit.

19. The appellate Court appears to have given its all considerations on the title and possession as if it was a suit for declaration of title and possession. It excluded the title deeds of the plaintiffs on the ground that the plaintiffs failed to examine neither the scribe nor the executant of their deeds. But record shows that Sahabuddin who sold the lands to the plaintiffs came before the Court and on oath admitted as PW 4 that he transferred the suit land to the plaintiffs by those sale deeds exhibit 9 series and delivered possession. It rejected the oral evidence of the plaintiffs without considering their entire evidence. It also failed to notice the fact that the plaintiffs have come from various parts of Bangladesh and on different dates purchased the land for the purpose of residence. One of them is not supposed to know every detail of the facts in respect of others. Besides, the notice dated 8-7-1998 issued by the Demra Police, the report of the Advocate Commissioner is the most important evidence on record on possession. When the defendant No.1 claimed the suit land as agricultural land, an Advocate Commissioner was appointed to ascertain the present position and nature of the suit land, namely, whether there is any paddy in the land and also the-number of structures standing thereon. After investigation, the Advocate Commissioner submitted his report on 11-5-1999 with a sketch map. The report was accepted without any objection. Sketch map clearly shows that the entire suit land is divided into plots for residential purposes with a road leading through the middle' of the land for access. Major portion of the land is occupied by different huts. Advocate Commissioner found 8 CI Sheet sheds, 6 semi-pucca and two pucca residential quarters. He definitely reported that he did not find any paddy field. This report together with the sketch map exhibit No.6 belies the case of defendant No.1 that the suit land is a nal land and his borgadar DW-1 cultivates the land with tractor. But such evidence was totally excluded by the appellate Court from consideration on the ground that why the Advocate Commissioner could not say the area of the land or the boundary thereof. The appellate Court failed to notice that such statements were made to questions asked beyond the terms of the reference for investigation, and he had to reply from his memory. Other PWs in chorus stated that the plaintiffs possess the suit land. Against the voluminous documentary evidence of the plaintiffs including rent receipts and RS khatian over a period of about 30 years, the defendant has got not an iota of evidence. But the Court of appeal below found that the plaintiffs do not know the suit land.

20. Curiously, the appellate Court has discovered that many of the plaintiffs did not sign the plaint. But we find that 16 out of 18 plaintiffs signed the plaint and the attorney signed on behalf of other two plaintiffs. In the nature of the suit, this is absolutely unnecessary exercise.

21. In the circumstances and on the evidence on record, the trial Court has correctly declared that the judgment and decree 24-5-1998 and 31-5-1998 respectively as obtained by defendant No. 1 in previous Title suit No. 51 of 1997 was obtained by collusion and practicing fraud in getting cancellation of the sale deed dated 14-5-1969, exhibit No.4. When such decree goes, whatever the cloud cast over the title of the plaintiffs is also cleared. It is also found that the findings of the Court of appeal below on title and possession and the decision in the appeal was arrived at on misreading and non-reading of the evidence on record and without application of any judicial mind. Such decision has no doubt resulted in serious miscarriage of justice. The judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below therefore cannot be sustained in law.

<u>22. Let me now consider the submission of Mr Garib Newaz that the suit is hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for failing of the plaintiffs to seek further declaration of title in the suit land. He also cites decisions in the case of MA Mallik vs NH Mallik, 1986 BCR (AD) 56 and that of Ishaque Mia and another vs Abdul Mazid and others, 48 DLR 465. According to him, the plaintiffs were further required to have prayed for declaration of title in the suit land. This issue was never raised before. Not even before the Court of appeal below. I shall however consider the question.</u>

In the case of MA Mallik, the Appellate Division has held.

"In view of the clear proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act there is no hesitation in saying that without prayer for consequential relief such suit should not be maintained."

23. The suit was brought for declaration that decree passed in Title Suit No. 69 of 1961 is fraudulent, void, collusive, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff. Leave granted to consider question whether the suit for declaration of title simpliciter could be maintained? Plaintiff was not a party to the suit. In coming to the above view, the Appellate Division did not elaborate what other relief ought to have been sought for. . Relying on the decision, a single bench in the case of Ishaque Mia held,

"Both the Courts below have held that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their title and possession and that in that circumstances it must be held that the plaintiffs were not entitled to a decree for simple declaration that the sale decree in Title Suit No. 561 of 1976 was obtained fraudulently, was illegal and not binding on him."

But in Moulavi Abdul Mannan vs Mohammed Rafiqul Islam, 46 DLR 493 another single bench held,

"when a decree adversely affects a person not a party to a decree he may file a suit for declaring the same not binding on him and get the same set aside if found illegal as in the present case."

The question was elaborately discussed by the Appellate Division 'in the case of Sufia Khanam Chowdhury vs Faizunnessa Chowdhury, 39 DLR (AD) 46, Appellate Division has held,

"If, by an instrument a person's right and title is clouded or threatened, he may seek a declaration under this section to the effect that by the instrument his right and title has not been affected or that any other person who denies his title or claims title in himself has not acquired any right or title. If the suit is for a declaration that a written instrument, whether it is a sale deed or a Court's decree, "is void", it clearly comes under section 39, since it is covered by the expression "any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable." But if a further prayer is included in the suit that by the void instrument the plaintiffs right has not been affected, then this prayer comes straight under section 42; similarly, if this prayer is framed in a different form, that is, the defendant acquired no right or interest thereby, it will make no difference, for this prayer is also covered by section 42. If this suit includes the reliefs that the instruments in question is void and his right has not been affected thereby and, or, the defendant acquired no right thereby, then the reliefs are covered by both sections 39 and 42. In such cases provisions of section 39 and 42 will overlap.

24. It appears that earlier decision was brought to the notice of the Appellate Division. Under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, no Court shall make any declaration of title where the plaintiff is able to seek 'further relief than mere declaration but omits to do so. It has now been settled by long line of decisions interpreting the phrase 'further relief that the 'further relief referred to in the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act must be a relief flowing directly and necessarily from the declaration sought and a relief appropriate to and necessarily consequent on, the right or title asserted.

Sometimes, it is called consequential relief and a relief is said to be consequential only when the relief of declaration is essential to the grant of that relief. No relief is consequential if it cannot be granted without declaration.

<u>25. In the suit before me, the plaintiffs impeached the decree passed in Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 on ground of collusion and fraud on the assertion that they are owners in possession of the suit since 1969 and the defendants having no right, title or possession obtained the decree in collusion with each other after about 30 years of their sale. The trial Court has found their title and possession in the suit land and also held the judgment and decree of the earlier Title Suit No. 51 of 1997 collusive and fraudulent. Appellate Court as stated above most erroneously reversed those findings. In such suit, the plaintiffs are not required to seek any other relief as further relief to their main relief of declaration. Furthermore, with due respect, a relief for further declaration of title in the suit land as submitted does not seem to be a further relief within the meaning of the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Submission has therefore no substance.</u>

26. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. No order as to costs. Impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below are set aside and those of the trial Court are hereby restored.

Send down the records.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha J : This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 25-4-1995 passed by the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong disallowing pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1948.

2. The case of the pre-emptee petitioner, in short, is that the case land belonged to Arifur Rahman, A. Barik and A. Khaleque and their names were duly recorded in the finally published RS Khatian. One Abdus Sobahan purchased the case land and other lands from the rightful owners by registered kabala dated 10-2-1939 and owned possessed the same. Thereafter Abdus Sobhan died leaving son Abdus Samad, daughter Aroba Khatun and wife Nasua Khatun to succeed him. Subsequently, Nasua Khatun died leaving opposite parties Abu Taher Abdus Samad, Arora Khatun and Sufia Khatun as her heir and heiresses. The aforesaid owners being in rightful possession of the case Land sold 22 decimals of Land to pre-emptee petitioner Abdul Latif Bhuiyan land the predecessor-in-interest or opposite parties Nos. 7-11, Abdul Latif Bhuiyan subsequently purchased the aforesaid 0.22 decimals of land by kabalas dated 27-7-1964 in the name of his wife Tarina Akhter Khatun. In this way the pre-emptor and opposite parties Nos. 7-15 are co-sharers in the case land and their names have been duly recorded in the relevant RS Khatian. It has been contended by the pre-emptor that by the disputed 4 kabalas dated 20-7-1991 opposite parties Nos. 4-11 sold the case land to opposite party Nos. 1-6, who are stranger purchasers, beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor. On coming to know about the disputed sales the pre-emptor obtained the certified copy of the kabalas in question and filed the pre-emption case on making the statutory deposit, impleading all necessary parties.

3. Opposite party Nos. 1-6 contested the case by filing the written objection denying all the material allegations of the pre-emption application and contended, inter alia, that the case is barred by limitation and it is bad for defect of parties. It has also been contended that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case land and as such the pre-emption case is not maintainable in law. It has been further contended that the disputed sales were not sales proper but these were conditional sales with agreement for re-conveyance of the same to the vendors on receipt of the sale money within the stipulated time. It has been also contended by the opposite parties that the case land has already been re-conveyed to opposite party Nos. 7-11 by registered Kabala dated 24-9-1992 in pursuance of the agreement dated 21-7-1991 for re-conveyance of the case land on stipulated terms and conditions and, as such, the pre-emption case is not maintainable in law. It has also been contended that before sale of the case land to opposite party Nos. 1-6, it was duly offered to the pre-emptor but he refused to purchase the same as be had no fund for the purpose and consequently, he is estopped from claiming pre-emption.

4. The pre-emptor examined only one witness in support of his case while the contesting opposite parties examined 3 witnesses in support Of their case.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge by his impugned judgment and order dated 25-4-1995 refused pre-emption on the ground that since the land under pre-emption has already been re- conveyed to the original vendors in pursuance of the agreement for re-conveyance, the pre-emptor is not entitled to pre-emption. The learned Subordinate Judge, however, found all other points in favour of the pre-emptor petitioner.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned judgment and order dated 25-4-1995, the pre-emptor petitioner filed the present appeal before this Court.

7. Mr Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that having regard to the fact that the kabalas under pre-emption were executed on 20-7-1991 without containing any recital for re-conveyance and the so- called unregistered deeds of agreement for re-conveyance having not being executed on 20-7-1991 to be contemporaneous documents but subsequent thereto, the learned Subordinate Judge was manifestly wrong in refusing pre-emption on the basis of the so-called agreements for re- conveyance subsequently created for defeating the pre-emptor's right of pre-emption. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the proviso to section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act providing that no transaction shall be deemed to be a mortgage by conditional sale, unless the condition is embodied in the document which effects or purports to effect the sale, the so-called agreements for re-conveyance cannot affect the pre-emptor's right of pre-emption. The learned Advocate also submits that the pre-emptor petitioner filed the pre-emption case on 10-3-1992 but the so-called re- conveyances by 4 registered deeds took place on 24- 9-1992, long after the filing of the pre-emption case and, as such, the disputed transactions are clearly hit by the principle of lispendens under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. The learned Advocate further submits that the so-called deeds of re-conveyances Ext. Ka series being the products of fraud and collusion between opposite party Nos. 1-11 and 7-11, the learned Subordinate Judge was manifestly wrong in refusing pre-emption without carefully considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the law bearing on the subject, and the same has occasioned failure of justice.

8. Mr M A Jalil, the learned Advocate appearing for the contesting opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that in the face of agreements for re-conveyances, which are contemporaneous documents, and in view of the admitted fact that the vendees have already reconveyed the case land to the vendors the learned Subordinate Judge was fully justified in refusing pre-emption.

9. The learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor petitioner has placed before us the impugned judgment. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge found that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the case land and he has locus standi to maintain the pre-emption case. The learned Subordinate Judge also found that the case is not barred by limitation and it is not bad for defect of parties. The only ground on which the learned Subordinate Judge refused pre-emption is that the land under pre-emption has already been re-conveyed to the vendors by the vendees in pursuance of agreements for re-conveyance. It is found that the learned Subordinate Judge failed to consider the vital fact that the deeds of reconveyance came into existence on 24-9-1992 whereas the present case for pre-emption had been filed on 10-3-1992. It is thus evident that the alleged deeds of re-conveyance have been brought into existence more than six months after the filing of the pre-emption case. Admittedly, the disputed sale deeds were executed on 21-7-1991 and this is why there is no mention about the alleged agreements for re-conveyance in the disputed sale deeds.

<u>10. It is a settled proposition of law that sale takes effect from the date of execution of the sale deed and not from the date of its registration. In the absence of any allegation of fraud and collusion in concluding the disputed sale deeds, the vendors lost all their interests in the case property on and from 20-7-1991, as a result of which they had no subsisting interest in the case property on 21-7-1992 to encumber the sales by subsequent agreements for re-conveyance on 21-7-1991. So the alleged deeds of re-conveyances dated 21-7-1991 cannot encumber any property which was already duly transferred by its vendors on 20-7-1991. In the facts of the case, the alleged agreements of re-conveyances dated 21-7-1991 cannot be considered as contemporaneous documents to affect in any way the earlier executed sale deeds. Moreover, the pre-emptee opposite parties have not stated even one word either in their written objection or in their evidence explaining the circumstances preventing them from mentioning in the disputed sale deeds the fact of the agreements for re-conveyance or why these were executed' one day after the admitted execution of the disputed sale deeds on 20-7-1991. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, we find that the alleged agreements for re-conveyances of the case land and the subsequent re-conveyance of the same by the vendors to the vendees long after the filing of the pre-emption case are fraudulent and colourable transactions brought into existence by the opposite parties in collusion with each other for the purpose of defeating the pre-emptor's right of pre-emption.</u>

<u>11. The pre-emptor petitioner deposing as a witness clearly stated in his evidence that the so-called deeds of re-conveyances witnessed by Ext. Kha series are fake and fraudulent documents created for defeating his right of pre-emption. PWs 1 to 3 stated in their evidence that in pursuance of deeds of re-conveyance the vendees of the disputed sales already re-conveyed the case land to: the vendors on 24-9-1992, evidently after more than six months of the filing of the pre-emption case. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, it must be found that the four deeds of agreements for re-conveyance are nothing but colourable transactions to defeat the right of pre-emption available to the pre-emptor, It is unfortunate that the learned Subordinate Judge failed to address himself to this vital question in the light of the evidence on record and the attending facts and circumstances of the case and thereby fell in error in refusing pre-emption. Moreover, the alleged deeds of re-conveyance Ext. Ka series dated 24-9-1992 are also hit by the principle of lispendens under section 52 of the TP Act. Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act also stands out prominently against contesting opposite parties. Mr Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor petitioner, has placed before us the case of Abul Hossain and other, vs Md Masim Ali and others reported in 19 DLR, 677. the case of Md Sukur Ali vs Sree Suresh Chandra Barmon and others, reported in 4 BLD (AD) 219 and the case of Khorshed Ali and another vs Aftauddin and others, reported in 47 DLR 607 in support of his contention while Mr MA Jalil, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee opposite parties, has referred to us the case of Shaft Khan vs Mannujan Hossain and others, reported in 35 DLR (AD) 225 in support of his submission.</u>

12. On going through the cited decisions we are of the view that the present case is fully covered by the cases cited by Mr Majumder. The facts and circumstances of the case reported in 35 DLR (AD), 225 are quite distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the present case, the cited decision is of no. assistance to the pre-emptee opposite parties.

<u>13. In view of the fact that the so-called agreements for re-conveyance of the case land by the vendees to the vendors have been found to be colourable transactions brought into existence for the sole purpose of defeating the pre-emptor's right of pre-emption are not bonafide re-conveyance, the pre-emptors right of pre-emption subsists and he is entitled under the law to pre-emption. The fraudulent and collusive manoeuvres resorted to by the opposite parties cannot be allowed to stand in the way of pre-emption, which is otherwise available to the pre-emptor.</u>

14. In view of the foregoing discussions, we are inclined to find that the learned Subordinate Judge was manifestly wrong in refusing pre-emption ignoring the vital facts and the attending circumstances of the case and the evidence on record.

15. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost and the impugned judgment and order dated 20-4-1995 passed by the learned 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong in Misc. Case No.10 of 1992 refusing pre-emption are set aside. Miscellaneous Case No. 10 of 1992 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for pre-emption is allowed.

Send down the lower Courts records immediately.

End.
