full_judgment:
Abdus Salam Mamun J : This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and decree dated 27-7-1993 decree signed on 31-5-1993 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon in Title Appeal No.19 of 1992 reversing the judgment and decree dated 28-5-1992, decree signed on 3-6- 1992 passed by the Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon in other Suit No.5 of 1985 should not be set aside.

2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule are that, one Mossammat Anowara Begum instituted the Other Suit No.18 of 1980 on 5-2-1980 in the Court of the Munsif, Thakurgaon, Dinajpur praying for setting aside the ex parte decree passed on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No. 100 of 1978 declaring the same illegal. collusive and not binding upon her and the learned Munsif by his judgment and decree dated 30-1-1982 has been pleased to decree the suit on contest with costs declaring the ex parte decree obtained by the defendant No.1, namely, Nurul Haque, on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 is not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. As against the said judgment and decree the defendants preferred the Other Appeal No.24 of 1992 and on 14-6-1984 the appeal was allowed by the learned appellate Court, by its Judgment and decree, setting aside the Judgment and decree of the learned trial Court and remanding the suit back to the trial Court with direction to the Learned Munsif to give an opportunity to the plaintiff to amend her plaint. On 25-2-1985 the case record was received by the trial Court from the appellate Court back on remand and the learned trial Court returned the plaint to the plaintiff for filling it before an appropriate Court and the 'plaintiff has re-filed it by amending the plaint in the Court of the Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon and the suit has been registered as the Other Suit No.5 of 1984 and during trial of the case neither party adduced any additional evidence, but relied upon the evidence recorded earlier in the Other Class Suit No.18 of 1980.

4. On conclusion of the trial the learned Subordinate Judge. Thakurgaon has been pleased to dismiss the suit by his judgment and decree dated 28-5-1992 and being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff has preferred the Title Appeal No.19 of 1992 and by judgment and decree dated 27-5-1993 the learned Additional District Judge. Thakurgaon, has been pleased to allow the appeal by setting aside the judgment and decree of the learned trial Court and declaring the ex parte decree passed in the Other Class Suit No.1 00 of 1978 on 24-5-1979. by the learned Assistant Judge, Thakurgaon illegal, void, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff- appellant also declaring the title of the plaintiff in the suit property directing the defendant No.1 to vacate the suit land by demolishing and removing structures and declaring also khas possession of the plaintiff in the suit land on eviction of the defendant No.1 as aforesaid.

5. As against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon in Title (Other) Appeal No.19 of 1992 the defendant-respondent has preferred this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule together with an order of stay of all further proceedings of the Title Execution Case No.5 of 1993 pending in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Thakurgaon.

6. Facts as appears from the pleadings of the parties and the judgments of the Courts below are that in the Other Class Suit No.18 of 1980 the plaintiff Mossammat Anowara Begum stated that the suit land originally belonged to one Subarna Probha Biswas and the CS Khatian No.420 was finally published in her name. Subsequently, the suit property was put to auction in the Certificate Case No.15311958-59 and she along with the defendant No.3 namely, Hanuman Das Agarwala purchased the entire land of the suit Khatian on auction held on 9-11-1959, with equal shares. The sale was confirmed on 9-1-1960 and they got delivery of possession of the suit land from the Court on 16-2-1960 and thus they acquired the right, title interests and possession of the suit land extinguishing the interests of Subarna Probha Biswas.

The defendant No.3 Hanuman Das Agarwala sold his half share to one Upendra Nath Barman who subsequently, filed a Partition Suit in the Court of Munsif: Thakurgaon, Dinajpur being No.143 of 1960 against the plaintiff and her husband and the suit was dismissed on contest. An appeal was preferred being Partition Appeal No.68 of 1961 and the learned Subordinate Judge. Dinajpur was also pleased to dismiss the appeal on contest.

Thereafter, Upendra Nath Barman again filed the Title Suit No.4 of 1963 in the same Court and obtained an ex parte decree on 2-9-1963. The present plaintiff, Mossammat Anowara Begum has then filed a suit for cancellation of that ex parte decree being the Other Suit No.37 of 1966 in the same Court and the said ex parte decree has been set aside and the original suit was restored to its original file and number and Upendra Nath ultimately, obtained a decree in that Title Suit.

The defendant No.1 in the present suit namely, Nurul Haque, was also a defendant in that Title Suit instituted by Upendra Nath Barman.

The defendant No.1. Nurul Haque was at the time residing in the suit land as a rental tenant of this plaintiff: The plaintiff then preferred an appeal against that decree passed in favour of Upendra Nath Barman being the Other Appeal No.31 of 1968 and the learned Subordinate Judge. Dinajpur has been pleased to dismiss the appeal. Ultimately, the present plaintiff Mossammat Anowara Begum, purchased those half share of the suit land from Upendra Nath Barman by a registered Kabala dated 8-8-1970 and thus she became owner of the entire 57 decimal of land in the suit Khatian No.420 and in the suit Plot No.460. But subsequently, land of this plot was declared Enemy Property by the Government in the year 1969 in Case No.19 (Non- Agricultural land) of 1969-1970. The case was heard on 9-5-1974 and it was dismissed on the same day on finding that the suit property in question was not Enemy Property.

7. The defendant No.1 of the present suit, Nurul Haque, though was a tenant under the plaintiff in some portion of the suit land on rent but took lease of 07 decimal of land from the Government in collaboration with the officers of the Enemy Property Cell. The said enemy property case was sent to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dinajpur for order who was pleased to release the entire 57 decimal of land from the list of enemy property on 28-1-1978 after proper hearing. Against that order of release the present defendant No.1 preferred an Appeal being No.14 of 1978 to the learned Divisional Commissioner, Rajshahi and upon full hearing the learned Divisional Commissioner, Rajshahi was pleased to reject the said Appeal.

8. The plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land by constructing pucca wall, bathroom, latrine and tubewell. She also planted various sorts of fruit bearing trees in the suit plot. She also paid holding taxes regularly in the Municipality and subsequently, transferred 14 decimal of land to several persons on several dates under kabalas and the purchasers are also in possession of the suit land in their respective shares by opening new holding and by paying rent to the Government. The remaining 41 decimal of land has been duly recorded in the name of the plaintiff and the defendants including the defendant No.1 have no right, title and possession in the suit land.

The defendant No.1 has obtained an ex parte decree from the Court of the Munsif, Thakurgaon, in the Other Class Suit No. 100 of 1978 after he was defeated in the VP Miscellaneous Caseie after release of the suit property and got the ex parte decree behind the knowledge of the plaintiff, in respect of 19 decimal of land on 24-5-1979. The plaintiff was not made a party in that suit intentionally and her title has been clouded by that ex parte decree and thus, she has been obliged to institute the instant suit.

9. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 have submitted two separate written statements and contested the suit. In his written statements the defendant No.1 stated that the plaintiff has no cause of action to file the suit nor locus standi for it. The suit is barred by law of limitation and hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and also by the principles of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence and that the .suit land originally belonged to one Subarna Probha Biswas who after the partition of the sub-continent has left for India. During the SA operation, the suit land was recorded in the name of one Hanuman Das Agarwala as forceful occupier of the suit plot who is also the defendant No.3 in the instant suit. The story of the Certificate Case No.153/1958-59 and the auction purchase or delivery of possession thereof, are all false and collusive and mere paper transactions. The plaintiff and defendant No.3, namely, Hanuman Das Agarwala, have never acquired any right, title and possession in the suit land by that auction. The suit that was instituted by Upendra Nath i-e the Partition Suit No.4 of 1963, was false for, no summons was served upon him in the suit. The plaintiff also instituted the Suit No.37 of 1966 challenging the title of Upendra Nath in the Partition Suit No.4 of 1963 where the husband of the present plaintiff admitted that the defendant No.3 Hanuman Das Agarwala had been in possession of the suit land before the initiation of the Certificate Case No.153 of 1958-59 and, as such, the plaintiffs averments that the defendant No.3 has no possession in the suit land is false. He has erected houses about 17/18 years ago in the suit plot, when it was covered by bushes and fallen land. A holding was opened in the Municipality in his name and he got receipts of payment of taxes. He has constructed houses on 7 (seven) decimal of land about 16/17 years ago within the full knowledge of the plaintiff and her husband and also the defendant No.3. He also possesses an area of excess 12 decimal of land adjacent to his house and, as such, he is in the possession of 12 + 7 = 19 decimals of land and thus, has acquired a good title by his adverse possession. He was never a tenant under the plaintiff. The plaintiff may have purchased 28.5 decimal of land from Upendra Nath on the basis of a collusive decree that he got in the Partition Suit No.4 of 1963, but has acquired no title on the basis of that collusive decree. The plaintiff was not affected by the decree passed in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978. No party was left out in that Other Class Suit and the plaintiff is bound by that decree. The plaintiff neither has possession nor homestead in the suit land as alleged and the authority i.e, the Government, at one point of time, advised him to take lease of his homestead measuring an area of 7 decimal ofland from the Government failing which, they will evict him therefrom and finding no other alternative, he took lease of 7 decimal of land under compulsion and thus, he retained possession of 19 decimal of land. He instituted the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 for declaration of his title as he has acquired his good title by virtue of his long standing adverse possession and got an ex parte decree in it. He also applied for mutation of his decretal land and then came to learn that the husband of the plaintiff has applied for demarcation of 16 decimal of land and the plaintiffs husband also tried to enter into the suit land with the help of the local wicked and dangerous people on 18-1-1980. The defendant with his sons have resisted them and also filed a criminal case, being No. MP 18/1980 which was subsequently renumbered as MR Case No.19/1980 in which the husband of the plaintiff and his men have been restrained from entering into the suit land under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, on 12-2-1980.

10. The defendant No.2, has, on the other hand, stated that he is not bound by the decree obtained by the defendant No.1 and that the suit land originally belonged to one Suburna Probha Biswas who was in possession and subsequently, left for India leaving the property uncared for. No auction was held as alleged. The PRR Khatian was prepared in the name of Subarna Probha, but subsequently, it was recorded in the name of Hanuman Das Agarwala as forceful occupier. The record was prepared in the name of Suborna Probha under section 46 and it was correct. The ex parte decree obtained by the defendant No.1 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 is collusive one between the defendant No.1 and the plaintiff and Upendra Nath. The defendant is not bound by the decree of the defendant No.1.

11. During the re-trial of the suit on remand, learned Munsif has framed two issues, namely, whether the suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and barred by limitation for the learned appellate Court has directed to decide those two points in its order of remand and the learned trial Court held that the plaintiff has proved her title in the entire land but the defendant No.1, Nurul Haque is in possession of 19 sataks of land and the plaintiff failed to prove that the defendant No.1 entered into the suit land' as tenant of the plaintiff. She did not produce any deed of tenancy agreement or rent receipts in this respect and her witnesses are partisan and their evidence are not reliable to the effect that the defendant No.1 entered into the suit land as tenant of the plaintiff.

12. On perusal of the document namely, the tax paying receipt of the Municipality of the year 1965, produced by the defendant No.1, the learned trial Court held that the defendant No.1 is in possession of that 19 sataks of land from 15/16 years ago. In accordance with the auction purchase dated 12-12- 1960. the plaintiff got possession in the southern portion or the suit plot and she could not explain as to how she got possession in 28'/2 steaks of land in the northern portion of the plot. By auction. Hanuman Das Agarwala got possession of this plot which he sold out to Upendra Nath Barman by a registered deed. Upendra Nath Barman instituted the Partition Suit praying for separate shaham where he lost upto appeal and, on the contrary, he won the Title Suit upto the appellate Court and in that Partition Suit this defendant No.1 was also a defendant. From that period this defendant is an illegal occupier in the suit land and his possession is adverse to all and continuous. The plaintiff has purchased from Upendra Nath Barman on 8-8-1970 by a registered deed measuring an area of 28-1/2 sataks in the northern portion of the plot but she could not prove acquiring her possession under the Kabala. The plaintiff also could not prove whether her vendor Upendra Nath Barman executed the decree which he obtained in his Partition Suit. The title of the plaintiff in the suit land is mere paper title and that she inserted her claim for recovery of possession on 29-9-1984 by way of amendment of the plaint. It could not be said that the possession of the defendant No.1 was not adverse to the plaintiff only because he took lease of it from the Government as Enemy Property. The defendant No.1 has enjoyed adverse possession and right, title thereof from 1963 to 1984. Though the ex parte decree was passed on 24-5-1979 in the Other Class Suit No.100 of 1978 without making the plaintiff a party and in her absence, but still it can be said that the decree was passed on finding his possession. The plaintiff has lost her cause of action by not suing from 8-8-1970. to 29-9-1984 and the suit is barred by section 144 of the Limitation Act. But the suit is maintainable in its nature and form. The suit is not hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

13. In the Other Suit No. 18 of 1980, the Learned Munsif held that the defendant No.2. i-e, the Government, could not produce any documentary evidence to prove that the suit land is an Enemy Property and the activities of the defendant No. 1 are not clean. From the volume of the SA Khatian the Suit Plot No.46D was found recorded in the name of Subarna Prova. The defendant No.1 has committed wrong in obtaining the ex parte decree. The plaintiff has good title over the suit land and her interests has been clouded by the ex parte decree. It was thus, not binding upon the plaintiff.

14. The findings of the Learned Appellate Court in the Other Appeal No. 19 of 1992, on the contrary, are that as soon as the defendant No.1 took lease of 7 decimal of land from the Government as Enemy Property, his claim of adverse possession stood relinquished and, as such, the limitation of more than 12 years has been completed. The findings of the learned trial Court on the point of limitation was erroneous. The defendant No. 1 has not acquired any title by adverse possession and he is liable to eviction. The defendant No.1 claimed that he is dwelling in an area of 0.07 sataks of land having his dwelling house and possessing another 12 sataks of contiguous land by growing vegetables and plantation which is a new claim, not raised in the Other Suit No. 100 of 1978.

15. Mr Mahbubey Alam appearing with Mrs Mafuza Begum, the learned Advocates, for the petitioner, has advanced mainly threefold arguments: namely, (a) the plaintiff by adducing oral and documentary evidence could not prove the date of her alleged dispossession from the suit land. Relying upon the cases of Jogendra Nath alias Govinda Sarker vs Amulya Chandra Sarker and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 147. Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 100, the learned Advocate submits that since the plaintiff failed to prove induction of the defendant No.1 as her tenant in the suit land, he will be treated under the law, as a hostile possessor and his possession is adverse possession under the law; (b) With reference to the cases of Radhamoni Debi vs Collector and others reported in 27 Indian Appeals 136, Secretary of State vs Debendra Lal, reported in 1934 (Privy Council) 23; Ejas Ali Qidwai and others vs Special Manager. Court of Wards. Balrampur Estate and others reported in 1935 (Privy Council) 53 and Musa Ali vs Nur Ahmed and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 154 the Learned Advocate submits that since the possession of the defendant No.1 was open, overt, continuous and competitive against his competitor, the same has conferred a good title against all except the real owner and since the defendant No.1 has proved by evidence that he is in possession of the suit land the onus of proof was shifted upon the plaintiff to prove that he was inducted by her as her tenant or was her permissive possessor or licensee and in the absence of such proof: the possession of the defendant No.1 is clearly an adverse possession and (c) the defendant No.1 is in possession of the suit land from 1963 without break as it was found by the Courts below and so he has acquired his title in the suit land by way of adverse possession and the Learned appellate Court has erred in law in not holding title in the suit land by adverse possession and the findings and conclusion of the learned appellate Court is liable to be set aside.

16. Mr Md Fazlul Karim with Mr ABM Mahbub, the learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party, submits on the other hand, that the suit property was declared Enemy Property in the year 1969 and it remained as such till its release in favour of the plaintiff in the year 1978 and the defendant No.1 got lease of 7 sataks of land from the Government acknowledging and admitting the property to be the property of the Government and thus this period running from 1969-78 could not be added to or deemed to be hostile or adverse possession against the plaintiff. The learned Courts below found that the defendant No.1 has entered into an unlawful possession in 1963 and since the property was declared Enemy Property in 1969 his possession was of only 6 years prior to declaration of Enemy Property. The suit was instituted in 1980 and; as such, the period of his possession is not more than 8 years in all and, as such, he has acquired no adverse possession or title in the suit land. The plaintiff need not prove her constructive possession, since the possession of the defendant No.1 was broken. The defendant No.1 cannot claim his adverse possession in the suit land as was held by their Lordships in the case of Kumar Basanta Roy and others vs Secretary of Stale for India in Council and others reported in 44 Indian Appeals 104.

17. Perused the application, heard the learned Advocates and considered their submissions.

18. There is no statutory definition of adverse possession. The limitation of adverse possession is a matter of practice ascribed to sections 26 and 27 of the Limitation Act which is also not categorical. From different textbooks and judicial pronouncements it appears that adverse possession comprises of possession (a) commenced in wrong; and (b) maintained against a right.

19. It has been variously described eg, (a) abnormal enjoyment. against all the world, but wrongly against the true owner (b) continuous possession against the title of the true owner if continued for the statutory period of limitation except making re-entry or bringing an action (c) Continuous exercise of right or title against the true owner which cannot afterwards be refused, either by re-entry or subsequent acknowledgment (Pannamma Velly vs Achu Thana Union. ILR 1966, 1 Kerala 689). Possession by continuous assertion against the title of the dispossessed owner and actual exclusive possession of the property commenced and continued to a clear right either openly or by a void claim' against a constructive claim adverse against the competitor and actual in continuity, in publicity and to the extent to show that its possession is adverse to the competitor.

Since title by adverse possession is relating to the possession which is not legal and obtained in some unlawful manner and by continuity for specific period, the person concerned is claiming title thereupon, it must be categorical and specific.

<u>20. In acquisition of ownership the maxim "qui prior est tempore potior est Jure" (whoever is prior in point of time has priority in law) applies. So, where two rights or title conflict the earlier prevails unless there be some reason to prefer the latter. Ownership is distinct from possession.</u>

<u>Ownership is de jure recognition of a claim to certain property. Possession is the objective realisation of ownership. It is the de facto exercise of a claim to certain property and a de facto counterpart of ownership. Possession is a right in the de facto relation of continuing exercise and enjoyment as opposed to the de jure relation of ownership. Possession is thus external form to justify and normally manifest in the possession in fact. Possession denotes the relationship between a person: (a) some actual power over the object possessed. i.e. physical (corporeal) control or actual possession; and (b) some amount of will to avail oneself of that power that is the desire to possess (animus). Thus, it expresses the physical relation of control exercised by a person over the thing. The possessor may be or may not be the owner of the thing. Possession confers more than a personal right to be protected against wrongdoers. It confers a qualified right to possess, a right in the nature of property which is valid against everybody who cannot show a prior or better right. The law under such circumstances assists not only the possessor himself but also those who stand in the place of the possessor by succession or transfer. The term dispossession, on the other hand, is, in essence, ouster of possession. The prefix of the term "dis" is "negative", "objection", "separation" and "deprivation". The dictionary meaning of the term "dispossession" is "to be out of possession from acquired or right of property. " In the case of Basanta Kumar Roy vs Secretary of State, reported in LR 44 of 104, their Lordships held that "the meaning of 'dispossession' is well settled. A man may cease to use his land because he cannot use it, since it is under water. He does not thereby discontinue his possession. Constructively, his possession continues until he is dispossessed: and upon the cessation of the dispossession before the lapse of the statutory period, constructively, it revives."</u>

21. In the case permissive possession is also an issue for the plaintiff claimed that the defendant No.1 has entered into the possession of the suit land as her tenant and remained there as her permissive possessor. Permissive possession does not amount to dispossession. If the person in permissive possession changes his animus and continued to hold continuous assertion of hostile title openly the possession becomes adverse to the owner after expiry of specific period of limitation. A trespasser, on the other hand, if continues in possession for the statutory period, the adverse possession is created, which may be covered by title of the trespasser, if the conditions of adverse possession are satisfied. Trespass means to enter into land or a building that does not have permission or the right to enter. Trespasser's possession is only unlawful possession and mere unlawful possession does not mean adverse possession.

A trespasser's possession becomes adverse only when the adverse nature of trespasser's claim entered into the knowledge of the true owner. Trespass literally means wrongful disturbance of another person's possession of immovable property by entering upon the premises in the possession of another or remaining upon such premises.

In order to make the possession adverse, it has to be proved on the part of the trespasser his explicit possession exclusive to the true owner.

In the case of Bush vs Smith, (1953) 6 PL 670 their Lordships held that: "Neither the use of force, nor the breaking of an enclosure or transgression of a visible boundary, nor even an unlawful intention, is necessary to constitute an actionable trespass." And in the case of Lawrence vs Tucker, (1938) 160 Ore 474: 85 it was held that: "The motive of the intruder is immaterial and the trespass cannot be justified even by showing that it resulted in a benefit to the occupier."

<u>22. On the other hand, the term licence has been defined in section 60 of the Easement Act meaning a licence to property is based on trust which makes the action lawful, which without it, would have been unlawful.</u>

<u>In the case of Play Fair vs Musgrove, 153 ER, 465 their Lordships held that: "A licensee must quit upon the termination of the licence and if he overstayed, he became a trespasser,"</u>

<u>Therefore, licensee means, In essence, possession or enjoyment, without passing any interest in the property to which it relates, which could be otherwise wrongful.</u>

23. In the instant case, admittedly the property belonged to one Subarna Probha and according to the plaintiff, the property was auction sold and she, together with one Hanuman Das Agarwala (defendant No.3) purchased that property in the auction proceeding and got possession thereof through the Court and subsequently, Hanuman Das sold out his share to one Upendra Nath who instituted a suit praying for his separate saham and he lost the suit upto appeal. He then instituted a Title Suit and obtaining a decree and won up to appeal. The plaintiff purchased the share of Upendra Nath, after being lost in that Title Suit and appeal, by her kabala and became owner of the entire property, in question. The case of the defendant No.1 is that the story of Certificate Case and Auction Sale of the suit property and purchase of the plaintiff are all false. Subarna Probha was the owner and possessor of the suit property and in the Khatian Hanuman Das was recorded as forceful possessor. When Subarna Probha left for' India sometime around the partition of the subcontinent, he got his possession in the property by making a house in the portion where Hanuman Das was the forceful possessor. Subarna Probha's property became Enemy Property and was listed as such in the year 1969 and he got lease of .07 sataks of land from the Government in whom the property was vested and in this area of land he has his homestead and the lease continued till its release in 1978.

The plaintiff has asserted her right from the proceeding of the certificate case, particularly after her purchase on auction. She had been involved in litigations in respect of the suit land where Hanuman Das got his possession followed by Upendra Nath and thereafter, by the Government and, last of all, the present defendant No.1.

The learned appellate Court found that the plaintiff's persuasion and chase to the equal share holder of Certificate purchase, Hanuman Das, has finally led to the point of her purchase from Upendra Nath. Upon purchase of the property in auction, the plaintiff got possession in the southern half and Hanuman Das in the northern half of the suit plot. While the plaintiff was trying to come to the northern half of the land in question by way of litigations with Hanuman Das he made an exit by way of transfer to Upendra Nath and Upendra Nath was in possession of this portion. From Upendra Nath the plaintiff has finally purchased it and Upendra Nath had his right, title and possession therein.

The learned first trial Court also found possession of the defendant No.1, but since the defendant No.1 could not explain his possession, the Learned Court held that it will not amount as hostile to the plaintiff. In the opinion of the learned remand Court, since before her purchase from Upendra Nath., the defendant No.1 was possessing the half share of Hanuman Das, so his possession was prior to the purchase of the plaintiff. It is hostile against Hanuman Das and also against the plaintiff. Though the plaintiff acquired title, but she did not get the possession of it.

In arriving at the aforesaid findings the Learned Courts below committed a grave omission in not looking into the fact, why Upendra Nath lost his Partition Suit upto its appeal against the present plaintiff and why he was compelled to institute a Title Suit instead: especially, why his prayer for separate saham was refused.

24. The other important factor in this case is the interruption. While the litigations were going on between the plaintiff and Hanuman Das or between the plaintiff and Upendra Nath, suddenly, the Government has entered into the scene and taken away the suit property declaring it Enemy Property. After its release from the list of Enemy Property, it again came back to the plaintiff, giving rise to the question as to with whom the possession remained during this period.

<u>25. The plaintiff has taken the plea of permissive possession. Plaintiff's possession, according to her, is one, where a true owner is neither dispossessed nor discontinued the possession because a third person has taken away the possession. But whether such a possession constitutes an adverse possession, is a mixed question of law and facts.</u>

<u>In a case of acquiring title by adverse possession, the possessor has to remain in an uninterrupted possession for the full period of 12 years. If the adverse dispossession discontinued, for however short a time before he completes his title, his previous possession loses its value. In Kumar Basanta Roy's Case. (Supra) their Lordships held that "where the Government after taking possession of re-formed lands has released them to persons claiming to be entitled, those persons do not derive their liability to be sued from or through the Government within the meaning of section 3 of the Act and upon a claim to possession they consequently cannot rely under Article 144 upon the period during which the Government had possession."</u>

<u>In the case of Thakur Singh vs Bhogeraj Singh, 'reported in ILR 27 (Cal) 29 their Lordships held that "in order to acquire title by adverse possession, the possession must not only be open and exclusive, but it must also be shown to have been adverse for the full statutory period i-e, it must be continuous for the full period (without any break or without interruption)." And as per decision given in the case of Badri vs Smt. Ram Rati, 1977 RD (BR) 224, it was held that the claimant has to specifically show his possession from year to year, particularly so, if he is a trespasser by continuity. " (also the case of Gouri Sanker vs Deputy Director, Consolidation, 1980 RD 250 continuity not found, presumption not drawn). In another case of Ganda Singh and others vs Ram Narain Singh, reported in AIR 1959 (Punjab) 147 it was held that "the claimant must show on what date he came into possession, what was the nature of his possession, whether the factum of his possession was known to the legal claimants and how long his possession continued."</u>

26. In the instant case, both the plaintiff and defendant No.1 have abstained from stating on what date the defendant No.1 came into possession and both of them have intelligently avoided the point of time on what date the defendant No.1 entered upon possession, in the suit land. In such a case, priority of possession is also relevant and the point was considered by their Lordships in the, case of Ramchandra Apaji vs Balaji Bhaurav, reported in ILR 9 (Bombay) 137 holding that "it is not difficult to find out where the plaintiff has been affected and deprived of certain property belonged to her for the defendant has wrong possession over it. The question is one of the title or ownership in the case and if the plaintiff can establish that she is the owner and the defendant cannot show a better title the latter must go out. The plaintiff may prove her prior possession out of use standing for such long period of time. But all adverse claims by law is subject to limitation."

27. In the instant case, the plaintiff is claiming possession by virtue of her ownership and by way of purchase from Upendra and even prior to it by virtue of her litigations with Hanuman Das on the point of share and possession and the defendant is claiming his wrongful possession based without any ante-dated deed and in view of the above decisions, the title holder shall have the priority.

28. Upendra Nath Das, the vendor of the plaintiff, has appeared in the suit as PW 2 supporting the plaintiffs possession in the suit land. The PW 3 Shahadat Hossain has completed his evidence by saying that he is also carrying on business in the suit land under the plaintiff and the plaintiff is possessing the suit land by growing fruit bearing trees, etc. The defendant No.1, on the other hand, has produced no other oral evidence except himself. But facts remain that his claim of possession has not been corroborated by any corroborative evidence, especially about the starting point of his possession. It is on record that the Government has interrupted his continuous possession that was adverse, according to him, to the title and possession of the plaintiff, for the period of 1969-78 and in view of the cases referred to above, the possession must be uninterrupted to acquire title to the property by adverse possession.

29. Mr Mahbubey Alam has relied upon the case of Jogendra Nath vs Amulya Chandra Sarker and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 147. But the dispute arose in that case was out of a Will and extinction of title on the basis of will by adverse possession.

He has also relied upon the case of Abdus Sattar vs Abdul Rahman and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 100. But in that case, the defendant took the plea of tenancy and encroachment.

He has relied upon another of Musa Ali vs Nur Ahmed and another [44 DLR (AD) 154] and this case is on the point of limitation.

I find these cases are distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

30. In the case of Nazira Begum vs Roushanara Begum, reported in 39 DLR (AD) 22 their Lordships held that "onus of proof is upon the defendant and apparent show of possession is not sufficient. Constructive possession is not equal possession. In the case of tenancy in common ownership are not examined."

In the case of Madaris Ali and others vs Biswamber Das, reported in 46 DLR 34 their Lordships held that "evidence of forcible entry in the suit land, cannot amount to adverse possession."

31. In view of the above, I find that the petitioner, Md Nurul Haque has not acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession, especially by virtue of his unspecified and interrupted possession. He is mere a trespasser, who acquired no title.

32. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 27-7-1993, decree signed on 31-5- 1993 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon, in Title Appeal No.19 of 1992, reversing the judgment and decree dated 28-5-1992, decree signed on 3-6-1992, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Thakurgaon, in Other Suit No. 5 of 1985 is hereby upheld.

Send down the lower Court's Record at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: This Rule was obtained by the preemptor upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and order dated 31-03-99 passed by Additional District Judge, Fifth Court at Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 223 of 1996 affirming those dated 12-10-96 passed by Subordinate Judge, Fourth Court at Dhaka in Preemption Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1992 which disallowed the prayer for preemption.

2. The preemptor made an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, in brief, the Act against the opposite parties for preemption of the transfer of 0.0907 acre of land of SA plot No. 54 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 48/1 out of CS plot No. 139 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 2 by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No.1. His case, in short, is that said khatian No. 2 consisted of 5 plots of which CS plot No.139 comprised of 3.49 acre of land. Owners of other plots got settlements from the Bhowal Raj Court of Wards Estate by opening separate holdings. The CS plot No. 139 was joint and still remained joint and other owners of other four plots were never co-sharers in this plot.

3. Lal Mahmud, Waz Mahmud, Shukur Mahmud and Noor Mahmud took settlement of 2.36 acres from said Court of Wards Estate and the rest 1.13 acre was given settlement to Ibrahim and his brother Wasimuddin. Said Lal Mahmud and three others transferred their land to Nishi Kanta Shome, Rebati Mohan Shome and Amrita Lal Shome. Then, one Golam Mowla purchased the said land from them by deed No. 5935 dated 27-08-51 and deed No. 6755 dated 27-09-51 and became owner in possession. Similarly, Ibrahim and his brother transferred their land to one Charu Bala. Thereafter, the land was sold in auction for arrears of rents and one Jamsher Ali purchased said land measuring 1.13 acre in the auction. The auction was confirmed on 23-12-49 and possession was delivered to him on 31-01-50.

4. While Jamsher Ali was thus owner in possession in 1.13 acre, he transferred 0.4050 acre by a registered deed dated 03-05-50 to one Mainuddin and the rest 0.7250 acre by another registered deed dated 22-01-51 to Hasina Shamsuddin, opposite party No. 7 Mainuddin on the same date re-transferred his land to Hasina Shamsuddin. Thus, Hasina Shamsuddin became owner in possession of said 1.13 acre of land.

5. Golam Mowla also on 27-08-51 transferred 0.70 acre to one Haji Tarikullah by a registered deed and to one Noor Akhter Khatun 0.5250 acre by another deed. He then on 30-04-53 transferred 11 decimals to late SM Nazmul Huque, father of the preemptor and 22 decimals to opposite party No. 29, mother of the preemptor, and on 20-07-54 further transferred 30 decimals to the father of the preemptor. Similarly, Golam Mowla transferred the rest of his land at different times to different persons, and thus, he exhausted all his interest in said 2.36 acre of land of CS plot No. 139. The parents of the preemptor thus became owners in possession in total 0.63 acre of land out of CP plot No.139.

6. Haji Tarikullah instituted Partition Suit No. 43 of 1993 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka for partition. Father of the preemptor is defendant No.3 in the suit. The parents of the preemptor jointly prayed for a 'Saham' in respect of their purchased land of 0.63 acre. The suit was on 15-12-54 decreed in the preliminary form the suit was then transferred to the Fourth Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka and was re-numbered as Partition Suit No. 584 of 1993. The suit is still pending for final decree. Further case of the preemptor is that CS plot No. 139 was never partitioned by metes and bound and, as such, he is still a co-sharer in said land and is therefore entitled to pre-empt. Having come to know about the transfer of the case land by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1, the application was filed on making the statutory deposit.

7. Opposite party, No. 1 opposed the prayer for preemption by filing a written objection. Main objection is that during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 number of plots was created out of said CS Khatian No. 139 under various khatians on the basis of possession of the persons. As the land measuring 0.63 acre was recorded in a new SA plot No.92 appertaining to first SA Khatian No.76 then 73 in the names of the parents of the preemptor, so, the land of opposite party No. 2 including the transferred land was recorded in separate SA plot No. 54 appertaining to SA khatian No. 48/1. The opposite party No. 2, vendor and others exclusively possessed their respective lands on payment of rents since the record of rights was finally published in 1964. Similarly, all other owners of the rest land of original CS plot No. 139 now exclusively possess their respective land either on the basis of SA record of rights or by subsequent mutations. The preemptor was not a co-sharer in the holding of opposite party No. 2 and, as such, his application was liable to be dismissed.

8. Opposite party Nos. 21 and 22 also filed an objection and adopted the case as made out by the preemptor as they appear to be the sisters of the preemptor.

9. On the aforesaid pleadings, five issues were raised of which the moot issue was whether the preemptor is a co-sharer in the disputed jote.

10. One witness each was examined on behalf of the preemptor and opposite party No. 1. Number of documents was produced by both the parties, which were marked as exhibits.

11. The learned Subordinate Judge found the preemptor not a co-sharer in the land and accordingly, disallowed the application. On appeal therefrom at the instance .of the preemptor, the learned Additional District Judge hearing the same was also pleased to affirm the decision of the trial Court, and dismissed the appeal by impugned judgment and order.

12. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner read section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 and submits that the preemptor is still a co-sharer in the land of CS plot No. 139 appertaining to CS Khatian No. 2 and the Courts below erred in law in disallowing preemption on the view that the preemptor is not a co-sharer in land. Elaborating, he submits that CS plot 139 was never partitioned by metes and bound and until a final decree in the Partition Suit is passed the preemptor must be held to be a co-sharer in said land. In support, he cites the decisions in the case of Muhammad Muzaffar Khan vs Muhammad Yusuf Khan, 11 DLR (SC) 78, SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 230 and Shafiuddin Chowdhury vs Md Abdul Karim and others, 52 DLR (AD) 41.

13. Opposing the Rule, Mr. Md Ismail, learned Counsel for the purchaser, opposite party No. 1 submits that the land measuring 3.49 as was recorded as CS plot in 1917-18 in the Cadastral survey was split up in numerous plots under various khatians during the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in 1964 and the persons including the preemptor have been exclusively possessing their respective land according to such record of rights. The parents of the preemptor were in exclusive possession in their 0.63 acre of land which was recorded as SA plot No. 92 under SA khatian No. 73 Exhibit 'Ka' while opposite party No. 2 was in exclusive possession in plot No. 54 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 4811. The preemptor is therefore not a co-sharer in the land transferred by the kabala Exhibit No. 8. He accordingly, submits that the learned Additional District Judge did not commit any error in affirming the order of the trial Court in disallowing preemption. He also submits that everyone of purchasers of land of said CS plot No. 139 including the parents of the preemptor got their names mutated and in view of provisions of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the parents of the preemptor ceased to be co-sharer in said land. In support, he cites the decisions in the case of Haladar Dutta vs Abdul Rob Chowdhury, 36 DLR 193 and Md Khairullah vs Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 338.

14. Only question facing us is whether the learned Additional District Judge is well founded in affirming the decision of the trial Court in disallowing the application for preemption. More precisely, the issue raised for our decision is whether the preemptor is a co-sharer in the land transferred by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1 by a sale deed No. 1677 dated 30-06-91, Exhibit No.8 within the meaning of section 24 of the Act, 1949.

15. We have perused the record, and heard the learned counsels at length. We shall first consider the cases as cited by them.

<u>16. Muhammad Muzaffar Khan vs Muhammad Yusuf Khan, 11 DLR (SC) 76 arose out of two suits for preemption. Khatian No. 324 of a village in the District of DI Khan, comprising of 54 Khasras and measuring 2664 kanals 1 maria in area were jointly owned and possessed by two brothers, Samundar and Qalandar in equal shares, and the rest half belonged to Alamgir Khan. Muhammad Muzaffar Khan, the appellant, purchased 480 kanals of different khasras of the khata from said Alamgir Khan. No partition was ever effected. Co-sharers possessed in severalty specific shares. Samundar and Qalandr jointly sold 62 kanals to respondent Muhammad Yusuf Khan. A mutation followed. Subsequently, Samundar sold another 30 kanals to said Yusuf Khan. The appellant instituted the suits for preemption of these two sales as co-sharer.</u>

<u>"A plain consideration of nature of the transaction in the circumstances of this case could, in our opinion, lead to but one conclusion. The vendee of a co-sharer who owns an undivided khata in common with another is clothed with the same rights as the vendor has in the property, no more and no less. If the vendor was in exclusive possession of a certain portion of the joint land and transfers its possession to his vendee, so long as there is no partition between the co-sharers, the vendee must be regarded as stepping into the shoes of his transferor qua his ownership rights in the joint property, to the extent of the area purchased by him, provided that the area in question does not exceed the share which the transferor owns in the whole property. Alienation of specific plots transferred to the vendee would only entitle the latter to retain possession of them till such time as an actual partition by metes and bounds takes place between the co-sharers. It is difficult to see in these circumstances why the vendee of specific plots acquired from a co-owner, in an undivided khata, does not become a co-sharer in the khata. It may be pointed out that the mutations in favour of the appellant, which are on the record, described the sale transactions in his favour as hissadari sales of the joint khata in suit.</u>

<u>Upon such finding, the Supreme Court of Pakistan restored the decision of first two Courts allowing preemption. What Khata, khasras, kanals etc, means, we could not ascertain. Nor we could ascertain the land law in Peshawar at the time. Unlike our land tenure, the land laws there, particularly, in the then West Pakistan was tilted a bit to big land holdings, Besides, unless the law for preemption in Peshawar is not in pari-materia with our law, i.e. the Act, 1949, in brief, the Act, 1949, it is very difficult for us to follow the opinion of the Pakistan Supreme Court. Moreover, if we take Khata meaning a tenancy or holding, the above view of the Supreme Court of Pakistan will be of no help because sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act have provided procedure for amalgamation and subdivision of a tenancy or holding, and after a valid subdivision of a holding and distribution of the rents, preemption at the instance of a co-sharer of the former joint holding is not maintainable.</u>

17. SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury, 35 DLR (AD) 230 arose out of an application under section 24 of the Act, 1949. The case land appertained to a permanent tenure recorded in CS Khatian No. 214 in the names of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani. Akshoy instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 for partition and by the decree passed, Akshoy got one-third share while Rangubala got the rest two-third. One Nafisa Khatun purchased the entire share of Akshoy by a registered sale deed dated 19-07-52 while Rangubala settled her share of two-third for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 with Ayesha Khatun, respondent No. 2. Then, Nafisa Khatun sold her share to respondent No. 1 by a registered deed of sale dated 18-04-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered deed of sale dated 10- 09-73. Against this sale, respondent No.1 filed the application for preemption, which was allowed by the trial Court. Against the order, appellant's appeal and revision failed. But the Appellate Division set aside the order and dismissed the application for preemption. But, we find, on different reasons.

18. The main issue as to whether respondent No.1 was a co-sharer in land along with other questions were considered and determined in the appeal. Mr Ruhul Islam, J, wrote the leading judgment. Construing the phrase, 'Non-Agricultural land' His Lordship was of the view,

"Different sub-sections of section 24 sufficiently indicate that the Legislature did not use the expression 'Non-Agricultural land' carrying the same meaning as the expression 'holding' defined in the Bengal Tenancy Act and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The expression 'Non-Agricultural land' may represent the entire land comprised in a tenancy or it may form a part as owned and possessed by a tenant or tenants on partition."

While concurring with the conclusion allowing the appeal, Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed, J, as his Lordship then was, on the point reserved his verdict as hereunder,

"Secondly, a Full Bench of the High Court in the case of 'Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury vs Rezia Begum'; 16 DLR 77 examined this question and by majority decision held that these two terms, 'Non-Agricultural land' and 'holding', are synonymous carrying the same meaning, Since this question is not necessary for disposal of the instant appeal, I would refrain from expressing any opinion as to the correctness of the decision of the High Court in that case."

19. Before this decision, it appears, the view of the Full Bench in the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury was holding the field that the phrase and word 'Non-Agricultural land' and 'holding', are synonymous carrying the same meaning.

20. In holding that the respondent No. 1 was a co-sharer in the land, their Lordships gave different reasons as well. Mr Ruhul Islam, J was of the view,

"In this case also by effecting partition on the basis of a decree of the Civil Court the co- sharers, namely, Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Chouwdhurani possessed separately the land in their respective share, but the tenancy with the jama of Rs 10 was not divided or split up."

Lastly, he found,

"In view of what has been stated above, in my opinion the respondents not being co-sharer in the land transferred, though they may be co- sharer in the tenancy, the right of preemption did not accrue in their favour and, as such, their application for preemption must fail."

Whereas, Mr Shahabuddin Ahmend, J finds,

"The principle of law on this subject is that where an under-raiyati is created by a raiyat, the latter is not a co-sharer of the former; and when the superior interest of the raiyat is extinguished and he disappears, the under-raiyat is upgraded into a raiyat but only in respect of his own share. If the previous raiyat or for that matter his co-sharer raiyat held khas any portion of the original tenancy, that portion becomes a separate raiyati under the Government with which the upgraded raiyat has got no connection. In view of the position, the under-raiyati held by Ayesha upgraded into an independent raiyati which got no connection with the raiyati previously held by Nafisa, now by respondent No.1 As such, respondent No.1 is not a co-sharer of the appellant and he got no right to pre-empt the land purchased by the appellant from Ayesha Khatun."

Mr Ruhul Islam, J found that respondent No.1 was not a co-sharer on the basis of the decree passed in the suit for partition, under which the land was separated though the tenancy remained the same while Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed J was of the view, that after the wholesale acquisition, the under-raiyati of Ayesha Khatun was upgraded into an independent raiyati which got no connection with the raiyati held by Nafisa, now by respondent No.I. Mr Ruhul Islam, J is therefore of the view that the decree in partition suit results in separation and division of the land. But Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed expressed himself as follows.

" .....by a decree in a partition suit the parties go into separate and exclusive possession of their respective shares in the land of a holding, but such a decree does not result in the splitting up of the holding along with its jama which may be done only by sub-division of the holding under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, corresponding to section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Right of preemption is not extinguished by partition as was rightly held in the case of Md Shukur vs Ram Chandra Kapali, 6 DLR 393. This principle however will apply only in the case of a 'holding'. Whether this principle will be applicable in the case of a non-agricultural tenancy will depend upon the question whether 'Non-Agricultural Land' under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the 'holding' under section 26 F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, corresponding to section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are synonymous carrying the same meaning."

As quoted above that he refrained from expressing any opinion on the question.

21. Before the above case, on May 5, 1982 the Appellate Division in the case of Md Khairullah vs Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury as cited above by a majority of 3:2 disallowed the prayer for preemption under section 24 of the Act, 1949 on the ground of amalgamation and separation of old holding. In the leading judgment written by Mr Ruhul Islam J, the preemptor was found to be not a co-sharer on the view.

"Amalgamation of tenancies made in Miscellaneous Case No. 89/72-73 under sections 116 and 117(1)(a) was given effect by amending khatian No. 14 after excluding plot No. 108 therefrom and revenue was collected on the basis of the new khatian No. 18. Prima facie the order was a valid one; its validity could not be challenged for a collateral purpose, that is, in a proceeding of preemption. The Civil Court while dealing with altogether a different matter cannot ignore the order passed by a competent Revenue Officer under section 117 of the Act."

22. In the Case of Shafiuddin Chowdhury vs Md Abdul Karim, in allowing a review of its earlier decision, the Appellate Division disallowed the prayer for preemption on the ground of partition of the land by a decree. It held that,

"the passing of the final decree in a partition suit finally determines the rights of the co-sharers in land. Hence, the application for the preemptor-respondents on the basis of co- sharer ship is not maintainable."

23. Ratio decidendi in the above decisions is that a decree of the Court in a partition suit brings separation and division in the joint possession and enjoyment of land. But such decree does not ipso facto result in the splitting of holding along with the jama till such subdivision of the holding and distribution of the rents takes place in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act or the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the case may be. Such division of the land may also be brought about by an amicable partition among the co-sharers in such land. But the main submission of Mr. Islam is that the total area of land in a plot as was plotted in the cadastral survey in 1917-18 must to be taken as an undivided unit. If such land was recorded in the names of more than one person, all such persons and/or their successors-in-interest must be held to be co-sharers in such plot till the land is partitioned by a decree of the Court or by amicable partition among such co-sharers. Even any sub-division of such CS plot and/or the holding to which such plot appertained in subsequent survey, say, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 will not result in the termination of co-sharer ship in such land and thereby, taking away the right of preemption under section 24 of the Act, 1949. The argument appears to be unique in the sense that it was never argued since the Act came into force in 1949. We are unable to accept such interpretation of the law.

<u>24. Firstly, we do not find any reason or authority to agree with Mr Islam that the word 'land' as used in the expression 'co-sharer in the land' in section 24(1) of the Act, 1949 should always mean the quantum of land in one plot only. As the word 'co-sharer' always implies the existence of more than one person jointly owning, similarly, such joint ownership may be in respect of land of one plot or several plots. It is now well settled rule of interpretation as to number that in every Act, unless the contrary intention appears, the words in the singular shall include the plural, the words in the plural shall include singular. The land is always recorded under a holding for the purpose of revenue record and payment of rents. This holding may be joint of several persons, or exclusive in the name of one person. It may also may be noted that the holding of any land, agricultural or non-agricultural, could only be sub-divided and rents distributed in accordance with the procedure under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. But the proposition of Mr Islam that such sub-division of the holding and distribution of rents will not affect the land appertaining to such holding is equally misconceived.</u>

<u>25. Secondly, who are the co-sharers in the expression, 'co-sharer in the land'? To find the answer, we need not go far just to refer to the holding, more popularly known as khatian, comprising of such land. The concept of 'co-sharer' cannot be conceived independent of any holding or tenancy. If the holding is recorded in the name of more than one person, then, each of such person or his successor-in-interest is the co-sharer to each other in such land. Such a co-sharer will deem to continue as such co-owner in both holding as well as in land so long the holding will continue to be joint. Contrary to such proposition as argued by Mr Islam that sub-division of such holding will not affect the land in any way appear to be fallacious. Because, after sub-division of the holding and creation of new plots in subsequent survey, or by mutation by the acts of parties, the previous co- owners in the holding and/or the land cannot be deemed to still continue as such co-owners.</u>

<u>26. Coming to the facts of this case, we find, on 30-04-53 and 30-07-54 parents of the preemptor purchased 0.63 acre of land. After the survey under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 their purchased land was recorded as plot No. 92 appertaining to first khatian No. 76 and then, No. 73, Exhibit 'Ka', Accordingly, they possessed since then, and after them, the preemptor has been in possession and enjoying the land on payment of rents in the separate jama. His possession and enjoyment are absolutely independent and exclusive of others. Similarly, the land transferred by opposite party No. 2 to opposite party No. 1 vide sale deed No. 1677 dated 30-06-91 was recorded as SA plot No. 54 appertaining SA khatian No.48/1. In the partition suit, the father of the preemptor as defendant No. 3 along with defendant No. 2 and defendant Nos. 4 to 6 prayed for saham and the preliminary decree dated 15-12-54 has allotted a saham to each of those defendants on the basis of their purchase. Mr Islam told that effecting partition by Advocate Commissioners failed four times. Mr Ismail submitted that chance of any final decree is far remote for the present successors of the original plaintiff have lost all their interest in such a decree. Be that as it may, the final decree that may ultimately be passed will just formalise independent and exclusive possession of present owners. The submission of Mr Islam that even after so many transactions and transfers since the final publication of CS record of rights, and the long and exclusive possession and enjoyment by the present occupiers on the basis of SA record of rights and/or mutation have not yet terminated the original co- sharer ship in CS plot No.139 as recorded in 1917-18 cannot be accepted.</u>

<u>27. In view of above decisions, there is no escape from the irresistible conclusion that even if the land in the expression, 'co-sharer in the land' in section 24(1) of the Act, 1949 is not synonymous to a holding but conceiving of such land without reference to the word 'co-sharer' is neither feasible nor possible. And the word 'co-sharer' in the phrase 'co-sharer in the land' is the key to find whether the preemptor is entitled to pre-empt. A final decree passed in a partition suit or amicable partition though separates and divides the land for the purpose of possession but does not ipso Jacto terminate co-ownership in such land till subdivision of the holding and distribution of rents takes place only in accordance with law. Sub-division of a holding and distribution of rents may also take place in a revenue survey subsequent to the cadastral survey with or without the plot or plots divided into different small plots. As stated above, such sub-division may also take place at the instance of one or more of the co-tenants of the holding in accordance with the provisions of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Such sub-division always terminates the joint tenancy or more precisely co-sharership in the land, no matter whether the land is sub-divided or separated or not and after such sub-division, the old co-owners of the holding in such land cannot be deemed to still continue as co-sharer in the land within the meaning of section 24(1) of the Act, 1949.</u>

28. Lastly, it is now well settled by the decision of our Appellate Division that all lands situate within a municipal area must be deemed to be non-agricultural land for the purpose of preemption. We cannot think of the disastrous consequence of the view as Mr Islam submits that the quantum of land as recorded in one plot in the name of more than one person during the cadastral survey in 1917-18 must be deemed to be an independent unit and in the joint ownership of those persons as recorded then till partition by metes and bound-to declare all such land still joint for the purpose of preemption. Such view will definitely go against the public policy as well.

29. In the facts and circumstances of the case, and on the above principles, we could not find any reason to differ from the concurrent conclusion of the Courts below that the preemptor ceased to be a co-sharer in the land in question and, as such, his application for preemption was rightly found to be not maintainable. No failure of justice has occasioned by the decision.

30. In the result, the Rule is discharged with costs. Impugned judgment and order affirming the order of the trial Court in disallowing the application for preemption are confirmed. Order of stay as granted at the time of issue of the Rule is hereby recalled and vacated.

Send down the records.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
Abu Sayeed Ahammed J: This Rule Nisi has been issued at the instance of the petitioner Sew Bihari Parsed, sole proprietor of Messers Bangladesh Traders, having his business office at Sena Kallyan Bhaban, Room 0.901, 9th Floor, 195 Motijheel Commercial Area Dhaka, calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order dated 6-5-95 (Annexure-E) issued by the respondent No. 3 the Appraiser, Chittagong Customs House, Chittagong, directing the petitioner to submit the bill of entry declaring the value of imported goods namely, sugar, for fixing the rate of customs duty on the basis of indicative value and declaring the same arbitrarily for the purpose of assessment of the Customs duty, VAT and other charges on the consignment of the petitioner, in question.

2. The petitioner according to SRO No. 214- ATN/93/1527/Shulka dated 28-10-1993, wherein the value of the questioned Sugar was affixed at US$ 350 per metric ton, by opening LC No. D/C/94240 dated 18-8-1994 through American Express Bank, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka, imported 10,500 metric tons of white crystal sugar. The SRO is Annexure-“A” and the L/C is Annexure “B”

3. After arrival of the goods, the clearing Agent of the petitioner submitted the bill of entry for releasing the goods' after assessment of customs duty at the aforesaid rate of the value as shown in the papers and documents of the petitioner importer. But the respondent No. 3 by his order dated 6-5-95 directed the petitioner to submit bill of entry declaring the value of the imported goods at the rate of US$ 401.55 calling it indicative value instead of declared value which was at the rate of US$ 350 per metric ton.

4. Bring aggrieved by that order (Annexure-C the petitioner has obtained the present Rule under Article 102 of the Constitution.

5. The Customs Authority has not filed affidavit-in-opposition and its case is that under section 25(1) of the Customs Act, the indicative value can be assessed and accordingly, the impugned order has been issued upon the petitioner asking him to value his goods accordingly and to pay customs duty upon that value which the customs authority call indicative value.

6. In this case, the tax has been imposed on the basis of the term 'indicative value' but this term indicative value is not found anywhere within the four comers of the Customs Act, 1969 and, as such, it is submitted for the petitioner that the impugned order is illegal and it has infringed the fundamental right of the petitioner.

<u>7. Mr Ramjan Ali Sikder, the learned Counsel for the petitioner in support of his argument cites the decision in the case of Russell Vegetable Oil Ltd vs Collector of Customs, Chittagong and others, reported in 5 MLR (HC) 121=52 DLR 382. In the said decision, in para 13 while opinion as to standard in fixation of value, their Lordships have held, as under:</u>

<u>"The price as mentioned in the letter of credit and the commercial invoice prima facie shows that the price mentioned in those documents is the market value between the seller and the buyer, in other words, the supplier and the consignee. Therefore, as per provision of section 25(1) said invoice price is to be taken to be the normal price unless of course, the Customs Authority have no arbitrary right to reject the invoice value. If they do not accept the invoice value they must have sufficient materials to support their action. There is no such material whatsoever which tends to show that the consignment in question has been under invoiced."</u>

<u>Section 25(1) also has proved that the value of any imported goods shall be fixed according to normal value of the Articles i.e. the price which they would fetch, on the date as referred to in section 30 on sale of the goods in open market between a buyer and a seller independent of each other.</u>

8. So we are of the opinion that the section 25(1) of Customs Act also recognise and accept the view that the price of the imparted goods should be affixed at the normal value vis-a-vis the market value. So nowhere, there is indicative value which has been accepted as the basis for imposition of customs duty in this particular case and the customs authority enhanced the value of the goods from US$ 305 per metric ton to US$ 401 per metric tons to the great prejudice of the petitioner.

<u>9. In another unreported decision of the High Court Division in which a bunch of cases have been decided their Lordships nave held as under:</u>

<u>"We are of the view that the age old methods determining the normal price with various adjectives i.e. indicative value, enhanced valuation price, recorded value, loaded value, Commissioner's value, etc have no sanction in law and, as such, we direct the respondents not to use such attributes or any other adjective so far the normal value is concerned. The name of parties in the bunch of cases are Md Ayub and others vs Collector of Customs and others in Writ Petition Nos.1495 of 1996 and others.</u>

<u>10. In another decision reported in 4 BLC 85 relevant page 99 in para 62 [Rahmania Vanaspati Product Ltd vs Collector of Customs], their Lordships have held as follows:</u>

<u>"From a reading of the provision of sections 25(1), (2)(3) and section 30(1) of the Act it is very much seen that if customs authority is authorised to assess customs duties on imported merchandise at the value prevalent on the date the Bill of entry is presented for assessment of customs duties. The undenied position is that the customs authority fixed the "indicative value" for the purpose of assessment of customs duties of the imported CDSO and CPO, the kind of merchandises imported by the petitioners, much long before the presentation of the Bill of Entry, This being the factual position, the 'indicative value' that has been fixed by the circular dated 3-6-1994 cannot be considered to have been fixed in the light of the provisions of section 25(1), (2) (3) and section 30(1) of the Act."</u>

<u>Mr Ramjan Ali Sikder, the learned Counsel for the petitioner submits that in this case, affixing value on the basis calling it indicative value, the customs authority has committed illegality against the vested legal right of the petitioner, because his goods are to be valued at the rate of normal value as per provisions of section 25(1) of the Customs Act.</u>

<u>11. We find force in this submission, because, we do not get anywhere the term. indicative value, which can be made the basis or standard legally for fixing the value of the imported goods for the purpose of imposing customs duty, rather, in the aforesaid decisions the same has been made nugatory.</u>

12. Our meticulous reading of the provision of Section 25(1) as a whole also does not approve the said term, namely, indicative value which is a mere dreaming one without any basis. The decision of the High Court Division although have no binding force upon us, but those have got persuasive value. So, we accept the opinions contributed by those decisions.

13. Mr Aminuddin, the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the respondent, in view of the impugned order passed vide Annexure-'F", submits that the petitioner avoiding to appear before the customs authority, has come up with this writ petition. So it is not maintainable.

14. We see that by the impugned order, the Customs authority did not, in fact, direct the petitioner to appear before the customs authority and to show cause, as to the grievance of the petitioner, rather, after fixing up the mind of the custom authority, illegally and arbitrarily, they have directed the petitioner to appear before them only for the purpose of converting the value of the goods to facilitate the customs authority to impose higher duty and tax. On hearing the submissions of both parties it led us to find that the customs authority should fix the value of the goods according to normal price which could be found from the bill of entry, to be considered along with the invoice value submitted by the by petitioner as to the consignment in question.

15. For the reasons and discussions made above, we find merits in this Rule. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The fixation of valuation and imposition of taxes by the impugned order is declared to have been made without lawful authority and ultra vires of the Constitution and are of no legal effect. The Customs authority, therefore, is directed to affix the value of the goods in question under section 25(1) of the Customs Act according to the normal value of the goods which is also called market value as incorporated in the bill of entry and the invoice.

The Commissioner of Customs is directed to release the bank guarantees furnished by the petitioner in terms of the Rule within 15 days from the date of receipt of this order.

No costs.

End.

Dr Kamal Hossain with Ramzan Ali Sikder; Tanjib-ul-Alam and Sara Hossain, Advocates ----- For the Contemner-Respondent Nos.1-4.

Md Faiz, Advocate of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh ------ Petitioner
vs
Ekramul Haque Bulbul, reporter of the Daily Prothom Alo and others  ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Matin J: This Rule was issued calling upon the condemner-respondents Nos.1 and 2, the reporters of Daily Prothom Alo, for the reports captioned হাইকোর্টের বিচারপতির সনদ জাল, published in the daily Prothom Alo on 30-10-2004 and also upon the respondents Nos. 3 and 4 Editor and Publisher respectively of the same paper for commission of contempt of this Court and this Rule was also issued upon the respondent No. 5 who is the reporter of Daily Bhorer Kagoj for the report captioned এলএলবি পাশ না করেই বিচারপতি” published in the Daily Bhorer Kagoj on 30-10-2004 and also upon the respondents Nos. 6 and 7 who are the Editor and Publisher respectively of Daily Bhorer Kagoj. Cutting of the said 2(two) reports have been annexed and marked as Annexures-A and B to the Contempt Petition.

2. The case of the petitioner is that both the reports i.e. Annexures A and B, having been published under red big-lettered bold misleading captions by distorting the truth that Mr Justice Faisal Mahmud Faizee's LLB certificate is forged and he never passed his LLB examinations interfered with the administration of justice and the public confidence has been fundamentally shaken thereby.

3. It has further been asserted that Justice Faisal Mahmud Faizee obtained the Bachelor of Arts degree from Chittagong University and studied Law at the Chittagong Law College under the Chittagong University wherefrom he obtained his LLB degree. Justice Faizee was enrolled as an Advocate in 1991 and obtained permission to practice in the High Court Division in January, 1994 and he became a member of the Bangladesh Supreme Court Bar Association on 11 July 1994.

4. Justice Faisal Mahmud Faizee sat for both the LLB preliminary and final examinations for the year 1989 under the University of Chittagong which were held in January and February, 1990. The results of the final examination was published through Gazette Notification No. 24269-77 dated 26-11-1990 under roll number 3652 and the result of the preliminary examination was published in the official Gazette Notification No. 24655-64 dated 9-12-1990 under roll number No. 1934, both duly issued under the signature of the Controller of Examinations, Chittagong University. The photocopies of the Gazette Notifications have been annexed and marked as Annexures C&D respectively and the Provisional Certificate of the Degree of Bachelor of Laws (LLB) dated 10 December 1990 has been annexed and marked as Annexure-E to the Contempt petition. It has further been asserted that the petitioner is the father of said Justice Faisal Mahmud Faizee and is a practicing lawyer of this Court and Justice Faisal Mahmud Faizee is the Additional Judge of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court.

5. It has been further asserted in the Supplementary Affidavit by the petitioner that even after publishing Annexures-A & B the respondents continued to publish similar contemptuous reports to tarnish the image of this Court. The cuttings of the reports have been annexed as Annexures-"F to S" to the Supplementary Affidavit filed by the petitioner.

6. The respondent Nos. 1-4 appeared and filed affidavit-in-opposition denying material allegations made in the petition and contended, inter alia, that the report was published on the basis of records of the Chittagong University in exercise of their right of freedom of press and they have a duty to publish the same and they never intended to bring the Court into disrepute or interfere with the administration of justice. Respondent Nos. 5 and 6 also filed a separate affidavit-in-opposition in line with the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent Nos. 1 to 4 and respondent No.7 also did the same. The respondents have admitted the publications but tried to justify the same.

7. Respondents have not annexed any inquiry report of the Chittagong University nor any resolution of the Senate but quoted some portion of the resolution Nos.353 to 362 passed by the Senate of the Chittagong University.

8. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and perused the petition, Supplementary Affidavit by the petitioner and also Affidavit-in- opposition by the contemner-respondents.

9. Before we adjudicate whether the offending reports constitute the offence of contempt of this Court, let us deal with certain preliminary jurisprudential aspects of this case as raised by the learned Counsels of the parties. It has been contended that in absence of any definition of contempt and in view of the protection of the freedom of press by Article 39 of the Constitution the law relating to contempt of Court must be construed afresh. The pre-constitutional decisions on contempt of Court should be construed as to harmonies them with the constitutional safeguard of freedom of press.

10. The learned Counsel Mr Ajmalul Hossain QC, appearing for the petitioner, has taken us through the history of the contempt law and submitted that in the remote past it was considered as a part of law of sedition and when the Supreme Court was established in Calcutta in 1774 it was made a Court of record having power to punish its contempt. Subsequently, all the High Courts were given the same power and our Constitution by Article 108 specifically provided that this Court shall be the Court of record having power to punish its contempt.

11. The Psalms of David cursed the tongue that imagined wickedness and with lies cut like a sharp razor. So, the publication of false reports affecting the character of others was prohibited by the Mosaic law. The laws of Solon punished calumniators by an arbitrary fine and the same penalty was sanctioned by the law of the Twelve Tables.
