full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: This Rule- was issued on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure calling upon the opposite party Nos.1-7 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 12-5-2010 passed by the learned District Judge, Rangpur in Other Appeal No. 49 of 2010 dismissing the appeal summarily and affirming the Judgment and decree dated 29-4-2010 (decree signed on 5-5-2010) passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge Sadar, Rangpur in Other Suit No.238 of 2009 rejecting the plaint should not be set-aside.

.

2. The material facts as necessary for disposal of this Rule are that the present petitioner as plaintiff brought a suit being Other Suit No. 238 of 2009 on 29-8-2009 in the Court of Senior Assistant- Judge, Sadar, Rangpur impleading the present defendant-opposite parties praying for permanent injunction in respect of the suit land as described in the schedule of the plaint .The plaintiff's case in short is that Shib Krishna Sen and MonikrishnaSen were the original owner of the suit land as described in the 'Ka' schedule of the plaint. Shib Krishna Sen executed a registered will in favour of his brother Monikrishna Sen, who obtained probate from the District Judge vide Probate Case No. 14 of 1971 and has been owing and possessing the suit land; that Monikrishna. Sen executed a will on 8-4-1991 in favour of Shankar Basu, who obtained probate vide Probate Case No. 43 of 1992 wherein, it has been stated that the executor of will is not entitled to sell the schedule property but to enjoy the same; that Shankar Basu established Monikrishna Sen Decree College and after the death of Shankar Basuthe suit land came under Monikrishna Sen Trust; that one NGO namely Grameen Samaj Kendra took loan from the Agrani Bank, Tejgaon Industrial Area Branch, Dhaka mortgaging the schedule property as security of loan but the said NGO failed to liquidate the loan and thereupon, the Bank instituted a suit for realization of its outstanding dues against the authority of Grameen Samaj Kendra and the said suit was decreed ex-parte beyond the knowledge of the trust authority; that Shankar Basu was not empowered to mortgage the suit and as per will, the defendant Nos .1-3 in connivance with each other created a kabala vide its No.9685 dated 22-7-1990 in the name of Ranjit Basu in order to grab the suit property with an ulterior motive; that after creating kabala deed the defendants with the help of bad people attempted to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land on 15-9-2009 and thereafter, the defendant Nos. 1-3 in connivance with the defendant Nos. 4- 6 on 26-7-2009 at 9-10 AM illegally entered into the suit land and also tried to evict the employees of Monikrishna Sen Trust. Hence, the suit.

3. After institution of the suit the plaintiff filed an application under Order XXXIX, rule 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restraining the defendants from evicting the plaintiff of the suit land.

4. Decree holder, Agrani Bank Ltd. Tejgaon Industrial Area Branch, Dhaka on knowing about the said suit filed an application for addition of party which was allowed resulting which Agrani Bank Ltd. became party as defendant No.7 in the suit.

5. The defendant No.7 thereafter, on 15-10- 2009 filed an application under order 7, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint stating, inter-alia, that the defendant No.7 as plaintiff instituted Artha Rin Suit 771 of 2004 before the Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka for recovery of its outstanding dues amounting to Taka 60,61,540 against the Grameen Samaj Kendra which was decreed vide ex-parte judgment and decree dated 2-9-2004 and thereafter, the defendant No.7 as decree-holder Bank put the decree into execution filing Artha in Execution Case No. 638 of 2004 on 30-11-2004 in which the decree-holder-Bank after exhausting all the legal formalities executed a sale deed in respect of the suit land as described in the 'Ka' schedule of the plaint in favour of the highest bidder namely, (1) Momtaz, Jafar Ahmed, (2) Md Ashif Wahed and (3) Md Rashidul Alam and as such the suit is impliedly barred by section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

6. The learned Senior Assistant Judge upon hearing the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and on considering the contents of the plaint was pleased to reject the plaint by his judgment and decree dated 29-4-2010 holding that the suit property was mortgaged to bank against loan and the Bank for recovery of its loan amount instituted a suit being Artha Rin Suit No. 638 of 2004 and the Artha Rin Adalat decreed the suit as prayed for and as such the suit is impliedly barred by section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

7. The unsuccessful plaintiff, thereupon as plaintiff-appellant took an appeal being Other Appeal No. 49 of 2010 before the learned District Judge, Rangpur, who upon hearing the plaintiff appellant by his judgment and order dated 12-5- 2010 dismissed the appeal summarily along with an application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction holding that the suit is barred by section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 inasmuch as earlier over the self-same suit land the Artha Rin Adalat passed a decree in Artha Rin Case No. 771 of 2004 and thereafter, the suit property was sold in auction in Artha Rin Execution Case No. 638 of 2004 in accordance with law.

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of two Courts below the present plaintiff-appellant-petitioner has come before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

9. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that both the Courts below under misconception of law and facts most erroneously arrived at a finding that the suit is impliedly barred by section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 inasmuch as it is apparent from the plaint of the suit that no relief was sought for against the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in Artha Rin Case No.638 of 2004

10. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff-petitioner is in exclusive physical possession over the suit land and admittedly he did 'not hand over delivery of possession in favour of the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-3 and, as such, both the Courts below in rejecting the plaint of the suit committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of just. He further submits both the Courts below having failed to consider that the mortgage deed dated 26-5-1996 (Annexure X-1) allegedly executed by Shankar Basu is contrary to the provisions of the Succession Act as well as Hindu law.

11. Referring to the plaint of the suit Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate further argues that the plaintiff-petitioner did not mention any case being Artha Rin Case No. 771 of 2004 in the body of the plaint and no relief was sought for against the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin case and as such without taking evidence there is no legal scope at all to decide the question whether the suit is barred by section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 or not. He adds that the proposition of law is well settled that in deciding the question as to whether the plaint should be rejected the Court may look into the averments made in the plaint and cannot go beyond the same to find whether the plaint is rejected or not and in this case both the Courts committed a serious error in taking into consideration the application of the defendant-bank and as such at any rate the judgment of two Courts below are liable to be set-aside.

12. Mr Abdul Quayum, the Learned Advocate to fortify his submission has relied on the decision reported in 7 ADC 291, 56 DLR (AD) 22, 10 BLC (AD) 8 and section 307 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925.

13. On the other hand, Mr Shamim Khaled Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No.7, Agrani Rank Ltd. supports the judgments of two Courts below, which were according to him just, correct and proper. He in the course of his argument upon placing the plaint of the suit submits that the plaintiff through a clever device under the camouflage of a suit for permanent injunction challenged the judgment and decree of the Artha  Rin Adalat, Dhaka passed in Artha Rin Case No. 771 of 2004 stating in the plaint that he came to know Shankar Basu and others took loan in the name of Grameen Samaj Kendro (NGO) from Agrani Bank mortgaging the suit land and since the loan amount was not paid and the Bank filed a suit and obtained a decree in respect of the suit t land from the Artha Rin Adalat.

14. He further submits that the present plaintiff-petitioner with an ulterior motive in order to frustrate the decree of the Artha Rin Adalat filed the present suit for permanent injunction in respect of the suit property as described in the schedule of the plaint; which already have been sold in auction in the proceedings of the Execution Case No 368 of 2004 and in that view of the matter both the Courts below rightly arrived at a concurrent finding that the suit is impliedly barred by section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and, as such, question of interference by this Court sitting under revisional jurisdiction does not arise at all .

15. Mr Shamim Khaled Ahmed, the learned Advocate finally relying on the decision reported in 15 BLT 425 = 12 BLC 723 submits that in this case it is apparent from the materials on record that the delivery of possession of the suit property has not yet been handed over to the auction purchasers and thus, it cannot be said that the execution case has been disposed of in accordance with law and in such situation the present petitioner's door is still open to ventilate his grievance, if any, as per the provisions of section 32 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

16. Zafarullah Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1-3, auction purchasers submits that the present defendant-opposite party No. 7 as plaintiff filed Artha Rin Suit No. 771 of 2004 in the Artha Rin Adalat. 1, Dhaka and obtained a decree for recovery of Taka 60,31,540 with interest till realization of the same by selling the mortgaged property as described in the schedule of the plaint and thereafter, in the execution proceeding the mortgaged property was sold in auction to the opposite party Nos.I-3 in accordance with law. He next submits that plaintiff- petitioner deliberately with malafide intention in a cunning manner filed other Suit No. 238 of 2009, seeking permanent injunction in respect of the property which is subject matter of judgment and decree passed in Artha Rin Suit No. 771 of 2004 as well as Execution case No. 368 of 2004 and both the Courts below on consideration of the materials on record together with section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 correctly allowed the application for rejection of the plaint holding that the suit is barred by section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 which does not call for any interference .

17. Mr Zafarullah Chowdhury, finally relying on a number of decisions namely the decisions reported in 49 DLR (AD) 135, 8 BLC 411, 59 DLR 695,51 DLR (AD) 221 and in an unreported judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 2046 of 2006 submits that the proposition of law is by now well settled that no separate suit lies against the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat even on the allegation of fraud and in the present Case from a plain reading of the plaint it is apparent that the plaintiff-petitioner very technically challenges the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat as such both the Courts below acted legally in rejecting the plaint of the suit.

18. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides at length and .perused the revisional application, affidavit-in-reply dated 27-1-2011, counter affidavits, judgments of two Courts below along with other connected documents as filed therewith. Now, to deal with the submissions of the learned Advocates, let us examine first whether the petitioner as plaintiff filed other Suit No. 238 of 2009, seeking permanent injunction in respect of the property which is subject matter of the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat passed in Artha Rin Suit No. 771 of 2004 as well as Artha Rin Execution Case No. 638 of 2004.

19. To resolve this dispute, we in it necessary to quote hereunder a portion of the plaint which reads as follows:

মনিকৃষ্ণ সেন উক্ত শংকর বসুকে ট্রাষ্টের চেয়ারম্যান মনোনীত করিয়াছিলেন। বিগত ২৮-২-১৯৮৫ ইংতারিখে অকস্মাৎ মস্তিস্কে রক্তক্ষরন হইয়া শংকর বসূ মৃত্যুবরণ করেন এবং উইলের মর্মানুযয়ী নালিশী সম্পত্তি সহ অপরাপর সম্পত্তি ট্রাষ্টের মালিকানায় চলিয়া আসে। তদন্ত ট্রাষ্টের কার্য্যক্রম উক্ত সম্পত্তির আয় দ্বারা পরিচালিত হইয়া আসিতেছে। সম্প্রতি জানা যায় যে, শংকর বসু এবং আরো অন্যান্য ব্যক্তিবর্গ গ্রামীন সমাজ কেন্দ্র নামক একটি এন,জি,ও জন্য অগ্রনী ব্যাংক শিল্প এলাকা শাখা ঢাকা হইতে নালিশী তপশীল বর্নিত সম্পত্তি বন্দক রাখিয়া ঋণ করিয়াছিলেন এবং উক্ত অর্থ পরিশোধিত না হওয়ায় ব্যাংক কর্তৃপক্ষ ঢাকায় মাননীয় অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করিয়া ডিক্রি পাইয়াছেন। এই বিষয়টি ট্রাষ্ট কর্তৃপক্ষসহ এলাকার কেহই জানিতে পারেন নাই। শংকর বসু নালিশী সম্পত্তি কোনভাবেই হস্থান্তর করার অধিকারী ছিলেন না। বাদী ট্রাষ্ট আশংকা করিতেছে যে, একটি ভূমি লোলুপ কিছু ব্যক্তিবর্গ ব্যাংকের সহিত যোগাসাজস করিয়া বেআইনী কাগজপত্র সৃষ্টি করিয়া উক্ত সম্পত্তি আত্বসাৎ করার একটি হীন অপচেষ্টা চালাইতেছে।

20. From a reading of the above quoted averments of the plaint, it transpires that the property as described in the schedule of the plaint is subject matter of the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat

21. Now, let us see the plaint of the Artha Rin Suit No. 771 of 2004 and other connected documents including the judgment and decree of the said Artha Rin Suit as well as orders of Executing Adalat passed in Artha Rin Execution Case No. 638 of 2004. It is found that Agrani Bank, Tejgaon Industrial Area Branch, Dhaka as plaintiff instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 771 of 2004 for realization of its outstanding dues amounting to Taka 60,31,540 as stood on 28-4-2004 against Managing Director of Grameeh Samaj Kendroand others. The suit was decreed ex-parte vide exparte judgment and decree dated 2-9-2004 by the Artha Rin Adalat and thereafter, the decree-holder-Bank put the decree into execution by filing Execution Case No 368 of 2004 in which the mortgaged property was sold in auction to the present opposite party Nos. 1-3 in accordance with law.

22. It is found that the said mortgaged property is the suit property of the present suit of permanent injunction. Now, let us look at the relevant provisions of both the old 'and new Artha Rin Adalat Ain.

23. Section 6 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 reads as follows:

৬। অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের সিদ্ধান্ত চুড়ান্ত। (১) ধারা ৭ এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের কার্য্যধারা, আদেশ, রায় ও ডিক্রী সর্ম্পকে কোন আদালত বা অন্য কোন কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট উথাপন করা যাইবেনা।

(২) উপ-ধারা(১) এ যাহা কিছুই থাকুকনা কেন, কোন অর্থ ঋণ আদালত কর্তৃক বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে প্রদত্ত কোন একতরফা ডিক্রি রদ করার জন্য বিবাদী Code of Civil Procedure, 1908(Act V of 1903)এর Order IX এর rule 13 এর বিধান মোতাবেক আদালতে দরখাস্ত করিতে চাহিলে তাহাকে তাহার বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রিকৃত অর্থের অন্তত: অর্ধেক অর্থ বা উহার সমপরিমান অর্থের ব্যাংক জামানত দরখাস্তের সহিত আদালতে জমা করিতে হইবে এবং উক্তরুপ জমা করা না হইলে তাহার দরখাস্ত গ্রহন যোগ্য হইবে না।”

24. Similar provision has been provided in section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 which reads as follows:

২০। অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের আদেশের চুড়ান্ততা। এই আইনের বিধান ব্যতিরেকে, কোন আদালত বা কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে বিচারাধীন কোন কার্যধারা বা উহার কোন আদেশ, রায় বা ডিক্রীর বিষয়ে কোন প্রশ্ন উথাপন করা যাইবেনা এবং এই আইনের বিধানকে উপেক্ষা করিয়া কোন আদালত বা কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট আবেদন করিয়া কোন প্রতিকার দাবী বা প্রার্থনা করা হইলে, এরুপ আবেদন কোন আদালত বা কর্তৃপক্ষ গ্রাহ্য করিবেনা।

25. From a plain reading of the above quoted provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990/2003 it appears that except the provisions of this Act, no question shall be raised before any Court. or authority about any pending proceeding in the Artha Rin Adalat, or its order, judgment or decree, and if any relief is claimed or prayed before any Court or authority ignoring the provisions or this Act, no Court or authority shall accept any such prayer, the judgment or decree of the Artha Rin Adalat is final and the same cannot be questioned in any other Court under any separate proceeding. In the connection it must bear in mind that the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is special law and the provision provided therein prevails over the general law.

26. Now, the only question for consideration is, whether the trial Court and the lower Appellate Court correctly held that the suit is impliedly barred by section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

27. It appears that the trial Court below on consideration of the materials on record allowed the application for rejection of the plaint stating as follows:

ইহার পর বন্ধকী তপশীল বর্নিত জমি নিলাম কার্য ধারা অর্থঋণ জারী ৬৩৮/০৪ নং মামলার মাধ্যমে চলিত থাকা অবস্থায় প্রমোদ সুন্দরী সেনকল্যান ষ্ট্রাষ্টে রংপুর এর পক্ষে নির্বাহী পরিচালক মো: আ: রহমান বাদী হইয়া ডিক্রিকৃত জমিতে নিজের স্বত্ব দখলজারী করিয়া অর্থ ঋণ আদালতের ডিক্রীকে Challenge করিয়া চিরস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার প্রার্থনায় অত্র অন্য ২৩৮/০৯ নং মোকদ্দমা আনায়ন করেন। যার অর্থ ঋণ আদালত আইন, ২০০৩ এর ২০ ধারা অনুযায়ী বারিত। কাজেই তৎকারনে বাদীর আরজী নাকচ হইবে।

28. The lower Appellate Court in its turn affirmed the above findings of the trial Court.

29. As already noticed that admittedly the property as described in the schedule of the plaint was sold in auction pursuant to the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in Artha Rin Suit No. 771 of 2004. Therefore, it is very difficult on our part to interfere with such concurrent findings sitting under revisional jurisdiction.

30. To meet the main argument of Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the plaintiff-petitioner in his plaint did not mention any case being Artha Rin Suit No. 771 of 2004, no relief was sought for against the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Suit and as such the findings of the trial Court is perverse being contrary to law and facts, we have carefully examined the entire averments of the plaint together with the connected materials on record.

31. We agree with the submission of Mr. Quayum that in deciding the question as to whether the plaint should be rejected the Court may look into the averments made in the plaint and cannot go beyond the same .to find whether the plaint is rejected or not. In this case on a close perusal of the averments of the plaint together with the other materials on record, it appears to us that the plaintiff-petitioner in a very cunning manner disputing the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat under the camouflage of the present suit for permanent injunction being Other Suit No.238 of 2009 seeking permanent injunction in respect of the property which is subject matter of the judgment and decree of Artha Rin Adalat passed in Artha Rin Suit No.771 of 2004. In view of this, we do not find any possible reason to differ with the view taken by the two Courts below.

32. In this connection we may refer to the view of Mr Murshed, CJ as given in the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd. Vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union reported in 18 DLR 709 which reads as follows:

"Turning, now, to the plaint in the present suit, it is obvious, from a mere perusal of the plaint itself, that it must be held the suit is prohibited under, if not by law. This being the position, even if the case does not come, literally and strictly, within the letter of Order 7, rule 11 the Code of Civil Procedure, there cannot be any manner of doubt that the suit is prohibited under the law in the sense that is barred under legal provisions. The Court should, therefore, have rejected the plaint in limine because the suit itself is barred under our legal system. If Order 7, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be prayed in aid, the inherent power of the Court should be invoked."

33. In support of that view Mr Murshed, CJ referred to various decisions and discussed them elaborately.

34. Now, it remains for us to consider the cases cited by Mr Abdul Quayum. On reading of the decisions reported in 7 ADC 291, 56 DLR (AD) 22, 10 BLC (AD) 8 and section 307 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, it seems to us that the principles as enunciated in those decisions as well as the provision of section 307 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

35. Mr Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate at the fag end of the hearing has repeatedly argued before us that after disposing of the execution case the present auction purchasers (opposite party Nos.I-3) threatened the plaintiff-petitioner to vacate the suit property and thereby finding no other way the plaintiff-petitioner in order to save his property filed the present suit.

36. To this, Mr Shamim Khaled Ahmed, the learned Advocate relying on the decision reported in 15 BLT 425 = 12 BLC 723 submits that sub- section 7 of section 33 of the Ain, 2003 envisages vesting of ownership of the property of the judgment-debtor upon the decree-holder and the said vesting of ownership includes delivery of possession of the property, without the delivery of possession, the execution case cannot be disposed of and admittedly, in this case the possession of the suit property has not yet been handed over to the auction on purchasers and as such it cannot be said that the execution case has already been disposed of.

37. To appreciate this last branch of argument, we have carefully examined the provisions of section 33 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 together with the decision reported in 15 BLT 425 = 12 BLC723, it appears to us that unless the possession of the property is handed over to the auction on purchasers, the execution case may not be finally disposed of. Therefore, we find no substance in either of the contentions as raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

<u>38. It is an admitted proposition that the present plaintiff-petitioner did not file any application before the executing Adalat under section 32 of the Ain, 2003 but he has filed the present suit without even approaching before the executing Adalat. The 3rd party petitioners have/had enough scope to file an application before the Artha Rin Adalat by way of filing an objection under section 32 of the Ain, 2003 against the execution of a decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat relating to the property. Therefore, it is clearly found that the plaintiff-petitioner took a wrong way to ventilate his grievances, other than the recourse prescribed by specific provisions governing the issue.</u>

39. The submission made by the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1-3 that the instant suit is misconceived in law and designed to frustrate the execution of the decree appears to have substance.

40. Hence for all these reasons above, the impugned judgments of both the Courts below does not call for any interference. The Rule is, therefore, discharged without any order as to cost

Let a copy of the Judgment along with lower Court's record be sent down at once.

End.

caseno: Writ Petition No. 201 of 1996 with Writ Petition No. 2035 of 1996
lawyer:
Dr Kamal Hossain with AF Hasan Arif, Sara Hossain and Md Ramzan AU Sikder, Advocates- For the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 201 of 1996 Syed Mahmudul Ahsan with Md Salahuddin, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2035 of 1996. 
KS Nabi, Attorney-General; with Kaiseruddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General and Shafiul Bashar Bhandari, Advocate ----- For Respondent No.5 in Writ Petition No. 201 of 1996 and Respondent No. 3 in Writ Petition No. 2035 of 1996 
Zakir Ahmed with Md Oziullah, Iqbal Ahsan Chowdhury and AKM Enayetullah Chowdhury, Advocates ----- For Respondent No.4 in Writ Petition No. 201 of 1996 and Respondent No. 2 in Writ Petition No. 2035 of 1996.
parties:
Nasiruddin Ahmed ------ 
[In WP No. 201 of 1996]
Road Impo ------ Petitioners [In WP No. 2035 of 1996]
vs.
Commissioner of Customs, Chittagong and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Mozammel Houque J: Since in these two writ petitions, namely, Writ Petition No. 201 of 1996 and Writ Petition No. 2035 of 1996 identical questions of law are involved,• these were heard together and are being disposed of by one judgment. 
2. In Writ Petition No. 201 of 1996, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned orders dated 14-1-1996 as endorsed in 17 Bills of Entry vide Annexures- V to V -16 pursuant to impugned Notification being SRO No. 215-Ain/951644/Shulko dated 12-12-95 video  Annexure-U refusing to assess customs duties on the  goods imported by the petitioner on the basis of  Clean Report of Finding (CRF) value vide Annexure- T pursuant to SRO No. 316-Ain/94  /1568/Shulko dated 3-11-94 vide Annexure-A should not be declared to be without lawful authority and  are of no legal effect. Pending hearing of the Rule, the respondents were directed to allow the petitioner to release the reconditioned cars on the basis of payment of duty on CRF value of the goods.  

3. In Writ Petition No. 2035 of 1996, Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned orders dated 6-6-96 vide Annexures-B Series should not be declared to void and without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and as to why the Respondents should not  directed to levy and collect customs duty, VAT and  other charges in respect of the said imported  consignments on the basis of R&F value as declared  by the petitioner. In this case also, pending hearing of the Rule, the respondents were directed to allow the petitioner to release the goods on payment of the duties on the cost and freight (C&F) value. 

4. In Writ Petition No. 201 of 1996, the petitioner stated that he is the sole proprietor of MIs Rising Traders of OR Nizam Road, Chittagong. In pursuance of Notification being SRO No. 316-Ain/94/1568/Sulko dated 3-11-1994, which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary on 5-11-1994, the customs duties were required to be assessed on the imported reconditioned cars on the basis of Clean Report of Finding (CRF as to their quality, quantity and value issued by an approved pre-Shipment Inspection Agent, in short, PSI Agent, enlisted at Appendix-l of the said SRO. The aforesaid SRO dated 3-11-1994 issued under section 25A of the Customs Act 1969 specifically provides that in the event of the Commissioner of Customs failing to approve the CRF, he may refer the matter to the National Board of Revenue, but must in the meantime allow provisional assessment and release of the goods on payment of customs duties on the basis of the value certified by the CRF. The petitioner opened letter of credit on 8-11-95 valued US dollar 32,800 at C&F, Chittagong, issued by the National Credit and Commerce Bank Limited, Khatunganj Branch, Chittagong, for import from Japan of a consignment of 17 units of used vehicles which is peculiarly known as re-conditioned vehicles in accordance with the pro forma invoice dated 1-11-95. The goods were duly shipped/rom Japan under a set of 17 commercial invoices dated 22-11-95 with related bills of lading dated 28-11-95. Prior to the shipment, the goods were duly inspected on 22-11-95 by Bureau Veritas, a duly enlisted PSI Agent, who issued CRF on 11-12-95 in respect of quality, quantity, price and NS Code thereof in compliance with the said SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 issued under section 25A of the Customs Act. 

5. After letter of credit had been opened and the said goods were shipped from Japan, the respondent No. 4 issued a Notification being SRO No. 215-Ain/95/1644/Shulko dated 12-12-95 (which is the impugned notification) which purported to amend SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 by excluding from its  ambit 12 kinds of goods including car/micro- bus/jeep/pick-ups classified under HS Code No. 87'03 and directing that CRF issued by PSI Agent would not be applicable in respect of such goods. The goods of the petitioner arrived at Chittagong Port on 23-12-95 on the vessel Morning Bright and then the petitioner submitted the shipping documents including the bills of entry and CRF to the Customs Authority through his Clearing and Forwarding Agent on 13-1-96 in order to take delivery of goods on payment of customs duties, V AT and other charges thereon on the basis of the CRF value. The petitioner thereafter came to learn that respondent No.2 has issued 17 impugned orders all dated 14-1-96 pursuant-to SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 refusing to allow the petitioners to clear the goods on payment of customs duties on the basis  CRF value and directing that the goods be  examined for the purpose of assessment of customs duties and other charges thereon instead of assessing the same on the basis of the invoice value as certified in the CRF pursuant to SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94. The respondent No. 1 failed to assess customs duties on the goods on the basis of CRF value and to release the same on payment of customs duties by the petitioner pursuant to SRO No: 316 dated 31-11-94. The petitioner then came to learn that respondent No. 2 had directed to assess the duties and taxes on the basis of 'Yellow Book' value instead of CRF value. 

6. It is submitted by the petitioner that the respondents are bound to release the goods on realising the duties on the basis of CRF value in pursuance of SRO No. 316 dated 3•11•94. It is further submitted that the very subsequent SRO No. 215 dated 1'2•12•95 is bad in law in view of the fact that the said amended SRO 215 is ultra vires section 25A of the Customs Act. It is further submitted that in respect of the goods of the present petitioner the SRO No. 215 dated 12•12-95 has no manner of application. This imposition of duties on Yellow Book value is absolutely without jurisdiction in view of the fact that this Yellow Book value has no legal sanction. The petitioner has also taken the ground that the actions of the respondents are violative of the provisions of Articles 27, 31, 40, 42 and 83 of the Constitution. 

7. The respondent Nos. 4 and 5 have filed affidavit-in-opposition and they also filed a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition in this case. In this affidavit-in-opposition the respondents have denied the allegations made by the petitioner in the writ petition. It is their case that in the instant case the duty should be assessed on the Yellow Book value inasmuch as this importation of used cars is out of the ambit of the CRF value. It is their case that there is no illegality in assessing the duties on the basis of Yellow' Book value. By the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition the respondents have annexed several papers and documents in order to show that the customs authority is entitled to assess customs duty on the basis of Yellow Book value. The petitioner also filed an affidavit-in-reply and a supplementary affidavit-in-reply stating that this Yellow Book value has got no legal sanction and, as such, this imposition of the duties upon the petitioner's goods is violative of the provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act. 

8. For our convenience, let us mention some facts which are relevant for the purpose of disposal of this case. Under section 25A of the Customs Act, 1969, the Notification being SRO No. 316-Ain/94/1568/Shulko was issued on 3-11-94' which was published in the Gazette Extraordinary on 5•11•94. When letters of credit were opened on 8•11•95 the aforesaid SRO dated 3•11•94 was in force. The invoice for importing the aforesaid goods were dated 22•11•95. Bills of lading of the goods were dated 28•11•95. CRF was granted by a PSI Agent, namely, Bureau Veritas, on 11•12•95. The amended notification vide SRO No. 215 came into force on 12•12•95. The bills of entry and all other connected papers were submitted to the authorities for releasing the goods on' 13•1-96 and the impugned orders were passed on 14.1•96. 

9. Dr Kamal Hossain and Mr AF Hasan Arif, the learned Advocates, appeared for the petitioner in this case. They submit that the Notification vide SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 was issued under section 25A of the Customs Act and in that Notification, 14 terms and conditions have been incorporated. In that Notification the Appendix-I shows 5 recognised PSI Agents one of whom was Bureau Veritas. The impugned Notification vide SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 shows that the appendix No.2 was amended by which the 12 kinds of goods were brought out from the ambit of Notification vide SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94. It shows that vide this impugned Notification dated 12-12-95 issued under section 25A of the .Customs Act simply these 12 kinds of goods were taken out from imposition of duties on the basis of CRF value. The learned Advocate submits that this Notification is repugnant to section 25A of the Customs Act and the earlier Notification dated 3-11-94.

10. Section 25A of the Customs Act as stood on 30th June, 1955, runs as follows: "25A. Assessment on the basis of certificate issued by pre-shipment inspection agencies: Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, declare that the quality, quantity, price and customs classification of goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment inspection agency will be accepted as the basis of assessment. Explanation-For the purpose of this section, "price" shall mean the normal price and (2) of section 25." The SRO 316 dated 3.11.94 was issued by the authority in pursuance of section 25A of the Customs Act. The amendment of the aforesaid SRO was also made by the self-same authority vide SRO No. 215 dated 12•12•95 in pursuance of the this amended SRO dated 12•12•95 authority only provisions of section 25A of the Customs Act. By amended the Appendix•2 and by that amendment provision was made to the effect that the 12 kinds of goods when the same will be imported, will not be subject to payment of customs duties on the basis of CRF value. So, the authority which issued the SRO dated 3•11•94 also amended the aforesaid SRO vide issuing another SRO No. 215 dated 12•12•95 under section 25A of the said Act. As such, we do not find any reason as to why this amended Notification dated 12•12•95 should be called ultra vires section 25A of 
11. The learned Advocates for the petitioner submit that when the letters of credit were opened on 8•11•95, invoices were issued on 22•11•95, bills of lading were issued on 28•11•95 and CRF was granted on 11•12•95, the previous SRO dated 3•11•94 was in force. As soon as the CRF was granted on 11•12•95 the vested right was created in favour of the petitioner to get the goods released on payment of duties on the CRF value. They submit that since the amendment was made vide SRO dated 12•12•95, the same will not be applicable in the case of the petitioner in view of the fact that the CRF was granted on 11•12•95 which was one day earlier of the amended Notification dated 12•12•95. Since before the subsequent Notification dated 12•12•95 came into force, the right of the petitioner was accrued on 11•12•95 and, as such, this amended Notification dated 12•12•95 has no manner of application in the case of the petitioner. 

12. The learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that section 2SA of the Customs Act will have independent application in view of the fact that non-obstante clause has been added• in that section itself. Since the provisions of section 2SA are completely and independently applicable in the matter of importing goods as covered under CRF, there is no option of the authority but to release the goods on imposing duty upon the CRF value. Since in the instant case by Gazette notification the PSI Agent has been appointed and upto the date of the  certificate granted by PSI Agent, the SRO No.315  dated 3•11•94 was in force, and as such, the respondents are under legal obligation to release the goods on the basis of imposition of duty upon CRF value. 

13. Mr KS Nabi, learned Attorney General, and Mr Zakir Ahmed, the learned Advocate (as he was),appeared on behalf of the respondent Nos 5 and 4 respectively. It is their submission that by the Finance Act No. 12 of 1995 dated 30th June, 1995 an explanation was added to section 25A of the Customs Act which runs as follows: "For the purposes of this section, 'price' shall mean the normal price determined in accordance with sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 25." The learned Advocates for the respondents submit that as soon as this explanation was added by an amendment dated 30th'June, 1995, section 2SA lost its original independent character in view of the fact that henceforth this section 25A must be read along with section 25( 1) and (2) of the Customs Act. They further submit that if we read section 25, we are required to read the same along with section 30 of the Act in order to ascertain the normal price of the goods; They further submit that now the position is that this section25A must be read along with section 25, 30 and 30A of the Customs Act. So, if we read now the section 25A along with the explanation together with the provisions of sections 25, 30 and 30A of the Customs Act, it appears to us that the normal price should be determined on the imported goods following the provisions of section 25, 30 and 30A of the ACL.

14. Two writ petitions, namely, Writ Petition No. 4337 of 1996 and Writ Petition No. 4336 of 1996 were heard and disposed of by this Bench on 17 -12-96 wherein this Court discharged the aforesaid two Rules. In that Judgment, this Court discussed different provisions of the Customs Act as well as some authorities and held that the price of the goods, prevailing or in force at the time of submission of bill of entry to the authority will be the basis for imposition of customs duty for the goods. In the instant case we also hold that the section 25A with explanation shall be read along with sections 25, 30 and 30A of the Customs Act and the customs duty will be imposed upon the value of the goods prevailing or in force at the time when the bill of entry along will other papers will be submitted to the authorities. Since in the instant case the bills of entry were submitted to the authority for clearance of the goods on 13-1-96, the petitioner shall have to pay the customs duties on the basis of the price of the goods fixed by the authority then prevailing that is on 13-1-96. 

15. Dr Kamal Hossain submits that CRF was granted on 11-12-95 and on that day the right of the present petitioner was accrued to get the goods released on paying customs duty on the basis of CRF value. It is difficult for us to accept the above contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

16. In support of the contentions that the importer will have to pay the duties on the value of the goods at the rate prevailing on the date of submission of bill of entry, the learned Advocate for the respondents have referred to several decisions in the cases of Glaxo Laboratories vs. A V Venkateswaran, AIR 1959 (Born) 372, Sharaf Faridi vs. Federation of Pakistan, PLD 1989 (Kar) 457, 621, Shah Devchand vs. Union of India, AIR 1991 (SC) 1931,764, Ramkrishna Theatres Ltd. vs. GI & C Corporation, AIR 1993 (Kerala) TC 98, Bharat Surfactant (Pv.) Ltd vs. Union of India, AIR 1989 (SC) 2059), Afgan Commercial Co vs. Union of India, AIR 1953 (Punj) 225, Public Prosecutor vs. Venkata Reddy, AIR 1961 (Andaw) 107, Kuwait Flour Mills Co vs. MV Kashmir, PW 1989 (Har) 60 end Assistant Controller of Customs and 3 others vs. Messrs Link Engineering Company Ltd. 1989 SCMR 1698. In our recent judgment this Bench also held the similar view following other decisions to the effect that the importers are liable to pay customs duties on the basis of the value of the goods which is in force on the day when the bill of entry is produced before the authority. So, we do not find any substance in the submissions of the learned Advocates for the petitioner. 

17. In the Writ application at paragraph 12 it is stated by the petitioner that the authorities arbitrarily directed to pay the customs duties on the basis of Yellow Book value instead of CRF value. In reply to the statement made in paragraph 12 of the writ petition, it is stated by the Respondent Nos. 4 in paragraph 10 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the customs duties 0:1 the imported cars was not assessed on the basis of CRF value because the CRF had already been withdrawn from the imported goods in question by SRO dated 12-12-95 and respondent No.2 had correctly and lawfully directed to assess the duties and taxes on the basis of Yellow Book value. It is further stated that this Yellow Book value has a basis and standard having authentic value of the goods in question as determined by the manufacturers' Association of Japan, a semi- government organization, with high credibility and standard in the country as well as other importing countries. When the bill of entry was submitted in the instant case on 13-1-96 the importer is required to pay the customs duty on the basis of the Yellow Book value which was in force at that time. 

18. The learned Advocates for the petitioner have vehemently challenged the imposition of the duties on the basis of Yellow Book value. It is their case that this Yellow Book has no legal sanction. It is neither a rule nor any notification nor any regulation under any authority of law of this country. Since this Yellow Book is neither any Act nor any Ordinance nor any Rule nor any Regulation in any manner whatsoever, imposition of the duties on the basis of such Yellow Book is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction. Not only that, it offends Article 83 of the Constitution. It is further submitted that without passing any law by the Parliament or by any other delegated authority, no Rule or Regulation can be made for imposition of duties and taxes upon any person. As such, this Yellow Book value has no legal basis. 

19. The learned Advocates for the respondents have produced before us a booklet named 'Yellow Book' from which they wanted to show the price of cars which were given by the manufacturers of different companies with regard to different kinds of motor vehicles manufactured in Japan. It is the case of the Respondents that the dishonest business people of the country with malafide intention to deprive the Government of having actual customs duties, in connivance with the foreign exporters and corrupt officers used to show the lesser value of the goods in their invoices so that they are required to pay customs duties in Bangladesh at a lesser rate. In order to stop this corrupt practice of these unscrupulous businessmen and also for the interest of the country, Government brought this booklet from Japan, namely, Yellow Book wherein the HS Codes of different cars with the prices have been incorporated. The authority, on the basis of such price of the different imported goods shown by the manufacturers in the Yellow Book used to impose the customs duties here, although in the invoices, the importers used to show the lesser price of the imported goods. In such a manner the customs authorities tried to stop mal-practice of the dishonest importers who used to deprive the country of having real and actual customs duties on the goods imported. 

20. In the supplementary affidavit given by respondent Nos. 4 and 5 dated 30-1-97 Annexure-2 shows that it was translation of JAAI's Yellow Book/Silver Book given by JETRO, means, Japan External Trade Organization, Official Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of International Trade and Industry. In this Annexure the retail price and whole-sale price of different manufactured vehicles have been given. In this Annexure-2 it is further stated that all the prices are shown in this Yellow Book in the unit of 1,000 Yen. It appears to us that the first cover of this booklet is of yellow color and that is why it is popularly know as Yellow Book. In fact, it is a booklet where the manufacturers of different cars and vehicles of Japan have given the manufacturing prices of the imported cars and vehicles which the customs authority has been following since 1993. 

21. It is submitted by the learned Advocates for the respondents that this Yellow Book is being used and followed since 1989 in respect of imposing duties on imported motor vehicles. Not only in this country, but also in other importing countries prices contained in this book are being followed. From Annexure-A(I) of this supplementary affidavit- in-opposition \ dated 30-1-79 it appears that the respondent No.4, namely, National Board of Revenue, issued a Standing Order on 9th June, 1994 vide Memo No. 1557/94/Cus in respect of imposing duties with regard to the imported re-conditioned cars and this Standing Order refers to section 30 of the Customs Act. From this Annexure-l(l) of the' supplementary affidavit-in-opposition it appears that imposition of duties upon motor vehicles on the basis of this Yellow Book in our country is being followed from 1993 and on 10th June, 1993 the First Standing Order was issued vide Memo No. 1514/93 Cus by NBR for imposing customs duties upon the imported re-conditioned cars after deducting the depreciation value. Then again another Standing Order was issued on 29th January, 1996 vide Memo No. 1653/96/Cus amending the earlier Standing Order dated 9th June, 1994. The rate of depreciation has also been shown in it and it appears that this Standing Order was issued by the National Board of Revenue for imposition of duties upon the imported goods, namely, reconditioned motor vehicles on the basis of the prices as given by the manufacturers from the exporting country. This Standing Order was modified by issuing another Standing Order on 29th1 January, 1996 and a chart has also been given showing as to how the depreciation value will be determined. The depreciation at any rate will not go above 60M. From this Standing Order it shows as to how the prices would be determined on the basis of the price given by the manufacturers and as to how the importers of this country will have to pay the import duties on the value.

22. The learned Advocates for the respondents submit that though there is no mentioning of any section of the Customs Act, yet in pursuance of sections 25 and 30 of the Customs Act the National Board of Revenue is competent to issue such Standing Order for fixation of price upon which duty is to be imposed. So, it appears that the respondents had not arbitrarily or suddenly imposed duties upon the re-conditioned vehicles on the basis of this Yellow Book, but this has been followed in our country since 1993. Further, it cannot be said to be arbitrary in view of the fact that this Yellow Book was procured from Japan External Trade Organisation, an Official Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of International' Trade and Industry and this is being used since 1993 and in the meantime hundreds of importers had paid their duties on the basis of this Yellow Book and the Government have been realising the duties upon the re-conditioned imported motor vehicles on the basis of this Yellow Book price from the importers.

23. In view of the above, the learned Advocates for the respondents submit that this imposition of duty upon the Yellow Book price of the imported re-conditioned cars and vehicles cannot be said to be illegal or arbitrary. It is their case that to fix such a duty on the price of the Yellow Book value is to stop the manipulation of the dishonest businessmen inasmuch as previously it appeared to the Government that the dishonest business people with a view to deprive the country of actual import duties on re-conditioned cars and vehicles used to show lesser prices in the invoices and bills of lading and in this way the Government was deprived of having the actual and real customs duties from the importers of re-conditioned cars and vehicles. It is their further case that only to save the country from being deprived of such huge amount of customs duties the Government has been following the imposed duty on Yellow Book price with reasonable depreciation so that the importers cannot deprive the Government of the usual duties which the dishonest business people did showing lesser value in their invoices and bills of lading. The booklet viz, the Yellow Book was produced before this Court. In that Yellow Book the prices of the cars and vehicles are written both in Japanese language and English language, particularly, the names, code numbers and prices are given in English language. As such, it cannot be said that there is no existence of any book called Yellow Book or that it has no legal existence. The aforesaid Standing Order of the National Board of Revenue relied upon this Yellow Book for the purpose of imposing customs duties upon used cars and vehicles imported from abroad and such Standing Order recognising the Yellow Book is being followed. From Annexure-I (1) of the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition it appears clearly that on 10th June, 1993, first Standing Order was issued with regard to the imposition of duties upon re-conditioned cars and vehicles and subsequently it was amended from time to time. Not only that the National Board of Revenue also has given a guideline in the Standing Order itself as to how and at what per cent the depreciation prices will be determined and allowed and also it shows that under section 30 of the Customs Act when the bill of entry will be produced, the new exchange rate will be applicable for the goods prevailing on that day. 

24. Further, the Annexure-I of that supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 30-1-96 also has given a guideline as regards depreciation and the money exchange rate when the bill of entry will be produced under section 30 of the Act. Since the Board of Revenue issued the Standing Order with respect to imposition of duties upon the used re-conditioned cars and vehicles on the basis of this Yellow Book from 1993 and since it is being used from that day till now and since hundreds of importers had already paid the customs duties on the basis of the Yellow Book value and the Government had already realised the duties from those business people on that basis and since nobody challenged such imposition of duties earlier and since it is being followed in our country, we are of the view that it cannot be said that the imposition of customs duties on the Yellow Book value for the imported re-conditioned cars and vehicles from abroad is illegal and without jurisdiction. In our view, in order to save the country from being deprived of getting legal and usual customs duties on the re-conditioned cars and vehicles from abroad and also in order to protect the interest of the country from the hands of unscrupulous and dishonest businessmen the Government had to take resort to this policy of imposing customs duties on the basis of Yellow Book value. So it cannot be said that such an action of the authorities is illegal and without jurisdiction, rather we hold that this is being done and followed for the greater interest of the country. 

25. In this connection it may be mentioned that if all the business' people or importers pay the import duties on the basis of Yellow Book, they will not be prejudiced in any manner whatsoever in view of the fact that whatever duties they will pay to the Government will be included in the real price of the goods concerned and when the importers will sell the goods to the customers, they will sell it at the price including the customs duty. As soon as duty of any kind is paid upon the goods it is merged with the price of the goods. So, the importers of the cars will not be prejudiced in any manner whatsoever if they pay the import duties on the basis of Yellow Book value. In several judicial pronouncements including judgment passed in Writ Petition No.4337 of 1996 and Writ Petition No.4336 of 1996, it had been held that importers will have to pay the duties on the price which is prevailing at the time when bill of entry is submitted If, according to the rate of duty imposed by the Government on the date of submission of the bill of entry the importers pay the duties, it will not cause any prejudice to the importers inasmuch as whatever customs duty they are required to pay to the authority, it will be merged with the price of the goods imported. This will, in fact, in our opinion, save the interest of the country from the hand of dishonest business people. We are also of the view that the Standing Orders issued by the National Board of Revenue from time to time are actually reasonable in view of the fact that the same have given the guideline as well as the rates for imposition of import duties on the re-conditioned cars and vehicles with the chart of the depreciation. In the supplementary affidavit dated 30-1-97 Annexure-2 shows that the booklet, namely, JAAI's Yellow Book/Silver Book was obtained by the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry, Federation Bhaban, Motijheel, Dhaka, from JETRO as stated above. This Yellow Book December, 1996 Edition, was sent by JETRO

26. Today before delivering judgment Dr. Kamal Hossain has submitted a supplementary affidavit-in-reply on behalf of the petitioner to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition dated 2-2-97 filed by respondent Nos. 4 and 5. In this supplementary affidavit-in-reply it is again stated that this Yellow Book has got no legal force as it cannot be treated as law in this country. In this supplementary affidavit-in-reply it is stated that this Yellow Book has got on legal force as it cannot be treated as low in this country. In this supplementary affidavit-in-replay it is stated that this translation extract from the Yellow book and silver Book is incorrect and misleading and malafide. It is Slated further that the petitioner contacted the office of the JETRO and one Mr. Kabir of JETRO confirmed the petitioner 'over telephone' that JETRO does not have any expert and they did not translate the Yellow Book into English, but they arrange to translate the same from elsewhere. Mr. Kabir further confirmed the petitioner that JETRO typed the translated pages on their letter head only and supplied the same under the signature of their own people. Mr. Kabir of JETRO further confirmed the petitioner that the translation of Yellow Book is not a complete translation of the Yellow Book and Silver Book, but the same was only a summary of the Yellow Book. From this paragraph 6 of this supplementary affidavit-in-reply it appears that in a sense Mr Kabir of JETRO had confirmed the existence of Yellow Book and Silver Book. Further, Annexure-2 of the supplementary affidavit shows that this book was procured by the Secretary, Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry, but the petitioner had confirmed the authenticity of this Yellow Book from one Mr. Kabir of JETRO over telephone, but nothing on paper or anything else. Even then Mr. Kabir also admitted the existence of this Yellow Book. So, we do not find any substance in the allegation as made in this supplementary affidavit-in-reply dated 26-2-97. In view of the submissions made by the learned Advocates and also our discussion as made above we do not find any substance in the contentions of the learned Advocates for the petitioner. 

 27. With regard to Writ Petition No.2035 of 1996 it appears that the customs duty has been imposed upon the Yellow Book value of the re-conditioned vehicles but not upon invoice value of the goods. In this writ petition the order dated 6-6-96 has been challenged by which it has been directed that the duties should be realised upon the Yellow Book value and not upon the invoice value. The learned Advocate Mr Syed Mahrnudul Ahsan, appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that the assessment of customs duty on the basis of Yellow Book is illegal and without jurisdiction. He submitted that the duties upon the re-conditioned motor vehicles ought to have been imposed upon C & F value which is the invoice value. In this case the letter of credit was opened on 22-4-96 and subsequently the vehicles arrived at Chittagong Port. But it appeared that on 12-12-95 the earlier SRO was amended and the customs duty was imposed upon the re-conditioned motor vehicles in pursuance of SRO dated 12-12-95. So, in this case there should not be any doubt about the imposition of customs duty on the basis of the Yellow Book value inasmuch as by the subsequent SRO dated 12-12-95 the cars and vehicles were taken out from the Appendix-2 of the earlier Notification dated 3-1-94. Now, upon his submission as regards the illegality of imposition of duty on the basis of Yellow Book value we need not give any further explanation inasmuch as we have already given our decision above in Writ Petition No.201 of 1996. The instant case is fully covered by the Yellow Book and, as such, our findings above with regard to Yellow Book value are fully applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case and no new explanation is necessary. In the writ petition he has challenged Annexure-D which is the subsequent SRO dated 12-12-95. With regard to this Notification we have given our reasoning’s and findings above and, as such, we do not find anything new in his submissions. For this reason we hold that no illegality was committed by the authority concerned by imposing duties on the basis of Yellow Book value. So, the contentions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner have got no substance.

28. Section 219 of the Customs Act provides that the National Board of Revenue may by notification in official Gazette make Rules for carrying out the purposes of the Customs Act. This Act came into force in the year 1969 and this is 1997 and for this long period of about 27 years the Government or the National Board of Revenue remained silent without framing any Rule whatsoever with regard to the import and export of the goods as covered under this Customs Act. This import-and export of goods is not a temporary affair for a particular period. In every year this country exports goods to foreign countries and imports goods from abroad. In order to facilitate the import and export of the goods and to give proper guideline for such importation and exportation and also to save the interest of the country from the hands of dishonest businessmen and corrupt officers of the Government the authority ought to have framed rules for realisation of duties upon the imported and exported goods under this Act 

29. This period of 27 years is more than a reasonable period. It is not that the period of six months or one year or two years or five years has passed from the date .of promulgation of Customs Act. This period of 27 years is sufficiently reasonable period during which the authority ought to have framed rules for greater economic interest of the country, but the Government as well as the National Board of Revenue slept over the matter for such a long period without any reason whatsoever. Had there been the relevant Rules for realisation of duties upon import and export of the goods under the Customs Act, country would have been saved from the curse of malpractice of the dishonest businessmen and corrupt officers in the matter of evading duties upon the goods exported and imported. Since there are no specific rules, it has given opportunities to the dishonest people to do corrupt practice and by this corrupt practice they are depriving the country of having its economic interest in the matter of imposition of duties upon the goods which are exported abroad and imported from foreign countries. We do not find any explanation as to why the authorities remained silent over this matter for such an unusually long period. It is reported that in the neighboring country namely, India, relevant rules of Customs Act have already been framed for the import and export of goods. So, it is desirable that the Government and the National Board of Revenue should frame necessary rules for imposition of duties upon the goods which are imported and exported under this Customs Act and if it is not done, the country will suffer more and more so far its economic interest is concerned. 

30. In Writ Petition No.5722 of 1996 the petitioner has annexed several newspaper cuttings one is the Daily Ittefaq dated 17-11-1996 Annexure-F. the Daily Purbokon, Chittagong dated 17th July, 1996, Annexure-F(l), the Daily Star dated 5-11-96 Annexure-F(2), the Weekly Nastra dated 31 October to 6 November, 1996 Annexure-F (3) and the daily Ittefaq dated 12-11-96 Annexure-F (4). In this Annexure-F (4) the news with the caption 

রীটের কারনে সরকার বিপুল রাজস্ব হারাইতেছে- অর্থ মন্ত্রী।” In this report the Finance Minister Mr S A M. S Kibria, in reply to an attention notice, stated that m the High Court Division  1276 writ pennons have been filed  which, in fact, creates difficulty to realise the duties from the importers. Some fake importers giving false .addresses imported goods from abroad and they released their goods after filing writ petitions in the High Court Division and as are suit there is apprehension that the rate of realisation of national revenue will not be fulfilled Several writ petitions were filed which are still pending, no doubt. But as soon as a few writ petitions were filed before this Court, the Government as well as National Board of Revenue ought to have come forward and try to get the matter heard and disposed of by this Court. But, unfortunately, no step was taken either from the side of the Government of from the National Board of Revenue. In many of the cases till today the Government or the National Board of Revenue have not yet filed the affidavit-in-opposition and taken any step for early disposal of these cases. 

31. At the insistence of this Court only two cases on tariff value were disposed of by a Judgment passed 10 Writ Petition NosA337 of 1-96 and 4336 of 1996 on 17-12-96. From the aforesaid newspaper report it appears to us that the Finance Minister made, some indication blaming the Court that because of the interim orders passed by the High Court Division in those writ petitions, country is going to suffer huge financial loss. In this connection it may not be irrelevant to mention that the relevant authorities were in deep sleep for an unusually long period and 'after about 27 years on one fine morning they' suddenly woke up from slumber and discovered that because of several writ petitions the Government is going to incur huge financial loss. But they failed to understand that, for non-framing of Rules, how many hundreds of crores  of money the country had already suffered loss during this long period of 27 years. If the relevant Rules are not framed this Customs Department will remain as unscrupulous businessmen and corrupt officers' paradise. When the petitioners come before this Court and prima facie show some irregularity and illegality, this Court cannot but interfere with those matters. But as soon as a few writ petitions were filed and petitioners obtained favourable release of goods from this Court, the Government as well as National Board of Revenue ought to have come forward for settling the matters by Court immediately. But they remained silent for long.

32. Further, we are drawing the notice of the  Government to consider as to why and how the Government and National Board of Revenue sat over  the matter for last 27 years without framing the Rules as require under section 219 of the Customs Act This section was added not to beautify the Customs Act, but It most have some definite purpose and the purpose IS that the relevant Rules ought to have been framed as early as possible so that the dishonest businessmen in connivance with the Corrupt Officers may not indulge into unholy alliance of depriving the State of its legal duties upon the imported goods. Such sitting over of the matter for about 27 years and the laches of the Government and .the Board o~ Revenue are totally disapproved by this Court. Taking advantage of such laches the dishonest businessmen in connivance with the corrupt officers are getting opportunity to cause huge financial loss to Public Exchequer. So, it is desired by this Court that both the Government and National Board of Revenue to make laws and rules for imposing duties upon the goods which are exported and imported so that the interest of the country may not suffer any more in future. 

33. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that these two writ petitions have got no. substance and, as such, the Rules are liable to be discharged. In the result, these Rules issued in these two Writ Petition Nos.201 of 1996 and 2035 of 1996 are discharged without any order as to cost. Let a copy of this judgment be sent to Mr Shah MAS Kibria the Finance Minister of Bangladesh and also to the Chairman. National Board of Revenue for information and necessary action. 

Petitioners of both the "Writ Petitions are directed to pay the balance duty immediately and the respondents are at liberty to realise the balance duty from the petitioners in accordance with law. 

End.

lawyer:
Amir Hossain with Farzana Hoque, Advocates ------ For the Appellants
Abdul Kuddus Mia, Advocate ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Mayurer Nessa and others ------ Appellants
vs
Julekha Khatoon and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment: This appeal by the contesting defendant Nos. 1 and 8 is against judgment and decree dated 26.9.1972 passed by the Addl. District Judge, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 95 of 1967 affirming the judgment and decree dated 18.3.1967 passed by Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Comilia in Title Suit No. 69 of 1965. 2. Respondent Nos. 1-14 as plaintiffs filed the aforesaid suit of partition of the suit property claiming plaintiffs’ No. 1-13 as heirs of one of the recorded tenant Rahmat Ali whose name was recorded in the CS Khatian Ext. 2 as owner of 0.08 annas share of the jote. According to the plaintiffs, plaintiff No. 14 is the purchaser from the plaintiff No. 2. The plaintiffs claimed that other recorded tenant of the suit kharian was Alabuddin, predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 1-19, and defendant Nos. 20-23 are purchasers from the said defendants. Plaintiffs claimed partition On the ground that there was no partition by metes and bounds and taking advantage of wrong entry regarding possession in the CS khatian the defendants had been disturbing their possession. On such allegations plaintiff filed the suit on 27.1.63. 3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 8 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying material allegations and stating that the suit property originally belonged to their predecessor Alabuddin who took lease of the same from the landlord on tile basis of kabuliyat and patta from the landlord Gouri Pria Debi at an annual jama of Taka 16.00 and as the taluk of Gouripria Debi was purchased by Nabin Chandra Chakraborty said Alabuddin executed a kabuliyat in favour of the purchaser landlord who also executed a paua in his favour on 24th Kartick, 1310 BS Ext. 'A'. Since then Alabuddin was in possession of the entire suit property. Further case of the defendants was that the said Alabuddin had a brother named Sona Guzi who married mother of plaintiffs predecessor Rahmat Ali who came to the house of Sona Gazi and after the death of Sonagazi and his 2nd wife out of compassion Alabuddin allowed Rahmat Ali to possess the Suit plot Nos.160, 224 and 226. Taking advantage of old age and ignorance of Alabuddin the said Rahmat Ali during the CS operation wrongly recorded 0.08 annas share of the suit land in the suit khatian though he had no title in the suit property. Further case of the contesting defendants is that Yusuf Ali and Jinnat Ali, two sons of Alabuddin while in title and possession of the suit land executed a confirmatory kabuliyat in favour of landlord, Nabin Chakraborty on 4th Agrahayan 1331 BS and got a paua on the same date from the said landlord Ext. A(1) and since then they are in possession of the entire suit land except those three suit plots on payment of rents from before CS khatian in the name of Alabuddin and his heirs vide Ext. 'B' series. Their further case is that sons of Rahmat Ali relinquished possession of plot Nos. 224 and 226 in favour of Ishab Ali and Jinnat Ali after taking settlement of some land from them by a kabuliyat dated 3rd Chaitra, 1330 BS Ext. C. Their further case is that Alabuddin and after his death his heirs paid rent of the suit property to the landlord. 4. On consideration of the evidence on record trial Court found that Rahmat Ali had 8 annas share in the suit land and decreed the suit for partition of 8 annas share in favour of the plaintiff in preliminary form of the entire suit property excepting plot No. 238. Court of appeal below affirmed the aforesaid finding of the trial Court. 5. Mr. Amir Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, submitted that both the Courts below failed to hold that the presumption of correctness of the entry in the CS khatian Ext. 2 recording 8 annas share in favour of plaintiffs' predecessor Rahmat Ali was rebutted by the paua Ext. 'A' registered on 16.11.1903 long before the preparation of CS khatian Ext. 2 and the payment of rents alone by Alabuddin. 6. It appears that trial Court found that Alabuddin had 8 annas share and Rahmat Ali had 8 annas share in the suit tenancy although the original patta stood in the name of Alabuddin alone and that Rahmat Ali was in possession of about half of the tenancy. On the other hand Court of appeal below found that Alabuddin took lease on his own behalf and on behalf of his nephew Rahmat Ali and the plaintiffs have possession in the suit land. But none, of the Courts below found in which suit plots plaintiffs have exclusive or joint possession. It is not denied that only plot Nos. 160, 224 and 226 having an area of 50 acres were recorded in exclusive possession of plaintiffs' predecessor Rahmat Ali in the CS khatian Ext. 2 and other 10 plots except homestead plot No. 224 were recorded in exclusive possession of defendants predeceassor Alabuddin in the said khatian. Though the plaintiffs stated in para 7 of the plaint that Alabuddin and Rahmat Ali possessed the suit land in equal share and entry regarding exclusive possession in the CS khatian was wrong they did not state in which other plots they had possession. Plaintiffs adduced evidence to the effect that before compromise they possessed 7/8 plots and after compromise they possess 5 plots but none of the PWs could say in which plots plaintiffs possessed before compromise. Trial Court without considering the presumption of entry regarding possession in the CS khatian, failure of the PWs to state the plot numbers in which plaintiffs had possession and reliability of the PWs erroneously opined that plaintiffs previously possessed 7/8 plots. If the entry in the CS khatian Ext. 2 regarding share of plaintiffs' predecessor Rahmat Ali and defendants' predecessor Alabuddin is found to be correct the entry regarding exclusive possession of the said two persons cannot be found to be incorrect. As a matter of fact none of the Courts below specifically found the said entry regarding exclusive possession in the said CS khatian to be wrong or incorrect. I do not find any illegality in the finding of the Courts below regarding share of the parties in the suit property as recorded in the CS khatian inasmuch as both the Courts below considered the patta Ext. A and rent receipts Ext. B series in the name of Alabuddin along with other evidence on record for arriving at the said finding. But I fail to agree with the finding of the Courts below regarding possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land as the same suffers from non-consideration of material evidence on record and presumption arising from entry in the CS Khatian. 7. CS khatian Ext. 2 clearly shows that except homestead plot No. 234 all other plots were recorded in exclusive possession of the said Alabuddin and Rahmat Ali respectively. From the same it is clear that long before the CS operation they possessed the suit plots except plot No. 234 separately and exclusively and homestead plot No. 234 was only in their ejmali possession. From their above conduct it can easily be inferred that there was amicable partition between them in respect of those plots recorded in their respective exclusive possession. When CS khatian records a jote in the name of several persons having distinct share therein but the lands are recorded in exclusive possession of the respective co-sharers then there remains nothing to partition the lands unless the entry regarding exclusive possession is found to be wrong and incorrect. Had the entry regarding exclusive possession in the CS khatian been wrong Rahmat Ali or his heirs would not have remained silent for about fifty years from the date of final publication of the CS khatian. Such exclusive possession of a party in the land for a long period should not be easily disturbed on the flimsy allegation of a co-sharer in the jote unless he can prove by evidence that presumption of correctness of such entry is erroneous. 8. It appears from judgment of the trial Court that the suit was decreed on compromise between the plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 12-17 on 4.3.61 and ex parte against the rest and subsequently appellants filed a Miscellaneous Case and got the decree set aside on 27.3.65 and thereafter they contested the suit and lost upto the Court of appeal below. The compromising defendants being male descendants of Alabuddin at the earliest opportunity compromised the suit with the plaintiffs by giving up their possession in same plots in favour of the plaintiffs in consideration of their relinquishing some share in the suit property in favour of defendants to avoid litigation and protect their possession in other plots in spite of their exclusive possession in 10 plots and even after setting aside of the ex parte decree they neither contested the suit nor disowned the compromise. Plaintiff No. 1 Kala Mia deposing as PW 1 stated that according to the terms of that compromise plaintiffs gave up possession of some lands and they are in possession of the remaining land. PW 2 also supported PW 1 as to plaintiffs' possession of 1.52 acres of land in plot Nos. 160, 161, 320, 367 and 400 in terms of compromise. It appears from joint petition of compromise dated 4.3.64 filed by the plaintiffs and aforesaid defendant Nos. 2, 3, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17 that the plaintiffs were given in possession in the aforesaid five plots having an area of 1.52 acres and they were allowed decree in 76/23 share of the suit property and they abandoned their claim in the rest of the suit property in favour of compromising defendants. Since none of the compromising parties abandoned the said compromise it is difficult to understand why the Courts below did not consider the same while passing the impugned judgment and decree. 9. Order 23 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that at any time after institution of the suit plaintiffs may as against all or any of the defendants withdraw his suit or abandon any part of his claim. Plaintiffs having abandoned their claim in respect of part of the suit property in the said petition of compromise effected at the intervention of relations and well-wishers of the parties and village matbars they cannot get a decree as claimed in the plaint in respect of 8 annas share of the suit property. None of the village Matbars came to support plaintiffs' claim of possession in 7/8 plots before the said compromise. From the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 it transpires that the said compromise was acted upon between compromising parties. Had the contesting defendants’ appellants been successful in dislodging the claim of the plaintiffs and establishing their claim that defendants were thel6 annas owners of the suit property then the compromise could not be considered and given effect to. But the defendant appellants having failed to establish that their predecessor Alabuddin was 16 annas owner of the suit property, male decendants of Alabuddin who are residents of the suit village could not be deprived of the benefit of the compromise acted upon between the compromising parties for the mere fancy and folly of non-resident female decendants of Alabuddin who never actually possessed any part of the suit property. 10. Partition is an equitable relief. Compromising defendants having given up their possession in favour of the plaintiffs in some of the suit plots in consideration of plaintiffs' relinquishing some portion of their share in the suit property in favour of the defendants and the same having been acted upon the plaintiffs are estopped from giving a go by to the same to the prejudice of the said defendants. 11. In the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case I find that decision of the Courts below is contrary to law in not giving effect to the compromise effected between the plaintiffs and non-contesting defendants though acted upon by those parties. 12. In view of the above I find substance in this appeal not on the ground as taken by the appellants but on the ground that the plaintiffs are estopped from claiming 8 annas share giving a go by to the compromise acted upon between the compromising parties. In the result, the appeal is allowed in part without cost and the judgments and decrees of the Courts below are modified and the suit is decreed in part in preliminary form in terms of compromise petition dated 4.3.1964. End.
