case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 8-6-2011 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3070 of 2010).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 8-6-2011 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3070 of 2010 discharging the Rule and affirming the judgment and decree dated 5-4-2010 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Sixth Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 07 of 2009 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 28-6-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 234 of 2003 dismissing the same.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this appeal, in brief, are:

Al-haj Md Serajuddin as the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. (number not stated) of 1998 renumbered as Title Suit No. 234 of 2003 in the Additional Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka praying for declaration of title and recovery of khash possession on removing the construction standing on the suit property. His case, in short, is that he purchased the land of 'Ka' schedule to the plaint with two storied building, garage, different plants situated on SA Dag No. 10 of Mouza-Kakrail under previous Lalbagh Police Station now Ramna within Dhaka Collector ate from Syed Farooq Mirja, son of Syed Fakrul Hasan Mirja in 1971. After purchase, the plaintiff got his name mutated and had been paying taxes regularly. While the plaintiff was abroad, the 'Ka' schedule was wrongly declared abandoned property. Having come to know of the aforesaid fact, the plaintiff filed an application to the Government of Bangladesh and the Government having been satisfied released the suit property in favour of the plaintiff and issued memo dated 19-6-1983 from the office of defendant No. 3 but defendant No. 1 did not return the land shown in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint. Consequently, the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 53 of 1988 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Fourth Court, Dhaka, which was decreed on 17-12-1988. After that, the plaintiff requested defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to deliver 'Kha' schedule land to him on a number of dates from 26-3-1989 up to 3-5-1997 and lastly, on 8-7-1997 but defendant No. 1 did not vacate or deliver 'Kha' schedule land to the plaintiff. As such the plaintiff issued legal notice upon defendant No. 1 on 1-9-1997. But defendant No. 1 did not pay any heed to the said request made by the plaintiff and consequently, the suit was filed. Along with plaint, the plaintiff filed sketch map showing position of the garage. During pendency of the suit, the sole-plaintiff died and his heirs were substituted as the plaintiffs.

3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 3 by filing written statements denying all the material statements made in the plaint. It appears that at first defendant No. 3 filed written statement on 30-3-2000 and subsequently on 2-5-2000. In the first written statement, it has been written by defendant No.3 that the suit land was allotted to defendant No. 1, vide memo No.2FV-123/72/2103 dated 9-12-1974 at a rental of Taka 1,000 per month and later on, vide memo No. Sef-V/1M/D7/ 70 (PT)/402 dated 3-8-1984 to the Ministry of Home Affairs for using the same for the police department. Since then police department had been enjoying the suit schedule-B land. It is further stated that Title Suit No. 53 of 1988 was decreed against defendant No. 3 on contest and ex parte against defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The aforesaid suit was filed by a person who had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. Summons of the aforesaid suit was not served upon defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The garage mentioned in the instant suit is unspecified and, as such, Civil Court Commissioner is required to be appointed to identify the location of the garage. It is further stated that defendant No. 1 has been possessing the property for more than 20 years and, as such, acquired title by adverse possession. In the second written statement, the Government stated that the suit land had been vested in the Government as per provision of PO (President's Order) No. 16 of 1972 as abandoned property by gazette notification No. 9762 (8) at serial No. 10 according to the provision of Ordinance LIV of 1985 on 23-9-1986 and it was allotted to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and they have been possessing the suit schedule-B property.

4. The trial Court upon hearing the parties by its judgment and order dated 28-6-2007 dismissed the suit.

5. Against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 07 of 2009 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. On transfer, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the then learned Additional District Judge, Sixth Court, Dhaka, who by his judgment and order dated 5-4-2010 allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court, the defendants filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 3070 of 2010. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 8-6-2011 discharged the Rule with direction affirming the judgment and decree of the appellate Court.

7. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the defendant-leave-petitioners have filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1887 2011 before this Division, in which, leave was granted on 15-9-2014 resulting in Civil Appeal No. 230 of 2014.

8. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the leave appellants, submits that the plaintiffs in the plaint alleged that they had been dispossessed in 1974 and Title Suit No. (number not stated) of 1998 renumbered as Title Suit No. 234 of 2003 having been filed on 19-2-1998 beyond the statutory period of limitation for recovery of possession, the plaintiffs are not entitled to a decree for recovery of possession in the instant suit. He also submits that the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 52 of 1988 for permanent injunction against the appellants and that decree was passed restraining the appellants from changing the nature and character of the suit land and that the plaintiff of that suit had not asserted his possession in the suit land ('Kha' schedule land to the plaint) and, as such, the decree passed in Title Suit No. 52 of 1988 is of no avail to the plaintiffs and even that suit for permanent injunction was also filed beyond the statutory period of limitation of 12 years from his dispossession in 1974.

9. Mr AM Aminuddin, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondents, on the other hand, submits that the suit has been filed within the statutory period of limitation and, as such, the High Court Division was justified in discharging the Rule.

10. We have considered the submission of the learned Attorney-General for the appellants and the learned Senior Advocate for the respondents, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

11. Before entering into the merit of the appeal, it would be pertinent to quote the grounds, for which, leave was granted as under:

"The land purchased by the plaintiffs from SA Plot No. 10 having been recorded in RS Plot No. 932, the Court of appeal below failed to take into consideration that the garage claimed by the plaintiffs is not within their RS Plot No. 932; rather the same is within RS Plot No. 933 which is an abandoned property and under the occupation of Police Department and the High Court Division committed an error in upholding the decision of the Court of appeal below.

The subject matter of the instant suit being a garage and whether the same is within the purchased land of the plaintiffs or beyond their purchased land being the subject matter of local investigation with reference to their title deeds and in the instant case the plaintiff having not taken any initiative for local investigation, the Court of appeal below illegally decreed the suit and the High Court Division committed error of law in upholding the said decree.

The plaintiff alleged that they have been dispossessed in the year 1974 and they having filed an earlier suit being Title Suit No. 52 of 1988 and in the said suit they having not prayed for recovery of possession from the defendant, the plaintiff is not entitled to a decree for recovery of possession in the instant suit in respect of which they have allegedly been dispossessed in the year 1974."

12. It transpired from the plaint that the original plaintiff, Al-haj Md Serajuddin purchased the suit land under Holding No.10, New Baily Road in 1971. After the death of the original plaintiff his heirs were substituted in his place as the plaintiffs. They claimed that the suit land is part and parcel of Holding No. 10, New Baily Road and not Holding No. 10/A, New Baily Road. The plaintiffs alleged that the defendants dispossessed them from the suit land treating it as an abandoned property.

13. Admittedly, the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 53 of 1988 for permanent injunction against (1). Superintendent of Police, Special Branch, 10/A, New Baily Road, Police Station-Ramna, Dhaka, (2) Deputy Inspector General, Special Branch, 10/A, New Baily Road, Police Station-Ramna, Dhaka and (3). Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works. The plaint of Title Suit No.53 of 1988 was not exhibited. From judgment delivered in Title Suit No.53 of 1988, we find that the learned Assistant Judge, Fourth Court, Dhaka, while describing the case of the plaintiff stated, amongst others, as under:

“বাংলাদেশ সরকারের র্পূত মন্ত্রণালয়ে ১০-এ বেইলী রোড ঢাকা সিটি স্পেশাল ব্রাঞ্চ ঢাকা কে বরাদ্দ করেন। তখন বাদীর অনুপস্থিতে ১/২ নং বাদীগণ বাদীর স্বত্ব দখলীয় অত্র আরজীর ‘খ’ তফসিল ভূক্ত গ্যারেজটি দখল নেয়।

14. From the aforesaid averment of the plaint, it appears that even in 1978 the sole plaintiff Al-haj Serajuddin was out of possession of the suit land prior to filing of Title Suit No. 53 of 1988 for permanent injunction.

15. From the judgment of Title Suit No. 53 of 1988, we find that the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works by filing written statement asserted that the disputed 'Kha' schedule land is part and parcel of Holding No. 10/A, of New Baily Road. Defendant No.3 further asserted that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 had been in possession of the suit land ('Kha' schedule land). Having gone through the judgment delivered in Title Suit No. 53 of 1988, we find that the learned Assistant Judge, Fourth Court, Dhaka, restrained the defendants of Title Suit No.53 of 1988 from changing the nature and character of 'Kha' schedule land to the plaint by a decree of permanent injunction. From the judgment, it appears that the plaintiff himself admitted that he was out of possession of 'Kha' schedule land when the suit for permanent injunction was filed.

16. Subsequently, the plaintiff filed present Title Suit No. 234 of 2003. The High Court Division having considered the documentary evidence came to a finding that the plaintiff acquired title from the original owner of the suit property who was a non-Bengali. The High Court Division also found that the defendants had no title to the suit land and that they were restrained by an order of permanent injunction for making construction or renovation in the suit land. The High Court Division also found that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 had been possessing the suit land on the strength of their possession in the garage defying the decree of the Court passed in Title Suit No. 53 of 1988.

17. We have already noticed that even in the plaint of Title Suit No. 53 of 1988 for permanent injunction, the plaintiff Al-haj Md Serajuddin, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff-respondents of Title Suit No. 234 of 2003, stated that he was out of possession of the 'Kha' schedule land. Subsequently, the present suit was filed for declaration of title and recovery of possession.

18. PW 1, Md Sharifuddin, in his evidence stated that within their boundary the Special Branch had been in possession. He further stated that they (defendants) took possession in 1974 and that subsequently his father filed the suit.

<u>19. Having gone through the record, the judgment delivered in Title Suit No. 53 of 1988 and the evidence of PW 1 given in Title Suit No. 234 of 2003, we find that the plaintiff had been out of possession of the suit land ('Kha' schedule land) according to their admission from 1974. The present suit for declaration of title and recovery of khash possession was filed in 1998. Therefore, the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. The plaintiff was required to file the suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession within 12 years from the alleged date of dispossession but they have been failed to do so and, as such, they are not entitled to get a decree for recovery of possession.</u>

20. In the case of Ahmed Miaji vs Eakub Ali Munshi 12 DLR 708 it has been held that where the plaintiffs have set up a case of possession followed by dispossession, they must prove possession within 12 years of the suit as contemplated under Article 142 of the Limitation Act.

<u>21. In the case of Syed Moin Ahmed vs Khondkar Mohiuddin 19 DLR 912, it has been held that under Article 142 of the limitation Act, it is the duty of the plaintiff first to prove to the satisfaction of the Court that he was in possession of the suit premises within 12 years prior to the filing of the suit and if he fails to do so he cannot get decree for declaration of title and recovery of possession.</u>

22. Reliance may be placed on the case of Amanatullah vs Ali Mohamnuni Bhuiyan 2 BLC (AD) 134 where it has been held as under:

"The last but not the least point that has been noticed by this Court at the time of hearing of the appeal is that there is no averment in the plaint of plaintiffs dispossession from the suit land within twelve years of bringing the suit which is for recovery of khas possession. Notwithstanding this, both the trial Court and the lower appellate Court concurrently found that the plaintiffs had never been in possession of the suit land. In such circumstances, the suit was not maintainable. On this ground alone the plaintiffs suit was liable for dismissal."

<u>23. On consideration of the cases referred to above, it appears that in a suit for declaration of title and recovery of khash possession, the plaintiffs in addition to proving their title to the suit land must prove that the suit has been filed within 12 years from the alleged date of dispossession. In the case in hand, the plaintiffs miserably failed to prove that the suit has been filed within 12 years from the alleged date of dispossession.</u>

24. In the light of the findings, we are of the view that the High Court Division erroneously decreed the suit for declaration of title and recovery of khash possession.

Accordingly, this appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division is set aside.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order. dated the 25th of October, 2011 passed by the High Court Division inWrit Petition NO.8806 of 2010)
full_judgment:
Md Imman Ali J: This civil petition for leave to  appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated i5-1 0-2011 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 8886 of 2010 discharging the Rule.

2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that the petitioner, Chowdhury Mohidul Haque, is one of .the Senior Executive Directors of the Bangladesh Bank. He was General Manager of Barisal Office of Bangladesh Bank during 2002-2004. During his tenure in Barisal Office, he played active role in constructing own Building of the Bank and eventually foundation of the new office building of Barisal Office was given and much of the construction work had been completed and foundation stone was laid by the then Prime Minister of the Country in January, 2004. Thereafter, Bangladesh Bank,. Barisal Office found prima facie case through internal audit arid inspection report conducted by Head Office of Bangladesh Bank that the Assistant Director of the Bank's Sanchay Patra section one Abul Kalam Azad misappropriated Taka 30,29,459.50. Thereafter, said Abul Kalam Azad was suspended. Bangladesh Bank conducted thorough investigation of the case by internal Audit Team and found Abul Kalam Azad guilty for misappropriation of the fund of Sanchay Patra section of the Bank. A First Information Report (FIR) was lodged by the Deputy Director, Bangladesh Bank, Barisal with Kotwali Police Station,Barisal on 2-7-2005 wherein allegation was made that offence was committed during the period 21-11-2002 to 29-10-2003, and on the basis of the FIR, Barisal Police Station Case No. 5/404 dated 2-7-2005 under sections 406 and 409 of the Penal Code was started. The FIR named accused Abul Kalam Azad was dismissed from his service by Bangladesh Bank under Bangladesh Bank Staff Regulations, 2003. Furthermore, Money Suit No. 3 of 2007 was instituted in the Court of Joint District Judge, Barisal for recovery of the. said misappropriated money and the said suit was decreed ex-parte on 20-7-2011 for an amount of Taka 46,49,008.95 with interest till recovery.

3. After investigation, the Investigating Officer found prima facie case against the FIR named sole accused Abul Kalam Azad and submitted charge-sheet being No. 348 dated 18-10-2006 under sections 406/409 and 201 0f the Penal Code. In the charge-sheet the petitioner was shown as Prosecution Witness No.11.

4. On 24-12-2006 the learned Magistrate, Barisal accepted the charge-sheet and sent the case record to the Court of Sessions Judge, Barisal for trial. On 23-1-2007 the learned Senior Special Judge, Barisal received the Case Record and on 18-2-2007 cognizance was taken under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and date was fixed on 14-3-2007 for framing charge, and then he transmitted the case record to the Divisional Special Judge, Barisal. On transfer, the case was renumbered as Special case No.2 of 2007. On 9-5-2007 the prosecution prayed for re- investigation of the case, but the learned Divisional Special Judge, Barisal did not pass any-order rather he postponed process of framing of charge and sent the case record to the Senior Special Judge, Barisal for obtaining sanction and taking necessary steps regarding the charge-sheet No. 348 under section 32(1) of the Anti- Corruption Commission Act, 2004 from respondent No.1. On 21-5-2007, the learned Senior Special Judge, Barisal sent the case record of Special Case No. 2 of 2007 to the concerned Magistrate for taking step under section 32(1) of Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. Thereafter, the concerned Magistrate, Barisal sent all the relevant papers and charge-sheet to the Investigating Officer for obtaining sanction from the Anti-Corruption Commission. The Anti-corruption Commission instead of giving sanction to the charge-sheet being No. 348 dated 18-10-2006 under sections 406, 409 and 201 of the Penal Code on which cognizance had been taken by the Divisional Special Judge, Barisal, took decision for re-investigation of the case. On the decision of the Anti Corruption Commission, respondent No. 4, the Investigating Officer of Anti-Corruption Commission, Barisal Office on 8-9-2008 took up the matter for re-investigation and thereafter, on 5-8-2010 submitted“বিকল্প অভিযোগপত্র”(Alternative charge-sheet) being No. 348I Ka under section 409/477 (Ka)/109 of the Penal Code road with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 on obtaining sanction from the concerned official of Anti-Corruption Commission. The petitioner has been implicated in the case through this “বিকল্পঅভিযোগপত্র” (Alternative charge-sheet).

5. After submission of "Alternative charge-sheet" “বিকল্প অভিযোগপত্র”the case, was re-numbered, as Special Case No. 11 of 2010 dated 22-7-2010. The learned Senior Special Judge, Barisal further took cognizance of alleged offence on the strength of the said “বিকল্প অভিযোগপত্র” (Alternative charge-sheet) No. 238IKa dated 5-8- 2010 without assignment of proper and cogent reasons.

6. Against the initiation and continuation, of the proceedings of Special Case No.11 of 2010 arising out of Kotwali Police Station Case No. 5 dated 2-7-2005 on the basis of alternative charge- sheet being No. 348/Ka dated 5-8-20 I 0 under sections 409/477 (Ka)/109 of the Penal Coderead with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 on the basis of sanction vide Memo. No. “দুদক/সি/১০/২০০৮ (অনুঃ ও তদন্ত-২) /বরিঃ১৪৬৮৯”, তারিখঃ২-৮-২০১০ ইং the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 8885 of 20 1 0 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule and an order of stay.

7. In due course, after hearing both the parties by the impugned judgment and order the said Rule was discharged. Hence the petitioner has filed the instant civil petition for leave to appeal before this Division.

8. Mr Moudud Ahmed, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submitted that there is no provision either in the Code of Criminal Procedure or in the relevant special law for re-investigation of any case after submission of a charge-sheet. There is also no provision for submitting an "alternative charge-sheet“বিকল্প অভিযোগপত্র”, and, as such prosecution of the petitioner, is without any lawful authority and hence the High Court Division erred in dis- charging the Rule. He submitted that there is a gulf of difference between re-investigation(পুনঃ তদন্ত) and further investigation (অধিকতরতদন্ত)the former is what was ordered in the instant case and is not contemplated by the law. He also submitted that further proceedings against the petitioner on the basis of an illegal alternative charge-sheet (বিকল্প অভিযোগপত্র)is illegal and hence the impugned judgment calls for interference by this Division.

9. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1-5 made submissions in support of the judgment and order of the high Court Division.

10. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the respective parties and perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

11. The Code of Criminal Procedure does not provide for re-investigation of any case. Whether or not the investigation done in any case subsequent to the submission of a charge-sheet after the initial investigation is completed, is the result of a re-investigation or a further investigation is a matter of semantics. We note from the order sheet of the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Barisal, annexed to the additional paper book, that the subsequent investigation arid the consequent report has been variously referred to as “পূর্ণঃ তদন্ত প্রতিবেদন”,“পূর্ণঃ তদন্ত প্রতিবেদন”,“পূর্ণঃ তদন্ত প্রতিবেদন”,and “অধিকতর তদন্ত প্রতিবেদন”. In the body of the report it is referred to as “বিকল্প অভিযোগপত্র” .In the writ petition, the petitioner preferred to it as "supplementary charge-sheet". The validity and legality of the subsequent investigation termed as "re-investigation" and the report termed as "alternative charge-sheet" was challenged by way of a supplementary affidavit on behalf of the petitioner. The question that may be posed is whether or not there would be any prejudice caused if instead of calling it "re-investigation", the second investigation was termed "further investigation", which is allowed by the law, i.e. the terms were simply transposed. Under normal circumstances, if on the basis of fresh evidence a supplementary charge-sheet is submitted, for example by adding name of accused person (s) who had not been included in the initial charge- sheet, there would be no questioning the legality of the supplementary charge-sheet. That clearly is the purpose of section 173(3B) of the Code.

12.In support of his submissions Mr Moudud Ahmed referred to the case of 66 DLR (AD) 286;AjiaKhatoonvs Ali reported in 1995 BLT (AD) 74=47 DLR (AD) 62,where this Division upheld ,the judgment and order of the High Court Division which held that the second charge-sheet appeared to be a result not of a further investigation but of re-investigation in the name of further investigation, which is barred by law. The principle that re-investigation is barred is established. However, the facts of the case mentioned above are somewhat peculiar, inasmuch as, in that case it was found that the subsequent investigation by the CID effectively exonerated the accused against whom prima facie case was found in the course of the initial investigation, by establishing an alibi for him. The High Court Division had found that the re-investigation by the CID was malafide, observing that by implicating the informant and other witnesses in the same case which was done by the ASP, cm in collusion with the main accused thereby cleverly creating a situation such that the trial against the first accused and others could not proceed.

13. Similarly, in another recent unreported case, this Division found that the second investigation and charge-sheet was malafide and done with the ulterior motive to exonerate the accused in the first charge-sheet against whom a prima facie case had been found. The second charge- sheet reportedly did not find any evidence against those accused persons. (Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 456 of 2011, judgment delivered on 11-9-2014). In that case we observed as follows:

"We would again reiterate that section 173 (3B) of the Code allows for further investigation and submission of a further report with further evidence, oral or documentary in respect of an offence, even after a report had been forwarded to the Magistrate under section 173( 1) of the Code. Hence, in this case, if it is felt necessary, a further investigation may be carried out and any other person could be implicated as an accused in the offence if prima facie evidence is found against him/her/them."

<u>14. However, in the facts of the instant case; it appears that although the initial charge-sheet was submitted against only one accused person, upon finding prima facie evidence against him, he still remains an accused in spite of the so called "re-investigation" of the case whereby the petitioner before us has been additionally named an accused, prima facie evidence having been found against him in the subsequent investigation. We do not find any indication of malafide in the conduct of the subsequent investigation.</u>

15. It is unfortunate that various terminologies have been used which do not reflect the relevant terminology used in the statutes. We would strongly urge that the learned Magistrates, Judges, investigating agencies and others who deal with such terminologies, should ensure that the terms they use are accurate and in accordance with the terminology used in the law.

16. We also note, incidentally that the sub-sequent charge-sheet was numbered as 348 Ka, whereas the first charge-sheet was numbered as 348. In a way, this indicates that the second charge-sheet is 'indeed a supplementary of the first.

<u>17. The High Court Division observed that under section 173(3B) of the Code the Investigating Officer does not require any permission from the court concerned for further 'investigation and hence after completion of further investigation filing of supplementary charge-sheet does not suffer from any illegality. The High Court Division has treated the subsequent investigation as a further investigation and the report as a supplementary charge-sheet.</u>

18. In view of our discussion, above, we do not, find any illegality or infirmity in the impugned judgment and order and accordingly the civil petition for leave to appeal is dismissed.

End.

parties:
Khairul Bashar (Md) and others ------ Petitioner
vs.
Collector of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: In all these Rules assessments of customs duty by the customs authority on the basis of SROs subsequent to the date of opening of Letters of Credit are under challenge. Common question of law having been involved in all these Rules these are being disposed of by this judgment. 

2. Learned Advocate for the petitioner of the respective Rule after placing the petitions and other materials on record submitted that tariff value as well as customs duty having been increased by the SROs published subsequent to the date of opening of the Letters of Credit in the respective Rule and the customs authority having claimed customs duty on the basis of subsequent SROs vested right of the respective petitioner to import goods and to pay custom duty on the basis of tariff value and custom duty prevailing at the time of opening of the letters of credit on the basis of SROs published before the date of opening of the letters of credit has been adversely affected. .Since under the impugned assessment orders customs duties have been charged on the basis of SROs issued subsequent to the date of opening of the respective letter of credit vested right of the respective petitioner has been adversely affected and such vested right cannot be taken away in view of the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Collector of Customs VS. Ahmed Hossain and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199. 

3. It appears from materials on record that under SRO No.155 dated 12-6-91 customs duty for milk and cream concentrated or containing added sugar or other sweetening matter in powder form in retail packing of upto 2.5 Kg was 20% ad valorem and in powder form in bulk imported in bags was 40% ad volorem Under SRO No.157 dated 12-6-91 tariff value of tin packed full cream and half cream milk powder per Kg was Taka 90.00 and tariff value of fat free milk powder imported in bags per metric ton was Taka 55,125.00. By SRO No: 394 dated 24-12-91 customs duty on milk and cream concentrated or containing added sugar or other sweetening materials in powder form in retail packing  upto 2.5 Kg was increased to 25% ad valorem and in powder form in bulk imported in bags was increased to 45% ad valorem. By SRO No. ll dated 20-1-92 tariff value of full cream or half cream milk powder per Kg continued at Taka 90.00 and tariff value of fat free milk powder imported in bag also continued at Taka 55,125.00 but tariff value of full cream and half cream milk in powder form imported in bags was fixed at Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton. By SRO NO.152 dated 18"6-92 tariff value of full cream and half cream milk powder packed in tin per Kg was fixed US dollars 2.50 and tariff value of full cream and half cream milk in powder form imported in bags was fixed at US dollars 1900.00 per metric ton and fat free milk powder imported in bags was fixed at US dollars 1560. Under SRO NO.152 dated 18-6-92 customs duty on milk powder packed in tin upto 2.5 Kg was 25% ad valorem and packed in bags was 45% ad valorem. Under SRO No.1 13 dated 10-6-93 rate of customs duty on milk and cream concentrated or containing added sugar or other sweetening matter in powder form was 30%: ad valorem and in other form was 45% ad valorem. By subsequent SRO No.1 33 dated 6-7-93 customs duty on milk and cream concentrated or containing added sugar or other sweetening matter in powder form was increased to 45% ad valorem. By SRO No.214 dated 28-10-93 tariff value of milk powder imported in bulk in bags was increased to US dollars 1950.00. 

4. Petitioner of the respective writ petition claim that he is entitled to pay custom duty at the rate which was in operation on the date of opening the Letter of Credit on the basis of tariff value which was also in operation on the date of opening the letter of credit. In the aforesaid case reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199 relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioner of the respective Rule it has been held that an importer acquired a vested right to- pay customs duty at the rate applicable on the date of opening of the letter of credit and he could not be charged with custom d~ at the rate imposed subsequent to the opening of the Letter of Credit. In the said decision as well as earlier decision of the Appellate Division in Abdul Hannan's case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 interpretation of sections 19 and 30 of the Customs Act was involved. But interpretation of section 25 of the Customs Act was not involved in those decisions. Learned Advocate for the petitioner of the respective Rule contended that principle enunciated in those decisions regarding  application of the rate of customs duty will also be  applicable in respect of normal value and tariff value under section 25 of the Act. But he could not point out any decision in which it has been held that an importer is entitled to assessment of customs duty on the basis of normal value or tariff value which was in force on the date of opening of the Letter of Credit. In the case of Mostafa Kamal vs. Commissioner of Customs and others (Writ Petition Nos.4336 and 4337 of 1996) another Division Bench of this Court by judgment dated 17-12-96 considered the question as to whether an importer entitled to pay customs duty on the basis of tariff value fixed before the opening of the letter of credit or he-was to pay customs duty on the basis of tariff value which was in force on the date when the Bill of Entry was presented for assessment' of customs duty. In that decision it has been noticed that tariff value is fixed by the Government according to the suggestions of the high powered committee. In that case it has been held as follows: "since in the instant case it appears that before submission of the bill of entry before the
authority the high powered committee considered the matter and suggested for enhancement of tariff value of the goods in question at US Dollar 220 per metric ton, it  cannot be said that it was fixed arbitrarily and  the notification as well as the law itself are ultra  vires of the Constitution on the point of excessive delegation without having any  guideline. Since the notification was issued as per the decision of the high powered committee which considered the matter according to the provisions of sections 25, 30 and 30 the Customs Act, we are of the view that the impugned notification or the law itself, that is section 25(7) of the Customs Act cannot be declared ultra vires or to have been made and passed without any lawful authority." 

5. Sub-sections (1)(2) and (3) of section 25 of the Customs Act 1969 provide for determination of value of imported goods and sub-sections (4), (5) and (6) of section 25 provide for determination of value of the exported goods and sub-section (7) provides for fixation of tariff value by the Government by notification in the official .Gazette, The said- sub-section (7) is as follows: "7. Notwithstanding anything contained in this section the Government may by notification in 'the official Gazette, fix for the purpose of levying customs duties, tariff values for any goods imported or exported as chargeable with customs duty ad valorem; Provided that any imported or exported goods the declared value of which is higher than its tariff value fixed under this sub-section shall be chargeable with customs duties on the basis of its declared value. "The aforesaid provision of .sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Act provides the Government may by notification published in the official Gazette fix for the purpose of levying of custom duty, tariff value for any imported or exported goods and the said power would be exercised by the Government in spite of the provisions for determination of value of such goods under the earlier sub-sections 1-6 of section 25. But if the declared value of any such goods is higher than its tariff value then the party concerned would be liable to pay customs duty on the basis of such declared value. 

6. Normally invoice value is the basis of assessment of customs duty. To prevent under invoicing or over invoicing widely practiced by the traders either to evade payment of proper duty or to smuggle out foreign exchange power has been vested in the Government under sub-section (7) of section 25 to fix tariff value of imported or exported goods by publishing notification in the official/Gazette.  When the Government finds from materials that traders have taken resort to under invoicing to evade payment of proper customs duty it fixes tariff value of the imported goods in exercise of power under-sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Act. On the basis of change in price of goods in the foreign market from time to time Government increases or decreases the tariff value of goods to be imported in the country. This power of Government to fix tariff value by publishing notification in the official Gazette is an exceptional power which is contrary to the provisions for determination of value of the goods under-sub-sections (1)(2) and (3) of section 25. But the non-obstante provision of sub-section 7) has resolved the aforesaid contradiction between the provision of sub-sections (1), (2), (3) and the provisions of sub-section (7) of section 25. It has already been noticed from the aforesaid decision in Writ Petition Nos. B36 and 4337 of 1966 that Government revises the tariff value from time to time on the basis of recommendation of High powered Committee. Tariff value is imposed to keep the value of the imported goods in conformity with the prevailing price in the foreign countries so that importers could not in collusion with the exporters under value the goods to be imported to evade payment of proper customs duty. That being the position there is no question of importers acquiring vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value existing at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit. The aforesaid decisions of the Appellate Division relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioner having not interpreted the provisions of section 25 of the Customs Act we are not inclined to apply the principle enunciated in those decisions as to the date of the application of invoice value or tariff value. We are of the view that custom duty is payable by the importer on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry and not on the basis of invoice value or tariff value which was in existence at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit. But in view of the aforesaid decision of the Appellate Division Customs Authorities cannot charge customs duty on the basis of rate imposed by SRO issued subsequent to the opening of the letter or credit and an importer is entitled to pay customs duty at the rate which was in force en the date of opening of the letter of Credit. 

7. In the light of the above discussion and determination let us now consider the merit of the respective Rule. 

8. In Writ Petition No. 1032 of 1992 and Writ Petition No.1071 of 1992 petitioner of the respective writ petition was asked to declare customs duty at the rate of 25% in the Bill of Entry on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91. Letter of credit opened by the petitioner of Writ Petition No.1032 992 on 8-12-91 and by the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 1071 of 1992 on 7-12-91 when customs duty for the milk powder imported by the respective petitioner was 20% ad valorem on the basis of SRO  dated 12-6-91 So, charging customs duty at the rate  of 25%. on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91 which was issued subsequent to the opening of letters of  credit on 7-12-91 and 8-12-91 is without lawful  authority and of no legal effect So, we find merit in  these two Rules. In Writ Petition No.278 of 1992 customs authority directed the petitioner to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% on the milk powder imported by him by opening letter of credit on 14-11-91. As customs duty on the said goods on the date of opening of the letter of credit on 14-11-91 was 40%   valorem on the basis of SRO dated 12-6-91 he  was not .liable to pay customs duty at the rate of 45% imposed by SRO dated 24-12-91 issued  subsequent to the opening of the Letter of credit. Charging customs duty at the rate of 45% from the petitioner is without lawful authority and of no legal effect So we find merit in this Rule. 

9. In Writ Petition Nos. 518, 718, 785,912, 1293, 1294, 1447 and 1708 of 1992 petitioner of the  respective Writ Petition was asked by customs  authority to declare customs duty at the rate 45% and tariff value per metric ton @ Taka 65,000.00.  Petitioner of the respective Rule opened Letter of Credit on 14-11-91 when customs duty on the milk powder imported by him was @ 40% on the basis of SRO dated 12-6-91 and, as such, he was not liable to pay customs duty on the basis of subsequent SRO dated 24-12-91 @ 45%. Under SRO No.157 dated 12-6-91 tariff value of fat free milk powder imported in bags was Taka 55,125.00 per metric ton but under SRO No.l1 dated 20-1-92 tariff value of fat free milk powder imported in bags per metric ton remained at Taka 55,125.00 and for the first time tariff value of full cream and half cream milk powder it imported in - bags was fixed at Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton. Petitioner having imported full cream milk powder is liable to pay customs duty @ 40% ad valorem on the tariff value of Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton on his imported full cream milk powder and he is not entitled to pay customs duty on his goods on the tariff value of Taka 55,125.00. So we find merit in these Rules in part and we hold that charging 45% customs duty instead of 40% on the petitioner is without lawful authority. But tariff value of Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton is not illegal and same is maintained for the reasons already stated. 

10. In Writ Petition No.2830 of 1992 petitioner was asked to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% and tariff value at US dollars 1900 per metric ton for the full cream milk powder imported by him in bags. He opened letter of credit on 14-11-91 and submitted Bill of Entry on 25-7-92 when tariff value was raised to US dollar 1900 by SRO dated 18-6-92 and, as such, he is to declare tariff value at the rate 1900 US dollar per metric ton. But he having opened letter of credit on 14-11-91 he was liable to pay customs duty at the rate of 40% and not 45% as demanded from him. So, we find merit in part in this Rule the charging customs duty at the rate of 45% instead of 40% from the petitioner is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. But tariff value of US dollars 1900 per metric ton is upheld. 

11. In Writ Petition No.2197 of 1992 customs authority directed the petitioner to declare customs duty @ 45% and tariff value at the rate of Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton for the milk powder imported in bags, Petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 9-3-92 when applicable rate of duty was 45% on the basis of SRO No.394 dated 24-12-91 and tariff value was Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton as per SRO. So we find no merit in this Rule which is liable to be discharged. 

12. In Writ Petition Nos.2584, 2728, 2831, 2974, 3067, 3189 and 3473 of 1992 Collector of Customs directed the petitioner of each of the Rules- to declare customs duty @ 45% and tariff value at the rate of US dollar 1900 per metric ton of full cream milk powder imported in bags. Petitioner of the respective Writ Petition opened letter of credit on 9-3-92 when applicable rate of duty was 45% on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91 and tariff value was Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton on the basis of SRO dated 20-1-92. Since customs duty was @ 45% from before the opening of the respective letter of credit petitioner of the respective Rule cannot claim to pay customs duty @ 40% on the basis of earlier SRO dated 12-6-91. In view of our opinion regarding the applicability of tariff value petitioner was liable to declare tariff value at the rate of US dollars 1900 per metric ton which was in operation on the basis of SRO dated 18-6-92 before presentation of the Bills of Entry on different dates in July, August and September, 1992. Petitioner of the respective Rule having opened letter of credit on 9-3-92 for importing full cream milk powder for which customs duty was 45% on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91 his claim that he is entitled to pay customs duty @40% on the basis of SRO No.155 dated 12-6-91 and to declare tariff value at the rate of Taka 55,125.00 per metric ton on the basis of SRO No.157 dated 12-6-91 is not tenable in view of the opinion we have already expressed. So, we find no merit in these Rules which are liable to be discharged. 
13. In Writ Petition Nos.1399, 1643, 1680, 1882 and 1883 of 1993 customs authority directed the' respective petitioner of the above writ petitions to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% on the basis of SRO No. 133 dated 6-7-93. By the said SRO customs duty was raised to 45% per metric ton on the milk powder imported packed in tins or in bags by amending the earlier SRO No.1l3 dated 10-6-93 under which customs duty was only 30% on the milk powder imported either packed in tins or in bags. Petitioner having opened letter of credit on 27-6-93 he was entitled to pay customs duty at the rate of 30% on the basis of SRO dated 10-6-93 which was in force on that date and he was not liableto pay customs duty @ 45% on the basis of' subsequent SRO dated 6-7-93. We therefore, find merit in these Rules and declare the orders in question asking the petitioner to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% under SRO dated 6-3-93 instead of SRO dated 10-6-93 to be without lawful authority customs authority directed the petitioner to declare 

14. In Writ Petition No.1321 of 1992 customs duty @25% on his imported milk powder on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91. Petitioner opened letter or' credit on 14-12-91 for import of milk powder in packed tins of 2.5 Kg and at that time customs duty for the said goods was 20% ad valorem on the basis of SRO dated 12-6-91 and, as such, he was not liable to pay customs duty @25% on the basis of subsequent SRO dated 24-12-91. So we find merit in this Rule and as such charging on 25% customs duty on petitioner's goods instead of 20% is declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect 

15. In Writ Petition No.1931 of 1993 customs authority directed the petitioner to declare customs duty @ 45% on the basis of SRO No.133 dated 6-7-93 and tariff value per metric ton at US dollar 1950 on the basis of SRO No.214 dated 28-10-93. Petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 27-6-93 when customs duty for milk powder both packed in tins and bags was @ 30% ad valorem and, as such', he was not liable to pay customs duty @ 45% ad valorem on the basis of subsequent SRO dated 6-7-93. But he having not acquired any vested right to pay customs duty on the basis of tariff value of US dollar 1900 per metric ton as per SRO dated 18-6-92 he is not entitled to declare tariff value at US dollar 1900 per metric ton. We, therefore, find merit in part in this Rule and declare the demand of customs duty @45% instead Of 30% is without lawful authority and uphold the tariff value of US dollars 1950 per metric ton. 
16. In writ Petition No.1360 of 1993 customs authority directed the petitioner to declare customs duty @ 45%. Petitioner opened the Letter of credit on 10-6-93. By SRO dated 1O-~-93 C4stOmS duty on his imported milk powder packed in tins as well as bags was @ 30% and, as such, he was entitled to pay customs duty at that rate and not @ 45% on the basis of subsequent SRO dated 6-7-93. So, we find merit in this Rule and declare demand of customs duty @ 45% instead of 30% to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

17. In Writ Petition Nos.1365, 1366, 1516, and 1405 of 1993 petitioner of the respective writ petition was directed to declare customs duty @ 45%. Petitioner of the respective Rule opened Letter of Credit on 18-5-93,' 13-1-93 and 11-4-93 respectively when customs duty on the milk powder imported by him packed in tins of 2.5 Kg was at the rate of 25% on the basis of SRO No.151 dated 18-6-92 and, as such, petitioner of the respective Rule was entitled to pay custom duty @ 25% on the basis of the said SRO dated 18-6-92 and not liable to pay custom duty at the rate of subsequent SRO dated 6-7 -93. So we find merit in these Rules and declare the impugned orders in each of the Rules directing each of the writ petitioners to declare customs duty @ 45% instead of 25% is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

18. Petitioner of Writ Petition No.1681 of 1993 was directed by the customs authorities to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% on the full cream milk powder imported by him in retail packing of 2.5 Kg. He opened letter of credit on 10-6-93 when custom duty on his imported goods was at the rate of 30% under SRO No.113 dated 10-6-93. So demand of customs duty at the rate of 45% on the basis Of subsequent SRO No.133 dated 6-7-93 is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. So we find merit in this Rule. 

In the result, Rules on Writ Petition Nos.278, 1032, 1071 and 1321 of 1992, Writ Petition Nos. 1399, 1643, 1680, 1882, 1883, 1360, 1365, 1366, 1516, 1681 and .J405 of 1993 are made absolute, Rule in Writ Petition Nos.518, 718, 785, 912, 1293, 1294, 1447, 1708, 2830 of 1992 and Writ Petition No. 1931 of 1993 are made absolute in part and Rules in Writ Petition Nos.2197, 2584, 2728,2831,2974,3067,3189 and 3473 of 1992 are discharged.

In the facts and circumstances there will be no order to costs. Respondents are at liberty to encash the bank guarantee in full in respect of the discharged Rules and in part in respect of the Rules made absolute in part. 

End.

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 3837 of 1991 (Dhaka) 
Civil Revision No. 61 of 1989
lawyer:
Shahabuddin Ahmad with Ferdaushi Shahab, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners
Golam Mostafa, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party Nos.1-3.
parties:
Fatick Chandra Dey and others ------ Petitioners
vs. 
Dipok Kumar Dey and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant- petitioners is against judgment and decree dated 29.12.88 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Khulna in Title Appeal No. 7 of 1984 dismissing the appeal and affirming judgment and decree dated 28.12.83 passed by the Munsif, 1st Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 679 of 1979.

2. Opposite parties along with two others filed the aforesaid suit on 18.12.87 for ejectment of the defendant-petitioners and another from the suit premises, and also for recovery of arrear rent and compensation, being holding No. 40 Quaid-e-Azam, Upper Jessore Road, Khulna comprising one semi-pucca tin-shed and two kuchcha sheds, etc. standing on 3 decimals of land of CS plot No. 2061 corresponding to SA plot No. 2434 recorded in CS Khatian No. 1233 corresponding to SA Khatian No.1238 on the allegation that plaintiffs' predecessor Bhojahari Dey got the suit land by patta dated 31.3.1930 from Abul Kashem (Ext.8) and thereafter Suresh Chandra Dey and Jogesh Chandra Dey, brother's sons of Bhojahari and predecessors of the plaintiffs inherited the same and they let out the suit premises to the defendants at first at a monthly rent of Taka 24.00 which was gradually increased to Taka 75.00 payable according to English calendar month and that they paid rents to the plaintiffs up to February, 1979 and since March 1979, they having defaulted in payment of rent their tenancy was terminated by notice dated 6.11.79 Ext. 1 series and the same were served by registered post vide Exts. 2-4 series and thereafter defendants having not amicably vacated the premises they filed the suit

3. Defendant-petitioner No.1 Fatick Chandra Dey alone contested the suit by filing written statement on 8.9.81 denying that the defendants had never been monthly tenants in the suit premises in CS plot No. 2061 under Jogesh Chandra Dey and Suresh Chandra Dey or under the plaintiffs and further alleged that plaintiffs' predecessor Bhojahari acquired share of Kashem Sk. only by patta dated 31.3.1930 and remaining share of that plot remained with other co-sharers in whose name SA Khatian No. 1237 (Exts. B1, B2) was finally published and without a suit for declaration of title plaintiffs' present suit was not maintainable as they had no title and possession in the remaining part of the suit plot and no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served upon the defendants. On 13.3.86 when the suit was fixed for peremptory hearing defendant No. 1 filed further and better statement stating that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 entered into an agreement with Barkat Ullah and Khurshed Sk. on 28.2.1961 Ext. E to purchase 8 decimals of land of CS plot No. 2064 of CS Khatian No. 1233 as they were in possession of the same and thereafter they purchased the land of entire plot No.2064 in a certificate case on 29.6.61 vide sale certificate Ext. 'C' and got delivery of possession on 26.9.61 vide writ of delivery of possession Ext. D and thereafter got entire land of plot No. 2061 and eastern part of plot No. 2064 by amicable settlement with Suresh Chandra Dey and Jogesh Chandra Dey and possessing the same by constructing structures and recording their names in the municipality.

4. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submitted that plaintiffs having failed to prove their case that the defendants were monthly tenants under them by oral or documentary evidence, Court of appeal below acted illegally in dismissing the appeal merely relying on an entry in the municipal assessment register Ext. 6 recording the name of defendant petitioner No. 1 as tenant under the predecessors of plaintiffs. He further submitted that Court of appeal below should not have decided complicated question of title in a suit for ejectment of monthly tenants which was essentially in the nature of Small Cause Court Suit.

5. It appears from the impugned judgment that Court of appeal below after considering the evidence of 3 PWs including plaintiff No. 1 and 2 DWs including the defendant No. 1, concluded that auction purchase claimed by the defendants was set aside in the proceedings of Title Suit No. 1162 of 1962 and their bainapatra Ext. E was a fraudulent document and, as such, defendants' claim in the suit property was not legally tenable. He further found that plaintiffs' have prima facie title in the suit land on the basis of patta Ext. 8 which has been admitted by the DW 1 Court of appeal below, further noticed that the plaintiffs could not produce any rent receipts in support of their claim that defendants are tenants under them but on consideration of oral evidence especially admission of DW 2 and municipal assessment register Ext. 6 found that defendants were tenants under the plaintiffs.

<u>6. Defendant No. 1 simply denied in his written statement that the defendants are tenants under Suresh Chandra Dey and Jogesh Chandra Dey, predecessors of the plaintiffs or under the plaintiffs and asserted that plaintiffs did not acquire any title in the entire land of CS plot No. 2061 on the basis of patta Ext. 8 and other co-sharers of that land have got title in the remaining land and he did not assert that suit premises and the suit land and structures standing thereon belong to defendants in his written statements. To fill up that lacuna he filed a further and better statement and asserted that he is the owner of the said land and structures standing thereon. Court of appeal below rightly found that deed of agreement of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 with Barkatullah and Khurshed Ext. E is fraudulent and contradictions in deposition and cross-examination of DW 1 regarding that document was noticed by the Court of appeal below. Court of appeal below also correctly held relying on the decree passed in Title Suit No. 1162 of 1962 on 19.12.74 Ext.9 that auction purchase of plot No. 2064 by the defendant No. 1 Fatick Chandra Dey in certificate Case No.15311 R/1959-60 vide Ext. 'C' and 'D' was set aside. It appears from Ext.9 that defendant petitioner No. 1 Fatick Chandra Dey was defendant No. 3 in that suit. In view of the same it does not lie in the mouth of the petitioners to say that they are in possession of entire land of suit plot No. 2061 and eastern part of plot No.2064 by amicable settlement with the predecessors of the plaintiffs especially when there is no corroboration of such assertion of DW 1 either by any document or by any oral evidence.</u>

<u>Order VI rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure is as follows:</u>

<u>"A further and better statement of the nature of the claim or defence, or further and better particulars of any matter stated in any pleading, may in all cases be ordered, upon such terms, as to costs and otherwise, as may be just."</u>

<u>In view of the fact that defendant No. 1 did not claim title and possession in suit plot No. 2061 in his written statement he could not raise the same by filing further and better statement asserting something which was not within the four comers of his written statement. Purpose of filing further and better statement is to elucidate the pleadings and not to amend the same by adding new claim or defence which was not in the pleading. So the defence case as made out in the trial was beyond the pleadings of the defendant petitioner No. 1 and not fit to be considered. Even then he failed to prove his claim of title and possession in the suit plot No. 2061.</u>

7. It is true plaintiffs could not produce any documents in support of their claim that the defendants had been in possession of the suit property as their tenants except Ext. 6. Court of appeal below correctly relied upon the admission of DW 2 and entry of the name of defendant No. 1 Fatick Chandra Dey in municipal assessment register for the year 1960-61 Ext.6 as a tenant under the assesses Jogesh Chandra Dey and Suresh Chandra Dey in old holding No. 38. It appears from municipal tax receipts filed by the defendant that Fatick Chandra Dey paid municipal taxes since 1961-62 in respect of holding No. 38. Receipt for the year 1967-68 shows old holding No.38 was renumbered as new holding No.40 vide Ext. G (13) and since then he has been paying municipal tax in respect of holding No.40 From the above documents it is clear that defendant No. 1 Fatick Chandra Dey was a tenant in holding No.38 and subsequently part of that holding was recorded in his name as holding No. 40 which is the present suit holding. By recording one's name in the municipal assessment register a tenant cannot disown his tenancy.

<u>8. No reason has been assigned by the trial Court for allowing compensation to the plaintiffs at the claimed rate of Taka 10.00 per day and the decree to that extent also has been upheld by the Court of appeal below without assigning any reason. It is now well settled that in the absence of any contract to the contrary measure of compensation for unauthorized use and occupation of the rented premises after termination of tenancy is the rate of rent of such tenancy. So, the plaintiff-opposite parties are entitled to recover compensation from the defendants at the rate of Taka 75.00 per month, which was the rate of monthly rent, for their unauthorized use and occupation of the suit premises from 1.12.79 till the date of their vacating the same on payment of Court fee on such amount in the trial Court. So the impugned judgment and decree need be modified to that extent.</u>

9. There is no error of law in the impugned judgment and decree resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice except the modification required to be made as noticed above.

10. Faced with such situation learned Advocate for the petitioners prays for allowing some time to the petitioners to vacate the suit premises. Learned Advocate for the opposite parties has no objection to the granting of reasonable time to the petitioners to vacate the suit premises provided they pay rent and compensation up to the date of their vacating the suit premises.

11. In the result, the Rule is discharged with cost and the order of stay passed earlier by this Court stands vacated and the compensation is reduced from Taka 10.00 per day to Taka 75.00 per month and the impugned judgment and decrees affirming those of the trial Court are modified to that extent. Petitioners are allowed time up to 31st December, 1994 to vacate the suit premises on condition of their depositing the decretal rent of Taka 675.00 along with costs and compensation of Taka 375.00 from August, 1994 to December, 1994 within one month from the date of receipt of the records by the Court below in favour of the plaintiff-opposite parties, in default the plaintiff opposite parties will be at liberty to take delivery of possession before that date. Plaintiffs will be entitled to recover compensation for the remaining period through Court on payment of court fees after the aforesaid amounts are paid by the defendants as directed.

End.

lawyer:
Dr Chowdhury Ishrak Ahmed Siddiky Advocate -----For the Petitioner. 
Amatul Karim DAG with AR Hasanuzzaman AA Gand Abu Saleh Md Fazle Rabbi Khan AAG -----For the Respondent No.5.
parties:
Jahurul Islam (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of an Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Tariq-ul-Hakim J: Rule Nisi has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the respondents should not be directed to appoint and absorb the petitioner into the revenue budget to. the Local, Government Engineering Department (LGED) under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives and/or pass such other Dr further order Dr orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper should not be passed.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule is that on 13-5-1985 the petitioner was appointed as a Coolie of Zilla Parishad Rajshahi on daily 'wage basis. Subsequently" on 21-8-1989 he was appointed in the Local Government Engineering Bureau on daily wage basis for the maintenance of various vehicles of the said Bureau. Thereafter on 1-2-1992 the petitioner was temporarily appointed as road-roller driver in the project titled 'Polli Unnoyan Prokalpa-7' under the Local Government Engineering Bureau in the District-of Nababgonj in the national. Pay Scale of Taka 1,200 -7/60-1620-EB-11 x 65-2335. Thereafter the petitioner has been working. under different projects of the Local Government Engineering Department. Lastly in 2003; he was working for the project titled "Polli Unnoyan. Prokalpa Abokathamo Unnoyan-26' under the office of the Executive Engineer, Local Government Engineering Department vide Memo. No. LGED/ CEIE-96/2001/8163/1(6) dated 1-4-8-2003. The said project ended in the year 2012 and the petitioner was not transferred to any other project but he was informed that the project was complete and his service was no longer required. As such after over 20 years of service at the prevailing National 'Pay Scale under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives the petitioner 's service was terminated.

3. It is further stated that the petitioner was 25 years old when he, was appointed under the National Pay Scale in the office of the Local Government Engineering Bureau and at the age of 46 years he was terminated from service as a result of which he is not eligible to get employment anywhere else. It is further stated that many of 'the employees in, the project titled polliUnnoyanProkalpaAbokathamoUnnoyan-26 where the petitioner was lastly employed has been regularized in the revenue budget, In fad there appears to be a practice of the Government to regularize employees in various projects of the LGED in the revenue budget of the Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives. The petitioner' 'therefore claims a legitimate expectation to be regularized and absorbed in the revenue budget. The petitioner made several representations to the Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives for appointing him in various posts but he, has not received any, satisfactory response, Finally the petitioner sent a Demand for Justice Notice on 9-3-2014(Annexure-k) to the  respondents through his learned Advocate to appoint/absorb him in the revenue budget of the Local Government Engineering Department under " the' Ministry 'of the Local-Government, Rural Development 'and Co-operatives 'in accordance with directions of several decisions of the Appellate Division as well as of this Court but has received no satisfactory response.

4. Being aggrieved the petitioner has come to this 'Court and obtained the present Rule. The Rule is being contested by the respondent No. 5 by filing Affidavit in Opposition where it has been stated inter alia that there is no 'suitable vacancy in the revenue budget of the Local Government Engineering Department and, as such, he is no entitled to be absorbed in the' same. It has been further stated that 'in the 'case of Chief Engineer; LGED vs Kazi Mizanur Rahman reported  in 17BLC (AD)91,11 (eleven) guide lines have been stated for absorbing, employees in the revenue budget including inter alia that whenever any vacancy In LGED 'IS created In the revenue set up, it shall consider for absorption employees' and/or officers of development projects, within the meaning' of section 2(ga)' of the উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিত পদের পদধারীদের নিয়মিতকরণ ও জ্যোষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা ২০০৫” hereinafter referred to as "the Rules" if the project in which she/he is working is completed and subject to the condition that such employees or officers have requisite qualifications for the said posts but in the instant case since there is no vacancy in permanent posts in the 'LGED as per the aforesaid guide lines the petitioner' is not entitled to be considered to be. absorbed in a permanent post in LGED.

5. It is further stated in the Affidavit-in': Opposition that the petitioner was never given assurance that his service would be regularized after the end of the project which is evident 'from' his appointment letter for various projects and, as such-there is no reason why the petitioner should he absorbed in the revenue budget. Thus as the petitioner's employment has come to an end and there being no 'vacancy in the permanent posts of LGED, he does not' have any tight for absorption or appointment in there venue budget. It is denied that the petitioner has satisfied all the criteria stated' in the' case of Chief Engineer, 'LGED vs Kazi Mizanur Rahman reported in17 BLC (AD)91 and, as such, the petitioner has no right to claim absorption lit 'the revenue budget.

6. Dr. Chowdhury Ishrak Ahmed Siddiky the learned' Advocate for' the petitioner submits thru the petitioner has been working continuously in temporary jobs for the last 20 years in the Local Government Engineering Department under the Ministry of Local Government. Rural Development and Co-operatives but all on a sudden at the age of 46 years he has been terminated and he is not .being given any employment either temporarily or permanent in the LGED. The learned Advocate, further submits that the petitioner having spent most of his life in the LGED as Road Roller Driver, it is difficult for him to find a job arty where at the age of 46 years. Furthermore, since his junior colleagues who have been in the Local Government Engineering Department , have' been appointed and regularized in the permanent set up the petitioner also, has a legitimate expectation to be employed in the permanent set up of LGED. The learned Advocate further points out that petitioner has requisite qualifications for the post in which he is seeking absorption along with experience of 20 years as road toller driver' without any complaint and, as such, he has a legitimate expectation to be absorbed: in the revenue budget. The learned Advocate further submits that the-petitioner has satisfied all the criteria-listed 'by the Appellate Division in the case of Chief Engineer; LGED vs Kazi Mizanur Rahman reported in 17 BLC (AD) 91'for absorption. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has' drawn' our attention to' an unreported judgment of this Court in Writ Petition No. 76580/2011 in the-case of Mousumi Akhter vs Government of Bangladesh wherein their Lordships stated that there are 2559 posts in the EGED Under the Ministry of Local Government, Rural 'Development and Co-operatives and, as such, there will be no complication if the petitioners are regularized in the revenue budget of LGED. In the said case 146 petitioners were 'directed' by this Court to be absorbed in permanent jobs and vacancies in LGED subject to satisfaction' of criteria given in the ECNEC resolution. The said decision has not been interfered with by the Appellate Division:

7. In, the instant ease, it appears that the petitioner has been working for different projects of the LGED under' the Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives and suddenly his service has been terminated. 'The petitioner has annexed a number, of documents showing that several other road rollers have been absorbed in the revenue budget in the said Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives but for some reason the petitioner has not been so absorbed in the revenue budget. In the aforesaid unreported judgment in Writ Petition No. 7658 of 2011 it has been stated that there was an unambiguous direction from the Economic Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) to the effect that subject to satisfaction of certain criteria, the project employees would be absorbed in permanent jobs. This resolution was taken on 10thJanuary, 2008 Besides, through a gazette notification dated 20th June, 2005 signed by a Secretary to the Government at the order of the Hon'ble President; the authorities stated; “উন্নয়ন প্রকল্পের কোন কর্মচারী কর্মকর্তাকে নিম্ন বর্ণিত শর্তে নিয়মিত করা যাইবে”

8. The aforesaid decision of 'ECNEC and the Government allow sufficient scope: for persons to be employed in the revenue set up of the Ministry of Local Government. Rural Development and Co-operatives from amongst those persons who worked in the "development project absorbed. In spite of the aforesaid guide lines, it appears that the respondents' are adopting a policy of pick and, choose. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the case of Chief Engineer, LGED vs Kazi Mizanur Rahman reported in 17 BLC (AD) 91 has given certain guide lines on' the basis of which employees may be absorbed in the revenue budget from amongst those who worked in the development project. The guide lines are as follows:

(i)	 Whenever any vacancy in the revenue set up LGED is created, it shall consider for absorption employees or officers from the development projects within the meaning of section 2 (ga) of the Rules, 2005, if the project in which she/he is working is completed subject to the condition that such employee or officer has . requisite qualifications for the said post;

(ii)   Whenever a vacant post is created in the revenue budget the LGED shall absorb/ transfer an employee or' officer from the development project mentioned in clause (1) 'to fill up that post in accordance with, Rules of 1985 and the ECNEC's decision dated 10th January.

2008.

(iii)An officer or employee: shall be absorbed if she/he was appointed in the development project 'within the meaning of rule 2 (ka) of Rules, 2005 in accordance with the procedures prescribed for appointment in public employment,

(iv) An officer or employee must have requisite qualifications for the post in which he is seeking absorption.

(v) An officer or employee must have continuity in, service in the project in which he is working. :

(vi). An officer or employee must have satisfactory service record before his case is considered for regularization in the revenue budget.

(vii) If an officer and employee whose rank and status .does not relate to the posts advertised by the impugned notifications' on the day of its publication such officer or employee would not be eligible for consideration for absorption.

(viii) The employees and officers who' have been working in' the development projects' mentioned in clause (I) 'on monthly pay basis would only be eligible for consideration for absorption in the revenue budget,

(ix) Unless and until vacancies in the revenue budget in the LEGD are created, the employees and officers of the development projects mentioned in clause (l) cannot claim as of right to be absorbed in the revenue budget.

(x) While considering and selecting an employee or officer of the development project for absorption in the revenue budget, the appointing authority shall maintain strictly the prevailing quota system for employment in the public employment being followed by the Government.

(xi). The LGED shall consider the cases of those, working on master roll basis for absorption in the revenue budget by phases if they have requisite qualifications subject to availability of vacancies according to their seniority.

<u>9. In several decisions this Court has directed the authorities to absorb/appoint employees in, the permanent set up from amongst those who have been working on temporary or master roll basis over a period of time provided that there is lie, contrary report against them. In the case of Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and 'Co-operatives vacancies: in permanent posts are all the time occurring due to huge nature of development projects; undertaken by the said Ministry. After 'utilizing, an employee for more than 20 years-by taking his service and then not giving him any employment without assigning any reason is highly unfair and undesirable. This is arbitrary and malafide exercise of power. In our view therefore the petitioner has a right to be employed  either in the development  budget or revenue  budget provided; his past employment history 'is 'satisfactory: The respondents are therefore  directed to employ the petitioner in the .revenue budget subject to satisfaction of criteria slated in the case of Chief Engineer; LGED vs Kazi Mizanur Rahman reported in 17 BLC (AD)91ofcourse if there is no vacancy in the revenue setup of the respondents, tile respondents are directed to consider him for employment in the development budget as per, decision in the case of the. Government of Bangladesh vs Mil Anisur Rahman reported in 18 MLR (AD) 372.</u>

10. Accordingly this Rule is made absolute.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
MI Farooqui with Salimullah, Khurshid Alam Khan and Raziaq Sultana, Advocates --- For the Petitioners in WP Nos. 781/94, 1377/95, 1855, 4893/96 and 79 of 1997.

HR Sharif with Rubaiya Rahman Sharif, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners in WP No. 1472 of 1996.

Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General with Mahbub Ali, Assistant Attorney-General ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Karamat Ali and others ------ Petitioners
vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mahfuzur Rahman J: All the writ petitions namely, Writ Petition Nos. 781/94, 1377/95, 1855/96, 4893/96, 79 of 1997 and 1472 of 1996 are taken up together for disposal since in all the cases vires of the Ordinance No.54/85 has been challenged.

<u>2. In all these writ petitions Rules Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the sub-section (2) of section 5 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance 54 of 1985) should not be declared to be void as being inconsistent with Articles 27 and 42 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. In the aforesaid 5 writ petitions, except Writ Petition No. 1472 of 1996, the judgment and order passed by the First Court of Settlement have been passed without jurisdiction and hence void, illegal and without lawful authority.</u>

<u>3. For the sake of convenience we like to take up the first point regarding the vires of the Ordinance as challenged in the writ petitions. Then we shall decide the next point regarding merit of the individual cases.</u>

<u>4. Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate in all the cases except Writ Petition No. 1472 of 1996 submits that the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 is ultra vires of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as it offends Articles 27, 31, 48 of our Constitution. Mr Farooqui referring to section 4 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1935 submits that it has been stated therein that in pursuance of a notice in any form issued thereunder at any time before 30th October, 1988 the Government may take over possession of any abandoned property or building. This power of issuing this type of notice in any form gives arbitrary power to the Government and hence it is void ab initio. In support of his contention he referred to the case of Government of Bangladesh vs. Dr Nurul Islam, reported in 33 DLR (AD) 201 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"Since neither the impugned provisions of the Act nor the rules provide any principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion by the Government when it proposes to retire a Government servant from amongst a group of Government servants similarly situated and holding similar jobs, there invariably exists the scope for arbitrary exercise of such discretion.</u>

<u>Discretion of the relevant authority must be seen to have been exercised on some such principles as are discernible in Fundamental Rule 56, Notes 2 of the East Bengal Service Rules and Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules 1973. Where such basis has been provided the concerned authority before exercising its discretion has to conform to the principles so provided therein."</u>

<u>But this case is not applicable in the present cases as because that was a case regarding retirement of Government employee and there was no guideline or Rules and the facts are also distinguishable. In this regard Mr. Additional Attorney-General submits that Article 25 of President's Order 16 of 1972 clearly provides that the Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of the order and in exercise of such power Government has framed the notice in the form in exercise of the power vested under Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over Possession) Rules 1972 and in Rule 6 residential and other buildings in the urban area have been classified as one category of abandoned property. For taking over possession of abandoned property, notice in Forms I, II, III & IV, as, the case may be, can be issued. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits that notice in any form means, depending on the category of abandoned property and notice in any form of the specimen given as per Rule 3 should be issued before taking over of the abandoned property. So, there is no violation of any law and it was nor arbitrary. Mr Farooqui referring to section 4(b) (ii) of Ordinance 54 of 1985 next contends that no building shall be taken possession of as abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972 except in pursuance of a notice in any form issued under President's Order 16 of 1972 and where no such notice is issued in respect of a building, in execution of a decree or order passed by a Court in a suit filed by the government. He submits that this is clear discrimination in equality and is hit by equality clause under Articles 27 and 31 of our Constitution. He submits that thereby classification has been made by this Ordinance.
